2.1 Why Containers? The "Works on My Machine" Problem

Every developer has lived this nightmare: easypj runs perfectly on your laptop, then explodes the moment it hits a server. A container ends the argument by packaging everything the app needs — code and its entire environment — into one immutable, portable unit.

The "works on my machine" problem — and the fix
   👩‍💻 your laptop                          🖥️ production server
   ┌────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj runs ✅          │   deploy →   │ 💀 ModuleNotFoundError: 'psycopg2'   │
   │ Python 3.13 · Django   │              │    (different Python · no psycopg2 · │
   │ psycopg2 · env vars set │              │     missing env vars · different OS) │
   └────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────────────────┘

   THE FIX — pack EVERYTHING into one image 📦, ship the box, not the recipe:
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 📦 easypj:v1                                                   │
   │   • Python 3.13            • Django 5.2.5                      │
   │   • gunicorn · psycopg2    • easypj source + settings          │
   │   • env / config baked in  • a slim Debian userland            │
   │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
   │  runs IDENTICALLY:   laptop ✅   staging ✅   production ✅      │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Key Term — Container

A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that bundles everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Crucially, containers share the host's OS kernel — which is what makes them far lighter and faster than virtual machines.

🚢 Analogy — the shipping container

Before standardized shipping containers, every cargo was loaded by hand and broke in transit. The steel box changed the world because the same sealed unit rides any ship, truck, or crane without anyone caring what's inside. A software container is the same idea: a standard box the cluster can pick up and run anywhere, without caring whether it holds easypj, nginx, or PostgreSQL.

The Four Properties That Matter

📦
Portable

The same image runs on Linux, Mac, Windows, cloud, or bare metal — identical behavior everywhere.

🔒
Isolated

Each container gets its own filesystem, network, and process space — no dependency conflicts between apps.

⚡
Fast

Starts in seconds (not minutes like a VM) — it shares the host kernel, so there's no full OS to boot.

📐
Lightweight

Megabytes, not gigabytes — run dozens (even hundreds) of containers on a single machine.

What's Inside a Container — and What Is Not

This is the misconception that trips up almost everyone, and clearing it up makes the rest of the chapter click: a container image does not contain an operating system. It bundles the app's userland — your code, language runtime, and shared libraries — but it borrows the host's kernel. That single fact is why containers are MB not GB, and why a Linux container needs a Linux kernel underneath.

✅ IN the image (userland — shipped)❌ NOT in the image (shared from the host)
Your code (easypj) + settingsThe Linux kernel itself
Python 3.13 runtime + pip packagesKernel modules & device drivers
System libs (libc, libpq) from a slim DebianThe CPU / memory scheduler
The default command (gunicorn …)Namespaces & cgroups (these are kernel features)
An image is userland on top of the host's kernel
   📦 easypj image  (everything you ship)        ── all containers share ──▶  one kernel
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj code · gunicorn         │            ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Python 3.13 · psycopg2         │  ───runs──▶ │ 🐧 HOST LINUX KERNEL                   │
   │ libc · libpq (slim Debian)     │   on top of │   scheduling · namespaces · cgroups ·  │
   │ (NO kernel in here!)           │            │   drivers · filesystems                 │
   └──────────────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 So how do containers run on a Mac or Windows?

They don't, directly — those OSes have no Linux kernel. Docker Desktop quietly runs a tiny Linux VM and starts your containers inside it. On a real Kubernetes node (which is Linux), there's no such trick — the container runs natively on the node's kernel. This is also why a Linux image can't run on a Windows kernel and vice-versa: the userland must match the kernel it's calling.

💡 Why this is the foundation of everything ahead

Kubernetes never runs your code — it runs your image. Every later topic (pods, deployments, rollouts, probes) is just the cluster choreographing copies of an image like easypj:v1. Get the image right here, and the rest of the guide is choreography.

2.2 Containers vs Virtual Machines

Both VMs and containers give you isolation — but at fundamentally different levels, and that difference explains every "containers are light and fast" claim. A VM virtualizes hardware (a full guest OS per app); a container virtualizes the OS (all containers share the host kernel).

VM architecture vs container architecture
   VIRTUAL MACHINES                          CONTAINERS
   ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐              ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐
   │  App A     │ │  App B     │             │ 🐍 easypj  │ │ 🌐 nginx   │
   │  Libs      │ │  Libs      │             │  Libs      │ │  Libs      │
   │ ┌────────┐ │ │ ┌────────┐ │             └─────┬─────┘ └─────┬─────┘
   │ │Guest OS│ │ │ │Guest OS│ │  ← a WHOLE         │   shared    │
   │ └────────┘ │ │ └────────┘ │    OS per app      ▼             ▼
   └───────────┘ └───────────┘             ┌────────────────────────┐
   ┌───────────────────────────┐           │ 🐋 container runtime     │ (containerd)
   │       Hypervisor           │           ├────────────────────────┤
   ├───────────────────────────┤           │   Host kernel  (SHARED) │ ← the key difference
   │         Host OS            │           ├────────────────────────┤
   ├───────────────────────────┤           │        Host OS          │
   │         Hardware           │           ├────────────────────────┤
   └───────────────────────────┘           │        Hardware         │
     heavy → GIGABYTES · MINUTES            └────────────────────────┘
                                              light → MEGABYTES · SECONDS
Feature🖥️ Virtual Machine📦 Container
SizeGigabytes (a full OS per VM)Megabytes (shares the kernel)
StartupMinutes (OS must boot)Seconds / ms (just a process start)
OSFull guest OS per VMShares the host kernel
IsolationStrong (hardware-level)Process-level (namespaces + cgroups)
PerformanceNear-native (hypervisor overhead)Native (direct kernel access)
Density~10–20 per server~100–1000 per server
Best forA different OS, or strong isolationSame OS, many microservices
💡 CKA reality: nodes ARE VMs (usually)

In most real clusters, Kubernetes worker nodes are themselves virtual machines in a cloud (EC2, Azure VM, GCE). So you actually use both layers: VMs as the host infrastructure, and containers for the workloads on top. The administrator manages both — VMs for the cluster machines, containers for what runs on them.

⚠️ The flip side of a shared kernel

Sharing the host kernel is what makes containers light — but it also means weaker isolation than a VM. A kernel exploit or a privileged container can potentially affect the host. That's why later chapters lock containers down: non-root users, dropped capabilities, seccomp, and Pod Security Standards (Ch 27). Light ≠ automatically safe.

The Isolation Spectrum — It's Not Just "VM or Container"

The VM-vs-container choice isn't binary — production platforms pick a point on a spectrum, trading isolation strength for weight. Kubernetes even lets different pods on the same cluster choose different points, via RuntimeClass (§2.7):

Weakest → strongest isolation (and what each costs)
  LIGHTER / FASTER ◄──────────────────────────────────────────────────────► STRONGER ISOLATION

  📦 plain container      📦🔒 hardened container       🛡️ gVisor            🧱 Kata            🖥️ full VM
  shared kernel,          + non-root, dropped caps,    user-space kernel    a micro-VM per     own guest OS
  default profile         seccomp, read-only rootfs    intercepts syscalls  pod (KVM)          per workload
  ──────────────          ──────────────────────        ─────────────       ─────────────      ───────────
  ms startup · no tax     ms startup · tiny tax        small syscall tax    ~100ms+ · some RAM  minutes · GBs
  easypj default ✅        production baseline ✅        untrusted code       multi-tenant/       different OS
                                                                            hostile workloads   needed
                             pods opt in via:  spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor | kata   (Ch 27 hardens further)
📖 How to choose (the practical rule)

Your own trusted code (easypj) → a hardened plain container is the norm. Running other people's code (CI runners, plugins, multi-tenant SaaS) → a sandboxed runtime (gVisor/Kata) buys VM-class isolation at container-like speed. A genuinely different OS or kernel version → only a real VM does it. Same cluster, per-pod choice — that's the point of the CRI + RuntimeClass design.

2.3 Docker Basics for Kubernetes Admins

Docker created the container ecosystem. Even though Kubernetes no longer uses Docker as a runtime, Docker's concepts and tooling are still how you build and reason about images — so the vocabulary is essential.

The Docker workflow — recipe to running container to registry
   📝 Dockerfile  ──docker build──▶  📀 Image  ──docker run──▶  📦 Container
   (the recipe)                      (read-only               (a running
                                      template)                instance)
                                         │
                                         │ docker push
                                         ▼
                                   🏪 Registry   ──docker pull──▶  🤖 a K8s node
                                   (Docker Hub / ECR / GCR)        pulls & runs it
📝
Dockerfile

A text recipe that defines how to build an image: the base OS, dependencies, your code, and the startup command.

📀
Image

The built, read-only template. Like a class in code — it defines the container but isn't running yet.

📦
Container

A running instance of an image. Like an object created from a class — live and executing.

🏪
Registry

Where images are stored & distributed: Docker Hub (public), ECR (AWS), GCR (GCP), ACR (Azure).

Image Layers — How Docker Images Are Built (and Cached)

An image isn't one blob — it's a stack of read-only layers, one per Dockerfile instruction. Each layer is content-addressed and cached, which is the single most important thing to understand for fast builds:

easypj image — layer stack (bottom = base, top = your code)
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Container layer (read-WRITE)                 │ ← runtime changes, ephemeral
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │  L5  CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi…"]         │ ← startup command
   │  L4  COPY . .            (easypj source)      │ ← changes MOST → put it LAST
   │  L3  RUN pip install -r requirements.txt      │ ← Python deps (slow; cache this!)
   │  L2  COPY requirements.txt .                  │ ← the deps list
   │  L1  FROM python:3.13-slim   (base OS+Python) │ ← shared base, pulled once
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   💡 Layers are cached. Edit L4 (your code) → only L4+L5 rebuild; L1–L3 are reused.
      THAT is why you COPY requirements.txt and pip install BEFORE COPY . .
📖 Why layer order matters for the CKA

When you debug an ImagePullBackOff, knowing images are layers helps you reason about where it broke — a missing base image, a build failure, or a registry-auth problem. As an admin you also configure imagePullSecrets so nodes can pull from private registries (Ch 23/25).

The Dockerfile Instructions You'll Actually Use

You don't need all 18 Dockerfile instructions — about ten do 99% of the work. Here's the full working set, each with what it does and the gotcha that bites people:

InstructionWhat it doesNote / gotcha
FROMThe base image to build onPin it (python:3.13-slim), never :latest
WORKDIRSets (and creates) the working dirUse it instead of RUN cd … (cd doesn't persist)
COPYCopies files from build context → imageOrder matters for caching; respects .dockerignore
ADDLike COPY but also untars / fetches URLsPrefer COPY — ADD's magic causes surprises
RUNExecutes a command at BUILD time → new layerChain with && to keep layers small
ENVSets an env var (persists into the running container)Available at build AND run time
ARGA build-time-only variableGone at runtime; don't use for secrets
EXPOSEDocuments the port the app listens onDocumentation only — doesn't publish the port
USERSwitches the user for later steps + runtimeSet a non-root user before CMD
CMD / ENTRYPOINTThe default process the container runsSee the breakdown below — the #1 confusion

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT — the Classic Confusion

Both define what runs when the container starts, but they combine in a specific way, and Kubernetes overrides them with its own fields. Get this straight once:

ENTRYPOINT = the program · CMD = its default arguments
   ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]          ← the fixed executable (hard to override)
   CMD ["easypj.wsgi","-b","0.0.0.0:8000"]   ← default args (easy to override)

   container runs:  gunicorn easypj.wsgi -b 0.0.0.0:8000
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   only CMD, no ENTRYPOINT:   CMD ["gunicorn","easypj.wsgi"]
        → runs that, but `docker run img python manage.py shell` REPLACES it entirely
   ENTRYPOINT + CMD:          `docker run img --workers 5`  → gunicorn easypj.wsgi --workers 5
                              (CMD's defaults are swapped, ENTRYPOINT stays)
In the DockerfileIn Kubernetes (pod spec)Overrides…
ENTRYPOINTcommand:the executable
CMDargs:the arguments
💡 The K8s payoff

When a pod sets command: / args:, it's directly overriding the image's ENTRYPOINT / CMD. That's how you run a one-off (e.g. python manage.py migrate) from the same easypj image without rebuilding it — exactly what Jobs do in Chapter 16. Use the exec form (["gunicorn","…"]), not the shell form, so signals (SIGTERM on pod stop) reach your process for clean shutdown.

💡 Layers also speed up pod startup

Because layers are cached on the node, once one easypj pod has pulled the base + deps layers, the next pod on that node reuses them and starts almost instantly. Shared base images across your apps = less to pull, faster scaling.

2.4 Building the easypj Image

Now let's package easypj into the image Kubernetes will pull and run as pods. We'll go straight to the production-grade, multi-stage, non-root pattern — the way you'd actually ship it.

Dockerfile.production — multi-stage 
# ── Stage 1: builder — compile/install deps with build tools ──
FROM python:3.13-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .                       # copy deps list FIRST (cache layer)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ── Stage 2: runtime — slim final image, NO build tools ──
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local       # just the installed packages
COPY . .                                      # easypj source (changes most → last)
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
RUN useradd -m app                            # create a non-root user…
USER app                                      # …and run as it (security!)
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
.dockerignore — keep junk & secrets out of the image 
# Don't copy these into the build context / image
.git/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
.env                # never bake secrets into an image!
db.sqlite3
venv/
env/
node_modules/
*.md
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
⚠️ Always run as non-root

Notice the useradd app + USER app lines. Running a container as root is a real risk — if an attacker breaks out, they land as root on the node. The image declares the intent; in Kubernetes you enforce it with a securityContext (runAsNonRoot: true) and Pod Security Standards (Ch 27).

Why Multi-Stage? Size & Safety

The builder stage has compilers and -dev headers; the runtime stage copies only the installed result and throws the builder away. Smaller image = faster pulls, less attack surface, fewer CVEs.

Multi-stage build — discard the toolchain, keep the app
   ❌ single stage:  python:3.13 + gcc + libpq-dev + build tools + app   →  ~900 MB 😬
   ✅ multi-stage:   python:3.13-slim + installed deps + app (no tools)  →  ~150 MB ✅

   ┌─────────────────────────┐   COPY --from=builder   ┌─────────────────────────┐
   │ Stage 1: BUILDER        │   only the /install     │ Stage 2: RUNTIME        │
   │  gcc, libpq-dev, headers │  ─────────────────────▶ │  slim base + deps + app │
   │  pip install …           │   (build tools are      │  runs as non-root        │
   │  💥 DISCARDED after build │    left behind)         │  ← THE FINAL IMAGE       │
   └─────────────────────────┘                         └─────────────────────────┘

Build & Test Workflow

terminal — build, run, verify, push 
# Build the image (tag it — never rely on :latest)
docker build -f Dockerfile.production -t easypj:v1 .

# Run it locally and map the port
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj-app easypj:v1

# Verify it serves /jobs/
curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/

# Inspect logs if it misbehaves
docker logs easypj-app

# Tag & push to a registry so Kubernetes can pull it later
docker tag easypj:v1 myregistry.io/easypj:v1
docker push myregistry.io/easypj:v1

Image Security Checklist

🛡️
Do ✅
  • Use slim / distroless base images
  • Run as non-root (USER app)
  • Pin versions (python:3.13-slim, not :latest)
  • Scan images (Trivy / Grype) in CI
  • Use .dockerignore to exclude secrets
  • Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in K8s
🚫
Avoid ❌
  • Running as root inside the container
  • :latest (unpredictable, non-reproducible)
  • Baking secrets / .env into the image
  • Full-OS base images (Ubuntu 1 GB+)
  • Leaving build tools in the final image
  • Skipping vulnerability scans

The Build Context — What docker build . Actually Sends

That trailing . in docker build -t easypj:v1 . is not "the Dockerfile" — it's the build context: the whole directory is tarred up and shipped to the build engine, which is why a fat context (a .git folder, a venv, node_modules) makes builds slow and can leak secrets into the image. The .dockerignore is what trims it.

docker build . — the context is the directory, not just the Dockerfile
   your project dir (the "context")            🔨 build engine (BuildKit)
   ┌───────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ Dockerfile                 │  ──tar the── │ reads Dockerfile, runs each   │
   │ requirements.txt           │   WHOLE dir  │ instruction → cached layers   │
   │ easypj/  manage.py         │  ──────────▶ │ (.dockerignore'd files never  │
   │ .git/  venv/  .env  ✂️       │   (minus     │  enter the context)           │
   │   ^ excluded by .dockerignore│  ignored)   └──────────────────────────────┘
   └───────────────────────────┘
   💡 A 5 MB context builds fast; a 2 GB context (venv/.git) crawls and risks leaking .env.

ENV vs ARG — Build-Time vs Run-Time Variables

A frequent source of broken builds and leaked secrets. They look similar but live in different worlds:

ARGENV
Available at…build time onlybuild time AND run time
In the running container?❌ gone✅ present (e.g. DEBUG=False)
Set viadocker build --build-arg VER=1.2baked in, or overridden by K8s env
Secrets?❌ no — visible in image history❌ no — use Secrets/ConfigMaps in K8s
⚠️ Never bake secrets into an image (any layer)

Both ARG and ENV values are visible in the image's layer history (docker history) — and anyone who can pull the image can read them. easypj's SECRET_KEY and DB password belong in Kubernetes Secrets, injected at runtime (Ch 23), never in the Dockerfile.

Going Smaller Still — Distroless & Scratch

Slim is good; distroless is the next level — an image with only your app and its runtime: no shell, no package manager, almost no OS userland. Tiny attack surface, tiny size.

📦
-slim

Minimal Debian + your runtime. Has a shell for debugging. The pragmatic default (what we used for easypj).

🛡️
distroless

gcr.io/distroless/python3 — just Python + your app. No shell, no apt. Hardest to attack; debug via ephemeral containers (Ch 31).

⚛️
scratch

Literally empty. Only for static binaries (Go/Rust). Not for Python, which needs a userland.

🧪 Drill

Build easypj:v1 from the multi-stage Dockerfile, run it with -p 8000:8000, and curl /jobs/. Then edit a source file and rebuild — watch the pip install layer stay cached while only the code layer rebuilds. Finally run docker history easypj:v1 to see the layers and prove no secret leaked in.

Show solution
terminal
# 1) build & run
docker build -f Dockerfile.production -t easypj:v1 .
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1
curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/          # → HTML/JSON from easypj ✅

# 2) edit a .py file, rebuild — note the cache
docker build -f Dockerfile.production -t easypj:v1 .
# => ... RUN pip install ...   ---> Using cache   ✅  (deps layer reused)
# => COPY . .                  ---> running        (only your code layer rebuilds)

# 3) inspect layers; confirm no secret baked in
docker history easypj:v1                   # each line = one layer; no .env / SECRET_KEY

What you should observe: the second build reuses the pip install layer (Using cache) and only re-runs COPY . . — proof that ordering deps before source pays off. docker history shows the layer stack with no secret values, because .env is excluded by .dockerignore and config comes from K8s at runtime.

2.5 Essential Container Commands

You'll build images with docker on your laptop, but on a real cluster node Docker often isn't installed — there you use crictl (the CRI CLI) to inspect what the kubelet is running. Know both, and know which to reach for.

docker — on your build host

CommandWhat it doesCKA relevance
docker build -t easypj:v1 .Build an image from a DockerfilePrep images for K8s
docker run -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1Run a container, expose a portTest before deploying
docker psList running containersDebug outside K8s
docker logs <id>View a container's logsMirrors kubectl logs
docker exec -it <id> shShell into a containerMirrors kubectl exec
docker imagesList local imagesCheck what's cached
docker push <registry>/easypj:v1Push an image to a registryRequired so K8s can pull it
docker pull <image>Pull an image from a registryPre-cache on nodes
docker stop <id>Stop a running containerGraceful shutdown
docker system pruneClean up unused images/containersReclaim node disk

docker ↔ crictl — the same moves, on a node

On a node, crictl talks straight to the CRI (containerd/CRI-O). The verbs are nearly identical to Docker, so the muscle memory transfers:

Task🐳 docker (build host)🔧 crictl / ctr (on the node)
List containersdocker pscrictl ps
View logsdocker logs <id>crictl logs <id>
Shell indocker exec -it <id> shcrictl exec -it <id> sh
Inspectdocker inspect <id>crictl inspect <id>
List imagesdocker imagescrictl images / ctr images ls
Runtime infodocker infocrictl info
📖 ctr vs crictl — don't mix them up

crictl is the Kubernetes-aware CRI client — it sees pods/containers the way the kubelet does. ctr is containerd's low-level tool and is namespace-scoped (use -n k8s.io to see K8s containers). For troubleshooting cluster workloads, reach for crictl.

The Three containerd CLIs — Which One, When

On a containerd node you'll meet three tools. They overlap, so people get lost — here's the one-line rule for each:

ToolWhat it isUse it for
crictlThe CRI debug CLI (K8s view: pods + containers)Troubleshooting cluster pods on a node — your default
nerdctlA Docker-compatible CLI for containerdBuilding/running containers by hand with familiar docker-style commands (nerdctl run, nerdctl build)
ctrcontainerd's raw, low-level clientDeep containerd internals; namespace-scoped (-n k8s.io) — rarely needed
💡 Mental model

nerdctl ≈ "docker, but for containerd" (great when you miss Docker's ergonomics on a node). crictl ≈ "what the kubelet sees" (great for debugging actual pods). ctr ≈ "the engine's bare-metal wrench." For the CKA, crictl is the one that earns points.

A Container's Lifecycle — the States You'll See

Whether via docker ps, crictl ps, or kubectl describe pod, a container moves through a small set of states. Recognizing them tells you instantly whether something is healthy, stuck, or dead:

Container lifecycle states
   📥 created ──start──▶ ▶️ running ──stop (SIGTERM→SIGKILL)──▶ ⏹️ stopped ──rm──▶ 🗑️ removed
                          │   ▲
                   pause  │   │ unpause
                          ▼   │
                       ⏸️ paused                  💥 exited (code ≠ 0)  ← crashed; K8s → CrashLoopBackOff
                                                  ✅ exited (code 0)    ← finished cleanly (e.g. a Job)
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   In Kubernetes you mostly see:  Running · Terminated(reason: Completed | Error | OOMKilled) · Waiting
   (Waiting covers ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff — the kubelet is retrying.)

The Debugging Altitude Ladder — Which Tool at Which Layer

You now have four CLIs that can all "look at containers" — the skill is knowing which altitude each one works at, and stepping down the ladder exactly when the layer above stops answering:

AltitudeToolTalks toReach for it when…
🛰️ clusterkubectlthe apiservernormal life — pods, logs, exec, describe (needs the control plane up)
🏔️ node / CRIcrictlthe runtime's CRI socketthe apiserver or kubelet is down but containers still run — your lifeline
🏠 runtime-nativectr -n k8s.io / nerdctlcontainerd directly (no CRI)runtime internals: images, snapshots, namespaces — below what crictl shows
🧱 build hostdockerthe Docker daemon (your laptop/CI)building, tagging, pushing images — usually absent on nodes
Step DOWN the ladder as each layer stops answering
   "pod is misbehaving"
        │
        ▼
   kubectl logs / exec / describe ────── works? → debug at cluster level ✅
        │ ✗ apiserver/kubelet dead
        ▼
   ssh node → crictl ps -a / logs / inspect ── works? → debug at CRI level ✅
        │ ✗ even crictl fails
        ▼
   systemctl status containerd · ctr -n k8s.io c ls ── runtime itself is the problem
        │ ✗ containerd dead
        ▼
   journalctl -u containerd · disk full? cgroup driver? ── OS level (Ch 32)
   💡 the k8s.io namespace matters: `ctr images ls` shows NOTHING without -n k8s.io,
      because Kubernetes keeps its containers in containerd's "k8s.io" namespace.
💡 Exam translation

Every "the node is broken" task is really testing whether you know this ladder: kubectl fails → don't fight it, drop one level to crictl on the node. The docker CLI is deliberately not installed on exam nodes — reaching for it instead of crictl is the classic time-sink.

2.6 Container Runtimes: Beyond Docker

Since Kubernetes v1.24, Docker is no longer a supported runtime. The kubelet now talks to runtimes directly through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) — and as the admin, you install & configure that runtime on every node.

📖 Key Term — CRI (Container Runtime Interface)

The CRI is the standard gRPC "socket" the kubelet uses to tell a runtime "run / stop / list this container." Any CRI-compliant runtime plugs in. This is one of the three extension interfaces from Chapter 1 (CRI · CNI · CSI) — the runtime is swappable, so Kubernetes itself never has to care which one you picked.

Container runtime evolution — Docker out of the data path (v1.24)
   BEFORE v1.24                          AFTER v1.24
   🤖 kubelet                            🤖 kubelet
      │                                     │  CRI (gRPC)
   dockershim  ❌ (removed)              ┌──┴───────┐
      │                                  ▼          ▼
   🐳 Docker daemon                  🐋 containerd   🔴 CRI-O
      │                                  │          │
   containerd                          📦          📦   containers
      │                              (direct — no Docker daemon, no shim)
   📦 containers
   💡 Docker IMAGES still work everywhere (they're OCI). Only the node-side
      runtime changed. You still BUILD with Docker; nodes RUN via containerd.
🐋
containerd

The industry standard, extracted from Docker itself. Default for kubeadm; used by GKE, EKS, AKS. Lightweight, stable, CNCF-graduated.

  • Default runtime for kubeadm clusters
  • CLIs: ctr (low-level), crictl (K8s-native)
  • Config: /etc/containerd/config.toml
🔴
CRI-O

Purpose-built for Kubernetes — nothing more. Preferred by Red Hat / OpenShift. Minimal footprint, releases version-aligned to K8s.

  • Used by OpenShift & Fedora CoreOS
  • Version-locked to Kubernetes versions
  • Config: /etc/crio/crio.conf
⚠️ The #1 runtime gotcha: cgroup-driver mismatch

The kubelet and the container runtime must use the same cgroup driver — on modern systemd hosts that means systemd. If containerd is left on the cgroupfs default while the kubelet expects systemd, the kubelet won't start and the node stays NotReady. The fix is to set SystemdCgroup = true in /etc/containerd/config.toml and restart containerd (you'll do this in Ch 9).

Runtime Troubleshooting — Start Here on a NotReady Node

terminal — on the node 
# Is the runtime even running?
systemctl status containerd

# Did the kubelet complain about the CRI?
journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i "container runtime"

# List containers + check the CRI endpoint, via crictl
crictl ps
crictl info | grep -i runtime

# Restart the runtime if it's wedged
sudo systemctl restart containerd

The Full Call Chain — Who Actually Starts the Container

"containerd runs the container" is true but vague. There are several layers between the kubelet's decision and a process appearing on the node, and knowing them tells you exactly which component to suspect when a container won't start:

From kubelet to a running process — the runtime stack
   🤖 kubelet            "start this pod's containers"
      │  CRI (gRPC over a unix socket: /run/containerd/containerd.sock)
      ▼
   🐋 containerd         high-level runtime: pulls image, unpacks layers (snapshots),
      │                  manages container lifecycle & the image store
      ▼
   🔧 containerd-shim    one per container; keeps the container alive & reparents it
      │                  if containerd restarts (so a runtime upgrade ≠ killing pods)
      ▼
   ⚙️ runc               low-level OCI runtime: the program that actually creates it —
      │                  clone() with namespace flags + cgroups + pivot_root, then exec
      ▼
   📦 your process       gunicorn (PID 1 inside the container) — easypj is now running
LayerJobIf it's broken you'd see…
kubeletDecides & calls the CRINode NotReady; nothing starts
CRI socketThe gRPC endpointcrictl "connect: no such file or directory"
containerdPull/unpack image, manage lifecycleImagePull errors; runtime down → NotReady
containerd-shimBabysit each containerRare; containers die when containerd restarts
runcclone()+cgroups+pivot_root, exec"failed to create container" / permission errors
📖 Why the shim matters (a real-world win)

Because each container has its own shim holding it, you can restart or upgrade containerd itself without killing running pods — the shims keep the containers alive and re-attach. That's the kind of detail that separates "knows the commands" from "understands the system," and it's why a runtime hiccup doesn't automatically take your workloads down.

Building Images Without a Docker Daemon

If nodes no longer run Docker, how does CI build the easypj image — especially when the build itself runs as a pod inside the cluster? You don't need the Docker daemon at all. Several tools build OCI images without it (and without root), which matters because giving CI access to a Docker socket is a serious security hole:

🧰
BuildKit

The modern build engine (now Docker's default too). Faster, parallel, better caching. Runs standalone as buildkitd — no full Docker needed.

🪄
kaniko

Builds from a Dockerfile inside a container/pod, no daemon, no privileged access. The go-to for building images in a K8s-based CI pipeline.

🔨
buildah

Red Hat's daemonless builder (pairs with podman). Scriptable, rootless, OCI-native. Common on OpenShift.

⚠️ Why this matters for security

The old pattern — mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a CI container so it can build — effectively grants root on the node (the Docker daemon runs as root). Daemonless, rootless builders (kaniko/buildah) exist precisely to kill that risk. You'll wire one into the easypj CI/CD pipeline in Chapter 39.

Node Image Garbage Collection — Keeping Disk From Filling

Every image a node pulls is cached on its disk (the imagefs). Over time that fills up — and a full disk triggers DiskPressure, which evicts pods. So the kubelet automatically garbage-collects unused images; as the admin, you tune the thresholds:

kubelet image garbage collection — high/low watermarks
   node disk usage (imagefs) ▲
   100% ┤
        │   imageGCHighThresholdPercent (default 85%) ─────────── ▶ GC TRIGGERS
    85% ┤■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■
        │   kubelet deletes UNUSED images, oldest-first, until…
    80% ┤■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■  ◀── imageGCLowThresholdPercent (default 80%)
        │   (images in use by running pods are NEVER removed)
     0% ┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ time
   ⚠️ cross 85% and never recover → DiskPressure taint → pods evicted (Ch 30/32).
💡 Admin takeaways on image GC
  • It's automatic, but the thresholds are yours to set in the kubelet config (imageGCHighThresholdPercent / LowThresholdPercent).
  • Manual cleanup on a node: crictl rmi --prune removes unused images now.
  • This is the K8s automation of docker system prune — and a frequent root cause when a node mysteriously goes NotReady with DiskPressure.
⚠️ A NotReady node your kubelet logs won't obviously explain: the CRI API version

Since Kubernetes v1.26, the kubelet requires the runtime to speak the v1 CRI API — an old/unsupported runtime (or a stale CRI shim) makes the kubelet refuse to register the node at all, and the same failure re-appears on every kubelet restart during an upgrade. This is a genuinely different root cause from the cgroup-driver mismatch above:

SymptomRoot causeWhere to look
node never appears in kubectl get nodesruntime doesn't implement the v1 CRI APIjournalctl -u kubelet: "CRI v1 runtime API is not implemented"
node fails to rejoin after a K8s upgraderuntime wasn't upgraded alongside the kubeletcheck the container runtime's own version/changelog

The fix is always the same: upgrade the container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) to a version that implements the current CRI API — never the kubelet's fault to patch around.

💡 Where this leads

You now know the artifact (an OCI image of cached layers), how it's built (with or without Docker), and the engine that runs it (the full kubelet → CRI → containerd → shim → runc stack). Chapter 3 zooms out to the whole control plane that decides where these containers run; Chapter 9 has you install & configure the runtime as part of kubeadm; and Chapter 32 returns here when a node goes NotReady.

2.7 Images in Kubernetes — Pull Policy, Registries & Failures

You built easypj:v1 in §2.4. Now the cluster side: how Kubernetes names, pulls, authenticates, and garbage-collects images — and the pull errors you'll diagnose on the exam.

① Image reference syntax & defaults

A full reference is [REGISTRY[:PORT]/]NAME[:TAG][@DIGEST]. Leave parts off and Kubernetes fills in surprising defaults:

You writeIt resolves to
easypjdocker.io/library/easypj:latest — default registry and default tag
easypj:v1docker.io/library/easypj:v1
registry.example.com:5000/easypj:v1your private registry on port 5000
easypj@sha256:9f2a…pinned by digest — exact bytes, ignores tags

⚠️ A bare image with no registry comes from Docker Hub (docker.io), not your private registry — a classic "why is it pulling the wrong thing?" surprise.

📖 If you give both a tag and a digest (easypj:v1@sha256:9f2a…), only the digest is used to pull — the tag becomes a purely human-readable label, so a stale :v1 next to a fresh digest is harmless, not a conflict.

①b Multi-architecture images — one tag, several real images underneath

Pull python:3.13-slim on an amd64 laptop and an arm64 CI runner and you get different bytes with the same tag — that's not magic, it's an image index (also called a manifest list): one small pointer object listing a manifest per architecture, and the runtime picks the one matching the node.

one tag → an index → the node's own architecture
   docker.io/library/python:3.13-slim   (the tag you pull)
        │
        ▼  1. GET the image INDEX (manifest list) — a small JSON pointer, not an image
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  index: python:3.13-slim                                        │
   │    linux/amd64  ──▶ manifest sha256:111…  (the real amd64 image) │
   │    linux/arm64  ──▶ manifest sha256:222…  (the real arm64 image) │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │  2. containerd reads the NODE's own arch, picks ONE manifest
        ▼
   node is amd64 → pulls sha256:111…'s layers only (never touches the arm64 bytes)
   💡 K8s itself does this for its own images: `pause` is the multi-arch index;
      `pause-amd64` is the old, single-arch, backward-compatible name.

This is why the same manifest works unmodified across a mixed amd64/arm64 cluster, and why docker manifest inspect / crane manifest on a "single" tag can show several platform entries.

② Tags vs digests — mutable name vs immutable bytes

🏷️ Tag (:v1)

Human-friendly but mutable — someone can re-push :v1 to different bytes, so two nodes may run different builds of "the same" tag.

🔒 Digest (@sha256:…)

Immutable & tamper-evident — the same digest is byte-identical everywhere, forever. Pin production with easypj:v1@sha256:….

③ imagePullPolicy — the default depends on your tag (exam favourite)

If you don't set imagePullPolicy, Kubernetes infers it from the tag — the single most-missed image fact on the exam:

Image tagDefault policyBehaviour
:latest or no tagAlwayspulls from the registry on every pod start
a fixed tag (:v1)IfNotPresentpulls only if the node lacks it (cached otherwise)
@sha256:… digestIfNotPresentcached; the digest already guarantees the bytes

Override explicitly with Always / IfNotPresent / Never (Never = it must already be on the node). Gotcha: running :latest in production means an unannounced re-pull can change your app under you — always deploy a fixed tag or a digest. One more gotcha: imagePullPolicy is set once, at pod creation, and does not update later even if you edit the image's tag/digest downstream.

📖 Force-always-pull cluster-wide: the AlwaysPullImages admission controller

Instead of trusting every pod author to set imagePullPolicy: Always, an admin can enable the AlwaysPullImages admission controller (--enable-admission-plugins on the apiserver) to force it cluster-wide. This has a real security use: it means a user who can only exec into pods (not pull images directly) can't get at an image they weren't authorized to access, because every pod creation re-triggers the pull-authorization check rather than trusting a node's local cache.

④ Private registries — imagePullSecrets

To pull from a private registry, create a docker-registry Secret and reference it — on the Pod, or (cleaner) on the ServiceAccount so every pod inherits it.

terminal — create the registry secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password=$PASS
pod spec — reference it
spec:
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred          # ← pod-level: this pod only
  containers:
  - name: easypj
    image: registry.example.com/easypj:v1

💡 Attach imagePullSecrets to the namespace's ServiceAccount and every pod using it pulls privately with no per-pod config. A missing/wrong secret shows up as ImagePullBackOff with an "unauthorized" event.

⑤ Pull failure states — read the event, fix the cause

StateMeansUsual cause → fix
ErrImagePulla pull attempt just failedtransient / registry hiccup → kubelet retries
ImagePullBackOffrepeated failures, backing off (up to ~5 min)wrong name/tag · missing imagePullSecrets · registry unreachable
InvalidImageNamethe reference is malformedfix the image string (typo / bad characters)

Diagnose with kubectl describe pod easypj-web → the Events section names the exact error.

⑥ Why a pod sits in ContainerCreating — serial pulls

By default the kubelet pulls images one at a time per node (serializeImagePulls: true, to avoid hammering the registry). Several big images on a fresh node = pods wait in ContainerCreating for minutes. Pre-pulling images onto nodes — or smaller images (§2.4) — makes pods start faster. To parallelize: set serializeImagePulls: false first — the kubelet won't accept a maxParallelImagePulls value otherwise — and note that leaving maxParallelImagePulls unset once parallel pulls are on means no concurrency limit at all, so set it deliberately.

⑦ Image garbage collection — the disk watermarks

The kubelet auto-deletes unused images when node disk crosses imageGCHighThresholdPercent (default 85%), oldest first, until it drops to imageGCLowThresholdPercent (default 80%). Images in use by running pods are never removed. If disk stays high the node gets a DiskPressure condition and starts evicting pods (Ch 3 §node health / Ch 30). Manual sweep: crictl rmi --prune.

⑧ Beyond — RuntimeClass (choosing a stronger sandbox)

What it is

A RuntimeClass object maps a name → a runtime handler the node supports; a pod opts in with spec.runtimeClassName. It's cluster-scoped (no namespace) with really just two fields that matter: metadata.name and handler.

Why you'd use it

Run untrusted / multi-tenant workloads in a stronger sandbox — gVisor (user-space kernel) or Kata (lightweight VM) — instead of default runc. Adds per-pod overhead.

Two more RuntimeClass fields matter for the exam because they answer "how does the cluster guarantee a gVisor pod actually lands on a gVisor-capable node?" — the class isn't just a label, it actively steers the scheduler:

RuntimeClass — scheduling + overhead
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: gvisor            # must match a handler the containerd config actually defines
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:             # MERGED (intersected) with the pod's own nodeSelector at admission
    sandbox.io/runtime: gvisor
  tolerations:              # MERGED (unioned) with the pod's own tolerations at admission
  - key: sandbox
    operator: Exists
overhead:                   # extra resources the SANDBOX itself consumes, on top of the pod's own
  podFixed:                 # — the scheduler/quota/eviction math all account for this automatically
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "120Mi"
FieldWhat it actually does
scheduling.nodeSelectormerged (intersection) with the pod's own nodeSelector during admission — guarantees the pod only lands on nodes that support this handler
scheduling.tolerationsmerged (union) with the pod's own tolerations — so gVisor-only nodes can be tainted to keep ordinary pods off
overhead.podFixedthe sandbox's own CPU/memory tax, added on top of the pod's container requests — the scheduler, ResourceQuota, and eviction logic all see the true total

📖 RuntimeClass assumes a homogeneous cluster by default (every node has every handler) — scheduling is exactly the escape hatch for clusters where only some nodes run gVisor/Kata.

Under the Hood — what a container REALLY is: namespaces, cgroups & union filesystems

A container is not a tiny VM. It's an ordinary Linux process with three kernel features applied: namespaces (what it can see), cgroups (what it can use), and a union filesystem (what it can read/write). That's the whole trick — and understanding it is what turns "OOMKilled" and "Exit 137" from mysteries into one-glance diagnoses.

① The three pillars of isolation
   ┌──────────────────────── HOST LINUX KERNEL (shared by all containers) ────────────────────┐
   │   🪟 NAMESPACES (visibility)     📊 CGROUPS (limits)        💾 UNION FS (layers)            │
   │   PID · NET · MNT · UTS          CPU · Memory · IO          overlay2 (lowerdir = image,    │
   │   IPC · USER · CGROUP · TIME     PIDs · HugeTLB             upperdir = writable top)        │
   └───────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                   │                       │                        │
                   ▼                       ▼                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────── 📦 the easypj container = a PROCESS ──────────────────────┐
   │  PID ns   → sees itself as PID 1            (host sees PID 48291)                          │
   │  NET ns   → its own eth0 (veth → host bridge); the whole POD shares this ns               │
   │  MNT ns   → sees /app as root              (host: /var/lib/containerd/…)                   │
   │  UTS ns   → hostname "easypj-web-6d8f9-x7k2"                                               │
   │  USER ns  → sees UID 0, mapped to UID 1000 on the host (rootless)                          │
   │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
   │  CPU cgroup    → limited to 500m (0.5 core) → over-use is THROTTLED (slowed)               │
   │  Memory cgroup → limited to 512Mi          → over-use is OOM-KILLED (Exit 137)             │
   │  PIDs cgroup   → max N processes            → fork() fails with EAGAIN                       │
   │  rootfs        → overlay2: read-only image layers + one writable upper layer               │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
② The 8 namespaces — how a container gets its own view of the world

When containerd starts easypj, it calls clone()/unshare() with namespace flags. Each namespace isolates one dimension:

NamespaceIsolatesWhy it matters in K8s
PIDProcess IDs — container sees its own PID 1kubectl exec PIDs ≠ host PIDs
NETInterfaces, routes, iptablesEach pod gets one NET ns, shared by its containers
MNTMount points / root filesystememptyDir, hostPath, PVC all mount here
UTSHostname & domainThe pod's hostname
IPCShared memory, semaphoresContainers in a pod share IPC
USERUID/GID mappingsrunAsUser, rootless containers
CGROUPThe cgroup root it can seeHides the host's cgroup tree
TIMEClock offsetsNewer kernels (5.6+)
③ Union filesystem — how image layers become a writable rootfs

overlay2 stacks the read-only image layers under a single writable layer, presenting one merged view:

   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ upperdir (READ-WRITE)  → all runtime writes land here          │ ← EPHEMERAL: gone when
   │   …/<container-id>/upper                                        │   the container dies!
   ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │            ▼  merged, overlaid view the process sees           │
   ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ lowerdir (READ-ONLY image layers, newest on top):             │
   │   L3  sha256:jkl…   easypj source code                        │
   │   L2  sha256:ghi…   pip packages                              │
   │   L1  sha256:def…   python:3.13-slim base                     │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   read:  check upper → L3 → L2 → L1 → ENOENT      write: copy-up from lower, then modify
🔑 CKA insight — Exit Code 137 = OOMKilled. 137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9). The container blew past its resources.limits.memory and the kernel's OOM killer terminated it. Confirm with kubectl describe pod easypj-web-… → State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled. The fix: raise the memory limit or cut the app's usage. And because upperdir is ephemeral, any data a restarted container wrote is gone — which is the whole reason Volumes (Ch 21) exist.
④ cgroups — how a memory/CPU limit is actually enforced (v1 vs v2)

"cgroups limit resources" is where most explanations stop. Here's the real mechanism, because it directly explains throttling, OOMKills, and the kubelet's QoS classes. A cgroup is a kernel-managed group of processes with accounting + limits; your easypj container is placed in one, and the kubelet writes its limits into special files:

Pod spec fieldcgroup setting (v2)What the kernel does
resources.requests.cpu: 250mcpu.weight (relative share)Under contention, you get a proportional slice — a guarantee, not a cap
resources.limits.cpu: 500mcpu.max (quota per period)Exceed it → process is THROTTLED (slowed), never killed
resources.limits.memory: 512Mimemory.maxExceed it → the OOM killer terminates it → Exit 137
resources.requests.memory(scheduling + memory.low)Used to place the pod; soft-protects that much memory
cgroups v1 (older)cgroups v2 (modern default)
HierarchyOne tree per controller (cpu, memory, … separate)One unified tree for all controllers
ConsistencyControllers could disagree / be mounted differentlyCleaner, consistent limits + pressure metrics (PSI)
KubernetesDeprecated (v1.35) — kubelet refuses to start on a v1 node by default (override: failCgroupV1: false)Recommended & the default; required for some features (PSI-based eviction, MemoryQoS)
🔑 This is exactly why CPU and memory behave differently. CPU is compressible → over-limit = throttle (your app just runs slower). Memory is incompressible → over-limit = OOMKill (you can't "slow down" RAM). That asymmetry drives every right-sizing decision in Chapter 15.
⑤ How an image pull actually works (manifest → config → layer blobs)

"It pulls the image" hides a precise OCI flow — and understanding it explains layer caching, multi-arch images, and most ImagePull failures:

   crictl/kubelet asks containerd for  easypj@sha256:abc…
        │
        ▼  1. GET the MANIFEST (or manifest LIST for multi-arch)
   🏪 registry  ──▶  manifest list:  amd64 → sha256:111…   arm64 → sha256:222…
        │            (containerd picks the node's architecture)
        ▼  2. GET the IMAGE CONFIG (json): env, CMD/ENTRYPOINT, user, the layer order
        ▼  3. GET each LAYER BLOB by digest (only the ones not already cached!)
   📦 layers:   sha256:def… (base)   sha256:ghi… (deps)   sha256:jkl… (easypj code)
        │
        ▼  4. containerd UNPACKS each blob into a snapshot, then overlay2 stacks them
   🗂️ ready rootfs  ──▶  runc creates the container from it
   💡 Step 3 is content-addressed: if another image already pulled sha256:def…, it's
      REUSED from the node — that's why shared base images make pods start fast.
🔑 ImagePull failures, decoded. Fails at step 1 (manifest) → wrong name/tag or "not found". Fails with "unauthorized" → private registry, no imagePullSecret. Fails at step 3 (a blob) → network/registry flake or disk-full on the node. Knowing which step broke turns a vague ImagePullBackOff into a targeted fix.
⑥ Which namespaces are shared inside a pod

A pod's containers don't each get 8 fresh namespaces — they share some (that's what makes them a pod) and isolate the rest:

NamespaceIsolatesShared across a pod's containers?
NETinterfaces, IP, ports✅ yes — one pod IP; that's why containers reach each other on localhost
IPCshared memory, semaphores✅ yes
PIDprocess IDsoptional — only with shareProcessNamespace: true
MNT · UTS · USER · CGROUPmounts · hostname · UID maps · cgroup view❌ no — each container is isolated
🔑 The pause container holds the shared NET + IPC namespaces open, so app containers join them — which is why the pod keeps its IP even as individual containers restart.
⑦ overlayfs — how the writable layer really behaves (copy-on-write)
   READ  /app/manage.py    → search top-down: upper? no → L3? no → L2? no → L1 base? YES   (no copy)
   WRITE /app/cache.txt    → the file is COPIED UP into the writable upper layer, then changed there
   DELETE /usr/bin/oldtool → can't touch the read-only image, so overlayfs writes a "whiteout"
                             marker that simply HIDES the file from the container's view
   ⚠️ the upper layer is the container's ephemeral R/W scratch — gone when the container is removed
      (exactly why durable pod data needs a Volume / PVC — Ch 6)
⑧ Exit codes — decode them at a glance
ExitMeansFirst move
0clean exitfine (Job done; restartPolicy: Always still restarts it)
1–128app error / crashkubectl logs <pod> --previous
137128 + 9 (SIGKILL) → usually OOMKilledraise the memory limit / fix a leak (describe shows OOMKilled)
143128 + 15 (SIGTERM)graceful stop — or shutdown ran past the grace period
139128 + 11 (SIGSEGV)app/runtime bug (segfault)

🔬 Deeper (exam + beyond): images and runtimes follow the OCI (Open Container Initiative) image & runtime specs, which is why a Docker-built image runs under containerd/CRI-O unchanged. Layers are content-addressed by @sha256: digest (pin these for true reproducibility). Every pod also has a tiny pause/sandbox container that holds the shared network + IPC namespaces so app containers can join them. Rootless & user namespaces map container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID, so "root in the container" is not root on the host — a major hardening win (and the mechanism behind the USER-ns row in the diagram above). privileged: true effectively switches namespace isolation OFF — which is why restricted Pod Security forbids it. For stronger isolation without a full VM, sandboxed runtimes like gVisor (user-space kernel) and Kata (lightweight microVM) plug in via RuntimeClass. And you don't need the Docker daemon to build: BuildKit, kaniko (in-cluster, daemonless) and buildah all emit OCI images — handy when CI itself runs on Kubernetes.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Containers share the host kernel — they're processes with namespaces (visibility) + cgroups (limits) + union FS (layers), so they're MB & milliseconds, not GB & minutes.
  • An image is a stack of cached layers. Order the Dockerfile cheap→expensive (deps before source) so edits don't bust the pip install cache.
  • Multi-stage + non-root = small, fast-pulling, lower-CVE production images.
  • Kubernetes runs containers via the CRI (containerd / CRI-O), not Docker — the dockershim was removed in v1.24. You still build with Docker.
  • crictl is your node-level lifeline when kubectl/kubelet is down.
  • Containers package code + deps + config so the app runs identically everywhere — the cure for "works on my machine." A container = image + a thin writable upper layer.
  • Image refs have hidden defaults — bare easypj means docker.io/library/easypj:latest; pin production by digest (@sha256:…); imagePullPolicy's default is inferred from the tag.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • cgroup-driver mismatch. containerd default (cgroupfs) vs kubelet's systemd → kubelet won't start, node stays NotReady. Set SystemdCgroup = true.
  • :latest is a trap. It's non-reproducible and defaults imagePullPolicy to Always (tagged images default to IfNotPresent) — surprise pulls and surprise versions.
  • Running as root. A container breakout as root = root on the node. Always USER + runAsNonRoot.
  • "Kubernetes removed Docker, so my images break." No — images are OCI; only the node runtime changed.
  • Using docker on a node. It may not be installed; use crictl (and ctr -n k8s.io for containerd internals).
  • Wrong/missing CRI socket path. If the kubelet can't reach the runtime socket (e.g. /run/containerd/containerd.sock), it can't start containers — node stays NotReady. On v1.35+, a cgroups-v1-only node won't start either.
  • Writing data into the container's ephemeral upper layer. It vanishes on restart/reschedule — anything worth keeping needs a Volume (Part 6).
  • Missing/bad imagePullSecret on a private image → ImagePullBackOff with "unauthorized" in the Events. Create the docker-registry Secret and reference it (or attach it to the ServiceAccount).
  • Fat single-stage images ship compilers and CVEs you never run — multi-stage the build.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Debug image issues fast: kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A8 Events — it names ImagePullBackOff vs OOMKilled vs CrashLoop instantly.
  • Order layers for cache hits — COPY requirements + pip install BEFORE COPY . ..
  • Pin digests (image@sha256:…) for reproducible, tamper-evident deploys.
  • ⚡ crictl is your lifeline — When the apiserver or kubelet is down, kubectl is useless — but the containers are still running on the node. crictl ps / crictl logs let you see and debug them directly via the runtime. This is exactly the move the Troubleshooting domain (30%) wants from you (Ch 32).
  • Multi-stage by default — discard the builder stage; the runtime image ships only installed packages + your code (small, fewer CVEs, faster pulls).
  • Tight .dockerignore (.git, __pycache__, *.pyc, db.sqlite3, .env, venv/) — shrinks the build context and keeps secrets out of the image.
  • Read the exit code first: 137 ⇒ OOMKilled (128+9), 143 ⇒ SIGTERM (128+15), 139 ⇒ segfault — it names the bug class instantly.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 2)

build host (docker) + node (crictl) 
# build host
docker build -t easypj:v1 .          # build image from Dockerfile
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1 # run + expose
docker push myregistry.io/easypj:v1  # push so K8s can pull
docker pull <image>                  # pull from a registry
docker ps                            # list running containers
docker logs <id>                     # view container logs
docker exec -it <id> bash            # shell into a container
docker images                        # list local images
docker stop <id>                     # stop a container (SIGTERM → SIGKILL)
docker system prune                  # clean up unused images/containers/networks

# on a node (Docker may be absent) — talk to the CRI directly
crictl ps                            # list running containers
crictl logs <container-id>            # view logs
crictl exec -it <id> sh              # shell into a container via the CRI
crictl inspect <id>                  # full container detail (incl. exit code)
crictl images                        # images cached on this node
crictl info | grep -i runtime        # which runtime + endpoint
ctr -n k8s.io images ls              # containerd-native image list
nerdctl ps                           # docker-compatible CLI for containerd (if installed)
systemctl status containerd          # is the runtime up?

# from the control plane — the Events line names the real pull/exit cause
kubectl describe pod <p>

🧠 Chapter 2 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
State two concrete differences between a VM and a container.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor (gigabytes, boots in minutes); a container shares the host kernel (megabytes, starts in milliseconds). (2) VM isolation is hardware-level/strong; container isolation is process-level via namespaces + cgroups.

🖥️ Virtual Machine📦 Container
Kernelits own full guest OS on a hypervisorshares the host kernel
Size · startGBs · boots in minutesMBs · starts in milliseconds
Isolationhardware-level (strong)process-level — namespaces + cgroups
Explanation

The shared kernel is the root cause of every "light & fast" property — and of the weaker isolation that later security chapters harden.

Q2
A pod is ImagePullBackOff. Give three likely causes and how to confirm.
Show Answer
Answer

Likely: (1) wrong image name/tag, (2) private registry with no imagePullSecrets, (3) registry unreachable / rate-limited. Confirm with kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events — it states the exact pull error.

Likely causeEvent says…Fix
wrong image name/tagnot found / manifest unknowncorrect the image reference
private registry, no credsunauthorizedadd an imagePullSecrets
registry unreachable / throttledtimeout / 429fix networking · mirror the image
Explanation

Events is always the first stop. "unauthorized" → credentials; "not found" → name/tag typo; "timeout" → network/registry.

Q3
Why does a multi-stage build produce a smaller, safer image?
Show Answer
Answer

The builder stage holds compilers and -dev headers; the runtime stage copies only the installed result and discards the builder. Less in the final image = smaller size, faster pulls, and a smaller attack surface / fewer CVEs.

what ships vs what's thrown away
  STAGE 1 builder (~900MB)                  STAGE 2 runtime (~150MB)  ← the ONLY stage shipped
  ┌───────────────────────────┐   COPY      ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ gcc · make · -dev headers │  --from=    │ python:3.13-slim base     │
  │ pip caches · build deps   │  builder    │ /install (the packages)   │
  │ /install  ────────────────┼──────────▶  │ easypj source · USER app  │
  └───────────── DISCARDED ✂️ ┘             └───────────── SHIPPED ✅ ──┘
Explanation

easypj's image drops from ~900 MB to ~150 MB this way, and nothing exploitable (gcc, build deps) ships to production.

Q4
kubectl is unavailable on a node. How do you list and log the containers?
Show Answer
Answer

Use crictl, which talks to the CRI directly:

on the node — talk to the CRI directly
crictl ps                  # list running containers
crictl logs <id>           # view a container's logs
crictl inspect <id>        # full details: mounts, env, state
Explanation

When the apiserver/kubelet is down, the containers still run — crictl is the node-level lifeline (Ch 32).

Q5
What is the CRI, and what replaced dockershim in v1.24?
Show Answer
Answer

The Container Runtime Interface is the standard gRPC API the kubelet uses to drive a runtime. v1.24 removed the dockershim translation layer; nodes now run containers via a CRI-native runtime — containerd (default) or CRI-O.

before vs after v1.24 — Docker leaves the data path
  BEFORE v1.24                          AFTER v1.24
  🤖 kubelet                            🤖 kubelet
     │ dockershim (translation)            │ CRI (native gRPC)
     ▼                                     ▼
  🐳 Docker daemon                      🐋 containerd / CRI-O ──▶ 📦 containers
     │
     ▼                                  (one hop fewer; same OCI images run unchanged)
  containerd ──▶ 📦 containers
Explanation

Docker-built images still work (they're OCI) — only the node-side runtime path changed.

Q6
Reorder a Dockerfile so pip install stays cached across code edits.
Show Answer
Answer

Copy the deps list and install before copying the source, so editing code only busts the last layer:

Dockerfile — deps before source
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # cached unless deps change
COPY . .                                             # only THIS layer busts on a code edit
Explanation

Layers cache top-down by content; put what changes least (deps) low, what changes most (your code) high.

Q7
Name three ways to shrink the easypj image.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Multi-stage build (drop build tools); (2) a slim/distroless base (python:3.13-slim not full python); (3) a .dockerignore to exclude .git, caches, venvs. (Bonus: combine RUN layers, --no-cache-dir for pip.)

TechniqueWhat it removesTypical saving
multi-stage buildcompilers, headers, pip caches (the whole builder)hundreds of MB
slim / distroless basethe OS packages a full base drags in~800MB → ~120MB base
.dockerignore.git, venv/, db.sqlite3, .env from the build contextMBs + keeps secrets out
pip --no-cache-dir / merged RUNspackage caches; dead intermediate layerstens of MB
Explanation

Smaller images pull faster (quicker pod starts/scaling) and expose fewer packages to scan/exploit.

Q8
Why run as non-root, and how do you do it?
Show Answer
Answer

If an attacker escapes a root container, they're root on the node. Declare a user in the image and enforce it in the pod:

image (Dockerfile) + pod (securityContext)
# Dockerfile
RUN useradd app
USER app
---
# Pod spec
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
Explanation

Defense in depth — the image declares intent; the cluster enforces it cluster-wide via Pod Security Standards, so a bad image can't slip through (Ch 27).

Q9
Why is :latest dangerous, and what should you use instead?
Show Answer
Answer

:latest is a moving pointer — two nodes can run different builds, and it defaults imagePullPolicy to Always. Use pinned tags (easypj:v1) or, best, an immutable digest (easypj@sha256:…).

ReferenceMutable?Default pull policyVerdict
easypj:latest (or no tag)✏️ yes — re-pushableAlways❌ non-reproducible; surprise pulls
easypj:v1✏️ technically yesIfNotPresent🟡 fine if your registry forbids re-push
easypj@sha256:…🔒 no — content-addressedIfNotPresent✅ exact bytes, tamper-evident — pin prod
Explanation

Reproducibility & rollback depend on knowing exactly which bytes ran. Digests are tamper-evident too.

Q10
A node's kubelet won't start, citing cgroups. What's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

The runtime and kubelet disagree on the cgroup driver. Set the runtime to systemd, then restart both:

/etc/containerd/config.toml → systemd driver
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options]
  SystemdCgroup = true

sudo systemctl restart containerd kubelet    # node should go Ready
Explanation

On systemd hosts both must use the systemd driver; a mismatch leaves the node NotReady (Ch 9).

⚙️ Chapter 2 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. You run kubectl describe pod easypj-web and see the event: "Failed to pull image 'myregistry.io/app:v2': rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Error response from daemon: unauthorized". What is the most likely cause and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The image is stored in a private registry and the pod doesn't have credentials configured. Fix by creating an imagePullSecret and referencing it in the pod spec:

fix the pull auth
# Create the secret with registry credentials
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=myregistry.io \
  --docker-username=myuser \
  --docker-password=mypass

# Add to pod spec under spec.imagePullSecrets:
# imagePullSecrets:
#   - name: regcred
Explanation

ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet failed to pull the container image. The "unauthorized" error specifically indicates authentication failure. Common causes: (1) Private registry without imagePullSecrets, (2) Expired/wrong credentials, (3) Wrong registry URL. On the CKA exam, always check the Events section of kubectl describe pod — it tells you exactly why the pull failed. Other ImagePullBackOff causes include typos in the image name or tag not existing.

Q2
What is the difference between crictl and docker commands? On a Kubernetes node running containerd, which tool should you use to list running containers and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Use crictl. It communicates directly with the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) and works with any CRI-compliant runtime (containerd, CRI-O).

Taskcrictl CommandDocker Equivalent
List containerscrictl psdocker ps
List imagescrictl imagesdocker images
View logscrictl logs <id>docker logs <id>
Inspect containercrictl inspect <id>docker inspect <id>
Explanation

Since Kubernetes v1.24 removed dockershim, Docker is no longer a supported runtime. Most clusters now use containerd directly. The crictl tool is the standard debugging tool for CRI runtimes. On the CKA exam, if you SSH to a node and need to inspect containers at the runtime level, crictl is the expected tool. Configure it via /etc/crictl.yaml to point at the runtime socket (e.g., unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock).

Q3
Explain the difference between the three imagePullPolicy values: Always, IfNotPresent, and Never. What is the default policy when you use the :latest tag versus a specific tag like :v1.2?
Show Answer
Answer
  • Always — kubelet always contacts the registry to check for newer image. Re-pulls if digest changed.
  • IfNotPresent — kubelet uses the local cached image if available; pulls only if not cached.
  • Never — kubelet never pulls; uses local image only. Fails if image isn't cached.

Defaults:

  • :latest tag → defaults to Always
  • Specific tag (e.g., :v1.2) → defaults to IfNotPresent
  • No tag specified → treated as :latest → defaults to Always
You writeEffective policyNode behaviour per container start
image: easypj (no tag)Alwayscontacts the registry every time
image: easypj:latestAlwayscontacts the registry every time
image: easypj:v1.2IfNotPresentuses the node cache; pulls once
image: easypj@sha256:…IfNotPresentuses the node cache; exact bytes
explicit imagePullPolicy: NeverNevercache only — fails if absent
Explanation

This is a common trap on the CKA. If you specify image: nginx without a tag, Kubernetes treats it as nginx:latest with imagePullPolicy: Always. This means every pod restart will contact the registry. In air-gapped or exam environments, this can cause unexpected ImagePullBackOff errors. Best practice: always use specific tags and explicitly set imagePullPolicy to avoid surprises.

Q4
What is a container image layer? Why are layers important for both storage efficiency and pod startup speed in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A container image is built from read-only layers. Each layer represents a filesystem change from a Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY, etc.). Layers are:

  • Cached and shared — If two images share a base layer (e.g., python:3.11-slim), the layer is stored and downloaded only once
  • Content-addressable — Each layer is identified by its SHA256 digest, enabling deduplication
  • Immutable — once built, a layer never changes; containers add a thin writable layer on top

For Kubernetes: shared layers mean that if node already has the base image cached, pulling a new version only downloads changed layers, dramatically speeding up pod startup.

v1 → v2: only the changed layer moves
  easypj:v1 (on the node)          easypj:v2 (being pulled)
  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ L3 app code  sha:jkl │         │ L3' app code sha:xyz │ ◄── ONLY this layer downloads
  │ L2 pip deps  sha:ghi │  ═══▶   │ L2 pip deps  sha:ghi │ ✅ cached — reused
  │ L1 base      sha:def │         │ L1 base      sha:def │ ✅ cached — reused
  └─────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────┘
  content-addressed by digest → identical layers are stored once, shared by all images
Explanation

While the CKA doesn't test image building, understanding layers helps diagnose issues: (1) Large images cause slow pulls and startup — use slim/alpine bases. (2) imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent leverages the layer cache. (3) If a node's disk fills up with cached images, use crictl rmi --prune to clean unused images. The kubelet also has garbage collection settings (imageGCHighThresholdPercent) that automatically clean old images when disk pressure is detected.

Q5
A pod spec references a multi-container pod with an init container and a sidecar container. Explain the difference between init containers and regular sidecar containers in terms of execution order and lifecycle.
Show Answer
Answer

Init containers:

  • Run sequentially before any app containers start
  • Must complete successfully (exit 0) before the next init container or app containers start
  • If an init container fails, the pod restarts according to its restartPolicy
  • Common uses: wait for a dependency, clone a git repo, populate a shared volume

Sidecar containers:

  • Run alongside the main app container for the entire pod lifetime
  • Share the pod's network namespace (communicate via localhost) and volumes
  • Common uses: log shipping, service mesh proxy, monitoring agent
yaml
spec:
  initContainers:            # Run first, sequentially
    - name: init-db-check
      image: busybox
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nslookup db-service; do sleep 2; done']
  containers:                # Run together after init completes
    - name: easypj-web       # Main container
      image: easypj:v1
    - name: log-shipper      # Sidecar
      image: fluentd:latest
Explanation

The CKA frequently tests multi-container pod patterns. Key points: (1) Init containers share volumes with app containers but NOT the same array — they're under initContainers:. (2) As of Kubernetes v1.28+, there's a native restartPolicy: Always for sidecar containers declared in initContainers that makes them true sidecars. (3) All containers in a pod share the same IP address and port space. A sidecar on port 8080 conflicts with the app on 8080.

Q6
You need to troubleshoot a pod on a worker node. The kubectl command is not available on the node. What tools can you use to inspect containers, view logs, and check images directly on the node?
Show Answer
Answer
on the worker node
# List all running containers on the node
sudo crictl ps

# List all containers (including stopped/failed)
sudo crictl ps -a

# View logs of a specific container
sudo crictl logs <container-id>
sudo crictl logs --tail 50 <container-id>

# Inspect container details (config, state, mounts)
sudo crictl inspect <container-id>

# List all pods on this node
sudo crictl pods

# List cached images
sudo crictl images

# Check kubelet status and logs
sudo systemctl status kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50
Explanation

On the CKA exam, you will encounter scenarios where you must SSH to a node and troubleshoot without kubectl. The two essential tools are: (1) crictl — for container-level inspection, and (2) journalctl -u kubelet — for kubelet logs showing why pods fail to start. Remember that crictl talks to the container runtime (containerd) via the CRI socket, while kubectl talks to the API server. They show different views of the same containers.

Q7
What is the OCI (Open Container Initiative) and why does it matter that Docker images are OCI-compliant? Can you use Docker-built images on a Kubernetes cluster running containerd?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes, absolutely. Docker-built images work perfectly on containerd or CRI-O clusters because they conform to the OCI Image Specification.

The OCI defines two standards:

  • OCI Image Spec — how container images are structured (layers, manifests, configs)
  • OCI Runtime Spec — how containers are executed (runc, crun)

Docker, containerd, CRI-O, and Podman all produce and consume OCI-compliant images. The tool you use to build the image is irrelevant — what matters is the resulting image format.

OCI is the neutral middle — any builder, any runtime
  BUILD with any of…                 ONE standard artifact              RUN on any of…
  🐳 Docker / BuildKit ─┐                                             ┌─▶ 🐋 containerd (runc)
  🧰 Buildah / Podman  ─┼──▶  📀 OCI image (manifest + config +  ────┼─▶ 📦 CRI-O (runc/crun)
  ☸️ kaniko (in-cluster)─┘        content-addressed layers)           └─▶ 🛡️ gVisor / Kata (RuntimeClass)
                              no conversion, ever — the FORMAT is the contract
Explanation

A common misconception is that removing Docker from Kubernetes means Docker images no longer work. This is false. The removal of dockershim only affects the runtime layer, not the image format. You can build with Docker, Buildah, Kaniko, or any OCI-compliant tool and run the images on any CRI-compliant runtime. The CKA may test this conceptual understanding in a scenario where someone incorrectly believes images need to be "converted" for containerd.

Q8
A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff state. What does this status mean, and what are the systematic steps to diagnose the root cause?
Show Answer
Answer

CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts, crashes, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with exponentially increasing delays (10s, 20s, 40s... up to 5 minutes).

Diagnostic steps:

bash
# Step 1: Check pod status and restart count
kubectl get pod easypj-web -o wide

# Step 2: Check events for clues
kubectl describe pod easypj-web | grep -A 20 "Events:"

# Step 3: Check container logs (current attempt)
kubectl logs easypj-web

# Step 4: Check previous crash logs
kubectl logs easypj-web --previous

# Step 5: Check if it's an OOMKill
kubectl describe pod easypj-web | grep -i "OOMKilled"

# Step 6: Check if command/args are wrong
kubectl get pod easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A 5 "command\|args"
Explanation

CrashLoopBackOff is one of the most common CKA troubleshooting scenarios. Common root causes: (1) Application error — app crashes on startup (check kubectl logs --previous), (2) Wrong command/args — container entrypoint fails, (3) Missing ConfigMap/Secret — referenced env vars don't exist, (4) OOMKilled — container exceeds memory limit, (5) Liveness probe failure — probe kills the container before it's ready. The --previous flag is crucial because it shows logs from the last crashed instance, not the currently starting one.

Q9
What is a container registry? Explain the full image reference format registry/repository:tag@sha256:digest and what each part means.
Show Answer
Answer

A container registry is a storage and distribution system for container images. The full reference format:

anatomy
registry.example.com/namespace/image-name:tag@sha256:abc123...

│                    │          │          │    │
├─ Registry host     │          │          │    └─ Digest (immutable hash)
│  (docker.io if     │          │          └─ Tag (mutable label)
│   omitted)         │          └─ Image name
│                    └─ Namespace/org
└─ Full reference

Examples:

  • nginx → docker.io/library/nginx:latest
  • mycompany/app:v2 → docker.io/mycompany/app:v2
  • gcr.io/my-project/app:v1 → explicit registry
Explanation

Understanding image references is critical for troubleshooting ImagePullBackOff errors on the CKA. Common mistakes: (1) Omitting the registry for private images, (2) Using :latest when a specific tag is needed, (3) Not specifying imagePullSecrets for private registries. The digest (@sha256:...) is the most reliable way to pin an image — tags are mutable and can be overwritten, but digests are content-addressable and immutable.

Q10
You SSH to a Kubernetes worker node and run crictl ps but get the error: "connect: no such file or directory". What is wrong and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The crictl tool cannot find the container runtime socket. Fix by configuring the runtime endpoint:

on the worker node
# Option 1: Set environment variable
export CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock

# Option 2: Create/edit crictl config file
sudo cat > /etc/crictl.yaml <<EOF
runtime-endpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
image-endpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
timeout: 10
debug: false
EOF

# Now try again
sudo crictl ps

Common socket paths:

  • containerd: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
  • CRI-O: unix:///var/run/crio/crio.sock
Explanation
