The CKA exam may present a node where crictl isn't configured. The tool needs to know which socket to connect to — this is the CRI endpoint. If /etc/crictl.yaml doesn't exist or has the wrong socket path, crictl will fail. To find the correct socket, check what runtime is installed: systemctl status containerd or systemctl status crio. Then set the endpoint accordingly. This is a quick fix that can save you from being stuck on a troubleshooting question.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.1 — Containerize easypj & Inspect It Like an Admin

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

A chapter capstone that exercises the whole pipeline — try each step before peeking:

  1. Build the multi-stage easypj:v1 and confirm it's slim.
  2. Run it and hit /jobs/.
  3. On a cluster node, use crictl (not docker) to find the running container, read its logs, and identify the runtime.
  4. Verify the node's cgroup driver is systemd.
Hint: crictl inspect + grep -i image shows which image is actually running; the cgroup driver must be systemd or the kubelet becomes unstable.
View Solution
1–2 · build & run (build host)
docker build -f Dockerfile.production -t easypj:v1 .
docker images easypj                 # ~150MB (slim, multi-stage) ✅ not ~900MB
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1
curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/     # easypj responds ✅
3–4 · inspect on a cluster node (no docker, no kubectl)
crictl ps | grep easypj              # find the container ID
crictl logs <container-id>            # its stdout/stderr (like kubectl logs)
crictl inspect <container-id> | grep -i image   # which image it runs
crictl info | grep -i runtime        # runtime = containerd, + the CRI endpoint

# 4) confirm cgroup driver matches the kubelet (must be systemd)
grep -i SystemdCgroup /etc/containerd/config.toml   # → SystemdCgroup = true ✅

Check yourself: easypj ships as a small OCI image; the node runs it via containerd (Docker is nowhere on the data path); crictl gives you full visibility without kubectl; and the cgroup driver lines up so the kubelet stays healthy. That's the entire Chapter 2 mental model exercised end-to-end.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.2 — Shrink the Image: Single-Stage → Multi-Stage

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Your single-stage easypj image is bloated with build tooling. Convert it to a multi-stage build (builder + slim non-root runtime), rebuild, and prove the size dropped with docker images. Add a .dockerignore so .env and db.sqlite3 can never leak into the image.

Hint: Stage 1 installs into --prefix=/install; stage 2 starts fresh from python:3.13-slim and copies only /install + your source. Add USER app so it runs non-root.
View Solution
Dockerfile.production + proof
# ── stage 1: builder (discarded) ──
FROM python:3.13-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ── stage 2: slim non-root runtime ──
FROM python:3.13-slim
RUN useradd -m app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn","easypj.wsgi:application","-b","0.0.0.0:8000"]
.dockerignore + build & compare
cat > .dockerignore <<'EOF'
.git
__pycache__
*.pyc
db.sqlite3
.env
venv/
EOF

docker build -t easypj:v1-fat -f Dockerfile .              # single-stage
docker build -t easypj:v1 -f Dockerfile.production .       # multi-stage
docker images | grep easypj
# easypj  v1-fat  ~900MB   ← compilers, caches, build deps
# easypj  v1      ~150MB   ← runtime only ✅
docker run --rm easypj:v1 whoami                            # app  (non-root ✅)

Check yourself: the builder stage — with pip's caches, compilers, and headers — was thrown away; only /install and your source reached the final image. Smaller image = faster pulls + fewer CVEs, and USER app means a breakout isn't root. This exact pattern is the production baseline for every image in this guide.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.3 — Fix an ImagePullBackOff (Private Registry)

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

A pod for registry.example.com/easypj:v1 is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. Diagnose the exact cause from the Events, fix it with a registry Secret, and verify the pod starts. (Assume the registry needs a login.)

Hint: describe first — "unauthorized" means credentials, "not found" means a bad name/tag. The fix for credentials is a docker-registry Secret referenced by imagePullSecrets.
View Solution
diagnose → fix → verify
# 1. DIAGNOSE — the Events line names the real cause
kubectl describe pod easypj-web | grep -A6 Events
#   Failed to pull image "registry.example.com/easypj:v1":
#   ... 401 Unauthorized  ← credentials, not a typo

# 2. FIX — create the registry credential Secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=deploy --docker-password='S3cret!' \
  --docker-email=ops@easypj.io

# 3. Reference it from the pod spec…
kubectl patch deployment easypj-web -p \
  '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}}}}'

#    …or attach it to the ServiceAccount so EVERY pod inherits it
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'

# 4. VERIFY — new pods pull successfully
kubectl get pods -w        # ContainerCreating → Running ✅
Events say…Real causeFix
unauthorized / 401missing/bad imagePullSecretdocker-registry Secret + reference it
not found / manifest unknownwrong image name or tagfix the ref (remember the docker.io/library/…:latest defaults)
timeouts / DNS errorsregistry unreachable from the nodecheck node network/proxy/rate-limits

Check yourself: ImagePullBackOff only means "a failed pull is being retried with backoff" — the Events name the actual failure. You fixed the credential case; the table gives you the other two family members so the whole error class is now routine.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.4 — Debug a Node with crictl (kubectl Is Dead)

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

The apiserver is down — every kubectl command times out — but easypj containers are still running on worker-1 and users report errors. SSH to the node and, using only runtime-level tools: list the running containers, read the easypj container's logs, find its exit code from its last crash, and confirm the runtime itself is healthy.

Hint: crictl talks straight to /run/containerd/containerd.sock — no kubelet or apiserver required. crictl ps -a shows exited containers too; crictl inspect carries the exit code.
View Solution
on worker-1 — the CRI is your only window
# 1. What's running (and what crashed)?  -a includes exited containers
sudo crictl ps
sudo crictl ps -a | grep easypj

# 2. Read the app's logs straight from the runtime
CID=$(sudo crictl ps -a --name easypj -q | head -1)
sudo crictl logs "$CID" | tail -30

# 3. Exit code of the last crash (137 = OOMKilled, 143 = SIGTERM, 139 = segfault)
sudo crictl inspect "$CID" | grep -i exitCode

# 4. Is the runtime itself healthy?
sudo systemctl status containerd
sudo crictl info | grep -iA2 runtime      # runtime name + socket endpoint

Check yourself: you diagnosed a live workload with zero Kubernetes control plane — because containers are just processes managed by containerd, and crictl speaks CRI directly to it. This is the exam's "node is broken, kubectl returns nothing" reflex: SSH in, switch tools, keep debugging. (Chapter 32 builds a full method on this.)

🔬 Practice Drill 2.5 — Kubelet Won't Start: the cgroup-Driver Mismatch

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

A freshly provisioned node refuses to join: systemctl status kubelet shows a crash-loop and the journal mentions cgroups. Diagnose the classic cause — the kubelet and containerd disagree on the cgroup driver — and fix both sides to systemd.

Hint: containerd's default is cgroupfs; kubeadm clusters expect systemd on both. The containerd side lives in /etc/containerd/config.toml under the runc options; the kubelet side in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
View Solution
diagnose → align both drivers → restart
# 1. DIAGNOSE — read the kubelet's own words
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -20
#   "failed to run Kubelet: misconfiguration: kubelet cgroup driver: \"systemd\"
#    is different from docker/containerd cgroup driver: \"cgroupfs\""

# 2. FIX containerd → systemd driver
sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml
#   ([plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options])

# 3. CONFIRM the kubelet side matches (kubeadm default is already systemd)
grep cgroupDriver /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml     # cgroupDriver: systemd

# 4. RESTART the pair, runtime first
sudo systemctl restart containerd
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# 5. VERIFY
sudo systemctl is-active containerd kubelet        # active active ✅
kubectl get nodes                                  # node Ready ✅

Check yourself: the kubelet and the runtime both write cgroup limits for containers, so they must speak the same dialect — systemd on modern distros. The journal names the mismatch outright, the fix is one line of TOML, and the restart order is runtime-then-kubelet. Bonus fact for v1.35+: the node must also be on cgroups v2 (v1 is deprecated) — check with stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/ (cgroup2fs = good).

📌 Chapter 2 Visual Summary — easypj source → image → running pod
   👩‍💻 your code            🔨 BUILD (laptop / CI)              🏪 REGISTRY            ☸️ KUBERNETES NODE
   ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ easypj source │ ─────▶ │ Dockerfile (multi-    │ ──push─▶ │ easypj:v1   │ ─pull─▶ │ 🤖 kubelet → CRI       │
   │ + requirements│  docker│ stage, non-root)     │         │ (cached     │        │ 🐋 containerd starts   │
   │               │  build │ → 📀 image = layers   │         │  layers)    │        │ 📦 the container       │
   └──────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘         └────────────┘        │   namespaces + cgroups │
                                                                                    │   + overlay2 rootfs    │
   ① build once  ──────────  ② push to a registry  ──────────  ③ nodes pull & run ──┘  :8000  ✅
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   One immutable image, built once, runs identically everywhere — and the cluster runs it via the CRI,
   not Docker. That artifact is the unit every later chapter schedules, scales, heals, and secures.

In words: You take the easypj source plus its dependencies and a Dockerfile (multi-stage, non-root) and docker build it into an image — a stack of read-only layers. You build it once, then push it to a registry where the layers are cached and shareable.

When a node needs to run it, the kubelet asks the container runtime (containerd) — through the CRI, not Docker — to pull the image and start a container. That container is just a normal Linux process that the kernel isolates with namespaces (what it can see), cgroups (what it can use), and an overlay root filesystem (its files).

The takeaway: the image is one immutable artifact that runs identically on every node — that reproducibility is why containers exist. From here on, this image is the unit every later chapter schedules, scales, heals, and secures.

Chapter 3 · Kubernetes Architecture — The Admin's Blueprint

Every troubleshooting question is really one question: "which component failed?" — and you can't fix what you can't name. This chapter is the map: every part of the control plane and every part of a worker node, what each does, what breaks when it's gone, and the exact end-to-end journey from kubectl apply to a running easypj pod. It is the foundation the entire rest of the guide stands on.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📖 Architecture 🎯 CKA Core (25%) 🐍 easypj / jobpost

🎯 What You'll Learn

🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% Troubleshooting 30%
🏗️ Architecture knowledge is CKA gold — it's the foundation for ~55% of the exam

Every troubleshooting task assumes you know how the components interact. Match the symptom to the component and you've half-solved it:

  • Node NotReady? → check the kubelet.
  • Pods stuck Pending? → check the scheduler.
  • State lost? → restore etcd (backup/restore is tested directly).
  • kubectl hangs? → the apiserver is down; debug from the node with crictl.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 3 Learning Arc

We zoom from the whole cluster, into each half (control plane, then nodes), then trace one pod's entire life across them, and finish with the network and the static-pod trick that bootstraps it all.

3.1 Cluster Architecture Overview

A Kubernetes cluster is two layers: a control plane (the brain — makes every decision) and one or more worker nodes (the muscle — actually run the workloads). As a CKA admin you install, configure, and repair both. Everything else in this chapter is a zoom-in on one of these two halves.

The complete cluster — brain + muscle
   ┌──────────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ───────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  🧠 CONTROL PLANE  (decides)                                                            │
   │   ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐    │
   │   │ 📡 apiserver  │ │ 🗄️ etcd     │ │ 📋 scheduler    │ │ 🔄 controller-manager       │    │
   │   │ the ONLY door │ │ ALL state  │ │ places pods    │ │ reconcile loops             │    │
   │   │ :6443         │ │ :2379/2380 │ │ filter→score→  │ │ (node · ReplicaSet ·        │    │
   │   │ authN/Z/admit │ │ (Raft)     │ │ bind           │ │  endpoint · serviceaccount) │    │
   │   └──────┬───────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────┘    │
   │          │   ⚠️ ONLY the apiserver talks to etcd; every component & kubectl goes        │
   │          │      THROUGH the apiserver (the single choke point).                          │
   │  ────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
   │  💪 WORKER NODES  (run)                                                                  │
   │   ┌──────▼──────────────────┐                  ┌─────────────────────────┐              │
   │   │ Node 1                   │                  │ Node 2                   │             │
   │   │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 kube-proxy │                  │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 kube-proxy │             │
   │   │ 🐋 containerd            │                  │ 🐋 containerd            │             │
   │   │ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐   │                  │ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐   │             │
   │   │ │📦 easypj│ │📦 easypj│   │                  │ │📦 easypj│ │🐘 postgres│ │             │
   │   │ │  web    │ │  web    │   │                  │ │  web    │ │  :5432   │ │             │
   │   │ └────────┘ └────────┘   │                  │ └────────┘ └────────┘   │             │

💪 Worker Nodes Run the actual workloads

🌐 Networking Layer Connects everything together

📖 The mental shortcut

For the rest of your CKA life, sort every problem into one bucket: is it a decision problem (control plane — won't schedule, won't reconcile, can't reach the API) or a run problem (a node — container won't start, NotReady, networking)? That single split routes you to the right component before you type a command.

Three Cluster Topologies — How the Same Components Get Arranged

Every cluster has the same components; what varies is how many copies and where they live. You'll build the first topology in Ch 9 and the HA ones in Ch 35 — but knowing all three now makes every "how many nodes / what fails when" question answerable:

Single control plane → stacked HA → external etcd
  ① SINGLE CONTROL PLANE (learning / dev — what kubeadm init gives you)
     ┌────────── CP node ──────────┐    ┌─ worker ─┐ ┌─ worker ─┐
     │ apiserver·etcd·sched·c-mgr  │    │  pods    │ │  pods    │
     └─────────────────────────────┘    └──────────┘ └──────────┘
     💥 CP node dies → no API, no scheduling (pods keep running "headless")

  ② STACKED HA (production default — etcd rides ON each CP node)
     ┌── CP-1 ──┐ ┌── CP-2 ──┐ ┌── CP-3 ──┐      🔀 LB in front of :6443
     │ api+etcd │ │ api+etcd │ │ api+etcd │      etcd quorum = 2 of 3
     └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘      lose 1 CP node → still healthy
     ⚠️ each CP loss costs an apiserver AND an etcd member at once

  ③ EXTERNAL ETCD (large/critical clusters — etcd on its own machines)
     ┌─ CP-1 ─┐ ┌─ CP-2 ─┐ ┌─ CP-3 ─┐   ┌─ etcd-1 ─┐ ┌─ etcd-2 ─┐ ┌─ etcd-3 ─┐
     │ api…   │ │ api…   │ │ api…   │──▶│          │ │          │ │          │
     └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘   └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘
     failure domains SEPARATED (6+ machines) — an apiserver loss never touches etcd
TopologyMachines (min)SurvivesUse when
① Single CP1 CP + workersnothing (CP is a SPOF)learning, dev, the exam's practice clusters
② Stacked HA3 CP + workers1 CP-node lossthe standard production choice
③ External etcd3 CP + 3 etcd1 of each, independentlylarge clusters where etcd needs its own I/O & blast radius
💡 Why always an odd number of etcd members?

etcd commits a write only when a majority (quorum) agrees: 3 members tolerate 1 failure (quorum 2), 5 tolerate 2 (quorum 3). An even count adds cost but no extra failure tolerance — 4 members still only tolerate 1 loss (quorum 3) and can split 2–2. Hence 1, 3, or 5 — never 2 or 4. Full quorum math in Ch 35.

3.2 Control-Plane Components — Deep Dive

These are the components you maintain, troubleshoot, and restore. For each, learn three things: its job, its config location, and — most exam-relevant — what breaks when it's gone.

🍽️ In plain English — the cluster as a restaurant

If the components feel abstract, map them to a busy restaurant — it makes every role (and every failure) intuitive:

RestaurantKubernetesSo if it's gone…
🛎️ the front desk — every order/request goes through it📡 kube-apiservernobody can place or change orders (no kubectl)
📖 the order ledger — the single written record of every order🗄️ etcdlose the ledger = lose the whole restaurant's state
🪑 the host who seats each party at the best table📋 schedulernew parties wait at the door (pods Pending)
🧑‍💼 the floor manager watching everything & fixing gaps🔄 controller-managerno one refills empty tables (no self-healing)
👨‍🍳 the line cook at each station who actually makes the food🤖 kubelet (on each node)that station stops cooking (node NotReady)
🏃 the runner delivering plates to the right table🌐 kube-proxyfood's made but never reaches diners (Services break)

Notice the front desk (apiserver) is the only one who reads/writes the ledger (etcd) — exactly like the real cluster. Keep this picture; the rest of §3.2 just adds detail to each role.

a) 📡 kube-apiserver — the front door

📡 kube-apiserver

🎯 Role
The only entry point. Every kubectl call, every kubelet, every controller talks to it — and it's the only component that reads/writes etcd.
🔐 Pipeline
Each request: authentication (certs/tokens) → authorization (RBAC) → admission (validate/mutate) → persist to etcd.
📂 Config
Static-pod manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
🔌 Port
6443 (secure HTTPS)
💀 If it fails
No kubectl, no new pods, nodes can't report status. Existing pods keep running — the kubelet is independent.

b) 🗄️ etcd — the cluster database

🗄️ etcd — the brain's memory

🎯 Role
A distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state under /registry/… — pods, services, secrets, RBAC, everything.
🔄 Consensus
Uses Raft — a quorum (majority) must agree on every write. That's why HA clusters run 3 or 5 etcd members.
🔌 Ports
2379 (client) · 2380 (peer)
📝 CKA
Backup & restore is directly tested — know etcdctl snapshot save / restore cold.
🚨 etcd lost = cluster lost

Lose etcd without a backup and your entire cluster — every pod, service, secret, and RBAC rule — is gone. This is precisely why "back up etcd" is the #1 admin task and a guaranteed exam item (Ch 29).

terminal — etcd backup (CKA skill)
# snapshot (cert paths come from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# verify it's readable
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table

c) 📋 kube-scheduler — the matchmaker

📋 kube-scheduler

🎯 Role
Watches for Pods with no node assigned, evaluates every node, and binds the pod to the best fit.
🔍 Process
Filter (which nodes can run it?) → Score (which is best?) → Bind (assign the winner).
📊 Considers
CPU/mem requests, nodeSelector, affinity/anti-affinity, taints/tolerations, PV topology, spread constraints.
💀 If it fails
New pods stay Pending (existing pods unaffected). Spot it: kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending.
1
Watch

See a Pod with empty nodeName

2
Filter

Drop nodes that can't fit (resources, taints, affinity)

3
Score

Rank the survivors (spread, balance, preferences)

4
Bind

Assign the top node → write to etcd → kubelet takes over

d) 🔄 kube-controller-manager — the watchdog

🔄 kube-controller-manager (many controllers, one process)

🖥️ Node ctrl
Watches node heartbeats; marks a node NotReady after ~40s of silence, evicts its pods after ~5 min.
📦 ReplicaSet ctrl
Keeps the pod count right — spec says 3, only 2 running → creates 1 more.
🔗 Endpoint ctrl
Wires Services to Pods by maintaining the EndpointSlice (the list of ready pod IPs).
👤 ServiceAccount ctrl
Creates the default ServiceAccount for each new namespace.
💀 If it fails
No self-healing: crashed pods aren't replaced, scaling/endpoints stall, dead nodes aren't acted on.
A controller loop — the heart of Kubernetes
   ┌─────────── CONTROLLER LOOP (runs forever) ───────────┐
   │  👁️ OBSERVE  ──▶  🧮 COMPARE  ──▶  🛠️ ACT  ──┐         │
   │  actual state    desired vs       reconcile          │
   │  "2 pods"        actual "want 3"  "create 1 pod"      │
   │      ▲                                    │           │
   │      └────────────────────────────────────┘           │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   easypj ReplicaSet: spec replicas=3, see 2 → create 1 → repeat

e) ☁️ cloud-controller-manager — the cloud glue (optional)

📖 Only on cloud clusters

The cloud-controller-manager integrates a cloud provider: provisioning LoadBalancers, managing routes, and handling node lifecycle (detecting deleted VMs). Bare-metal/kubeadm clusters don't run it. It exists so the core controllers stay cloud-agnostic — another example of Kubernetes keeping vendor specifics behind a plug.

3.3 Worker-Node Components — Deep Dive

Every node — worker and control-plane — runs three things that actually make containers happen: the kubelet (agent), kube-proxy (service routing), and a container runtime. These are where "run" problems live.

a) 🤖 kubelet — the node agent

🤖 kubelet

🎯 Role
Receives PodSpecs from the API server, drives the runtime to start/stop containers, runs probes, and reports status back.
⚡ Key fact
The kubelet is NOT a pod — it's a systemd service on the node. Check it with systemctl status kubelet.
📂 Config
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
🔌 Port
10250 (HTTPS API)
🔍 Troubleshoot
journalctl -u kubelet -f — most common causes: expired cert, runtime down, swap on, or cgroup-driver mismatch.

b) 🌐 kube-proxy — the network plumber

🌐 kube-proxy

🎯 Role
Programs each node's dataplane so a Service VIP load-balances to the right backing Pod IPs.
⚙️ Modes
iptables (still the upstream default), nftables (GA since v1.33, needs kernel ≥5.13 — the recommended target for new clusters), IPVS (was the faster-at-scale option, but deprecated as of v1.35 in favor of nftables — don't build new deployments on it).
📦 Runs as
A DaemonSet (one pod per node) in kube-system — unlike the kubelet, it is a pod.
💡 Remember
kube-proxy handles Service networking; the CNI handles pod-to-pod networking. Pods ping by IP but Services fail → suspect kube-proxy.

c) 🐋 container runtime

🐋
containerd

The default for kubeadm, EKS, AKS, GKE. CNCF-graduated. Drives the actual container lifecycle via the CRI.

🔴
CRI-O

Kubernetes-native, minimal. Used by OpenShift; versioned in lockstep with K8s.

⚠️ CKA triage: node shows NotReady? Check in this order
  • systemctl status kubelet — is the agent running?
  • journalctl -u kubelet — what's the error? (cert / swap / CNI / cgroup)
  • systemctl status containerd — is the runtime up?
  • crictl ps — can the runtime even list containers?

Everything the kubelet Actually Does

"The kubelet runs containers" undersells it — it's the busiest agent in the cluster and the prime suspect in most node problems. Knowing its full job list tells you exactly what can break:

🤖 the kubelet's responsibilities

📝 Register
Registers the node with the apiserver on startup (creates the Node object, advertises capacity/labels).
💓 Heartbeat
Renews a node Lease (in kube-node-lease) every few seconds so the control plane knows it's alive — stop renewing → NotReady.
👁️ Watch
Watches the apiserver for Pods bound to its node (and the static-pod dir on disk).
🐋 Run
Drives the CRI to pull images and start/stop containers; sets up the pod sandbox.
💾 Mount
Attaches/mounts volumes via the CSI before starting containers (emptyDir, PVC, configMap/secret).
🩺 Probe
Runs liveness/readiness/startup probes → restarts dead containers, gates traffic on readiness.
📊 Report
Reports pod & node status back to the apiserver; exposes stats (cAdvisor) for kubectl top.
🧹 Evict
Under node pressure (disk/memory) it evicts pods and applies the matching taint (e.g. DiskPressure).
📖 Why this matters: the kubelet is "trusted" but standalone

Because the kubelet reads its work from the apiserver but acts independently, two important things follow: (1) if the apiserver dies, running pods keep running — the kubelet doesn't need it to keep containers alive; and (2) the kubelet can run static pods with no control plane at all, which is exactly how kubeadm bootstraps the cluster (§3.6). It's the one component that bridges "declared in the API" and "actually running on Linux."

3.4 How a Pod Is Born — The Full Journey

This is the single most important sequence in Kubernetes — every troubleshooting task assumes it. Watch what happens after kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml, and notice that no single component runs the show: each one reconciles its own slice and the pod emerges.

1
kubectl → apiserver

HTTPS request to :6443 with a client cert.

2
authN → authZ → admit

Who are you? (cert) · Allowed? (RBAC) · Valid? (admission).

3
apiserver → etcd

The Deployment object is persisted — desired state recorded.

4
controllers

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod objects (still nodeless).

5
scheduler

Sees a nodeless Pod → filter → score → binds to a node.

6
kubelet

On that node: pulls easypj:v2, starts the container, CNI gives it an IP.

7
kube-proxy

Programs Service routing to the new Pod IP.

8
Running ✅

kubelet reports status → apiserver → etcd; the loops keep watching.

kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml → a Running pod
   👩‍💻 kubectl apply
        │ ① HTTPS :6443 + client cert
        ▼
   📡 apiserver ──② authN → authZ(RBAC) → admission──┐
        │ ③ persist Deployment                       │
        ▼                                            │
   🗄️ etcd  (desired state)  ◀───────────────────────┘
        │ ④ controller-manager: Deployment → ReplicaSet → 3 Pod objects (Pending)
        ▼
   📋 scheduler ── ⑤ filter → score → BIND each Pod → a node
        ▼
   🤖 kubelet (on the node) ── ⑥ 🐋 pull easypj:v2 · start container · 🌐 CNI assigns IP
        ▼
   🌐 kube-proxy ── ⑦ program Service routing to the new Pod IP
        ▼
   📦 easypj Running :8000 ── ⑧ status ─▶ apiserver ─▶ etcd     (loops keep reconciling)
💡 The troubleshooting map — match the symptom to the broken step
  • Connection refused / kubectl hangs → step 1–3 (apiserver/etcd down)
  • Forbidden / Unauthorized → step 2 (RBAC or certs)
  • Pod stuck Pending → step 5 (scheduler can't place it)
  • ImagePullBackOff → step 6 (kubelet can't pull the image)
  • CrashLoopBackOff → step 6 (container starts, then dies)
  • Service unreachable → step 7 (kube-proxy / endpoints)
🍽️ In plain English — the same journey, as a restaurant order

Tie it back to §3.2's restaurant: "You hand your order to the front desk (apiserver), which checks you're allowed and writes it in the ledger (etcd). The floor manager (controllers) turns 'a table of 3' into three seat requests; the host (scheduler) seats each at a table (node); the line cook there (kubelet) actually makes the dish (starts the container); and the runner (kube-proxy) makes sure diners can find it (Service routing)."

Same eight steps, zero jargon — and the failure map still works: nobody seated = the host (scheduler) is out; food never delivered = the runner (kube-proxy) is out.

3.5 Cluster Networking Overview

Kubernetes networking has one founding rule: every Pod gets its own unique IP, and all Pods can reach all Pods without NAT — one flat network. A CNI plugin makes that real. Keep the layers straight and networking stops being scary (full depth in Part 5).

The four network layers — from the wire up to the user
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🌍 EXTERNAL traffic (users, internet)                          │
   │    enters via: NodePort · LoadBalancer · Ingress · Gateway     │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 🔗 SERVICE network  (stable virtual IPs, e.g. 10.96.0.0/12)    │
   │    kube-proxy DNATs a Service VIP → a ready Pod IP             │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 📦 POD network  (real pod IPs, e.g. 10.244.0.0/16)            │
   │    assigned by the CNI · flat · every pod reaches every pod     │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 🖧 NODE network  (the machines/VMs, e.g. 192.168.1.0/24)       │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   easypj-web pod 10.244.1.5  ──reaches──▶  easypj-db 10.244.2.4 (no NAT)
   a client hits the Service VIP → kube-proxy picks a ready easypj-web pod

CNI Plugins — Your Choice as Admin

🐯
Calico

Most popular. Full NetworkPolicy, BGP routing. Common in CKA environments.

🐝
Cilium

eBPF-based, deep observability (Hubble), high performance. NetworkPolicy +.

🟦
Flannel

Simple VXLAN overlay, easy setup — but no NetworkPolicy.

🕸️
Weave

Encrypted mesh, auto-discovery, NetworkPolicy support.

📖 CKA task: install a CNI right after kubeadm init

A fresh cluster's pods (including CoreDNS) sit Pending and nodes stay NotReady until a CNI is installed — e.g. kubectl apply -f calico.yaml. "No CNI" is a classic NotReady cause: the fix is install a CNI, not restart the kubelet.

Why it's all pluggable — the three "sockets" (CRI · CNI · CSI)
   🤖 kubelet   ──CRI──▶  🐋 containerd / CRI-O          RUN containers
   pod network ──CNI──▶  🌐 Calico / Cilium / Flannel   WIRE pods (give IPs)
   volumes     ──CSI──▶  🧱 EBS / PD / Ceph / NFS driver ATTACH storage
   📖 CRI = runtime · CNI = network · CSI = storage — swap the plug, K8s is unchanged.

The Rules of the Kubernetes Network Model

Every CNI must honour the same contract — four rules that make the "flat network" promise concrete. Memorize these; they're the foundation of all Part 5 troubleshooting:

#RuleWhy it matters
1Every Pod gets its own unique IPNo port-mapping juggling — each pod is a "real host" on the network
2All Pods reach all Pods without NATThe destination sees the real source pod IP (flat L3 network)
3Nodes reach all Pods without NATThe kubelet & health checks talk to pods directly
4A Pod sees its own IP as others see itNo surprising address translation inside the pod
📖 CoreDNS — names instead of IPs

Pods come and go with changing IPs, so apps address each other by name. CoreDNS (a Deployment in kube-system, fronted by the kube-dns Service, usually 10.96.0.10) resolves Service names to ClusterIPs — e.g. easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local. Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points at it. If name resolution breaks cluster-wide, suspect CoreDNS first (full chapter: Ch 19).

⚠️ kube-proxy vs CNI — keep them separate when debugging

The CNI implements rules 1–4 (pod-to-pod). kube-proxy implements the Service abstraction on top (VIP → pod). So: pods can ping each other by IP but a Service is unreachable → kube-proxy/endpoints problem; pods can't reach each other by IP at all → CNI problem. That one split routes most networking tickets.

3.6 Static Pods — an Admin-Only Concept

Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet on one node — not by the scheduler or API server. They're how kubeadm runs the control plane itself, and they're tested directly on the CKA.

📦
Regular pods

Created via the API server (kubectl) → stored in etcd → scheduled by the scheduler → managed by controllers.

📌
Static pods

Created by the kubelet from YAML in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet watches that dir and owns the lifecycle. Drop a file → pod appears; remove it → pod gone.

💡 The control plane IS static pods

On a kubeadm cluster, the apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, and etcd all run as static pods — which is why you configure them by editing YAML in the manifests dir (the kubelet reloads automatically):

terminal — the control-plane static pods
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane
# etcd-controlplane                       1/1  Running   ← note the -<nodename> suffix
# kube-apiserver-controlplane             1/1  Running
# kube-controller-manager-controlplane    1/1  Running
# kube-scheduler-controlplane             1/1  Running

Creating a Custom Static Pod

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-easypj
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: easypj
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
⚠️ Static-pod facts the exam loves
  • You cannot kubectl delete a static pod — the kubelet instantly recreates it. Remove the manifest file instead.
  • The kubelet creates a read-only "mirror pod" in the API so you can see it; that's why the name carries a -<nodename> suffix.
  • The watched directory is set by staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
  • Static pods (kubelet-managed) ≠ DaemonSets (API-managed) — both put one pod per node, but only DaemonSets are API objects.

etcd Restore — the Companion Procedure

You saw backup in §3.2; restore is the other half (and a classic exam task). Always restore to a new data dir, then repoint the etcd static pod at it:

terminal — etcd restore
# 1) restore the snapshot into a NEW directory
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

# 2) edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml → point the data hostPath
#    volume from /var/lib/etcd  →  /var/lib/etcd-restored

# 3) the kubelet sees the manifest change & recreates etcd automatically
# 4) verify
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get nodes
🚨 Restore gotcha

--data-dir must be a new path (e.g. /var/lib/etcd-restored), then repoint the manifest. Restoring over the live dir while etcd runs can corrupt it. Full DR drill in Chapter 29.

Component Quick Reference — Ports · Config · Logs

ComponentPortConfig / manifestLogs
kube-apiserver6443/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-*
etcd2379/2380/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system etcd-*
kube-scheduler10259…/kube-scheduler.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-*
controller-manager10257…/kube-controller-manager.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-*
kubelet10250/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamljournalctl -u kubelet -f
kube-proxy10256ConfigMap kube-proxykubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-*
