CoreDNS53ConfigMap corednskubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-*
💡 Key file paths to memorize
  • /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — static-pod manifests (control plane)
  • /etc/kubernetes/pki/ — all cluster certs (CA, server, client)
  • /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf — the admin kubeconfig
  • /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — kubelet config (incl. staticPodPath)
  • /var/lib/etcd/ — etcd data directory
  • /etc/cni/net.d/ & /opt/cni/bin/ — CNI config & binaries

3.7 Node Health & Control-Plane ↔ Node Communication

§3.3 named the node's components; this is how the control plane knows a node is alive, how much it can schedule onto it, and how the two halves talk securely. It's the backbone of "node NotReady" troubleshooting (30% domain).

① Node status conditions — the health report

Each Node object carries a set of conditions (see them with kubectl describe node). Ready=True means healthy & schedulable; the four "pressure" conditions are early-warning flags.

ConditionProblem stateTypical cause
ReadyTrue = healthy · False/Unknown = problemkubelet down, lost heartbeat, runtime/CNI broken
MemoryPressureTrue = low memorynode RAM nearly exhausted → starts evicting pods
DiskPressureTrue = low diskfull disk / image cache → eviction + image GC
PIDPressureTrue = too many processesfork bomb / runaway workload
NetworkUnavailableTrue = node network not configuredCNI not installed / route missing

② Heartbeats, the node Lease & the eviction timeline

A node proves it's alive two ways: the kubelet renews a lightweight Lease in the kube-node-lease namespace (one per node, ~every 10s — the cheap, frequent heartbeat) and posts a fuller .status update whenever something changes (or periodically). When heartbeats stop, the node controller runs a fixed clock:

what happens when a node goes silent
   t = 0s     kubelet stops renewing its Lease / status   (node crashed, network cut)
   t ≈ 50s    node controller marks the node  Ready = Unknown   (node-monitor-grace-period)
              └─ adds taint  node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute   (or …/not-ready)
   t ≈ 5min   pods without a matching toleration are EVICTED & rescheduled elsewhere
              └─ eviction is rate-limited so a big outage doesn't stampede the cluster
   kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease     ← see each node's heartbeat

🔑 This is why "I rebooted a node and my pods vanished a few minutes later" is expected — the ~5-minute eviction timer fired. A pod's tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/unreachable / not-ready (with tolerationSeconds) control how quickly it's moved.

③ Capacity vs Allocatable — what the scheduler actually sees

A node's Capacity is its total hardware; Allocatable is what's left for your pods after reservations for the kubelet, the OS, and an eviction buffer. The scheduler only ever fills Allocatable — which is why a pod can sit Pending even though the node "looks" half-empty.

Capacity vs Allocatable — the slice the scheduler actually fills
   NODE CAPACITY   (e.g. 4 CPU / 16Gi)
   ├─ kube-reserved       kubelet, container runtime
   ├─ system-reserved     OS, sshd, systemd
   ├─ eviction-threshold  safety buffer (e.g. memory.available < 100Mi)
   └─ ALLOCATABLE   ◀── the only slice the scheduler can place pods into
   kubectl describe node node-1     → shows Capacity and Allocatable side by side

④ Control-plane ↔ node communication — the trust asymmetry

Traffic from a node into the control plane is secured by default; traffic from the control plane out to nodes is the leg you must harden.

DirectionPathSecurity
Node → control planekubelet / kube-proxy → apiserver :6443✅ TLS + auth + RBAC by default — the one hub everything dials
CP → kubeletapiserver → kubelet :10250 (logs, exec, port-forward, metrics)⚠️ HTTPS, but the apiserver won't verify the kubelet's cert unless you set --kubelet-certificate-authority
CP → nodes / pods / servicesapiserver → cluster IPs⚠️ plain HTTP by default — unsafe over untrusted networks; use the Konnectivity service for a secured tunnel

💡 Mental model: everything dials the apiserver (secure, single front door); the apiserver dialing back out to nodes is the weaker leg — Konnectivity (the konnectivity-agent/server pair) wraps it in a managed tunnel for production.

📖 Konnectivity replaced SSH tunnels — and it dials the OTHER way

Older Kubernetes docs mention securing apiserver→node traffic with SSH tunnels — that approach is now deprecated ("don't use it unless you know exactly why"). Its replacement, Konnectivity, flips the connection direction on purpose: the konnectivity-agent (running near the nodes) initiates the connection to the konnectivity-server (beside the apiserver) and keeps it open. The apiserver's outbound calls then ride that pre-established tunnel — which is why Konnectivity works even when nothing on the control-plane side could otherwise dial into a node's network (a common shape in locked-down or NAT'd cloud VPCs).

📖 How pods reach the apiserver, symmetrically: every namespace gets a kubernetes Service (check kubectl get svc kubernetes in default) whose ClusterIP kube-proxy redirects to the real apiserver endpoint — so a pod never needs to know the apiserver's real address, only the name kubernetes. And on the node-registration side, production clusters normally automate kubelet certificate issuance via kubelet TLS bootstrapping rather than hand-copying client certs to every node (Ch 26 covers the CSR mechanics behind it).

⑤ Node registration — how a node joins, and the cordon-vs-drain distinction

A node doesn't need to be manually "added" to the cluster object list — by default the kubelet self-registers (--register-node, true by default) the moment it starts and can reach the apiserver, which is exactly what happens during kubeadm join. Two commands then let you control whether a registered node accepts new work — and they are not the same operation:

CommandMarks unschedulable?Evicts existing pods?Use when
kubectl cordon <node>✅ yes (taints SchedulingDisabled)❌ no — running pods stay putyou want to stop new pods landing there, but not disturb what's already running
kubectl drain <node>✅ yes (cordons first)✅ yes — evicts everything (respecting PDBs)you're about to take the node down (OS patch, decommission) — full depth in Ch 30
kubectl uncordon <node>reverses cordonn/abring a node back into scheduling after maintenance

📖 cordon alone is the safer first move when you just want to freeze a node's pod count while you investigate — nothing gets rescheduled, so you can debug a suspect node without an eviction storm. drain is the deliberate "empty this node" operation you reach for only once you actually intend to take it offline.

Under the Hood — how the control plane stays consistent & highly available

The components in §3.2 are simple to name; the machinery that makes several copies of them cooperate without conflict is where real understanding lives. Four mechanisms do the heavy lifting.

① Leader election via Lease — how scheduler & controller-manager run HA

You can run 3 schedulers and 3 controller-managers for high availability, but if all of them acted at once they'd fight (three controllers each creating the "missing" pod). So they're active-passive: only one is the leader at a time, chosen by a Lease object the others watch.

   3 kube-scheduler replicas         🗄️ a Lease object in kube-system
   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ sched-1  │ │ sched-2  │ │ sched-3  │ ────▶ │ Lease "kube-scheduler"    │
   │ LEADER ✅ │ │ standby  │ │ standby  │      │ holder: sched-1           │
   └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘      │ renewTime: …(every ~2s)   │
        │ only the leader schedules            └──────────────────────────┘
        └─ stops renewing (crash) → a standby grabs the Lease → becomes leader
   kubectl get lease -n kube-system   ← see who holds it
🔑 Why it matters: "I have 3 control-plane nodes but only one scheduler seems to work" is correct — the other two are hot standbys. Check kubectl get lease -n kube-system to see the current holder.
② The Binding subresource — how the scheduler actually places a pod

The scheduler doesn't "move" a pod. It computes the best node, then makes a tiny API call — a Binding — that sets the pod's nodeName. The kubelet on that node then notices "a pod is assigned to me" and runs it. Scheduling is just one field being written.

   scheduler picks node2  ──POST /api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods/easypj-web-x/binding──▶ 📡 apiserver
   apiserver sets pod.spec.nodeName = "node2"  ──▶ 🗄️ etcd
   🤖 kubelet(node2) is watching pods where nodeName == its own → sees it → starts it
   💡 you can hand-schedule by setting nodeName yourself (bypasses the scheduler entirely)
③ API Priority & Fairness (APF) — keeping the apiserver alive under load

Because everything goes through the apiserver, a flood of requests (a buggy controller, a stampede of kubelets) could starve it. APF classifies incoming requests into priority levels and fair-queues them, so critical traffic (leader election, node heartbeats) isn't drowned out by bulk list calls.

ConceptWhat it does
FlowSchemaMatches requests (by user/verb/resource) → assigns them to a priority level
PriorityLevelConfigurationReserves concurrency shares + a fair queue per level
EffectA misbehaving client is throttled (HTTP 429) instead of taking down the API for everyone
④ The aggregation layer — extending the API itself

Beyond CRDs, you can register a second API server behind the main one via an APIService. The apiserver proxies a slice of the API path to it. That's how metrics-server serves metrics.k8s.io (powering kubectl top) — it's not a CRD, it's an aggregated apiserver.

⑤ REST + watch — the API machinery everything is built on

The apiserver is a RESTful server: every object is a URL, and the usual HTTP verbs act on it. The magic extra is WATCH — a long-lived stream of changes that lets components react instantly instead of polling. That single mechanism is how the scheduler, controllers, and kubelets all stay in sync.

   REST verbs on a resource:
     GET    /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments/easypj-web   read one
     LIST   /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments              read all
     POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE                                     create / replace / modify / remove

   WATCH (the key to reactivity):
     GET …/deployments?watch=true&resourceVersion=4821
        ──▶ keeps the connection OPEN and streams events as they happen:
            ADDED {…}   MODIFIED {…rv:4822}   MODIFIED {…rv:4830}   DELETED {…}
     each event carries the new resourceVersion → a client can resume the stream
     after a disconnect from exactly where it left off (no missed & no duplicate work)
ConceptWhat it gives you
LIST then WATCHGet the full state once, then only the deltas — the pattern every informer uses
resourceVersionA cursor: "stream changes since here" + the basis of optimistic concurrency
watch cacheThe apiserver serves watches from memory, so thousands of watchers don't hammer etcd
kubectl get -wIs literally a watch stream you can see in your terminal
🔑 Why this is the whole design: components never call each other — they all watch the apiserver and react to changes. That's the loose coupling that makes Kubernetes resilient: a component that was briefly down just re-LISTs and resumes watching, catching up to current state automatically.
🔑 Tie it together: the apiserver isn't just a CRUD endpoint — it's a REST + watch hub (the API machinery), a consistency & fairness hub (APF), a placement coordinator (Binding), an HA arbiter (Leases), and an extensible surface (aggregation). Master these and "the control plane" stops being a black box.

🔬 Deeper (exam + beyond): reads can be served from the apiserver's watch cache (fast, slightly behind) or forced consistent; every object carries a resourceVersion for optimistic concurrency (Ch 1 UTH); controllers are built on informers (shared list-watch + cache) feeding workqueues with rate-limiting and retries — packaged for reuse as the controller-runtime library, which is what most operators (Ch 38) are built on; and the node controller's NotReady (~40s) → eviction (~5min) timers are why a briefly-down node doesn't instantly lose its pods.

⑥ The full pod-creation trace — what happens inside §3.4's 8 steps

§3.4 showed the journey; here is the internal trace — the named admission plugins, the scheduler's filter/score plugins, and the exact CRI calls the kubelet makes. This is the depth CKA troubleshooting questions live at.

kubectl run easypj-web --image=easypj:v1
   │
   ▼  STAGE 1 — apiserver: authN → authZ → admission → etcd
 📡 kube-apiserver
   ├─ a. AuthN      validate the bearer token (who are you?) → user: easypj-admin
   ├─ b. AuthZ      RBAC: may easypj-admin CREATE pods in ns easypj? → yes
   ├─ c. Admission chain (mutate, then validate):
   │       MutatingAdmissionWebhook   → inject sidecars / defaults
   │       LimitRanger                → apply default requests & limits
   │       PodSecurity                → enforce baseline / restricted
   │       ValidatingAdmissionWebhook → reject if a policy is violated
   ├─ d. WRITE      /registry/pods/easypj/easypj-web  → 🗄️ etcd (quorum write)
   └─ e. RETURN     201 Created → "pod/easypj-web created"
   │
   ▼  STAGE 2 — scheduler: watch → filter → score → bind
 📋 kube-scheduler  (watches pods where .spec.nodeName == "")
   ├─ FILTER (predicates) — drop nodes that CAN'T run it:
   │     NodeReady? · CPU/mem fits requests? · nodeSelector/affinity? · taints tolerated? · hostPort free?
   ├─ SCORE  (priorities) — rank the survivors 0–100:
   │     NodeResourcesFit(LeastAllocated) · NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation · ImageLocality · NodeAffinity
   └─ BIND: POST …/pods/easypj-web/binding → sets .spec.nodeName = "node-1" → 🗄️ etcd
   │
   ▼  STAGE 3 — kubelet → CRI → containerd → runc
 🤖 kubelet(node-1)  (watches pods assigned to it)
   └─ calls the CRI (gRPC), in order:
        RunPodSandbox   → create the pause container + network namespace (CNI assigns the IP)
        PullImage       → fetch easypj:v1 layers from the registry
        CreateContainer → set up namespaces + cgroups + overlay rootfs
        StartContainer  → exec the easypj process
      containerd builds the OCI bundle → runc create → runc start
        runc: clone() with namespace flags · write cgroups · pivot_root · exec
   └─ kubelet reports status → Running → Ready (once probes pass) → 🗄️ etcd
🔑 Map a failure to its stage: hangs at kubectl → Stage 1 (apiserver unreachable); stuck Pending → Stage 2 (nothing survived filtering — taints / resources / selector); stuck ContainerCreating → Stage 3 RunPodSandbox/PullImage (CNI, or image/registry); CrashLoopBackOff → Stage 3 StartContainer (the app itself — read kubectl logs).
⑦ Static pods — the bootstrap paradox solved

The control plane (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) runs as pods — which is a chicken-and-egg problem: how do you run pods before the apiserver that schedules them even exists? The answer is the static pod — the kubelet reads manifests straight from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and runs them itself, with no apiserver and no scheduler involved.

   boot order on a control-plane node
   ① kubelet starts             (a systemd service — it does NOT need the API)
   ② reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
   ③ runs the apiserver static pod    (CRI → containerd → runc)
   ④ the apiserver is now up
   ⑤ kubelet registers a read-only MIRROR pod for it in the API
        → visible as kube-apiserver-<nodename>   (that's where the suffix comes from)
   ⑥ kubelet runs the remaining manifests: etcd, scheduler, controller-manager
   ⑦ control plane operational → normal, API-driven scheduling begins
🔁 Restarting a static pod (you can't kubectl delete it): move the manifest out and back — sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/ && sleep 20 && sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet sees the file vanish (stops the pod), then reappear (recreates it). Editing the manifest in place also triggers a restart.
🔑 CKA insight: if you SSH to a control-plane node and kubectl won't respond, the apiserver static pod may be down — there's no API to ask. Check it directly: sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver (is the container running?) and sudo ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (is the manifest present?). A missing or corrupt manifest takes the entire control plane down.
⑧ A few more control-plane internals worth knowing
TopicWhat to know
Lease fieldsa leader-election Lease carries holderIdentity (who holds it), leaseDurationSeconds (TTL — ~15s for scheduler/controller-manager) and renewTime (the leader rewrites it every couple of seconds). If a renewal is missed past the TTL, a standby claims the Lease — so failover takes up to about one lease duration.
APF: 429 vs 503429 Too Many Requests = API Priority & Fairness fair-queued you and the queue/wait was exceeded → back off & retry. 503 = a priority level with no queueing, or the server is genuinely overloaded → investigate. exempt flows (e.g. system:masters, health checks) bypass APF so a misconfig can't lock you out of the API.
Admission failurePolicyif a webhook errors or times out: Fail (default) rejects the request — safe for policy/security; Ignore lets it through — for optional webhooks. Mutating runs before validating by design, so validators judge the final object (after sidecars/defaults are injected).

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Control plane decides, worker nodes run — sort every problem into "decision" vs "run" and you've found the half to look in.
  • Only the apiserver talks to etcd — and everything else talks only to the apiserver (the single choke point).
  • The kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod — debug it with systemctl / journalctl, never kubectl.
  • The control plane runs AS static pods in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — edit the YAML, the kubelet reloads.
  • CRI · CNI · CSI are the three plug points (runtime · network · storage).
  • etcd uses Raft — ports 2379 (client) / 2380 (peer); a write commits only when a quorum acks. Back it up or lose the cluster.
  • Scheduler = FILTER → SCORE → BIND — and it only fills Allocatable (Capacity − reservations), never raw Capacity.
  • Everything DIALS the apiserver — via authN → authZ (RBAC) → admission → etcd; node health is tracked by Leases in kube-node-lease.
  • Match symptom → component: NotReady=kubelet · Pending=scheduler · lost state=etcd · kubectl dead=apiserver.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • kubelet ≠ pod. It's systemd — kubectl get pods won't show it; systemctl status kubelet will.
  • You can't kubectl delete a static pod — the kubelet recreates it. Remove the manifest file from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  • apiserver is the single choke point. If it's down, kubectl is useless — switch to crictl / journalctl on the node.
  • Static pod vs DaemonSet. Both = one pod per node, but static = kubelet-managed (mirror pod, -<nodename> suffix), DaemonSet = API object.
  • Scheduler vs controller-manager. Scheduler only places pods; the controller-manager handles replication, nodes, endpoints. Don't conflate.
  • A half-empty node can still reject a pod. The scheduler counts Allocatable (Capacity − kube/system-reserved − eviction threshold), so a pod sits Pending though the node "looks" free.
  • kubectl get componentstatuses is deprecated. Use the health endpoints instead: kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'.
  • apiserver → kubelet (:10250) doesn't verify the kubelet's cert unless --kubelet-certificate-authority is set — a trust asymmetry worth knowing (everything else dials the apiserver over verified TLS).
⚡ Speed Tips
  • apiserver down? Debug from the node: crictl ps -a, crictl logs <apiserver-id>, journalctl -u kubelet.
  • Pods Pending? Suspect the scheduler — kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending then check the scheduler pod/logs.
  • Editing a control-plane component? Just edit its manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet restarts it for you.
  • Force-restart a control-plane static pod: move its manifest out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, wait for the pod to vanish, move it back.
  • Node NotReady? Check in this order: kubelet (systemd) → CNI (/etc/cni/net.d/) → runtime (crictl) — it's the dependency chain.
  • Per-check apiserver health: kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' breaks the health down check-by-check (etcd, informers, post-start hooks).
  • Pod stuck Pending? kubectl describe pod → the scheduler's Events name the exact filter that rejected every node (taints, insufficient CPU, affinity…).
  • Find the HA leader: kubectl get lease -n kube-system.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 3)

inspect the cluster's anatomy
kubectl get pods -n kube-system            # control-plane + CNI + CoreDNS pods
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'       # apiserver health, per-check (cs is deprecated)
kubectl get componentstatuses             # cs — control-plane health (older clusters)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system          # who holds leader election
kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease      # the node heartbeats
kubectl describe node <node>              # conditions + Capacity vs Allocatable
kubectl cordon <node>                     # mark unschedulable (existing pods stay)
kubectl drain <node>                      # cordon AND evict (Ch 30)
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/             # the static-pod manifests
kubectl get nodes -o wide                 # node roles, versions, IPs

# node-level (when the apiserver is down)
crictl ps -a                              # containers via the CRI
crictl logs <container-id>
journalctl -u kubelet -f                  # live kubelet logs

🧠 Chapter 3 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the architecture — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Which component is the ONLY one that reads/writes etcd?
Show Answer
Answer

The kube-apiserver. Every other component (scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet) reaches state through the apiserver, never etcd directly.

the star topology — one gateway to state
  📋 scheduler ─┐                      ┌─ 🤖 kubelets
  🔄 ctrl-mgr ──┼──▶ 📡 apiserver ◀───┼─ ⌨️ kubectl
  controllers ──┘         │           └─ 🌐 kube-proxy
                          ▼  the ONLY client
                       🗄️ etcd  (all state)
Explanation

This star topology is why an etcd backup = a cluster backup, and why securing/operating the apiserver is so critical.

Q2
A node shows NotReady. Which agent do you check first, and how?
Show Answer
Answer

The kubelet (it's a systemd service, not a pod), then the runtime and CNI:

node NotReady — first checks (on the node)
systemctl status kubelet        # is the agent even up?
journalctl -u kubelet -f        # why did it fail?
systemctl status containerd     # runtime alive?
ls /etc/cni/net.d/              # CNI configured?
Explanation

NotReady = the node can't report healthy. Usual causes: kubelet down, swap on, expired cert, missing CNI, cgroup-driver mismatch.

Q3
Trace what happens after kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml.
Show Answer
Answer

Each actor reconciles its own slice — no central script:

what kubectl apply sets in motion
 kubectl apply ─▶ 📡 apiserver (authN → authZ → admission) ─▶ 🗄️ etcd   (persist desired state)
                       │
                       ├─ 🔄 controller-manager:  Deployment ─▶ ReplicaSet ─▶ Pods
                       └─ 📋 scheduler:  filter → score → BIND (sets nodeName)
                              ▼
                    🤖 kubelet:  pull image → start container → 🌐 CNI assigns the pod IP
                              ▼
                    🔀 kube-proxy programs Service routing ─────▶ Running ✅
Explanation

No central script — each actor reconciles its own slice. Knowing the order lets you map any symptom to a step (§3.4).

Q4
The scheduler is down. What symptom appears, and on which objects?
Show Answer
Answer

New pods stay Pending (no node gets assigned). Existing pods keep running. Spot it: kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending, then check the scheduler pod/logs.

With the scheduler down…Why
❌ new pods: Pending, nodeName empty, no scheduling eventsnobody performs the Bind
✅ existing pods: unaffectedalready bound — kubelets keep running them
✅ kubectl / apiserver: finethe scheduler is a consumer of the API, not part of its path
Explanation

The scheduler only sets nodeName; with it down, pods are created but never bound.

Q5
Create a static pod on a node, then delete it. Which files/commands?
Show Answer
Answer

The kubelet watches a directory; creating/deleting the file creates/deletes the pod:

static pod — create & delete (on the node)
# create: drop a manifest where the kubelet watches
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml   # path = staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# delete: remove the FILE — `kubectl delete` just gets recreated
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml
Explanation

Static pods are owned by the kubelet, not the API; the API only shows a read-only mirror pod.

Q6
Name the network layers and what routes each.
Show Answer
Answer

Three layers, each programmed by a different actor (all riding on the node/infra network):

LayerAddressesWho programs it
Pod networkreal pod IPs (flat, no NAT)the CNI plugin
Service networkstable virtual IPs (ClusterIP)apiserver assigns the IP · EndpointSlice controller tracks Ready pods · kube-proxy programs the routing
ExternalNodePort · LoadBalancer · Ingress/Gatewaythe cluster edge
Explanation

Pods can fail to reach each other (CNI) independently of Services failing (kube-proxy) — keep the layers separate when debugging.

Q7
Which ports does etcd listen on, and for what?
Show Answer
Answer

Two ports, two jobs:

PortPurpose
2379client traffic — the apiserver (and etcdctl) connect here
2380peer traffic — etcd member ↔ member for Raft; only matters in multi-member HA
Explanation

etcdctl uses --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379; 2380 only matters in multi-member HA.

Q8
Why is the apiserver the cluster's single choke point?
Show Answer
Answer

Every read/write of state, every component's watch, and every kubectl call flows through it — and it's the only thing that touches etcd. Down apiserver → no scheduling, no reconciliation, no kubectl (though running pods continue).

apiserver down: ❌ stops✅ keeps working
kubectl (every command)already-running pods (kubelets act on cached state)
scheduling & reconciliation (all watches are blind)Service routing on each node (kube-proxy rules already programmed)
new deploys, scaling, self-healingnode-level debugging: crictl, journalctl
Explanation

That's also why it gets HA replicas behind a load balancer and APF to stay alive under load (UTH).

Q9
Explain a controller's reconcile loop using the ReplicaSet example.
Show Answer
Answer

OBSERVE → COMPARE → ACT, forever — a deleted pod is just the next gap to close:

the reconcile loop, one ReplicaSet tick
        ┌──────────── reconcile loop (runs forever) ───────────┐
        ▼                                                      │
   OBSERVE actual ──▶ COMPARE to desired ──▶ ACT to close gap ─┘
   (2 pods now)        (spec replicas: 3)     (create 1 pod)
   delete a pod → next pass sees 2 ≠ 3 again → recreates it
Explanation

Level-triggered: it reacts to current state, not events, so it self-heals even if an event is missed.

Q10
What is a "mirror pod" and why does its name end in -<nodename>?
Show Answer
Answer

When the kubelet runs a static pod, it creates a read-only mirror pod in the API so you can kubectl get it. The kubelet appends its node name (e.g. etcd-controlplane) to show which node owns it — and to keep names unique across nodes.

the file is the truth; the mirror is a reflection
  📁 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml     ← SOURCE OF TRUTH (a file on the node)
        │ kubelet watches the folder & runs it
        ▼
  📦 real pod on the node  ──registers──▶  📡 API: mirror pod "etcd-controlplane"
                                              │ read-only: kubectl can SEE it,
                                              ▼ but delete = it comes right back
  to manage it: edit/move the FILE, never the mirror
Explanation

You can view but not control a mirror pod via the API; the real lifecycle lives with the kubelet and the manifest file.

⚙️ Chapter 3 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — a broken state or a "trace it" question, with the real answer.

Q1
You SSH to the control plane node and find that kubectl get nodes returns "The connection to the server was refused". The kubelet is running. What is the most likely problem and how do you diagnose it?
Show Answer
Answer

The kube-apiserver is down. Since it's a static pod, diagnose as follows:

check if the api server container is running
# 1. Check if the API server container is running
sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver

# 2. If not running, check the static pod manifest
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 3. Check kubelet logs for manifest errors
sudo journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i "error\|apiserver" | tail -20

# 4. Common fixes:
#    - Fix YAML syntax errors in the manifest
#    - Fix wrong certificate paths (--tls-cert-file, --tls-private-key-file)
#    - Fix wrong etcd endpoints (--etcd-servers)
#    - Fix port conflicts (--secure-port)
Explanation

This is a classic CKA troubleshooting scenario. The kube-apiserver runs as a static pod managed by the kubelet. If the manifest file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ has errors, the kubelet cannot start the pod. Key diagnostic path: crictl ps → journalctl -u kubelet → check manifest → fix → kubelet automatically restarts the static pod. No kubectl apply needed — static pods are managed by the kubelet directly from filesystem watching.

Q2
What are static pods? Where are they defined, which component manages them, and how are they different from regular pods created via the API server?
Show Answer
Answer

Static pods are pods managed directly by the kubelet on a specific node, without going through the API server.

Feature Static Pods Regular Pods
Managed by kubelet (filesystem watcher) API server → scheduler → kubelet
Defined in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ etcd (via kubectl/API)
Visible in API Yes, as a mirror pod (read-only) Yes, fully managed
Can be deleted via kubectl No — delete the file to remove Yes
Explanation

Static pods are how the control plane bootstraps itself — kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, and kube-controller-manager all run as static pods. The kubelet watches the staticPodPath (configured in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml) and automatically creates/restarts pods from YAML files found there. On the CKA, you may be asked to create a static pod: simply place a valid pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and the kubelet will start it.

Q3
Explain the kube-scheduler's decision process. When a new pod is created without a nodeName, what steps does the scheduler take to place it on a node?
Show Answer
Answer

The scheduler follows a two-phase process:

Phase 1: Filtering — Eliminates nodes that can't run the pod:

  • Insufficient CPU/memory resources
  • Taints that the pod doesn't tolerate
  • Node affinity rules not satisfied
  • PodAntiAffinity constraints
  • Unschedulable nodes (cordoned)

Phase 2: Scoring — Ranks remaining nodes by preference:

  • Resource balance (spread workloads evenly)
  • Node affinity preferences (soft rules)
  • Pod topology spread constraints
  • Image locality (node already has the image cached)

The highest-scoring node wins. The scheduler then sets spec.nodeName via the API server.

filter → score → bind, on a 4-node cluster
  new pod (nodeName: "")   requests: cpu 500m · toleration: none
        │
        ▼ FILTER (who CAN run it?)
  node-1 ✅ fits     node-2 ❌ insufficient cpu    node-3 ❌ NoSchedule taint    node-4 ✅ fits
        │
        ▼ SCORE (who's BEST?)          node-1: 82 (image cached, balanced)
                                       node-4: 61 (image must pull)
        ▼ BIND
  POST …/pods/<pod>/binding  →  spec.nodeName = node-1  →  kubelet(node-1) starts it
Explanation

The CKA tests scheduling concepts heavily (15% of the exam). Key scenarios: (1) Pod stuck in Pending — all nodes filtered out (check taints, resources, node selectors). (2) Pod scheduled to wrong node — scoring preferences not configured correctly. (3) Manually bypass the scheduler by setting spec.nodeName directly in the pod spec. If a pod is Pending, kubectl describe pod events will show "0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had taint..." — this tells you exactly which filter failed.

Q4
The kube-controller-manager runs many controllers. Name at least 5 built-in controllers and describe what each one is responsible for.
Show Answer
Answer
Controller Responsibility
Node Controller Monitors node heartbeats (every 10s), marks NotReady after 40s, evicts pods after 5min
ReplicaSet Controller Ensures the correct number of pod replicas are running at all times
Deployment Controller Manages ReplicaSets for rolling updates, rollbacks, and scaling
Endpoint Controller Populates Endpoints objects (maps Services to pod IPs)
ServiceAccount Controller Creates default ServiceAccount + token for every new namespace
Job Controller Tracks Job completions and creates new pods until the desired completion count is reached
Namespace Controller Cleans up resources when a namespace is deleted (cascading deletion)
Explanation

All these controllers run as goroutines inside a single kube-controller-manager binary/pod. Each controller follows the same Observe → Diff → Act pattern. On the CKA exam, understanding controllers helps diagnose issues: if replicas aren't being created, the controller-manager might be down. If nodes stay NotReady for too long without pod eviction, check the node controller's --pod-eviction-timeout flag.

Q5
How does the kubelet know which static pod manifests to watch? What configuration file controls the staticPodPath, and how would you find it?
Show Answer
Answer
find kubelet's config file
# Find kubelet's config file
ps aux | grep kubelet | grep -- --config
# Typically: --config=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# Check the staticPodPath in kubelet config
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep staticPodPath
# Output: staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests

# List static pod manifests
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml
Explanation

On the CKA exam, you may need to create a static pod on a specific node. The steps are: (1) SSH to the target node, (2) Find the staticPodPath from the kubelet config, (3) Place your pod YAML file in that directory, (4) The kubelet automatically detects and creates the pod. To find the kubelet config: systemctl status kubelet shows the systemd unit file, which contains the --config flag pointing to the config file. Default path is almost always /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

Q6
What is the role of CoreDNS in a Kubernetes cluster? If DNS resolution fails inside a pod, what troubleshooting steps would you take?
Show Answer
Answer

CoreDNS provides cluster-internal DNS resolution. It runs as a Deployment in the kube-system namespace and resolves:

  • service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local → ClusterIP
  • pod-ip-dashed.namespace.pod.cluster.local → Pod IP

Troubleshooting DNS failure:

check if coredns pods are running
# 1. Check if CoreDNS pods are running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

# 2. Check CoreDNS logs
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

# 3. Verify the kube-dns Service exists
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system

# 4. Test DNS from inside a pod
kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never \
  -- nslookup kubernetes.default

# 5. Check pod's /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec easypj-web -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Should point to kube-dns ClusterIP (usually 10.96.0.10)
Explanation

DNS is critical infrastructure in Kubernetes. Every pod gets a /etc/resolv.conf pointing to the CoreDNS service's ClusterIP. If DNS fails, almost everything breaks — service discovery, external API calls, etc. Common causes: (1) CoreDNS pods not running, (2) kube-dns Service ClusterIP changed, (3) Network policy blocking DNS traffic on port 53, (4) CoreDNS ConfigMap misconfigured, (5) kube-proxy not programming iptables rules for the kube-dns service. This is a high-priority CKA troubleshooting topic.

Q7
Explain the difference between the kube-apiserver's authentication, authorization, and admission control stages. What happens at each stage when a request arrives?
Show Answer
Answer

Every API request passes through three stages in order:

  1. Authentication — "Who are you?" — Verifies identity via client certificates, bearer tokens, or service account tokens. If authentication fails → 401 Unauthorized
  2. Authorization — "Are you allowed to do this?" — Checks RBAC rules (Role/ClusterRole + RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding). If denied → 403 Forbidden
  3. Admission Control — "Should we modify or reject this?" — Webhooks and built-in plugins that can mutate (change defaults) or validate (reject invalid) requests. Examples: LimitRanger (set default resource limits), NamespaceLifecycle (reject requests to terminating namespaces)
bash
Request → [Authentication] → [Authorization] → [Admission] → etcd
              401?                  403?              Reject/Mutate
Explanation

Understanding this pipeline is critical for CKA RBAC and security questions. When you get a "forbidden" error, it's authorization (RBAC). When you get "unauthorized", it's authentication (bad/expired cert or token). Admission controllers can silently modify your objects — for example, DefaultStorageClass adds a storage class to PVCs that don't specify one. The CKA tests RBAC extensively (creating Roles, ClusterRoles, Bindings). Remember: Roles are namespace-scoped, ClusterRoles are cluster-wide.

Q8
A Kubernetes node's kubelet is configured with --pod-cidr=10.244.1.0/24. What does this mean, and how does the CNI plugin use this information to assign IP addresses to pods?
Show Answer
Answer

The --pod-cidr defines the subnet of IP addresses allocated to pods on that specific node. Each node gets a unique pod CIDR from the cluster's overall pod network CIDR (e.g., 10.244.0.0/16).

one cluster CIDR, carved into per-node /24s
  cluster pod CIDR  10.244.0.0/16   (set at kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr)
        │ controller-manager hands each node a unique slice
        ├────────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                ▼
  node-1: 10.244.0.0/24  node-2: 10.244.1.0/24  node-3: 10.244.2.0/24
  📦 .0.2  📦 .0.3        📦 .1.2  📦 .1.4        📦 .2.7
        └──────── CNI assigns pod IPs from its OWN node's slice ────────┘
  💡 read an IP like an address: 10.244.1.x lives on node-2 — handy when tracing traffic

How it works:

  • Controller-manager assigns each node a unique /24 subnet from the cluster CIDR
  • The CNI plugin (Flannel, Calico, Cilium) reads the node's pod CIDR
  • When a pod is created, the CNI assigns an IP from that node's subnet
  • Node 1: 10.244.0.0/24 → pods get 10.244.0.2, 10.244.0.3, etc.
  • Node 2: 10.244.1.0/24 → pods get 10.244.1.2, 10.244.1.3, etc.
Explanation

Understanding pod networking is essential for the CKA's "Services & Networking" domain (20%). The pod CIDR is configured during cluster initialization (kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16). Each node gets a unique subnet. The CNI plugin handles the actual IP assignment and inter-node routing. If pods can't communicate across nodes, check: (1) CNI plugin is installed, (2) pod CIDRs don't overlap with node IPs, (3) firewall rules allow inter-node pod traffic.

Q9
You run kubectl get componentstatuses and see that scheduler shows Unhealthy. What could cause this, and how would you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer
check if the scheduler pod is running
# 1. Check if the scheduler pod is running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler

# 2. If not running, check the static pod manifest
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml

# 3. Check kubelet logs for scheduler errors
sudo journalctl -u kubelet | grep scheduler

# 4. Check scheduler logs directly
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-controlplane

# 5. Common issues:
#    - Wrong kubeconfig path (--kubeconfig flag)
#    - Certificate expired or wrong path
#    - Port conflict (--secure-port)
#    - YAML syntax error in manifest file
Explanation

Note: kubectl get componentstatuses (or cs) is deprecated since v1.19, but may still appear on the CKA. It checks health endpoints of control plane components. If the scheduler is unhealthy: (1) The scheduler static pod may have crashed — check its manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, (2) The scheduler's health endpoint may be unreachable. Symptoms of a dead scheduler: new pods stay in Pending state because nothing assigns them to nodes. Existing pods continue running — only new scheduling decisions are blocked.

Q10
Draw or describe the complete communication flow between all Kubernetes components when a user runs kubectl delete pod easypj-web. Which components are involved and what happens at each step?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod deletion flow:

bash
kubectl delete pod easypj-web
        │
        ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│  kube-apiserver  │ ← Receives DELETE request
│  1. Authenticate │
│  2. Authorize    │
│  3. Set deletion │
│     timestamp    │
└────────┬────────┘
         │ Updates etcd: pod.deletionTimestamp = now
         │ pod.deletionGracePeriodSeconds = 30 (default)
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│    kubelet       │ ← Watches API, sees deletionTimestamp
│  1. Send SIGTERM │
│  2. Wait 30s     │    to containers
│  3. Send SIGKILL │    (if still running)
│  4. Report back  │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│  kube-apiserver  │ ← kubelet confirms termination
│  Remove from     │
│  etcd            │
└─────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Endpoint ctrl    │ ← Removes pod IP from Service endpoints
└─────────────────┘
Explanation

Key points for the CKA: (1) Deletion is graceful by default — containers get SIGTERM and 30 seconds to shut down. (2) The --grace-period=0 --force flags skip the grace period (useful for stuck pods). (3) The Endpoint controller removes the pod from Service endpoints concurrently with the grace period, so in-flight requests may still reach a terminating pod. (4) preStop hooks run before SIGTERM — use them for graceful shutdown logic. Understanding pod lifecycle is critical for troubleshooting stuck deletions and graceful application shutdown.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.1 — Map the Control Plane

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

On a control-plane node — predict each output before running it:

  1. List the static-pod manifests.
  2. List the control-plane pods and note the -<nodename> suffix.
  3. Identify the leader of the scheduler/controller-manager.
  4. Tail the apiserver logs.
Hint: The API server is the only component that talks to etcd directly — every other component goes through it.
View Solution
terminal
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/              # etcd · kube-apiserver · kube-scheduler · kube-controller-manager
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane   # all 4 Running, -controlplane suffix (mirror pods)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager   # HOLDER column = leader
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-controlplane | tail -20        # apiserver logs

Check yourself: the control plane is just static pods the kubelet runs; their mirror pods carry the node-name suffix; HA components elect one leader via a Lease; and you can read any control-plane component's logs with kubectl logs (or crictl logs if the apiserver itself is down).

🔬 Practice Drill 3.2 — Create & Destroy a Static Pod (the Exam Classic)

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

On a node, create a static pod named static-web running nginx:1.27 — without using kubectl create. Prove it appears in the API as a mirror pod, prove kubectl delete can't kill it, then remove it the right way.

Hint: Static pods are files in the kubelet's staticPodPath (kubeadm default: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/). The kubelet watches that folder — file in = pod up, file out = pod gone.
View Solution
on the node — file in, pod up; file out, pod gone
# 1. CREATE — drop a manifest into the watched folder
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
  labels:
    role: static
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
EOF

# 2. VERIFY — the kubelet starts it in seconds; note the -<nodename> suffix
kubectl get pods                        # static-web-worker-1   1/1   Running

# 3. PROVE kubectl can't kill it — the kubelet recreates it immediately
kubectl delete pod static-web-worker-1
kubectl get pods                        # …it's back (mirror pod is read-only)

# 4. DESTROY — remove the FILE; the kubelet stops & removes the pod
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml
kubectl get pods                        # gone ✅

Check yourself: the pod's name gained a -<nodename> suffix — that's the read-only mirror pod the kubelet publishes so you can see it via the API. Deleting the mirror did nothing because the source of truth is the file. This is exactly how the control plane itself runs — and a recurring exam task.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.3 — Restart the API Server Without kubectl

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

You need to force-restart the kube-apiserver on the control-plane node (say, to pick up a config change that isn't applying). kubectl delete is useless against a static pod — use the manifest-move trick, and watch the whole lifecycle with crictl since kubectl dies the moment the apiserver stops.

Hint: The kubelet stops a static pod when its manifest leaves the folder and starts it again when it returns. Move it out to /tmp, wait, move it back — and observe via crictl ps, not kubectl.
View Solution
on the control-plane node
# 1. Move the manifest OUT — the kubelet stops the apiserver (~seconds)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/

# 2. kubectl is now DEAD (the front door is gone) — watch via the runtime
kubectl get pods                        # connection refused ❌ (expected!)
sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver      # container Exited

# 3. Move it BACK — the kubelet recreates the pod
sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# 4. Watch it come up, then confirm the front door is open again
sudo crictl ps | grep apiserver         # Running again
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | head   # per-check health ✅

Check yourself: two deep truths just became muscle memory — (1) the control plane is files run by the kubelet, so its lifecycle is controlled from the filesystem; (2) when the apiserver is down you observe the node through crictl, because kubectl's only door is closed. The brief outage didn't touch running workloads — the data plane kept serving.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.4 — Node Health Forensics: Conditions, Allocatable & Heartbeats

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

Answer three questions about a live node using only kubectl: (1) what are its five conditions right now? (2) how much CPU/memory can the scheduler actually place on it (vs the hardware total)? (3) when did its last heartbeat land — and where do heartbeats live?

Hint: Everything is in kubectl describe node (Conditions, Capacity, Allocatable) — except the fast heartbeat, which is a Lease in the kube-node-lease namespace.
View Solution
node forensics in three reads
# 1. CONDITIONS — Ready + the four pressure flags
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A8 "Conditions:"
#   MemoryPressure  False   DiskPressure  False
#   PIDPressure     False   Ready         True   (Unknown = lost contact)

# 2. CAPACITY vs ALLOCATABLE — what the scheduler may actually use
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A6 -E "^Capacity|^Allocatable"
#   Capacity:    cpu: 4    memory: 8Gi     ← the hardware
#   Allocatable: cpu: 3800m memory: 7.2Gi  ← Capacity − kube/system-reserved − eviction

# 3. HEARTBEATS — the kubelet renews this Lease ~every 10s
kubectl get lease worker-1 -n kube-node-lease -o yaml | grep -E "holderIdentity|renewTime"
Question on the examWhere the answer lives
"Why is this pod Pending though the node looks free?"Allocatable, not Capacity — the scheduler only fills the reserved-out slice
"Why did the node flip NotReady?"Conditions + the kubelet's stopped Lease renewals (→ Unknown after ~50s)
"Is the node under pressure?"MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure conditions → the kubelet is evicting

Check yourself: you can now read a node like a chart — conditions for health, Allocatable for schedulable room, the Lease for liveness. Those three views solve most "what's wrong with this node?" tasks before you ever SSH in.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.5 — The Scheduler Vanishes: Diagnose Pending Pods

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Simulate a scheduler outage on a test cluster: stop the kube-scheduler (manifest-move trick from Drill 3.3), create a new easypj pod, and observe exactly what breaks — and what doesn't. Then restore the scheduler and watch the queued pod get placed. Explain the symptom chain.

Hint: The scheduler's only job is writing the Binding (setting spec.nodeName). No scheduler → new pods exist in etcd but have no node, forever Pending. Existing pods don't care.
View Solution
break → observe → restore → verify
# 1. BREAK — stop the scheduler (control-plane node)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/

# 2. OBSERVE — create a pod; it lodges as Pending with NO node
kubectl run easypj-test --image=nginx
kubectl get pod easypj-test -o wide            # STATUS Pending · NODE <none>
kubectl get pod easypj-test -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}'   # (empty!)
kubectl describe pod easypj-test | grep -A3 Events
#   (no scheduling events at all — nobody is even TRYING to place it)

# existing pods? completely unaffected — they were already bound
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Running | head

# 3. RESTORE — bring the scheduler back
sudo mv /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# 4. VERIFY — the queued pod is bound within seconds
kubectl get pod easypj-test -o wide            # Running · NODE worker-2 ✅
kubectl delete pod easypj-test                 # cleanup

Check yourself: the tell for "scheduler down" is precise — Pending pods with an empty nodeName and no scheduling events whatsoever (vs. a resource problem, where Events actively list the filter that rejected each node). And nothing already running was touched: the control plane decides, the data plane runs. That distinction — plus the instant catch-up when the scheduler returned (level-triggered!) — is Chapter 3 in one experiment.

📌 Chapter 3 Visual Summary — the whole cluster, annotated
   ┌──────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ───────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🧠 CONTROL PLANE (decides)        every request & watch flows through apiserver │
   │   📡 apiserver :6443  ── the ONLY door, the ONLY etcd client                    │
   │        │  authN → authZ(RBAC) → admission                                       │
   │        ├── 🗄️ etcd :2379/2380   ALL state (Raft quorum)                          │
   │        ├── 📋 scheduler          filter → score → BIND (sets nodeName)           │
   │        └── 🔄 controller-mgr     reconcile loops (node·RS·endpoint·SA)           │
   │  ───────────────────────────── apiserver ⇅ nodes (watch) ──────────────────────│
   │ 💪 WORKER NODE                                                                   │
   │   🤖 kubelet (systemd, not a pod) · 🌐 kube-proxy (Service routing) · 🐋 runtime  │
   │   🌐 CNI gives each 📦 pod a flat IP   ·   💾 CSI attaches volumes                │
   │   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐                                                 │
   │   │📦 easypj-web│ │🐘 postgres  │   the control plane itself = static pods in     │
   │   │  :8000      │ │  :5432      │   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (kubelet-run)      │
   │   └────────────┘ └────────────┘                                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Decide (control plane) vs Run (nodes) · only apiserver→etcd · symptom→component = the exam.

In words: A cluster splits cleanly into two halves. The control plane decides; the worker nodes run. The apiserver (:6443) is the only way in and the only component that talks to etcd — every request first passes authentication → authorization (RBAC) → admission. etcd (:2379) holds all cluster state, kept consistent by Raft quorum.

Behind the apiserver, the scheduler filters and scores nodes then binds each pod (sets nodeName), and the controller-manager runs the reconcile loops (node, ReplicaSet, endpoint, service-account…). On each worker node, the kubelet runs the containers (it's a systemd service, not a pod), kube-proxy programs Service routing, the runtime executes containers, CNI gives each pod a flat IP, and CSI attaches storage. The control plane itself runs as static pods the kubelet starts from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

The takeaway: hold the "decide vs run" split and "only the apiserver touches etcd" in your head, and troubleshooting becomes a lookup — match the symptom to the responsible component. That mapping is the heart of the exam's Architecture and Troubleshooting domains.

Chapter 4 · Core Kubernetes Objects — The Admin's Toolkit

These six objects are the nouns of every exam task and every easypj manifest: Pod, ReplicaSet, Deployment, Service, Namespace, and the labels that wire them together. Chapter 3 showed you the machines; this chapter shows you the things you actually create on them. Master how they nest and reference each other and you can read any manifest at a glance.

4.1 Pods — The Smallest Unit

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, reachable over localhost) and storage volumes. You rarely create pods directly (you use Deployments), but you debug them constantly.

Pod anatomy — single vs multi-container (sidecar)
   SINGLE-CONTAINER POD (most common)        MULTI-CONTAINER POD (sidecar pattern)
   ┌──────────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 📦 POD   IP 10.244.1.5     │             │ 📦 POD   IP 10.244.1.8  (shared net)   │
   │  ┌────────────────────┐   │             │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐    │
   │  │ 🐍 easypj-web        │   │             │  │ 🐍 easypj      │ │ 🌐 nginx       │    │
   │  │ Django gunicorn:8000│   │             │  │ Django :8000 │ │ static :80   │    │
   │  └────────────────────┘   │             │  └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘    │
   │                            │             │         │   localhost     │            │
   │                            │             │         └────────┬────────┘            │
   │                            │             │              ┌───▼────┐ shared 💾       │
   │                            │             │              │ volume │ (emptyDir)      │
   │                            │             │              └────────┘                │
   └──────────────────────────┘             └──────────────────────────────────────┘
   one container = the norm                   localhost:8000 = Django · localhost:80 = nginx
💡
Key pod facts
  • Every container in a pod shares the same IP
  • They talk to each other over localhost
  • Pods are ephemeral — replaced, never repaired
  • Never rely on a pod's name or IP — both change
🔧
Essential pod commands
  • kubectl get pods -o wide
  • kubectl describe pod <name>
  • kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>
  • kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
easypj-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-pod
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: web                # labels = how other objects find this pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: easypj
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "128Mi"        # scheduling floor (guaranteed)
        cpu: "250m"
      limits:
        memory: "256Mi"        # hard ceiling (OOMKilled if exceeded)
        cpu: "500m"
📖 Why "ephemeral" is the whole point

A bare Pod is a pet: delete it and it's gone for good — nothing recreates it, and its IP vanishes. That's exactly why you wrap pods in controllers (next) and why apps reach each other through Services (§4.4), never by pod IP. Treat pods as disposable cattle and Kubernetes' design suddenly makes sense.

Init Containers, Sidecars & the Pause Container

A pod can hold more than one container, and they don't all behave the same way. There are three roles worth knowing — and one hidden container you never write but always have:

KindWhen it runseasypj example
init containerBEFORE app containers, to completion, in order — the next won't start until it exits 0wait for easypj-db to accept connections, or run manage.py migrate
app containerThe long-running main process(es)gunicorn easypj.wsgi on :8000
sidecarALONGSIDE the app for its whole life (a special init container with restartPolicy: Always)an nginx static-file server, or a log shipper
🔒 pauseThe hidden "sandbox" — created first, holds the pod's network + IPC namespacesauto-created; app/sidecar containers join its namespaces
🩺 ephemeralInjected after the pod is already running, purely for debugging — never in pod.spec, never restarted, can't be removedkubectl debug -it easypj-web --image=busybox --target=easypj (full depth in Ch 6)
Pod startup order — init runs to completion, then the rest share the sandbox
   pod created
      │
      ▼  🔒 pause container starts → reserves the pod IP + network namespace
      ▼  ⏳ initContainer "wait-for-db"   runs → exits 0
      ▼  ⏳ initContainer "migrate"       runs → exits 0   (ordered, must succeed)
      ▼  ▶️ app: 🐍 easypj  +  sidecar: 🌐 nginx   start together, share the sandbox
   Running ✅
   ── if an init container fails → pod stuck in Init:0/2 → it never reaches Running
💡 Why init containers are the clean answer to "wait for X"

Instead of baking retry/wait logic into easypj's startup, an init container does the waiting (e.g. until easypj-db:5432 answers) and the app container starts only once the dependency is ready. And the pause container is why all containers in a pod share one IP: they all join its network namespace — so a crashing app container can restart without the pod losing its IP. You'll use init containers for real in Chapter 16 (Jobs/migrations).

The Three Named Multi-Container Patterns — Sidecar, Ambassador, Adapter

"Sidecar" above was really one instance of a family. Kubernetes documentation names three canonical multi-container patterns — same mechanism (shared network + volumes), three different jobs the helper container does for the app:

📎
Sidecar

Extends or enhances the main container — runs alongside it for the pod's whole life. easypj: an nginx container serving Django's collected static files from a shared volume.

📡
Ambassador

A local proxy the app talks to on localhost, which forwards out to the real (often complex/remote) service. easypj: a local proxy on localhost:5432 that forwards to a sharded/replicated PostgreSQL cluster — Django just sees "a database on localhost."

🔌
Adapter

Transforms the app's output into a standard format for the outside world. easypj: a container that reads Django's plain-text logs and re-emits them as structured JSON for a cluster-wide log collector.

Same shared-network mechanism, three different jobs
   📦 POD (one IP, one localhost)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  🐍 easypj (app)                                                       │
   │     │ writes static files ──▶ 📎 sidecar (nginx) ──▶ serves them       │
   │     │ talks to localhost:5432 ──▶ 📡 ambassador ──▶ real Postgres cluster │
   │     │ writes plain-text logs ──▶ 🔌 adapter ──▶ JSON out to log collector│
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   💡 the app container never knows the helper is there — that's the whole point:
      it talks to "a file", "localhost:5432", or "stdout" and the helper does the rest.
💡 Why this taxonomy is worth knowing (beyond naming things)

All three patterns exist because the pod's shared network + volumes let you bolt on capability without touching app code — easypj's Django code never needs a Postgres-proxy library or a JSON logging formatter; the sidecar/ambassador/adapter container handles it. This is also the exact mechanism a service mesh sidecar (Istio/Linkerd, §1.5) uses to add mTLS and traffic policy to every pod with zero app changes.

4.2 ReplicaSets — Maintaining the Count

A ReplicaSet keeps a desired number of identical pods running, using a label selector to know which pods are "its." If one dies, it creates a replacement — that's self-healing. You rarely create a ReplicaSet directly; a Deployment manages it for you.

ReplicaSet self-healing — always 3 replicas
   ReplicaSet easypj-web-rs   (replicas: 3, selector: app=easypj,tier=web)

   HEALTHY                        POD 2 CRASHES                  SELF-HEALED
   ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐          ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐          ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐
   │📦 1│ │📦 2│ │📦 3│          │📦 1│ │💀 2│ │📦 3│          │📦 1│ │🆕 4│ │📦 3│
   └────┘ └────┘ └────┘          └────┘ └────┘ └────┘          └────┘ └────┘ └────┘
   3/3 Running ✅                 2/3 ⚠️                          3/3 Running ✅
                                     │ RS: "want 3, see 2"          ▲ new pod created
                                     └──────────────────────────────┘
📖 ReplicaSet vs Deployment

A ReplicaSet only ensures count. A Deployment adds rolling updates, rollback history, and version tracking on top — and creates/owns the ReplicaSet for you. In practice you always use Deployments; ReplicaSets are the layer doing the actual self-healing underneath.

Where the Hash in a Pod Name Comes From — pod-template-hash

You've seen pod names like easypj-web-7f8b4-abc1 — that middle segment isn't random. When a Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, it computes a hash of the pod template (image, env, labels — everything that would produce a genuinely different pod) and stamps it onto the ReplicaSet's name and onto every pod it owns as the label pod-template-hash.

why the hash exists: one label per template version, forever
   Deployment easypj-web  changes image v1→v2
        │ computes a NEW hash for the changed template
        ▼
   🎛️ ReplicaSet easypj-web-7f8b4   pod-template-hash: 7f8b4   (OLD template — v1, now 0 replicas)
   🎛️ ReplicaSet easypj-web-9c2e1   pod-template-hash: 9c2e1   (NEW template — v2, scaled up)

   💡 the Deployment's own selector doesn't include the hash — but each ReplicaSet's
      selector DOES, which is exactly how two ReplicaSets can share a Deployment
      without ever fighting over the same pods.

⚠️ Never hand-edit pod-template-hash — it's Kubernetes' own bookkeeping for "which template version is this pod running," and it's what makes rollouts/rollbacks able to tell ReplicaSets apart cleanly.

🚨 The bare-pod adoption trap

A ReplicaSet doesn't just create pods matching its selector — it adopts any existing, unowned pod whose labels happen to match too. So a "harmless" throwaway debug pod labeled app: easypj can get silently swallowed into a Deployment's ReplicaSet count (and later killed when the RS decides it's now "one too many"). The rule: never label a one-off pod with the same labels a real Deployment's selector uses — give debug pods a distinct label (e.g. app: debug-tmp) instead.

📖 The legacy predecessor — ReplicationController

Before ReplicaSets, Kubernetes had ReplicationController (RC) — same job, but its selector only supported simple equality (key=value), not the richer matchExpressions (in/notin/exists) a ReplicaSet supports. RC still technically exists but is effectively legacy — every current tool, including Deployments, is built on ReplicaSet. You'll see the name in older docs/blogs; treat it as history, not something to use.

4.3 Deployments — Managing the Application Lifecycle

The Deployment is the standard way to run a stateless app. You declare desired state (image, replicas, resources); the controller makes it real and adds rolling updates, rollbacks, and revision history — by managing a chain of ReplicaSets.

Deployment ownership chain (old ReplicaSets kept for rollback)
   🚀 Deployment: easypj-web
   ├── manages ─▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-7f8b4  (current, v3)
   │                ├── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc1
   │                ├── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc2
   │                └── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc3
   ├── keeps ──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-6d5a2  (old v2, scaled to 0)
   └── keeps ──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-5c3f1  (old v1, scaled to 0)
   💡 old ReplicaSets at 0 replicas = your instant rollback history.
🪆 In plain English — the wrapping (nesting) model

Pod, ReplicaSet, and Deployment aren't competing things — each wraps the one below and adds a single capability. Think Russian dolls, smallest inside — see the picture below.

Russian dolls — each layer wraps the one inside it
   🚀 Deployment        "give me rolling updates + rollback + history"
     └─ 🎛️ ReplicaSet    "keep exactly N copies alive"   (self-healing)
          └─ 📦 Pod      "schedule these container(s) together, one IP"
               └─ 🐋 Container   "run my easypj process"

You create the outermost doll (the Deployment) and it builds the rest. That's why you almost never make a bare Pod or a lone ReplicaSet — you'd give up the capabilities the outer wrappers add. Need a one-off task instead of a long-running app? Swap the Deployment for a Job (Ch 16): same Pod inside, different outer doll.

easypj-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  labels:
    app: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj                  # ← MUST match the template labels below
      tier: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1                   # at most 1 EXTRA pod while rolling
      maxUnavailable: 0             # zero-downtime: never dip below desired
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj                 # ← MUST match the selector above
        tier: web
        version: v3
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: easypj
        image: easypj:v3
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"         # scheduling floor (guaranteed)
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"         # hard ceiling (OOMKilled if exceeded)
            cpu: "500m"

Pod Lifecycle — the Phases & Statuses You'll See

Pod phases + the STATUS column you read in kubectl get pods
   ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌───────────┐
   │ Pending │──▶ │ Running │──▶ │ Succeeded │ (exit 0 — Jobs)
   └────┬────┘    └────┬────┘    └───────────┘
        │              └──▶ ┌────────┐
        └──────────────────▶│ Failed │ (exit ≠ 0)
                            └────────┘
   STATUS column (what kubectl actually shows):
   ContainerCreating  image pulling / volumes mounting
   Running            at least one container up
   Completed          all containers exited 0
   CrashLoopBackOff   container keeps crashing (growing backoff)
   ImagePullBackOff   can't pull the image
   Pending            not yet scheduled to a node
   Terminating        being gracefully deleted
   Init:N/M           init containers still running
⚠️ Reading those statuses for the exam
  • Pending → scheduler can't place it (no fit), ResourceQuota, or unbound PVC
  • ImagePullBackOff → wrong image/tag, private registry without imagePullSecrets
  • CrashLoopBackOff → kubectl logs <pod> --previous for the crash reason
  • Init:0/1 → an init container is stuck — kubectl logs <pod> -c <init>

Deployment Operations (CKA Speed)

terminal — the rollout toolkit
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3   # fast create
kubectl scale deployment easypj-web --replicas=5                      # scale
kubectl set image deployment/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v4              # rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj-web                         # watch it
kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj-web                        # revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web                           # roll back 1
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web --to-revision=2           # to a specific rev
💡 The strategy knobs

maxSurge: 1 allows one extra pod during the update; maxUnavailable: 0 means never drop below the desired count → zero downtime. Deep dive (incl. canary/blue-green) in Chapter 13.

4.4 Services — Stable Network Endpoints

Pods get random IPs that change on every restart — so you can never point a client at a pod IP. A Service gives a stable virtual IP + DNS name and load-balances across the pods its selector matches (its "endpoints").

TypeReachable fromUse casePort
ClusterIPInside the cluster onlyInternal (the default)any
NodePortOutside, via <nodeIP>:portDev / testing30000–32767
LoadBalancerOutside, via a cloud LBProduction (cloud)any
ExternalNameDNS alias (CNAME)Point at an external hostn/a
Service types — who can reach each
   🔒 ClusterIP (default)        🚪 NodePort                  ☁️ LoadBalancer
   ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐
   │ in-cluster only   │         │ <nodeIP>:30080    │        │ cloud LB          │
   │ VIP 10.96.0.10    │         │      │            │        │ 203.0.113.50      │
   │      │            │         │      ▼            │        │      │            │
   │      ▼            │         │ VIP 10.96.0.11    │        │      ▼            │
   │ 📦 easypj  📦 easypj│         │      │            │        │ VIP 10.96.0.12    │
   └──────────────────┘         │      ▼            │        │      │            │
                                │ 📦 easypj 📦 easypj│        │      ▼            │
                                └──────────────────┘        │ 📦 easypj 📦 easypj│
                                                             └──────────────────┘
   all three pick a READY pod by label selector (app=easypj) and load-balance to it
easypj-service.yaml — ClusterIP + NodePort
# internal Service (default) — stable VIP inside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-svc
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: easypj           # matches the pod labels
    tier: web
  ports:
  - port: 80              # the Service port (what clients call)
    targetPort: 8000      # the container port (gunicorn listens here)
---
# external dev access — same pods, reachable from outside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-nodeport
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: easypj
    tier: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
    nodePort: 30080       # reachable at <nodeIP>:30080 (range 30000–32767)
terminal — expose fast (CKA)
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000          # ClusterIP
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 \
  --type=NodePort --name=easypj-nodeport
kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc      # the pod IPs this Service routes to (empty = bug!)

Service DNS — How Pods Find Each Other by Name

Every Service gets an automatic DNS name from CoreDNS, so easypj-web can reach easypj-db without ever knowing its IP:

Service DNS resolution & cross-namespace access
   from a pod in the easypj namespace, all of these reach the DB Service:
     easypj-db                              ← same namespace (short)
     easypj-db.easypj                       ← name.namespace
     easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local     ← the full FQDN
   pattern:  <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local

   cross-namespace:  easypj-web (ns: easypj)  ──curl postgres.data.svc.cluster.local──▶
                     🐘 postgres Service (ns: data)
💡 Debugging DNS & endpoints

Service unreachable by name? Check CoreDNS (kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns) and test from a pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nslookup easypj-db. Unreachable by VIP? Check kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc — empty endpoints = the selector doesn't match any ready pod (the #1 Service bug; full depth in Part 5).

Two More Service Behaviours Worth Knowing

Beyond the four types, two knobs come up constantly — especially the moment you hit stateful apps like easypj's database.

🎯
Headless Service (clusterIP: None)

No VIP, no load-balancing. DNS returns the individual pod IPs directly. This is what StatefulSets use so clients can address a specific replica by a stable name like postgres-0.easypj-db… (Ch 16).

📌
sessionAffinity: ClientIP

Pins a client to the same backend pod for a timeout window instead of load-balancing every request — useful for sticky sessions. Default is None (spread freely).

Services Without a Selector — Manually Wiring Endpoints

Every example so far has Kubernetes compute the endpoints for you from a label selector. You can also create a Service with no selector at all and manage its EndpointSlice yourself — the escape hatch for pointing a stable in-cluster name at something Kubernetes doesn't manage, like an external database or a service living in another cluster.

easypj-external-db.yaml — a selector-less Service pointing outside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-external-db      # pods reach it as easypj-external-db, same as any Service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 5432                  # NO selector — nothing auto-populates endpoints
---
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: easypj-external-db-manual
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: easypj-external-db   # ← links it to the Service above
addressType: IPv4
ports:
- port: 5432
endpoints:
- addresses: ["203.0.113.42"]   # the real, off-cluster database IP

💡 easypj's Django code never needs to know the real database address changed — it always talks to easypj-external-db:5432. This is also how a plain ExternalName Service (a CNAME, no proxying at all) differs: selector-less-with-EndpointSlice still gets a real ClusterIP and load-balancing; ExternalName is pure DNS aliasing with neither.

Naming Every Port — the Rule Multi-Port Services Must Follow

Every Service example above exposed one port. The moment a Service exposes more than one, each port entry needs a unique name — the apiserver rejects an un-named multi-port Service outright:

a Service exposing both HTTP and metrics
spec:
  selector: { app: easypj }
  ports:
  - name: http           # REQUIRED once there's more than one port entry
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
  - name: metrics
    port: 9100
    targetPort: 9100

📖 The names also make targetPort referenceable by name from the pod side (containerPort: { name: http }) instead of by number — handy when the container port might change without the Service definition needing to.

📖 How kube-proxy actually routes (iptables vs IPVS)

A Service VIP isn't a real interface — it's a rule. kube-proxy programs the node so traffic to the VIP is DNAT'd to a ready pod IP:

  • iptables (default): a chain of rules with random probability per endpoint — simple, but rule lookup is O(n) at thousands of services.
  • IPVS: a kernel load-balancer with hash tables — O(1), better at large scale, more LB algorithms (round-robin, least-conn).
  • nftables: the newer successor to iptables mode.

Check the mode: kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-proxy | grep -i proxier. This is why "Services are slow at scale" historically meant "switch to IPVS" — but IPVS is deprecated as of v1.35, so on modern clusters the scale answer is nftables instead (Ch 18/34).

The Service Types Aren't Alternatives — They're Layers

The biggest unlock for remembering the four types: each external type is built on top of the one below it. A LoadBalancer contains a working NodePort, which contains a working ClusterIP — so every Service always has its internal VIP, no matter how it's exposed:

Each type = the previous type + one more door
   🌍 type: LoadBalancer      = NodePort  +  a cloud load balancer in front
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  ☁️ cloud LB 203.0.113.9:80 ──▶ <nodeIP>:31234 on every node      │
   │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
   │  │ 🚪 type: NodePort        = ClusterIP  +  a port on EVERY node│  │
   │  │   <anyNodeIP>:31234 ──▶ the ClusterIP                       │  │
   │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
   │  │  │ 🔌 type: ClusterIP     = the base: internal VIP + DNS  │  │  │
   │  │  │   10.96.142.10:80 ──▶ ready pod IPs :8000 (endpoints) │  │  │
   │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
   │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   (ExternalName is the odd one out: no VIP, no proxying — just a DNS CNAME alias)

   💡 consequence: a LoadBalancer Service ALSO answers on <nodeIP>:nodePort and on its
      ClusterIP — three valid doors to the same pods. On bare metal (no cloud), a
      LoadBalancer simply sits <pending> forever and behaves as its NodePort layer.
💡 Why this matters on the exam & in production

Exam clusters are kubeadm (no cloud): asked to "expose externally," reach for NodePort — a type: LoadBalancer will hang <pending> (that's expected, not broken). And when debugging, test the layers inside-out: ClusterIP from a pod → NodePort from a node → the LB last. The failing layer names the broken component (endpoints → kube-proxy → cloud controller).

4.5 Namespaces — Virtual Clusters

Namespaces are logical partitions of one cluster — used to isolate teams and environments. Each can carry its own ResourceQuota, RBAC, and NetworkPolicy, so easypj-dev and easypj-prod live side-by-side without colliding.

Namespace isolation — the easypj example
   ┌──────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ────────────────────────────────┐
   │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
   │  │ 🟢 easypj-dev         │        │ 🔴 easypj-prod        │                    │
   │  │  1 replica · DEBUG=on │        │  3 replicas · DEBUG=off│                   │
   │  │  low limits           │        │  high limits           │                   │
   │  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘                     │
   │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
   │  │ 🔧 kube-system        │        │ 📊 monitoring         │                    │
   │  │  CoreDNS · kube-proxy │        │  Prometheus · Grafana  │                   │
   │  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘                     │
   │  each namespace can have its OWN: ResourceQuota · RBAC Roles · NetworkPolicy │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Four Built-in Namespaces

📦
default

Where objects land with no namespace set. Avoid it in production.

🔧
kube-system

Control-plane add-ons: CoreDNS, kube-proxy, metrics-server. Don't deploy apps here.

🌍
kube-public

Readable by all (even unauthenticated). Holds the cluster-info ConfigMap.

💓
kube-node-lease

Node heartbeat Lease objects — used for fast node-health detection.

terminal — namespace commands
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl get namespaces
