🐳 Docker Engine

The core. Includes the daemon (dockerd), the CLI (docker), and the container runtime (containerd). This is what actually builds and runs containers.

🎼 Docker Compose

Tool for defining and running multi-container apps. One YAML file (compose.yaml) defines your entire stack. One command (docker compose up) starts everything.

🐝 Docker Swarm

Docker's native clustering and orchestration tool. Turns a pool of Docker hosts into a single virtual host. Simpler than Kubernetes but less feature-rich.

🖥️ Docker Desktop

All-in-one package for Mac/Windows/Linux: Docker Engine, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Docker Scout, and a GUI dashboard. The recommended way to run Docker on development machines.

Every one of these tools attaches to the one engine three different ways: Compose and Buildx ship as CLI plugins (docker compose, docker buildx), Swarm is compiled straight into dockerd with nothing extra to install, and Scout, Hub, and Build Cloud are hosted services the CLI simply talks to over the network. Knowing which category a tool falls into tells you whether you need to install anything at all.

TaskToolOne-liner
Run my app locallyEngine + CLI 🐳docker run
Multi-container dev stackCompose 🎼docker compose up
Build faster / multi-archBuildx 🏗️docker buildx build
Store + share imagesHub / registry 🗄️docker push
Find CVEs before productionScout 🔍docker scout quickview
Cluster without KubernetesSwarm 🐝docker swarm init
GUI + batteries on a laptopDesktop 🖥️(install once)
📱 Analogy — The Phone and Its Apps

Docker Engine is the phone — the one thing everything else needs to exist at all. Compose, Scout, Buildx, and Swarm are apps installed around it, each solving one specific job. You'll never need every app installed, but you always need the phone.

Match blind, no peeking at the table above: "the team needs the same 5-service stack every time" → Compose. "This image has 120 CVEs" → Scout. "Build for ARM Macs and AMD64 servers from one command" → Buildx. If those three came straight to mind, you've got the ecosystem's shape, not just its list of names.

Concretely, on easypj: docker compose up starts easypj + PostgreSQL together from one file (Part 4); docker scout quickview easypj:v1 lists CVEs in that exact image before it ever reaches production (Part 7).

📖 The Rest of the Tool Belt

Four more subcommands round out the ecosystem, each solving a smaller, specific job: docker init (scaffolds a Dockerfile + compose file for a new project by detecting your language), docker sbom (generates a Software Bill of Materials — every package inside an image, for supply-chain audits), docker context (switches which daemon your CLI talks to — local, remote, or cloud, without retyping -H every time), and docker extension (installs third-party panels directly into the Desktop GUI).

⚠️ The Surprise Every New Team Hits: Hub Pull Rate Limits

Docker Hub throttles anonymous and free-tier pulls — a busy CI pipeline pulling python:3.11-slim on every build can burn through the limit fast, failing with toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. The fix is a free docker login in CI (authenticated pulls get a much higher ceiling) or mirroring base images to your own registry/ECR.

1.6 Docker Editions & Installation Overview

FeatureDocker DesktopDocker Engine (CE)
TargetDev machinesServers
GUI Dashboard✅ Yes❌ No
Windows/Mac support✅ Yes❌ Linux only
WSL2 integration✅ YesN/A
Kubernetes built-in✅ Yes❌ No
Production-grade⚠️ Not recommended✅ Yes
Security scanning✅ Scout includedOptional
LicenseFree tier, then Pro/Team/Business subscriptionAlways free (Apache 2.0), any company size

Editions are subscription tiers on one product, not different engines underneath. Desktop wraps Engine inside a lightweight Linux VM (WSL2 on Windows, Apple's Virtualization.framework on macOS) — that hidden VM is precisely how Linux containers run on a non-Linux machine, and it bundles every extra (GUI dashboard, built-in Kubernetes, Scout) for one device at a time. Engine (CE) is the free, self-hosted tier running as a bare systemd service — nothing extra, built for a fleet of servers, not one laptop, and it stays Apache 2.0 free forever regardless of company size.

📖 If You See "Docker EE" or "Mirantis" in Older Material

Older docs, courses, and even some real exam-prep material still describe a three-way split: Desktop / Engine CE / Engine EE (Enterprise Edition). That product no longer exists under that name — Mirantis acquired Docker's enterprise business in 2019, and Docker's own current commercial model is entirely subscription tiers on Desktop (Personal → Pro → Team → Business), while Engine itself has stayed free and open-source the whole time. If a question or article mentions "Docker EE," mentally translate it to "Docker Business subscription" — the underlying engine hasn't changed.

60-second install verification, any OS
# Client AND Server both answer = the daemon is up
docker version

# Storage driver, cgroup version, which runtimes are registered
docker info

# Full pull → create → run → exit path, self-cleaning
docker run --rm hello-world

# Verify: hello-world printed its message above, AND --rm already
# cleaned up after itself — confirm with:
docker ps -a                    # stays EMPTY, nothing to clean up

# Now drop --rm and look again — the container lingers as "Exited":
docker run hello-world
docker ps -a                    # hello-world   Exited (0)

On a laptop, Desktop's GUI gets easypj and PostgreSQL running in minutes with zero terminal knowledge required. The server actually hosting easypj in production only ever installs Engine (CE) — no GUI, no accidentally-enabled Kubernetes toggle, nothing running that isn't earning its keep.

⚠️ Desktop Isn't Free Forever

Docker Desktop's free tier covers individuals, small businesses, personal use, and education. Once a company grows past a certain size (roughly 250 employees or $10M+ annual revenue, per Docker's own published terms), Desktop requires a paid subscription — Engine (CE) never does, at any company size, which is one more reason production servers run bare Engine rather than Desktop.

1.7 Real-World Docker Use Cases

🏗️
Microservices

Each service in its own container — independent deploy, independent scale. Django easypj app, Auth service, Payment service, Celery worker — each gets its own container with its own dependencies.

🚀
CI/CD Pipeline

Build → Test → Push → Deploy — every step runs in an identical Docker container. No more "it works in CI but not in prod." The exact same image that passed tests is what gets deployed.

💻
Development Environment

docker compose up starts PostgreSQL, Redis, Django, and Nginx in 30 seconds. No installing databases, no configuring caches. Team members get identical environments instantly.

🏚️
Legacy Modernization

Old PHP 5.6 app? Containerize it with a PHP 5.6 Apache image. NO rewriting needed. It runs the SAME on modern infrastructure. This is how enterprises migrate to the cloud without rewrites.

📊
Data Science

docker run jupyter/scipy-notebook — the exact Python version, every ML library, fully reproducible. "It worked on my laptop" becomes "it works everywhere," notebook and all.

Use caseThe easypj moment that proves it

CI/CDEvery push builds & tests easypj automatically (Part 8)
Dev environmentsA new hire runs the full stack in 30 seconds (Part 4)

🎭 Analogy — A Touring Stage Show, Five Venues, Never Repainting the Set

Microservices is five small acts each touring on its own truck. CI/CD is the dress rehearsal run in the exact same venue as opening night. The dev-environment card is a pop-up matinee assembled in 30 seconds. Legacy modernization re-stages an old script under a new rig without rewriting a line. Data science ships the same traveling exhibit to every museum, pixel for pixel. Five different economic wins — the same one mechanic underneath every single one of them.

Every card above reduces to the same mechanic: pin the runtime and libraries inside an image so the same artifact moves from a laptop's docker compose up, through a CI runner's build/test steps, to the production scheduler — no reinstalling, no version drift, at any of the five stops. One caution worth holding onto: containerizing a legacy app freezes its known vulnerabilities too — modernization buys portability, not a free security upgrade (Part 7 covers scanning them away).

1.9 Containers Beyond Docker — OCI Standards & the Runtime Landscape

Docker didn't just build a tool — it drove the creation of an open standard. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines three specs: image-spec (how an image is packaged), runtime-spec (how a container starts from it), and distribution-spec (how images move between registries).

The practical consequence: Docker images ARE OCI images. They run unmodified on any OCI-compliant runtime — not just Docker's own containerd/runc chain (1.4).

💿 Analogy — The DVD Standard

OCI is the DVD standard; Docker is one brand of DVD player. When Kubernetes swapped players (dropping dockershim for talking to containerd directly), every movie — every image — still plays exactly the same. The standard, not the player, is what makes the disc portable.

Who Implements Which OCI Spec
  image-spec (how it's packaged):    docker build │ buildah │ kaniko
  runtime-spec (how it starts):      runc │ crun │ gVisor │ Kata Containers
  consumers (who runs it):           dockerd │ Podman │ containerd ◀── Kubernetes (via CRI)
The Runtime Landscape
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     📐 OCI-COMPLIANT RUNTIMES                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │   easypj:v1  (one OCI image, built once with `docker build`)             │
  │        │                                                                │
  │        ├──▶ 🐳 Docker (containerd + runc) — dev laptops, CI runners      │
  │        ├──▶ 🦭 Podman (daemonless, rootless by default)                  │
  │        └──▶ ☸️ Kubernetes nodes (containerd or CRI-O, via CRI)           │
  │                                                                          │
  │   Same image, three different places it can run — UNMODIFIED.            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Concretely: the easypj:v1 image built with docker build is an OCI image — it runs unmodified under Podman or a Kubernetes node's containerd, no dockerd required at all, the day this guide reaches Part 9.

📖 Key Term — dockershim

Kubernetes 1.24 removed dockershim — a compatibility SHIM that let Kubernetes talk to Docker Engine directly instead of through the standard Container Runtime Interface (CRI). It did NOT remove Docker images: those are OCI images and still run fine on containerd/CRI-O nodes. Only the glue that let Docker itself act as the node runtime was dropped.

Under the Hood — from docker run to an isolated Linux process: the full internals

A container has NO virtualization hardware underneath it — it is an ordinary host process wrapped in kernel primitives. Everything in this chapter's architecture diagram (1.4) is real, inspectable machinery, not a black box. This section walks the whole chain once, end to end, then opens up each layer in turn.

🗺️ The Full Trace — Running easypj from Command to Process, Step by Step

Here's every hop a single docker run easypj:v1 actually makes, numbered start to finish:

  1. YOU type:  docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1

  2. Docker CLI (client) builds an HTTP request and sends it over the
     Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) to dockerd's REST API.

  3. dockerd checks: is easypj:v1 present locally?
     No  → pulls it from the registry first (1.9's OCI image-spec)
     Yes → skip straight to step 4

  4. dockerd calls containerd over gRPC: "create a container from this image,
     with this config" — dockerd itself never touches Linux namespaces/cgroups.

  5. containerd unpacks the image's layers (via its snapshotter, see ⑤),
     assembles an OCI "bundle" directory (rootfs + config.json, see ④),
     and spawns a containerd-shim process for this one container.

  6. The shim execs runc, handing it the bundle directory.

  7. runc reads config.json and makes the kernel syscalls that build the
     container: clone()/unshare() for namespaces, cgroup creation, mount
     the rootfs, set up networking — then execs YOUR process inside it.

  8. runc's job is done — it exits immediately. Your process (gunicorn)
     is now PID 1 inside the container, parented by the shim, not runc.

  9. The shim stays alive for the container's whole lifetime, relaying
     stdio and exit status back up to containerd, then to dockerd.
LayerWhat it actually does
dockerdThe Docker daemon. Handles the Docker API, builds images, manages networks. Does NOT directly run containers.
containerdThe container runtime. Manages the complete container lifecycle: image transfer, container execution, storage, and networking. Originally spun out from Docker, now a CNCF graduated project used by Kubernetes too.
containerd-shimA small process that stays between containerd and the container. Allows containerd to be restarted without killing running containers, and handles STDIO.
runcThe OCI runtime. Creates and starts containers by setting up Linux namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS, USER, CGROUP) and cgroups, then exits. This is where the actual Linux magic happens.
🔑 Why This Matters for DCA. The exam expects you to understand this architecture chain, especially for the Installation & Configuration domain (15%). Questions may ask about containerd's role, how to configure the daemon (daemon.json), or what happens when you restart dockerd with live-restore enabled (the shim keeps containers alive — see ⑥ below, and Practice Drill 1.2 later in this chapter for the hands-on proof).
① The Docker REST API — What docker run Really Is Over the Wire

The CLI is nothing but a thin HTTP client. Every command you type becomes a specific REST call against dockerd's API — there is no other channel, no hidden shortcut.

  docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
       │
       │  the CLI actually issues (roughly) THREE calls:
       ▼
  ① POST /images/create?fromImage=easypj&tag=v1      (only if not cached locally)
  ② POST /containers/create?name=easypj-web           body: {Image, ExposedPorts, HostConfig...}
       ◀── {"Id": "a1b2c3...", "Warnings": []}
  ③ POST /containers/a1b2c3.../start
       ◀── 204 No Content  (success, no body)
Endpoint (abbreviated)What docker subcommand triggers it
GET /containers/jsondocker ps
GET /containers/{id}/logsdocker logs
POST /containers/{id}/execdocker exec
DELETE /containers/{id}docker rm
🔑 Prove it yourself: run docker -D run hello-world (the -D debug flag) or inspect traffic on the socket — every single CLI action is one of these plain HTTP calls. This is also exactly how tools like Portainer, Docker Compose, and the VS Code Docker extension work: they're all just other REST clients talking to the same API you do.
② Namespaces in Detail — What Each of the Seven Types Isolates
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOST KERNEL (one, shared by every container)                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  easypj-web container                                       │ │
  │  │  NAMESPACES: PID·NET·MNT·UTS·IPC·CGROUP (USER: opt-in)      │ │
  │  │  CGROUPS   (what it CAN USE): --memory 512m · --cpus 1.5    │ │
  │  │  PID 1 inside: gunicorn (easypj.wsgi)                       │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  Other containers on the SAME host get their OWN namespaces —   │
  │  none can see each other's processes or files by default.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
MechanismControlsDetail
NamespacesWhat the process can SEEEach type virtualizes one resource: PID (its own process tree, PID 1 inside), NET (its own interfaces/routes/ports), MNT (its own filesystem view), UTS (its own hostname), IPC (its own shared memory/semaphores), and CGROUP (its own view of the cgroup hierarchy). These six are created for every container by default. A seventh type, USER (remapping container UID/GID to an unprivileged host range), is NOT on by default — root inside a container IS root on the host unless the daemon is explicitly configured with userns-remap. (Chapter 3 has the full 7-namespace reference table.)
CgroupsWhat the process can USECPU shares/quota, memory limits, block I/O, PID count. A container hitting its cgroup memory limit is OOM-killed by the kernel, not by Docker.
⚠️ Namespaces are NOT a hard security boundary the way a hypervisor is — a kernel exploit can cross them. That gap is exactly why Part 7 (Docker Security) exists: userns-remap, seccomp, and capabilities.
③ Cgroups v1 vs v2 — the Split the Exam Expects You to Know

runc's job (①) is calling the kernel syscalls that create namespaces and attach cgroups, then exec-ing your process inside them — after that, runc exits and the shim babysits. But WHICH cgroup implementation it talks to depends on the host, and the two versions behave differently enough to matter.

  cgroup v1 (legacy) — one SEPARATE tree per controller:      cgroup v2 (unified, modern default) — ONE tree:
  /sys/fs/cgroup/                                             /sys/fs/cgroup/
  ├── cpu/docker/easypj-web/        (CPU limits here)         └── docker/easypj-web/
  ├── memory/docker/easypj-web/     (memory limits here)          ├── cpu.max
  └── blkio/docker/easypj-web/      (I/O limits here)              ├── memory.max
       3 trees to walk to see the full picture                     └── io.max      ← ALL controllers, one place
cgroup v1 (legacy)cgroup v2 (unified, modern default)
HierarchyOne SEPARATE hierarchy per controller (cpu, memory, blkio each mounted separately)ONE single unified hierarchy for all controllers
Resource limits it can expressCPU, memory, block I/O (each independently)Same, plus more accurate memory pressure reporting (PSI) and cleaner delegation
Who uses it todayOlder distros, some legacy CI imagesDefault on modern Ubuntu, Fedora, and Docker Desktop's VM since ~2021
which cgroup version is this host actually running?
docker info | grep -i "Cgroup Version"
# Cgroup Version: 2

# Or check the kernel directly:
stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/   # "cgroup2fs" = v2, "tmpfs" = v1
🔑 Why it's exam-relevant: --memory/--cpus flags work the same either way from the CLI, but low-level troubleshooting (reading raw cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup/ to see exactly why a container was OOM-killed) looks in a different place on each version — v1 splits files across /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/, /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/, etc.; v2 keeps everything under one unified /sys/fs/cgroup/<container>/ path.
④ The OCI Runtime Spec — What runc Actually Reads

Step 7 of the full trace said "runc reads config.json." That file is not a Docker invention — it's the literal OCI runtime-spec (1.9) in JSON form, and it's the actual contract between containerd and runc.

  containerd assembles an OCI "bundle" — a directory containing:

    bundle/
    ├── config.json     ← the OCI runtime-spec: namespaces to create, cgroup
    │                       limits, mounts, capabilities, the process to exec,
    │                       env vars, working dir — EVERYTHING about this
    │                       one container, as plain JSON
    └── rootfs/          ← the container's actual filesystem (image layers,
                             already unpacked and merged by the snapshotter)

  runc create --bundle bundle/ easypj-web
       reads config.json  →  builds the namespaces/cgroups it describes
                          →  execs config.json's "process.args" (your CMD)
🔑 This is precisely WHY Docker images run unmodified under Podman or a Kubernetes node (1.9): any tool that can produce a valid config.json + rootfs bundle can hand it to runc (or crun, or any other OCI runtime) and get an identical container — the spec, not Docker's code, is the actual portability guarantee.
⑤ containerd's Own Internal Architecture — a Second, Different Kind of "Namespace"

Here's a genuine trap: containerd has its own concept called a "namespace" — and it has nothing to do with the kernel namespaces in ②. A containerd namespace is a logical partition INSIDE containerd itself, used to keep separate callers' containers and images from colliding.

  ONE containerd installation on a self-managed Kubernetes node, serving TWO callers:

  🐳 dockerd ──creates in──▶  containerd namespace "moby"   ──▶  📦 easypj-web (your container)
  🤖 kubelet ──creates in──▶  containerd namespace "k8s.io" ──▶  📦 coredns, kube-proxy, etc.

  Same containerd binary, same host — but "moby" containers and "k8s.io" containers
  are invisible to each other's default tooling (docker ps sees ONLY "moby").
containerd namespaceUsed by
mobyThe Docker Engine (dockerd) — every container you create with docker run lives here
k8s.ioA Kubernetes node's kubelet, talking to the SAME containerd installation via CRI
see containerd's own namespace, not the kernel's
# List containerd namespaces (needs ctr, containerd's own low-level CLI)
sudo ctr namespaces list
# NAME
# moby      ← docker's containers live here

# List containers docker created, via containerd directly (bypassing dockerd!)
sudo ctr -n moby containers list
🔑 This is exactly HOW a single containerd installation can serve both Docker AND a Kubernetes kubelet on the same machine (common on self-managed nodes) without their containers colliding — two totally separate containerd namespaces, one shared binary. Don't confuse this with kernel namespaces in ② — same word, two unrelated isolation mechanisms at two different layers of the stack.
⑥ Live-Restore in Practice — What Actually Survives a Daemon Restart, and What Doesn't

Q8's Scenario Drill and Practice Drill 1.2 (later in this chapter) both make this concrete: running containers survive a dockerd restart ONLY when this flag is set — it is not automatic on any install by default.

  WITHOUT live-restore                          WITH live-restore: true
  ────────────────────────                      ────────────────────────
  dockerd restart                                dockerd restart
       │                                              │
       ▼                                              ▼
  dockerd sends SIGTERM to ALL                   shims are left ALONE —
  containers it manages, then                    dockerd simply reconnects
  they stop  ❌  visible outage                   to them once it's back up
       │                                              │
       ▼                                              ▼
  dockerd back up → containers                  containers never stopped
  must be started again manually                 running the whole time  ✅
/etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "live-restore": true
}
Survives a dockerd restart with live-restore ONDoes NOT survive
Already-running containers (parented by the shim)An in-flight docker build (dockerd owns the build process directly)
Their network connectivity and published portsAn open docker exec -it session's TTY (though the process it started keeps running)
Containers that crash and need restarting per their restart policy — the shim itself re-execs themA docker pull or docker push in progress
🔑 The rule of thumb: anything the shim owns (a running container) survives; anything only dockerd itself is actively driving (a build, a pull, an attached exec session) does not. This single flag is exactly why production hosts enable it — a routine daemon upgrade shouldn't cause a visible outage.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Docker solves environment drift by shipping the whole userspace (interpreter + libraries + code) as one immutable image.
  • Image = read-only blueprint; container = running instance with one writable layer on top (class vs object).
  • Containers share the ONE host kernel via namespaces (what you see) and cgroups (what you can use) — no hypervisor, no guest OS.
  • A docker run travels CLI → REST API → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc; the shim is why containers survive a daemon restart.
  • The ecosystem is one engine with satellite tools bolted on three ways: CLI plugins (Compose, Buildx), compiled-in (Swarm), or hosted services (Hub, Scout, Build Cloud).
  • Desktop wraps Engine in a VM for laptops; production servers run bare Engine (CE) — Desktop is never a production runtime.
  • Docker images are OCI images — they run unmodified under Podman or a Kubernetes node's containerd; "K8s removed Docker" only removed the dockershim glue.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Containers are lightweight VMs" → Containers share the host kernel; VMs have their own. Completely different architectures.
  • docker stop = docker kill → stop sends SIGTERM (graceful); kill sends SIGKILL (immediate).
  • EXPOSE publishes ports → EXPOSE is documentation only. Use -p or ports: to actually publish.
  • Data survives container deletion → All container data is lost on deletion unless stored in volumes.
  • "Docker packages the kernel too" → The kernel always comes from the host (1.3); "identical everywhere" means userspace only.
  • Docker Desktop runs Linux AND Windows containers natively → Windows containers need a Windows kernel, Linux containers need a Linux kernel — Desktop only "does both" by hiding a Linux VM underneath.
  • ":latest" means the newest, freshest image → :latest is just a tag NAME, not a freshness guarantee — it's whatever was last pushed without an explicit tag, which can be stale or simply wrong.
  • "Kubernetes dropped Docker" → It dropped the dockershim CRI glue (1.9), not Docker-built images — those still run fine.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker version before anything else. If Client answers but Server doesn't, connectivity is the problem, not the daemon.
  • docker info | grep -i runtime any time you need to prove which OCI runtime (almost always runc) sits under this engine.
  • Read an image reference right to left when confused: TAG, then REPOSITORY, then NAMESPACE, then REGISTRY — defaults fill every gap.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 1)

orient yourself & sanity-check the daemon 
# Client AND server — daemon reachability
docker version

# Runtime, storage driver, cgroup version
docker info

# Full pull→create→run→exit path, self-cleaning
docker run --rm hello-world

# Running containers only
docker ps

# Every container, including exited
docker ps -a

# Local images with their immutable digest
docker images --digests

# Which platforms an image tag covers (classic; still works everywhere)
docker manifest inspect <image>

# Same job, the actively-maintained Buildx equivalent (prefer this)
docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>

# Disk used by images/containers/volumes
docker system df
run, inspect & ship a container (memorize these) 
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name app IMAGE
docker logs -f CONTAINER
docker exec -it CONTAINER sh
docker inspect CONTAINER
docker build -t name:tag .
docker push REGISTRY/name:tag
docker history IMAGE
docker scout quickview IMAGE

🧠 Chapter 1 — DCA Practice Questions (15)

Quick recall of the mental model — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What is the primary problem that Docker solves in software development?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker solves the "works on my machine" problem by packaging applications and ALL their dependencies into standardized containers that run identically across any environment — development, staging, and production.

EXPLANATION

Before Docker, each environment (dev, staging, prod) could have different OS versions, library versions, and configurations. A container bundles the application code WITH its exact runtime environment, ensuring consistency everywhere.

# Before Docker — "Works on my machine"
# Dev: Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04
# Prod: Python 3.10, CentOS 7

# With Docker — identical everywhere:
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
What is the key architectural difference between containers and virtual machines?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Virtual Machines virtualize the HARDWARE and each runs a full guest OS with its own kernel. Containers virtualize the OPERATING SYSTEM and share the host's kernel.

EXPLANATION

This is why containers are so much lighter: they don't need to boot a full OS, don't need a hypervisor, and can share memory and disk resources. A VM needs GBs of RAM for the guest OS alone; a container adds only MBs on top of the host.

  VIRTUAL MACHINES:                    CONTAINERS:
  ┌──────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ App A │ App B        │             │ App A │ App B        │
  │ Bins/  │ Bins/        │             │ Bins/  │ Bins/        │
  │ Libs   │ Libs         │             │ Libs   │ Libs         │
  │┌──────┐│┌──────┐     │             │        │             │
  ││Guest │││Guest │     │             │  Docker Engine       │
  ││OS    │││OS    │     │             │  (containerd+runc)   │
  │└──────┘│└──────┘     │             │        │             │
  │   Hypervisor         │             │   Host OS (kernel)   │
  │──────────────────────│             │──────────────────────│
  │   Host OS (kernel)   │             │   Hardware            │
  │──────────────────────│             └──────────────────────┘
  │   Hardware            │              Each VM = GBs RAM
  └──────────────────────┘              Each container = MBs RAM
   Each VM = full guest OS               All share ONE kernel
Q3
Name the three main components of Docker's architecture and their roles.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Docker Client — CLI that sends commands to the daemon via REST API.
2. Docker Daemon (dockerd) — Background service that builds images, runs containers, manages networks/volumes.
3. Docker Registry — Stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, ECR, etc.)

EXPLANATION

The client and daemon can run on the same machine or different machines. Communication happens over a Unix socket (default: /var/run/docker.sock) or TCP. The registry is where images are pushed to and pulled from — Docker Hub being the default public registry.

# Docker Client ↔ Daemon communication
# Local (Unix socket — default):
docker run nginx          # → /var/run/docker.sock → dockerd

# Remote (TCP — requires TLS):
docker -H tcp://192.168.1.10:2376 run nginx    # 2376 = TLS-secured
# NEVER expose port 2375 (plaintext, no auth) to an untrusted network —
# anyone who can reach it can run any container as root on that host.

# Registry interaction:
docker pull nginx         # ← Docker Hub (default)
docker pull myreg.com:5000/app:v1  # ← Private registry
docker push myreg.com:5000/app:v1  # → Private registry
Q4
A developer says "Docker containers are just like lightweight VMs." Is this accurate? Explain.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Not accurate. While both provide isolation, containers share the host OS kernel and do NOT include a full operating system. VMs each have their own kernel, making them fundamentally different architecturally.

EXPLANATION

This misunderstanding is common. Containers feel like VMs because they provide process isolation, but under the hood they use Linux namespaces and cgroups — NOT hardware virtualization. This is why you can't run a Windows container on a Linux host (kernel must match).

# Linux namespaces — the isolation building blocks:
# PID namespace:    container sees only its own processes
# NET namespace:    container has its own network stack
# MNT namespace:    container has its own filesystem mount
# UTS namespace:    container has its own hostname
# IPC namespace:    container has isolated shared memory
# USER namespace:   container UIDs mapped to host UIDs (opt-in, see Under the Hood)

# Verify isolation:
docker run --rm alpine ps aux
# Shows only container processes — NOT the host's 200+ processes

# cgroups limit resources:
docker run --memory=256m --cpus=1 nginx
# Kernel enforces: container cannot exceed 256MB RAM
Q5
Which container runtime does modern Docker use, and what is its role?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Modern Docker uses containerd as the container runtime. containerd manages the complete container lifecycle: image transfer, container execution, storage, and networking. It uses runc (an OCI-compliant runtime) to actually create and start containers.

EXPLANATION

Docker's architecture evolved: originally dockerd did everything. Now dockerd delegates to containerd, which delegates to runc. This modular design means you can swap components (e.g., use CRI-O instead of containerd in Kubernetes).

  DOCKER RUNTIME CHAIN (from high-level to low-level):

  docker CLI ──REST API──▶ dockerd ──gRPC──▶ containerd ──shim──▶ runc ──▶ CONTAINER
  (user types)            (daemon)          (runtime)   (per-ctr) (OCI)

  KEY INSIGHT: The shim keeps containers alive
  even when dockerd restarts!

  # Check runtime:
  docker info | grep Runtime
  # Runtime: runc

  # Containers survive daemon restart (with shim):
  sudo systemctl restart docker
  docker ps  # Containers still running!
Q6
What is "dependency hell," and where exactly does it bite easypj?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Environment drift: unpinned interpreter versions and libraries that differ between machines. easypj's laptop has Python 3.11 + Django 5.2; staging has 3.8 → python manage.py runserver dies on syntax it has never seen. Docker ends this by shipping the interpreter + libraries + code as one frozen artifact.

MachinePythonDjangoResult
Your laptop3.115.2✅ Works
Staging server3.84.2❌ SyntaxError on startup
Either, as a containerFrozen inside easypj:v1✅ Identical everywhere
EXPLANATION

This is the concrete version of the "works on my machine" problem from 1.1 — the fix isn't discipline or documentation, it's packaging the whole userspace so there's nothing left to drift.

Q7
Using ~1.5 GB of idle VM overhead and ~50 MB per container, how many easypj containers fit in the RAM ONE idle VM wastes before running any app code?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1.5 GB ÷ 50 MB ≈ 30 containers — pure overhead, before a single line of easypj has executed.

  1,500 MB (one idle VM's overhead)
  ─────────────────────────────────  =  30 easypj containers
        50 MB (one container)             doing REAL work, for free
EXPLANATION

This is the density argument from 1.3 turned into a concrete number: the RAM one VM burns just existing is enough to run 30 easypj containers doing real work.

Q8
What role does a registry play, and what travels over the wire on push?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A registry stores image layers + manifests for distribution (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR, Harbor...). A push uploads only the layers the registry doesn't already hold — content-addressed dedup — then the manifest.

  easypj:v1 = [layer-A: base][layer-B: deps][layer-C: your code]
  easypj:v2 = [layer-A: base][layer-B: deps][layer-C': your code CHANGED]
                 ✅ registry already has it   📤 only THIS layer + manifest travel
EXPLANATION

This is why re-pushing an image after a small code change is fast: only the changed layer (and the manifest) actually travels — everything else the registry already has, byte-identical, from the previous push.

Q9
You docker rm -f a running easypj container that was never given a volume. What data survives, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing written inside the container survives. A container's writable layer holds all its runtime changes (per 1.2's image/container split); deleting the container deletes that layer. Only data written to a mounted volume (outside the container's own filesystem) would survive.

EXPLANATION

This is a critical concept for the DCA exam. The mantra: "Containers are cattle, not pets." They should be disposable. Persistent data belongs in volumes — the reason Part 6 (Docker Storage) exists.

# DATA LOST — No volume:
docker run -d --name mydb postgres:15
# ... use database, store 5GB of data ...
docker rm mydb              # ❌ ALL 5GB LOST!

# DATA SAFE — With volume:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name mydb -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
docker rm mydb              # Container gone
docker volume ls            # pgdata STILL EXISTS with 5GB ✅
Q10
What do the three OCI specs each define, and who commonly implements them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

image-spec (how an image is packaged: docker build, buildah, kaniko), runtime-spec (how a container starts from it: runc, crun, gVisor, Kata), distribution-spec (how images move between registries). Consumers include dockerd, Podman, and containerd (used directly by Kubernetes via CRI).

SpecDefinesImplementers
image-specHow an image is packageddocker build, buildah, kaniko
runtime-specHow a container starts from itrunc, crun, gVisor, Kata
distribution-specHow images move between registriesDocker Hub, ECR, GCR, Harbor
EXPLANATION

This is 1.9's core lesson made concrete: because Docker images conform to image-spec, ANY OCI-compliant runtime can run them — that's the guarantee that carries every image built in this guide into Kubernetes without a rebuild.

Q11
Sort these terms into their BUILD / RUN / SHIP / PLUMBING bucket: Dockerfile, container, registry, containerd, tag, ENTRYPOINT, digest, namespace.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
BUILDRUNSHIPPLUMBING
Dockerfilecontainerregistrycontainerd
ENTRYPOINTtagnamespace
digest
EXPLANATION

The buckets are grouped by where each term acts in the pipeline, not alphabetically — the same four families the 1.8 bicycle-factory analogy uses, and the same four families this whole guide reuses in every later chapter.

Q12
Docker Desktop claims to run Linux containers on a Mac or Windows laptop. What's actually happening underneath, and why can't Desktop simply run a native Windows container's process directly on that same Linux engine?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Desktop wraps Docker Engine inside a hidden, lightweight Linux VM (WSL2 on Windows, Apple's Virtualization.framework on macOS). Linux containers run inside that hidden VM's Linux kernel. A Windows container needs a Windows kernel — Desktop cannot run one on that same hidden Linux VM; it must switch the whole engine into "Windows containers" mode, which uses a different (Windows-based) backend.

  Your Mac/Windows laptop
  └── 🐳 Docker Desktop
        └── 🐧 hidden Linux VM  ──▶  Linux containers run HERE ✅
              (Windows containers need a Windows kernel — NOT in this VM ❌)
EXPLANATION

This is 1.6's editions table plus 1.3's "kernel must match" rule combined: the hidden VM is why Linux containers work on non-Linux hardware at all, and it's also exactly why "Desktop runs Windows and Linux containers natively at the same time" is a myth — the kernel constraint from 1.3 never goes away, Desktop just hides where the Linux kernel is coming from.

Q13
Your company wants to move a legacy PHP 5.6 job board onto modern cloud infrastructure without rewriting a single line of it. Which real-world use case is this, how does Docker make it possible, and what's the one thing this migration does not automatically fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Legacy modernization. Containerize it with a matching PHP 5.6 Apache base image — the container ships the exact old runtime, so nothing in the app has to change to run on brand-new infrastructure. It does not fix security: containerizing an old app freezes its known vulnerabilities right along with it.

PortabilitySecurity
Containerizing the legacy app✅ Solved — runs anywhere Docker runs❌ NOT solved — old CVEs frozen in too
Needs a separate step—docker scout quickview (Part 7)
EXPLANATION

Portability and security are two separate wins, and Docker only automatically buys you the first one. Scanning and patching the frozen vulnerabilities is a distinct, deliberate step — covered in this guide's Part 7 — not a side effect of containerizing.

Q14
A team needs to run an old Windows-only desktop application, but their entire fleet is Linux servers. Using the 1.3 decision guide, should they reach for a container or a VM here — and why does a container structurally not qualify?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A VM. Containers share the host's kernel (1.3) — a Linux host can only run Linux containers, no matter how the image is built. The Windows app needs an actual Windows kernel underneath it, which only a VM (or a Windows host) can provide.

  Linux fleet + Windows-only app
       │
       ▼
  "Need a DIFFERENT kernel/OS than the host?"  ──YES──▶  🖥️ VM  (the only option)
       │ NO
       ▼
  🐳 Container (not applicable here)
EXPLANATION

This is the first row of 1.3's decision-guide diagram turned into a real scenario: "need a different kernel/OS than the host" is the one case containers structurally cannot solve, regardless of how much lighter they are for everything else.

Q15
Your CI pipeline must produce ONE image that runs correctly on both Apple Silicon (arm64) laptops and x86 (amd64) cloud servers, without maintaining two separate Dockerfiles. Which ecosystem tool solves this, and what's the one-line command?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Buildx 🏗️ — docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v1 . builds one multi-architecture manifest from a single Dockerfile.

  ONE Dockerfile ──buildx--platform──▶  ONE tag, TWO platforms inside
                                          easypj:v1
                                          ├── linux/amd64  (cloud servers)
                                          └── linux/arm64  (Apple Silicon)
EXPLANATION

Straight off the 1.5 "which tool, when" table: multi-platform builds are Buildx's job specifically, distinct from Compose (multi-container) and Scout (vulnerability scanning) — picking the right tool from that table in one step is exactly what the exam rewards.

⚙️ Chapter 1 — Scenario & Command Drills (16)

Exam-style and hands-on — 16 drills that mirror how the DCA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
You type docker ps and the shell replies docker: command not found. What's actually missing, and what's the fastest way to confirm it?
Show Answer
Answer

The Docker CLI isn't installed, or isn't on this shell's PATH — this is purely a client-side problem, nothing to do with a daemon.

confirm the CLI itself is missing
# Is docker anywhere on PATH?
which docker

# If nothing prints, it's genuinely not installed (or not on PATH) —
# install Docker Desktop (laptop) or Engine (server), per 1.6
Explanation

Don't confuse this with "daemon down" (Q2) — a missing binary means the client was never installed. Install the right edition for the machine (1.6): Desktop for a laptop, Engine (CE) for a server.

Q2
docker ps fails with Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running? The CLI itself clearly works. What's broken, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The daemon (dockerd) isn't running, or the client is pointed at the wrong socket. Start it and re-check.

Linux server — start the daemon
sudo systemctl status docker
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

# Confirm Client AND Server both answer now
docker version
Explanation

This is 1.4's architecture diagram made concrete: the CLI is just an API client — if dockerd is down, the client has nothing to talk to over the Unix socket, no matter how correctly it's installed.

Q3
The daemon is confirmed running (a teammate's session works fine), but your session gets permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket. What's different about your user, and how do you fix it without sudo on every command?
Show Answer
Answer

Your user isn't in the docker group, so it lacks permission on /var/run/docker.sock. Add it, then start a fresh login session.

grant socket access
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# Log out and back in (group membership is read at login)
newgrp docker   # or just open a new shell
docker ps       # no sudo needed now
Explanation

Membership in the docker group is effectively root-equivalent on the host — the daemon runs as root, so anyone who can talk to its socket can do anything root can. Grant it deliberately, not by habit.

Q4
You started an easypj container ten minutes ago, but docker ps now shows an empty list. Before assuming it crashed, what's the very next command, and what might it reveal?
Show Answer
Answer

docker ps -a — it lists every container, including stopped/exited ones. docker ps alone only shows running containers.

running vs. everything
docker ps          # empty — nothing RUNNING right now
docker ps -a       # easypj-web   Exited (1) 3 minutes ago
docker logs easypj-web   # read why it exited
Explanation

An empty docker ps is not proof a container is gone — it only proves nothing is currently running. This one-flag habit (-a) prevents a lot of wasted "where did it go?" panic.

Q5
docker pull registry.example.com/team/easypj:v2 fails with pull access denied, repository does not exist or may require authorization. The image name is definitely correct. What's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

You're not authenticated to that private registry. Log in first, then pull.

authenticate to a private registry
docker login registry.example.com
# Username / password (or token) prompt

docker pull registry.example.com/team/easypj:v2   # now succeeds
Explanation

Docker deliberately reports "does not exist or may require authorization" as one message — it never confirms whether a private repo exists to an unauthenticated caller, which is itself a small security feature, not a bug.

Q6
A colleague built easypj:v3 on their Apple Silicon Mac and pushed it. You pull it on an x86 cloud server and docker run fails with exec format error. What actually went wrong, and what's the fix going forward?
Show Answer
Answer

The image was built for arm64 only; the server's CPU is amd64 — the binary inside the image literally cannot execute on that architecture. Rebuild with Buildx targeting both platforms.

build for both architectures at once
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t easypj:v3 --push .

# Verify the manifest actually covers both
docker manifest inspect easypj:v3
Explanation

This is exactly the failure mode 1.5's Buildx row and Lab Q&A Q15 exist to prevent — a single-architecture image is a ticking time bomb the moment your team's hardware isn't uniform.

Q7
A teammate says "easypj works perfectly for me" but it crashes immediately for you with a syntax error Python shouldn't produce. Both of you have Docker installed. Where do you look first, and what's the permanent fix?
Show Answer
Answer

Compare interpreter/dependency versions outside any container first — if either of you is running easypj directly on the host (not inside Docker yet), that's environment drift (1.1), not a Docker bug. The permanent fix is pinning everything inside a Dockerfile so nobody's host Python version matters anymore.

stop trusting the host, pin it in the image
FROM python:3.11-slim   # exact interpreter, not "whatever's on my machine"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt   # exact pinned versions
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
Explanation

"Works on my machine" (1.1) is diagnosed the same way every time: find what's unpinned, then freeze it into the image. Once both of you run the same image, the bug either reproduces for both or it was never an environment issue at all.

Q8
Ops needs to restart the Docker daemon on a production server (sudo systemctl restart docker) to pick up a config change. Will the currently-running easypj containers go down during that restart?
Show Answer
Answer

It depends on live-restore — and it's OFF by default. Out of the box, when dockerd shuts down it stops every running container along with it, so yes, they'd briefly go down and come back once the daemon and its containers restart. Only with live-restore: true explicitly set in daemon.json do containers stay up — parented by their containerd-shim instead of by dockerd — through a restart.

prove the default first, then enable live-restore
# WITHOUT live-restore (the actual default):
docker run -d --name proof nginx
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps   # "proof" is GONE — dockerd stopped it on shutdown

# Enable live-restore, THEN repeat the test:
echo '{"live-restore": true}' | sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker run -d --name proof2 nginx
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps   # "proof2" is still Up — the shim kept it alive this time
Explanation

This is 1.4's daemon-internals chain in action: dockerd → containerd → shim → runc. Without live-restore, dockerd's own shutdown handler proactively stops containers before the shim gets a chance to babysit them alone — that opt-in flag is exactly what changes the outcome, verified hands-on in Practice Drill 1.2.

Q9
Parse myregistry.com:5000/team/easypj:v2 into its four parts (registry, namespace, repository, tag) without looking anything up.
Show Answer
Answer
PartValue
Registrymyregistry.com:5000
Namespaceteam
Repositoryeasypj
Tagv2
Explanation

The chapter's Speed Tips pay off here: read right to left — tag first, then repository, then namespace, then registry — and every gap (no registry given? assume Docker Hub. No namespace? assume library) has a documented default.

Q10
You need to prove, right now, which OCI runtime this engine actually uses underneath — not guess, prove. One command.
Show Answer
Answer
prove the runtime, don't assume it
docker info | grep -i runtime
# Default Runtime: runc
Explanation

Straight from the chapter's Speed Tips. It's almost always runc, but "almost always" isn't "always" — gVisor and Kata Containers are real, less-isolated-by-default alternatives you might find on a hardened host.

Q11
A junior developer insists "a Docker container is basically a lightweight VM." Give ONE command that disproves this directly, and explain what it proves.
Show Answer
Answer
prove there's no guest OS in here
docker run --rm alpine ps aux
# Shows only 1-2 processes — NOT a full OS process tree
# A real VM's `ps aux` would show dozens of boot/OS processes
Explanation

A container has no init system, no boot sequence, no kernel of its own — ps aux inside one shows only what you started, isolated by a PID namespace (1's Under the Hood), on top of the one host kernel. A VM's process list would look nothing like this.

Q12
docker rm easypj-web fails: Error response from daemon: You cannot remove a running container... Stop the container before attempting removal or force remove. What are your two options, and what's at risk if this container was never given a volume?
Show Answer
Answer

Either docker stop first, then docker rm — or force it in one step with docker rm -f. Either way, if no volume was mounted, everything the container wrote is deleted with it.

graceful vs. forced removal
docker stop easypj-web && docker rm easypj-web   # graceful — SIGTERM first
# or, equivalently in one step:
docker rm -f easypj-web                          # SIGKILL, then remove
Explanation

This is 1.2's writable-layer concept plus the chapter Gotchas combined: the running-container guard exists precisely so you don't accidentally destroy that writable layer's data by reflex — -f removes the guard, not the risk.

Q13
You're provisioning a brand-new CI runner (a headless Linux server, no GUI, ever). Which Docker edition do you install, and what's the ONE-command sanity check once it's up?
Show Answer
Answer

Docker Engine (CE) — never Desktop, which is a dev-machine tool with a GUI this headless server will never use (and would need a license for at scale).

sanity-check a fresh Engine install
docker run --rm hello-world   # full pull → create → run → exit path
Explanation

Straight off 1.6's editions table: Desktop's entire value (GUI, WSL2 integration, built-in Kubernetes toggle) targets a single developer's laptop. A CI runner needs the bare engine as a systemd service — nothing else is even running there to click on.

Q14
You docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v3 --push . — how do you actually confirm, from the registry side, that BOTH architectures made it into the pushed image?
Show Answer
Answer
verify the multi-arch manifest, don't just trust the build log
docker buildx imagetools inspect easypj:v3
# Look for TWO platform entries in the output:
#   linux/amd64
#   linux/arm64
Explanation

A successful build log is not proof of a correct manifest. imagetools inspect reads what the registry actually stored — the same check that would have caught Q6's single-architecture mistake before it ever reached a server.

Q15
docker version prints a full Client section but the Server section is missing entirely, with no error. What are the two most likely causes, and which command tells them apart?
Show Answer
Answer

Either (a) the daemon isn't running, or (b) the client is pointed at the wrong socket/host (a stale DOCKER_HOST env var, or a remote context). Check the raw error, not just the summary.

tell the two causes apart
# See the real connection error, not just a blank Server section
docker info

# Is DOCKER_HOST pointing somewhere unexpected?
echo $DOCKER_HOST

# Which context is active?
docker context ls
Explanation

Same root category as Q2, but the client-only output here means the CLI ran fine and simply couldn't reach a daemon — the follow-up commands separate "nothing is listening" from "I'm asking the wrong address."

Q16
A container was docker stopped (not removed) and was never given a volume. Is the data it wrote still recoverable if you docker start it again?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. stop only halts the process — the container object and its writable layer still exist on disk. docker start resumes the exact same container, data intact. Only docker rm destroys the writable layer.

stop/start preserves data — rm does not
docker stop easypj-web    # process halted, writable layer intact
docker start easypj-web   # resumes — same data, same container

docker rm easypj-web      # ❌ THIS is the point of no return, not stop
Explanation

The chapter's data-loss warnings (Q9 in Lab Q&A, this chapter's Gotchas) are specifically about deletion, not stopping. Confusing the two is a common, entirely avoidable mistake — the container lifecycle has real stages between "running" and "gone forever."

🔬 Practice Drill 1.1 — Sketch the Architecture from Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, sketch the 1.4 architecture diagram from memory — label CLI, dockerd, containerd, shim, runc, and the registry — then say out loud which ONE box would still be running if dockerd crashed right now (with live-restore on).

Hint: Trace the chain in one direction only — CLI talks to exactly one thing, and the thing closest to your actual running process is the one that outlives a daemon crash.
View Solution 
  🖥️ Docker CLI  ──REST API──▶  ⚙️ dockerd (daemon)  ──gRPC──▶  📦 containerd
                                       💥 CRASHES                      │
                                  (live-restore: OK, no             ┌──┴──┐
                                   containers touched)          🛡️ shim   🗄️ registry
                                                                     │      (uninvolved,
                                                                🏃 runc      just storage)
                                                                (already exited
                                                                 after creating
                                                                 the container)
                                                                     │
                                                                📦 easypj-web
                                                                 STILL RUNNING ✅

Check yourself: the box still running is the container itself, kept alive by its containerd-shim — not by dockerd, and not by runc (which already exited right after creating the container, per 1.4's daemon-internals chain). If you drew the shim as the container's true parent process, you've got the chain cold — verify it for real in Practice Drill 1.2.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.2 — Prove Live-Restore Is Opt-In, Then Prove It Works

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

On any machine with Docker installed, start a throwaway container and restart the daemon underneath it before touching any config — prove with real commands that it does NOT survive by default. Then enable live-restore and prove the opposite. This is the same behavior Q8's Scenario Drill described; here you make both halves happen yourself.

Hint: Start a container with docker run -d --name proof nginx, restart the daemon, check docker ps — then edit /etc/docker/daemon.json, restart the daemon once to pick up the config, and repeat the test with a fresh container.
View Solution
default OFF, then explicitly ON
# 1. WITHOUT live-restore (the default) — start fresh, restart, check
docker run -d --name proof nginx
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'   # "proof" is GONE — dockerd stopped it on shutdown

# 2. Enable live-restore in the daemon's own config
echo '{"live-restore": true}' | sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json
sudo systemctl restart docker   # picks up the new config

# 3. WITH live-restore — start fresh again, restart, check
docker run -d --name proof2 nginx
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'   # proof2   Up 2 seconds
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'   # proof2   Up 40+ seconds (never restarted!)

docker rm -f proof2   # cleanup

Check yourself: step 1 proves the real default — no flag, no survival. Step 3's "Up" duration kept climbing straight through the daemon restart instead of resetting, because once live-restore: true is set, the container's actual parent process becomes containerd-shim, not dockerd — and only dockerd itself proactively stops containers on shutdown. Skipping straight to step 3 is the mistake that leaves people thinking this is automatic when it never was.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.3 — Do the Density Math

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Using 1.3's stat table (~1.5 GB idle overhead per VM, ~50 MB per container), work out two numbers by hand: (1) how many easypj containers fit in the RAM ONE idle VM wastes before running any app code, and (2) if your team's 8 microservices each need 50 MB as containers, how much total RAM would the SAME 8 services cost as 8 separate VMs instead?

Hint: Part 1 is pure division. Part 2 multiplies each side out separately, then compares the two totals directly.
View Solution
QuestionWorkingAnswer
Containers that fit in 1 VM's idle overhead1.5 GB ÷ 50 MB≈ 30 containers
8 microservices as containers8 × 50 MB400 MB total
Same 8 microservices as 8 VMs8 × 1.5 GB (idle overhead alone)12 GB total

Check yourself: the 8-VM number (12 GB) is pure overhead — before any of the 8 services has done a single unit of real work — versus 400 MB for the same 8 services as containers. That 30x gap is exactly why "just run everything in its own VM" stops being a serious option the moment a team grows past a handful of services.

  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In one line: dependency drift is the disease (1.1), Docker packaging the full userspace into an image/container pair is the cure (1.2), sharing one kernel instead of many is WHY the cure is cheap (1.3), the client-to-runc chain is HOW a single docker run turns an image into a live process (1.4), the ecosystem and editions are WHERE you get that engine depending on laptop or server (1.5-1.6), and OCI is the guarantee that everything you just built travels — untouched — into every chapter after this one, including the day this guide reaches Kubernetes (1.9).

The takeaway: nothing here is Docker-proprietary magic — it's an open standard (OCI) implemented by a specific, inspectable chain of components (dockerd → containerd → runc), running on kernel primitives (namespaces + cgroups) any Linux admin can go look at directly.

Chapter 2 · Docker Core Concepts — Images, Containers & Registries

Now that you understand why Docker exists, let's dive into the what — the fundamental building blocks: Images, Containers, Registries, Layers, and Tags. These five concepts form the foundation of everything you'll do with Docker.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📖 Core Concepts

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The difference between Images (blueprints) and Containers (running instances)
  • ✅ How image layers work and why they make builds fast
  • ✅ How registries store and distribute images
  • ✅ Container lifecycle — created, running, paused, stopped, deleted
  • ✅ Tagging strategies and multi-architecture images
  • ✅ Configuring the Docker daemon via daemon.json
🎓 DCA Relevance
Image Creation, Management & Registry 20%
🎯 This Chapter IS the Graded Domain

Chapter 1 told you WHY Docker exists; this one hands you the five nouns everything else conjugates: image, container, registry, layer, tag. This chapter maps almost section-for-section onto the Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%) domain — image references, layers/caching, tags, manifests, and registries are graded directly.

  • A full image reference is registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest — every omitted part defaults; only the digest is immutable.
  • Cache rule: a layer reuses only if EVERY layer before it matched too.
  • daemon.json (2.7) also feeds Installation & Configuration-domain questions about host-level daemon configuration.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 2 Learning Arc

The seven stops below build on each other in strict order: a blueprint (2.1) only matters once you can run it as a live instance (2.2); that instance had to come FROM somewhere, which is what a registry is for (2.3); registries and rebuilds are fast because of cached layers (2.4); tags and digests (2.5) are how anyone — human or machine — points at one exact image; a manifest list (2.6) lets one tag fan out across CPU architectures; and daemon.json (2.7) is the single file deciding how every container on this host behaves once it's running.

2.1 Docker Images — The Blueprint

A Docker image is a read-only template containing your application code, runtime, libraries, environment variables, and configuration files. Think of an image as a class in programming — it's a blueprint. A container is an instance of that class — a running object.

Images are identified by repository:tag (e.g., easypj:v1.0, python:3.11-slim). If no tag is specified, Docker defaults to :latest.

Image vs Container — Class vs Object Analogy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            📦 IMAGE (Blueprint)  →  ▶️  CONTAINER (Running Instance)       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │  Class in Python:       │         │  Object in Python:       │        │
  │  │  class Car:             │         │  my_car = Car()          │        │
  │  │      wheels = 4         │ create  │  my_car.wheels → 4       │        │
  │  │      color = "red"      │────────▶│  my_car.start()          │        │
  │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │  Docker Image:          │         │  Docker Container:       │        │
  │  │  easypj:v1.0            │ docker  │  docker run easypj:v1.0  │        │
  │  │  (read-only layers)     │  run    │  (read-write layer on    │        │
  │  │  stored on disk         │────────▶│   top, running process)  │        │
  │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧬 Analogy — Tag Is a Name Plate, Digest Is DNA

The class/object picture above explains the image↔container relationship; tags and digests explain how you point at a specific class. A tag is a sticky note stuck on the class definition — anyone can peel it off and stick it on a different class tomorrow. A digest (sha256:…) is that class's DNA — content-addressed, so the same digest can only ever mean the exact same bytes, forever.

✅
Official Images

Curated by Docker's Docker Official Images program (e.g. python, nginx, postgres, redis) — reviewed for best-practice Dockerfiles, regularly rebuilt for security patches, and continuously scanned. They live under docker.io/library/… with no namespace — exactly why python:3.11-slim needs no username in front of it.

👤
Community / Personal Images

Anyone can push docker.io/anyuser/anything:tag — no vetting, no guaranteed rebuild cadence, no security review. Fine for experimentation; treat as untrusted for anything you'll run in production until you've read the Dockerfile yourself or scanned it (see Chapter 8's image scanning).

Every image also carries an immutable digest — a SHA256 hash computed from its content. Two builds that produce byte-identical layers get the SAME digest even under different tags; change a single byte and the digest changes completely. docker.io/you/easypj:v1.0 is convenient to type; ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:3f29a1c... is what a production deployment should actually pin — no one can silently repoint a digest the way they can repoint a tag.

📍 The Full Syntax, Piece by Piece

The complete grammar is REGISTRY[:PORT]/NAMESPACE/REPOSITORY:TAG@DIGEST — every part except REPOSITORY has a default. A self-hosted or on-cluster registry is commonly reached through an explicit port, e.g. localhost:5000/easypj:v1 or registry.internal:5000/team/easypj:v1. Docker tells a registry host from a Docker Hub namespace by one rule: if the first segment before the first / contains a . or a :, or is literally localhost, it's treated as REGISTRY[:PORT] — otherwise Docker assumes docker.io and treats that first segment as your NAMESPACE. This is exactly why easypj:v1 and myuser/easypj:v1 both resolve to Docker Hub, while registry.internal:5000/easypj:v1 does not.

🧪 Practice — Compare Tag, Digest & Image ID

docker pull python:3.11-slim, then docker images --digests. Verify: you can point at the repository, tag, digest, and IMAGE ID columns and state in one sentence how each one differs from the others.

2.2 Docker Containers — The Running Instance

A container is a runnable instance of an image. You can create, start, stop, move, or delete a container using the Docker CLI. Containers are ephemeral by design — treat them like cattle, not pets. If one dies, you spin up a new one from the same image.

Key characteristics: containers are isolated (process, network, filesystem, and IPC — each container gets its own PID namespace, network namespace, mount namespace, and inter-process-communication namespace), lightweight (share host kernel), and portable (run anywhere Docker runs).

Container Lifecycle State Machine
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 CONTAINER LIFECYCLE                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │ 📦 IMAGE ──docker create──▶ ▶️ CREATED ──docker start──▶ ▶️ RUNNING       │
  │(blueprint)                (on disk, not started)         (process active)│
  │                                                                          │
  │ RUNNING ──┬── docker pause ─────────────▶ ⏸️  PAUSED (frozen)            │
  │           │                                     │                        │
  │           │                              docker unpause                  │
  │           │                                     ▼                        │
  │           │                              (loops back to RUNNING)         │
  │           │                                                              │
  │           ├── docker stop (SIGTERM) ────▶ ⏹️  STOPPED                    │
  │           │                               (Exited 0 or 143)              │
  │           │                                     │                        │
  │           └── docker kill (SIGKILL) ─────▶ (also lands here — Exited 137)│
  │                                                   │                      │
  │                                             docker rm                    │
  │                                                   ▼                      │
  │                                             💀 DELETED (gone)             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The diagram above stops at PAUSED/STOPPED/DELETED, but two arrows loop back to RUNNING: docker unpause thaws a paused container exactly where it froze, and docker start restarts a stopped one (same writable layer, same filesystem state — only the process re-launches). The full command → mechanism → resulting-state map:

CommandMechanismFrom → To
docker createAllocates filesystem + config, no process started(none) → Created
docker startLaunches PID 1 inside the prepared filesystemCreated / Stopped → Running
docker stopSIGTERM, then SIGKILL after --time (default 10s) — gracefulRunning → Stopped (Exited 0 or 143)
docker killSIGKILL immediately — no grace periodRunning → Stopped (Exited 137)
docker pausecgroup freezer — process never even sees a signalRunning → Paused (frozen)
docker unpausecgroup freezer releasedPaused → Running
docker rmDeletes the writable layer + metadata permanentlyStopped → Deleted (gone)
🏢 Analogy — Leaving the Building Three Different Ways

docker stop is "please save your work and leave the building" — the process gets a chance to finish and exit cleanly. docker kill is cutting the power — whatever was mid-flight is gone, no goodbye. docker pause is stopping time in the room — nothing finishes, nothing is lost, everyone is simply frozen until docker unpause lets the clock run again.

🔬 easypj: docker stop easypj-web lets gunicorn finish any in-flight job-post request before exiting (graceful, exit code 0 or 143); docker kill easypj-web drops those same requests mid-response (exit code 137 = 128 + SIGKILL's signal number 9).

🧪 Practice — Watch Every State Transition

Run docker run -d --name lc-demo nginx, then walk it through stop → start → pause → unpause → kill, checking docker ps -a's STATUS column after each move. Verify: Exited (0) after stop, Up ... (Paused) after pause, and Exited (137) after kill.

2.3 Docker Registries — The Storage

A registry is a storage and content delivery system for Docker images. You push images to a registry and pull them from it. Docker Hub is the default public registry, but enterprises typically use private registries.

Docker Registry Push/Pull Workflow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🗄️ DOCKER REGISTRY WORKFLOW                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │   DEVELOPER LAPTOP                      🗄️ REGISTRY                      │
  │   ┌────────────────┐                ┌────────────────────┐              │
