🗄️ Docker Registry (OSS) vs. Harbor — Not the Same Thing

The plain, self-hosted Docker Registry is the open-source distribution/distribution project — you get it running with one command, docker run -d -p 5000:5000 registry:2, and it speaks nothing but the registry HTTP API (push/pull, no UI, no RBAC, no scanning). Harbor is a separate CNCF project that wraps a registry with a web UI, role-based access control, image vulnerability scanning, and replication — it's the "GitHub Enterprise" layered on top of plain "git-daemon." Reach for the bare registry for a quick lab or air-gapped CI cache; reach for Harbor when a team needs auth, audit, and scanning around it.

🚦 Docker Hub Pull Rate Limits — the CI Gotcha

Docker Hub throttles image pulls (not pushes) on a rolling 6-hour window: 100 pulls / 6h for anonymous, unauthenticated requests — counted per IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 subnet, which is exactly why a shared office network or a pool of CI runners behind one NAT IP burns through it fast — 200 pulls / 6h for an authenticated free Docker Hub (Personal) account, and unlimited pulls on Pro, Team, and Business plans. Hitting the ceiling returns HTTP 429. In CI/CD the usual fixes are a docker login with a service account (jumps you from 100→200/6h immediately) or routing pulls through a pull-through cache via registry-mirrors (2.7) so only the cache itself counts against Docker Hub's limit.

🐙 Analogy — A Registry Is GitHub for Images

Docker Hub is the public GitHub of images: anyone can pull. ECR/GCR/ACR/Harbor are the company's private Git server: only your team can push/pull, and traffic never leaves your network. docker push/docker pull are git push/git pull — and just like unchanged files are never re-uploaded to Git, unchanged layers are never re-uploaded to a registry. That dedup is exactly what the workflow diagram above is showing.

🔬 easypj: docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 && docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 — the python:3.11-slim base layers are almost certainly already on the registry from someone else's push, so only easypj's own COPY/RUN layers actually travel.

⚠️ The Image Name Decides the Destination

easypj:v1 implicitly means docker.io/library/easypj:v1 — you cannot docker push easypj:v1 straight to ghcr.io without re-tagging it ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 first. The registry hostname lives INSIDE the image reference, not as a separate push argument.

🧪 Practice — Prove the Dedup

Push easypj:v1 twice in a row with no changes in between. Verify: the second push prints Layer already exists for every single layer — nothing actually re-uploads.

2.4 Image Layers — The Secret to Docker's Speed

Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer. Layers are stacked to form the final image. Layers are cached — if a layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses it instead of rebuilding. This is why Docker builds are so fast after the first one.

Docker Image Layer Cake — easypj Example
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Layer 6 (R/W): Container Writable Layer      │  ← Container-only (ephemeral!)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 5: CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:app"] │  ← Startup command (~0 bytes)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 4: COPY . /app/                        │  ← Your code! (~500 KB)
  │  (models.py, views.py, urls.py, settings.py)  │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 3: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt │  ← Dependencies (~80 MB)
  │  (Django 5.2, gunicorn, psycopg2, etc.)      │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 2: COPY requirements.txt .             │  ← Deps list (~200 bytes)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 1: FROM python:3.11-slim               │  ← Base image (~150 MB)
  │  (Debian 12 + Python 3.11)                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Layer Caching Strategy

Order your Dockerfile from LEAST to MOST frequently changing. Copy requirements.txt BEFORE copying your source code. This way, when you change your code (Layer 4), Layers 1-3 remain cached — saving minutes of rebuild time!

Layer Caching — Why Order Matters (Bad vs Good)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🏎️ LAYER CACHING — WHY ORDER MATTERS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BAD ORDER (cache useless after code change):                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/              │ ❌ REBUILT (code changed!)       │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .   │ ❌ REBUILT (previous layer       │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req..  │ ❌ REBUILT  changed!)            │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GOOD ORDER (only changed layers rebuilt):                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .   │ ✅ CACHED (same requirements)    │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req..  │ ✅ CACHED (same install)         │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/              │ ❌ REBUILT (only code changed!) │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RESULT: Good order = 3 layers cached (fast!), Bad order = 3 rebuilt     │
  │  For easypj: Good build ≈ 3 seconds (only code changed)                  │
  │              Bad build ≈ 45 seconds (pip install reruns)                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 The Cache Invalidation Rule

If layer N changes, layers N, N+1, N+2… ALL rebuild — Docker never asks whether a later layer actually depends on the earlier one, it just invalidates everything downstream. For easypj's good order (base → requirements.txt → pip install → code), roughly 99% of day-to-day changes land in the last layer alone: 3 layers get their cache checked, only 1 gets rebuilt.

🍰 Analogy — You Can't Swap a Middle Layer of a Cake

Back to the layer cake diagram above: you cannot pull out and replace a middle layer without re-baking every layer stacked above it — frosting included. The BAD/GOOD ORDER boxes above are that same cake baked two different ways: identical ingredients, wildly different rebuild cost depending on which layer you frosted (changed) last.

🧪 Practice — Watch the Cache Boundary Move

Build easypj twice back-to-back (second build should print CACHED for every step). Then touch one .py file and rebuild. Verify: every step up through RUN pip install still prints CACHED; only COPY . /app/ and later steps actually re-run.

2.5 Tags and Versioning

A tag is a human-readable label for a specific version of an image. The :latest tag is convenient but dangerous — it always points to the most recent build, which can cause unexpected changes in production.

StrategyExampleProsCons
Semantic Versioningeasypj:1.2.3Clear, predictableManual tagging
Git Commit SHAeasypj:abc1234Traceable to codeNot human-friendly
Date-basedeasypj:2026-06-12ChronologicalNo semantic meaning
Environmenteasypj:stagingClear intentMutable (changes over time)
Combinedeasypj:1.4.2-a1b2c3dBest of both — human-readable AND exactly traceableLonger tag string
🚪 Analogy — Name Plate vs Fingerprint

A tag is the name plate on an office door; a digest is the occupant's fingerprint. People swap offices all the time — the name plate on "Room 204" might read a different name next month. Fingerprints don't change. If you need to prove exactly WHO is in the room right now, you check the fingerprint, not the door.

🧪 Practice — One Image ID, Three Tags

Tag one build as 1.0.0 AND latest AND its git SHA in the same docker build, then run docker images | grep easypj. Verify: one IMAGE ID, three tag rows, zero extra disk used — tags are free pointers to the same layers.

2.6 Docker Manifest and Multi-Architecture Images

A manifest is a JSON file that describes an image — its layers, digests, architecture, and OS. Multi-architecture images use a manifest list to point to different platform-specific images. One tag (easypj:v1) can serve linux/amd64, linux/arm64, and windows/amd64 — Docker automatically pulls the right one for your platform.

One Tag, Many Platforms — Manifest List
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             $ docker pull easypj:v1                       │
  │                        │                                  │
  │              ┌─────────▼─────────┐                        │
  │              │   MANIFEST LIST   │  ("fat manifest")      │
  │              │   easypj:v1       │                        │
  │              └─────┬───────┬─────┘                        │
  │        linux/amd64 │       │ linux/arm64                  │
  │            ┌───────▼──┐ ┌──▼───────┐                      │
  │            │ manifest │ │ manifest │                      │
  │            │ + layers │ │ + layers │                      │
  │            └──────────┘ └──────────┘                      │
  │   Your CPU architecture decides which one downloads.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📚 Analogy — One Book Title, Many Translations

You ask the shop for "easypj v1" and are handed the edition printed in YOUR language — the title on the cover never changes, only the edition that lands in your hands. That's a manifest list: one tag on the spine, per-architecture "translations" (amd64, arm64…) behind it, and the registry hands you the one that matches your machine.

📖 Buildx for Multi-Arch

Use docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v1 . to build a single tag that works on both Intel/AMD and Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) machines. This is essential for modern development teams with mixed hardware. Buildx builds non-native platforms via QEMU emulation, registered automatically by Docker Desktop — an arm64 layer built on an amd64 CI runner is a REAL, fully functional image, just noticeably slower to produce than a native build. Docker's own build docs are explicit that emulation trades speed for correctness: for genuinely compute-heavy builds (large compilations, dense RUN steps) the recommended pattern is a buildx builder pool with one REAL node per architecture, or cross-compiling inside the Dockerfile, rather than leaning on QEMU for the slow part.

StepSingle-ArchMulti-Arch (Buildx)
BuilderDefault builderdocker buildx create --use
Builddocker build -t easypj:v1 .--platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64
Pushdocker push easypj:v1append --push to the buildx command
Registry result1 manifest, 1 platformmanifest list + N per-platform images
ARM pull risk"exec format error"Correct architecture auto-picked
Audit commanddocker image inspectdocker manifest inspect
🧪 Practice — Count the Platforms

docker manifest inspect python:3.11-slim and count how many platforms are listed. Verify: linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 both appear.

📌 Two Different --platform Flags — Don't Confuse Them

docker buildx build --platform ... (above) is for building — it decides which architectures get produced and pushed into the manifest list. A separate flag, docker pull --platform linux/arm64 easypj:v1 (or docker run --platform ...), is for pulling/running — it forces Docker to fetch one specific entry out of an existing manifest list, overriding the auto-detected host architecture. This is the tool for deliberately testing an arm64 image on an amd64 laptop (via QEMU emulation) without touching the build pipeline at all.

2.7 Docker Daemon Configuration — daemon.json Deep Dive

The Docker daemon is configured via /etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux. This single JSON file controls logging, storage, networking, security, and runtime behavior. Invalid JSON = daemon won't start. The DCA Installation & Configuration domain (15%) tests this heavily.

🏘️ Analogy — daemon.json Is the Building's House Rules

daemon.json is the apartment building's house rules: every tenant (container) inherits them automatically, and changing the rules requires a building-wide meeting (a daemon restart) — everyone feels it at once. live-restore: true is the clause letting tenants stay home during that meeting instead of being evicted onto the street while it's in session.

daemon.json — Complete Configuration Map
  /etc/docker/daemon.json
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  {                                                         │
  │    // ── LOGGING ──                                        │
  │    "log-driver": "json-file",     // json-file|syslog|     │
  │    "log-opts": {                  //   journald|gelf|      │
  │      "max-size": "10m",           //   fluentd|awslogs|    │
  │      "max-file": "3",             //   splunk|gcplogs      │
  │      "labels": "env,service"                               │
  │    },                                                      │
  │    // ── STORAGE ──                                        │
  │    "storage-driver": "overlay2",  // overlay2|btrfs|zfs|   │
  │    "storage-opts": [               //   devicemapper|vfs   │
  │      "overlay2.override_kernel_check=true"                 │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    "data-root": "/var/lib/docker",// Custom data directory │
  │    // ── NETWORKING ──                                     │
  │    "icc": false,                  // Inter-container comm  │
  │    "dns": ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"],                         │
  │    "dns-search": ["example.com"],                          │
  │    "bip": "172.17.0.1/16",       // Default bridge IP      │
  │    "default-address-pools": [                              │
  │      {"base": "10.10.0.0/16", "size": 24}                 │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    // ── SECURITY ──                                       │
  │    "userns-remap": "default",     // User namespace remap  │
  │    "live-restore": true,          // Keep containers alive │
  │    "tls": true,                   // Daemon TLS            │
  │    "tlscert": "/etc/docker/cert.pem",                      │
  │    "tlskey": "/etc/docker/key.pem",                        │
  │    "tlsverify": true,                                      │
  │    // ── REGISTRY ──                                       │
  │    "registry-mirrors": [                                   │
  │      "https://mirror.gcr.io"                               │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    "insecure-registries": [                                │
  │      "my-registry:5000"                                    │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    // ── RUNTIME ──                                        │
  │    "default-runtime": "runc",                              │
  │    "runtimes": {                                           │
  │      "nvidia": {"path": "nvidia-container-runtime"}       │
  │    },                                                      │
  │    "default-ulimits": {                                    │
  │      "nofile": {"Name": "nofile", "Hard": 64000}         │
  │    }                                                       │
  │  }                                                         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
Logging Drivers

json-file (default): logs to host disk. syslog: central syslog server. journald: systemd journal. gelf: Graylog. fluentd: EFK stack. awslogs/splunk/gcplogs: cloud-native. Set rotation: {"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"} to prevent disk exhaustion.

💾
Storage Drivers

overlay2: default, recommended for all modern kernels. devicemapper: RHEL7 legacy, needs direct-lvm for production. btrfs/zfs: advanced snapshots. vfs: no CoW, testing only. aufs: overlay2's predecessor on old Ubuntu/Debian hosts — deprecated, not selectable on modern kernels. Check current: docker info | grep "Storage Driver". Changing loses all data.

🔒
Security Config

userns-remap: container root maps to high UID on host. icc: false: blocks inter-container communication on default bridge. live-restore: true: containers survive daemon restart. tlsverify: true: mutual TLS for Docker API. no-new-privileges: block privilege escalation.

⚠️ Critical: live-restore

Without "live-restore": true in daemon.json, restarting the Docker daemon (systemctl restart docker) KILLS all running containers. With live-restore, containers keep running during daemon updates or crashes. This is essential for production — set it in every production daemon.json. Docker Desktop enables it by default.

daemon.json KeyValuesDCA Exam Context
log-driverjson-file, syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, splunk, gcplogsConfigure logging for production; set rotation to prevent disk full
log-opts{"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"}Prevent unbounded log growth; json-file default has no rotation
storage-driveroverlay2 (default), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfsoverlay2 for all modern kernels; devicemapper needs direct-lvm
data-root/var/lib/docker (default) or custom pathMove Docker data to separate partition/disk
icctrue (default), falsefalse = containers on default bridge cannot communicate
userns-remap"default" or "username:userns"Container root → host high UID; strongest user isolation
live-restoretrue, false (default)Keep containers alive when daemon stops/restarts
registry-mirrors["https://mirror.example.com"]Cache Docker Hub images locally; reduces pull latency
insecure-registries["my-registry:5000"]Allow HTTP (non-HTTPS) registries; testing only
tlsverifytrue/falseEnable mutual TLS for Docker daemon API (port 2376)
default-address-pools[{"base":"10.10.0.0/16","size":24}]Control subnet allocation for custom networks
daemon.json DCA Checklist: 1. Know default location: /etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux — the same file exists at %programdata%\docker\config\daemon.json on native Windows, and at $HOME/.docker/daemon.json under Docker Desktop. 2. Always validate JSON: python3 -m json.tool /etc/docker/daemon.json, or let dockerd check it for you with dockerd --validate (returns non-zero on a bad file without ever starting the daemon). 3. Restart to apply most keys: sudo systemctl restart docker. 4. docker info shows active config. 5. Bad JSON = daemon won't start (check journalctl -u docker). 6. Docker Desktop: the Docker Engine settings tab IS a raw JSON editor for this exact file — editing it by hand (there or in a text editor) is the intended workflow, not something the UI hides from you. 7. A handful of keys — live-restore, registry-mirrors, insecure-registries, max-concurrent-downloads/max-concurrent-uploads, debug, labels — apply live with zero downtime via sudo systemctl reload docker (SIGHUP); most others, like storage-driver, still demand the full restart from step 3.
🧪 Practice — Prove live-restore Without Notes

Apply a daemon.json with log-opts rotation and "live-restore": true, start a long-running nginx container, then sudo systemctl restart docker. Run docker info | grep -A2 "Logging Driver" afterward. Verify: json-file shows your rotation limits AND the nginx container never stopped running — that's live-restore, proven, not just read about.

🔧 Under the Hood — how the five nouns actually work: digests, kernel signals, the registry wire protocol & overlay2

Every noun in this chapter is a friendly name for a precise mechanism underneath. A digest isn't a random ID — it's computed math. A "push" isn't magic — it's a small, well-defined HTTP protocol. docker stop isn't guaranteed to work — it depends on a Linux kernel quirk almost nobody knows about. This section walks each of 2.1–2.7's nouns down to the metal, in the same order you met them.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Dockerfile → BUILD → layers (① content digests) → IMAGE (① manifest)    │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼ docker push  (③ registry HTTP API v2 — blobs, then manifest)    │
  │  REGISTRY  ◀──────────────────────── docker pull ─────────────────────── │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼ docker run                                                      │
  │  RUNNING CONTAINER — filesystem = ④ overlay2 CoW; one tag can mean       │
  │  ⑤ several platforms; every command above obeys ⑥ daemon.json            │
  │  and every stop/kill/pause obeys ② the kernel's signal rules             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
① Content-Addressable Storage — how a digest is actually computed

2.1 said two byte-identical builds get the SAME digest even under different tags. Here's why: a digest is never invented, it's computed FROM content. Each layer's compressed tarball is hashed (SHA256) to get that layer's own digest. The image's config blob — a JSON document holding env vars, entrypoint/cmd, history, and the uncompressed digest of every layer (its diff_id) — is hashed separately. Finally the manifest, a JSON document that simply lists the config blob's digest and every layer's digest in order, is itself hashed — and THAT hash is the digest docker pull image@sha256:… pins.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MANIFEST  (application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json)        │
  │  {                                                                        │
  │    "config": { "digest": "sha256:c3fa19e...", "size": 8433 },  ◀── the   │
  │    "layers": [                                              config blob  │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:a1b2c3d...", "size": 157326671 },  ← FROM ...   │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:9c8d7e6...", "size": 194 },        ← COPY req.  │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:7e6f5a4...", "size": 83912011 },   ← RUN pip .. │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:5d4c3b2...", "size": 512040 }      ← COPY . .   │
  │    ]                                                                      │
  │  }                                                                        │
  │        │  sha256(exactly these bytes — key order and all)               │
  │        ▼                                                                  │
  │  sha256:3f29a1c9...  ◀── THIS is what @digest pins. Change ANY byte      │
  │                          above — even reordering keys — and it changes.  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
BlobContainsIts digest covers
Layer blobcompressed tar of the files that one Dockerfile instruction added/changedonly that layer's own bytes
Config blobenv, entrypoint/cmd, build history, every layer's uncompressed diff_idthe image's runtime config, not file bytes directly
Manifestordered pointers (digests) to the config blob + every layer blobthe WHOLE image — this is the digest you pull, pin, or see in docker images --digests
🔑 This is also why docker tag is instant and free — it never touches a single content byte, it only writes a new name→digest pointer locally (or, on push, on the registry). A tag (2.5) is just a mutable label pointing AT one of these immutable manifest digests; move the label and the digest underneath doesn't change at all.
② Container Lifecycle at the Kernel Level — SIGTERM, SIGKILL, the cgroup freezer & the PID-1 signal trap

2.2's table said stop=SIGTERM, kill=SIGKILL, pause=cgroup freezer. Each is a genuinely different kernel mechanism, and one of them hides a trap that silently breaks graceful shutdown in a huge number of real images:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  docker stop app        docker kill app        docker pause app         │
  │       │                      │                       │                  │
  │       ▼                      ▼                       ▼                  │
  │  SIGTERM → PID 1        SIGKILL → PID 1        cgroup FREEZER            │
  │  wait --time (10s       dies immediately —       (cgroup.freeze=1)       │
  │  default), then still   no grace, no cleanup,    suspended by the        │
  │  up? → SIGKILL           in-flight work lost      SCHEDULER — no signal  │
  │       │                                            delivered AT ALL,     │
  │       ▼                                            the process never     │
  │  exit 0 (clean) or                                 even knows it froze   │
  │  143 (128+15, SIGKILL   exit 137 (128+9)                                 │
  │  fallback fired)                                                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Here's the trap: on Linux, a signal's default action is skipped for PID 1 unless PID 1 explicitly installs a handler for it (SIGKILL/SIGSTOP are the only exceptions — nothing can block those). Your app, run bare with docker run myapp, IS PID 1 inside its own PID namespace. If it's a plain script or framework that never calls signal.signal(SIGTERM, …), the kernel simply swallows the SIGTERM that docker stop sends — nothing happens, the app doesn't know, and Docker burns the ENTIRE grace period every single time before finally landing SIGKILL.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  $ docker run myapp        your app IS PID 1 — no handler for SIGTERM?  │
  │     python app.py           the kernel skips the default action.        │
  │                              docker stop always burns the full 10s.     │
  │                                                                            │
  │  $ docker run --init myapp  docker-init (tini) becomes REAL PID 1;      │
  │                              your app runs as PID 2 — tini forwards      │
  │                              SIGTERM to it AND reaps zombie children.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ActionSignal / mechanismGrace periodKernel-level detail
docker stopSIGTERM, then SIGKILL--time (default 10s)Ordinary signal delivery — but the PID-1 exemption above can swallow it entirely
docker killSIGKILL (or --signal)noneUnblockable, unhandleable, no exemption applies
docker pausecgroup freezer (v1 freezer.state, v2 cgroup.freeze)n/aScheduler-level suspend — no signal is ever delivered
docker run --initadds tini as real PID 1n/aFixes both the PID-1 exemption AND orphaned-zombie reaping
🔑 If a container ALWAYS takes the full grace period to stop — never faster, even when idle — suspect the PID-1 exemption before you suspect a hung process. Add --init (or a real init like tini/dumb-init inside the image) to any app that doesn't explicitly trap SIGTERM itself.
③ The Registry Wire Protocol — HTTP API v2, blobs & why dedup is automatic

2.3's practice drill said pushing an unchanged image twice prints Layer already exists for every layer. That message is literally the client reporting the result of one HTTP request per blob — the Docker Registry HTTP API V2 is built entirely around "ask before you upload":

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            $ docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1                          │
  │                                                                            │
  │  for EACH blob (config + every layer), the client asks FIRST:            │
  │    HEAD /v2/you/easypj/blobs/sha256:a1b2...   ◀── "do you have this?"   │
  │       200 OK  →  SKIP upload  ("Layer already exists")                  │
  │       404     →  upload it:                                             │
  │         POST /v2/you/easypj/blobs/uploads/       → 202 + upload URL     │
  │         PATCH <upload URL>   (stream the bytes, chunk by chunk)        │
  │         PUT   <upload URL>?digest=sha256:a1b2...  → 201 Created         │
  │                                                                            │
  │  once every referenced blob exists on the registry:                     │
  │    PUT /v2/you/easypj/manifests/v1   { the manifest JSON from ① }       │
  │       registry checks every digest it names actually exists → 201        │
  │       response header: Docker-Content-Digest: sha256:3f29a1c...          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
EndpointVerbPurpose
/v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>HEADDoes the registry already have this EXACT blob? (the dedup check)
/v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/POSTStart a new blob upload session
/v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/<uuid>PATCH / PUTStream the blob's bytes, then finalize with ?digest=
/v2/<name>/manifests/<tag-or-digest>GET / PUTFetch or publish the manifest itself
🔑 The HEAD check IS the dedup — nothing clever happens server-side. python:3.11-slim's base layers are already on ghcr.io from someone else's push (2.3), so their HEAD requests return 200 and easypj's push skips them entirely; only the layers whose digest the registry has never seen actually PATCH/PUT any bytes.
④ Copy-on-Write & Union Filesystems (Overlay2)
🗺️ How Docker Stores Images Efficiently

Docker uses two key Linux technologies to make images fast and space-efficient:

Copy-on-Write (CoW) — When a container modifies a file from the image, Docker doesn't copy the entire image. Instead, it copies ONLY the specific file being modified to the container's writable layer. This means 100 containers from the same image share 99.9% of the storage — only their changes take extra space.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   📋 COPY-ON-WRITE (CoW) IN ACTION                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Image Layers (READ-ONLY, shared)       Container Layer (READ-WRITE)      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ /app/models.py   ← SHARED │       │ (no copy needed!)           │   │
  │  │ /app/views.py    ← SHARED │       │                             │   │
  │  │ /usr/lib/python  ← SHARED │       │                             │   │
  │  │ /etc/os-release  ← SHARED │──COPY▶│ /etc/os-release (modified)  │   │
  │  │                  100 containers     │ ← ONLY this file copied!    │   │
  │  │                  share these!       │   (rest still shared)       │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Union Filesystem (Overlay2) — The default storage driver. It "stacks" the read-only image layers and the read-write container layer into a single unified view. The container sees one filesystem, but it's actually composed of multiple layers. Overlay2 uses:

  • LowerDir — The read-only image layers (your Dockerfile instructions)
  • UpperDir — The writable container layer (changes made at runtime)
  • Merged — The unified view the container sees (LowerDir + UpperDir combined)
  • WorkDir — Internal working directory for Overlay2 operations

Docker's default storage driver, overlay2, stacks read-only image layers and one writable container layer into a SINGLE merged view using the kernel's OverlayFS:

  • lowerdir = the read-only image layers (the "layer cake" from 2.4), stacked, never written to again.
  • upperdir = the container's one writable layer — every new or changed file the running process creates lands here.
  • workdir = OverlayFS-internal scratch space.
  • merged = the single view the container's process actually sees — reads fall through top-to-bottom to the first layer that has the file; writes always go to upperdir.

Changing a file that exists in a lower (read-only) layer triggers copy-on-write: the file is copied UP into upperdir first, then modified there — the original lower-layer bytes are untouched, which is exactly why many containers can share the same image layers on disk simultaneously.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  upperdir  (writable) │ logs/, /tmp/*  ← new files land HERE      │
  ├───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  lowerdir  (RO, top)  │ COPY . /app/         (your code)          │
  │  lowerdir  (RO)       │ RUN pip install...   (dependencies)       │
  │  lowerdir  (RO, base) │ FROM python:3.11-slim                     │
  ├───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  merged    = what the container's process sees as "/"            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
docker inspect key (.GraphDriver.Data)Role
LowerDircolon-separated list of read-only layer paths, top layer first
UpperDirthis ONE container's writable layer on the host disk
WorkDirOverlayFS-internal scratch space — never touch it directly
MergedDirthe actual mount point the container's / resolves to
⚠️ docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <container> prints the real LowerDir/UpperDir/MergedDir/WorkDir paths on the host — useful the day you need to prove where a "missing" file actually went.
⑤ Manifest Lists / OCI Image Index — the JSON buildx actually pushes

2.6 showed the manifest list as a routing diagram. Underneath, it's the exact same JSON+SHA256 pattern as ① — just one extra layer of indirection, with a platform field added to each entry so the daemon can pick the right one:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MANIFEST LIST (app/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json,       │
  │                  or the OCI-native app/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json)      │
  │  {                                                                        │
  │    "schemaVersion": 2,                                                   │
  │    "manifests": [                                                        │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:aaa111...",                                     │
  │        "platform": { "architecture": "amd64", "os": "linux" } },        │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:bbb222...",                                     │
  │        "platform": { "architecture": "arm64", "os": "linux",            │
  │                       "variant": "v8" } }                                │
  │    ]                                                                      │
  │  }                                                                        │
  │        each digest above IS an ordinary single-platform manifest (①) —   │
  │        this list is nothing more than one more level of pointer.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
StepWhat buildx does
1. Build each platformone full image (config + layers + manifest) per --platform value, via QEMU emulation for non-native ones
2. Push each manifestevery platform's manifest and blobs are pushed individually, using ③'s protocol
3. Push the listone manifest list referencing all of them is published under the shared tag
4. Client pullsthe daemon reads the host's own OS/architecture and picks the ONE matching entry
🔑 The "exec format error" gotcha, explained precisely: the daemon's platform-pick logic only runs if the tag actually resolves to a manifest LIST. Push a single-arch image under a tag someone expects to be multi-arch, and there's no list to choose from — Docker hands over the one manifest it has, and the kernel refuses to execute a binary built for the wrong CPU.
⑥ Inside daemon.json — startup parsing & why storage drivers aren't interchangeable

A daemon.json key that's also passed as a CLI flag to dockerd is a fatal conflict, not a merge — flagged in this chapter's Gotchas box below. Here's why: at startup, dockerd reads the file, parses it as JSON (any syntax error aborts immediately), then validates every key against its own flag set — if a key is ALSO supplied on the command line, dockerd refuses to guess which one wins and exits rather than silently picking one:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  $ sudo systemctl start docker                                           │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼  1. read /etc/docker/daemon.json                                │
  │  bad JSON syntax? ──────────────────────────▶ ❌ abort, daemon never starts│
  │        │  valid JSON                                                     │
  │        ▼  2. validate every key against dockerd's known flags            │
  │  key ALSO passed as a CLI flag to dockerd? ──▶ ❌ abort — "conflicting    │
  │        │  no conflicts                             options" fatal error │
  │        ▼  3. apply config → open the storage driver, start listening    │
  │  ✅ dockerd is up, `docker info` now reflects this exact file             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Step 3 above is also where storage-driver stops being a config string and becomes a real kernel mechanism. overlay2, devicemapper, btrfs, and zfs are NOT interchangeable formats for the same on-disk data — each stores layers in its own incompatible directory structure under /var/lib/docker/<driver-name>/:

DriverCoW granularityBacking mechanismProduction status
overlay2per-filekernel OverlayFS (④'s lowerdir/upperdir/merged)Default; recommended on every modern kernel
devicemapperper-blockdevice-mapper thin-provisioned block deviceRHEL7 legacy; needs direct-lvm, not loopback, in production
btrfsper-subvolumenative filesystem CoW + snapshots (no overlay needed)Advanced snapshotting; requires a btrfs-formatted /var/lib/docker
zfsper-datasetnative filesystem CoW + checksummed snapshotsSimilar use case to btrfs; strong data-integrity guarantees
vfsnonea full plain directory copy per layerNo CoW at all — testing / Docker-in-Docker fallback only
🔑 This is what "changing the storage driver loses all data" (2.7's card grid) actually means: it's not corruption, it's invisibility — every existing image and container lives under the OLD driver's subdirectory, and the new driver starts from a completely empty one. Switching drivers is a fresh install of the image/container store, not a migration.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A full image reference is registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest — every omitted part defaults (docker.io/library/…:latest); only the digest is immutable.
  • Container lifecycle: created → running → {paused|stopped|deleted}; stop = SIGTERM (graceful), kill = SIGKILL (immediate), pause = cgroup freezer (no signal at all).
  • A push/pull only moves layers the far side doesn't already have — content-addressed dedup, just like git.
  • Cache rule: a layer reuses only if EVERY layer before it matched too — one early change invalidates everything after it, so order Dockerfiles rarely-changing before always-changing.
  • Tags are mutable pointers (a name plate); digests are immutable (a fingerprint) — never deploy production from :latest.
  • A manifest list ("fat manifest") maps one tag to per-architecture images; Buildx is how you produce multi-arch images yourself.
  • daemon.json sets host-wide defaults (log rotation, live-restore, storage driver); live-restore works because the shim, not dockerd, parents running containers.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • apt install docker → The package is docker.io on Ubuntu/Debian, not "docker" (which is a system tray app).
  • Forgetting to add user to docker group → Without it, every docker command needs sudo. Run usermod -aG docker $USER then log out/in.
  • Editing daemon.json with invalid JSON → Bad JSON prevents daemon startup. Always validate with python -m json.tool first.
  • ":latest is a freshness guarantee" → It's a name, not a guarantee — pulling a newer :latest never updates containers already running from the old one.
  • "docker rm just tidies up, no data risk" → Deleting a container permanently deletes its writable layer — anything not on a volume or already pushed to a registry as a new layer is gone for good (2.2, and Part 6 covers volumes).
  • A lone RUN apt-get update is harmless → It caches a stale package index forever — always chain update && install && clean in ONE layer.
  • Building multi-arch without --platform "just works" → On an ARM Mac it ships an image that greets an AMD64 server with "exec format error."
  • A daemon.json key can also be passed as a CLI flag to dockerd → That's a fatal conflict, not a merge — dockerd refuses to start.
  • "The default json-file log driver is fine left alone" → With no max-size/max-file set it has NO rotation and grows forever — unbounded container logs are the #1 silent disk-filler on real production Docker hosts (2.7). Always set log-opts rotation.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Order Dockerfiles rarely-changing → always-changing (base image, deps, code) so docker build reuses cache by default, not luck.
  • Multi-tag every build (semantic + git SHA) in one docker build — one IMAGE ID, several handles, zero extra disk.
  • docker manifest inspect <image> proves which platforms a tag actually covers before someone's ARM pull fails.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 2)

images, registries & the daemon 
# Local images + immutable digest
docker images --digests

# Move layers to/from a registry
docker pull <image>
docker push <image>

# Re-point a tag before pushing
docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1

# Every platform a tag covers
docker manifest inspect <img>

# Real overlay2 lowerdir/upperdir/merged paths
docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <container>

# Disk used by images/containers
docker system df

# Store registry credentials
docker login <registry>
install & run the daemon itself 
sudo apt install docker.io
sudo systemctl start docker
sudo systemctl enable docker
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
docker run hello-world
cat /etc/docker/daemon.json
sudo journalctl -u docker -f

🧠 Chapter 2 — DCA Practice Questions (11)

Quick recall of the five nouns — 11 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What is the relationship between a Docker image and a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An image is a read-only template (like a class). A container is a runnable instance of an image (like an object). One image can spawn many containers, just as one class can create many objects.

EXPLANATION

Think of the image as a frozen snapshot — it contains the OS, libraries, application code, and configuration ALL bundled together. When you docker run, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top and starts the process. You can run 100 containers from the same image — each gets its own writable layer but shares the read-only image layers. This is why containers start in milliseconds.

  📦 easypj:v1.0  (ONE read-only image, stored on disk once)
        │ docker run (×N)
        ├──▶ 📦 container-A   own thin R/W layer, shares image layers
        ├──▶ 📦 container-B   own thin R/W layer, shares image layers
        └──▶ 📦 container-C   own thin R/W layer, shares image layers
  Only each container's writable layer is unique — the shared
  read-only image layers are never duplicated on disk.
Q2
How do Docker image layers work, and why does layer order matter?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a read-only layer. Layers are cached. If a layer changes, ALL layers after it are rebuilt. Therefore, put frequently-changing layers (source code) LAST and rarely-changing layers (base image, dependencies) FIRST.

EXPLANATION

Docker cache is sequential: Layer 1 → Layer 2 → Layer 3. If Layer 2 changes, Layers 3+ ALL rebuild. For easypj: FROM python:3.11-slim (never changes) → COPY requirements.txt (changes weekly) → RUN pip install (depends on requirements) → COPY . . (changes constantly). Code changes only rebuild the last layer — pip install stays cached, saving 2-3 minutes per build.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q3
What is the difference between Docker Hub and a private registry like ECR?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Hub is a public registry with free tier. Private registries (ECR, GCR, ACR) are cloud-managed, provide lower latency, better security (IAM integration), and are typically used for production workloads.

EXPLANATION

Docker Hub is like GitHub for images — anyone can pull public images, rate-limited for anonymous users. Private registries run in your VPC: images never leave your network, IAM controls who can push/pull, and latency is sub-millisecond. The DCA exam expects you to know how to authenticate to both: docker login for Hub, aws ecr get-login-password | docker login ... for ECR.

Docker HubPrivate (ECR/GCR/ACR)
VisibilityPublic by defaultPrivate, IAM-gated
Network pathPublic internetInside your VPC
Authdocker loginaws ecr get-login-password | docker login ...
Token lifetimeSession-basedECR tokens expire every 12h
Q4
What are the valid states in a container's lifecycle?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Created → Running → Paused / Stopped → Deleted. A container starts as "created" (on disk but not started), transitions to "running," can be "paused" (frozen) or "stopped" (exited), and finally "deleted" (gone).

EXPLANATION

The container lifecycle is fundamental to the DCA exam. Created: filesystem prepared but process not started. Running: PID 1 is executing. Paused: all processes frozen (SIGSTOP) — useful for debugging without destroying state. Stopped: process exited but filesystem and metadata preserved. Deleted: everything gone. Check state with docker ps -a and inspect with docker inspect CONTAINER.

  CREATED ──start──▶ RUNNING ──┬──pause───▶ PAUSED  ──unpause──▶ RUNNING
                                 ├──stop────▶ STOPPED ──start────▶ RUNNING
                                 └──(stop+rm)────────▶ DELETED (gone)
  docker ps -a shows: Created | Up ... | Up ... (Paused) | Exited (N) | (row gone)
Q5
Why is the :latest tag considered dangerous for production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

:latest is mutable — it points to whatever was most recently built/pushed. This means docker pull easypj:latest can silently pull a completely different version than expected, causing production incidents. Always use explicit version tags.

EXPLANATION

:latest is a moving target. If you docker push easypj:latest today and someone pulls tomorrow, they get whatever was pushed most recently — not necessarily your image. In production, this means your deployment could silently change versions. Always tag with semver (easypj:v1.2.3) or Git SHA (easypj:abc1234). For ultimate immutability, use digests: easypj@sha256:def5678...

  easypj:latest  is a pointer that keeps moving:
  Day 1   easypj:latest ──▶ sha256:aaa111  (v1.0, tested)
  Day 5   easypj:latest ──▶ sha256:bbb222  (v1.1, re-pushed — nobody told prod)
  Day 9   easypj:latest ──▶ sha256:ccc333  (v2.0-broken build, pulled by accident)
  easypj@sha256:aaa111  always ──▶ sha256:aaa111   (never moves, ever)
Q6
What is a multi-architecture image and how is it built?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A multi-architecture image uses a manifest list to serve different platform-specific images (amd64, arm64) under a SINGLE tag. Built with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v1 .

EXPLANATION

Multi-arch images solve the "works on my Mac (ARM) but not on the server (x86)" problem. A manifest list contains pointers to platform-specific images. When you docker pull easypj:v1, Docker automatically selects the image matching your architecture. Build with docker buildx: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t easypj:v1 .. This pushes a manifest list + both platform images.

                    easypj:v1  (ONE tag)
                        │
                 MANIFEST LIST ("fat manifest")
                    ┌───────┴───────┐
              linux/amd64      linux/arm64
                    │                │
            image+layers      image+layers
  docker pull easypj:v1 auto-selects the branch matching your CPU.
Q7
What happens to data stored inside a container when the container is deleted?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

All data inside the container's writable layer is permanently lost. Only data stored in Docker volumes or bind mounts survives container deletion. This is by design — containers are meant to be ephemeral.

EXPLANATION

This is the #1 mistake beginners make: storing database files inside the container. When docker rm CONTAINER runs, the writable layer is destroyed — all data gone forever. The solution: use volumes or bind mounts. docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres stores the database in a named volume that survives container deletion. Containers are cattle, not pets — they should be disposable.

Where data livesSurvives docker rm?
Container writable layer (default)❌ No — destroyed with the container
Named volume (-v pgdata:/…)✅ Yes — lives on until docker volume rm
Bind mount (-v /host/path:/…)✅ Yes — it's the host's own filesystem
Q8
What command authenticates you to a private Docker registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker login <registry-url> — e.g., docker login (Docker Hub), docker login ghcr.io (GitHub), or aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <aws-account-id>.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com (ECR).

EXPLANATION

docker login stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json. For security, Docker uses credential helpers (osxkeychain, wincred, pass) instead of storing plaintext passwords. After login, docker push and docker pull automatically include authentication. Tokens for ECR expire after 12 hours.

RegistryLogin command
Docker Hubdocker login
GitHub (ghcr.io)docker login ghcr.io -u USER --password-stdin
Amazon ECRaws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com
Q9
How does Docker's layer caching decide whether to rebuild a layer?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker compares the instruction text AND the files being copied (checksums). If either changed, the layer is rebuilt — and ALL SUBSEQUENT layers are also rebuilt. This is why order matters: keep frequently-changing layers at the bottom.

EXPLANATION

Docker computes checksums for COPY/ADD instructions. For RUN instructions, it hashes the command string. If an earlier layer's hash matches the cache, Docker reuses it. If ANY layer changes, all subsequent layers are rebuilt from scratch. This is why COPY requirements.txt . should come before COPY . . — requirements changes are rare, code changes are frequent.

InstructionWhat Docker hashesRebuild trigger
COPY / ADDChecksum of the copied file(s)File bytes change
RUNThe command string itselfCommand text changes
Any layer N—Any layer before N was invalidated
Q10
What is an image digest and why is it more reliable than a tag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An image digest is a SHA256 hash of the image's content — it's immutable. Tags like :latest can be moved to point to different images, but a digest always identifies the EXACT same image. Use easypj@sha256:abc123... for guaranteed reproducibility.

EXPLANATION

Tags are like symlinks — they can be moved. A malicious actor who gains push access could retag a compromised image as :latest and no one would notice. Digests are content-addressable: the hash is computed FROM the image content, so any change produces a different digest. For production deployments, always pin by digest. Docker Content Trust (DCT) also signs images to verify publisher identity.

Tag (:v1)Digest (@sha256:…)
Mutable?Yes — can be re-pushed to point elsewhereNo — content-addressed, byte-locked
Human-readable?YesNo — 64 hex chars
Production useConvenient for humansWhat you actually pin/deploy
Q11
Which two daemon.json settings guarantee running containers survive a daemon restart AND that container logs never grow unbounded — and what's the mechanism behind each?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

"live-restore": true keeps containers running through a daemon restart or crash, and "log-opts": {"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"} under "log-driver":"json-file" caps and rotates logs so they can never silently fill the disk.

EXPLANATION

live-restore works because running containers are actually parented by containerd-shim, not by dockerd itself — when the daemon restarts, the shim keeps the container's process tree alive and dockerd simply re-attaches afterward. Without it, systemctl restart docker kills every running container immediately. Separately, the default json-file log driver has NO rotation unless max-size/max-file are set — unbounded logs from one chatty container are one of the most common silent disk-fillers on a real production Docker host. Of the two, only live-restore is on the short list of keys dockerd reloads live via sudo systemctl reload docker (SIGHUP) (2.7's DCA Checklist); log-opts/log-driver aren't on that list, so they still need the full restart.

KeyProtects againstApply without a full restart?
live-restoreContainers dying when the daemon restarts✅ Yes — systemctl reload docker
log-opts.max-size / max-fileDisk filling silently from unbounded logs❌ No — needs sudo systemctl restart docker

🔬 Practice Drill 2.1 — Prove the Cache Rule

Build easypj once, touch one .py file, rebuild, and circle every line that prints CACHED — then edit requirements.txt and rebuild again, circling every line that does NOT print CACHED this time. If your two circles don't match 2.4's GOOD ORDER table exactly, your Dockerfile order is inverted.

  Expected output — GOOD ORDER Dockerfile (base → requirements.txt → pip install → code):

  touch app.py && docker build .          edit requirements.txt && docker build .
  ┌───────────────────────────┐            ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ FROM python:3.11-slim      │ CACHED     │ FROM python:3.11-slim      │ CACHED
  │ COPY requirements.txt .    │ CACHED     │ COPY requirements.txt .    │ REBUILT ← changed
  │ RUN pip install -r req..   │ CACHED     │ RUN pip install -r req..   │ REBUILT ← upstream changed
  │ COPY . /app/                │ REBUILT ← changed │ COPY . /app/       │ REBUILT ← upstream changed
  └───────────────────────────┘            └───────────────────────────┘
  Only 1 of 4 lines rebuilds for a code touch; ALL lines downstream of
  requirements.txt rebuild for a dependency change — that asymmetry IS the cache rule.

  • Do you know where daemon.json lives and what live-restore actually protects against?
📌 Chapter 2 Visual Summary — the five nouns
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 🍰 LAYERS (2.4)      cached diffs, order = rebuild cost             │
  │        │ stack into                                                │
  │        ▼                                                           │
  │ 📦 IMAGE (2.1)       registry/repo:tag@digest — read-only layers    │
  │        │ named by 🏷️  TAGS (2.5) — mutable name, digest = immutable│
  │        │                                                           │
  │        ├── docker run ─────────▶ ▶️ CONTAINER (2.2)                │
  │        │                        created→running→{paused|stopped|   │
  │        │                        deleted}; governed by daemon.json  │
  │        │                        (2.7)                              │
  │        │                                                           │
  │        └── docker push/pull ───▶ 🗄️  REGISTRY (2.3)                │
  │                                   Hub/ECR/GCR/ACR/Harbor — only    │
  │                                   missing layers travel            │
  │                                                                    │
  │ 🏷️  TAGS (2.5) fan out via 📐 MANIFEST (2.6) — one tag → per-arch   │
  │ images (amd64, arm64...); daemon.json (2.7) governs logging,       │
  │ storage & restart behavior for every container on this host.   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In one line: an IMAGE is a read-only, digest-addressed template stored in a REGISTRY; docker run turns it into a CONTAINER with its own writable LAYER; the image itself is built from cached LAYERS whose order decides rebuild cost; humans find images by mutable TAGS while machines pin the immutable digest; a MANIFEST list lets one tag serve many CPU architectures; and daemon.json is the one file deciding how every container on this host logs, survives a restart, and stores its files on disk.

The takeaway: every later chapter just operates on these five nouns — nothing new gets introduced, only deeper mechanics for image, container, registry, layer, and tag.
