3.1 Installing Docker Desktop (Windows/Mac)

Docker Desktop is the recommended way to run Docker on development machines. It includes Docker Engine, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Docker Scout, and a GUI dashboard — all in one package.

📖 Installation Steps

1. Download from docker.com
2. Run the installer (Windows: enable WSL2 if prompted — Docker Desktop uses WSL2 as its Linux backend for better performance)
3. Launch Docker Desktop — the whale icon appears in your system tray
4. Open a terminal and verify: docker --version and docker run hello-world

📖 Before You Install — System Requirements

Windows: 64-bit Windows 10/11 (current supported builds only — Docker drops the oldest build the moment a new one ships, so always check the live requirements page) with a SLAT-capable 64-bit CPU and hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x / AMD-V) enabled in the BIOS/UEFI, and WSL2 enabled (Desktop's default backend) — the older Hyper-V backend is still available as a fallback but needs Pro/Enterprise/Education (Home edition is WSL2-only). Docker's official current minimum is 8GB of system RAM for either backend — noticeably more than many assume. macOS: Apple Silicon (M-series) or Intel, on a currently-supported macOS release (officially: the current release plus the two previous major versions — support for the oldest drops the instant a new major version ships), with at least 4GB of RAM. Apple Silicon runs both native arm64 and emulated amd64 images (via Rosetta), though emulation costs performance. Both platforms: those RAM figures are the OS-level minimum just to install Desktop — separately, Settings → Resources lets you cap how much of that RAM the Linux VM itself is allowed to use, worth raising if you'll run multiple services at once (Compose stacks, covered later in this guide). Linux: none of this applies — Engine (3.2) talks to the host kernel directly, no VM check needed, which is exactly why bare-metal Linux gets the best raw performance per core.

💡 Windows + WSL2

On Windows, Docker Desktop runs inside WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux 2). This gives you a real Linux kernel, near-native performance, and full compatibility with Linux containers. Make sure WSL2 is installed and set as the default: wsl --install and wsl --set-default-version 2. Docker's current published requirement is WSL version 2.1.5 or later — and if you turn on the newer Enhanced Container Isolation setting (extra sandboxing between containers and the Desktop VM), that floor rises to WSL 2.6 or later. Run wsl --version to check what you're on before filing a "Docker won't start" bug that's really just a stale WSL install.

📖 What Desktop Actually Is

Docker Desktop is not a separate engine — it's the same Docker Engine and CLI you'd install on Linux, wrapped in a managed Linux virtual machine (WSL2 backend on Windows, Apple's Virtualization.framework on macOS), plus a GUI dashboard and bundled Compose/Buildx/Scout. Containers never run "on Windows" or "on macOS" directly — they always run inside that hidden Linux kernel, which is also why a native Windows container needs a Windows kernel underneath (a much rarer setup covered later in this guide).

🧠 Analogy — An Aquarium Starter Kit

Docker Desktop is an aquarium starter kit: the tank (the Linux VM), the pump (the engine), and an illustrated instruction booklet (the GUI dashboard) all arrive in one box, ready to go. Installing Docker Engine on Linux (3.2) is buying just the pump — no tank needed, because the "water" (a Linux kernel) is already there on the host.

🖥️ Docker Desktop Dashboard — the 5 tabs

📦 Containers tab
Every container, running or stopped. Start/stop/restart/delete with a click, tail live logs, open an in-browser terminal into a running container, and see its published ports — all without touching the CLI.
🐳 Images tab
Every local image. Pull new ones, inspect layer history, run a container straight from an image, and prune unused images to reclaim disk space.
💾 Volumes tab
Every named volume. Create, delete, and browse a volume's file contents directly — handy for peeking at a database's data directory without exec-ing in.
🏗️ Builds tab
History and live logs for every docker build/buildx run, including a cache-hit breakdown per layer — the GUI view of what the build chapters later in this guide do at the CLI.
🔎 Docker Scout
A built-in vulnerability/CVE summary for images pulled or built locally — the GUI entry point to the image-scanning workflow covered in a later chapter.
📖 Kubernetes Is Bundled, But Not Turned On

That "Kubernetes" in the bundle line above is a real, standalone single-node Kubernetes cluster that ships inside every Docker Desktop install — but per Docker's own current docs it is not enabled by default. It stays off until you open the Dashboard's Kubernetes view and explicitly create/activate a cluster, precisely so a beginner installing Desktop just for containers (this chapter's scope) doesn't pay the extra RAM/CPU cost for a Kubernetes control plane they never asked for.

💡 GUI or CLI — Same Daemon

Every click in the Dashboard is just a REST API call to the same dockerd your terminal talks to — docker ps in a terminal and the Containers tab always agree, because they're reading the same daemon state, not two separate sources of truth.

🔬 easypj — Why This Matters Immediately

Once Docker Desktop reports healthy, docker pull python:3.11-slim — the exact base image 3.4 uses to run easypj interactively — succeeds from either the GUI or a terminal. Desktop is the only thing standing between this laptop and running easypj at all.

🧪 Practice — Prove Desktop Is Actually Healthy

Install Docker Desktop, then run docker run --rm hello-world. Verify: the "Hello from Docker!" message prints, AND (Windows only) Settings → Resources → WSL Integration shows the WSL2 backend enabled.

3.2 Installing Docker Engine on Linux

For Linux servers, install Docker Engine directly (no Desktop GUI). The process varies by distribution:

⚠️ Read This First — docker-ce Isn't In Ubuntu's Or RHEL's Default Repos

The docker-ce package the two boxes below install does not exist in Ubuntu/Debian's or CentOS/RHEL/Fedora's own default repositories — it lives only in Docker's own apt/yum repository, and nothing adds that repository automatically. Skipping this step is the single most common reason a fresh apt-get install docker-ce fails outright with E: Unable to locate package docker-ce: apt genuinely never searched a repo that contains it. (Ubuntu's own docker.io package is a DIFFERENT, older, community-maintained build — installing that instead silently leaves you on a stale Engine version missing the buildx/Compose v2 plugins the rest of this guide assumes are present.)

add the official repo — run once, BEFORE the install commands below 
# Ubuntu/Debian
$ sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl
$ sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
$ sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
$ sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
$ echo \
  "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] \
  https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
$ sudo apt-get update

# CentOS/RHEL/Fedora
$ sudo yum install -y yum-utils
$ sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo
📖 Ubuntu/Debian

sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
Then: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER (add yourself to docker group, log out and back in — or run newgrp docker to activate the new group in your current shell without a full logout). The docker-ce package creates the docker group for you automatically — the official docs still list sudo groupadd docker as their literal step one, only needed if you're on a stripped-down install where the group is somehow missing.
Start on boot: sudo systemctl enable docker.service — Docker's own post-install guide enables containerd.service right alongside it: sudo systemctl enable containerd.service.

📖 CentOS/RHEL/Fedora

sudo yum install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
Then: sudo systemctl enable --now docker

⚡ Quick Install — the Convenience Script

For any distro (fast box spin-up, CI runners, quick testing), Docker publishes a one-line convenience script: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh. It detects your distro and installs the same docker-ce packages the manual apt/yum steps above do. It's not recommended for hardened production hosts (review and pin it first) but is perfect for a scratch VM.

📖 Engine-Only Inside WSL2 — Skipping Desktop's License Entirely

Every command in this section works completely unmodified inside a WSL2 distro on Windows — Ubuntu-on-WSL2 is a real Linux kernel environment, so the identical apt-get install docker-ce steps above install a real dockerd, with no Docker Desktop involved at all. This has become a common pattern specifically to dodge Desktop's commercial-use license: a company past the 250-employee/$10M-revenue threshold (Chapter 1 has the exact terms) can still hand every developer a free, fully-featured Docker CLI by running Engine directly inside their existing WSL2 Ubuntu distro — trading away Desktop's GUI, one-click Kubernetes, and Scout dashboard for zero license cost, while every command in this chapter stays identical. The catch: a dockerd started this way does not automatically survive a Windows reboot the way Desktop's does — either enable systemd in that distro's /etc/wsl.conf ([boot] section, systemd=true, supported on current WSL2) so systemctl enable docker from earlier in this section actually takes hold, or start it by hand (sudo service docker start) at the top of each session.

💡 Verify Installation

After installation, verify with: docker version (shows BOTH the client AND the server/Engine version, in two clearly labeled sections) and docker info (shows detailed system info including Storage Driver, Cgroup Driver, number of containers/images). Both must succeed before proceeding. Don't confuse this with docker --version (double-dash) — per the official CLI reference, that flag prints a single line for the CLI client only and says nothing about whether the daemon is even reachable.

⚠️ A Second Permission Trap — Root-Owned ~/.docker

If you ever ran sudo docker ... even once BEFORE completing the docker-group setup above, the sudo run silently created ~/.docker (config, cache, contexts) owned by root. Later, plain docker commands as your own user then fail with confusing permission errors that groups/newgrp won't fix, because the socket permission is fine — it's this directory that's wrong. Docker's own Linux post-install docs give the exact repair: sudo chown "$USER":"$USER" /home/"$USER"/.docker -R followed by sudo chmod g+rwx "$HOME/.docker" -R. Worth knowing as a DISTINCT gotcha from the /var/run/docker.sock one — same symptom family ("permission denied"), two completely different root causes.

💡 Reading docker version's Two Halves — and Why They Can Legitimately Differ

Client and Server are two separate binaries that can genuinely report different version numbers — the CLI talks to whatever daemon it's currently pointed at (3.6's --context), and the two sides negotiate DOWN to the lower of their two API versions automatically:

TERMINAL 
$ docker version
Client:
 Version:           27.0.0
 API version:       1.46
 Go version:        go1.21.9
 OS/Arch:           linux/amd64
 Context:           default

Server: Docker Engine - Community
 Engine:
  Version:          27.0.0
  API version:      1.46 (minimum version 1.24)
  OS/Arch:          linux/amd64
 containerd:
  Version:          1.7.15
 runc:
  Version:          1.1.12
📖 The "minimum version" Line Is the One That Bites

The daemon advertises a floor (minimum version 1.24 above) alongside its own current API version. A client too OLD for that floor is refused outright: Error response from daemon: client version 1.20 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.24. A client too NEW fails the other direction — rare day-to-day, but common when a freshly-updated CLI points at a much older remote server via --context. Either error means exactly one thing: stop debugging the command you typed and check docker version's two halves first — a version SKEW, not a real bug, is very often the actual cause.

📖 Rootless Mode — the Direct Answer to "docker Group = root-equivalent"

Everything above installs Docker in its default (rootful) mode, where dockerd itself runs as root and docker group membership is a straight line to host root. Docker also ships a rootless mode: install the docker-ce-rootless-extras package for your distro, then run dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install — this starts dockerd itself as your own unprivileged user, using a user namespace to remap container "root" to a non-root host UID, so even a full container escape doesn't hand over real root. The trade-off: no binding to ports below 1024 without extra setup, and a few storage/network features are unavailable — which is why most production fleets still run rootful Engine with docker-group membership carefully guarded instead (Part 7 covers exactly how).

🧠 Analogy — Wiring a Building Into the Power Grid

Installing Engine on Linux is wiring a building straight into the power grid: the apt/yum repo is the utility crew wiring the service, the systemd unit is the meter that keeps current flowing after they leave (systemctl enable docker = "keep the power on after reboot"), and docker group membership is a key to the breaker panel — anyone holding it can cut power to (or root) anything on the box. Part 7 walks back exactly how dangerous that key is.

🔬 easypj — Same Engine, Same Behavior

Once docker version and docker run --rm hello-world both succeed, docker run -d -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1 on this Linux VM behaves identically to the same command on a laptop running Docker Desktop — it's the same engine underneath either way.

🧪 Practice — Verify Without sudo

Install Engine on any free-tier cloud VM. Verify: docker run hello-world succeeds WITHOUT sudo — proof the docker group membership (and the relogin/newgrp that activates it) actually took effect.

3.3 Your First Docker Command — Hello World

The docker run hello-world command is the "Hello World" of Docker. It pulls a tiny image (~13KB), runs it, and prints a message confirming Docker is working. Let's understand exactly what happens:

docker run hello-world — 5 Steps
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ⚡ docker run hello-world — WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS                │
  │                                                                              │
  │  1. You type: $ docker run hello-world                                       │
  │  2. Docker Client sends command to Docker Daemon (dockerd)                   │
  │  3. Daemon checks local images → "hello-world" NOT FOUND                     │
  │  4. Daemon PULLS hello-world image from Docker Hub (~13 KB)                  │
  │  5. Daemon creates a container FROM the image → runs → prints message → EXITS│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Key Insight

Notice that Docker automatically PULLS the image when it's not found locally. You don't need to run docker pull separately. Every docker run implicitly checks local images first, then pulls from the registry if needed.

🧠 Analogy — Ordering a Pizza You Don't Have in the Freezer

The first docker run hello-world is ordering a pizza you don't have in the freezer: delivery (the pull) happens once, and takes a moment. Every later run of the same image is just reheating — the local image cache means step 3 never happens again until you delete the image or its tag moves.

🧪 Practice — Watch the Cache Kick In

Run docker run hello-world twice in a row. Verify: the second run shows NO "Pulling from library/hello-world" lines — you just proved the local image cache exists and is being used.

3.4 Running easypj in Docker — First Contact

Let's run Python interactively inside a container. We'll pull the official Python image, get a shell inside it, and explore:

TERMINAL 
# Pull the Python base image (only needed once)
$ docker pull python:3.11-slim

# Run interactively with a bash shell
$ docker run -it python:3.11-slim bash

# Now you're INSIDE the container!
root@abc123:/# python --version
Python 3.11.9

root@abc123:/# ls
bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

root@abc123:/# exit
$ # Back on your host machine

# See the container (now stopped)
$ docker ps -a
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                COMMAND   CREATED         STATUS
abc123def456   python:3.11-slim     "bash"    2 minutes ago   Exited (0)
📖 Understanding -it Flags

-i = interactive (keep STDIN open). -t = TTY (allocate a pseudo-terminal for proper shell display). Together, -it gives you an interactive shell session inside the container.

📖 Why exit Kills the Whole Container — Not Just the Shell

Inside that -it session, bash isn't just "a shell you're using" — Docker made it PID 1, the very first process in the container's own private process tree (its PID namespace). A container's lifecycle is tied directly to PID 1's lifecycle: the container is considered "running" for as long as PID 1 is running, and the instant PID 1 exits — for any reason, including you typing exit — the container stops, whether or not anything else was still running inside it. That's why docker run -it IMAGE bash then exit stops the whole container rather than just closing your shell: there was never a separate "container process" running quietly in the background — bash itself WAS the container's one and only tracked process.

This also previews a subtlety Chapter 6 covers in full: if PID 1 spawns child processes of its own, those children die too the moment PID 1 exits — there's no separate init system reaping orphans by default, which is exactly why some multi-process images run a tiny init process (like tini) as PID 1 instead of the app itself.

🧠 Analogy — Scuba Gear

-it is scuba gear: -i is the air hose (STDIN stays connected even without a terminal literally attached), -t is the mask (a terminal you can actually see through — the shell prompt, colors, and control characters render correctly instead of arriving as raw bytes).

🧪 Practice — Add --rm and Watch the Cleanup

Repeat the session above with --rm added: docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim bash. Verify: after typing exit, docker ps -a shows NOTHING — the container was auto-removed the instant its PID 1 (the bash shell) exited.

📖 docker run vs. docker start vs. docker exec

These three commands look similar but do fundamentally different things — mixing them up is one of the most common early confusions:

CommandWhat it doesRequires
docker run IMAGECreates a brand-new container FROM an image, then starts itAn image (pulls it if missing)
docker start NAMEResumes an EXISTING stopped container with its original config (same name, mounts, env, entrypoint)A container that already exists — see it in docker ps -a
docker exec -it NAME shStarts a NEW process inside an ALREADY-RUNNING container, alongside PID 1A container currently running
🧠 Analogy — Moving Into a House

docker run is building a new house and moving in on day one. docker start is unlocking the front door of a house you already built and left empty. docker exec is a guest letting themselves in through a side door while you're already home — a second person inside the same house, not a new one.

💡 Reading docker inspect

docker inspect CONTAINER dumps the full JSON state Docker holds for that object — network settings (IP, ports), mounts, environment variables, restart count, exit code, and the exact config it was created with. Use --format to pull one field without wading through the JSON: docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' CONTAINER or docker inspect --format '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' CONTAINER. It works on images too — docker inspect IMAGE shows layers, env, and the exact command that built it.

3.5 Essential docker run Flags

FlagPurposeExample
--nameGive container a name--name easypj-dev
-dDetached mode (background)-d
-pPort mapping (host:container)-p 8000:8000
-PPublish all exposed ports to random ports-P
-eSet environment variable-e DEBUG=False
--env-fileLoad env vars from a file--env-file ./.env
-vMount a volume-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql
--rmAuto-remove container on exit--rm
--restartRestart policy (no/on-failure/always/unless-stopped)--restart always
--memoryRAM limit (e.g., 512m, 2g)--memory=512m
--cpusCPU limit--cpus=1.5
--networkConnect to a Docker network--network my-bridge
--hostnameSet container hostname--hostname easypj.local
--add-hostAdd host-to-IP mapping in /etc/hosts--add-host db:192.168.1.100
-wSet working directory inside container-w /app
📖 The 15 Flags, Sorted Into 4 Jobs

Every flag in the table above exists to do exactly one of four jobs — memorize the job, and the specific flag becomes easy to guess:

JobFlagsQuestion it answers
🪪 Identity & lifecycle--name -d --rm --restartWhat is it called, does it block my terminal, does it clean up after itself, does it come back after a crash?
🌐 Networking-p -P --network --hostname --add-hostHow does traffic reach it, and how does it reach other things?
⚙️ Configuration-e --env-fileWhat settings/secrets does it need at startup?
💾 Resources & filesystem-v --memory --cpus -wWhat can it read/write, and how much host CPU/RAM can it use?

Flag order before the image name is free — Docker parses them regardless of sequence. The image name itself is what's NOT free: it marks a hard boundary, and everything typed after it is passed to the container as its command, not interpreted as a docker flag at all.

🧠 Analogy — Prepping a Race Car Before It Leaves the Pit

Composing a full docker run is prepping a race car before it leaves the pit: --name paints the car's number on the door, -p assigns which lane it exits onto, -e/--env-file load the fuel-mixture settings before the engine starts, -v wires it to a spare-parts bin it can reach mid-race, and --restart is the standing order to push it back onto the track if it stalls.

⚡ Compose It From Memory

docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1 — named, detached, port-mapped, env-fed, restartable. This exact line is 3.5's goal: build it without looking anything up.

Decision Guide — dev run vs. prod run: which flags fire?
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ docker run easypj — dev laptop, or prod server?                     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ DEV (laptop, iterate fast)                                          │
  │   -v $PWD:/app        live code, no rebuild needed                  │
  │   --rm  -it            throwaway container, live tracebacks         │
  │   (skip --restart & --memory — you control the lifecycle by hand)   │
  │                                                                     │
  │   $ docker run --rm -it -v $PWD:/app -p 8000:8000 \                 │
  │       easypj:v1 python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ PROD (server, stays up unattended)                                  │
  │   --restart unless-stopped   survives crash & reboot                │
  │   --env-file .env            secrets in, never bare -e              │
  │   --memory 512m --cpus 1.5   caps the noisy neighbor                │
  │                                                                     │
  │   $ docker run -d --name easypj-web \                               │
  │       --restart unless-stopped --env-file .env \                    │
  │       --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ --rm and --restart Are Mutually Exclusive

Docker enforces the DEV/PROD split drawn above at the CLI level, not just by convention: docker run --rm --restart unless-stopped IMAGE fails instantly with conflicting options: --restart and --rm. Combining them wouldn't make sense anyway — --rm promises "clean up the instant this exits," and --restart promises "keep recreating this forever"; Docker refuses the command outright rather than silently picking a winner.

🧪 Practice — Build It, Then Break It

Type the ⚡ line above from memory, then break it on purpose two ways: use -p 8000 alone (no colon), and put the image name BEFORE the flags. Verify: you can read both resulting error messages and explain, in one sentence each, exactly what's wrong.

📖 15 Flags Today, 100+ in the Reference

The table above is the 15 daily-driver flags covering roughly 95% of daily docker run usage. The official docker run reference on docs.docker.com documents well over 100 flags in total (health checks, cgroups, GPUs, ulimits, security options, device access, and more) — see Appendix A.11 for the complete official flag reference.

3.6 Docker CLI Structure & Help System

The Docker CLI follows a consistent structure: docker <command> <subcommand> [options] [arguments]. Understanding this pattern makes the entire CLI predictable.

the same grammar, three real commands 
docker container run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1
docker image ls --filter "reference=easypj*"
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d
🧠 Analogy — Sentence Grammar

Read the anatomy diagram above as sentence grammar: management group = subject, subcommand = verb, flags = adverbs, target = object. Commands stop being memorization the day you start parsing them as grammar instead of as strings to recall.

💡 Legacy Shortcuts Are Aliases, Not a Different Path

docker ps, docker images, docker rm, and docker rmi predate the container/image management groups and still work today — they're aliases for docker container ls, docker image ls, docker container rm, and docker image rm respectively, resolving to the exact same code path inside the CLI. Either form is correct; the longer group-based form is what the anatomy diagram above describes, and it's what makes brand-new subcommands with no legacy shortcut (docker network ls, docker volume ls) just as guessable from the same grammar.

📖 The Full Global Flags List

Beyond --help/--version/--config, the CLI also accepts --context (switch which daemon you're talking to), --log-level, --tls, and --host (rarely used directly — --context has replaced most manual --host use). They all sit in the same GLOBAL_OPTIONS slot, before the management group.

⚡ Turn On Tab Completion

Modern Docker CLI versions can generate their own completion script: docker completion bash / zsh / fish / powershell prints a script for that shell — source it once (add it to ~/.bashrc, or drop it wherever your shell's completion system already looks) and Tab starts completing management groups, subcommands, flags, and even running container/image names. Combined with the grammar in the diagram above, completion turns "guess the flag name" into "type two letters, hit Tab."

🧪 Practice — Translate Without Running

Without running them, translate into plain English: docker network ls, docker volume rm pgdata, docker image prune -a. Then verify each guess with --help (e.g. docker volume rm --help) — every guess should match.

3.7 When docker Commands Fail — Reading Error Messages

The five errors every beginner hits in week one, decoded: permission denied on docker.sock → not in docker group (see 3.2). Cannot connect to the Docker daemon → daemon not running. port is already allocated → host port taken: change -p or free it. No such container → name typo, or it was --rm'd or never started. exec format error → wrong CPU architecture image (see 2.6).

💡 Triage First: Client or Daemon?

Before reading the error string closely, decide: did the CLIENT reject the command (bad flag, bad grammar — fails instantly, no network involved) or did the DAEMON reject the request (image not found, port conflict, out of disk — takes a moment, involves the API)? This one question halves your search space every time.

Error stringReal meaningFirst command to run
permission denied ... docker.sockYou're not in the docker group (or never re-logged in after joining it)groups — check membership, then newgrp docker
Cannot connect to the Docker daemondockerd isn't running (or Desktop hasn't finished starting)sudo systemctl status docker (Linux) / check the whale icon (Desktop)
Bind for 0.0.0.0:8000 failed: port is already allocatedSomething already owns the host port — often a forgotten container, not another appdocker ps (check Docker first, lsof -i :8000 second)
No such container: NAMETypo'd name, or the container was --rm'd / never starteddocker ps -a — confirm it actually exists
exec format errorWrong CPU architecture image (e.g. an amd64-only image on an arm64 host with no emulation)docker inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}' IMAGE
🧠 Analogy — Waiter vs. Kitchen

Client errors are the waiter rejecting your order — you misread the menu (bad flag, bad grammar), and it fails before anything reaches the kitchen. Daemon errors are the kitchen reporting a problem after taking the order — out of stock, oven busy (image not found, port conflict, disk full). You complain to a different person depending on which one happened, and the fix is different too.

🧪 Practice — Cause All Five On Purpose

Deliberately trigger all five errors above (stop the daemon, double-book a port, typo a container name, request an arm64-only image on amd64...). Verify: for each one, you can say "client-side" or "daemon-side" BEFORE reading the fix.

🔧 Under the Hood — from a typed command to an isolated Linux process: sockets, runc, namespaces, cgroups & the network rules underneath

Every reflex this chapter built — installing, running hello-world, getting a shell with -it, composing 15 flags, reading CLI grammar, triaging an error — sits on top of six real mechanisms most engineers never see. None of it is magic: it's a Unix socket, a chain of small programs, seven kernel namespaces, a resource accountant, a packet filter, and a watcher loop. Here's the whole chapter, one layer deeper.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  $ docker run -d --name web -p 8000:8000 --restart unless-stopped IMAGE  │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼  3.6's "grammar" is really an HTTP request — see ①              │
  │  docker CLI ──POST /containers/create──▶ dockerd  (over the socket)      │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼  dockerd never forks a container itself — see ②                │
  │  containerd ──▶ containerd-shim-runc-v2 ──▶ runc create / runc start     │
  │        │                                              │                  │
  │        ▼ ③④ isolation                                 ▼ ⑤⑥ policy        │
  │  7 namespaces + cgroup limits            iptables DNAT (-p) · exit watch │
  │  ("what it sees" / "what it can use")    (--restart)                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
① The Docker Socket — Why Every Command Is Really an HTTP Request

The docker binary you've typed all chapter is a thin REST client — it never touches the kernel directly. By default it opens a connection to a UNIX domain socket at /var/run/docker.sock and sends plain HTTP over it; dockerd is the only process listening on that socket, and it's the one actually holding root and talking to the kernel. 3.6's "grammar" (group → verb → flags → target) is just the CLI's translation layer over a small, well-defined API:

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ docker CLI ── HTTP (no TLS by default) ──▶ /var/run/docker.sock                │
  │                                                  │                             │
  │                                 owned root:docker, mode 660 (rw owner+group)   │
  │                                                  ▼                             │
  │                                     dockerd  (listens here, runs AS root)      │
  │                                                                                │
  │ in `docker` group ──▶ socket OPENS ──▶ every request dockerd honors            │
  │   (opening the socket IS the authorization check — nothing finer-grained)      │
  │   ⇒ docker-group membership = a straight line to host root, not a sandbox      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Command you typedREST call dockerd actually receives
docker versionGET /version — client AND server version, in one round trip
docker ps / docker ps -aGET /containers/json / GET /containers/json?all=true
docker run IMAGEPOST /images/create (only if missing) → POST /containers/create → POST /containers/{id}/start
docker inspect NAMEGET /containers/{id}/json (or /images/{id}/json for an image)
docker logs -f NAMEGET /containers/{id}/logs?follow=true — the connection is held open and streamed

The socket file itself is owned root:docker, mode 660 — read/write for owner and group, nothing for anyone else. That's the entire mechanism behind 3.2's "docker group is root-equivalent" gotcha: membership doesn't grant a sandboxed permission, it grants a direct line to a process that already IS root. A member can, for example, POST /containers/create with a bind mount of the host's / into the container, then write anywhere on the host filesystem — no exploit required, just a documented feature used deliberately. This is precisely why 3.2's rootless mode remaps dockerd itself off of root instead of trying to sandbox the socket.

🔑 This is also the exact mechanical reason 3.7's "client or daemon?" triage question works. If the CLI can't even open the socket, you get a CLIENT-side failure before a single HTTP request is sent — Cannot connect to the Docker daemon. Once the request DOES reach dockerd, every failure after that is the DAEMON replying with a real HTTP status (a 404 for "no such container," a 409 for a port conflict) — "client-side or daemon-side" is really just "did we ever reach the socket, or did the socket answer back."
② From docker run to runc create/start — the OCI Handoff

dockerd doesn't fork containers itself. Since the containerd split (Docker 1.11), it delegates over gRPC to containerd, which spins up one small containerd-shim-runc-v2 process per container. The shim calls runc — the actual OCI runtime binary — exactly twice: runc create sets up the 7 namespaces and cgroup limits and then PAUSES the new process at a barrier, waiting on a FIFO pipe; runc start writes to that FIFO, releasing the process to finally exec your real command. Once start returns, runc itself exits — the shim, not dockerd and not runc, stays behind as the container's actual parent process.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  dockerd ──gRPC──▶ containerd ──▶ containerd-shim-runc-v2 (1 per container)│
  │                                          │                                │
  │                                          ├─ runc create → namespaces +    │
  │                                          │   cgroups set up, process      │
  │                                          │   PAUSED at a FIFO barrier     │
  │                                          ├─ runc start  → FIFO written,   │
  │                                          │   process finally exec()'s     │
  │                                          │   (runc now EXITS — done)      │
  │                                          └─ shim stays alive as the       │
  │                                             REAL parent process           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
3.3's 5-step diagram, stepWhich component actually does it
1. You type docker rundocker CLI → HTTP POST over the socket (①)
2. Client sends command to daemondockerd receives the request
3. Daemon checks local imagesdockerd's local image store (no network yet)
4. Daemon pulls the imagecontainerd's content store, via the registry HTTP API
5. Creates → runs → exitscontainerd-shim-runc-v2 + runc create/start, exactly as above
🔑 This is why dockerd restarting for an Engine upgrade doesn't kill your running containers (with --live-restore enabled): the shim, not dockerd, is the real OS-level parent. It's also why a container's "process" is really two separate bookkeeping records that merely agree by convention — dockerd's own container object, and the OS process the shim is actually parenting.
③ Linux Namespaces — "What a Container Can See"

Namespaces limit what a process can see. runc create (②) allocates a fresh set for every container, making it believe it's the only thing running on the system. There are 7 types:

🧱 The 7 Linux Namespaces — "what a container can see"

🔢 PID
Isolates process IDs — the container sees its own PID 1 (init) and can't see host processes.
🌐 NET
Isolates network interfaces — the container gets its own eth0, routing table, and iptables rules.
📂 MNT
Isolates mount points — the container has its own root filesystem view.
🏷️ UTS
Isolates hostname & domain — the container can carry its own hostname.
📡 IPC
Isolates inter-process communication — the container's shared memory is isolated.
👤 USER
Isolates user/group IDs — UID 0 (root) in the container ≠ root on the host (with userns).
🧮 CGROUP
Isolates the control-group view — the container sees only its own cgroup limits.

3.4's root@abc123:/# prompt is a genuine PID 1 — but only inside its own PID namespace. Every containerized process actually carries two PID numbers at once, because a PID namespace is a translation, not a fence:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  INSIDE the container's PID namespace     ON the host's PID namespace    │
  │  (what `ps` shows you at the -it prompt)  (what `ps -ef` shows the host) │
  │                                                                            │
  │     PID 1  ←  bash (3.4's shell)     ═══▶     PID 48213  ←  same process │
  │     PID 12 ←  a child it spawned     ═══▶     PID 48221  ←  same process │
  │                                                                            │
  │  the container's kernel view starts counting from 1; the HOST kernel     │
  │  (there is only ever ONE real kernel) still sees the real, global PID    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 "PID 1 inside" and "PID 48213 on the host" are the SAME process, described through two different namespaces — which is also exactly why docker run --pid=host is dangerous: it skips allocating a new PID namespace entirely, so the container's ps sees (and can kill -9) every real host process, not just its own.
④ Control Groups (cgroups v2) — "What a Container Can Use"

cgroups limit what a process can use. When you type docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 (3.5), runc create writes those numbers into a dedicated cgroup directory under /sys/fs/cgroup/ — one per container — and the kernel itself enforces every limit from there on, with no further Docker involvement. Modern hosts default to the unified cgroup v2 hierarchy, which renamed several files from the older v1 layout you'll still see referenced in older docs:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ $ docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 --name web IMAGE                           │
  │         │                                                                        │
  │         ▼  runc create (②) writes the limits into ONE cgroup dir per container   │
  │ /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<container-id>.scope/                         │
  │     ├── memory.max   = 536870912        (512m, from --memory)                    │
  │     ├── cpu.max      = "150000 100000"   (1.5 cpus, from --cpus)                 │
  │     └── pids.max     = max               (unset by default — a fork-bomb risk)   │
  │                                                                                  │
  │ cross memory.max ──▶ kernel OOM killer scans ONLY this cgroup (never the host)   │
  │                   ──▶ SIGKILLs the biggest process inside it ──▶ Exit Code 137   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Resourcecgroup v1 filecgroup v2 file (current default)
Memory hard limitmemory.limit_in_bytesmemory.max
CPU weight/prioritycpu.shares (2–262144)cpu.weight (1–10000)
CPU hard quotacpu.cfs_quota_us / cpu.cfs_period_uscpu.max ("quota period" in one file)
Process count cappids.maxpids.max (unchanged)
Block I/Oblkio.*io.max

Exceed --memory and nothing gentle happens: the kernel's cgroup-aware OOM killer looks ONLY inside that container's cgroup (never the whole host) and SIGKILLs a process there — the container exits with code 137 (128 + SIGKILL's signal number 9), the exact same code you'd see from a manual docker kill.

🔑 Exit code 137 is a fingerprint, not a mystery: 128+9 always means SOMETHING sent SIGKILL — either you (docker kill), or the kernel's OOM killer because a cgroup limit from ④ was exceeded. docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' tells you which one happened without guessing.
⑤ Port Publishing — the iptables/nftables DNAT Chain

Publishing a port is not "opening a port on the container" — it is dockerd programming the HOST's own packet filter. On Linux, every -p hostPort:containerPort adds a DNAT rule to the DOCKER chain in iptables/nftables: a packet hitting the host's hostPort is rewritten to the container's private IP:containerPort on the bridge network, before it ever reaches the container's own network namespace. (Desktop hides an extra hop: host → WSL2/VM → the same iptables rule → container.)

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  client :80 ──▶ host eth0:8000 ──▶ iptables DNAT (DOCKER chain)   │
  │                                          │                        │
  │                                          ▼                        │
  │                docker0 bridge ──▶ easypj-web (172.17.0.x:8000)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 The Port-Publishing Chains

🔀 DOCKER
Written by dockerd, automatically. Holds the actual DNAT rule for every -p you've ever run — flushed and rebuilt as containers come and go.
✋ DOCKER-USER
Written by you, manually. Always evaluated BEFORE the DOCKER chain; dockerd never touches it, so custom filtering rules here survive every container restart.
🧩 docker-proxy (userland)
Started by dockerd, one process per published port. A fallback path alongside the iptables rule for loopback/hairpin traffic that pure kernel DNAT doesn't always cover.
⚠️ This is why a host firewall that blocks the DOCKER chain silently breaks every published port — the container is fine, the RULE never fired. It's also why custom port-blocking rules belong in DOCKER-USER, not the default INPUT/FORWARD chains: anything you add there runs ahead of Docker's own rule, every time, without dockerd ever overwriting it.

Current Docker Engine versions actually split this further than the two-chain sketch above: a DOCKER-FORWARD chain is now the true FIRST stage — it fast-paths already-established connections and hands new candidate packets off to DOCKER (the DNAT/port-mapping decision) and a handful of narrower chains (DOCKER-BRIDGE, per-network DOCKER-CT connection tracking, plus DOCKER-INGRESS for Swarm) that didn't exist in older Docker versions' simpler DOCKER-only layout. DOCKER-USER's promise is unchanged — it still runs before all of them — but if you ever run iptables -L on a modern host and see chain names beyond the two taught here, this is why.

⑥ --restart Policies — dockerd's Exit-Event Reconciliation Loop

--restart is not a kernel feature — dockerd subscribes to containerd's task-exit events over the same gRPC connection from ②, and on each exit it reads that container's stored policy (persisted to disk in config.v2.json under /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/) to decide whether to call containerd again for a fresh create→start:

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ container's PID 1 exits (crash, OOM, or `docker stop`)                         │
  │         │                                                                      │
  │         ▼                                                                      │
  │ containerd emits a TaskExit event over ②'s same gRPC connection                │
  │         │                                                                      │
  │         ▼                                                                      │
  │ dockerd reads THIS container's stored policy from                              │
  │     /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/config.v2.json                             │
  │         │                                                                      │
  │    ┌────┴──────────────────────────┐                                           │
  │    ▼ policy says restart?          ▼ no (or `no` / exhausted on-failure:N)     │
  │ containerd.create()+start()   container just stays Exited — nothing revives    │
  │   (②'s pipeline, again,        it until you `docker start` by hand             │
  │    against a BRAND-NEW process)                                                │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
PolicyReconciles after a crash?Reconciles when dockerd itself starts up (reboot/upgrade)?
nonevernever
on-failure[:N]only non-zero exit, up to N timesyes, resumes counting
unless-stoppedyesyes — UNLESS the last human action was an explicit docker stop
alwaysyesyes, even if it was last explicitly stopped

That startup pass is why "restarts across a reboot" needs no per-container systemd unit at all — only docker.service (the thing that keeps dockerd itself alive) has to be enabled; every container's own survival is dockerd re-walking its container list and re-asserting each stored policy.

🔑 It's the same instinct running the whole chapter: a stored intent (a RestartPolicy, a -p mapping, a namespace boundary) plus a small watcher that keeps re-asserting it. "Restart" is nothing more than dockerd re-running ②'s exact POST /containers/create → POST /containers/{id}/start pipeline against a brand-new process, every single time the old one exits.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Desktop = Engine wrapped in a managed Linux VM (WSL2 on Windows, Virtualization.framework on macOS) — containers never run "on Windows/macOS" directly, only inside that hidden Linux kernel.
  • On Linux, membership in the docker group is root-equivalent — it owns the daemon socket, not a sandboxed permission.
  • docker run hello-world = (pull if absent) → create → start; the exited container still exists until removed or --rm'd.
  • -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY; together they make a shell PID 1 inside the container, and exit stops the whole container.
  • docker ps shows only RUNNING containers; docker ps -a shows every container, including exited ones holding a name or port.
  • The 15 daily-driver run flags split into four jobs: identity/lifecycle, networking, configuration, and resource/filesystem control.
  • The CLI's real grammar is docker <group> <verb> [flags] [target] — legacy shortcuts (docker ps, docker images) are aliases for the same code path.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • docker build (forgot -t) → Without -t, image gets a random name. Always tag: docker build -t app:v1 .
  • docker run (forgot -d for daemon) → Without -d, the container runs in foreground and blocks your terminal.
  • docker attach for debugging → Use docker exec -it CONTAINER sh instead. attach connects to PID 1; exec starts a new process.
  • Forgetting --rm on temporary containers → Without --rm, stopped containers accumulate and waste disk space.
  • "Docker is eating my RAM" is a Docker Desktop bug → On Windows it's almost always the WSL2 VM's appetite — tune .wslconfig, not Docker Desktop settings.
  • --rm and --restart can be combined → They're mutually exclusive at the CLI level — docker run --rm --restart unless-stopped ... fails instantly with "conflicting options: --restart and --rm"; Docker refuses the command, it does not silently pick one.
  • Adding yourself to the docker group takes effect immediately → Group membership is read when a shell session STARTS. Skipping the relogin (or newgrp docker) is the #1 cause of "permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock."
  • hello-world exiting means something failed → It exits instantly BY DESIGN once its one job (print a message) is done — a stopped container is not an error, it's a finished process.
  • "I'm inside a container, so easypj's code must be here" → A base image like python:3.11-slim is an empty stage — no app code. COPYing easypj in is Chapter 4's job, not something 3.4's -it session does.
  • Flags can go anywhere on the command line → Everything typed AFTER the image name is the container's COMMAND, not a docker flag — position is grammar, not style.
  • "port is already allocated" means another app grabbed it → It usually means a FORGOTTEN container already holds it — run docker ps before reaching for lsof.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker ps -a --filter status=exited finds every leftover container before it silently squats on a name or a port.
  • --help works at every level (docker --help, docker image --help, docker image ls --help) — the fastest docs you own.
  • When a command errors, decide CLIENT vs DAEMON first (bad grammar vs API failure) — it halves the search space before you even read the string.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 3)

prove the daemon is alive, run your first containers 
# Client AND server — daemon reachability
docker version

# Full pull→create→run→exit path
docker run --rm hello-world

# Running containers only
docker ps

# Every container, incl. exited
docker ps -a

# Interactive shell, PID 1 inside
docker run -it <image> bash

# Named, detached, port-mapped, env-fed, restartable
docker run -d --name <n> -p H:C --env-file .env --restart unless-stopped <img>

# What a detached (-d) container printed
docker logs <container>
build, run & manage the day-to-day 
docker build -t name:tag .
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name app IMAGE
docker stop CONTAINER
docker rm -f CONTAINER
docker exec -it CONTAINER sh
docker logs -f CONTAINER
docker inspect CONTAINER

🧠 Chapter 3 — DCA Practice Questions (18)

Quick recall of install + first-run fluency — 18 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What happens when you run docker run hello-world for the first time?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. You type docker run hello-world. 2. Docker Client sends the command to the Daemon. 3. Daemon checks local images (not found). 4. Daemon pulls "hello-world" from Docker Hub. 5. Daemon creates a container from the image, runs it, prints a message, and exits.

  1️⃣ You type: $ docker run hello-world
       │
       ▼
  2️⃣ Client ──▶ Daemon: "run hello-world"
       │
       ▼
  3️⃣ Daemon checks local image cache ── not found
       │
       ▼
  4️⃣ Daemon PULLS "hello-world" from Docker Hub
       │
       ▼
  5️⃣ Daemon CREATES a container ──▶ RUNS ──▶ prints message ──▶ EXITS (code 0)
EXPLANATION

The hello-world container is the simplest possible Docker demonstration: it prints a message and exits with code 0 (success). Key insight: Docker does NOT keep containers running after their main process exits. For long-running services, your CMD must be a process that stays alive (web server, database, etc.).

Q2
What do the -i and -t flags do in docker run -it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-i = interactive (keep STDIN open so you can type input). -t = TTY (allocate a pseudo-terminal for proper shell display). Together they give you an interactive terminal session.

FlagStands forGives youAlone (missing the other)
-iinteractiveSTDIN stays openCommands run, but no prompt renders
-tttyPseudo-terminal allocatedPrompt renders, but you can't type input
-itboth combinedA real interactive shell session—
EXPLANATION

-i and -t are almost always used together because an interactive shell needs STDIN (to read your keystrokes) AND a TTY (to render the shell prompt, colors, and control characters). Memory aid: -it = "interactive terminal." Running with only -i (no -t) still works — commands execute — but you get no rendered prompt or proper line editing, so the session "looks broken" even though it functions.

Q3
How do you run a container in the background (detached mode)?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use the -d flag: docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1. The container runs in the background and prints the container ID.

ModeCommandYour terminal
Foregrounddocker run -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1Blocked — Ctrl+C kills the container
Detacheddocker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1Free — prints container ID and returns
EXPLANATION

-d (detach) is essential for production and most development work. Without it, docker run blocks your terminal — the container's stdout streams to your screen and Ctrl+C kills it. With -d, the container runs as a background daemon, printing only the container ID.

Q4
What's the difference between docker ps and docker ps -a?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker ps shows only RUNNING containers. docker ps -a shows ALL containers — running, stopped, exited, created. This is crucial for debugging: a container that immediately exited won't show in docker ps but WILL show in docker ps -a.

docker psdocker ps -a
Running containers✅ shown✅ shown
Stopped / exited containers❌ hidden✅ shown
Use whenChecking what's liveDebugging a container that crashed on start
EXPLANATION

A container that crashes immediately after starting (wrong CMD, missing file, port conflict) will show in docker ps -a with status "Exited (1)" but won't appear in docker ps. Always use -a when troubleshooting.

Q5
How do you map port 8000 on your host to port 8000 in the container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1. The format is -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT. This makes the container's port 8000 accessible at http://localhost:8000 on your host.

  HOST (your machine)                          CONTAINER
  http://localhost:8000  ──▶  -p 8000:8000  ──▶  :8000 (app listening)
                               HOST_PORT : CONTAINER_PORT
EXPLANATION

The -p flag creates iptables DNAT rules that forward host port traffic to the container port. You can bind to specific interfaces: -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 (localhost only, more secure) or -p 8000:8000 (all interfaces). To publish all EXPOSEd ports: -P (capital). Verify mappings: docker port CONTAINER.

Q6
What is the Docker CLI command structure pattern?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker [GLOBAL_OPTIONS] COMMAND [SUBCOMMAND] [OPTIONS] [ARGUMENTS]. Example: docker container run -d -p 8000:8000 --name web nginx:alpine.

  docker   container   run   -d -p 8000:8000 --name web   nginx:alpine
    │         │          │              │                       │
  binary    GROUP      VERB       FLAGS/OPTIONS            TARGET (image)
EXPLANATION

Docker's CLI follows a consistent pattern: GLOBAL options come first (before the command), then the command, then command-specific options, then arguments. This structure applies to ALL docker commands.

Q7
Why is python:3.11-slim preferred over python:3.11 for web apps?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The -slim variant is based on Debian but strips out build tools, documentation, and unnecessary packages. It's ~150 MB vs ~900 MB for the full image — faster pulls, less attack surface, and sufficient for running web applications.

VariantBaseApprox. size
python:3.11full Debian~900 MB
python:3.11-slimDebian, no build tools~150 MB
python:3.11-alpineAlpine (musl libc)~50 MB
EXPLANATION

Docker image variants: python:3.11 (~900 MB, full Debian with build tools), python:3.11-slim (~150 MB, Debian without build tools), python:3.11-alpine (~50 MB, uses musl libc instead of glibc). Slim is the sweet spot for web apps.

Q8
How do you see the logs of a detached container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs <container-name-or-id>. Add -f to follow (like tail -f): docker logs -f easypj-dev. Add --tail 100 to see only the last 100 lines.

docker logs easypj-dev             # dump everything so far
docker logs -f easypj-dev          # follow, like tail -f
docker logs --tail 100 easypj-dev  # last 100 lines only
docker logs --since 10m easypj-dev # last 10 minutes only
EXPLANATION

docker logs reads stdout/stderr from the container's PID 1. Key flags: -f (follow), --tail N (last N lines), --since 10m, --timestamps. Logs persist even after the container stops — they're only deleted when the container is removed.

Q9
What does docker run --rm do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The --rm flag automatically removes the container when it exits. This keeps your system clean — no accumulation of stopped containers. Great for one-off commands and CI/CD pipelines.

EXPLANATION

--rm is the CI/CD best practice flag. Without it, every docker run leaves behind a stopped container that consumes disk space. Combine with meaningful names: docker run --rm --name test-${BUILD_ID} easypj:v1 pytest.

# Without --rm — stopped containers pile up
docker run --name test1 easypj:v1 pytest
docker run --name test2 easypj:v1 pytest
docker ps -a   # test1, test2 ... both still listed, wasting disk

# With --rm — auto-cleaned the instant it exits
docker run --rm --name test-${BUILD_ID} easypj:v1 pytest
docker ps -a   # nothing left behind
Q10
After installing Docker Engine on Linux, a user runs docker ps and gets "permission denied." What's the fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add the user to the docker group: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in. The Docker daemon socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is owned by root:docker — only users in the docker group can access it without sudo.

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER   # add yourself to the docker group
newgrp docker                   # OR log out / back in
docker ps                       # now works without sudo
EXPLANATION

The Docker socket is owned by root:docker with permissions 660. Adding a user to the docker group grants them effective root access on the host (via the daemon). After adding yourself: newgrp docker avoids logging out.

Q11
On a Windows laptop, where do Linux containers actually run, and why doesn't that contradict "containers share the host kernel"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Inside Docker Desktop's managed Linux VM (the WSL2 backend) — the container still shares THAT Linux kernel with every other container in the VM. The "host" from the container's point of view is the VM, not Windows itself: Windows → WSL2 Linux VM → dockerd → containers (shared kernel).

  Windows host
   └── 🐳 Docker Desktop
         └── 🐧 WSL2 Linux VM   (the REAL "host" kernel, from a container's view)
               └── dockerd
                     ├── container A ─┐
                     ├── container B ─┤  all share THIS ONE Linux kernel
                     └── container C ─┘
EXPLANATION

This is why Linux containers run identically on Windows, macOS, and Linux hosts — Desktop simply hides one extra hop (host → VM → daemon) that bare Engine on Linux doesn't need. It also explains why a native Windows container needs a Windows kernel underneath, not a Linux one — the "shared kernel" rule never bends, only the VM layer changes what kernel is being shared.

Q12
Why does sudo usermod -aG docker $USER require a new login/shell before it takes effect, and what error appears if you skip it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Group membership is read when a shell session STARTS — an already-open shell keeps its OLD group list in memory. Skipping the relogin (or newgrp docker) produces "permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock" even though usermod already succeeded.

EXPLANATION

This trips up almost every first-time Linux install: the command that grants the permission runs successfully, but the CURRENT shell can't see the change yet. newgrp docker starts a new shell with the updated group list without a full logout; a fresh SSH session works too.

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
docker ps
# permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock  ← still using the OLD group list

newgrp docker      # starts a NEW shell with the updated group list
docker ps          # works now, no sudo
Q13
After docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim bash and then typing exit, what does docker ps -a show, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing. --rm auto-removes the container the instant its main process (the bash shell, PID 1) exits — before ps -a could ever list it.

EXPLANATION

This is the key difference from a plain docker run -it without --rm: without the flag, the exited container lingers in docker ps -a until you manually docker rm it. With --rm, removal is synchronous with the exit — there's no window where you could catch it in ps -a even if you tried.

docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim bash
root@abc123:/# exit
docker ps -a
# (nothing — --rm removed it the instant bash exited)

# Compare, WITHOUT --rm:
docker run -it python:3.11-slim bash
root@def456:/# exit
docker ps -a
# def456   python:3.11-slim   Exited (0)   ← lingers until you `docker rm` it
Q14
Write, from memory, a production docker run for easypj: named, detached, port 8000, an env file, capped at 512m RAM/1.5 CPUs, restart unless-stopped.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1

EXPLANATION

Every clause maps to one job from the four-job split in 3.5: -d --name --restart is identity/lifecycle, -p is networking, --env-file is configuration, and --memory --cpus is resource control. Flag ORDER before the image name is free — only the image name's POSITION (last, before any container command) is fixed.

ClauseJob
-d --name easypj-web --restart unless-stoppedIdentity / lifecycle
-p 8000:8000Networking
--env-file .envConfiguration
--memory 512m --cpus 1.5Resource control
Q15
Compare the four --restart policies, and say which one a production stack should prefer over always.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Production prefers unless-stopped: it survives crashes and reboots but still respects a deliberate docker stop during maintenance — always would fight you by restarting even after you explicitly stopped it.

EXPLANATION

The full comparison:

PolicyRestarts after crashRestarts after docker stop
nonevernever
on-failure[:N]only non-zero exit, up to N timesnever
unless-stoppedyesno (until explicitly started again)
alwaysyesyes, even after a manual stop
Q16
Translate docker volume rm pgdata and docker image prune -a into plain English using group/verb/flag/target grammar, without running them.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

volume rm pgdata: management group "volume," verb "rm" (remove), target "pgdata" — delete the named volume. image prune -a: management group "image," verb "prune," flag -a (all) — remove ALL unused images, not just dangling ones.

CommandGroupVerbFlagTarget
docker volume rm pgdatavolumerm—pgdata
docker image prune -aimageprune-a—
EXPLANATION

This is 3.6's whole point in miniature: once you can parse group → verb → flags → target as grammar instead of memorized strings, ANY docker command becomes guessable from its shape alone — including ones you've never typed before.

Q17
A teammate reports "port is already allocated" starting easypj-web on 8000. What are your first two commands, and in what order?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker ps first (find a forgotten container already publishing 8000), then lsof -i :8000 (or netstat) only if docker ps comes back clean.

  "port is already allocated" on 8000
       │
       ▼
  1️⃣ docker ps      ── forgotten container already publishing 8000? (check Docker's OWN state first)
       │ clean
       ▼
  2️⃣ lsof -i :8000  ── some OTHER OS process holding the port
EXPLANATION

Checking Docker's own state before the OS's avoids chasing the wrong process — "port is already allocated" almost always means a container YOU started earlier (and forgot about) still holds the port, not some unrelated system service.

Q18
Sort these into CLIENT-side vs DAEMON-side, and state the rule that sorts them: "unknown flag: --nam," "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon," "No such container: easypj-old," "exec format error."
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CLIENT: "unknown flag: --nam" (bad grammar, never reaches the API). DAEMON: "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon," "No such container: easypj-old," "exec format error" (all require the daemon to process the request and refuse it).

ErrorSideWhy
"unknown flag: --nam"CLIENTBad grammar — never reaches the API
"Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"DAEMONDaemon unreachable / not running
"No such container: easypj-old"DAEMONDaemon looked it up and it doesn't exist
"exec format error"DAEMONDaemon tried to run a wrong-architecture binary
EXPLANATION

The rule: if it fails before the API call, it's the CLIENT; if the daemon itself reports the problem, it's the DAEMON. This is the same triage rule from 3.7 — apply it BEFORE reading the error string closely, and you've already halved your search space.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.1 — Predict docker ps -a

Run nginx four different ways — plain, --rm, -d --name, and -it bash inside it — predicting docker ps -a's output BEFORE you run each one. Score yourself: 4/4 correct means Chapter 3 is muscle memory.

  Predict BEFORE you run — then check docker ps -a:

  1. docker run nginx                   (plain, foreground)  → Ctrl+C → Exited    (ps -a: present)
  2. docker run --rm nginx              (foreground)          → Ctrl+C → REMOVED   (ps -a: absent)
  3. docker run -d --name web nginx     (detached)            → Up, running        (ps AND ps -a: present)
  4. docker run -it nginx bash          (interactive shell)   → exit → Exited (0)  (ps -a: present)

  Score: ___ / 4 correct predictions

Docker Concepts — What You Now Know

You started asking why "works on my machine" keeps happening; now you can explain the image/container split, trace a docker run all the way from CLI to runc, and read any image reference down to its digest. You've installed Docker for real and run your first containers by hand — the vocabulary and reflexes every later chapter assumes are already yours.

🔑 Part 1 — Key Takeaways

  • Docker packages the whole userspace — interpreter, libraries, code — into one portable image; containers share the host kernel (no hypervisor, no guest OS), which is why they're MB & milliseconds instead of GB & minutes (Ch 1).
  • Docker images ARE OCI images — an open image-spec/runtime-spec chain (dockerd → containerd → shim → runc) means the exact image you build here runs unmodified under Podman or a Kubernetes node's containerd (Ch 1).
  • Everything is built from five nouns: image (read-only blueprint), container (running instance), registry (storage), layer (cached diff, order = rebuild cost), and tag (mutable name vs. immutable digest) — a full reference is registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest, and daemon.json governs the host (Ch 2).
  • Docker is installed and proven alive — Desktop (Mac/Win) or Engine (Linux); docker run hello-world walks all 5 steps (pull → create → start → run → exit); and the CLI's group → verb → flags → target grammar makes every future command guessable, not memorized (Ch 3).
  • 🎯 Exam: this Part underwrites two graded DCA domains directly — Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%, Ch 2) and Installation & Configuration (15%, Ch 3) — plus every domain after it.
  • 🔑 docker run · docker build · docker ps -a · docker logs -f · docker exec -it · docker inspect
📌 Part 1 Visual Summary — problem → the five nouns → hands-on

                                                        │ built from 🍰 layers, named by 🏷️ tag@digest
                                                        ▼
   🗄️ registry (Hub/ECR/GCR/Harbor) ◀──push/pull──▶ 📦 registry/repo:tag@digest  (Ch 2: the five nouns)

   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   one app, packaged once as an OCI image, that runs identically everywhere Docker exists. 🐳

In words: Docker exists to kill "works on my machine": it packages your whole userspace into one image, then runs it as a container that shares the host kernel instead of booting a guest OS — cheap because there's no hypervisor per app (Ch 1). That image is just one of five nouns everything else conjugates — image, container, registry, layer, tag — addressed by a full reference like registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest, with layer order deciding how much of a rebuild your next code change costs (Ch 2).

From there it's hands: you install Docker Desktop or Engine, prove it's alive with docker run hello-world's five steps, and learn to read any command as group → verb → flags → target grammar instead of memorizing it — the CLI reflexes (-d -p -e -v --name --rm) every later chapter assumes are already automatic (Ch 3).

The one idea to keep: Docker isn't a proprietary black box — it's an open standard (OCI) implemented by an inspectable chain (dockerd → containerd → runc) on ordinary kernel primitives, which is exactly why the image you build in Chapter 2 still runs, byte-for-byte, wherever an OCI runtime exists.

The Dockerfile is where you define your application's environment. It's a simple text file with instructions that tell Docker how to build your image. Master the Dockerfile, and you master Docker itself.
