4.1 What is a Dockerfile?

A Dockerfile is a text file containing a series of instructions that Docker reads to automatically build an image. Each instruction creates a layer. Think of it as a recipe: Dockerfile → docker build → Image → docker run → Container.

📝
Dockerfile

A text file named Dockerfile (no extension). Contains instructions like FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD. This is what YOU write.

📦
Image

The output of docker build. A read-only template containing your app + all dependencies. This is what gets STORED and SHARED.

▶️
Container

A running instance of an image. Created by docker run. Has its own writable layer, network, and process space.

🍰 Analogy — Recipe Card → Baked Cake → Plated Slice

The Dockerfile is a recipe card: a declarative list of steps that describes the RESULT, not a live process. docker build follows the card once and produces a baked cake — the image, an immutable artifact anyone can slice from identically. docker run plates one serving — a container. You never serve the recipe card itself, and eating a bite off one plated slice never rewrites the card in the kitchen — to change the cake, you edit the card and bake again from scratch.

Because a Dockerfile is executed top-to-bottom by BuildKit and most instructions freeze their result into a real image layer, committing the Dockerfile to git is enough for anyone on the team to rebuild an identical cake — that's what "declarative" buys you. For easypj specifically, a 10-line Dockerfile sitting next to manage.py replaces an entire "install Python 3.11, pip install these 40 packages, remember these six env vars" onboarding wiki page: git clone + docker build is the whole setup.

📄 Parser Directives Must Come First — Before Even Comments

Three special directives — # syntax=, # escape=, # check= — must sit as the literal FIRST lines of the file, before any other content, even regular comments. # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 is what unlocks newer BuildKit-only features like Appendix B.6's heredoc RUN blocks (Appendix B.9 has the full parser-directive syntax). Put one after a comment or blank line by mistake and Docker silently ignores it, parsing the file with old default rules instead.

4.2 Dockerfile Instruction Reference

Every Dockerfile instruction serves a specific purpose. Here are ALL the instructions you need to know for the DCA exam:

InstructionPurposeeasypj Example
FROMBase image (MANDATORY, always first)FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIRSet working directoryWORKDIR /app
COPYCopy files from host to imageCOPY requirements.txt .
ADDLike COPY, but also handles URLs and tar extractionADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /app/
RUNExecute commands during buildRUN pip install -r requirements.txt
ENVSet environment variables (persist at runtime)ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
ARGBuild-time variables (NOT in final image by default)ARG DJANGO_VERSION=5.2
EXPOSEDocument which port the app listens on (NOT publish!)EXPOSE 8000
CMDDefault command (overridable at runtime)CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application"]
ENTRYPOINTFixed executable (harder to override)ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]
USERSwitch to non-root user for securityUSER appuser
VOLUMECreate a mount point for external volumesVOLUME ["/app/static"]
HEALTHCHECKCommand to check container healthHEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/
LABELAdd metadata to imageLABEL version="1.0" maintainer="easypj"
SHELLChange default shell for RUNSHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
STOPSIGNALSignal to stop containerSTOPSIGNAL SIGTERM
The Build-Time / Run-Time / Metadata Axis
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │      BUILD TIME  (image layers)  ║  RUN TIME (container)       │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ FROM      ●         ║           base layer, always first       │
  │ ARG        ●        ║           build-only, discarded after    │
  │ COPY        ●─●     ║           files baked into a layer       │
  │ RUN         ●──●    ║           executes; result frozen in     │
  │ EXPOSE    ○         ║           metadata only — no publish     │
  │                                                                │
  │ WORKDIR   ●───────  ║───●       sets CWD, stays true at run    │
  │ ENV       ●───────  ║───●       baked in, still there at run   │
  │                                                                │
  │ USER                ║  ●        drops root before CMD          │
  │ CMD                 ║      ●    the process, every start       │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ● act now   ─ stays in effect   ○ documented, not enforced     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
InstructionPhaseWhat that means
FROMbuildBase layer, always resolved first
WORKDIRbuild + runSets CWD once; still true at container start
COPYbuildFiles baked into a real layer
RUNbuildExecutes once; result frozen into a layer
ENVbuild + runBaked in AND visible at runtime (and in docker inspect)
ARGbuild onlyGone once the build finishes — invisible to docker inspect
EXPOSEmetadataDocuments a port; publishes nothing (-p does that)
USERrunDrops root right before CMD/ENTRYPOINT executes
CMDrunThe actual process, resolved fresh every start
🧑‍🍳 Analogy — Prep Steps vs. Serving Notes

A recipe has prep steps done once, before service — "chop the onions" is RUN: it happens during the build and its result (chopped onions / an installed package) is frozen into the dish. It also has serving notes applied fresh every time a plate goes out — "serve warm" is CMD: re-evaluated at every docker run. EXPOSE is a note scribbled in the margin for the waiter — useful documentation, but it doesn't itself get a plate to the table.

Concretely, in easypj's own Dockerfile: RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt bakes Django, gunicorn, and psycopg2 into a single layer exactly once, at build time — while CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", ...] is re-evaluated fresh at every single docker run. That's the prep-steps/serving-notes split above, in the actual file you'll write in 4.4.

💡 ARG vs ENV — Same Shape, Opposite Lifetimes

ARG and ENV look alike but sit on opposite sides of the build/run axis: an ARG value is gone the moment the build finishes — docker inspect on the finished image shows nothing — while an ENV value is baked into the image AND visible in every container's docker inspect output, forever. That's exactly why secrets belong in neither: use --secret mounts (5.7) instead of either one.

💡 MAINTAINER Is Deprecated — and ADD Has More Tricks Than "COPY Plus Extraction"

Docker's own guidance: MAINTAINER is deprecated — "use the LABEL instruction instead, as it enables setting any metadata you require," e.g. LABEL maintainer="team@easypj.dev". The current docs.docker.com reference goes one step further and recommends the OCI-standard key specifically: LABEL org.opencontainers.image.authors="team@easypj.dev" — the informal maintainer key still works and is what most existing Dockerfiles use, but org.opencontainers.image.authors is the one tooling that understands OCI image annotations (registries, SBOM generators, Scout) recognizes by convention. Separately, ADD is more than "COPY plus tar/URL": it can also pull straight from a Git repository URL and verify a --checksum against the fetched content — Appendix B.11 documents the full flag set and exactly when each extra behavior earns its place instead of being an audit red flag.

4.3 CMD vs ENTRYPOINT — The Most Confusing Part

This is the #1 source of confusion for Docker beginners — and a favorite DCA exam topic. The key difference:

CMD = Default command that can be easily overridden when you docker run.
ENTRYPOINT = Fixed command that always runs; arguments to docker run are appended to it.

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT Decision Matrix
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                🎯 CMD vs ENTRYPOINT — WHICH TO USE?                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │              │      CMD             │       ENTRYPOINT             │  │
  │  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤  │
  │  │ Purpose      │ Default command      │ Fixed executable             │  │
  │  │ Overridable? │ ✅ Easily            │ ❌ Needs --entrypoint flag   │  │
  │  │ Use When...  │ App has one main     │ App is a wrapper/tool that   │  │
  │  │              │ purpose but may vary │ should always run the same   │  │
  │  │ Analogy      │ Default radio station│ Car ENGINE (not optional!)   │  │
  │  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  [6 COMBINATIONS — What Happens?]                                        │
  │  # | Dockerfile                    | docker run img | Result            │
  │  1 | CMD ["echo", "hello"]        | (none)          | echo hello        │
  │  2 | CMD ["echo", "hello"]        | world            | error (no cmd)   │
  │  3 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]           | (none)          | echo (no arg)    │
  │  4 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]           | hello           | echo hello        │
  │  5 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]+CMD["Hi"]| (none)          | echo Hi           │
  │  6 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]+CMD["Hi"]| world (OVERRIDES!)| echo world      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏆 Best Practice for easypj

ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"] (always run gunicorn) + CMD ["easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"] (default WSGI app + bind, but you can override with different worker count at runtime).

🚗 Analogy — Car Engine vs. Radio Preset

ENTRYPOINT is the car's engine: it's not optional, the car always drives, and swapping it out needs a mechanic (--entrypoint). CMD is the radio preset: a sensible default station the driver overrides freely just by turning the dial (anything typed after the image name on docker run). The rule that makes all six matrix rows predictable: the final command Docker executes is always ENTRYPOINT + CMD, concatenated — arguments typed at docker run replace CMD only, never ENTRYPOINT; --entrypoint is the only flag that replaces ENTRYPOINT itself.

That split makes runtime overrides safe and predictable in practice: docker run easypj:v1 easypj.wsgi:application --workers 4 only swaps CMD's arguments — bumping the worker count — while ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"] itself is never up for negotiation; gunicorn still runs, just with a different worker count than the Dockerfile's default.

Shell form vs. exec form is the actual syntax choice behind that SIGTERM/PID 1 behavior — CMD and ENTRYPOINT can each be written either way:

shell form — avoid for the main process 
# bare command string
CMD python manage.py runserver
ENTRYPOINT gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application
exec form — the default choice 
# JSON array, double-quoted strings
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver"]
ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application"]
BehaviorShell formExec form
How Docker runs itWrapped: /bin/sh -c "python manage.py runserver"Direct — execve() the binary, no shell involved
What becomes PID 1The shell (/bin/sh)Your process itself (gunicorn)
docker stop's SIGTERMHits the shell — most shells don't forward it, so it's ignored until the 10s grace period expires and SIGKILL hits mid-requestHits your process directly — clean, immediate shutdown
$VARIABLE expansion✅ Works — the shell substitutes it❌ Does not work — no shell means no substitution
Pipes, &&, wildcards✅ Work — full shell syntax available❌ Not available — it's a literal argv array
DCA / production guidanceOnly when you specifically need shell featuresDefault — correct signal handling, predictable argv
⚠️ The Trap: Exec Form Doesn't Expand Environment Variables

A very common exam-style gotcha runs the other direction: CMD ["echo", "$HOME"] prints the literal string $HOME, not its value — exec form never invokes a shell, so nothing expands $HOME. If you genuinely need variable expansion AND correct signal handling, the fix is not shell form; it's exec form calling the shell explicitly and then handing off: CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT"] — the explicit exec inside the string is what makes gunicorn (not sh) become PID 1, the same trick 4.7's entrypoint script relies on.

⚠️ Shell-Form ENTRYPOINT Silently Discards CMD Entirely

The six-combination matrix above only ever shows an exec-form ENTRYPOINT — because shell-form ENTRYPOINT changes the rules completely. Docker's own reference table is explicit: whatever CMD says (or omits), a shell-form ENTRYPOINT ALWAYS resolves to just /bin/sh -c "<entrypoint string>" — CMD never gets appended, never gets a chance to matter.

  ENTRYPOINT gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application     # shell form
  CMD ["--workers", "4"]                           # SILENTLY IGNORED — never appended

  Actual process every time: /bin/sh -c "gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application"   (no --workers, ever)

Anything typed after the image name on docker run is appended too — but since a shell-form entrypoint string like "gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application" never references $@ or $1, those trailing words arrive as unused positional parameters and still never show up in what actually runs. Combining shell-form ENTRYPOINT with CMD (or expecting docker run args to reach it) is a real anti-pattern — switch ENTRYPOINT to exec form whenever CMD or runtime args need to matter.

💡 --entrypoint Takes ONE Executable, No Arguments — and an Empty String Clears It

The docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it easypj:v1 command in this chapter's Commands list only accepts a single executable path on that flag — it can't carry arguments the way ENTRYPOINT's exec-form JSON array can; any arguments go as ordinary trailing docker run arguments instead, exactly like CMD would receive them (docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it easypj:v1 -c "ls /app"). If you need to run a completely different program with NO entrypoint honored at all — not even overridden to a shell — pass an empty string: docker run --entrypoint "" easypj:v1 python manage.py shell clears ENTRYPOINT entirely and runs the trailing command directly as PID 1.

4.4 Building an easypj Dockerfile — Step by Step

Let's build the complete Dockerfile for our easypj Django application. We'll evolve from a naive first attempt to a production-ready multi-stage Dockerfile. Every line is explained:

🥚
Stage 1
Naive Dockerfile

FROM python:latest
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver"]

❌ ~950 MB, runs as root
🐣
Stage 2
Slim Base + Layer Order

FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

⚠️ ~230 MB, better caching
🐔
Stage 3
Production Server

+ --no-cache-dir (drops ~100 MB pip cache)
+ gunicorn instead of runserver
+ ENV variables
+ EXPOSE
+ non-root USER

✅ ~180 MB, production-ready
🦅
Stage 4
Multi-Stage Mastery

FROM python:3.11 AS build
... build stage ...
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=build ...

🏆 ~180 MB, minimal attack surface
DOCKERFILE 
# Step 1: Choose the base image
# python:3.11-slim = Debian + Python 3.11, stripped down (~150 MB)
# Why slim not alpine? Alpine uses musl libc, can cause issues with some Python packages
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Step 2: Set working directory (all subsequent commands run here)
WORKDIR /app

# Step 3: Copy requirements FIRST (layer caching trick!)
# If requirements.txt hasn't changed, this layer is CACHED
COPY requirements.txt .

# Step 4: Install dependencies
# --no-cache-dir: don't cache pip packages (saves ~100 MB in image)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Step 5: Copy application code (changes most often, so goes LAST)
COPY . .

# Step 6: Set environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings

# Step 7: Document the port (does NOT publish it — use -p flag with docker run)
EXPOSE 8000

# Step 8: Command to run when container starts
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
📖 Why This Order?

The order is intentional: FROM (never changes) → requirements.txt (rarely changes) → pip install (rarely changes) → source code (changes constantly). This maximizes layer caching. When you edit views.py, only the last COPY layer rebuilds — everything else is cached!

Layer Visualization — Which Line Creates Which Layer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🍰 HOW THE easypj DOCKERFILE MAPS TO LAYERS                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DOCKERFILE LINE                          →  IMAGE LAYER                 │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  FROM python:3.11-slim                    →  Layer 1: Base (~150 MB)     │
  │  WORKDIR /app                             →  Layer 2: Directory (0 B)    │
  │  COPY requirements.txt .                  →  Layer 3: Deps list (~200 B) │
  │  RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \         →  Layer 4: Packages (~80 MB)  │
  │      -r requirements.txt                                               │
  │  COPY . .                                 →  Layer 5: Your code (~500KB) │
  │  ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 ...        →  Layer 6: Config (0 B)       │
  │  EXPOSE 8000                              →  Layer 7: Metadata (0 B)     │
  │  CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:app", ...] →  Layer 8: Startup (0 B)     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYERS 1-8 = READ-ONLY (shared by all containers)                      │
  │  CONTAINER gets an additional READ-WRITE layer on top                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CACHING: Change models.py → only Layer 5 rebuilds (~0.5s)             │
  │           Change requirements.txt → Layers 3-4 rebuild (~45s)            │
  │           Change base image → ALL layers rebuild (~2 min)                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧳 Analogy — Packing a Suitcase

Pack a suitcase the way this Dockerfile is ordered: heavy, rarely-touched items go in FIRST at the bottom (the base image, the dependency list), things you swap out daily go on TOP, easiest to reach (your source code). Repacking for a new trip (rebuilding after a code change) never means unpacking the whole case — you only touch what's on top.

📖 Why slim, Not alpine, for easypj

Alpine's tiny size comes from swapping glibc for musl libc — and psycopg2 (easypj's PostgreSQL driver) ships prebuilt wheels compiled against glibc, not musl. On alpine, pip falls back to compiling psycopg2 from source, which needs build tools present anyway and is slower and more fragile than just installing a prebuilt wheel. python:3.11-slim keeps glibc (still far smaller than the full python:3.11 image) so pip install stays a fast binary download — 8.2 runs the full slim-vs-alpine duel with real numbers.

4.5 Multi-Stage Dockerfiles — Smaller, Safer Images

A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a new stage. You can copy artifacts from earlier stages into later ones — keeping build tools OUT of your final image.

Multi-Stage Build Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🏗️ MULTI-STAGE BUILD ARCHITECTURE                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 1: BUILDER (python:3.11)              STAGE 2: FINAL (slim)        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────┐              ┌───────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11 AS build │              │ FROM python:3.11-slim     │ │
  │  │                           │              │                           │ │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .   │              │ COPY --from=build         │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install --user    │   COPY       │      /root/.local          │ │
  │  │   -r requirements.txt     │─────────────▶│      /root/.local          │ │
  │  │                           │  artifacts   │                           │ │
  │  │ RUN python manage.py      │              │ COPY --from=build         │ │
  │  │   collectstatic --noinput │─────────────▶│      /app/static           │ │
  │  │                           │  static      │                           │ │
  │  │ Includes: gcc, make,      │              │ NO gcc, NO build tools!   │ │
  │  │   git, headers, dev libs  │              │ Only runtime deps.        │ │
  │  │                           │              │                           │ │
  │  │ SIZE: ~850 MB             │              │ SIZE: ~180 MB (5x smaller!)│ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┘              └───────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
MetricSingle-StageMulti-StageImprovement
Image Size~850 MB~180 MB✅ 5x smaller
Build Time45s42s (similar)✅ Slightly faster
Attack SurfaceLarge (gcc, git, make)Small (only runtime deps)✅ 70% fewer CVEs
CVEs (vulnerabilities)120+30-40✅ 3-4x fewer
Pull Time (10 Mbps)~11 min~2.4 min✅ 4.5x faster
Disk Usage (10 deploys)8.5 GB1.8 GB✅ 4.7x less storage
🏆 The Multi-Stage Advantage

Multi-stage builds aren't just about size — they're about security. Build tools like GCC, make, and git are powerful attack vectors. By keeping them out of your production image, you eliminate entire classes of vulnerabilities. The DCA exam expects you to know when and why to use multi-stage builds.

🪑 Analogy — Workshop vs. Showroom

A furniture maker saws, sands, and paints in a sawdust-covered workshop (the builder stage) — full of tools nobody wants customers to see. Only the finished chair gets carried into the clean showroom (the final stage) that customers actually walk through. The architecture diagram above draws exactly that left-to-right move, and the size table prices what leaving the sawdust behind is worth.

🤔 4.4 Said slim Never Needed gcc — So Why Does the Builder Stage Start From the Full Image?

easypj's own requirements.txt happens to need nothing compiled — psycopg2 ships glibc wheels (4.4). The size table above prices the GENERAL case every growing Django project eventually hits: the moment one dependency needs a compile (Pillow, lxml, cryptography, numpy), a single-stage Dockerfile is stuck shipping gcc/headers/dev-libs in production forever, while a multi-stage builder absorbs that exact cost for free — none of it crosses the COPY --from=build line into the final stage. Starting the builder stage from the full python:3.11 image is insurance a real app needs sooner or later, not something this week's requirements.txt is forcing.

DOCKERFILE: Multi-Stage for easypj 
# ═══════ STAGE 1: BUILD ═══════
FROM python:3.11 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
# Install to /root/.local so we can copy just the packages
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# Collect static files (Django)
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ═══════ STAGE 2: FINAL (PRODUCTION) ═══════
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Copy ONLY the installed packages from build stage
COPY --from=build /root/.local /root/.local
# Copy ONLY the collected static files
COPY --from=build /app/static /app/static
# Copy application code
COPY . .
# Ensure scripts in .local are findable
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
EXPOSE 8000
# Create non-root user for security
RUN groupadd --system appuser && useradd --system --group appuser
USER appuser
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
💡 Two Multi-Stage Tricks Beyond COPY --from=build

Docker's official build docs describe two more moves worth knowing: docker build --target build -t easypj:builder . stops the build at ANY named stage instead of the last one — hand this to a teammate debugging why pip install failed, without ever building the final slim stage at all. And COPY --from= isn't limited to a stage inside THIS Dockerfile — it also accepts a published image reference directly, e.g. COPY --from=nginx:1.27 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf lifts one file out of a completely separate image with no extra stage, no extra FROM, and nothing else from that image shipping in yours.

4.6 Dockerfile Best Practices

Production Dockerfiles follow well-established conventions. These best practices are tested on the DCA exam and expected in real-world Docker environments:

✅ DO❌ DON'T
Use specific tags: python:3.11-slimUse :latest (unpredictable builds)
Chain RUN commands with && to reduce layersSeparate RUN for each package (more layers)
Clean up after package managers: rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*Leave package caches in the image (wasted space)
COPY requirements.txt BEFORE source codeCOPY everything at once (breaks caching)
Use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary filesSend entire project directory as build context
Run as non-root user: USER appuserRun as root (critical security risk)
Use multi-stage builds for smaller, safer imagesInclude build tools (gcc, git) in production image
Use COPY instead of ADD for local filesUse ADD for local files (COPY is explicit)
Run docker scout quickview before every releaseShip without ever scanning for known CVEs
🔢 The 9-Point Dockerfile Quality Checklist

✅ 1. Specific base tag   ✅ 2. WORKDIR set   ✅ 3. .dockerignore present   ✅ 4. COPY before RUN (cache)   ✅ 5. Chained RUNs   ✅ 6. Non-root USER   ✅ 7. Exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT   ✅ 8. One process per container   ✅ 9. docker scout quickview run before shipping

✈️ Analogy — The Pre-Flight Checklist

Pilots don't debate each item on a pre-flight checklist before every flight — every single line exists because something once crashed without it. Treat this 9-point list the same way: run it mechanically, every build, without re-litigating whether any one line is "really necessary" this time.

Concretely for easypj: adding RUN groupadd --system appuser && useradd --system --group appuser + USER appuser (4.5) costs two lines — skip them and a Django remote-code-execution bug (a real, common web-app vulnerability class) hands an attacker root inside the container instead of a throwaway unprivileged account. The "one process per container" rule is just as concrete: PostgreSQL belongs in its own container, never bundled inside the easypj image itself — two processes means tangled logs, confused restarts, and no single target for HEALTHCHECK to probe. Docker's own build docs soften the rule's wording slightly — "a good rule of thumb, but not a hard and fast rule" — and name legitimate exceptions like an init process supervising children, or Celery/Apache spawning worker processes of their own accord; the test that still applies is whether the extra processes are one COHESIVE service (fine) or two INDEPENDENT services duct-taped together (easypj + PostgreSQL is the second kind, and belongs in two containers).

ViolationReal failure it causes
Unpinned base tag (:latest)Silent drift — today's build ≠ tomorrow's (2.5)
Wrong COPY orderDead build cache — every edit rebuilds everything (2.4)
Split apt-get update / install across two RUNsStale apt index cached in an earlier layer (2.4)
Running as rootA container escape lands as root on the HOST (Part 7)
Shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINTLost SIGTERM — docker stop hangs 10s then SIGKILLs (4.3)
Two processes in one containerTangled logs, confused restarts, no single healthcheck target

4.7 The Entrypoint Script Pattern — Migrations at Startup

The problem: easypj needs migrate + collectstatic BEFORE gunicorn starts. A single CMD can only run one command — Django needs a sequence. The fix is an entrypoint script: wait for PostgreSQL → migrate → exec "$@".

docker-entrypoint.sh — the pattern in full 
#!/bin/sh
set -e
until pg_isready -h "$DB_HOST" -p 5432 -q; do
  echo "waiting for PostgreSQL..."; sleep 1
done
python manage.py migrate --noinput
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
exec "$@"        # replace shell with CMD → gunicorn = PID 1

The wiring: ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"] + CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"].

📖 exec "$@" Is the Load-Bearing Line

exec REPLACES the shell process with CMD's process, so gunicorn inherits PID 1 and docker stop's SIGTERM reaches it directly. Without exec, the shell stays PID 1 and swallows every signal (4.3) — docker stop then hangs 10 seconds before SIGKILLing gunicorn mid-request.

💡 The Theatre Stage Manager Analogy

The script checks the orchestra is seated (pg_isready), sets the props (migrate), then steps OFF the stage and hands the spotlight to the actor (exec "$@") — the manager never stands in front of the performance. Without the wait loop, compose starting postgres and easypj together races the DB and migrate dies with "connection refused"; the loop turns a crash-loop into a 2-second wait.

Under the Hood — from instruction to layer, to image, to running PID 1

Every FROM/RUN/COPY/ADD instruction that touches the filesystem makes BuildKit open a NEW layer: it snapshots the diff (files added, changed or deleted) and stores it, content-addressed by a SHA-256 digest, in the storage driver (overlay2 on Linux — 2.4). Metadata-only instructions — WORKDIR, ENV, EXPOSE, ARG, USER, LABEL, CMD, ENTRYPOINT — never touch the filesystem, so BuildKit records them as a 0-byte entry in the image's config JSON instead of a real layer. The image itself is nothing more than an ORDERED LIST of layer digests plus that one config file.

Every layer-producing instruction gets a deterministic CACHE KEY: hash(parent layer digest + exact instruction text + [for COPY/ADD] a checksum of every file copied). Change any one input and that layer — and every layer stacked on top of it — must rebuild; nothing downstream can trust a parent that changed.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    → layer A   (150MB, real files)       │
  │ WORKDIR /app             → metadata only (0B, config JSON)     │
  │ COPY requirements.txt .  → layer B   (~200 B, real files)      │
  │ RUN pip install ...      → layer C   (~80MB, real files)       │
  │ COPY . .                 → layer D   (~500KB, real files)      │
  │ ENV / EXPOSE / CMD       → metadata only (0B, config JSON)     │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ IMAGE = [A, B, C, D layer digests] + config JSON (env/cmd/…)   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 Only four of the eight instructions above ever touch disk — WORKDIR, ENV, EXPOSE and CMD all folded into the config JSON instead, leaving just four real layers (A–D) behind, exactly what 7.6's docker history output shows you as 0B rows.
① Layer Cache Keys, Precisely — diffID, chainID & a Different Digest Than 2.1's

Chapter 2's Under the Hood ① opened up the digest a REGISTRY stores once you push — a hash of the compressed blob, chained up through the config blob into the manifest. Locally, DURING a build, BuildKit is answering a completely different question, over and over: "have I already built a layer with exactly this content, so I can skip re-running this instruction?" That lookup uses a different pair of hashes entirely — diffID and chainID — computed over UNCOMPRESSED layer content and never touching a registry at all.

  diffID(layer)  = sha256 of that layer's OWN uncompressed tar diff — content only, no parent involved

  chainID(A) = diffID(A)                                      ← base layer, FROM python:3.11-slim
  chainID(B) = sha256( chainID(A) + " " + diffID(B) )         ← COPY requirements.txt .
  chainID(C) = sha256( chainID(B) + " " + diffID(C) )         ← RUN pip install ...
  chainID(D) = sha256( chainID(C) + " " + diffID(D) )         ← COPY . .

  BUILD CACHE LOOKUP for layer C on your NEXT build:
    same diffID(C)  AND  chainID(B) still matches upstream?  →  HIT, skip RUN pip install
    either one differs                                        →  MISS — C rebuilds, D's chainID
                                                                    recomputes too (it depends on C)
HashComputed overUsed forChanges if…
diffIDone layer's uncompressed tar content, aloneidentifying THIS layer's bytes, independent of historyany file that layer adds/changes/removes is different
chainIDthe PARENT chainID + this layer's diffID, chained from the basethe actual local build-cache lookup keythis layer's own diffID changes, OR any ancestor's does
Distribution digest (2.1)the COMPRESSED blob, then the manifest JSON that lists itwhat a registry stores/serves and @sha256:… pinssame content can still differ — gzip implementation/level affects compressed bytes even when diffID matches
🔑 This chainID chain is the literal mechanism behind 4.4's "Why This Order?" box: chainID(D) depends on chainID(C) depends on chainID(B). Put COPY . . before COPY requirements.txt . and every downstream chainID recomputes on EVERY build, cache or not — reordering isn't a style preference, it's rewriting which hash chain your build cache can even attempt to match.
② Which Instruction Writes Which Config Field

2.1's Under the Hood told you the config blob holds "env vars, entrypoint/cmd, build history" — true, but generic. Since this whole chapter is about writing instructions, here's the exact map: every metadata-only instruction from 4.2's table — the ones that produced 0-byte layers in this section's opening diagram — writes to ONE specific named field inside that same JSON document docker inspect prints as .Config:

Dockerfile instructiondocker inspect fieldeasypj value
WORKDIR /app.Config.WorkingDir"/app"
ENV KEY=value.Config.Env["PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1", …]
EXPOSE 8000.Config.ExposedPorts{"8000/tcp": {}}
CMD [...].Config.Cmd["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", …]
ENTRYPOINT [...].Config.Entrypoint["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"]
USER appuser.Config.User"appuser"
LABEL key="val".Config.Labels{"maintainer": "team@easypj.dev"}
VOLUME [...].Config.Volumes{"/app/static": {}}
STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM.Config.StopSignal"SIGTERM"
HEALTHCHECK ....Config.Healthcheck{"Test":[…], "Interval":30000000000, …}
🔑 This is the same JSON object 7.6's docker inspect audits and ③ below reads Cmd/Entrypoint from — one document, written one field at a time by the instructions you choose in 4.2, forever frozen the moment the build finishes.
③ From Config JSON to execve() — What runc Actually Starts

Chapter 3's Under the Hood ② walked the handoff — containerd → shim → runc create/start — that turns a container object into a real Linux process. Here's exactly what crosses that handoff for CMD/ENTRYPOINT. The image's Config.Cmd/Config.Entrypoint arrays (②) are BAKED IN at build time and never change again. What actually runs is computed FRESH at docker run time — merged from that static Config plus anything typed after the image name — into a single Process.Args array inside a completely different, per-container document (the OCI RUNTIME spec, confusingly also called config.json, that dockerd hands to containerd). runc start then does exactly one mechanical thing with it: resolve Process.Args[0] and execve() it.

  Dockerfile (build time)              Config blob (②, frozen)         docker run (fresh, per-container)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ ENTRYPOINT [...]          │──────▶ │ Config.Entrypoint = [...]│────▶│ Process.Args =                │
  │ CMD [...]                 │──────▶ │ Config.Cmd = [...]        │────▶│  Entrypoint ++ (run-args        │
  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘     │              OR Cmd if none)   │
                                                                        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                                                                       ▼
                                                              runc start (Ch3 ②) → execve(Args[0], Args, envp)
4.3 formWhat ends up in Config.CmdProcess.Args[0]PID 1 program
Exec: CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application"]["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application"] — literal"gunicorn"gunicorn itself
Shell: CMD python manage.py runserver["/bin/sh", "-c", "python manage.py runserver"] — rewritten AT BUILD TIME"/bin/sh"the shell (python is its child)
🔑 This is the precise mechanical reason behind 4.3's whole decision matrix and Chapter 6's SIGTERM story: shell form doesn't "sometimes" make /bin/sh PID 1 — Config.Cmd already CONTAINS /bin/sh, literally, frozen in at build time, long before docker run ever computes Process.Args.
④ Multi-Stage Builds & the Local Build Cache — Where Do Builder-Stage Layers Actually Go?

4.5 is exactly right that the FINAL image's manifest never references the builder stage's layers. But "not in the final image" and "gone from disk" are two different claims. Every layer BuildKit produces while executing ANY stage — including a builder stage nothing downstream ever COPY --from's again — stays behind in the local, chainID-indexed build cache (①), specifically so your NEXT build can reuse it even though those exact layers will never ship inside an image tag again.

  STAGE 1 (build) produces:  E [FROM python:3.11] F [COPY reqs] G [RUN pip --user] H [RUN collectstatic]
  STAGE 2 (final) produces:  I [FROM slim] J [COPY --from=build .local] K [COPY --from=build static] L [COPY . .]

  Final image MANIFEST references:  [ I, J, K, L ]   ← E,F,G,H never appear here — 4.5's size table
  Local BUILD CACHE still holds:    [ A..D, E,F,G,H, I,J,K,L ]  ← every layer any stage ever produced

  `docker images`     → only sees I,J,K,L worth of size, under your tag
  `docker system df`  → "Build Cache" row still counts E,F,G,H (and A-D) until pruned
CommandWhat it actually reclaims
docker image prune -a (this chapter's own Commands list)untagged/dangling IMAGES only — never touches the separate build cache
docker builder prunethe build cache itself — the one command that frees E-H above
docker system dfreporting only — shows "Build Cache" as its own line, distinct from "Images"
🔑 4.6's checklist item "use multi-stage builds" shrinks the SHIPPED image and its CVE surface — it does not, by itself, shrink local disk usage the way people assume. docker builder prune is the companion habit multi-stage builds quietly create.
⑤ Three Different "$VAR"s — Builder Substitution, Shell Expansion & No Expansion At All

4.2's ARG/ENV note and 4.3's exec-form trap both hinge on a distinction most Dockerfiles get wrong by assuming ONE substitution mechanism when there are actually THREE, triggered by different instructions:

  1. BUILDER SUBSTITUTION — parser-native, no shell ever runs
     Applies ONLY to: FROM, LABEL, COPY, ADD, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR, STOPSIGNAL, ONBUILD
     FROM ${BASE_IMAGE}:${TAG}   ← works even though FROM runs before any shell exists (4.1)

  2. SHELL EXPANSION — the actual /bin/sh Docker wraps shell-form commands in (③)
     RUN echo $HOME                        ← real POSIX substitution, only ENV is visible to it
     CMD python manage.py runserver        ← shell form: $VAR here would expand too

  3. NO EXPANSION AT ALL — exec-form JSON array items are frozen literal strings (②, ③)
     CMD ["echo", "$HOME"]   ← prints the 5 literal characters $HOME — nobody's job to expand this
MechanismWho performs itWhenApplies to
Builder substitutionBuildKit's Dockerfile parserparse time, before any layer buildsFROM, LABEL, COPY, ADD, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR, STOPSIGNAL, ONBUILD
Shell expansion/bin/sh (or SHELL-configured shell)build time (RUN) / container start (shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT)shell-form RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT only
No expansionnobody—exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT JSON arrays
🔑 4.3's fix — CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec gunicorn ... --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT"] — works because it deliberately invokes mechanism 2 from inside mechanism-3 territory: the array itself isn't expanded, but its ONE literal string element is handed to a real shell, and the explicit exec still hands PID 1 to gunicorn per ③.
⑥ HEALTHCHECK's Daemon-Side State Machine — a Second Process That Never Touches PID 1

4.2 lists HEALTHCHECK as one instruction; what it actually configures is a small state machine dockerd runs forever, entirely separate from your app's own PID 1. Every interval, the daemon launches the HEALTHCHECK command INSIDE the container the exact same way docker exec does — Chapter 6's takeaway that "exec never disturbs PID 1" is precisely why a failing health probe can never itself crash gunicorn.

  every `interval` (default 30s), dockerd execs the probe INSIDE the container (same path as docker exec):
       exit 0 → SUCCESS → failure counter resets to 0 → status: (healthy)
       exit 1 → FAILURE → failure counter += 1
                           counter < retries → status: (health: starting) / stays (healthy)
                           counter ≥ retries → status: (unhealthy), a health_status event fires

  start-period (default 0s) shields the FIRST N seconds differently:
       failure during start-period  → NOT counted toward retries at all
       success during start-period  → ends the shield immediately, normal counting begins
Probe resultDuring start-periodAfter start-period
Failsignored — doesn't touch the retries counterincrements the counter toward retries
Succeedsends the shield immediately, status → healthyresets the counter to 0, status → healthy
🔑 easypj's --start-period=15s shields exactly the window 4.7's entrypoint script spends waiting for PostgreSQL and running migrations — without it, three slow probes fired DURING that legitimate startup work would flip a brand-new, perfectly healthy container to (unhealthy) before it ever got a fair chance to answer.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A Dockerfile is a declarative recipe: FROM/RUN/COPY/ADD create layers, everything else writes metadata.
  • CMD sets an overridable default; ENTRYPOINT is fixed and needs --entrypoint to change — together they decide what PID 1 is.
  • Order by volatility: stable instructions first, COPY . . last, to protect the build cache.
  • Multi-stage builds let you use heavy build tools (gcc, headers, git) without ever shipping them in the final image.
  • The 9-point checklist (pin tags, drop root, exec form, one process per container, scan before shipping…) catches most real Dockerfile mistakes.
  • An entrypoint script plus exec "$@" is how a container waits for dependencies and still hands PID 1 to the real app.
  • EXPOSE, LABEL and similar instructions document intent; they never change runtime behavior by themselves.
  • DCA relevance: this entire chapter is examinable under Image Creation, Management & Registry — instruction syntax, the CMD/ENTRYPOINT table, and multi-stage mechanics are all fair game.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • COPY . /app (wrong order) → COPY source code LAST. COPY requirements.txt first, then RUN pip install, THEN COPY . .
  • Using ADD instead of COPY → Use COPY for local files. ADD only when you need tar auto-extraction.
  • RUN apt update && apt install (no cleanup) → Always chain with cleanup: RUN apt update && apt install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT confusion → ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable. CMD = default arguments. Combined: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"]
  • Shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT is equivalent to exec-form → Shell form wraps your app in /bin/sh -c — SIGTERM hits the shell, not the app, so docker stop hangs 10s then SIGKILLs mid-request.
  • Forgetting exec "$@" is harmless → It leaves the shell as PID 1, swallowing every signal meant for gunicorn.
  • Changes made inside a running container are permanent → They die with the container — nothing you edit by hand inside a container ever flows back into the Dockerfile or the image. Edit the recipe, rebuild, never patch the slice.
  • ENV values are only visible inside the container → They're baked into the image and visible forever via docker inspect on ANY machine that pulls it — never put secrets in ENV.
  • MAINTAINER is still the right way to set an image author → MAINTAINER is deprecated — use LABEL maintainer="team@easypj.dev" instead.
  • A multi-stage final stage automatically finds pip install --user packages → You must explicitly COPY --from=build /root/.local /root/.local AND set ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH in the final stage, or the installed packages are invisible.
  • "Minimize layers" means cramming everything into one giant RUN → Collapse only genuinely related commands (e.g. update+install+cleanup) — readability and cache granularity still matter.
  • The 4.4 Dockerfile is already production-ready → It still runs as root with no migrations/static-files story — 4.6's checklist and 4.7's entrypoint script (and 9.7's final version) are what finish the job.
  • A CMD will always append its args onto ENTRYPOINT → Only if ENTRYPOINT is exec form. Shell-form ENTRYPOINT (e.g. ENTRYPOINT gunicorn app.wsgi) makes Docker ignore CMD entirely — always resolves to /bin/sh -c "gunicorn app.wsgi", no matter what CMD says.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Keep a personal Dockerfile skeleton (FROM/WORKDIR/COPY reqs/RUN install/COPY ./ENV/EXPOSE/CMD) to adapt instead of writing one from memory every time.
  • Run docker history <image> immediately after any new Dockerfile — see your real layer sizes before you ship them.
  • Default to exec-form ["cmd","arg"] for CMD/ENTRYPOINT; only reach for shell form when you specifically need shell features.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 4)

build, inspect & ship the recipe 
# Build the recipe
docker build -t easypj:v1 .

# Ignore all cache
docker build --no-cache -t easypj:v1 .

# Instruction → layer
docker history easypj:v1

# Sanity-check CMD
docker run --rm easypj:v1

# Override ENTRYPOINT
docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it easypj:v1

# See the baked-in CMD
docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Cmd}}' easypj:v1

# Confirm the tag exists
docker images easypj
tag, push & transfer images 
docker build -t app:v1 -f Dockerfile .
docker tag app:v1 app:latest
docker push registry.example.com/app:v1
docker images
docker rmi IMAGE
docker save -o app.tar app:v1
docker load -i app.tar
docker image prune -a

🧠 Chapter 4 — DCA Practice Questions (18)

Quick recall of Dockerfile mechanics — 18 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Which Dockerfile instruction is mandatory and must always be the first instruction?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

FROM — it specifies the base image. Every Dockerfile must start with FROM (or ARG before FROM if you need a build arg in the FROM line).

  Dockerfile instruction order:
  ARG <name>            ← the ONLY thing allowed before FROM (a build-time arg for the FROM line itself)
  FROM <base-image>     ← MANDATORY, must be the first REAL instruction
  WORKDIR / COPY / RUN / ENV / CMD / ...   ← everything else follows FROM
EXPLANATION

FROM can appear multiple times in a multi-stage build. The only instruction allowed before the first FROM is ARG. Without FROM, Docker has no base to build upon.

Q2
What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT? When would you use each?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CMD provides defaults that can be overridden at runtime. ENTRYPOINT defines a fixed executable — arguments to docker run are appended to it. Use CMD when you want flexibility, ENTRYPOINT when the container should always run the same binary.

CMDENTRYPOINT
Overridable by docker run args?✅ Yes — fully replaced❌ No — needs --entrypoint
RoleDefault argumentsFixed executable
easypj example["easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]["gunicorn"]
EXPLANATION

For easypj: ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"] ensures gunicorn always runs. CMD ["easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"] provides default arguments that can be overridden: docker run easypj --workers 5 overrides CMD but gunicorn still runs.

Q3
Why should you COPY requirements.txt BEFORE copying your source code?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

For layer caching optimization. requirements.txt changes rarely; source code changes constantly. When you change source code, Docker reuses the cached layer for pip install — saving minutes of rebuild time.

  GOOD ORDER (reqs first)                  BAD ORDER (code first)
  COPY requirements.txt .                  COPY . .
  RUN pip install -r requirements.txt      RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
  COPY . .

  Edit one .py file, then rebuild:
  GOOD → only "COPY . ." reruns, pip layer stays CACHED
  BAD  → pip install RERUNS too, every single time
EXPLANATION

Docker's cache invalidation is sequential: if layer N changes, layers N+1, N+2, etc. ALL rebuild. By putting requirements.txt (rarely changes) BEFORE source code (frequently changes), only the last COPY layer rebuilds on code changes.

Q4
What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements. The first stage builds the app with all tools (compilers, dev headers). Later stages copy only the built artifacts — resulting in a much smaller, more secure final image without build tools.

  STAGE 1 "build"   (~850 MB — gcc, headers, pip cache)
  FROM python:3.11 AS build
  RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
         │
         │  COPY --from=build   (only the BUILT ARTIFACTS cross over)
         ▼
  STAGE 2 "final"   (~180 MB — no compilers, no headers)
  FROM python:3.11-slim
  COPY --from=build /root/.local /root/.local
EXPLANATION

Without multi-stage, you'd need two Dockerfiles: one for building, one for running. Multi-stage combines them into one. The key is COPY --from=build — it copies artifacts from an earlier stage. Typical reduction: 850 MB (with build tools) → 180 MB (runtime only).

Q5
What does EXPOSE 8000 actually do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

EXPOSE is documentation only. It does NOT publish the port or make it accessible from the host. It's a hint that the container listens on port 8000. To actually publish the port, use docker run -p 8000:8000.

Setupcurl localhost:8000
EXPOSE 8000 in Dockerfile only❌ connection refused — documentation only
docker run easypj:v1 (no -p)❌ connection refused
docker run -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1✅ answers
EXPLANATION

This is a common exam trap. EXPOSE only adds metadata to the image. The -p flag in docker run actually maps ports. You can publish a port not listed in EXPOSE, and EXPOSEd ports won't be accessible without -p (or -P to publish all EXPOSEd ports).

Q6
What's wrong with this Dockerfile? FROM python:latest
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Using :latest makes builds non-reproducible. Today's build might use Python 3.11, tomorrow's might use 3.13 — with breaking changes. Always pin to a specific version: FROM python:3.11-slim.

Build dayFROM python:latest resolves toResult
Monday's buildPython 3.11✅ works
Friday's build (new upstream push)Python 3.13❌ breaking changes, non-reproducible
Any day, FROM python:3.11-slimPython 3.11, always✅ reproducible
EXPLANATION

The :latest tag is mutable — it moves to point to whatever was most recently pushed. Two builds one day apart can produce completely different images. For production, always use specific tags or digests.

Q7
What's the difference between COPY and ADD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

COPY copies local files into the image. ADD does the same PLUS can fetch URLs and auto-extract tar archives. Docker recommends COPY for local files (more explicit, less surprising). Use ADD only when you need its extra features.

FeatureCOPYADD
Copies local files✅✅
Fetches remote URLs❌✅ (surprising side effect)
Auto-extracts tar archives❌✅ (surprising side effect)
Docker's recommendation for local files✅ preferredonly when you need the extras
EXPLANATION

ADD has two extra behaviors: (1) If the source is a URL, it downloads it. (2) If the source is a tar archive, it automatically extracts it into the destination. These "magic" behaviors can be surprising — COPY is more predictable.

Q8
How do you set an environment variable that's available at RUNTIME but NOT during build?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

You can't set it in the Dockerfile if you want it ONLY at runtime. Use docker run -e VAR=value or --env-file at runtime. ENV in Dockerfile sets it at both build AND runtime. ARG is build-time only.

Build-timeRuntimeVisible in docker history?
ARG✅❌ gone after buildpartially (build args)
ENV✅✅✅ baked in forever
docker run -e❌✅❌ never in the image
EXPLANATION

The three options: ARG (build only, gone after), ENV (build + runtime, visible in history), docker run -e (runtime only, not in image). For secrets like API keys, never use ENV — it's visible in docker history.

Q9
What does docker build -t easypj:v1 . do with the dot at the end?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The dot (.) is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon for the build. Docker sends ALL files in this directory (except those in .dockerignore) to the daemon. The Dockerfile is expected to be in this directory.

  docker build -t easypj:v1 .
                             │
                             ▼
                 tar up "." minus .dockerignore entries
                             │
                             ▼
              send build context ──▶ Docker daemon
                             │
                             ▼
      daemon reads the Dockerfile FROM the context, then builds layers
EXPLANATION

The build context is the FIRST thing Docker does. Before reading the Dockerfile, it tars up the context directory and sends it to the daemon. That's why .dockerignore is so critical — it slims the context before the tar is created.

Q10
What instruction would you use to switch to a non-root user for security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

USER appuser (after creating the user with RUN groupadd --system appuser && useradd --system --group appuser — the same Debian shadow-utils commands 4.5's multi-stage Dockerfile uses, since python:3.11-slim is Debian-based). Running as non-root is a critical security practice — if an attacker compromises your container, they won't have root privileges.

No USER (default)USER appuser
Process runs asroot (UID 0)appuser (non-root)
If attacker compromises the app❌ root inside the container✅ unprivileged, contained
EXPLANATION

By default, Docker containers run as root. If an attacker exploits your app, they get root inside the container — and potentially on the host if they break out. Creating a non-root user and using USER is a fundamental security hardening step.

Q11
What's the difference between a Dockerfile, an image, and a container — and why is editing a running container never the right fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Dockerfile = the versioned recipe; image = the immutable bake produced from it; container = one served, disposable slice of that bake.

  Dockerfile (recipe)  ──docker build──▶  Image (the bake, immutable)  ──docker run──▶  Container (one slice)
       ✅ edit HERE                                                          ✗ never edit here —
       rebuild to change it                                                    changes die with the container
EXPLANATION

Changes made inside a running container die with it — they never flow back into the Dockerfile or the image. To change the "cake" you edit the recipe card and rebuild; patching the slice on the plate never changes what the next slice looks like.

Q12
Classify FROM, ARG, COPY, RUN, EXPOSE, WORKDIR, ENV, USER and CMD as build-time, run-time, or metadata-only.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
PhaseInstructions
buildFROM, ARG, COPY, RUN
build + runWORKDIR, ENV
runUSER, CMD
metadataEXPOSE (documents, never publishes)
EXPLANATION

Build-time instructions bake their result into a layer; run-time ones only take effect when a container actually starts. This one axis is the fastest way to reason about any instruction you haven't memorized yet.

Q13
Fill in what runs for all six ENTRYPOINT/CMD combinations from the 4.3 decision matrix.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
#Dockerfilerun argsResult
1CMD ["echo","hello"](none)echo hello
2CMD ["echo","hello"]worlderror (no cmd)
3ENTRYPOINT ["echo"](none)echo (no arg)
4ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]helloecho hello
5ENTRYPOINT["echo"]+CMD["Hi"](none)echo Hi
6ENTRYPOINT["echo"]+CMD["Hi"]worldecho world (OVERRIDES)
EXPLANATION

Final command = ENTRYPOINT + CMD concatenated; anything typed after the image name on docker run replaces CMD only — never ENTRYPOINT.

Q14
Why does easypj's Dockerfile use python:3.11-slim instead of an alpine base?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

psycopg2 needs glibc wheels; alpine's musl libc forces slow, fragile source compiles instead of fast prebuilt wheels.

Base imagelibcpip install psycopg2
python:3.11-slimglibc✅ fast prebuilt wheel
python:3.11-alpinemusl❌ slow, fragile source compile
EXPLANATION

4.4 calls this out directly when building easypj's Dockerfile; 8.2 revisits the slim-vs-alpine trade-off in more depth with real size and build-time numbers.

Q15
Name four items from the 4.6 best-practices checklist and the specific failure each one prevents.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Pin base tags → prevents silent :latest drift; (2) .dockerignore excludes .git/env//__pycache__ → prevents a leaked secret or bloated build context; (3) USER appuser → prevents a container escape from landing as root on the host; (4) exec-form CMD → prevents a lost SIGTERM on docker stop.

#Checklist itemFailure it prevents
1Pin base tagssilent :latest drift
2.dockerignore excludes .git/env//__pycache__leaked secret or bloated build context
3USER appusercontainer escape landing as root on the host
4exec-form CMDlost SIGTERM on docker stop
EXPLANATION

Each checklist line maps to a named failure class in 4.6's violation table — the checklist is a compressed postmortem, not an arbitrary style preference.

Q16
What does exec "$@" do at the end of docker-entrypoint.sh, and why is it called "load-bearing"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

exec REPLACES the running shell process with CMD's process (gunicorn), so gunicorn inherits PID 1 directly instead of running as a child of the shell.

  WITHOUT exec "$@"                          WITH exec "$@"
  PID 1 = /bin/sh (entrypoint.sh)            PID 1 = gunicorn (shell REPLACED)
    └── gunicorn = PID 2 (child)               docker stop → SIGTERM → gunicorn directly ✅
  docker stop → SIGTERM → sh swallows it
    → 10s timeout → SIGKILL mid-request ❌
EXPLANATION

Without exec, the shell stays PID 1 and swallows docker stop's SIGTERM — the container hangs 10 seconds then gets SIGKILLed mid-request. It's "load-bearing" because removing that one word is invisible until the exact moment a graceful shutdown is needed.

Q17
Why must docker-entrypoint.sh wait on pg_isready before running manage.py migrate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

"Container up" does not mean "PostgreSQL accepting connections" — Compose starts postgres and easypj together, so migrate can race the database and crash with "connection refused" if it runs too early.

  WITHOUT the pg_isready wait loop             WITH the pg_isready wait loop
  0s: postgres + easypj start together         0s: postgres + easypj start together
  0s: migrate runs immediately                 0-2s: entrypoint polls pg_isready
      → "connection refused" ❌ crash          2s: postgres ready → migrate runs ✅
EXPLANATION

The wait loop turns a crash-loop into a harmless 2-second wait — exactly what the Theatre Stage Manager analogy in 4.7 describes.

Q18
You write ENTRYPOINT gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application (shell form) and CMD ["--workers", "4"] in the same Dockerfile. What actually runs?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Just gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application — with no --workers 4. Shell-form ENTRYPOINT makes Docker ignore CMD entirely, so the flag never reaches gunicorn.

  ENTRYPOINT gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application     ← shell form
  CMD ["--workers", "4"]                           ← SILENTLY IGNORED, not appended

  Actual process: /bin/sh -c "gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application"   (no --workers anywhere)
EXPLANATION

This only happens with shell-form ENTRYPOINT — the six-combination matrix earlier in 4.3 assumes exec-form ENTRYPOINT throughout, where CMD (or trailing docker run args) really is appended. Switching ENTRYPOINT to exec form — ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application"] — is what makes CMD's --workers 4 actually take effect.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.1 — Override CMD Live

Write a 3-instruction Dockerfile (FROM, COPY, CMD) for a one-line Python script, build it, run it once as written, then run it again passing a different argument on the command line WITHOUT editing the file. Verify: the second run's output changes — you just overrode CMD, live.

  docker build -t hello .            (FROM + COPY + CMD ["python","hello.py"])
  docker run hello                   → prints the DEFAULT message   (CMD as-written)
  docker run hello "custom text"     → prints "custom text"         (CMD overridden, LIVE — no rebuild)

Create a Dockerfile containing only FROM python:3.11-slim and run docker build -t probe .. Verify: docker images probe shows an image — one instruction was already a buildable recipe.

  Dockerfile:
  FROM python:3.11-slim        ← the only line

  docker build -t probe .      → succeeds, 1 layer
  docker images probe          → probe   latest   <IMAGE ID>   ~150MB

Build an image with EXPOSE 8000 but run it WITHOUT -p, then curl localhost:8000. Verify: connection refused — EXPOSE alone published nothing; rerun with -p 8000:8000 and it answers.

  touch jobpost/views.py && docker build -t easypj:v1 .

  COPY . .                      REBUILT  ← only this layer (and nothing before it)

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RECIPE (Dockerfile) ──build──▶ LAYERS ──config──▶ IMAGE        │
  │       │                                               │        │
  │  instructions:                                  CMD/ENTRYPOINT │
  │  FROM/COPY/RUN = layers                           decide PID 1 │
  │  WORKDIR/ENV/EXPOSE = metadata                         │        │
  │       │                                               ▼        │
  │  entrypoint.sh: wait → migrate → exec "$@" ──▶ gunicorn = PID 1 │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In one line: instructions become layers or metadata, CMD and ENTRYPOINT together decide what actually runs, multi-stage builds keep the toolchain out of the final image, and an entrypoint script with exec "$@" is what lets a container wait, prepare itself, and still behave correctly when Docker sends it a signal.

The takeaway: every later chapter's Dockerfile — including 9.7's production version — is this same chain with more discipline applied to it.

Chapter 5 · Building Images — docker build Deep Dive

Now that you can write Dockerfiles, let's master the build process itself. Understanding build context, layer caching, build arguments, and multi-platform builds is essential for the DCA exam and daily Docker work. Chapter 4 wrote the recipe; this chapter masters the oven — the difference between a ~3-second cached rebuild and a ~45-second cold one lives entirely in what you're about to learn. The problems this chapter solves: your build is slow, your context is huge, and your ARM Mac's image dies with "exec format error" the moment it hits the AMD64 server.

Image Creation, Management & Registry 20%
🎯 Cache Mechanics Are a Favorite Scenario Question

docker build/buildx internals and multi-stage builds are explicitly graded under Image Creation, Management & Registry — expect scenario questions on cache invalidation, ARG-vs-ENV leak surfaces, and multi-platform manifest lists.

  • A cache key is parent-layer + instruction TEXT + file checksums — RUN lines are matched by text, never re-executed to check for a match.
  • ARG dies at the end of the stage that declares it; ENV survives into every container, forever, visible in docker inspect.
  • Any ARG consumed by a RUN line is permanently recoverable via docker history --no-trunc — ENV needs no such trigger at all, since its own instruction always gets a history entry and populates Config.Env unconditionally. Use --mount=type=secret for real credentials.

5.1 docker build Fundamentals

docker build reads a Dockerfile and builds an image from it. The basic syntax is: docker build [OPTIONS] PATH. The PATH is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon.

🛍️ Analogy — The Shopping Bag You Hand the Baker

The build context is the shopping bag you hand the baker: the recipe (Dockerfile) may call for only the flour, but you still carried the WHOLE bag to the bakery — every jar, every unused ingredient — before a single line of the recipe ran. A bag stuffed with things the recipe never touches still costs you the walk there, which is exactly why 5.2 teaches you to pack light with .dockerignore.

TERMINAL
# Basic build
$ docker build -t easypj:v1 .

# Build with BuildKit (recommended — faster, better output)
$ DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t easypj:v1 .

# Build with no cache (force full rebuild)
$ docker build --no-cache -t easypj:v1 .

# Build from a specific Dockerfile
$ docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t easypj:prod .

# Build with build arguments
$ docker build --build-arg DJANGO_VERSION=5.2 -t easypj:v1 .

# Build and tag with multiple tags
$ docker build -t easypj:v1 -t easypj:latest -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 .
Build Output (Annotated)
$ docker build -t easypj:v1 .
[+] Building 45.3s (11/11) FINISHED
 => [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile    0.1s  ← Reads Dockerfile
 => => transferring dockerfile: 502B                    0.0s
 => [internal] load .dockerignore                       0.1s  ← Reads .dockerignore
 => => transferring context: 185B                       0.0s
 => [internal] load metadata for docker.io/library/     2.1s  ← Checks for base image updates
    python:3.11-slim
 => [1/5] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.11-slim       3.2s  ← Pulls/uses base image (CACHED)
 => [internal] load build context                       0.3s  ← Sends files to daemon
 => => transferring context: 15.82MB                    0.2s
 => [2/5] WORKDIR /app                                  0.1s  ← Layer 2: Working directory
 => [3/5] COPY requirements.txt .                       0.1s  ← Layer 3: Dependencies list (CACHED)
 => [4/5] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \             38.2s  ← Layer 4: Install packages
    -r requirements.txt
