# Notice: Layers marked "CACHED" took 0.1s each
# The pip install layer took 38.2s (only runs when requirements change)
# Total: 45s first build, ~3s on code-only changes!
💡 Always Pass -t — Or Meet Your First Dangling Image

-t easypj:v1 names the finished image. Forget it and the build still succeeds — but the result is a "dangling" <none>:<none> image, findable only by its IMAGE ID (docker images --filter "dangling=true", covered in 7.1). It still runs fine with docker run <IMAGE_ID>, but nobody else on the team can guess which build it came from.

🧪 Prove the Cache to Yourself — Run It Twice

Run the exact same docker build -t easypj:v1 . a second time, with no file changes at all, and count the CACHED lines in the output. Verify: total build time collapses from ~45s to roughly ~1-3s — every step reports CACHED because nothing changed, and BuildKit does nothing but cache-key lookups. This is the single fastest way to build intuition for 5.3's cache mechanics before touching the theory.

📖 docs.docker.com: The PATH Doesn't Have to Be a Local Directory

Official Docker docs confirm the build context accepts more than a local path. docker build https://github.com/you/easypj.git clones the repo straight into a temporary context on the daemon — append #branch:subdir to target a non-default branch or a subdirectory. docker build https://example.com/context.tar.gz streams a remote tarball the same way. And docker build - < context.tar.gz pipes a local tarball in over stdin. All three skip your working directory entirely — useful for CI jobs that build straight from a tag without a local checkout at all.

💡 --progress Controls How Verbose the Build Log Is

The default --progress=auto renders the fancy multi-line TTY view seen in this section's annotated output — but it auto-detects a non-interactive shell (a CI runner, a log redirected to a file) and silently falls back to a flatter format. Set it explicitly with --progress=plain for one line per step, ideal for CI logs and for piping through grep, or --progress=tty to force the fancy view even when output isn't a real terminal. The BUILDKIT_PROGRESS=plain environment variable sets the default for every build in that shell, so you don't have to repeat the flag.

5.2 Build Context & .dockerignore

The build context is ALL files in the specified directory that Docker sends to the daemon. A large context means slow builds. .dockerignore excludes unnecessary files — just like .gitignore for Git.

.dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.pyo
*.egg-info/
dist/
build/

# Django
*.sqlite3
media/
staticfiles/

# Virtual environment
env/
venv/
.venv/

# Git
.git/
.gitignore
.gitattributes

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp

# OS
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Documentation
README.md
docs/

# Docker
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml
🛂 Analogy — The Airport's No-Fly List, In Reverse

.dockerignore is an airport packing list run backward — a no-fly list for files. Your local virtualenv is a hair dryer with the wrong plug: it still gets packed, adds weight, and cannot work once it lands, because the container ships its own interpreter and its own compiled wheels for the container's OS/architecture, not your laptop's.

⚠️ Two Different Ways a Missing .dockerignore Bites

A stray env/ virtualenv directory can add ~200 MB to every single build upload — pure waste, since the image never uses your local venv's binaries. Worse: COPY . . with no .dockerignore happily copies a committed .env straight into a shareable image layer — a leaked SECRET_KEY the moment anyone docker pulls the image. .dockerignore is a SECURITY control here, not a tidiness nicety.

📖 Syntax Is .gitignore-Like — Globs, Negation, Directory Suffixes

.dockerignore supports the same pattern language as .gitignore: shell-style globs (*.pyc, **/*.log), a trailing / to match directories only (env/), and ! to re-include something an earlier pattern excluded — !important.log after a broad *.log rule un-ignores that one file. Docker evaluates patterns top-to-bottom, so a narrow re-inclusion must come AFTER the broad exclusion, never before it.

📖 A Dockerfile Can Have Its OWN .dockerignore

Docker also looks for a file named <Dockerfile-name>.dockerignore — for easypj's -f Dockerfile.prod build from 5.1, that's Dockerfile.prod.dockerignore. If that file exists, it takes precedence over the root .dockerignore for that build ENTIRELY, not merged with it. Handy when Dockerfile.prod needs a stricter or looser exclusion list than the everyday Dockerfile — but easy to forget exists, since most projects only ever see the root file and never notice the override is possible.

🗂️ Why .git/ Specifically

A repo's .git/ directory holds the FULL commit history — including any secret ever committed and later "deleted" in a newer commit. It is almost always the single largest and riskiest thing a missing .dockerignore ships into a build context.

🐍 Why __pycache__/ Specifically

Host-compiled .pyc bytecode is tied to your LOCAL Python's version/platform. It buys nothing inside the container — Python recompiles it from source on first import anyway — so it's pure upload weight with zero runtime benefit.

🖼️ Why media/ Specifically

User-uploaded files belong in a mounted VOLUME, not baked into an image layer — Part 6 covers volumes in depth. Excluding media/ keeps uploads out of the context AND stops a stale snapshot of user data from ever getting frozen permanently into an image tag.

📄 Why Dockerfile / .dockerignore Themselves

The recipe isn't an ingredient: excluding Dockerfile and .dockerignore from their own build context is mostly hygiene rather than a security fix — without it, COPY . . would happily copy the build instructions into the image right alongside the code they describe.

🧪 Prove It: Build With and Without .dockerignore

Build the SAME project once with .dockerignore deleted/renamed and once with it in place, watching the "transferring context" line both times. Verify: the upload size drops by orders of magnitude — then run docker run --rm easypj:v1 ls -a /app against the resulting image and confirm the listing shows no .env, no env/, and no .git — proof that what never enters the context can never end up in a layer either.

5.3 Layer Caching Deep Dive

Layer caching is Docker's superpower. When rebuilding, Docker checks if each instruction's result is already cached. If it is, Docker SKIPS that instruction and uses the cached layer. This is why smart Dockerfiles rebuild in seconds.

🧮 Analogy — The Meticulous Accountant

Layer caching behaves like a meticulous accountant filing invoices: identical invoice number and identical amounts means reusing last year's filing without even reopening the box. Change one digit anywhere on that invoice, though, and every filing that came after it in the drawer has to be redone too — the accountant never partially trusts a box once something inside it changed.

How BuildKit Judges One Step — the Cache Decision Flow
   parent layer unchanged?    ──no──▶  REBUILD this step + every later step
            │ yes
            ▼
   instruction text same?     ──no──▶  REBUILD this step + every later step
            │ yes
            ▼
   COPY/ADD checksums same?   ──no──▶  REBUILD this step + every later step
            │ yes
            ▼
         CACHED ✅  (instruction is SKIPPED, never re-executed)
Cache Hit vs Cache Miss
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🏎️ LAYER CACHING — WHY ORDER MATTERS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BAD ORDER (cache useless after code change):                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (code changed!)       │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ❌ REBUILT (previous changed)    │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ❌ REBUILT (rerun install!)     │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GOOD ORDER (only changed layers rebuilt):                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ✅ CACHED (same requirements)    │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ✅ CACHED (same install)         │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (only code changed!) │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RESULT: Good = 3 layers cached (~3 sec) | Bad = 4 layers rebuilt (~45s)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 --cache-from: External Cache for CI/CD

In CI/CD pipelines, each build starts with an empty cache (fresh runner). Use --cache-from to pull a previous build's layers from a registry as cache: docker build --cache-from=easypj:latest -t easypj:v2 .. For multi-stage builds, specify each stage: --cache-from=easypj:build --cache-from=easypj:final. This can cut CI build times from minutes to seconds — exactly the trick that makes cold CI runners tolerable in Part 8's pipelines.

📖 Beyond --cache-from=image:tag — Registry Cache Exporters

The --cache-from=easypj:latest shown above pulls cache from an image's ordinary layers — simple, but it only ever sees the FINAL stage's layers, which starves a multi-stage build's discarded builder stage of any cache at all. BuildKit's explicit exporters go further: docker build --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/you/easypj:cache,mode=max --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/you/easypj:cache . writes a dedicated cache blob to the registry with mode=max — exporting EVERY stage's layers, builder stage included, not just the final image's. mode=min (the default if you omit it) matches the old behavior and only exports what ends up in the final image.

⚠️ Cache Gotchas

1. COPY/ADD checksums are content + metadata, NOT timestamps — Docker's own docs are explicit that last-modified/last-accessed times are never part of the checksum. What DOES bust the cache: file content, permissions, and ownership (COPY --chmod/--chown change both). A fresh git clone with a new mtime does NOT invalidate cache by itself. 2. Combining apt-get update && apt-get install into ONE RUN line doesn't make it immune to caching — if that line's TEXT never changes between builds, the WHOLE line (update included) stays cached and can serve a stale index forever. What combining buys you: adding a package changes the line's text, which forces the update to re-run too. Split into two RUN lines, and the update layer can stay cached while a later, separately-cached install layer changes — installing new packages against an old index. 3. BuildKit's real edge over the legacy builder is parallelism and cache import/export (--cache-from/--cache-to, above) — an invalidated layer inside one linear stage still cascades to every layer after it, in BOTH builders alike; BuildKit does not selectively skip that rule.

📖 easypj: Where NOT to Put a Volatile ENV

An ENV APP_VERSION=... line placed near the TOP of a Dockerfile re-invalidates the expensive pip install layer on every single version bump — because everything after an invalidated layer must rebuild too. Volatile, frequently-changing metadata like a version stamp belongs LAST, below COPY . ., exactly where the stable FROM / COPY requirements.txt / RUN pip install sequence in 5.1's build output stays cached.

💡 COPY --link — a Layer That Skips the Chain Entirely

COPY --link requirements.txt . produces a layer that is NOT chained to the layer beneath it for cache-key purposes — it stays CACHED even if an earlier FROM or RUN layer changes, something an ordinary COPY can never do (this section's cache decision flow always checks the parent layer first). The same decoupling pays off on push, too: BuildKit can append a linked layer directly onto whatever base already sits in the registry instead of re-uploading everything beneath it. Needs the same # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 parser directive as 5.7's mount flags.

5.4 Build Arguments (ARG) & Environment Variables (ENV)

The distinction is critical for the DCA exam:

🎂 Analogy — A Note Taped to the Oven vs. Icing Text

ARG is a note taped to the oven door while the cake bakes — useful during baking, gone the moment the cake leaves the kitchen. ENV is icing text piped onto the finished cake: written once, and read by literally everyone who ever gets a slice, forever.

AspectARGENV
Available during build?✅ Yes✅ Yes
Available at runtime?❌ No (gone after build)✅ Yes (persists)
Visible in docker history?⚠️ Only the variable itself is gone at runtime — but if a RUN line consumes it, the value is baked into that layer's command string and IS visible via docker history --no-trunc (5.7)✅ Yes (caution with secrets!)
How to set--build-arg VAR=value-e VAR=value at runtime
Use caseBuild-time config (version, env name)Runtime config (settings, URLs)
DOCKERFILE: ARG vs ENV
# ARG — build-time only, NOT in final image
ARG DJANGO_VERSION=5.2
ARG ENVIRONMENT=production
RUN echo "Building for Django ${DJANGO_VERSION} in ${ENVIRONMENT}"
# Docker build: docker build --build-arg DJANGO_VERSION=5.2 -t easypj .
# At container runtime: ${DJANGO_VERSION} is EMPTY (ARG doesn't persist!)

# ENV — persists into the final image AND at runtime
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# PYTHONUNBUFFERED must be ENV, never ARG — gunicorn reads it at RUNTIME,
# not at build time, so it has to survive past the build (unlike ARG)
# At container runtime: these vars are available to your app

# TIP: To use ARG value at runtime, persist it to ENV:
ARG VERSION=unknown
ENV APP_VERSION=${VERSION}  # Now available at runtime!
⚠️ SECRET_KEY Belongs to NEITHER ARG NOR ENV

A version stamp is safe as ARG APP_VERSION=dev baked into a LABEL version=$APP_VERSION for CI traceability — that's metadata, not a secret. Django's SECRET_KEY is different: it must never appear as ARG (leaks into docker history the moment a RUN line touches it) or ENV (ships to every registry the image is ever pushed to, forever). Pass it at docker run time instead, with --env-file (3.5) — never bake it into the image at all.

📖 ARGs You Never Have to Declare

HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, FTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY (and their lowercase variants) are predefined by BuildKit and automatically available to proxy-aware RUN steps — no ARG line needed at all. ARG and ENV values also accept bash-style modifiers like ${VAR:-default} (fall back if unset) and ${VAR:+alt} (substitute only if set) — the full modifier table lives in Appendix B.10.

5.5 Multi-Platform Builds with Buildx

Modern development teams use a mix of Intel (amd64) and Apple Silicon (arm64) machines. Buildx lets you build ONE image that works on BOTH — and on cloud servers too.

📚 Analogy — Printing a Book in Two Languages at Once

A multi-platform build is printing a book in two languages simultaneously: one manuscript (the Dockerfile), two presses running in parallel (the amd64 and arm64 builders), and one ISBN (the tag) that hands every reader their own edition automatically — the same manifest-list machinery from 2.6, just built instead of just inspected.

TERMINAL
# Create a new builder instance
$ docker buildx create --name multiarch --use

# Build for multiple platforms simultaneously
$ docker buildx build \
    --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 \
    --push .

# Verify the image supports multiple architectures
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
Name:      ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
MediaType: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json
Manifests:
  Name:      ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1@sha256:abc... (linux/amd64)
  Name:      ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1@sha256:def... (linux/arm64)
📖 How Buildx Works: QEMU Emulation

When you build for linux/arm64 on an amd64 machine (or vice versa), Buildx uses QEMU — a processor emulator — to run the foreign architecture's binaries. This is automatic when you create a Buildx builder: docker buildx create --name multiarch --use sets up QEMU binfmt_misc handlers. Native builds (matching host arch) are faster than emulated ones. For CI/CD, consider using native ARM64 runners (like AWS Graviton) for faster ARM64 builds.

📖 Why buildx create --use Comes Before --platform, Not After

Buildx builders run on one of several DRIVERS. The default docker driver reuses the BuildKit instance already living inside the Docker daemon — convenient, but it has limited support for exactly the features this section needs: building for a platform other than the daemon's own, and exporting a real manifest list. docker buildx create --name multiarch --use switches to the docker-container driver, which runs a dedicated BuildKit instance inside its own container and unlocks --platform with multiple values, --cache-to exporters, and --output types the default driver can't do. Skip this step and a multi-platform --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 build fails outright — it never gets far enough to hit the QEMU emulation this section is actually about.

📖 docs.docker.com: on Docker Engine 29+, the Extra Builder Is Often Optional

The driver-switch above is still the safe, universal answer, but current Docker documentation narrows exactly when it's required. Docker Desktop and Docker Engine 29.0+ use the containerd image store as their default storage backend, and that store supports multi-platform images out of the box — on those versions, the plain default docker driver can run a --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 build directly, with no buildx create --use step at all. The docker-container driver from this section's workflow stays mandatory on an older Engine, or on any install upgraded from a version that still runs the classic (non-containerd) storage driver — there, either the containerd image store must be turned on by hand in the daemon config, or a dedicated docker-container builder remains the only path to a real multi-platform result.

🎯 DCA Exam Tip: Manifest Lists

A multi-platform build produces a manifest list (also called a "fat manifest") — not a single image. When a user runs docker pull, Docker automatically selects the correct platform-specific image from the list. This is transparent: your Intel Mac, your colleague's M2 Mac, and your production AMD64 server all use the same tag — Docker handles the architecture matching automatically.

💡 Which Half Is Slow Depends on Your Build Machine

On an Apple Silicon (M-series) laptop, the linux/arm64 half of a build runs natively in roughly ~40 seconds, while the emulated linux/amd64 half can take ~4 minutes for the same pip install step. Flip to an amd64 CI runner and the slow half flips too — whichever architecture is NOT the build machine's native one always pays the QEMU emulation tax.

📖 Automatic Platform ARGs — Zero --build-arg Plumbing

--platform unlocks a set of ARGs BuildKit fills in automatically, with no ARG declaration needed: TARGETPLATFORM, TARGETOS, TARGETARCH, TARGETVARIANT describe the platform being built FOR, and their BUILD* counterparts (BUILDPLATFORM, BUILDOS, BUILDARCH, BUILDVARIANT) describe the machine doing the building. A Dockerfile can branch RUN logic per architecture using these directly, with zero extra --build-arg plumbing:

DOCKERFILE: branching on TARGETARCH
# TARGETARCH is filled in automatically per platform — no ARG line needed
RUN case "$TARGETARCH" in \
      amd64) echo "installing amd64 wheel" ;; \
      arm64) echo "installing arm64 wheel" ;; \
    esac
📖 docs.docker.com: QEMU Is the EASIEST Option, Not the Fastest One

Docker's own multi-platform guidance is explicit that QEMU is a starting point, not the finish line: "emulation with QEMU can be much slower than native builds, especially for compute-heavy tasks like compilation." For easypj's pure-Python pip install step this mostly just costs time (5.5's ~40s vs ~4min split); for a language with a real compiler in the mix, Docker recommends two faster alternatives instead — cross-compilation (pin the build STAGE to the native --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM, then cross-compile a binary for $TARGETARCH, if your toolchain supports it) or multiple native builder nodes (one real amd64 machine, one real arm64 machine, joined into a single buildx builder) — both skip emulation entirely instead of just tolerating its tax.

📖 A Managed Third Option: Docker Build Cloud

Standing up and maintaining a fleet of native amd64 and arm64 builder machines is real infrastructure work — Docker's current offering for teams that want native-speed multi-arch builds without owning that fleet is Docker Build Cloud, a subscription service that supplies managed native builders for both architectures behind the same buildx CLI. It slots in as a THIRD point on the QEMU-vs-native-nodes spectrum above: same zero-emulation speed as self-hosted native nodes, but Docker operates the machines instead of your team.

💡 Stitching a Manifest List From Images Built on DIFFERENT Machines

QEMU emulation isn't the only way to get a multi-platform tag. If a real arm64 machine builds and pushes easypj:v1-arm64 natively, and a separate amd64 CI runner does the same for easypj:v1-amd64, docker buildx imagetools create -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1-amd64 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1-arm64 combines the two ALREADY-PUSHED images into one manifest list — zero rebuilding, zero emulation, just new index metadata pointing at digests that already exist. This is how many real-world CI pipelines dodge the QEMU tax entirely: native builders per architecture, stitched together as a last step.

5.6 docker buildx bake — Advanced Builds

When you need to build multiple related images simultaneously (e.g., your app + a worker + a migrations runner), docker buildx bake orchestrates them in parallel — much faster than sequential builds.

🧾 Analogy — A Bakery Order Sheet, Not One Shouted Order at a Time

Running docker build once per image is shouting orders into the kitchen one at a time. docker buildx bake is handing the kitchen a single order sheet: it sees every order at once, preps shared dough (cached layers) exactly once, and bakes everything in parallel ovens instead of queuing.

docker-bake.hcl
# Define build targets for easypj variants
group "default" {
  targets = ["django", "celery-worker", "migrations"]
}

target "django" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
  tags       = ["easypj:latest", "easypj:django"]
  platforms  = ["linux/amd64", "linux/arm64"]
}

target "celery-worker" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile.worker"
  tags       = ["easypj:worker"]
  args = {
    WORKER_CONCURRENCY = "4"
  }
}

target "migrations" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile.migrations"
  tags       = ["easypj:migrations"]
}

# Build all targets in parallel:
# $ docker buildx bake
📖 When to Use Bake

Use bake when you have a microservice architecture with 3+ Dockerfiles that need to be built together. It handles parallel builds, shared layers, and multi-platform output — all from a single command. For simple single-image projects, stick with docker build.

docker-bake.hcl — the inherits keyword
# "prod" reuses everything "dev" defines, then overrides/extends just what differs
group "default" { targets = ["dev", "prod"] }

target "dev" {
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
  tags       = ["easypj:dev"]
  args       = { APP_VERSION = "dev" }
}

target "prod" {
  inherits   = ["dev"]
  tags       = ["ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1"]
  platforms  = ["linux/amd64", "linux/arm64"]
}

# $ docker buildx bake dev   → builds only easypj:dev
# $ docker buildx bake      → builds dev AND prod, sharing cached layers

inherits copies another target's ENTIRE configuration — dockerfile, args, tags — as a starting point, then lets the new target override or extend just the fields that differ. Here prod inherits dev's dockerfile and APP_VERSION arg, but adds its own registry tag and multi-platform list, with zero duplication of the shared config.

📖 docs.docker.com: bake Doesn't Require an HCL File At All

Official Docker docs confirm docker buildx bake reads three file formats interchangeably — HCL, JSON, AND a Compose file. If easypj already has a compose.yaml with a build: block per service, docker buildx bake with no -f flag picks it up directly and treats each service as a target — no separate docker-bake.hcl to maintain at all. Reach for the HCL file specifically once you need things Compose's build: block can't express, like inherits or per-target platforms lists.

5.7 BuildKit Cache Mounts & Build Secrets

A cache mount is a persistent directory BuildKit re-attaches to a RUN step on every build — when requirements.txt changes, the layer rebuilds but pip finds its wheel cache warm. A secret mount appears as a file only DURING that one RUN and is never written to any layer; ARG/ENV values, by contrast, are recoverable by anyone with the image.

Dockerfile fragments — cache mount + secret 
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
# build with: docker build --secret id=pipconf,src=pip.conf .
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pipconf,target=/etc/pip.conf \
    pip install -r requirements.txt  # private index, no trace
💡 The Baker's Pantry Analogy

Cache mount = the baker's pantry: every cake is baked fresh, but flour is not re-bought per cake. Secret mount = a door code whispered to the builder — used, never written on the blueprints (ARG writes it on the blueprint in pen).

⚠️ Don't Pair --no-cache-dir With a Cache Mount

Plenty of copy-pasted Dockerfiles keep pip install --no-cache-dir out of old habit — but that flag tells pip to throw away its own download cache immediately, which defeats the entire point of --mount=type=cache. With a cache mount, drop --no-cache-dir entirely: the mounted directory IS the cache pip should reuse across builds.

📖 easypj: Cache Mounts in Practice

requirements.txt edits drop from ~45s to ~8s because Django/psycopg2 wheels come from the mounted cache, not PyPI. --mount has 5 official types, not just cache and secret — bind, tmpfs and ssh exist too (full table in Appendix B.7). RUN also takes two more independent flags: --network (default | none | host) and --security (sandbox | insecure) — both covered with an easypj example in Appendix B.8.

⚠️ The Leak-Audit Command

Build once with ARG TOKEN=hunter2 consumed by a RUN line, once with --mount=type=secret. Then run docker history --no-trunc easypj:v1 | grep hunter2 — the ARG build leaks the token in history; the secret build shows nothing anywhere: history, inspect, or layers.

⚠️ These --mount Flags Need a Parser Directive First

RUN --mount=type=cache,... and RUN --mount=type=secret,... are BuildKit-frontend-only syntax. Without # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 as the literal FIRST line of the Dockerfile (Ch 4 / Appendix B.9), the classic parser doesn't recognize --mount at all and the build fails with an "unknown flag" error — the two RUN fragments above only work once that directive is in place.

📖 Layer Cache HIT vs. Cache MOUNT — Not the Same Reuse

A layer cache hit (5.3) skips an instruction entirely — the whole RUN never re-executes. A cache mount is different: when requirements.txt changes, the RUN pip install layer's cache key IS invalidated, so the instruction DOES re-execute — but pip finds its downloaded wheels already sitting in the mounted directory, so it skips re-downloading from PyPI instead of skipping the whole step. One reuses a finished layer outright; the other reuses only what's inside a layer that still has to rebuild.

💡 Two More BuildKit Flags Worth Knowing

--secret id=mysecret,env=MY_TOKEN sources a secret straight from an environment variable instead of a file — no src= path needed. docker build --output type=local,dest=out/ . (or the shorthand -o out/) exports the build's filesystem result as plain files instead of producing an image at all — useful for using a Dockerfile purely as a build pipeline, e.g. compiling a static binary or bundling static assets without ever running docker run.

⚠️ Buildx Cache Isn't Cleaned by docker system prune

A container-based Buildx builder (docker buildx create --use, 5.5) keeps its own cache store, separate from the classic builder's. docker system prune (Ch 7, Appendix A.18) does NOT touch it. Use docker buildx du to see how much space a builder's cache is using, and docker buildx prune to reclaim it — cache mounts and layer cache both accumulate here and can quietly consume tens of GB on a busy CI runner.

Under the Hood — BuildKit's dependency graph solver, LLB, and the OCI plumbing beneath it

The legacy Docker builder executed a Dockerfile strictly top to bottom. BuildKit (the default builder) instead parses the file into a DEPENDENCY GRAPH of steps: it knows which steps depend on which outputs, so it can skip stages nothing needs, run independent steps CONCURRENTLY, and reuse any step whose cache key (5.3) still matches — regardless of where that step sits in the file. This is why a multi-stage build's builder and final stages can progress in parallel whenever they share no dependency, and why the => timing lines in 5.1's build output do not necessarily print in strict file order.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Dockerfile steps          BuildKit's graph view                │
  │  ────────────────          ──────────────────────               │
  │  FROM base (builder)  ──▶  [independent] ─┐                     │
  │  RUN gcc/build deps        runs in parallel ├─▶ COPY --from=    │
  │  FROM base (final)    ──▶  [independent] ─┘    build (joins)    │
  │  COPY --from=build         waits for BOTH branches above        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 The two FROM lines in 4.5's multi-stage Dockerfile open two independent branches of this graph — BuildKit builds both at once and only serializes at the COPY --from=build step, which is the first point that genuinely needs both branches finished.
① LLB — the content-addressable graph a Dockerfile actually compiles to

"Parses into a dependency graph" hides a specific intermediate representation: LLB (Low-Level Build definition). A frontend (the built-in dockerfile.v0 frontend) reads your Dockerfile and emits LLB — a Merkle DAG of primitive ops (ExecOp for a RUN, FileOp for a COPY, SourceOp for a FROM/image pull). Every vertex's digest is a hash of its own op PLUS the digests of everything it depends on, so identical instructions produce an identical digest regardless of where they sit in the file.

   Dockerfile line          LLB vertex (op)                digest = hash(op + input digests)
   ─────────────────        ───────────────────             ────────────────────────────────
   FROM python:3.11-slim ─▶ SourceOp(image ref)         ──▶  sha256:aaa… (no inputs)
   COPY requirements.txt ─▶ FileOp(copy)  inputs:[aaa]  ──▶  sha256:bbb… (depends on aaa)
   RUN pip install …     ─▶ ExecOp(cmd)   inputs:[bbb]  ──▶  sha256:ccc… (depends on bbb)
   COPY . .              ─▶ FileOp(copy)  inputs:[ccc]  ──▶  sha256:ddd… (depends on ccc)

   The Solver walks this DAG and asks ONE question per vertex:
   "does a vertex with THIS EXACT digest already have a cached result?" → yes = CACHED
AspectLegacy builder cache keyBuildKit LLB cache key
What's hashedparent layer + instruction text + file checksum (5.3)the vertex's own op description + the digests of its inputs — a full content hash
Position sensitivitystrictly linear — a step's identity is really "everything before it, in order"graph-shaped — two vertices with no shared ancestor can be reordered or run in parallel with no cache impact
Granularityone cache key per Dockerfile lineone cache key per LLB op — a single COPY can decompose into several file ops
🔑 5.3's "cache key = parent + text + checksum" rule is the legacy builder's version of this same idea. BuildKit generalizes it to a graph: a vertex is CACHED the instant its digest matches something already solved, whether that solve happened earlier in THIS build or in a completely different one that shares the same base layers.
② Getting the context to the daemon — tar walk, ignore filter, session stream

5.1's "transferring context" line and 5.2's .dockerignore are the visible tip of a concrete pipeline. The CLI compiles .dockerignore into a pattern matcher FIRST, then walks the context directory: every file that survives the filter is written into a tar stream. With the classic builder that tar is POSTed whole to the daemon's HTTP API; with BuildKit/buildx the CLI instead opens a gRPC session to buildkitd and streams the directory over the fsutil diff-copy protocol — comparing local file stat metadata against what the daemon already has cached from a prior build and sending only what actually changed, conceptually similar to how rsync avoids re-sending unchanged bytes.

   docker build .                          docker buildx build .
   ─────────────                           ──────────────────────
   1. walk dir, apply .dockerignore        1. walk dir, apply .dockerignore
   2. tar the survivors                    2. open gRPC session to buildkitd
   3. HTTP POST the whole tar               3. fsutil diff-copy: stat-compare vs
      to the daemon, every build               daemon's last-seen tree, stream
                                                only CHANGED files this time
   4. daemon untars into a build context   4. daemon assembles context from the
      before ANY instruction runs             diff — same "before any step runs"
                                               guarantee, less repeated I/O
🔑 This is why a huge but UNCHANGING context (a large vendor/ tree that never edits) costs almost nothing on repeated buildx builds even without a perfect .dockerignore — the diff-copy protocol only pays for what moved. It's still not a substitute for 5.2's .dockerignore: the FIRST build, and any file that DOES change, still crosses the wire in full.
③ What a layer physically is — diffIDs, distribution digests & OverlayFS

Every RUN/COPY/ADD step that produces a layer is really a filesystem DIFF — the set of files created, modified, or deleted versus the layer beneath it. That diff gets hashed TWICE, for two different jobs: the diffID is a sha256 of the UNCOMPRESSED tar (used to identify the layer locally and inside the image config's rootfs.diff_ids), and the distribution digest is a sha256 of the COMPRESSED blob (used as the layer's address when pushing/pulling a registry). On disk, the default overlay2 snapshotter stacks these diffs as OverlayFS lowerdirs, with a fresh upperdir opened for whichever layer is currently being built.

   OverlayFS view during "RUN pip install -r requirements.txt":

   upperdir  ── (this step's writes land here — becomes the new layer's diff)
       │
   lowerdir  ── COPY requirements.txt .    diffID sha256:bbb…
       │
   lowerdir  ── FROM python:3.11-slim      diffID sha256:aaa…

   merged view = union of ALL dirs above, read top-down, exactly what the RUN step sees
   (WORKDIR /app never appears in this stack at all — a metadata-only instruction
    produces no filesystem diff and therefore no diffID of its own; see ④)
HashComputed fromUsed for
diffIDuncompressed tar difflocal layer identity; rootfs.diff_ids array in the image config (④)
distribution digestcompressed tar blobthe address a registry stores/serves the layer under; what docker pull matches against
🔑 This is the mechanism behind 5.3's cache gotcha that COPY --chmod/--chown bust the cache: permissions and ownership are part of the tar entry, so they change the diff's bytes and therefore BOTH hashes — even when the file's actual content is byte-identical.
④ The image config JSON — where ENV, ARG, and docker history really come from

An image is not just layers — it's layers PLUS a small JSON document, the image config (OCI Image Spec), that docker inspect and docker history both read directly. Two of its fields explain 5.4 and 5.7's ARG/ENV behaviour precisely: Config.Env is a flat array of KEY=value strings — ONLY ever populated by ENV, never by ARG — and history is an ARRAY with one entry per Dockerfile instruction, each carrying a created_by string (the literal instruction text, ARG substitution already applied) and an empty_layer: true flag for instructions that touch metadata only.

   image config.json (abridged)
   {
     "config": { "Env": ["DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings", "PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1"] },
     "rootfs": { "diff_ids": ["sha256:aaa…", "sha256:bbb…", "sha256:ccc…"] },
     "history": [
       { "created_by": "WORKDIR /app",                     "empty_layer": true  },
       { "created_by": "COPY requirements.txt .",          "empty_layer": false },
       { "created_by": "RUN pip install --extra-index-url https://user:hunter2@pip.example.com/simple …", "empty_layer": false },
       { "created_by": "ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings", "empty_layer": true  }
     ]
   }
InstructionNew layer (diffID)?Shows up in history[].created_by?In Config.Env at runtime?
RUN / COPY / ADD✅ yes — empty_layer: false✅ always, verbatim textn/a
ENV❌ no — empty_layer: true✅ yes✅ yes — this is HOW it persists
ARG (consumed by a later RUN)n/a — ARG itself never runs✅ inside that RUN's own created_by text❌ never
WORKDIR / LABEL / EXPOSE❌ no — empty_layer: true✅ yesn/a
🔑 This is the EXACT mechanism behind 5.7's leak audit: docker history --no-trunc isn't scanning file contents at all — it is printing history[].created_by straight out of this JSON. An ARG that a RUN line consumed is sitting in that string in plain text forever; an ARG that no RUN line ever touched leaves no trace anywhere, because ARG itself never gets its own history entry.
⑤ Manifest lists — one tag, N independent LLB solves, one platform-matching pull

5.5's "manifest list" is itself just JSON: an OCI Image Index (or Docker's older-format equivalent) whose manifests array holds one entry PER PLATFORM, each pointing at its own separate image manifest + config + layers by digest, tagged with a platform object (architecture, os, optionally variant). docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 runs TWO independent LLB solves — separate graphs, separate caches, separate config JSONs from ④ — and only unifies them into one manifest list at the very end, on --push.

   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1  (OCI Image Index / manifest list)
   {
     "manifests": [
       { "digest": "sha256:abc…", "platform": {"architecture":"amd64","os":"linux"} },
       { "digest": "sha256:def…", "platform": {"architecture":"arm64","os":"linux"} }
     ]
   }
        │                                              │
        ▼                                              ▼
   full image manifest (amd64)                  full image manifest (arm64)
   → its OWN config.json (④) + its OWN layer diffIDs (③) — built by a SEPARATE LLB solve

   docker pull on an M-series Mac  →  reads the index  →  matches "arm64"/"linux"
                                    →  pulls ONLY that one manifest's layers
🔑 QEMU is what makes the amd64-branch solve possible on an arm64 build machine (or vice versa) in the first place: docker buildx create --use registers static QEMU interpreter binaries with the kernel's binfmt_misc facility, which recognizes a foreign architecture's ELF magic bytes and transparently routes execution through the matching QEMU interpreter — so every RUN step in the "wrong-arch" LLB graph runs for real, just emulated, which is exactly why that half of a build (5.5) is the slow one.
⑥ Cache mounts & secret mounts — extra rootfs, deliberately excluded from the diff

③ established that a layer is whatever changed between a step's lowerdir and its upperdir. Cache mounts and secret mounts (5.7) both work by attaching EXTRA storage to a RUN step's merged view that BuildKit deliberately excludes from that diff calculation — so neither one can ever end up inside a layer, by construction, not by convention.

   RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
       --mount=type=secret,id=pipconf,target=/etc/pip.conf \
       pip install -r requirements.txt

   merged rootfs seen by THIS process:
     ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ image layers (lowerdir chain, ③)   ── included in the diff │
     │ this step's upperdir (writes)      ── included in the diff │
     │ cache mount  /root/.cache/pip      ── EXCLUDED — a separate│
     │   (persistent snapshot, keyed by "cache id", reused        │
     │    across builds; sharing=shared/private/locked)           │
     │ secret mount /etc/pip.conf         ── EXCLUDED — tmpfs,     │
     │   torn down the MOMENT this RUN's process exits, before    │
     │   BuildKit even computes what changed                      │
     └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Mount typeLifetimePart of the layer diff (③)?Part of image config (④)?
Regular rootfs (image + upperdir)permanent — becomes the next layer✅ yes, by definition✅ yes — new diffID + history entry
--mount=type=cachepersists ACROSS builds, keyed by cache id❌ excluded — a sibling mount, not the step's own diff❌ never appears
--mount=type=secretthis ONE RUN process only, then unmounted❌ excluded — gone before the diff is even taken❌ never appears
🔑 Compare this to ④'s ARG mechanism: an ARG leaks because its TEXT gets written into history[].created_by — a metadata leak, not a filesystem one. A secret mount leaks NOTHING because its bytes were never even offered to the diff algorithm that produces a layer OR a history entry. Two completely different reasons for the same outcome in Drill 5.5 — one is "the wrong storage location," the other is "true isolation."

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The build context is whatever directory follows docker build — only files inside it are ever COPYable, and the whole thing is tarred and sent to the daemon before any instruction runs.
  • .dockerignore trims context size and keeps secrets and virtualenvs out of both the upload AND the final image.
  • A cache key is parent-layer + instruction TEXT + file checksums — RUN lines are matched by text, never re-executed to check for a match.
  • ARG dies at the end of the stage that declares it; ENV survives into every container, forever, visible in docker inspect.
  • buildx + --platform + --push produces one tag that serves every CPU architecture via a manifest list (2.6).
  • bake replaces repeated docker build invocations with one declarative HCL/JSON file; targets share cache across builds.
  • Cache mounts persist downloads across cache misses; secret mounts use credentials without ever writing them to a layer.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: this whole list is examinable under Image Creation, Management & Registry.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • One --cache-from flag warms an entire multi-stage build → Each stage needs its own --cache-from entry (--cache-from=easypj:build --cache-from=easypj:final) — name only one and the other stage's layers rebuild from scratch anyway.
  • Emulated QEMU builds need a second physical machine → docker buildx create --use registers QEMU binfmt_misc handlers on your EXISTING machine — no separate ARM/AMD hardware required, just a slower "wrong-arch" half of the build.
  • Forgetting .dockerignore → Build context size affects build speed. Always exclude node_modules, .git, venv.
  • HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY need their own ARG line to reach a RUN step → BuildKit predefines proxy ARGs automatically — no ARG declaration needed at all.
  • docker build . from any directory is safe → Run from the wrong directory it ships everything beneath it — always watch the "transferring context" line.
  • A cached RUN apt-get update expires by time → It never expires by time — it can silently serve a year-old package index forever.
  • Skipping --push on a buildx build just keeps it local → Skipping --push (or --load for single-arch) discards the result entirely — it exists nowhere afterward.
  • An ARG that a RUN line consumes is "safe" because ARG itself doesn't persist into the running container → The consumed VALUE is still written into that layer's history[].created_by text forever — docker history --no-trunc recovers it from anyone who ever gets the image, regardless of whether ARG "persists." Use --mount=type=secret for real credentials (5.7).
  • ENV SECRET_KEY=... at build time is fine as long as nobody else pulls the image → It ships the secret to every registry the image ever touches, forever — pass secrets at docker run with --env-file, never bake them in.
  • docker buildx bake starts and manages containers too → bake is BUILD orchestration only — it never starts a container; Compose owns runtime.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Check the "transferring context" line on every project's FIRST build — an oversized context is a five-second fix once caught.
  • Give docker buildx bake a default group so both dev and prod images build with a single word.
  • Add a pip/npm cache mount to every Dockerfile that installs dependencies — it is close to free after the first build.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 5)

standard, cache-busting & multi-arch builds 
# Standard build
docker build -t easypj:v1 .

# Bust the cache
docker build --no-cache -t easypj:v1 .

# Build-time value
docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2 -t easypj:v1 .

# Multi-arch
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    --push -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 .

# Build all targets
docker buildx bake

# Secret mount
docker build --secret id=pipconf,src=pip.conf -t easypj:v1 .

# Leak audit
docker history --no-trunc easypj:v1 | grep -i secret
multi-stage & layer inspection 
docker build --target builder -t app:dev .
docker history IMAGE --no-trunc
docker images --format "{{.Size}}"

🧠 Chapter 5 — DCA Practice Questions (16)

Quick recall of build mechanics — 16 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What exactly is the build context, and why is docker build . from your home directory dangerous?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The context is the directory named after docker build — it is tarred and streamed to the daemon whole, BEFORE any instruction runs.

  docker build .   (run from $HOME — dangerous)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. tar EVERYTHING under $HOME  (before the Dockerfile │
  │                                  is even parsed)      │
  │ 2. stream the whole tar to the daemon                 │
  │ 3. ONLY THEN does the first instruction run           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Photos/, .ssh/, node_modules/ all get tarred — even though
  not one COPY line will ever touch them.
EXPLANATION

From $HOME, that tar includes your entire home directory, whether or not anything in it is ever COPYed — a slow upload at best, an accidental secrets leak at worst.

Q2
How do you force a complete rebuild without using any cached layers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build --no-cache -t app:v1 . — forces every instruction to re-execute, ignoring all cached layers.

SituationCommand
Suspect the cache itself is corrupteddocker build --no-cache -t app:v1 .
Base image updated upstream, want fresh packages toodocker build --no-cache --pull -t app:v1 .
Debugging a build that "should" fail but doesn'tdocker build --no-cache -t app:v1 .
EXPLANATION

Use --no-cache when you suspect cache corruption, when base images have been updated and you want fresh packages, or when debugging build issues.

Q3
What's the purpose of .dockerignore?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Excludes files from the build context, making builds faster and preventing sensitive files (secrets, local config) from being accidentally copied into the image.

Excluded patternRisk if shipped anyway
.git/full commit history — the biggest accidental secret-leak surface
node_modules/ / env/host-platform binaries, reinstalled inside the image anyway
.envlocal secrets baked permanently into a shareable layer
EXPLANATION

Without .dockerignore, Docker sends EVERYTHING in the context directory — including .git (potentially huge), node_modules, .env files with secrets, and IDE configs.

Q4
What's the difference between ARG and ENV?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ARG is build-time only (gone after build). ENV persists into the final image and is available at runtime. Use ARG for build configuration, ENV for runtime configuration. Never put secrets in ENV — they're visible in docker history.

AspectARGENV
Survives into the running container?❌ No✅ Yes
Set with--build-arg VAR=valueENV VAR=value in the Dockerfile
Safe place for a secret?❌ Never — visible via docker history --no-trunc❌ Never — ships in every pulled image
EXPLANATION

To make an ARG value available at runtime, persist it to ENV: ARG VERSION=unknown; ENV APP_VERSION=$VERSION. The DCA exam frequently tests this distinction.

Q5
What tool builds images for multiple platforms (amd64 + arm64) simultaneously?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Buildx — docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t app:v1 .

  docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t app:v1 --push .
                                │
                   ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                   ▼                          ▼
        app:v1@sha256:...(amd64)     app:v1@sha256:...(arm64)
                   └────────────┬────────────┘
                       ONE tag = manifest list
             `docker pull app:v1` auto-picks the right entry
EXPLANATION

Buildx uses QEMU emulation (or native builders) to compile for different architectures. The result is a manifest list — a single tag that automatically serves the correct platform-specific image.

Q6
What happens to the cache when a layer changes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

That layer AND ALL subsequent layers are rebuilt. Docker cannot know if later layers depend on the changed one, so it rebuilds everything after the changed layer.

  Layer 1    Layer 2    Layer 3    Layer 4    Layer 5
  ✅CACHED   ✅CACHED   ❌CHANGED  ❌REBUILD  ❌REBUILD
                            └──────────┴──────────┘
                    everything AFTER a change rebuilds too
EXPLANATION

This is the "cache avalanche" effect. If Layer 1 changes, all N layers rebuild. If Layer N changes, only layer N rebuilds. That's why you put the most stable layers FIRST and the most volatile LAST.

Q7
How do you pass a value to an ARG during build?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.0 -t app:v1 . — sets ARG VERSION to "1.0" during the build.

TERMINAL
docker build \
  --build-arg VERSION=1.0 \
  --build-arg ENVIRONMENT=production \
  -t app:v1 .
EXPLANATION

Multiple ARGs can be passed: --build-arg VAR1=val1 --build-arg VAR2=val2. If an ARG has a default in the Dockerfile, the --build-arg flag overrides it.

Q8
What does DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 enable?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

BuildKit — Docker's next-generation build engine. Provides faster builds, better caching, parallel stage execution, secrets mounting, and improved output formatting. It's the default in recent Docker versions.

FeatureLegacy builderBuildKit
Independent stagessequentialparallel
Build secrets (--secret)❌✅
Remote cache (--cache-from/--cache-to)limited✅
SSH forwarding (--ssh)❌✅
EXPLANATION

BuildKit is backward-compatible but dramatically better. Key features: parallel multi-stage builds, build secrets (--secret), remote cache (--cache-from), and SSH forwarding (--ssh).

Q9
How do you build from a Dockerfile with a different name?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t app:prod . — the -f flag specifies a custom Dockerfile path/name.

FileCommand
Dockerfile (default)docker build -t app .
Dockerfile.proddocker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t app:prod .
Dockerfile.devdocker build -f Dockerfile.dev -t app:dev .
EXPLANATION

The -f flag is useful for projects with multiple Dockerfiles (e.g., Dockerfile, Dockerfile.prod, Dockerfile.dev). Without -f, Docker looks for a file named Dockerfile in the build context root.

Q10
Your build is slow because the build context is 2 GB. How do you fix this?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create a .dockerignore file to exclude large/unnecessary files (node_modules, .git, databases, logs, virtual environments). This reduces the build context sent to the daemon, dramatically speeding up builds.

Common culpritTypical size
.git/hundreds of MB, sometimes GBs
node_modules/200 MB – 1 GB+
local env/ / venv/~200 MB
media/log filesvaries, often the silent majority
EXPLANATION

You can check context size with docker build --no-cache 2>&1 | grep "transferring context". A good target is < 50 MB for the build context.

Q11
List four entries a Django project's .dockerignore should have, and why each one specifically matters.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

.git/ (full commit history — the biggest secret-leak surface of the four), __pycache__//*.pyc (host-compiled bytecode, rebuilt inside the container anyway), env/ (a virtualenv built for your LAPTOP's platform, not the container's), .env (runtime secrets that must be injected at docker run, never baked into a build).

EntryWhy it matters
.git/full commit history — the biggest secret-leak surface of the four
__pycache__/ / *.pychost-compiled bytecode, rebuilt inside the container anyway
env/a virtualenv built for your LAPTOP's platform, not the container's
.envruntime secrets that must be injected at docker run, never baked into a build
EXPLANATION

Each entry maps to a concrete, different failure mode (5.2): .git/ and .env are security risks; __pycache__/ is pure upload waste; env/ is waste AND a platform mismatch that would never even run correctly if somehow copied in.

Q12
What's the difference between what's reused on a layer cache HIT versus what's reused with a cache MOUNT?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A layer cache hit reuses an entire finished layer and skips the instruction outright. A cache mount reuses only the DOWNLOADS inside a layer that still has to rebuild — the instruction re-executes because its cache key was invalidated, but the tool it runs (e.g. pip) finds its files already warm in the mounted directory.

Layer cache HITCache MOUNT
Instruction re-executes?❌ No — skipped entirely✅ Yes — cache key was invalidated
What's reusedthe whole finished layeronly the downloads inside the mounted dir
requirements.txt edit, timedN/A — an edit is a miss, not a hit~45s → ~8s (5.7)
EXPLANATION

5.7's cache mount drops requirements.txt-edit rebuilds from ~45s to ~8s this way — the RUN pip install layer still reruns (its checksum input changed), but PyPI itself is never re-hit.

Q13
Why does moving ENV APP_VERSION=... near the TOP of a Dockerfile hurt the build cache more than placing it near the bottom, below COPY . .?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Any change below an invalidated layer must rebuild too — a volatile ENV placed early invalidates the (expensive) RUN pip install layer on every single version bump.

  BAD  (early ENV invalidates everything after it)
  FROM python:3.11-slim
  ENV APP_VERSION=1.4.2        ← changes every release
  COPY requirements.txt .      ❌ REBUILD (below the change)
  RUN pip install -r req..     ❌ REBUILD (38s, wasted every bump)
  COPY . .                     ❌ REBUILD

  GOOD  (volatile ENV moved LAST)
  FROM python:3.11-slim
  COPY requirements.txt .      ✅ CACHED
  RUN pip install -r req..     ✅ CACHED (38s saved)
  COPY . .                     ❌ REBUILD (code always changes anyway)
  ENV APP_VERSION=1.4.2        ❌ REBUILD (but free — nothing sits below it)
EXPLANATION

Volatile, frequently-changing metadata belongs LAST, below COPY . . — exactly 5.3's guidance on where the stable FROM / COPY requirements.txt / RUN pip install sequence should sit relative to anything that changes on every single build.

Q14
Which ARGs need NO explicit ARG line in the Dockerfile to be available during a build?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, FTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY — and their lowercase variants — are predefined by BuildKit and automatically available to proxy-aware RUN steps, with no ARG declaration required at all.

Predefined ARGPurpose
HTTP_PROXY / http_proxyproxy for plain HTTP requests during the build
HTTPS_PROXY / https_proxyproxy for HTTPS requests during the build
FTP_PROXY / ftp_proxyproxy for FTP requests during the build
NO_PROXY / no_proxyhosts that should bypass the proxy entirely
EXPLANATION

Covered in 5.4's proxy callout; the full ARG/ENV bash-style modifier syntax (${VAR:-default} and friends) is tabled in Appendix B.10.

Q15
What role does QEMU play when a buildx build targets linux/arm64 from an amd64 CI runner, and why is --push mandatory for a multi-platform result?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

QEMU provides user-mode emulation so the foreign architecture's instructions actually run — slowly, but automatically, via the kernel's binfmt_misc handlers that docker buildx create --use registers. --push is required because the local image store has no concept of holding a multi-arch manifest-list result — only a registry can.

Flag / toolRole
QEMU (via binfmt_misc)runs the "wrong-arch" half of the build for real, just emulated — an actual foreign-CPU interpreter, not a shortcut
--pushmandatory: writes the finished manifest list to a registry, the only place a multi-arch result can live
--loadan alternative to --push, but single-platform ONLY — loads one result into the local image store
EXPLANATION

5.5's buildx workflow always ends multi-platform builds with --push for exactly this reason — skip it (and skip --load) and the result exists nowhere afterward (5.5's gotcha).

Q16
What does the inherits keyword do in a docker-bake.hcl target, and what does it NOT do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It copies another target's ENTIRE configuration — dockerfile, args, tags — as a starting point, then lets the new target override or extend just the fields that differ. It does NOT merge field-by-field beyond that copy-then-override behavior, and a target can only inherit from a target defined in the same file.

  target "dev"  { dockerfile = "Dockerfile"; tags = ["easypj:dev"]; args = { APP_VERSION = "dev" } }
  target "prod" { inherits = ["dev"]; tags = ["ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1"]; platforms = [...] }
  # prod = dev's dockerfile + args, PLUS its own tags/platforms — zero duplication
EXPLANATION

Shown directly in 5.6's docker-bake.hcl example — prod inherits dev's dockerfile and APP_VERSION arg, then adds its own registry tag and multi-platform list, with zero duplication of the shared config.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.1 — Measure the Context Drop

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Add a .dockerignore excluding .git/ and env/ to any repo with a Dockerfile, rebuild, and compare the "transferring context" line before and after. Verify: upload size drops by an order of magnitude with zero change to the build's output image.

Hint: BuildKit prints the transfer size on its own progress line — look for "load build context" / "transferring context" right at the top of the output, before any instruction runs (5.1's annotated build output).
View Solution
TERMINAL
# BEFORE — no .dockerignore
docker build -t app:v1 .
# => [internal] load build context
# => transferring context: 340.20MB

# AFTER — exclude .git/ and env/
printf '.git/\nenv/\n' > .dockerignore
docker build -t app:v1 .
# => [internal] load build context
# => transferring context: 4.10MB

Check yourself: the transfer size drops by roughly two orders of magnitude because .git/ (full history) and env/ (a laptop-only virtualenv) were the two heaviest, and most pointless, things being tarred on every single build — while the built image's layers stay byte-for-byte identical, since neither directory was ever COPYed into it (5.2).

🔬 Practice Drill 5.2 — ARG vs ENV, Proven at Runtime

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Build easypj with --build-arg APP_VERSION=9.9, where the Dockerfile both consumes that ARG in a RUN line AND persists it into a LABEL version=$APP_VERSION. Then run docker run --rm easypj:v1 printenv APP_VERSION and separately check docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Labels.version}}' easypj:v1. Predict which command comes back empty and which one still holds "9.9" — then prove it.

Hint: ARG values that are never persisted to ENV don't survive into the running container's environment at all — but anything written into a LABEL is baked into image metadata, and metadata isn't a container environment variable.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=9.9 -t easypj:v1 .

docker run --rm easypj:v1 printenv APP_VERSION
# (empty output — the ARG evaporated at the end of the build stage)

docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Labels.version}}' easypj:v1
# 9.9  — the LABEL kept the value permanently

Check yourself: printenv comes back empty because ARG only ever exists DURING the build — it was never written into the image's runtime environment. The LABEL, by contrast, is baked straight into the image's config metadata, which is why docker inspect still reports "9.9" long after the container that built it is gone. This is the exact ARG/ENV split 5.4's table describes, just proven with real commands instead of a table.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.3 — Predict the Cache Before You Trigger It

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Using 5.3's cache decision flow, before running anything, write down which layers will show CACHED and which will REBUILD for two separate one-line edits to an easypj-style Dockerfile: (a) editing README.md, which is excluded by .dockerignore, versus (b) editing requirements.txt. Then run both builds and check your predictions against the real => output lines.

Hint: A file that never enters the build context in the first place can't invalidate anything — trace which instruction is the FIRST one whose checksum input actually changed.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# (a) touch README.md (excluded by .dockerignore), then rebuild
docker build -t easypj:v1 .
# every step shows CACHED — README.md never reached the daemon at all

# (b) edit requirements.txt, then rebuild
docker build -t easypj:v1 .
# CACHED through the layer BEFORE "COPY requirements.txt .",
# then REBUILD from that COPY onward — including the pip install layer

Check yourself: (a) is entirely CACHED because .dockerignore stopped README.md from ever entering the tarred context — it can't invalidate a checksum it was never part of. (b) rebuilds starting at COPY requirements.txt . and every instruction after it, because that's the FIRST step whose checksum input changed — matching 5.3's rule that a cache miss cascades forward, never backward.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.4 — Ship One Tag, Two Architectures

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Create a buildx builder, build AND push easypj for both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 under one tag, then use docker buildx imagetools inspect to prove the tag really is a manifest list with two platform-specific entries underneath — not one image that "just works everywhere" by magic.

Hint: --push is not optional here — the local image store has no concept of holding a multi-arch result at once, so skipping it silently discards the whole build (5.5's gotcha).
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker buildx create --name multiarch --use

docker buildx build \
    --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 \
    --push .

docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
# MediaType: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json
# Manifests:
#   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1@sha256:abc... (linux/amd64)
#   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1@sha256:def... (linux/arm64)

Check yourself: one tag, two Manifests: entries — that's the manifest list from 2.6, built instead of just inspected. If you skipped --push, the imagetools command finds nothing at all, because a multi-platform result is never written to the local image store; it only exists once pushed to a registry.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.5 — The Secret Leak Audit

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Build the SAME credential-consuming Dockerfile fragment TWICE — once with ARG TOKEN=hunter2 consumed by a RUN line, once with --mount=type=secret. Run docker history --no-trunc against both resulting images and grep for the token. Prove to yourself which build leaks and which one doesn't.

Hint: docker history --no-trunc reads each layer's recorded command string — anything a RUN line ever touched as ARG text is sitting right there in plain sight.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# Build 1 — ARG consumed by a RUN line (leaks)
docker build --build-arg TOKEN=hunter2 -f Dockerfile.arg -t leak-test:arg .
docker history --no-trunc leak-test:arg | grep hunter2
# FOUND — sitting right in the RUN command string

# Build 2 — secret mount (no trace anywhere)
docker build --secret id=token,src=token.txt -f Dockerfile.secret -t leak-test:secret .
docker history --no-trunc leak-test:secret | grep hunter2
# nothing — zero matches in history, inspect, or any layer

Check yourself: the ARG build's history line literally contains hunter2 in plain text, permanently, in every copy of that image ever pushed or pulled. The secret-mount build shows nothing because the credential existed only as a temporary file DURING that one RUN step and was never written to any layer — exactly 5.7's proof workflow, run yourself instead of just read.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.6 — One File, Every Variant, Built in Parallel

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Write 5.6's docker-bake.hcl (the dev/prod version with inherits), then run docker buildx bake dev alone. Verify: only easypj:dev exists afterward. Then run docker buildx bake with no target argument and watch the output tree — both dev and prod build in the same run, sharing whatever cached layers they have in common.

Hint: the group "default" { targets = [...] } block is what a target-less docker buildx bake falls back to — naming one target explicitly (bake dev) bypasses the group entirely and builds only that one.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# Build only "dev" by naming it explicitly
docker buildx bake dev
docker images easypj:dev
# easypj:dev   ...   (exists — "prod" was never touched)

# Build the whole "default" group — both targets, one command
docker buildx bake
# [+] Building ... => [dev] ... => [prod] ...  (both progress in the same tree,
# and any layer dev and prod share — e.g. the pip install — builds only once)

Check yourself: naming dev explicitly builds exactly one target — the group "default" block never even gets consulted. Running bare docker buildx bake falls back to that default group and builds every target it lists in parallel, and because prod inherits from dev, BuildKit recognizes their shared layers as the same cache key and builds the common dependency-install step only once for both (5.6, 5.3).

✅ Chapter 5 — Verify Your Knowledge
  • Can you explain exactly what the build context is, and why running docker build . from the wrong directory is dangerous?
  • Do you know what goes in a .dockerignore file, and why it's a security control, not just a speed optimization?
  • Can you trace a cache key (parent-layer + instruction text + file checksums) to predict which layers stay CACHED after a one-line edit?
  • Can you explain the difference between ARG and ENV, and why neither is safe for secrets?
  • Can you build and push a multi-platform image with buildx, and explain what a manifest list is?
  • Do you know when to reach for docker buildx bake instead of repeated docker build calls?
  • Can you explain why a secret mount leaves no trace in docker history but ARG does?
📌 Chapter 5 Visual Summary — the mechanics under docker build
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  docker build -t easypj:v1 .                                    │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  [context: tar, minus .dockerignore] ──▶ [BuildKit graph solve] │
  │       │                                          │              │
  │  cache key = parent + text + checksum   parallel independent    │
  │       │                                  steps, shared cache    │
  │       ▼                                          │              │
  │  ARG (gone at stage end)  ENV (baked in forever)  │              │
  │       │                                          ▼              │
  │  buildx --platform ──▶ per-arch build ──▶ manifest list --push  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In one line: the context decides what CAN be built, the cache-key algorithm decides what MUST be rebuilt, ARG and ENV decide what SURVIVES past the build, and buildx/bake scale the same recipe across every architecture and every variant your fleet needs — all without changing a single line of the Dockerfile Chapter 4 taught you to write.

The takeaway: Chapter 5 is the mechanics under the one command you already knew how to type.

Chapter 6 · Running Containers — docker run & Container Management

Building images is half the battle. Running and managing containers is where the real work happens. This chapter covers everything from basic docker run to advanced container lifecycle management. An image sitting on disk earns nothing — value only starts the moment a container actually RUNS and someone keeps it alive; this chapter is the answer to "the container started yesterday… how do I see inside it, and why did it die at 3 AM?"

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~4-5 hours 🏃 Runtime

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Choose correctly among -it, -d and --rm run modes, and pick the right restart policy for a service that must survive reboots
  • ✅ Drive every container lifecycle transition — create, start, stop, pause, kill, rm — and know exactly what each one destroys
  • ✅ Triage a running or crashed container using ps, logs, stats, top and inspect, in the correct cheap-to-expensive order
  • ✅ Use docker exec to run one-off commands and open interactive shells inside a LIVE container without restarting it
  • ✅ Move files across the container boundary with docker cp, and know when it is the wrong tool
  • ✅ Cap CPU and memory so one runaway container cannot starve the host, and correctly read OOM evidence
  • ✅ Add a HEALTHCHECK and read docker events to see real liveness, not just "the process exists"
🎓 DCA Relevance
Orchestration background Networking background Security background
🎯 Not Its Own Domain, But Assumed Everywhere

This chapter isn't graded as its own domain, but it's assumed by Orchestration (service health, restarts), Networking (port publishing) and Security (least-privilege exec) — expect its commands embedded inside scenario questions from those domains.

  • Triage order: ps (is it up?) → logs (what did it say?) → stats/top (is it healthy right now?) → inspect (full JSON truth) — cheap checks first, full dump last.
  • A --memory breach KILLS the process (exit 137, OOMKilled:true); a --cpus breach only THROTTLES it — the app stays alive but slow.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 6 Learning Arc

This chapter is the operator's manual for the image Chapters 4 and 5 taught you to build: start it right, move it through its lifecycle deliberately, observe it cheaply, reach inside it, cap what it can consume, and give it a real health signal.

Chapter 6 Roadmap — from docker run to a real health signal
   ▶ YOU ARE HERE — "I have an image. How do I actually operate it?"
        │
        ▼
   ┌── 6.1 ─ 🚀 RUN MODES & RESTART POLICIES ─────────────────────────────┐
   │   -it / -d / --rm, and no / on-failure / always / unless-stopped     │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │   (…the full state machine?)
        ▼
   ┌── 6.2 ─ 🔄 LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT ─────────────────────────────────────┐
   │   create → start → pause → stop → kill → rm                          │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │   (…is it actually healthy right now?)

   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │   (…get inside without restarting it?)

   │   exec adds a process to an EXISTING container's namespaces          │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        │   (…stop one container starving the host?)

   │   --memory kills; --cpus throttles                                    │

        │   (…is "Up" actually healthy?)
        ▼

6.1 docker run — The Complete Reference

docker run is your most-used command. It creates AND starts a container in one step. Understanding every option is critical for both the DCA exam and daily work.

Run Modes

ModeFlagsUse Case
Foreground (interactive)-itDebugging, exploring inside container
Detached (background)-dProduction, long-running services
Ephemeral (auto-cleanup)--rmOne-off commands, CI/CD, testing

Port Mapping

-p HOST:CONTAINER — Maps a port on your host to a port in the container. Example: -p 8000:8000 makes the container's port 8000 accessible at http://localhost:8000. Use -P to publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports.

Environment Variables

-e VAR=value sets a single variable. --env-file .env loads variables from a file. Environment variables are the primary way to configure containers at runtime — they keep configuration out of your image.

Naming (--name)

--name easypj-web gives a container a stable, memorable handle instead of a random Docker-generated name like epic_turing or fervent_hopper. Every later command targets this name instead of a long container ID — docker logs easypj-web, docker exec -it easypj-web bash, docker stop easypj-web all read cleanly in scripts, aliases and incident-response runbooks.

A name must be unique among every container on the host, running OR stopped — Docker doesn't garbage-collect the name the instant a container exits. Re-running the same docker run --name easypj-web … line against a container that already exited fails with the container name "/easypj-web" is already in use until you either docker rm easypj-web the old one first or launch the old one with --rm so it deletes itself on exit (this section's own ephemeral mode, above).

Restart Policies

PolicyBehavioreasypj Use Case
noNever restart (default)One-off scripts
on-failure[:max-retries]Restart only on non-zero exit code, up to N timesMigrations, cron jobs
alwaysRestarts on crash/reboot; a manual stop holds only until the NEXT daemon restart, then it comes back regardlessRarely what you actually want
unless-stoppedSame as always, except a manual stop stays stopped through any FUTURE daemon restart tooeasypj-web in single-host prod

Restart policies are enforced by dockerd itself, not by a separate cron job or watchdog script — which is exactly why they also survive a full host reboot, as long as the Docker daemon's own service is enabled to start on boot (systemctl enable docker on most Linux distributions). One more official rule worth knowing cold: a policy only "arms" after a container has stayed up for at least 10 seconds and Docker has started monitoring it — a container that dies faster than that (a bad CMD typo, a missing env var) is treated as a failed START, not a crash needing a restart, which is exactly why a badly broken image doesn't loop-restart forever on its own.

Forgot to set --restart at launch, or need to change it on a container that's already running important work? docker update --restart unless-stopped easypj-web changes the policy on a LIVE container — no rm and no fresh run required (see 6.6 for the rest of what docker update can change on the fly).

TERMINAL — the canonical single-host production start
$ docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env \
             --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1
💡 easypj in Practice — Every Flag Above Earned Its Place

That one line is the payoff of this whole section: -d because a web service must outlive your terminal, --name so every later logs/exec/stop targets it by a stable handle, -p 8000:8000 for an exact reproducible port instead of -P's random one, --env-file .env to keep secrets out of the image, and --restart unless-stopped so it survives crashes and reboots without fighting a deliberate maintenance stop. Nothing on this line is decorative.

🐾 Analogy — Pet-Care Instructions Taped to the Container

A restart policy is a pet-care instruction taped to the container's cage — but read the fine print. always says: "stand it back up whenever it falls — and if YOU deliberately lay it down, that instruction is only suspended, not cancelled: the next time the building's power comes back on (a Docker daemon restart), the instruction re-applies and it gets stood up again whether you wanted that or not." unless-stopped reads the same card with one line struck out permanently: once you've laid it down yourself, it stays down through any number of future power-outages. That single struck line is the entire reason production defaults to unless-stopped — both policies survive crashes and reboots identically, but only unless-stopped remembers, forever, that YOU were the one who stopped it.

🚀 docker run — Every Flag, One Reference (easypj examples)

🏷️ --name
--name easypj-web — gives the container a stable, memorable handle instead of a random epic_turing-style name; every later command (logs, exec, stop) targets this name.
🔌 -p / -P
-p 8000:8000 maps an EXACT host port; -P auto-publishes every EXPOSEd port to a RANDOM host port. -p is the safer, reproducible choice for production.
🧬 -e / --env-file
-e DEBUG=False sets one variable; --env-file .env loads a whole file — the primary way to keep configuration out of the image itself.
💾 -v / --mount
-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data attaches a named volume; -v $(pwd):/app bind-mounts the host directory for live-reload development (full detail in Part 6).
🌐 --network
--network easypj-net attaches to a user-defined bridge network so containers can resolve each other by NAME (Part 5 covers Docker networking end to end).
🔄 --restart
--restart unless-stopped — see the policy table above; mutually exclusive in spirit with --rm, since a container can't both auto-delete and auto-relaunch.
💪 --memory / --cpus
--memory=512m --cpus=1.5 caps RAM and CPU — the full resource-limit reference is 6.6.
👤 -u
-u appuser (or -u 1000:1000) runs PID 1 as a non-root user, overriding whatever USER the Dockerfile set — a favorite last-minute security fix.
🏠 --hostname / -h
--hostname easypj-web-1 sets the container's internal hostname, visible to uname -n and often used in log correlation across replicas.
📂 -w
-w /app overrides the working directory for THIS run only, without touching the Dockerfile's WORKDIR — handy for one-off diagnostic commands run from a different path.
🎯 --entrypoint
--entrypoint bash replaces the image's baked-in ENTRYPOINT for a single debugging run — the emergency hatch when the normal PID 1 won't even start.

6.2 Container Lifecycle Management

Containers have a well-defined lifecycle. Understanding the states and transitions helps you debug and manage containers effectively.

Container Lifecycle State Diagram
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 CONTAINER LIFECYCLE STATES                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │                            docker create                                 │
  │                        ┌───────────────────┐                            │
