  │                        ▼                   │                            │
  │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐                      │
  │  │  Image   │   │ ▶️ CREATED  │     │ ▶️ RUNNING  │                      │
  │  │         │──▶│             │────▶│             │                      │
  │  │(blueprint)│  │ (exists on  │     │ (process     │                      │
  │  └─────────┘   │  disk, not   │     │  active,     │                      │
  │                │  started)    │     │  CPU running)│                      │
  │                └──────┬──────┘     └──┬──┬──┬───┘                      │
  │                       │               │  │  │                            │
  │                       │ docker start  │  │  │ docker stop (SIGTERM,     │
  │                       └───────────────┘  │  │  then SIGKILL after       │
  │                                          │  │  10s grace period)         │
  │                                   docker │   │                           │
  │                                   pause  │   │ docker kill (SIGKILL)     │
  │                                          ▼   ▼                           │
  │                                    ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌─────────┐   │
  │                                    │ ⏸️     │ │ ⏹️      │ │ 💀      │   │
  │                                    │PAUSED  │ │STOPPED │ │ DELETED │   │
  │                                    │(frozen │ │(exited │ │ (gone)  │   │
  │                                    │ processes)│ │process)│ │         │   │
  │                                    └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └─────────┘   │
  │                                        │         │                       │
  │                             docker unpause  docker start                │
  │                                        │         │                       │
  │                                        ▼         ▼                       │
  │                                   ┌────────────────┐                    │
  │                                   │  ▶️ RUNNING     │                    │
  │                                   └────────────────┘                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docker restart is simply docker stop + docker start executed back-to-back against the SAME container ID — the writable layer (and anything written to it) survives completely untouched. Only docker rm actually deletes it. That is the one fact that makes the whole state machine safe to explore: every arrow except rm is reversible. Even rm has one exception this chapter hasn't introduced yet: data written to a named volume or bind mount lives OUTSIDE the container's writable layer entirely, so it survives an rm too — Part 6 covers exactly how.

🎭 Analogy — A Stage Play

create is actors waiting in the wings; start is curtain up; pause freezes the scene mid-line; stop is a graceful bow and exit; kill is a fire alarm that clears the building instantly, no bow; rm strikes the set entirely — the props (the writable layer) are gone for good. It's the same stage from Chapter 2's state diagram, just walked with the real commands instead of arrows.

📖 Containers Are "Cattle, Not Pets"

In traditional server management, servers are treated like pets — you name them, nurse them back to health, and panic when they go down. Containers are cattle — you number them, expect them to die, and automatically replace them from the same image. This mindset shift is fundamental to Docker: never manually fix a broken container; just docker rm it and docker run a fresh one from the same image.

💡 easypj in Practice — Why the Grace Period Matters

docker stop easypj-web gives gunicorn a full 10 seconds to finish in-flight JobPost requests before SIGKILL lands. A deploy script that uses docker rm -f instead skips that grace period entirely — SIGKILL fires immediately, and any request mid-flight is dropped on the floor at every single release. Always prefer stop (or stop -t 30 for slower shutdowns) in deploy tooling; save -f for truly stuck containers.

TERMINAL
# Create a container (but don't start it)
$ docker create --name easypj-dev easypj:v1

# Start a stopped container
$ docker start easypj-dev

# Stop a running container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after grace period)
$ docker stop easypj-dev

# Force kill immediately (SIGKILL)
$ docker kill easypj-dev

# kill isn't ONLY SIGKILL — send any signal by name or number instead
$ docker kill --signal=SIGHUP easypj-dev   # e.g. nginx reloads config on SIGHUP, no restart
$ docker kill -s SIGUSR1 easypj-dev        # -s is the short flag

# Pause / Unpause (freeze all processes)
$ docker pause easypj-dev
$ docker unpause easypj-dev

# Restart a container
$ docker restart easypj-dev

# Remove a container (must be stopped first, or use -f)
$ docker rm easypj-dev
$ docker rm -f easypj-dev  # Force remove (even if running)

# Rename in place — same ID, same writable layer, new handle
$ docker rename easypj-canary easypj-web

# Block until a container stops, then print its exit code
$ docker wait easypj-dev

# Delete every STOPPED container in one shot (prompts unless -f)
$ docker container prune -f
💡 Three More Lifecycle Commands Worth Knowing

docker rename OLD NEW renames a container in place — same ID, same writable layer, just a new handle. It's the clean way to promote a container that passed a smoke test: run the new version as easypj-canary, verify it, docker rm the old easypj-web, then docker rename easypj-canary easypj-web so every downstream script that hardcodes the name keeps working. docker wait CONTAINER blocks and prints the exit code the instant the container stops — the scriptable alternative to polling docker ps in a loop after a one-off job. docker container prune removes EVERY stopped container in one shot — the "cattle, not pets" cleanup command for a host that's accumulated a graveyard of exited debug and CI containers; add -f to skip the confirmation prompt in scripts.

📖 docker kill Isn't Only SIGKILL

The name is misleading: docker kill just means "send a signal now, no grace period" — the default signal happens to be SIGKILL, but --signal (or its short form -s) lets you send ANY signal instead, by name or number. This turns kill into a general-purpose signaling tool, not only a destructive one: docker kill --signal=SIGHUP easypj-web can trigger an app's own config-reload logic (nginx and many daemons treat SIGHUP that way) with zero downtime and no restart at all, and docker kill -s SIGUSR1 is a common hook for custom app-defined behavior (e.g. dumping a goroutine stack, rotating an internal log). Only the SIGNAL differs — everything else about delivery is identical to plain docker kill: it goes straight to PID 1, immediately, with no 10-second grace timer.

6.3 Viewing & Inspecting Containers

Five read-only commands, run in four triage stages, answer "what is this container doing RIGHT NOW?" in under thirty seconds — provided you hit them in the right order: cheap looks first, the full JSON dump last.

🏥 Analogy — A Hospital Ward Round

ps is the bed chart clipped to the foot of the bed (is the patient even here, and for how long?); logs is the patient's own account of what happened; stats is the live vitals monitor beeping beside the bed, with top as the nurse standing right next to it listing exactly who's in the room; inspect is the complete medical file in the records office. A good doctor reads them in exactly that order — nobody pulls the full chart before glancing at the vitals monitor first.

TERMINAL
# List running containers
$ docker ps
$ docker container ls  # same command, newer syntax

# List ALL containers (including stopped)
$ docker ps -a

# Filter instead of eyeballing the whole list
$ docker ps --filter status=exited        # only dead containers
$ docker ps --filter health=unhealthy     # only failing HEALTHCHECKs (6.7)
$ docker ps --filter name=easypj          # only names matching a substring

# Disk footprint per container (writable layer vs. total)
$ docker ps -s                            # adds a SIZE column: "12.4kB (virtual 850MB)"

# Just the port mappings, no full ps table needed
$ docker port easypj-dev                  # 8000/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:8000

# View logs
$ docker logs easypj-dev           # Show all logs
$ docker logs -f easypj-dev        # Follow (like tail -f)
$ docker logs --tail 50 easypj-dev # Last 50 lines
$ docker logs --since 10m easypj-dev # Last 10 minutes

# Live resource usage (CPU, RAM, Network, Disk)
$ docker stats easypj-dev

# Show processes running inside container
$ docker top easypj-dev

# Detailed JSON metadata about container
$ docker inspect easypj-dev
$ docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' easypj-dev  # Just the IP
📖 --filter Beats Eyeballing the List

docker ps and docker container ls accept the SAME --filter flag (they're the same command). --filter status=exited finds crashed containers worth a docker logs look before you prune them away; --filter health=unhealthy is the fastest way to answer "which of my 30 containers is the sick one" without reading 30 STATUS columns by eye. Filters combine — docker ps --filter status=exited --filter name=easypj narrows to exactly the dead easypj containers.

📖 Two Small Commands Worth Knowing: -s and docker port

docker ps -s (or --size) appends a SIZE column showing TWO numbers per container — the writable layer alone, then in parentheses the "virtual" size which also counts every shared, read-only image layer underneath it. A container reporting 12.4kB (virtual 850MB) has written almost nothing new to disk; the 850MB is the shared image, not duplicated once per container. docker port easypj-dev is a dedicated one-line lookup for "what's this container's port mapping again?" — the same information docker ps's PORTS column shows, but scriptable and grep-free when you only need the answer to that one question.

📖 Where docker logs Actually Reads From

docker logs isn't reading a live stream off the process — it's reading whatever the container's configured logging driver captured from PID 1's stdout/stderr, and by default that's the json-file driver writing to disk under /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/ (rotation and size limits for that file are set once, daemon-wide, in daemon.json — see §2.7). That's exactly why gunicorn must log to stdout and never to its own file inside the container: a driver can only capture what PID 1 actually writes to those two streams.

The observation toolkit on easypj-web — annotated real output
$ docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
NAMES        STATUS                  PORTS
easypj-web   Up 2 hours (healthy)    0.0.0.0:8000->8000/tcp
# ↑ "Up 2 hours" = alive that long; "(healthy)" only appears with a HEALTHCHECK (6.7)

$ docker logs --tail 5 -f easypj-web    # last 5 lines, then follow
[2026-07-02 09:14:02] "GET /jobs/ HTTP/1.1" 200
# ↑ this is PID 1's own stdout — the app's account of what just happened

$ docker stats --no-stream easypj-web   # one-shot CPU / MEM snapshot
$ docker top easypj-web                 # processes, mapped to HOST pids
$ docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' easypj-web
💡 easypj in Practice — Reading the Evidence After a Crash

After a crash, docker logs --tail 50 easypj-web shows the Django traceback that PID 1 printed right before it died — usually the fastest path to a root cause. The ExitCode template then tells you HOW it died: 137 means OOM-killed or a manual docker kill (disambiguate with .State.OOMKilled, 6.6); 0 is a clean exit; 1 is an uncaught application error.

6.4 Executing Commands Inside Containers

docker exec runs commands inside an already-running container. This is how you debug, run migrations, or check application state.

🍳 Analogy — Stepping Through the Kitchen Door

docker exec is stepping through the kitchen door to taste the sauce while the chef keeps cooking — a second person briefly joins an existing kitchen, tastes, and leaves without the meal ever stopping. docker run would instead build a WHOLE second kitchen next door. run = new container; exec = visit an existing one — the distinction the whole section rests on.

TERMINAL
# Get an interactive shell inside the container
$ docker exec -it easypj-dev bash

# Run a single command
$ docker exec easypj-dev python manage.py check --deploy

# Run Django migrations
$ docker exec easypj-dev python manage.py migrate

# Check the Django settings
$ docker exec easypj-dev python -c "from django.conf import settings; print(settings.DEBUG)"

# Run as a specific user
$ docker exec -u appuser easypj-dev whoami

# Interactive Django ORM shell — live query against real data, zero downtime
$ docker exec -it easypj-dev python manage.py shell
>>> JobPost.objects.filter(location__name="Remote").count()
42
#Scenariodocker exec CommandWhy This Works
1Get a shelldocker exec -it easypj-dev bash-i (stdin open) + -t (TTY) = interactive shell
2Run Django migrationsdocker exec easypj-dev python manage.py migrateExecutes the command, prints output, exits — no TTY needed
3Check Django deploymentdocker exec easypj-dev python manage.py check --deployValidates settings for production readiness
4Create Django superuserdocker exec -it easypj-dev python manage.py createsuperuserNeeds -it because createsuperuser prompts for password
5View environment variablesdocker exec easypj-dev env | sortShows all env vars the container sees (including Dockerfile ENV)
6Check installed packagesdocker exec easypj-dev pip freezeLists all Python packages and versions inside the container
7Test database connectivitydocker exec easypj-dev python -c "import psycopg2; print('OK')"Quick connectivity check without running the full app
8Clear Django cachedocker exec easypj-dev python manage.py clear_cacheClears app cache without restarting the container
9View running processesdocker exec easypj-dev ps auxShows all processes inside the container (alternative to docker top)
10Run as specific userdocker exec -u root easypj-dev apt updateTemporarily runs as root (use sparingly — breaks security model)
11Django ORM shell (live queries)docker exec -it easypj-dev python manage.py shellNeeds -it for the interactive prompt; queries the REAL PostgreSQL, no separate connection needed
⚠️ Golden Rule: Don't Modify Running Containers

Use docker exec for read-only inspection and debugging — not for making permanent changes. An ordinary docker restart won't erase an exec'd change (6.2's writable layer survives that untouched); the real trap is that the change lives ONLY in this one container's writable layer while the image on disk never changed. The instant this container is replaced instead of merely restarted — a fresh docker run, a redeploy, scaling out to a second replica — the replacement boots from the unmodified image and the fix is gone without a trace. Update your Dockerfile and rebuild instead. Containers are immutable — treat them that way; only the IMAGE should ever carry the source of truth.

💡 exec's Exit Code Is the Real Command's Exit Code

docker exec passes the exit code of whatever it ran straight back out to your shell — it never swallows it. That's what makes it trustworthy in a CI pipeline: docker exec easypj-dev python manage.py check --deploy run as a build step fails the pipeline HONESTLY the instant Django's own check command returns non-zero, with no wrapper script needed to translate "the command failed" into "the build failed." The same is true of Row 3's deployment check and Row 2's migration above — a non-zero exit from either one propagates all the way out of docker exec itself.

⚠️ docker exec vs docker attach — Not the Same Door

docker attach easypj-web connects your terminal directly to PID 1's OWN stdin/stdout/stderr streams — it doesn't start anything new, it plugs you into the exact process that's already running. That sounds convenient, but it's a trap for debugging: hitting Ctrl+C sends SIGINT straight to PID 1 and can kill the very container you were trying to inspect, and if two people attach to the same container they see (and can type into) the SAME session. docker exec -it easypj-web bash is almost always the right tool instead — it opens an independent second process (Drill 6.4 proves it with real PIDs), so Ctrl+C and exit only affect your exec'd shell, PID 1 keeps running undisturbed, and any number of engineers can exec in side by side without colliding. Reach for attach only when you deliberately need PID 1's own console — e.g. watching an interactive TUI app that was started with docker run -it — and detach without killing it using the escape sequence Ctrl+P Ctrl+Q (not Ctrl+C).

6.5 Copying Files To/From Containers

docker cp copies files between your host and a container — useful for extracting logs, backups, or injecting config files. It streams a tar through the daemon API — no network, no SSH — and it works even on a STOPPED container.

🚪 Analogy — A Prison Visitation Slot

docker cp is a prison visitation slot: you can pass a single document in or out through the tray, but you would never try to run the entire mailroom through it. Regular, recurring traffic deserves a proper door — that door is a bind mount or named volume (Part 6). Use the slot for what it's for: a one-off backup, a one-off fixture, a one-off debug pull — never an ongoing sync.

TERMINAL
# ─── SCENARIO 1: Extract a pg_dump SQL backup from a container ───
$ docker cp easypj-dev:/tmp/backup.sql ./backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).sql

# ─── SCENARIO 2: Inject updated settings ───
$ docker cp ./new-settings.py easypj-dev:/app/easypj/settings.py
$ docker restart easypj-dev  # Restart to pick up new settings

# ─── SCENARIO 3: Backup entire static files directory ───
$ docker cp easypj-dev:/app/static ./static-backup/

# ─── SCENARIO 4: Extract logs from a crashed container ───
$ docker cp crashed-container:/var/log/app/error.log ./debug-error.log

# ─── SCENARIO 5: Seed database from host ───
$ docker cp ./fixtures.json easypj-dev:/tmp/
$ docker exec easypj-dev python manage.py loaddata /tmp/fixtures.json

# ─── SCENARIO 6: Pull a file out WITH its original ownership intact ───
$ docker cp -a easypj-dev:/app/uploads/user-avatar.png ./restore/
# -a (--archive) preserves the container's own UID:GID instead of
# stamping the file with whoever ran this docker cp command
📖 docker cp vs Volumes

docker cp is a one-time, manual file transfer. For ongoing file sharing (development, config files, persistent data), use bind mounts (-v /host/path:/container/path) or named volumes (-v myvolume:/container/path). These sync automatically — no need to manually cp each time you change a file. docker cp is best for one-off operations: backups, debugging, injecting configs.

⚠️ Who Owns the File After docker cp Pulls It Out?

Files copied OUT of a container land on the host owned by the UID:GID of whoever ran the docker cp command — not automatically root, and not automatically the container's own UID. Run it as your normal user and backup-20260710.sql is yours to read and edit; run the identical command under sudo and that same file comes out root-owned, which is the usual reason a follow-up script gets a confusing "permission denied" on a file it just created. When scripting Practice Drill 6.5's backup, decide UP FRONT which user runs the cp — don't let it be whatever the CI runner happened to default to. Need the ORIGINAL ownership instead — e.g. restoring a user-uploaded file where the in-container UID actually matters — add -a (--archive, Scenario 6 above) to preserve the container's own UID:GID on the way out instead of stamping the host user's. A second, unrelated cp flag worth knowing: -L (--follow-link) copies the TARGET of a symlink at the source path instead of the symlink itself — without it, copying a symlinked config file often lands you a broken link on the other side rather than the file's actual contents.

6.6 Container Resource Limits

Without limits, one container can consume all available CPU and RAM — the "noisy neighbor" problem. Unlimited is Docker's own default: guarding against it is entirely OPT-IN, never opt-out, which is exactly why resource limits are essential for production deployments rather than a rare special case.

FlagPurposeExample
--memory or -mRAM limit — HARD cap; a breach gets OOM-killed (6 MB minimum)--memory=512m (512 MB)
--memory-reservationRAM SOFT limit — only kicks in when the host is actually under memory pressure, and never kills--memory=512m --memory-reservation=256m
--memory-swapTotal memory + swap limit--memory=512m --memory-swap=1g
--cpusCPU limit (fractional OK)--cpus=1.5 (1.5 cores)
--cpu-sharesCPU relative weight (default 1024)--cpu-shares=512 (half priority)
--pids-limitMax number of processes--pids-limit=100
--blkio-weightBlock I/O relative weight--blkio-weight=500
📖 --memory Is a HARD Cap; --memory-reservation Is a SOFT One

--memory is the ceiling from the diagram below — cross it and the kernel OOM-kills the container, no negotiation. --memory-reservation sets a lower, SOFT target that Docker only starts enforcing once the host itself is genuinely low on memory; below that pressure point a container can freely burst above its reservation (right up to its hard --memory ceiling) with zero penalty. Pairing both — e.g. --memory=512m --memory-reservation=256m — lets easypj-web use extra headroom during a traffic spike but still yields memory back first if the whole host gets tight, before any hard OOM-kill is ever on the table.

🏨 Analogy — A Hotel's Electricity vs Its Gym

Think of a hotel: the room's electricity has a breaker (memory) — trip it and the lights go out completely, no warning shots. The shared gym has a booking cap (CPU) — you simply wait your turn; nobody gets thrown out of the building. That's the whole memory-vs-CPU asymmetry in one picture: a memory breach is a hard, permanent trip; a CPU breach is a queue.

Same Cap, Two Different Fates Over Time — easypj hits its limits
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         easypj hits --memory 512m: two fates over time         │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ MEMORY  --memory 512m                                          │
  │  128MB ─▶ 256MB ─▶ 384MB ─▶ 504MB ─▶ 512MB ✖ OOM-KILL          │
  │  t=0      t=30s    t=60s    t=90s    t=120s  exit 137          │
  │                                                                │
  │ CPU  --cpus 1.5                                                │
  │  40%   ─▶ 90%   ─▶ 150%(cap)─▶ THROTTLED ─▶ THROTTLED          │
  │  t=0      t=10s     t=20s        t=30s        t=40s+           │
  │                                           (slow, alive)        │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ memory breach KILLS the process; CPU breach just WAITS         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 --memory-swap Is NOT Independent

Omit --memory-swap and Docker quietly defaults it to 2× your --memory value — handing the process swap space to thrash around in for a while BEFORE the OOM killer above ever fires, which turns a clean, fast kill into a slow, disk-thrashing stall. Set both flags to the SAME value (e.g. --memory=512m --memory-swap=512m) to disable swap for the container entirely and get the clean 137 exit in the diagram above.

📖 easypj in Practice — Sizing the Cap

gunicorn running 3 workers at roughly 90 MB each fits comfortably inside --memory 512m with headroom to spare. Capping it means a memory-leaking view now kills only ONE container — which --restart unless-stopped then resurrects automatically — instead of a leak slowly starving the entire host, PostgreSQL included.

TERMINAL — docker update: change limits on a LIVE container
# Bump the memory cap on easypj-web without touching the writable layer
$ docker update --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g easypj-web

# Tighten the CPU cap on a noisy neighbor, live, no downtime
$ docker update --cpus=0.5 easypj-web

# docker update also edits the restart policy (see 6.1)
$ docker update --restart unless-stopped easypj-web
💡 Every --memory/--cpus/--restart Flag Above Is Also a docker update Flag

Everything in this section's table so far describes limits set at docker run time — but every one of those cgroup values (--memory, --memory-swap, --cpus, --cpu-shares, --pids-limit, --blkio-weight) plus --restart can also be changed on a container that's ALREADY running, via docker update — no rm, no fresh run, no lost writable layer, and (for CPU/memory) no restart of the process inside either. This is the tool for "production is under memory pressure right now" — raise the cap in one command while gunicorn keeps serving requests, then fix the Dockerfile/deploy script afterward so the next rollout starts with the corrected value. The one thing docker update can NOT do is change -p port mappings or -v mounts — those are fixed at create time and genuinely require a new container.

6.7 Health Checks & Logs in Daily Operations

A HEALTHCHECK is the container's own liveness probe, baked into the image. Without one, docker ps's STATUS column only means "PID 1 is alive" — it can still be broken. With one, STATUS shows Up (healthy), Up (unhealthy), or Up (health: starting).

HEALTHCHECK for easypj — Dockerfile lines
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
            --start-period=15s \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/healthz/ || exit 1

The daemon runs the HEALTHCHECK command INSIDE the container on the interval; 3 straight failures flip STATUS to (unhealthy) and emit a health_status event — Docker alone does NOT restart unhealthy containers (Compose/Swarm act on it in Parts 4/10; Kubernetes takes the same idea much further with dedicated liveness, readiness AND startup probes — a separate CKA/CKAD-track topic, but built on this exact same "ask the app a question, don't just check the pulse" foundation). start-period shields slow Django startup (4.7's migrations!) from false alarms.

OptionDefault if omittedWhat it controls
--interval30sTime between probe runs once the container is past its start period
--timeout30sA single probe run longer than this counts as a FAILURE, not a hang
--retries3Consecutive failures required before STATUS flips to (unhealthy)
--start-period0sFailures during this window don't count toward --retries at all
--start-interval5sHow often to probe DURING the start period specifically (Docker Engine 25.0+) — lets a slow-booting easypj be declared healthy fast without shortening the safety margin for genuinely broken startups

easypj's example above only bothers overriding --timeout (3s, since /healthz/ should answer almost instantly) and --start-period (15s, for migrations) — --interval=30s and --retries=3 are actually just restating Docker's own defaults for clarity.

💡 A Pulse vs a Conversation

docker ps without HEALTHCHECK checks the pulse (PID 1 exists); the health command asks the patient a question every 30 seconds and writes the answer on the chart — the (healthy) tag in ps. A /healthz/ Django view that runs SELECT 1 against PostgreSQL means "healthy" covers app AND database connectivity — deadlocked gunicorn workers surface in minutes, not from user complaints.

📖 The Probe's Own Exit Code Drives Everything

The CMD in a HEALTHCHECK is graded on its own exit code, same as any shell command: 0 means healthy, 1 means unhealthy, and 2 is reserved by Docker itself and should never be returned deliberately. That's the whole reason the example ends in || exit 1 — curl -fsS already exits non-zero on any HTTP error or connection failure, but explicitly forcing exit code 1 keeps the probe's contract unambiguous no matter what curl's own exit code happens to be.

⚠️ curl Must Exist in the Image

The probe binary (e.g. curl) must actually exist in the image — slim bases often lack it by default. A missing binary fails every probe and marks a perfectly good easypj (unhealthy). Verify with docker events --filter event=health_status — the unhealthy transition appears in both ps and events, your first real-time daemon feed.

📖 Log Discipline Is Part of "Daily Operations" Too

The other half of this section's title: stdout/stderr is the ONLY place PID 1 should ever log to — never a file inside the container — and rotation for whatever the daemon captures from those streams is a one-time, host-wide setting in daemon.json (§2.7), not something any individual docker run flag controls. A HEALTHCHECK that's green and a docker logs that's silent are two independent signals — a healthy process can still be logging nothing useful, which is exactly why 6.3's triage order checks logs before ever reaching for inspect.

Under the Hood — signals, cgroups, the OOM killer and exec's namespace trick, all kernel primitives

Every command in this chapter is a thin CLI wrapper over the same two kernel mechanisms Part 1 introduced: NAMESPACES and CGROUPS. docker stop sends SIGTERM into the container's PID namespace, targeting PID 1 specifically, then dockerd runs a grace timer (-t, default 10s) before escalating to SIGKILL. docker kill skips the grace period and sends SIGKILL immediately. docker pause uses the cgroup FREEZER controller — it suspends every process in the container mid-instruction at the scheduler level, with no signal delivered at all, which is why a paused process cannot even catch SIGTERM. --memory and --cpus are literally cgroup controller settings (memory.max and cpu.max under cgroup v2); when memory.max is exceeded, the KERNEL's own OOM killer — not Docker — terminates the process, which is why the exit code is the generic 137 (128 + SIGKILL's signal number 9).

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ docker stop  → SIGTERM → PID 1 (namespace) → grace timer (10s) │
  │                                            → SIGKILL if ignored│
  │ docker kill  → SIGKILL immediately, no grace period             │
  │ docker pause → cgroup freezer → frozen mid-instruction, no sig │
  │ --memory 512m → cgroup memory.max → kernel OOM killer → 137    │
  │ --cpus 1.5    → cgroup cpu.max → CFS throttling, never killed  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 Nothing in this chapter is Docker-specific magic — dockerd is orchestrating namespaces and cgroups the kernel already provides, which is exactly why docker stats and docker inspect can read the same numbers the kernel is enforcing.
① Signals really are signals — the syscall path from docker stop to a dead PID 1

dockerd never calls kill(2) itself. docker stop is an API call that hops from dockerd to containerd (gRPC), then to the per-container containerd-shim-runc-v2 process — one shim stays alive for the ENTIRE life of a container specifically to relay signals and reap its zombies — which finally issues the real kill(2) syscall against the container's PID 1. That PID 1 is not some fictional in-container-only number: namespaces only change what a process can SEE, not what can signal it, so it is simultaneously a perfectly ordinary PID on the HOST. The one genuine wrinkle is that Linux gives PID 1 of any PID namespace special treatment — it silently IGNORES any signal for which it has not installed an explicit handler (SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are the only two exceptions), even signals like SIGTERM that would normally just kill a process outright. An app that never calls signal(SIGTERM, …) is therefore functionally deaf to docker stop until the grace timer expires and SIGKILL — which cannot be caught, ever — finishes the job.

  docker stop easypj-web
       │  (1) HTTP call over /var/run/docker.sock
       ▼
  dockerd ──(2) gRPC──▶ containerd ──(3) ttrpc──▶ containerd-shim-runc-v2
                                                    (one per container, lives the
                                                     whole time — shepherds PID 1,
                                                     relays every future signal)
                                                          │ (4) kill(2)
                                                          ▼
                                    real HOST pid e.g. 48213
                                    == PID 1 inside the container's PID namespace
                                          │
                             has a SIGTERM handler? ──NO──▶ signal silently ignored
                                          │ YES                  (PID-1 kernel rule)
                                          ▼                        │
                                just shuts down                10s grace timer (dockerd)
                                                                    │ still alive?
                                                                    ▼
                                                          shim sends SIGKILL (uncatchable)

  docker kill easypj-web  → same path, skips the grace timer, SIGKILL immediately
  docker pause easypj-web → shim never sends ANY signal — jumps straight to ② instead
PID 1 setupReaction to docker stop's SIGTERMReaction to docker kill's SIGKILL
App installs its own handler (gunicorn does)Handler runs → graceful shutdown inside the 10s windowDies instantly, no cleanup — SIGKILL can't be caught
App installs NO handler, runs directly as PID 1Kernel silently ignores it — the container "hangs" the full 10s doing nothing, then SIGKILL lands anywayDies instantly
Launched with docker run --init (injects tini as real PID 1)tini forwards SIGTERM to the app AND reaps zombie processes the app itself never waited onDies instantly (tini included)
🔑 --init is the fix for BOTH problems in one flag — a lesser-known docker run option belonging right next to 6.1's flag reference. It doesn't touch your Dockerfile's CMD/ENTRYPOINT at all; it just inserts a 4 KB tini binary as the REAL PID 1, which forwards signals to your app (fixing the deaf-PID-1 problem above) and reaps orphaned zombie processes your app never wait()'s on — the second problem no signal handler alone can solve.
② cgroups v2 unified hierarchy — where --memory, --cpus and --pids-limit actually live

6.6's resource flags are not enforced by Docker code running some kind of watchdog loop — they are single numbers written into plain text files inside the kernel's cgroup v2 filesystem, and the KERNEL itself does all the enforcing from that point on. Every container gets its own cgroup directory the moment it's created; docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 --pids-limit=100 is really three echo-style writes into that directory, and docker stats reading "live" numbers is really the daemon re-reading the SAME files on an interval — no top, no free, no shell-out at all.

  /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<64-char-container-id>.scope/
       (systemd cgroup driver — the default on most modern distros;
        the cgroupfs driver instead uses the flatter /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/<id>/)
       │
       ├── memory.max      ← docker run --memory=512m   writes "536870912" (bytes) here
       ├── memory.current   ← docker stats' MEM USAGE column reads this, live, every poll
       ├── memory.swap.max  ← --memory-swap (6.6) writes here
       ├── cpu.max          ← docker run --cpus=1.5      writes "150000 100000" here (④)
       ├── cpu.stat         ← nr_periods / nr_throttled / throttled_usec counters (④)
       ├── pids.max         ← docker run --pids-limit=100 writes "100" here
       ├── pids.current      ← live process count inside the cgroup right now
       └── cgroup.freeze     ← docker pause writes "1" here — see the freezer note below
docker run flagcgroup v2 file it writesWhat lands in it
--memory=512mmemory.max536870912 (bytes) — the hard cap the kernel OOM-kills on (③)
--memory-swap=1gmemory.swap.maxswap ceiling on top of memory.max — omit it and Docker defaults it to 2× the memory value
--cpus=1.5cpu.max"150000 100000" — quota/period pair, decoded in ④
--pids-limit=100pids.max100 — a fork-bomb inside the container hits EAGAIN, not the host
🔑 This is what makes 6.6's docker update --memory=1g easypj-web instant and restart-free: it is nothing more than overwriting memory.max in this SAME directory while PID 1 keeps running untouched — there is no container-side code to reconfigure, because the container's own process was never aware a limit existed in the first place. It's also what docker pause (①) actually flips: cgroup.freeze is a cgroup v2 file, not a signal — writing 1 tells the kernel scheduler to stop giving every process in this cgroup CPU time at all, which is why a paused process can't even catch SIGTERM: nothing is being delivered, it is simply never scheduled to run.
③ The OOM killer — why a memory breach is always exit code 137, and two DIFFERENT killers that can cause it

6.3's crash-evidence box calls exit 137 "OOM-killed or a manual docker kill" for a reason: both paths end in the exact same SIGKILL, and 137 is simply 128 + 9 (the POSIX convention for "killed by signal N"), so the number alone can't distinguish them — only docker inspect's .State.OOMKilled boolean can. What "OOM-killed" hides is that there are genuinely TWO different killers that can produce it. When ②'s memory.max is breached, the kernel runs a cgroup-scoped OOM kill that considers ONLY processes inside that one cgroup — this is what a normal --memory breach triggers, and it can never touch a process outside the container. Separately, if the WHOLE HOST runs low on memory (regardless of any container's own limit), the kernel's global OOM killer scans EVERY process on the box and picks a victim using a "badness" score based on RSS pages, adjusted by each process's oom_score_adj — a value docker run --oom-score-adj lets you tune directly, per container.

  PATH 1 — a single container exceeds ITS OWN --memory cap:
    memory.current climbs → hits memory.max → cgroup-scoped OOM kill fires
       → scans ONLY this cgroup's processes → picks the biggest → SIGKILL → exit 137
       → .State.OOMKilled = true

  PATH 2 — the WHOLE HOST is low on memory (uncapped containers, or the host itself):
    global available memory → critically low → system-wide OOM killer fires
       → scans EVERY process on the box, scored by RSS + oom_score_adj
       → --oom-score-adj tunes THIS container's odds of being picked, host-wide
       → victim gets SIGKILL → exit 137 too → but .State.OOMKilled reflects
         whichever container's process the global killer actually chose

  Either path → same signal (SIGKILL=9) → same exit code (128+9=137)
  → the ONLY way to tell them apart after the fact is .State.OOMKilled + dmesg
TriggerScope of the OOM scanWhat decides the victim
Cgroup-scoped (this container's memory.max)only processes inside THIS container's cgrouplargest resident-memory process in that cgroup
System-wide (host itself is critically low)every process on the whole host, across every container and cgroupRSS-based badness score, adjusted by oom_score_adj — --oom-score-adj tunes it
🔑 Practical upshot for 6.6's "size the cap" advice: setting a tight --memory on every container doesn't just protect the HOST from one runaway process — it also converts an unpredictable, host-wide, any-process-could-die PATH 2 event into a predictable, contained, PATH 1 event that only ever kills the one offending container. That containment is the entire reason 6.6 recommends capping every production container, not just the historically leaky ones.
④ CFS bandwidth throttling — how --cpus=1.5 becomes the two numbers inside cpu.max

The Completely Fair Scheduler's bandwidth controller enforces --cpus using two numbers written to ②'s cpu.max: a period (Docker always uses the kernel default, 100000 microseconds = 100ms) and a quota — the total CPU time, summed across ALL cores, the cgroup may consume within one period. --cpus=1.5 means "1.5 cores' worth," so Docker writes quota = 1.5 × 100000 = 150000, giving cpu.max = "150000 100000". Every 100ms the kernel refills the cgroup's bucket to 150ms of runnable time; the instant that bucket empties — because processes could burn it FASTER than real time passes, e.g. 150ms used up in only 60ms of wall-clock if running across 3 busy cores — every thread in the cgroup is pulled off the run queue and THROTTLED (not killed, not paused, just refused CPU time) until the next period resets the bucket.

  --cpus=1.5  →  cpu.max = "150000 100000"   (quota, period — both in microseconds)

  one 100ms period, cgroup running hot across 3 host cores at once:
    t=0ms  ───────────────────────────────────────────────▶ t=100ms
    │←────────── 60ms of wall-clock burns the full 150ms quota ──────►│
    │            (3 cores × 50ms each = 150ms of CPU-seconds spent)   │
    │                                                        ▲        │
    │                                            quota EXHAUSTED here │
    │◄───────────── remaining ~40ms: THROTTLED, 0% CPU ────────────►│
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    next period (t=100ms) → bucket refills to 150000 → cycle repeats

  cpu.stat (readable live, even from INSIDE the container — see callout):
    nr_periods      42918     total 100ms windows observed
    nr_throttled     6104     how many of those windows hit the wall
    throttled_usec  891234    total microseconds spent throttled, all-time
--cpus valuecpu.max quota (period fixed at 100000)Meaning
--cpus=0.550000 100000half of one core's worth, summed across however many cores it actually uses
--cpus=1100000 100000exactly one full core's worth of time per period
--cpus=1.5150000 1000006.6's example — 150ms of CPU-seconds per 100ms window, however it's split across cores
🔑 This is the exact mechanism behind 6.6's diagram — "150%(cap) → THROTTLED → THROTTLED, slow, alive." docker stats shows CPU% capped at the quota's ceiling, but never shows THROTTLING itself; to prove a slow app is throttled rather than just idle, read nr_throttled directly — because containers get their own cgroup NAMESPACE by default, docker exec easypj-web cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat transparently shows THIS container's own counters from the inside, no host access needed.
⑤ docker exec vs docker run — joining namespaces with setns(), not creating new ones

Drill 6.4 asks you to prove exec never touches PID 1 — here is exactly why it can't. docker run builds a container by calling clone(2)/unshare(2) with a stack of CLONE_NEW* flags — CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWUTS, CLONE_NEWIPC — which allocates entirely FRESH namespaces and makes the new process PID 1 inside the new PID namespace. docker exec does the opposite: it opens the file descriptors at /proc/<PID-1>/ns/* for the ALREADY-RUNNING container and calls setns(2) against each one, which makes the NEW process JOIN those exact same existing namespaces rather than creating its own. Inside the shared PID namespace, the kernel simply hands out the next free PID — 2, 3, 4… — so an exec'd process can NEVER become PID 1; that identity, and the PID-1-specific signal-ignoring behaviour from ①, belongs to the original process alone.

  docker run easypj:v1                         docker exec -it easypj-web bash
  ────────────────────                         ────────────────────────────────
  clone(2) / unshare(2) with                   open /proc/<PID1>/ns/{pid,net,mnt,
    CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNET |                 uts,ipc,cgroup} for the RUNNING
    CLONE_NEWNS  | CLONE_NEWUTS |                 container's PID 1
    CLONE_NEWIPC                                       │
       │                                          setns(2) against EACH fd
       ▼                                                │
  BRAND NEW, empty namespaces                           ▼
       │                                          JOINS the SAME namespaces —
       ▼                                          nothing new is created at all
  process becomes PID 1                                 │
  inside its own fresh                                   ▼
  PID namespace                                   kernel hands out next free PID
                                                    (2, 3, 4…) — CAN'T be PID 1
  → new writable layer, new cgroup              → SAME writable layer, SAME cgroup
                                                    (6.6's --memory/--cpus caps
                                                     apply to this process too)
Aspectdocker rundocker exec
Namespace callclone(2)/unshare(2) — creates newsetns(2) — joins existing
Becomes PID 1?Yes, alwaysNever — gets the next free PID inside the shared namespace
Cgroup (②)New cgroup created for the containerPlaced into the SAME cgroup — subject to the SAME --memory/--cpus caps
Ctrl+C behaviourSIGINT hits whatever PID 1 is doingSIGINT hits only the exec'd process — PID 1 is undisturbed
🔑 This is also why 6.4's warning box draws such a sharp line between exec and attach: attach doesn't create ANY new process at all — it connects your terminal's stdio straight to PID 1's own streams — while exec's setns() path always spins up a genuinely separate process sitting beside PID 1. That's the mechanical reason an exec'd shell's exit only kills your shell, while attach's Ctrl+C can take the whole container down with it.
⑥ HEALTHCHECK's real engine, and why docker cp is the one command in this chapter that skips exec entirely

6.7's HEALTHCHECK doesn't run as some separate daemon process watching from outside — dockerd keeps one lightweight "health monitor" goroutine per container, and on each --interval tick it runs the PROBE command through the EXACT SAME setns() exec path as ⑤, just triggered by a timer instead of a human typing docker exec. The probe's exit code is appended to a short rolling history; only after --retries CONSECUTIVE failures does the daemon flip .State.Health.Status and publish a health_status event onto dockerd's internal event bus — the same bus every docker events client subscribes to, over the identical Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) every other command in this chapter already uses, just kept open as a long-lived stream instead of one request/response. docker cp (6.5) is built completely differently, and deliberately skips exec: for a RUNNING container it resolves the requested path through /proc/<PID-1>/root/ — a "magic symlink" the kernel maintains straight into that process's own mount namespace — and for a STOPPED one (no living PID to borrow a symlink from) it instead asks the overlay2 storage driver to mount the layer stack directly. Either way it tars the result and streams it over the SAME socket. No exec, no new process inside the container at all — which is exactly why, alone among every command in this chapter, docker cp works on a container that isn't running.

  HEALTHCHECK path (6.7):                       docker cp path (6.5):
  ─────────────────────                         ─────────────────────
  --interval timer fires                        running container?
       │                                              │
       ▼                                         YES ─┴─ NO
  setns() exec the CMD                            │        │
  inside the container (⑤)                        ▼        ▼
       │                                    /proc/<PID1>/  overlay2 driver
       ▼                                    root/ (magic    mounts the layer
  exit code → rolling                       symlink into    stack directly —
  history window                            its mountns)    no process needed
       │                                              │        │
  --retries straight failures?                        └───┬────┘
       │ YES                                              ▼
       ▼                                            tar the requested path
  flip .State.Health.Status                                │
  + publish "health_status"                                ▼
  event on dockerd's event bus                    stream over /var/run/docker.sock
       │                                                    (same socket, no network,
       ▼                                                     works even when STOPPED)
  docker events (long-lived
  stream over the SAME socket)
MechanismUses setns() exec (⑤)?Works on a STOPPED container?Crosses the network?
HEALTHCHECK probe✅ yes, on a timer❌ no — needs a live PID 1 to join❌ never — local Unix socket only
docker exec✅ yes, on demand❌ no❌ never
docker cp❌ no — reads the filesystem directly✅ yes — the whole reason it's the exception❌ never
docker eventsn/a — subscribes to the event busn/a — reports on ALL containers❌ never — same local socket
🔑 Every single command explored across this whole chapter — stop/kill/pause (①), stats/update (②), the OOM path (③), throttling (④), exec (⑤), and now HEALTHCHECK — funnels through the SAME two primitives: the container's namespaces/cgroup on one side, and dockerd's local Unix socket API on the other. docker cp is the one deliberate exception, and knowing exactly WHY (no exec needed, just a filesystem read) is what tells you it's also the one command in this entire chapter you can trust against a container that has already exited.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • -it/-d/--rm decide HOW a container attaches and cleans up after itself; --restart decides whether it comes back after dying.
  • create/start/stop/pause/kill/rm walk the same state machine — only rm destroys the writable layer.
  • Triage order: ps (is it up?) → logs (what did it say?) → stats/top (is it healthy right now?) → inspect (full JSON truth) — cheap checks first, full dump last.
  • exec adds an extra process inside an EXISTING container's namespaces; it never starts a new container and never disturbs PID 1.
  • docker cp streams a tar over the API in either direction, even into stopped containers — it moves bytes, not deployed state.
  • A --memory breach KILLS the process (exit 137, OOMKilled:true); a --cpus breach only THROTTLES it — the app stays alive but slow.
  • HEALTHCHECK upgrades "Up" from "PID 1 exists" to "the app actually answered"; docker events broadcasts every transition.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: this vocabulary underlies Orchestration, Networking and Security scenario questions — it isn't graded on its own, but every one of those domains assumes you already know it cold.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • --restart always respects a manual stop → It resurrects containers you stopped manually the moment the daemon restarts — prefer unless-stopped to keep control.
  • Exit code 137 always means OOM-kill → It has two unrelated causes (OOM-kill or a manual docker kill) — only .State.OOMKilled in inspect tells them apart.
  • docker logs shows everything the app logs → It shows ONLY stdout/stderr from PID 1 — an app that writes its own log file inside the container is invisible to it.
  • You can exec into a crashed container → exec requires a RUNNING container; you cannot exec into a crashed one — read docker logs instead.
  • docker stop always shuts down within a couple seconds → If it times out EVERY time and always needs the full grace period before SIGKILL, PID 1 is ignoring SIGTERM — almost always a shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT from Chapter 4.3, where the shell (not your app) is PID 1 and never forwards the signal.
  • docker cp into a running container is a safe way to patch code → It changes files behind the app's back — copied code is not deployed code, and the change vanishes the instant the container is replaced. Rebuild the image instead.
  • A HEALTHCHECK failing means the app itself is broken → It can just as easily mean the probe binary (e.g. curl) doesn't exist in the image — slim bases often lack it, and a missing binary fails EVERY probe and marks a perfectly good container (unhealthy).
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Default every long-lived service to --restart unless-stopped — the one policy that respects a manual stop AND survives host reboots.
  • Keep a docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}" alias for a legible one-line dashboard.
  • Make docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' your first move on any exit-137 mystery.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 6)

start, triage & cap a production container 
# Prod start
docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env \
    --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1

# Every container
docker ps -a

# Tail + follow
docker logs --tail 100 -f easypj-web

# Shell in
docker exec -it easypj-web bash

# One-shot snapshot
docker stats --no-stream easypj-web

# Why did it die
docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' easypj-web

# Capped start
docker run -d --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 easypj:v1

# Live health feed
docker events --filter event=health_status
live updates, filtering & cleanup 
# Change limits/restart policy on a container that's already running
docker update --memory=1g --cpus=2 --restart unless-stopped easypj-web

# Rename in place, block for an exit code, sweep the graveyard
docker rename easypj-canary easypj-web
docker wait easypj-dev
docker container prune -f

# Find the sick one without reading every STATUS column by eye
docker ps --filter health=unhealthy

🧠 Chapter 6 — DCA Practice Questions (18)

Quick recall of container operations — 18 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What's the difference between docker run and docker start?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run creates a NEW container from an image and starts it. docker start starts an EXISTING stopped container. Run = create + start. Start = start only.

CommandCreates new container?Starts it?Use when
docker run✅ Yes✅ YesFirst time launching from an image
docker start❌ No✅ YesRestarting an existing stopped container
EXPLANATION

docker run is actually docker create + docker start combined. Each docker run creates a UNIQUE container — even from the same image. Running docker run nginx twice creates two separate containers.

Q2
How do you run a container in the background and automatically remove it when it exits?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -d --rm --name temp easypj:v1. -d detaches, --rm auto-removes on exit. Perfect for one-off tasks and CI pipelines.

EXPLANATION

Without --rm, stopped containers accumulate and consume disk space. In CI/CD, this can fill up build agents quickly.

  docker run -d --rm --name temp easypj:v1
                │        │
                │        └─ container exits ──▶ AUTO-REMOVED (no docker ps -a entry)
                └─ runs detached, in the background

  without --rm:  container exits ──▶ stays in "Exited" state ──▶ manual docker rm needed
Q3
What's the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, 10s default grace period), then SIGKILL if still running. docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately — no cleanup, no grace period.

CommandSignalGrace periodApp can clean up?
docker stopSIGTERM → SIGKILL10s (default)✅ Yes
docker killSIGKILL immediatelyNone❌ No
EXPLANATION

SIGTERM allows the app to gracefully shut down (close database connections, finish in-flight requests, clean up temp files). Always use stop for production; use kill only when the container is frozen.

Q4
How do you see the logs of a container that's running in detached mode?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs easypj-dev. Add -f to follow (stream), --tail 100 for last 100 lines, --since 10m for last 10 minutes.

FlagEffect
-fFollow — stream new lines live
--tail 100Show only the last 100 lines
--since 10mShow only logs from the last 10 minutes
--timestampsPrefix each line with when it was logged
EXPLANATION

Logs are stdout/stderr from the container's PID 1. They persist even after the container stops. Use docker logs --timestamps to see when each line was logged.

Q5
How do you get an interactive bash shell inside a running container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec -it easypj-dev bash. -i keeps STDIN open, -t allocates a TTY. Without both, you won't get a proper shell.

EXPLANATION

-i (interactive) = you can type. -t (TTY) = proper terminal formatting (colors, cursor positioning, tab completion).

FlagMeaningMissing it
-iKeep STDIN open (interactive)Can't type input into the shell
-tAllocate a pseudo-TTYNo prompt, colors, or tab completion
Q6
What restart policy would you use for a production web server that should ALWAYS be running?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--restart unless-stopped. It restarts the container if it crashes, and survives Docker daemon restarts. It only stays stopped if YOU manually stop it.

EXPLANATION

The four policies: no (default, never restart), on-failure (only on non-zero exit — and per Docker's own docs it explicitly does NOT restart a container purely because the daemon restarted, only on an actual failing exit), always (restarts on crash/reboot, and even a manual stop is only respected until the NEXT daemon restart — annoying for maintenance), unless-stopped (same as always, but a manual stop stays stopped through future daemon restarts too — best for production).

PolicyRestarts on crash?Survives daemon restart?Stays down after manual stop?
no (default)❌❌✅
on-failure✅ (non-zero exit only)❌ — a container already exited when the daemon restarts stays down; only always/unless-stopped bring one back purely BECAUSE the daemon restarted✅
always✅✅❌ — only until the NEXT daemon restart, then it reappears
unless-stopped✅✅✅ — the production pick
Q7
How do you limit a container to 512 MB of RAM and 1.5 CPU cores?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 easypj:v1. Without limits, the container can use ALL host resources.

EXPLANATION

Resource limits are enforced via Linux cgroups. If a container exceeds --memory, it gets OOM-killed. --cpus throttles CPU time. For production, always set limits to prevent the "noisy neighbor" problem.

  docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 easypj:v1
                 │                │
                 │                └─ cgroup CPU quota  ──▶ throttled once 1.5 cores are used
                 └─ cgroup memory cap ──▶ OOM-killed (exit 137) if exceeded
Q8
How do you copy a file from a container to your host?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker cp easypj-dev:/app/backup.sql ./backup.sql. The syntax is docker cp CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH (or vice versa).

  docker cp easypj-dev:/app/backup.sql  ./backup.sql     # container ➜ host
  docker cp ./config.yml  easypj-dev:/app/config.yml     # host ➜ container (reversed)
EXPLANATION

docker cp works whether the container is running or stopped. It's a one-time copy, not a sync. For ongoing file sharing, use volumes or bind mounts instead.

Q9
What command shows real-time CPU, memory, and network usage for all running containers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stats. Shows live CPU %, memory usage/limit, network I/O, block I/O, and PIDs for each container. Like top but for containers.

ColumnMeaning
CPU %Current CPU usage
MEM USAGE / LIMITMemory used vs. the --memory cap
NET I/ONetwork bytes in / out
BLOCK I/ODisk bytes read / written
PIDSNumber of processes inside the container
EXPLANATION

docker stats --no-stream gives a one-shot snapshot (useful for scripting). docker stats --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}" customizes the output.

Q10
A container exited immediately. How do you debug what happened?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. docker ps -a — find the exited container. 2. docker logs <container-id> — see what it printed before crashing. 3. docker inspect <container-id> — check exit code, mounts, env vars.

EXPLANATION

Exit code 0 = normal exit, 1 = application error, 137 = SIGKILL (OOM or manual kill), 139 = SIGSEGV (segfault). Also check: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Error}}' <id> for daemon-level errors.

Exit codeMeaning
0Normal exit
1Application error
137SIGKILL (OOM-killed or manual docker kill)
139SIGSEGV (segfault)
Q11
What's the difference between -p and -P, and which is safer for a reproducible production config?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-p host:container maps an EXACT host port to a container port. -P auto-publishes every EXPOSEd port to a RANDOM host port instead. -p is safer for production because the port is known and stable ahead of time.

FlagPort chosenReproducible?Typical use
-p 8000:8000Exact, you specify it✅ YesProduction, docs, firewall rules, reverse proxies
-PRandom, Docker picks it❌ NoQuick local testing, avoiding port collisions
EXPLANATION

6.1 pairs -p 8000:8000 with easypj's canonical production start line for exactly this reason — a random port is fine for a five-minute local test, but breaks any downstream config, reverse proxy, or firewall rule that expects a stable, known port.

Q12
Walk the lifecycle state machine: what does each of create/start/pause/stop/kill/rm do, and which ONE destroys the writable layer?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

create allocates the container and its writable layer without starting it; start launches PID 1; pause freezes every process via the cgroup freezer (no signal at all); stop sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after a grace period; kill sends SIGKILL immediately; rm deletes the container AND its writable layer — the only one of the six that's destructive to data.

CommandWhat it doesDestroys the writable layer?
createAllocates container + writable layer, doesn't start it❌ No
startLaunches PID 1❌ No
pause/unpauseFreezes/thaws via cgroup freezer — no signal delivered❌ No
stopSIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period❌ No
killSIGKILL immediately❌ No
rmDeletes the container + its writable layer✅ Yes — the only destructive one
EXPLANATION

docker restart reuses the SAME writable layer — it's just stop+start back to back; only rm actually erases it. That's exactly what Practice Drill 6.2 proves by leaving a marker file through a restart and then losing it after rm.

Q13
A container "looks fine" but users report errors. What's the correct triage order, and why that order specifically?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ps (confirm it's actually Up) → logs (read what PID 1 said) → stats/top (check live resource pressure) → inspect (pull the full JSON state as a last resort).

OrderCommandAnswersCost
1docker psIs it actually Up?Cheapest — one line
2docker logsWhat did PID 1 just print?Cheap — reads existing output
3docker stats / topLive CPU/RAM pressure, process countModerate — live sampling
4docker inspectFull JSON state (exit code, mounts, env)Most expensive — last resort
EXPLANATION

Cheap, read-only checks come first; the full JSON dump is for when the cheap checks didn't explain it. This is also why this chapter's DCA Relevance box calls out triage order twice — it's the single most exam-transferable habit in this chapter, reused verbatim inside Orchestration and Networking scenario questions.

Q14
What is fundamentally different about what docker exec starts, compared to what docker run starts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

exec starts an ADDITIONAL process inside an EXISTING container's namespaces, leaving PID 1 completely untouched; run always creates a brand-new container with its own fresh namespaces and its own new PID 1.

Aspectdocker rundocker exec
NamespacesCreates brand-new onesJoins the SAME existing ones
Becomes PID 1?Yes, alwaysNever — gets the next free PID
Writable layerNew, empty oneSame one the container already has
Effect of Ctrl+CCan hit PID 1 (whole container)Only kills the exec'd process
EXPLANATION

This is "stepping into the kitchen to taste the sauce," never "building a second kitchen" — Practice Drill 6.4 proves it with real PIDs, and Under the Hood ⑤ shows the exact setns() syscall that makes it structurally impossible for exec to ever become PID 1.

Q15
Why is docker cp the wrong tool for deploying a code fix, and what's the correct alternative?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker cp changes files inside a running container's writable layer behind the app's back — copied code is not deployed code, and the moment this container is replaced (a fresh docker run, a redeploy, scaling to a second replica) the replacement boots from the unmodified image and the fix vanishes without a trace. The correct fix is updating the Dockerfile and rebuilding the image.

  docker cp fix.py  easypj-web:/app/fix.py
                │
                └─ writable layer ONLY ──▶ container replaced/redeployed ──▶ FIX LOST, no trace

  correct fix:  edit Dockerfile ──▶ docker build ──▶ new IMAGE ──▶ docker run ──▶ survives every replacement
EXPLANATION

docker cp is for ad-hoc, one-off transfers — backups, fixtures, log extraction — never a deployment mechanism. Containers are meant to be immutable and disposable ("cattle, not pets," 6.2); only the IMAGE should ever carry the source of truth, which is exactly the discipline Chapter 9 builds a whole pipeline around.

Q16
A container exits with code 137. What TWO unrelated events could cause this, and which single field tells them apart?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An out-of-memory kill by the kernel, OR a manual docker kill — both end in the exact same SIGKILL, and 137 is simply 128 + 9 either way. docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' is the single field that disambiguates them: true means the kernel's OOM killer fired; false means something else — almost always a manual docker kill — sent the SIGKILL.

FieldManual docker killKernel OOM-kill
Exit code137137 — identical, no help here
.State.OOMKilledfalsetrue
TriggerSomeone/something ran docker kill--memory cap exceeded
EXPLANATION

Practice Drill 6.6 demonstrates OOMKilled:true paired with exit code 137 side by side, and Under the Hood ③ goes one level deeper still — there are actually TWO different OOM killers that can produce this exact signature (a cgroup-scoped one triggered by this container's own --memory cap, and a system-wide one triggered by the whole host running low), and only .State.OOMKilled plus dmesg can tell which of the underlying causes actually fired.

Q17
Table the four core resource-limit flags with what happens on breach.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
FlagCapsOn breach
--memory 512mRAM, including page cacheOOM-kill (exit 137)
--memory-swap 512mRAM + swap combinedNo swap escape once matched to --memory
--cpus 1.5CPU time (CFS quota)Throttled — stays alive, just slower
--pids-limit 200Process count inside the containerFork fails (EAGAIN) — nothing already running is killed
EXPLANATION

Memory breaches kill; CPU breaches merely slow the app down; a --pids-limit breach doesn't kill or slow anything already running — it just refuses to let the container fork any MORE processes, which is exactly what stops a fork bomb inside a container from ever reaching the host. Never confuse these three very different failure modes.

Q18
What are the three states docker ps can show for a HEALTHCHECK-enabled container, and what moves it between them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(health: starting) → (healthy) or (unhealthy). --start-period shields early probe failures from counting toward --retries at all; once that window closes, the daemon runs the HEALTHCHECK command on the configured --interval, and --retries consecutive failures flip the state to (unhealthy), publishing a health_status event.

  docker run (HEALTHCHECK set)
        │
        ▼
  (health: starting) ──── --start-period: probe failures don't count yet ────┐
        │                                                                    │
        │ --interval elapses, probe runs                                    │
        ▼                                                                    │
  --retries consecutive successes ──▶ (healthy) ◀── probe recovers ─────────┘
        │
        │ --retries consecutive failures
        ▼
  (unhealthy) ──▶ publishes a health_status event
EXPLANATION

Practice Drill 6.7 watches this exact transition live in both docker ps and docker events — the same underlying fact (the daemon's internal health monitor flipping .State.Health.Status) surfacing in two different places: a one-shot snapshot, and a live subscription.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.1 — Prove the Restart Asymmetry

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Start easypj with --restart unless-stopped, docker kill it and confirm it restarts on its own, then docker stop it and confirm it stays down. Verify: name the ONE flag responsible for that asymmetry.

Hint: Both kill and stop end the container's process — the difference is entirely in what happens AFTER it dies, not in how it dies.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker run -d --name easypj-web --restart unless-stopped -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1

docker kill easypj-web
sleep 3
docker ps --filter name=easypj-web
# easypj-web   Up 2 seconds   → dockerd auto-restarted it, unprompted

docker stop easypj-web
sleep 3
docker ps -a --filter name=easypj-web
# easypj-web   Exited (0) 3 seconds ago   → stays down, no auto-restart
Commanddockerd sees it asRestart policy reacts?
docker killAn unexpected death (crash-like)✅ Yes — restarts it
docker stopA deliberate, user-requested stop❌ No — unless-stopped means exactly that

Check yourself: the ONE flag is --restart unless-stopped itself — it restarts the container after ANY death EXCEPT one caused by an explicit docker stop. That's the asymmetry: kill looks like a crash to dockerd, so the policy fires; stop is the policy's own "stay down" signal.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.2 — Find the Writable Layer's Exact Lifespan

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Run docker exec easypj-web touch /tmp/marker, then docker restart easypj-web and check whether /tmp/marker is still there. Then docker rm -f easypj-web, run a fresh container with the SAME name and image, and check again. Verify: the marker survives the restart but dies with rm — prove the writable layer's exact lifespan with your own hands, not just the Key Takeaways bullet.

Hint: restart is stop+start against the SAME container ID; rm deletes that ID and its writable layer entirely — a fresh docker run afterward is a brand-new container, even with an identical name and image.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker exec easypj-web touch /tmp/marker
docker restart easypj-web
docker exec easypj-web ls /tmp/marker
# /tmp/marker  — SURVIVES: same container ID, same writable layer

docker rm -f easypj-web
docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
docker exec easypj-web ls /tmp/marker
# ls: cannot access '/tmp/marker': No such file or directory
# — GONE: rm deleted the old writable layer; this is a fresh container

Check yourself: the marker survives restart because restart never touches the writable layer — it's the same container ID coming back up. It's gone after rm + a fresh run because that's a brand-new container with its OWN empty writable layer, regardless of sharing a name and image with the one you just deleted. This is exactly why "cattle, not pets" works: the replacement looks identical from the outside but starts with a clean slate.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.3 — Thirty-Second Triage, No Guessing

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

On a running easypj-web container, run ps, logs, stats --no-stream, top, and inspect — in that exact order. Verify: without guessing once, you can state its uptime, the last request it served, its current RAM usage, its worker/process count, and its exit code if it has one.

Hint: Cheap-to-expensive means ps answers "is it up," logs answers "what did it just say," stats/top answer "how is it doing right now," and only inspect gives you the full JSON truth — resist jumping straight to inspect.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
# easypj-web   Up 2 hours (healthy)   0.0.0.0:8000->8000/tcp   → uptime answered

docker logs --tail 5 easypj-web
# [2026-07-02 09:14:02] "GET /jobs/ HTTP/1.1" 200   → last request answered

docker stats --no-stream easypj-web
# CPU 3.2%   MEM 210MiB / 512MiB   → RAM usage answered

docker top easypj-web
# 4 gunicorn processes listed   → worker count answered

docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' easypj-web
# 0 false   → not exited, no OOM — full JSON truth confirms the rest

Check yourself: each command answered exactly one question and nothing more — that's the point of triage order. If ps alone had shown "Restarting" or "Exited," you'd have skipped straight to logs and never needed stats/top/inspect at all; cheap checks first means you often never pay for the expensive one.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.4 — Prove exec Never Touches PID 1

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

docker exec -it easypj-web bash, run ps aux inside that shell, then exit, then run docker ps from the host. Verify: gunicorn was PID 1 the whole time your bash shell was a high-numbered PID alongside it, and exiting bash left the container still Up — proving exec added a process rather than replacing one.

Hint: Look at the PID column, not just the process names — PID 1 belongs to whatever the image's CMD/ENTRYPOINT started, and your exec'd bash will always land at a much higher number.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker exec -it easypj-web bash
root@easypj-web:/app# ps aux
# PID   USER   COMMAND
#   1   app    gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application
#  47   root   bash          <- this exec'd shell, a high PID, PID 1 untouched
root@easypj-web:/app# exit

docker ps
# easypj-web   Up 2 hours (healthy)   → still Up, exec never restarted anything

Check yourself: gunicorn held PID 1 before, during, and after the exec session — your bash shell was always a second, independent process inside the SAME namespaces, never a replacement. Exiting bash only ends that one extra process; the container's actual PID 1 (and every in-flight request it's serving) is completely unaffected. That's the entire "kitchen door" analogy proven with real PIDs.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.5 — A Real Backup, Landed on the Host

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Take a real PostgreSQL dump from inside a running easypj-db container, then docker cp it out to your host. Verify: head -3 backups/easypj.sql shows real SQL DDL sitting on the HOST filesystem — your data now survives anything Docker itself does to the container.

Hint: docker exec runs the dump INSIDE the container (that's where pg_dump and the database both live); docker cp only moves the resulting file OUT — two different tools for two different jobs.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker exec easypj-db pg_dump -U easypj -f /tmp/easypj.sql easypj
docker cp easypj-db:/tmp/easypj.sql ./backups/

head -3 backups/easypj.sql
-- PostgreSQL database dump
-- Dumped from database version 16.x
-- Dumped by pg_dump version 16.x

Check yourself: the dump itself happens entirely INSIDE the container's namespace via docker exec — pg_dump only exists there, next to the running PostgreSQL. docker cp's only job is streaming that one finished file across the container boundary onto your host disk. If easypj-db is destroyed a second later, the backup on your host is still perfectly intact — proof that cp moved real bytes, not a live reference.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.6 — Force an OOM-Kill on Purpose

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Run docker run -d --name probe --memory 64m easypj:v1 — deliberately far too small for Django/gunicorn to start in. Verify: it exits fast, and docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' probe prints true 137. Clean up with docker rm probe.

Hint: 64 MB is well under what even gunicorn's own startup needs, before a single Django worker is spawned — you're forcing the kernel OOM killer to fire almost immediately, not waiting for a slow leak.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker run -d --name probe --memory 64m easypj:v1
docker ps -a --filter name=probe
# probe   Exited (137) 2 seconds ago

docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' probe
# true 137

docker rm probe

Check yourself: OOMKilled: true paired with exit code 137 is the unambiguous kernel OOM signature — this is the ONE field that tells a memory-cap kill apart from a manual docker kill, which also exits 137 but leaves OOMKilled: false. Bump --memory up to 512m and rerun to confirm the same image starts cleanly — proof the limit itself, not the image, was the cause.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.7 — Watch STATUS Move From Starting to Healthy, Then Break It On Purpose

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Rebuild easypj with the HEALTHCHECK from this section, run it, and watch docker ps move from (health: starting) to (healthy). Then break the /healthz/ view on purpose (rename the URL, or stop the database) and run docker events --filter event=health_status in a second terminal. Verify: the transition to (unhealthy) appears in BOTH docker ps AND docker events — your first real-time daemon feed, proven with your own eyes.

Hint: The --start-period=15s window means failures in the first 15 seconds never count toward the 3 --retries — don't panic if STATUS still says (health: starting) a few seconds in, that's the safety margin working as designed, not a bug.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# Terminal 1 — watch the transition live
docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
watch -n2 'docker ps --filter name=easypj-web --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"'
# easypj-web   Up 3 seconds (health: starting)
# ... 15s later ...
# easypj-web   Up 18 seconds (healthy)

# Terminal 2 — subscribe to the daemon's own event feed
docker events --filter event=health_status

# Now break it on purpose (e.g. stop the DB the /healthz/ view queries)
docker stop easypj-db

# Terminal 1, ~90s later (3 retries × 30s interval):
# easypj-web   Up 3 minutes (unhealthy)
# Terminal 2, same moment:
# 2026-07-10T14:22:07Z container health_status: unhealthy  easypj-web

Check yourself: both terminals report the SAME transition at the SAME moment, because they're reading the SAME underlying fact — the daemon's internal health-monitor flipping .State.Health.Status after 3 consecutive probe failures. docker ps is a one-shot snapshot of that state; docker events is a live subscription to every change to it, which is exactly why alerting tooling watches events instead of polling ps in a loop.
