In one line: Chapter 6 is the operator's manual for the image Chapters 4 and 5 taught you to build: start it the right way, move it through its lifecycle deliberately, observe it cheaply before diving into JSON, reach inside it without restarting it, cap what it can consume, and give it a real health signal instead of a bare pulse.

The takeaway: every command here operates on a container that already exists — Part 3 goes back to make the IMAGE it started from smaller and safer.

🛠️ Part 2 · Recap · Complete

Docker Hands-On — Write It, Build It, Run It

You started able to only describe a container in theory; now you can write a Dockerfile from memory, explain exactly what docker build does to it before a single instruction runs, and take a container through its full operational lifecycle without guessing. Recipe, mechanics, operator's manual — Part 2 is the hands-on core the rest of the guide assumes is automatic.

🔑 Part 2 — Key Takeaways

  • A Dockerfile is a declarative recipe: FROM/RUN/COPY/ADD create layers, everything else writes metadata only; CMD and ENTRYPOINT together decide what becomes PID 1, and multi-stage builds keep heavy build tools out of the shipped image (Ch 4).
  • The build context sets the ceiling before a single instruction runs: it's tarred and sent to the daemon first, so .dockerignore controls both speed and leak risk; the cache key is parent-layer + instruction text + checksums, and buildx/bake scale one recipe across every architecture (Ch 5).
  • A running container is a lifecycle, not a single state: create → start → pause → stop → kill → rm, with exec adding a process to an existing container (never a new one) and --memory/--cpus enforcing hard-kill vs soft-throttle caps via the same cgroups the kernel already provides (Ch 6).
  • 🎯 Exam: Dockerfile authoring, build mechanics, and container lifecycle commands are the hands-on backbone the DCA's image-management and troubleshooting questions draw from.
  • 🔑 docker build · docker history · docker run · docker exec · docker inspect · docker stats
📌 Part 2 Visual Summary — recipe → build mechanics → running, operated container
   📝 Dockerfile (FROM/COPY/RUN=layers, ENV/EXPOSE=metadata)                    (Ch 4: the recipe)
          │ CMD/ENTRYPOINT decide PID 1
          ▼
   🧱 docker build ── context[tar, minus .dockerignore] ──▶ cache-key match?    (Ch 5: the mechanics)
          │ ARG dies at build end · ENV bakes in forever
          ▼
   📀 easypj:v1 image ── buildx --platform ──▶ manifest list (multi-arch)
          │
   🚀 docker run (-it/-d/--rm, --restart) ──▶ 📦 RUNNING container              (Ch 6: the operator's manual)
          │ lifecycle: create→start→pause→stop→kill→rm
          ├─ exec = extra process, same namespaces   cp = bytes in/out
          ├─ ps→logs→stats→inspect (cheap checks first, full JSON last)
          └─ --memory/--cpus caps · HEALTHCHECK ──▶ docker events
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   one Dockerfile, built once, run and operated with full command of its lifecycle. 🐋

In words: Chapter 4 gives you the recipe — a Dockerfile whose instructions either create a layer or write metadata, with CMD/ENTRYPOINT deciding what process actually becomes PID 1. Chapter 5 opens up the mechanics underneath the one command that turns that recipe into an image: the build context is tarred and sent before anything runs, a cache key of parent-layer + instruction text + checksums decides what gets rebuilt, and buildx stretches the same Dockerfile across every CPU architecture.

Chapter 6 is the operator's manual for what comes out the other end: docker run starts a container that then moves through a real lifecycle (create → start → pause → stop → kill → rm), exec reaches inside it without disturbing PID 1, cheap checks (ps, logs, stats) come before the full inspect dump, and --memory/--cpus cap what it's allowed to consume.

The one idea to keep: writing, building, and running are three separate skills with three separate failure modes — a bad Dockerfile, a bad build context, and a mismanaged running container all look different when they break. Part 2 gives you a clean mental model for each, so Part 3 can focus purely on making the image itself smaller and safer.

Chapter 7 · Image Management — docker image Commands

Now that you can build and run containers, let's master the complete image lifecycle: listing, tagging, pushing, pulling, saving, loading, and cleaning up. These are your day-to-day Docker operations. Builds multiply fast — within a week of normal iteration you can own fifty images, a dozen <none> ghosts, and a suspiciously full disk. This chapter is image custody: the answer to "which of these easypj images is actually production, why did /var/lib/docker quietly grow to 40 GB, and how do I ship an image to a server with no internet connection at all?"

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📦 Images 🎯 DCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ List and filter local images by name, dangling state, or reference pattern, and format output for scripts
  • ✅ Explain why one IMAGE ID can carry many tags, and re-tag easypj for release, latest, and registry-prefixed names
  • ✅ Log in, push, and pull easypj to/from a registry, and pin a deploy to a digest instead of a movable tag
  • ✅ Choose save/load over export/import for moving a full image offline, and state exactly what export loses
  • ✅ Run the cleanup ladder (prune → prune -a → system prune -a --volumes) and read docker system df before doing it
  • ✅ Read docker history to rank an image's fattest layers and docker inspect to audit its Env/User/digest

Image Creation, Management & Registry 20%
🎯 This Chapter IS the "Registry" Half of the Domain

Chapter 7 IS the "Registry" half of the 20%-weighted Image Creation, Management & Registry domain — expect exam items on tagging, push/pull, and removal semantics.

  • A tag is a free-to-create, free-to-delete pointer; the IMAGE ID (and the bytes behind it) is the only real identity.
  • push/pull move manifests + missing layers; the printed DIGEST is the deploy-safe identifier — tags can move, digests can't.
  • The cleanup ladder is ordered by blast radius: prune (dangling only) → prune -a (all unused) → system prune -a --volumes (everything).

7.1 Listing & Filtering Images

docker images (or docker image ls) shows all images on your system. With filters and formatting, you can find exactly what you need.

📋 Analogy — A Warehouse Manifest

Treat the local image store like a warehouse manifest: a --filter is a clipboard query ("aisle easypj*", "show me the unlabeled boxes"), --format picks which columns the printout shows, and -q prints barcode stickers only — just the IDs, nothing else — which is exactly what feeds docker rmi $(docker images -f dangling=true -q), this chapter's Speed Tip for clearing every ghost in one line.

🔬 easypj in Practice — Why the Ghosts Keep Appearing

Every rebuild of easypj:v1 with the same tag demotes the PREVIOUS build to <none>:<none> — the tag moved, the old bytes didn't disappear, they just lost their name. Iterate on a Dockerfile for a single afternoon and you can easily accumulate a dozen of these dangling ghosts. docker images --filter "dangling=true" is how you find them here in 7.1; docker image prune deletes them in 7.5 — this section only lists them.

TERMINAL
# List all images
$ docker images
REPOSITORY    TAG          IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
easypj        v1.0         abc123def456   2 hours ago    180MB
easypj        latest       abc123def456   2 hours ago    180MB
python        3.11-slim    xyz789ghi012   3 days ago     150MB
nginx         alpine       def456jkl345   5 days ago     42MB

# List with newer syntax (same output)
$ docker image ls

# Filter: show only dangling images (untagged, <none>:<none>)
$ docker images --filter "dangling=true"

# Filter: show images matching a pattern
$ docker images --filter "reference=easypj*"
$ docker images --filter "reference=python:*"

# Filter: show images created before/after a date
$ docker images --filter "before=easypj:v1.0"

# Format output (Go templates)
$ docker images --format "table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}"
$ docker images --format "{{.ID}}: {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} ({{.Size}})"

# Show only image IDs (useful for scripting)
$ docker images -q
abc123def456
xyz789ghi012
🕵️ Does -a Actually Show More Images?

docker images -a (or docker image ls --all) is documented as "show all images (default hides intermediate images)" — but on a modern BuildKit-powered Docker (the default builder since Docker 23.0), it usually prints the exact same rows as a bare docker images. BuildKit never commits each Dockerfile instruction as its own tagged intermediate image the way the legacy (pre-BuildKit) builder did; its layer cache lives in a separate store you inspect with docker system df's Build Cache row or clear with docker builder prune (7.5) — not with docker images -a. If a study guide claims -a reveals hidden "intermediate build layers," it's describing the classic builder, not the BuildKit default most DCA candidates actually run today.

7.2 Tagging Images Properly

A tag is a human-readable label pointing to a specific image. One image can have multiple tags. Understanding this is key for registry pushes and version management.

🪪 Analogy — Name Badges, Not a New Person

One IMAGE ID is one person; each tag is a name badge — a work alias, a nickname, a passport name for crossing a registry's border. docker tag hands out another badge; it never clones the person. Shredding a badge (docker rmi by name) never harms the person underneath — only running out of badges does.

🔬 easypj in Practice — The Release Ritual

A real release does two tags in a row: docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest && docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1 — one build, three names, each with a different job (the version pin, the convenience default, and the push destination). The registry prefix in that third name isn't decorative: it's what docker push in 7.3 reads to know WHERE to send the bytes.

TERMINAL
# Tag an existing image
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 easypj:latest
# Both tags now point to the SAME Image ID!

# Tag for a specific registry
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/easypj:v1.0

# Tag with multiple labels
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 easypj:stable
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 easypj:2026-06-12
$ docker tag easypj:v1.0 easypj:abc1234  # git commit SHA

# See all tags for an image
$ docker images easypj
REPOSITORY  TAG           IMAGE ID       CREATED
easypj      v1.0          abc123def456   2 hours ago
easypj      latest        abc123def456   2 hours ago
easypj      stable        abc123def456   2 hours ago
# All same IMAGE ID — they're the SAME image!
One Image ID → Multiple Tags
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🏷️ TAGS POINT TO IMAGE IDs                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │                        ┌─────────────────┐                              │
  │      easypj:v1.0 ─────▶│                 │                              │
  │      easypj:latest ───▶│  IMAGE ID:      │                              │
  │      easypj:stable ───▶│  abc123def456   │                              │
  │      easypj:20260612──▶│                 │                              │
  │                        └─────────────────┘                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  docker rmi easypj:v1.0  → removes the TAG only (image stays!)          │
  │  docker rmi abc123def456  → removes the IMAGE (all tags gone!)          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔡 Why docker build -t MyApp . Fails but easypj:MyTag Doesn't

An image reference splits into a REPOSITORY part and a TAG part, and only one of them is case-sensitive-hostile. The repository (everything left of the last :) may only contain lowercase letters, digits, and the separators . _ - — never leading/trailing, never doubled up carelessly. Try docker build -t MyApp . or docker tag easypj:v1 EasyPJ:v1 and Docker refuses instantly with invalid reference format: repository name must be lowercase, before a single layer is touched. The tag (right of that colon) plays by different, looser rules: letters of either case, digits, . _ -, up to 128 characters, just not starting with a . or -. So easypj:V2.0-RC1 is completely valid Docker syntax — the uppercase is fine there, it's only the part before the colon that's case-locked.

Reference partCase ruleFails examplePasses example
Repository (before :)lowercase ONLYdocker tag easypj:v1 EasyPJ:v1docker tag easypj:v1 easypj-prod:v1
Tag (after :)upper OR lowercaseeasypj:.v1 (leading dot)easypj:V2.0-RC1

7.3 Pushing & Pulling Images

Images flow between your local machine and registries via push and pull. This is how you share images with your team and deploy to servers.

✉️ Analogy — Registered Mail, Not a Guess

A push is registered mail: the layers are parcels the post office may already partly hold (dedup — identical layers already on the registry are skipped, see 2.3), the manifest is the delivery slip, and the printed DIGEST is the tracking number. Quote the tracking number in a dispute, not "the brown box" — a tag (:latest) can be reused for a different parcel tomorrow; a digest can't.

🔬 easypj in Practice — CI Pushes, Deploy Pulls by Digest

A CI pipeline pushes ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1, records the digest Docker prints on push (e.g. sha256:4be2...), and the deploy step pulls by that digest — docker pull ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:4be2... — so what was tested is byte-for-byte what runs, immune to anyone re-tagging :v1.1 in between. Docker Hub names omit the registry entirely (you/easypj:v1.1 implies docker.io); every other registry needs the full prefix, which is also what docker login must target.

TERMINAL
# Login to a registry first
$ docker login                              # Docker Hub (default)
$ docker login ghcr.io                      # GitHub Container Registry
$ docker login registry.example.com         # Self-hosted registry
# (AWS ECR uses a different auth method — see below)

# Push an image
$ docker push easypj:v1.0                  # Push to Docker Hub
$ docker push ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0 # Push to GitHub
# Sample output — note the DIGEST, not the tag, is the deploy-safe ID:
# 9d3a1b2c: Pushed   f2c1e4d5: Layer already exists   (dedup, see 2.3)
# v1.0: digest: sha256:a7c9e21f... size: 1786

# Push all tags for an image
$ docker push -a easypj                     # Pushes ALL tags of "easypj"

# Pull an image
$ docker pull python:3.11-slim
$ docker pull ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0

# AWS ECR login (special — uses AWS CLI)
$ aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
  123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
# That token is temporary — it expires after 12 hours, so CI pipelines
# re-run this exact login step at the start of every single job.
Push/Pull Flow Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        📤 PUSH / 📥 PULL FLOW                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │    YOUR MACHINE                          REGISTRY                        │
  │  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────┐               │
  │  │              │    docker push     │                  │               │
  │  │  easypj:v1.0 │──────────────────▶│  easypj:v1.0     │               │
  │  │  (local)     │                    │  (remote copy)   │               │
  │  │              │◀──────────────────│                  │               │
  │  │              │    docker pull     │                  │               │
  │  └──────────────┘                    └──────────────────┘               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Registry Types:                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Docker Hub       │ GHCR (GitHub)     │ AWS ECR                      │  │
  │  │ docker.io/…      │ ghcr.io/…         │ aws_account_id.dkr.ecr.…    │  │
  │  │ Public + Private  │ GitHub integrated  │ IAM auth (temporary token)  │  │
  │  │ docker login      │ docker login ghcr  │ aws ecr get-login-password  │  │
  │  └─────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  docker tag easypj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0  ← registry prefix │
  │  docker push ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔒 You Can Pin a Tag AND a Digest at Once

The full image reference grammar is name[:tag][@digest] — tag and digest aren't mutually exclusive. docker pull ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1@sha256:4be2a1c9... is valid syntax: the :v1.1 stays purely for a human-readable log line, while @sha256:... is what Docker actually resolves and verifies against. That's the best-of-both form for a deploy manifest that needs to stay readable in a CI log or kubectl describe output AND stay byte-pinned — a readable name with an immutable resolution, in one string.

📊 The Exact Numbers Behind 1.5's Rate-Limit Warning

1.5 already flagged that Docker Hub throttles pulls — here are the current figures worth knowing cold: an unauthenticated pull is capped at 100 pulls per 6 hours, measured per IPv4 address (or per IPv6 /64 subnet) — brutal for a shared office network or a CI runner that never authenticates. A free, authenticated Personal Docker Hub account (nothing paid — just the docker login already shown above) doubles that ceiling to 200 pulls per 6 hours; Pro, Team, and Business subscriptions remove the pull-rate limit entirely. Hit the ceiling and Docker Hub returns HTTP 429 with toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit — the fix is almost always the docker login this section already teaches, not a retry loop.

7.4 Saving & Loading Images (Offline Transfer)

When you can't use a registry (air-gapped environments, USB transfer), docker save and docker load let you move images as tar files.

CommandWhat It DoesUse Case
docker save -o file.tar image:tagExports image + layers + tags as a tar archiveTransfer to another machine
docker load -i file.tarImports an image from a tar archiveReceive from another machine
docker export -o file.tar containerExports container FILESYSTEM (flat, no layers/history)Create a "snapshot" of container state
docker import file.tar image:tagCreates an image from a flat filesystemImport from export (no layers!)
⚠️ Critical: save vs export

docker save preserves layers, tags, and history. docker export creates a FLAT filesystem — all layers are merged, tags and history are lost. Always use save/load for image transfer.

Offline Transfer Flow — save → USB → load, across the air-gap
   ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
   │ easypj:v1.1    │   │ docker save    │   │ USB stick      │   │ gunzip -c |    │
   │ image          │──▶│ | gzip         │──▶│ air-gap,       │──▶│ docker load    │
   │ (ONLINE host)  │   │ -> .tar.gz     │   │ hand-carry     │   │ (OFFLINE host) │
   └────────────────┘   └────────────────┘   └────────────────┘   └────────────────┘
      layers + tags + CMD all survive the whole trip — export/import would not.
🖨️ Analogy — Printing Plates vs. a Photocopy

docker save ships the printing plates: reprint the exact edition anytime, every layer and every metadata field intact. docker export photocopies one printed book — readable, but the plates, the edition history, and the cover (CMD/ENV/EXPOSE) are all gone. An imported photocopy doesn't even know how to open itself.

🔬 easypj in Practice — Air-Gap via USB

docker save easypj:v1.1 | gzip > easypj-v1.1.tar.gz — piping straight into gzip (instead of saving, then compressing separately) skips a multi-GB intermediate file and typically shrinks the tarball by roughly 40%. Carry it over on a USB stick, then on the offline host: gunzip -c easypj-v1.1.tar.gz | docker load. Layers, tags, and CMD all arrive untouched — docker inspect on the loaded image still shows CMD ["gunicorn", ...]; the same round trip through export/import would leave Cmd: null and a container that exits instantly on docker run.

7.5 Removing Images & Cleanup

Docker images accumulate quickly. Regular cleanup prevents running out of disk space — especially important on CI/CD build agents.

🧹 Analogy — Cleaning a Garage

docker system df is the inventory walk — see what's actually in the garage before touching anything. docker image prune tosses the unlabeled boxes (dangling images). docker image prune -a tosses everything not bolted to a car (any image no running container references). docker system prune -a --volumes sells the garage — nothing survives that isn't currently in use. Each rung is cheaper to regret than the next; never jump straight to the last one.

🔬 easypj in Practice — A Week of Iteration

A week of rebuilding easypj:v1 typically leaves about a dozen dangling images behind. docker image prune frees the gigabytes they cost — but it can never touch easypj:v1.1 while a container like easypj-web is still running from it; that live reference is what protects a tagged image from every rung of the ladder except -f. docker rmi itself refuses to remove an image referenced by ANY container, even a stopped (Exited) one — remove the container first.

TERMINAL
# Remove a specific image (by tag or ID)
$ docker rmi easypj:v1.0
$ docker rmi abc123def456          # Remove by IMAGE ID
$ docker rmi -f abc123def456       # Force remove (even if in use)
$ docker image rm easypj:v1.0      # "docker image rm" = "docker rmi", same command, different noun

# Remove dangling images (<none>:<none>)
$ docker image prune
# WARNING! This will remove all dangling images.
# Are you sure? [y/N] y
# Deleted: sha256:abc...
# Total reclaimed space: 1.2 GB

# Remove ALL unused images (not referenced by any container)
$ docker image prune -a

# Surgical instead of blanket -a: only touch images idle 24h+, or
# spare anything explicitly labeled to survive — CI-safe cleanup rungs
$ docker image prune -a --filter "until=24h"
$ docker image prune -a --filter "label!=keep=true"

# Remove unused BUILD CACHE too (separate accounting from images)
$ docker builder prune

# Check disk usage
$ docker system df
TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          15        8         3.2 GB    1.8 GB (56%)
Containers      6         2         150 MB    120 MB (80%)
Local Volumes   4         2         500 MB    200 MB (40%)

# Nuclear option: remove EVERYTHING unused
$ docker system prune -a --volumes
# Removes: all stopped containers, unused networks,
#          dangling images, unused build cache, ALL unused volumes
📥 The Hidden Cost of prune -a: Re-Pulls, Not Errors

docker image prune -a doesn't just free space — it removes every image with zero containers currently pointing at it, tagged or not. The next time anything needs one of those images — a fresh docker run, a restarted stack, a scaled-up replica — Docker has to re-pull it from the registry from scratch, because the local copy is simply gone. That's not a bug, it's the entire point of the -a widening (plain prune would have left it alone), but on a slow link or against a rate-limited registry, an over-eager prune -a run right before you need to scale up can turn a two-second docker run into a multi-minute wait — plan the "-a" rung for a quiet moment, not mid-incident.

7.6 Image History & Inspection

Understanding what's INSIDE your images is critical for debugging and optimization.

🪨 Analogy — Core Sample vs. Lab Report

docker history is a geological core sample — every layer's thickness on display, oldest at the bottom. docker inspect is the lab report on that same rock: composition (Env, Cmd, User), provenance (RepoDigests), fingerprint (the Config digest). Read the core sample to find what's heavy; read the lab report to find what's hidden.

🔬 easypj in Practice — Audit Before You Trust

Before basing anything on a community image you didn't build, run docker history on it first — a surprise curl … | sh layer or an unexplained 400 MB RUN step is visible in seconds, before that image ever runs on your machine. docker history --no-trunc shows the full, untruncated command string for every layer.

TERMINAL
# Show image layers (each with size and command)
$ docker image history easypj:v1.0
IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                           SIZE
abc123def456   2 hours ago    CMD ["gunicorn" "easypj.wsgi:app"]   0B
<missing>      2 hours ago    COPY . /app/                         500kB
<missing>      2 hours ago    RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  80MB
<missing>      2 hours ago    COPY requirements.txt .              200B
<missing>      3 days ago     /bin/sh -c #(nop) WORKDIR /app       0B
<missing>      3 days ago     /bin/sh -c #(nop) CMD ["python3"]    0B
<missing>      3 days ago     /bin/sh -c set -ex; ...              150MB

# Detailed JSON metadata
$ docker image inspect easypj:v1.0
# Returns: ID, Created, Architecture, OS, Layers, Env, CMD, Entrypoint,
#          Volumes, WorkingDir, Labels, and more...

# Extract specific fields with --format (Go template)
$ docker image inspect -f '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}' easypj:v1.0
linux/amd64

$ docker image inspect -f '{{range .RootFS.Layers}}{{println .}}{{end}}' easypj:v1.0
sha256:abc...
sha256:def...
🔑 Image ID vs Digest — Critical Distinction

Image ID is the (truncated) sha256 of the image's own CONFIG blob (e.g., abc123def456) — pull the exact same image on two machines and the Image ID matches exactly, but two INDEPENDENT docker build runs of "the same" Dockerfile usually produce different Image IDs anyway, since build timestamps and other config metadata differ even when the resulting files don't. Digest is the sha256 a registry hands back on push/pull (e.g., sha256:abc123...) — content-addressable and IDENTICAL everywhere, regardless of who's asking. Always reference images by digest for guaranteed reproducibility: python:3.11-slim@sha256:abc.... Tags are mutable, digests are immutable.

🔐 Docker Content Trust (DCT) — Image Signing (Legacy)

Docker Content Trust uses Notary to sign images, ensuring the image you pull is exactly what the publisher intended — not tampered with in transit. Enable with export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. When enabled: docker pull only succeeds if the image is signed by a trusted publisher. docker push automatically signs images. ⚠️ Status check (2026): Docker has announced DCT's underlying Notary v1 service (notary.docker.io) is being retired — shutting down December 8, 2026, so treat DCT as legacy plumbing, not the current recommendation. The DCA exam's Security domain has historically listed DCT by name, so know the mechanics above for exam purposes — but for a real supply-chain-security answer today, reach for BuildKit build attestations (--sbom/--provenance, generated in the in-toto format and inspectable without pulling the whole image) and Docker Scout's SBOM + CVE scanning (8.5, 21.1) instead.

Under the Hood — how the local image store actually stores things

Every image is really three things glued together by digests, never by name: a MANIFEST (lists layer digests + the config digest), a CONFIG (the JSON docker inspect prints — Env, Cmd, User...), and the LAYERS themselves (each a tarball, content-addressed by its own sha256). Tags are just human labels in a small local index — ⑤ below names the exact file (it's keyed by Image ID, not a manifest digest) and confirms it's ALL docker tag ever edits. docker rmi deletes an index entry; the layer BYTES only leave disk when the last image referencing them, across every tag, is gone — which is why ten easypj tags sharing one FROM python:3.11-slim layer cost that layer's bytes exactly ONCE.

   ┌────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────┐
   │ TAG (name)      │────▶│ MANIFEST         │────▶│ LAYERS (sha256)   │
   │ easypj:v1.1     │     │ digest sha256:.. │     │ shared across ALL │
   │ just a pointer  │     │ + CONFIG digest  │     │ tags that need    │
   │ in local index  │     │ (env/cmd/user)   │     │ that exact layer  │
   └────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └───────────────────┘
🔑 Retagging rewrites the left box only; deleting an image walks right-to-left and only frees a layer when NOTHING points at it.
① OverlayFS on disk — what a "layer" really is inside /var/lib/docker/overlay2/

The diagram above says "LAYERS (sha256)" as if they were abstract — on a real Linux host running the (default) overlay2 storage driver, every layer is one ordinary directory: /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<cache-id>/diff, holding ONLY the files that ONE Dockerfile instruction added, changed, or whited-out. Nothing merges those directories until something needs to actually SEE a full filesystem — the union view is a live kernel mount, not a copy. Because overlay's mount options list every lowerdir by full path and the kernel caps mount-option strings at one memory page (4096 bytes), a chain of 20+ layers would overflow that limit — so Docker keeps a second directory, overlay2/l/, full of short (26-character) symlinks like l/FJKW5ZFF… pointing back at the real diff folders, and builds the mount option string out of THOSE short names instead.

  /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
    ├── l/                                    ← short-symlink dir (dodges the
    │     FJKW5ZFF2K7… ──▶ ../a1b2c3.../diff      4096-byte mount-option limit)
    │     Q9XPLM3N8R2… ──▶ ../d4e5f6.../diff
    │
    ├── a1b2c3.../diff/     (python:3.11-slim base layer's own files)
    ├── d4e5f6.../diff/     (COPY requirements.txt .   → just that 1 file)
    ├── g7h8i9.../diff/     (RUN pip install -r …      → site-packages/)
    ├── j1k2l3.../diff/     (COPY . /app/               → the app source)
    │     ├── link          (this layer's own short name, written into l/)
    │     └── lower          "l/FJKW5ZFF2K7:l/Q9XPLM3N8R2:…"  ← parents, oldest→newest
    │
    └── <container's own writable id>/
          ├── diff/      (empty until the container writes something — 6.2's layer)
          ├── work/      (overlay's private scratch dir, never read directly)
          └── merged/    (the union view — ONLY exists while a container is running)

  kernel mount actually issued for a RUNNING container:
    mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=l/Q9XPL…:l/FJKW5…:…,\
      upperdir=<container-id>/diff,workdir=<container-id>/work  <container-id>/merged
DirectoryExists for…Holds
<id>/diffevery layer, image or containeronly THAT layer's own added/changed/deleted files — this IS the "layer" 7.1 lists and 7.6's SIZE column measures
<id>/lowerevery non-base layera plain text file listing this layer's parent chain, oldest-to-newest, by their short l/ names
l/<short-name>every layera symlink back to its own diff — exists purely to keep mount strings short
<id>/merged, workonly a RUNNING container's own top idthe live union mount and overlay's scratch space — an image on disk has neither
🔑 This is the mechanical reason 7's gotcha calls SIZE additive-but-wrong: docker images prints the FULL size of every layer a tag's chain touches, but two tags sharing a parent are pointing their lower file at the exact SAME diff directory on disk — that directory's bytes exist once, full stop. docker system df's RECLAIMABLE column is computed from these real, deduplicated directories; adding up SIZE column entries by hand never is.
② The Registry API v2 handshake — what docker push/pull actually put on the wire

7.3's "registered mail" analogy hides an HTTP protocol with a strict order of operations. A bare request to any endpoint gets 401 Unauthorized back with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="…",service="…",scope="repository:you/easypj:pull,push" header — that's the registry telling the client WHERE to fetch a short-lived token from and what scope to ask for; docker login's credentials are spent once, against that token endpoint, and the resulting bearer token rides on every subsequent call. For each layer, docker push issues a HEAD /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest> BEFORE sending a single byte — a 200 response IS the "Layer already exists" line 7.3's terminal output prints; only a 404 triggers the actual upload (POST to open a session, PATCH chunks, PUT to finalize with the digest in the querystring). The image's MANIFEST — the JSON document listing every layer digest plus the config digest — is always the very LAST thing PUT, specifically so a manifest is never visible to a puller while any blob it names might still be missing.

  docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1
       │
       ▼
  GET /v2/                                   ─▶ 401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearer …
       │
       ▼
  GET <token endpoint>?scope=…               ─▶ 200 { "token": "eyJhbGci…" }
       │  (every call below carries: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci…)
       ▼
  for EACH layer, cheapest check first:
    HEAD /v2/you/easypj/blobs/sha256:f2c1e4d5…  ─▶ 200 = "Layer already exists" (skip!)
                                                 ─▶ 404 = must upload:
         POST /v2/you/easypj/blobs/uploads/    ─▶ 202 Accepted, Location: …/uploads/abcd
         PATCH …/uploads/abcd  (raw layer bytes, possibly chunked)
         PUT   …/uploads/abcd?digest=sha256:f2c1e4d5…   ─▶ 201 Created
       ▼
  (config blob pushed the exact same HEAD/POST/PATCH/PUT way — it's just another blob)
       ▼
  PUT /v2/you/easypj/manifests/v1.1
      Content-Type: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json
      body lists: config digest + every layer digest, in order
       ─▶ 201 Created,  Docker-Content-Digest: sha256:4be2a1c9…   ← the DIGEST 7.3 prints
CallPurposeWhat 7.3 sees in the terminal
HEAD .../blobs/<digest>"do you already have this exact layer?"f2c1e4d5: Layer already exists
POST/PATCH/PUT .../blobs/uploads/…upload a genuinely new blob9d3a1b2c: Pushed
PUT .../manifests/<tag>publish the tag, LAST, only once every blob it names is confirmed presentv1.1: digest: sha256:4be2a1c9… size: 1786
🔑 The DIGEST 7.3 tells you to trust over a tag isn't invented by Docker locally — it's the Docker-Content-Digest the REGISTRY itself computes and returns from that final manifest PUT, which is exactly why two different registries holding "the same" push always agree on it: it's a hash of bytes, not an opinion either server holds.
③ Four sha256es, four different jobs — the compressed blob digest, diffID, chainID, and the Image ID

7.6's info-box draws one line between "Image ID" and "digest" — the full picture actually has FOUR distinct hashes, and confusing them is the single most common Docker-internals mistake. The compressed blob digest is what ② pushes/pulls and what a manifest lists — it changes if you merely re-gzip the identical bytes at a different compression level. The diffID is the sha256 of that same layer's UNCOMPRESSED tar stream, stored in the config's rootfs.diff_ids array — this is the layer's true content identity, immune to compression choices. The chainID folds a layer's diffID together with its PARENT's chainID (chainID(L0)=diffID(L0); chainID(Ln)=sha256(chainID(Ln-1)+" "+diffID(Ln))) — this is the value the layerdb/sha256/<chainID>/ directories (⑤ below) are actually named after, so two DIFFERENT images sharing an identical parent chain resolve to the identical chainID and therefore the identical on-disk layer. Last, the Image ID that docker images prints (truncated to 12 hex chars) is simply the sha256 of the CONFIG JSON blob itself — one hash covering Env, Cmd, the whole diff_ids list, and everything else docker inspect shows.

  compressed blob (what the registry stores/transfers, ②)
        sha256:f2c1e4d5…  ← changes if gzip level changes, content doesn't
                 │  gunzip
                 ▼
  diffID (uncompressed tar hash — the layer's TRUE content identity)
        sha256:9a8b7c6d…  ← stored in config.rootfs.diff_ids[i]
                 │  chainID(Ln) = sha256( chainID(Ln-1) + " " + diffID(Ln) )
                 ▼
  chainID (this layer's cumulative identity WITH its parent chain)
        sha256:3e2f1a0b…  ← names the layerdb/ dir (⑤) — shared by ANY image
                              with this exact same parent chain, even a
                              totally different repository

  config JSON  { "Env":[…], "Cmd":[…], "rootfs":{"diff_ids":[…]}, "history":[…] }
                 │  sha256 of the WHOLE config blob
                 ▼
  IMAGE ID  =  sha256:abc123def456…   ← what `docker images` truncates to 12 chars
                                          this is what 7.2's "same Image ID, many
                                          tags" diagram is actually pointing at
HashHashes…Changes if…Where you see it
Compressed blob digestthe gzip'd layer bytes on the wirecompression level/tool changes, even with identical contentregistry manifest, ② push/pull output
diffIDthe uncompressed tar streaman actual file inside the layer changesconfig.rootfs.diff_ids (not printed by any CLI command directly)
chainIDdiffID + its whole parent chainany ancestor layer changeslayerdb/sha256/<id> directory names (⑤)
Image IDthe entire config JSON blobEnv/Cmd/User/diff_ids/history — anything in config changesdocker images IMAGE ID column, docker inspect .Id
🔑 7.6's @sha256:… pin is a FIFTH thing again — the MANIFEST digest ②'s final PUT returns, which hashes the manifest JSON (the list of layer+config digests), not the config JSON itself. That's why docker inspect's Image ID and a pulled image's RepoDigests entry are never the same string even though both are "a sha256 for this image" — they hash two completely different documents one level apart.
④ Inside a docker save tarball — manifest.json, repositories, and per-layer blobs

7.4's "printing plates" analogy is literal: docker save writes a tar containing exactly the documents ③ just described, laid out so docker load can reconstruct the image without ANY registry involved. At the top level sits manifest.json — a JSON array with one entry per image naming its Config file (the config JSON blob, saved as <imageID>.json), its RepoTags, and an ordered Layers list of <legacy-id>/layer.tar paths. A legacy repositories file duplicates the tag→ID mapping in an older format purely so a pre-1.10 Docker daemon could still load it. Critically, docker save itself writes an UNCOMPRESSED tar — gzip is never applied — which is exactly why 7.4's "easypj in Practice" box pipes straight into gzip: the layer.tar files inside are the same bytes as ③'s diffIDs, highly redundant text/binary that gzip typically shrinks by ~40%, and piping avoids ever writing that multi-GB uncompressed intermediate to disk at all.

  easypj-v1.1.tar   (docker save easypj:v1.1 -o easypj-v1.1.tar)
    ├── manifest.json
    │     [{ "Config": "abc123def456….json",
    │        "RepoTags": ["easypj:v1.1"],
    │        "Layers": [ "9a8b7c…/layer.tar",     ← base (python:3.11-slim)
    │                    "d4e5f6…/layer.tar",     ← COPY requirements.txt
    │                    "g7h8i9…/layer.tar",     ← RUN pip install
    │                    "j1k2l3…/layer.tar" ] }]  ← COPY . /app/
    ├── repositories                              (legacy tag index, back-compat only)
    ├── abc123def456….json                        (the FULL config blob — Env/Cmd/history)
    ├── 9a8b7c…/  { layer.tar, VERSION, json }     (VERSION="1.0", json=legacy v1 stub)
    ├── d4e5f6…/  { layer.tar, VERSION, json }
    ├── g7h8i9…/  { layer.tar, VERSION, json }
    └── j1k2l3…/  { layer.tar, VERSION, json }

  docker export tmp-easypj -o v1.1-fs.tar   (Drill 7.4's trap, for contrast)
    └── (one single flat tar of the merged filesystem — NO manifest.json,
         NO config blob, NO per-layer split at all — Cmd/Env/history
         were never IN a tar that has no config.json to hold them)
File in the tarballRead byCarries
manifest.jsondocker load, firstwhich config file, which tags, which layers, in what order
<imageID>.jsondocker load, docker inspect after loadingEnv, Cmd, User, rootfs.diff_ids, history — everything ⑥ reads
<id>/layer.tardocker load, unpacked into a fresh overlay2/<cache-id>/diffthe exact same bytes as that layer's diffID (③), just uncompressed on disk
repositoriesonly pre-1.10 daemonsa legacy duplicate of the RepoTags mapping
🔑 Drill 7.4's proof that export/import loses Cmd isn't a missing FLAG someone forgot to pass — docker export's tar format has no slot for a config JSON at all, so there is nothing for import to read Env/Cmd/User back OUT of. save/load survive the round trip only because manifest.json + the config blob travel in the tarball alongside the layers.
⑤ What docker rmi actually deletes, and in what order — refcounts across three on-disk stores

Beyond ①'s overlay2 directories, the daemon keeps three more small on-disk stores under /var/lib/docker/image/overlay2/: repositories.json (the tag→Image-ID index — the ONLY file docker tag and a by-NAME docker rmi ever touch), imagedb/content/sha256/<imageID> (one raw config-JSON blob per image, keyed by ③'s Image ID), and layerdb/sha256/<chainID> (one refcounted entry per chainID (③), pointing back at the real overlay2/<cache-id> diff directory ① described). docker rmi easypj:v1.0 removes exactly one entry from repositories.json — nothing more — and prints Untagged: easypj:v1.0. Only once an image's LAST tag is gone, no OTHER image's config lists it as a parent, and no container (running OR stopped) references it, does the daemon delete its imagedb blob and print Deleted: sha256:… — then walks that image's chainID chain (③) from the top down, decrementing each layer's reference count in layerdb/sha256/<chainID>/, and only physically rm -rfs an overlay2/<cache-id> diff directory once ITS OWN refcount hits zero. This is precisely why two tags sharing a base layer (①'s callout) never double-delete it: the shared chainID's refcount simply drops from 2 to 1.

  BEFORE:  easypj:v1.0 ──┐
                          ├─▶ imageID abc123…  (refcount via repositories.json: 2 tags)
           easypj:latest ┘         │
                                    ▼  chainID chain, each layer refcounted separately
                          base(2) → +reqs(2) → +pip(2) → +copy(2)   (2 tags reference all 4)

  docker rmi easypj:v1.0
       │  repositories.json: remove "easypj:v1.0" entry only
       ▼
  Untagged: easypj:v1.0                    ← by-NAME rmi stops HERE if another tag remains
       (imageID abc123… still has 1 tag: "latest" → refcount 1, nothing deleted)

  docker rmi easypj:latest   (now the LAST tag)
       │  repositories.json: remove "easypj:latest" too → imageID has 0 tags left
       │  no other image's config parents THIS imageID; no container uses it
       ▼
  Deleted: sha256:abc123…                  ← imagedb blob removed
  Deleted: sha256:j1k2l3… (+copy)          ← chainID refcount 2→0, dir rm'd
  Deleted: sha256:g7h8i9… (+pip)           ← chainID refcount 2→0, dir rm'd
  Deleted: sha256:d4e5f6… (+reqs)          ← chainID refcount 2→0, dir rm'd
  (base layer SURVIVES — python:3.11-slim's own tag still references it!)
CommandStore(s) it touchesCan it strand a container?
docker rmi <tag>repositories.json only (plus imagedb/layerdb IF that was the last tag)refuses outright if any container references the image
docker rmi -f <tag>same, but skips the container-reference checkyes — the container's own layer still points at a now-gone parent chain
docker image pruneimagedb entries with ZERO RepoTags AND ZERO RepoDigests (7.1's dangling definition) → their layerdb chainsno — dangling images can't have a running container by definition
docker image prune -aevery imagedb entry with no CONTAINER reference, tagged or notno, but removes far more than plain prune (7.5's ladder)
🔑 7.5's rule that docker rmi refuses an image referenced by even a STOPPED container isn't a courtesy check — that stopped container's own top layer is a real overlay2 directory whose lower file names the image's chainID chain by path. Delete those parent directories out from under it with -f and the container becomes un-start-able: the very next docker start tries to mount a lowerdir= list that no longer exists.
⑥ Where docker history's data really comes from — the config's history array and why <missing> is cosmetic

docker history never re-runs a build or re-reads any Dockerfile — every column it prints comes from ONE place: the history array inside ③'s config JSON, an ordered list where each entry carries created, created_by (the exact instruction string — this is WHY a secret an ARG/RUN actually consumed shows up here, per 7's gotcha table), and an empty_layer boolean. Filesystem-touching instructions (RUN, COPY, ADD) get empty_layer omitted/false and correspond 1-to-1 with the NEXT entry in rootfs.diff_ids — that's the diffID docker history resolves a real SIZE for. Metadata-only instructions (ENV, CMD, WORKDIR, EXPOSE, LABEL, USER, ARG, STOPSIGNAL) touch no files at all, so Docker marks them empty_layer: true, they consume NO diffID, and history prints them at 0B. The <missing> in the IMAGE column (7's Q18) is simpler than it looks: since Docker 1.10 only the image's OWN top config gets a real Image ID locally — the classic per-layer v1 IDs that used to exist for every intermediate step were retired, so history has nothing legitimate to print for older/pulled entries except the literal placeholder. SIZE and CREATED BY are unaffected either way, because both were always sourced from this same array, never from those retired per-layer IDs.

  config.json → "history": [
    { "created_by": "/bin/sh -c #(nop) ADD file:… in /",                      ← real layer
                                                          empty_layer: (absent) → pops diff_ids[0]
    { "created_by": "/bin/sh -c #(nop) WORKDIR /app",    empty_layer: true    → NO diffID consumed
    { "created_by": "COPY requirements.txt .",           empty_layer: (absent) → pops diff_ids[1]
    { "created_by": "RUN pip install -r requirements.txt", empty_layer:(absent)→ pops diff_ids[2]
    { "created_by": "COPY . /app/ # buildkit",           empty_layer: (absent) → pops diff_ids[3]
    { "created_by": "/bin/sh -c #(nop) CMD […]",         empty_layer: true    → NO diffID consumed
  ]
  config.json → "rootfs": { "diff_ids": [ sha256:base…, sha256:reqs…, sha256:pip…, sha256:copy… ] }
                                             ▲ exactly 4 entries — one per NON-empty history item

  docker history reads history[] top-to-bottom, printing:
    IMAGE column:  <missing> for every entry except the image's own top config ID
    SIZE column:   diff_ids.pop() size for empty_layer:false, else "0B"
    CREATED BY:    created_by, verbatim — unredacted, forever
Instruction typeempty_layer?Consumes a diff_ids entry?SIZE shown
RUN, COPY, ADDfalse (omitted)yes — one real diffID eachthat layer's actual byte size
ENV, CMD, WORKDIR, EXPOSE, LABEL, USER, ARG, STOPSIGNALtrueno0B, always
🔑 This is the full mechanism behind the ARG/secret gotcha in this chapter's Gotchas list: there is no separate "build log" being leaked — created_by is a permanent, unredacted field inside the SAME config blob docker inspect reads, which is why docker history --no-trunc alone is enough to recover any value a RUN instruction ever consumed, no registry access or build logs required.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • docker images/image ls read the local index; filters and --format turn it into a queryable, scriptable list.
  • A tag is a free-to-create, free-to-delete pointer; the IMAGE ID (and the bytes behind it) is the only real identity.
  • push/pull move manifests + missing layers; the printed DIGEST is the deploy-safe identifier — tags can move, digests can't.
  • save/load preserve the whole image (layers+tags+config); export/import flatten a container's filesystem and lose CMD/ENV entirely.
  • The cleanup ladder is ordered by blast radius: prune (dangling only) → prune -a (all unused) → system prune -a --volumes (everything) — docker system df shows which rung you need.
  • docker history ranks a layer's SIZE and origin instruction; docker inspect exposes Config + RepoDigests — audit any image you did not build with both before trusting it.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: tagging semantics, push/pull/digest behavior, and prune/rmi reference rules are classic graded items here.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • SIZE in docker images is additive across tags → It double-counts shared layers — trust docker system df's RECLAIMABLE column, not mental arithmetic.
  • docker rmi <ID> with multiple tags always works → It either refuses or (-f) nukes every tag at once — untag by NAME, delete by ID only once one name remains.
  • "denied: requested access" on push means a bad password → It's almost always a missing registry NAMESPACE in the tag.
  • docker load asks before overwriting a tag → It overwrites an existing tag on the target host with zero confirmation — diff docker images before/after on any host you don't fully control.
  • docker save easypj saves just the base tag → With no tag specified, it silently bundles EVERY easypj tag into one tarball.
  • docker system prune -a is always safe to run on a CI build agent → It also evicts the very images a --cache-from build relies on — the next build goes fully cold; prune surgically (dangling-only or age-based) on cache-dependent runners.
  • A secret consumed only via ARG is invisible once the build finishes → Any ARG/ENV value a RUN instruction actually consumed is preserved forever in docker history's CREATED BY column — readable by anyone who can run history on the image.
  • docker images -a always reveals extra "intermediate" build layers → Only true for the legacy builder — BuildKit (the default since Docker 23.0) keeps its layer cache in a separate store; check docker system df's Build Cache row or docker builder prune instead.
  • docker rm and docker rmi are just two spellings of the same command → docker rm removes a CONTAINER, docker rmi (= docker image rm) removes an IMAGE — mixing them up under exam time pressure is the classic image-chapter trap.
  • Tag names follow the same lowercase-only rule as repository names → Only the REPOSITORY part (left of the colon) is lowercase-locked — the TAG part can mix case (easypj:V2.0-RC1 is valid syntax); it's docker build -t MyApp . that fails with "invalid reference format," not docker build -t app:MyTag .
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker rmi $(docker images -f dangling=true -q) — kill every ghost in one line.
  • docker inspect -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' easypj:v1.1 — grab a pinnable digest without parsing JSON by hand.
  • Pipe docker save … | gzip in one command instead of saving then compressing separately — one less multi-GB temp file.
  • docker image prune -a --filter "until=24h" — surgical, CI-safe pruning that won't evict a --cache-from source built earlier the same day.
  • Push hanging or timing out on a slow link? The progress bars docker push prints show the UNCOMPRESSED size, which reads scarier than what's really crossing the wire — but on a genuinely constrained connection, lower the daemon-level --max-concurrent-uploads (default 5) so fewer layers race for the same limited bandwidth at once instead of all timing out together.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 7)

the full image custody lifecycle 
# Find ghost images
docker images --filter "dangling=true"

# Free re-name, same ID
docker tag SRC DST

# Move; note the DIGEST
docker push registry/repo:tag
docker pull registry/repo:tag

# Full image, offline
docker save -o f.tar IMAGE
docker load -i f.tar

# One image, by name or ID (docker image rm is the exact same command)
docker rmi IMAGE

# Dangling / all unused
docker image prune
docker image prune -a
docker builder prune

# Honest disk accounting
docker system df

# Layer-by-layer cost
docker history IMAGE

# Audit injected env
docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' IMAGE

🧠 Chapter 7 — DCA Practice Questions (19)

Quick recall of the image custody lifecycle — 19 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command lists all Docker images on your system with their sizes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker images or docker image ls. Shows REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED, and SIZE for each image.

EXPLANATION

docker images is the older syntax, docker image ls is the newer Docker CLI structured syntax. Both produce identical output. The docker image subcommand group includes ls, pull, push, rm, prune, history, inspect — all image management operations under one namespace.

REPOSITORYTAGIMAGE IDCREATEDSIZE
easypjv1.19f8e7d6c5b4a2 hours ago181MB

Q2
How do you tag an existing image for pushing to GitHub Container Registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker tag easypj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0

EXPLANATION

The tag format for registries is registry/namespace/repository:tag. For Docker Hub, the registry prefix (docker.io) is implicit and can be omitted. For all other registries, you must include the full registry URL.

  docker tag  easypj:v1.0    ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
              └─ SOURCE           └──────────┬──────────┘ └┬┘
                (local image)     registry/namespace/repo  tag
Q3
What's the critical difference between docker save and docker export?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker save preserves ALL image layers, tags, and metadata. docker export creates a flat filesystem snapshot of a container's files — layers and history are LOST. Always use save/load for image transfer, never export/import.

EXPLANATION

Think of save as "serialize the complete image with its layer cake intact" and export as "flatten the container's filesystem into a single blob." The difference becomes critical in air-gapped environments.

docker savedocker export
Sourcean IMAGEa CONTAINER
Layers preserved?✅ Yes❌ No — flattened to one layer
Metadata (CMD/ENV) kept?✅ Yes❌ No
Use forimage transferfilesystem snapshot only
Q4
What command removes all unused Docker images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker image prune -a — removes all images not referenced by at least one container. Without -a, only dangling images (<none>:<none>) are removed.

EXPLANATION

Dangling images occur when you rebuild with the same tag — the old image loses its tag and becomes <none>:<none>. For complete cleanup: docker system prune -a --volumes adds containers, networks, build cache, and unused volumes.

CommandRemoves
docker image pruneOnly dangling (<none>:<none>) images
docker image prune -aAll images not used by any container, tagged or not
docker system prune -a --volumes+ stopped containers, unused networks/volumes, build cache
Q5
How do you filter images to show only those matching "easypj*"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker images --filter "reference=easypj*"

EXPLANATION

The --filter flag supports multiple filter types: reference (name:tag pattern), dangling (true/false), before/since (filter by image), and label (metadata). You can chain filters.

  docker images --filter "reference=easypj*"
  REPOSITORY   TAG      IMAGE ID       SIZE
  easypj       v1.1     9f8e7d6c5b4a   181MB
  easypj       latest   9f8e7d6c5b4a   181MB
  # rows outside the "easypj*" pattern are hidden, not deleted
Q6
What happens when you docker rmi easypj:v1.0 and the image also has the tag easypj:latest?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Only the :v1.0 TAG is removed — the image itself stays because it's still referenced by :latest. The image is only deleted when ALL tags pointing to it are removed.

EXPLANATION

Docker uses reference counting for images. Each tag increments the reference count. docker rmi <tag> decrements it. When the count reaches zero AND no container references the image, the layers are actually deleted.

  IMAGE ID 9f8e7d6c5b4a  ◀── easypj:v1.0    (rmi target)
                         ◀── easypj:latest  (still pointing here)

  docker rmi easypj:v1.0
     → only the ":v1.0" pointer is deleted
     → IMAGE ID survives — ":latest" still references it
Q7
How do you check total Docker disk usage and reclaimable space?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker system df — shows disk usage by Images, Containers, Local Volumes, and Build Cache, with RECLAIMABLE percentages.

EXPLANATION

docker system df -v gives verbose output showing each image/container/volume individually with its size. Use this before docker system prune to see exactly what you'll reclaim.

TYPETOTALACTIVESIZERECLAIMABLE
Images2349.8GB7.1GB (72%)
Containers62320MB180MB (56%)
Build Cache4102.1GB2.1GB (100%)
Q8
What authentication method does AWS ECR use that's different from other registries?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ECR uses aws ecr get-login-password piped to docker login --password-stdin — it generates a temporary token via AWS IAM, not a permanent username/password. The token expires after 12 hours.

EXPLANATION

This is more secure than a static password: the token is short-lived and tied to your AWS IAM credentials. In CI/CD, you typically run this command in every pipeline job.

  aws ecr get-login-password  ──pipe──▶  docker login --password-stdin
         │                                        │
    IAM-issued token                     dockerd caches it
    (expires in 12h)                     for that registry only
Q9
How do you see the size contribution of each layer in an image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker image history easypj:v1.0 — shows each layer with its SIZE column. This is how you identify which layers are bloating your image.

EXPLANATION

Each layer's SIZE is the delta from the previous layer. Use docker image history --no-trunc to see full command strings. For even deeper analysis: dive <image> (third-party tool) shows per-file changes in each layer.

IMAGECREATED BYSIZE
9f8e7d6c5b4aCMD ["gunicorn" "easypj.wsgi:app"]0B
<missing>RUN pip install -r requirements.txt80MB
<missing>FROM python:3.11-slim150MB
Q10
How do you transfer a Docker image to an air-gapped server with no internet access?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker save -o easypj.tar easypj:v1.0 on the connected machine, transfer the tar via USB, then docker load -i easypj.tar on the air-gapped server. This preserves all layers, tags, and metadata.

EXPLANATION

You can also pipe save/load over SSH to skip the intermediate tar file: docker save easypj:v1.0 | ssh user@airgap 'docker load'. The tar contains layer blobs + a manifest.json describing how to reassemble them.

  CONNECTED MACHINE                       AIR-GAPPED SERVER
  docker save -o easypj.tar   ──USB──▶    docker load -i easypj.tar
  (all layers + tags + metadata packed into one file, no registry involved)
Q11
docker images shows easypj:v1.0 and easypj:v1.1 both at ~181 MB. Does deleting easypj:v1.0 free ~181 MB?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Almost never — no, not if the two images share layers.

EXPLANATION

SIZE is per-tag, but layers are shared (7's gotcha). docker rmi easypj:v1.0 only frees layers v1.1 does NOT also reference — typically just the small COPY . . layer that changed; the shared python:3.11-slim base survives untouched. Check docker system df's RECLAIMABLE column for the real number, not the listed SIZE.

  easypj:v1.0 = [python:3.11-slim][pip install][COPY . . (v1.0 code)]
  easypj:v1.1 = [python:3.11-slim][pip install][COPY . . (v1.1 code)]
                 └────────┬────────┘             └───────┬───────┘
                 SHARED — survives rmi          UNIQUE — actually freed
Q12
After docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest, how many images exist on disk, and how many names?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

One image, two names.

EXPLANATION

docker tag never copies bytes — it adds a second pointer to the same IMAGE ID (7.2). docker images prints two ROWS with the same IMAGE ID column; that repeated ID is the proof.

  IMAGE ID 9f8e7d6c5b4a
        ▲                 ▲
        │                 │
   easypj:v1.1      easypj:latest    ← 2 names, 1 image, 0 bytes copied
Q13
docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1 fails with "denied: requested access to the resource is denied." You are logged in correctly. What's the first thing to check?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The NAMESPACE in the image name, not your credentials.

EXPLANATION

This error almost always means the repo path (you/easypj) doesn't match your logged-in account/org, or the repo doesn't exist yet on that registry (7.3) — a bad password produces a different (401 unauthorized) error.

SymptomLikely cause
"denied: requested access to the resource is denied"Wrong namespace/org in the image name, or the repo doesn't exist yet
"unauthorized: authentication required"Bad or expired credentials — a DIFFERENT error
Q14
Why should a deploy script pull by DIGEST (ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:...) instead of by tag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because tags are mutable pointers and digests are not.

EXPLANATION

Another tag/push can silently repoint easypj:v1.1 at different bytes tomorrow; the digest printed at push time (7.3) always resolves to the exact manifest that was tested — it is content-addressed, not name-addressed.

  ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1                ← MUTABLE, can repoint tomorrow
  ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:4be2a1c9…    ← IMMUTABLE, always the same bytes
Q15
You run docker load -i easypj-v1.1.tar.gz on a server that already has an image tagged easypj:v1.1. What happens?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The existing easypj:v1.1 tag is silently overwritten — no confirmation prompt.

EXPLANATION

This is 7.4's most dangerous gotcha. Always run docker images before AND after load on any shared or production host, especially in scripted deploy pipelines.

  docker load -i easypj-v1.1.tar.gz
     → easypj:v1.1 already exists locally
     → tag SILENTLY reassigned to the loaded image's ID, no prompt
Q16
docker system df reports Images: TOTAL 23, RECLAIMABLE 7.1GB (72%). You run docker image prune (no -a). Roughly how much of that 7.1GB comes back?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Only the DANGLING portion — likely much less than 7.1GB.

EXPLANATION

Plain prune removes only <none> images (7.1's ghosts); prune -a is required to reclaim images that are merely unused-by-a-container but still tagged. Re-run docker system df after each rung of the ladder (7.5) to see the real delta.

MetricBefore pruneAfter plain prune
RECLAIMABLE7.1GB (72%)4.8GB (64%)
Freed this run—~2.3GB (dangling only)
Q17
On a CI runner you rely on --cache-from to speed up builds. A teammate runs docker system prune -a to "clean up disk." What breaks?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The next build goes fully cold — the --cache-from source images were exactly what "unused" prune -a just deleted.

EXPLANATION

7.5's gotcha: CI hosts should prune surgically (dangling only, or age-based) rather than blanket prune -a, because "unused by a running container" and "needed as a cache source" are different things prune cannot distinguish.

  BEFORE: cache-from image sitting locally ──▶ build reuses cached layers (fast)
  docker system prune -a  ── deletes "unused" images, including the cache source ──▶
  AFTER: cache-from image gone ──▶ next build starts from a cold cache (slow)
Q18
docker history easypj:v1.1 shows a layer <missing> next to RUN pip install .... Is the image broken?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — <missing> is cosmetic.

EXPLANATION

7.6: since Docker 1.10, only an image's OWN top config keeps a real local Image ID — the retired per-layer IDs mean every other layer (virtually all of them, especially after a pull) has nothing legitimate to print but the placeholder — the layer's SIZE and CREATED BY stay accurate and usable for the size audit Chapter 8 depends on.

IMAGECREATED BYSIZE
<missing>RUN pip install -r requirements.txt80MB — still accurate
Q19
You need to know whether a downloaded community image injects a suspicious environment variable before running it. Which single command answers that, with zero risk?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' <image>.

EXPLANATION

inspect reads the CONFIG blob (7.6's Image ID vs Digest info-box) without ever starting a container — a completely static, safe read of exactly what that image would set at runtime, which is the whole point of auditing BEFORE you trust it.

  docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' easypj:v1.1
     → reads the CONFIG blob only — no container ever starts
     → zero risk of the image's ENTRYPOINT/CMD actually executing

🔬 Practice Drill 7.1 — Trace a Dangling Ghost

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Rebuild easypj:v1 once (touch any file first), then in order run docker images -f dangling=true, tag the new build both latest and with a registry prefix, then docker system df. Done when you can point at the dangling ghost, name all three tags sharing its predecessor's ID, and quote the RECLAIMABLE number.

Hint: the OLD image ID doesn't disappear when you rebuild with the same tag — it just loses its name and becomes the dangling <none>:<none> row 7.1 warned about; the two new tags you apply both point at the NEW build, not the ghost.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# 1. Touch a file and rebuild with the SAME tag
touch app.py
docker build -t easypj:v1 .

# 2. The old build loses its name -> becomes dangling
docker images -f dangling=true
# REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED           SIZE
# <none>       <none>    a1b2c3d4e5f6   3 minutes ago     181MB   <- the ghost

# 3. Hand the NEW build two more names
docker tag easypj:v1 easypj:latest
docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1

docker images easypj
# REPOSITORY           TAG      IMAGE ID       CREATED
# easypj               v1       9f8e7d6c5b4a   1 minute ago
# easypj               latest   9f8e7d6c5b4a   1 minute ago
# ghcr.io/you/easypj   v1       9f8e7d6c5b4a   1 minute ago
# ^ three tags, one NEW IMAGE ID -- none of them point at the ghost

docker system df
# TYPE      TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images    24      4        10.0GB    7.3GB (73%)   <- ghost inflated this

Check yourself: the dangling row's IMAGE ID must be DIFFERENT from the three tags you just applied — that mismatch is the proof the rebuild orphaned the old layer instead of updating it in place. If your RECLAIMABLE number went up by roughly the ghost's own size, you've connected 7.1's filter straight to 7.5's cleanup ladder.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.2 — Untag Without Fear

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Apply both release tags to easypj:v1.1 — docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest and docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1 — then run docker images and confirm all three rows share one IMAGE ID. Now docker rmi the :latest tag only. Verify easypj:v1.1 still runs.

Hint: docker rmi by NAME only removes that one badge — the underlying IMAGE ID needs zero surviving names before its bytes actually go away.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# 1. Hand out two more badges to the same IMAGE ID
docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest
docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1

docker images easypj
# REPOSITORY          TAG      IMAGE ID       CREATED
# easypj               v1.1     3f9a12bc77de   2 hours ago
# easypj               latest   3f9a12bc77de   2 hours ago
# ghcr.io/you/easypj   v1.1     3f9a12bc77de   2 hours ago
# ^ same IMAGE ID on all three rows — one image, three names

# 2. Shred ONE badge
docker rmi easypj:latest
# Untagged: easypj:latest        <- only the badge is gone

# 3. The person underneath is still there
docker run --rm easypj:v1.1 echo "still alive"
# still alive

Check yourself: all three original rows printed the identical IMAGE ID — proof docker tag never copied a single byte. After rmi easypj:latest, docker images easypj shows two rows, not zero, because two other names still hold the image's reference count above zero. If you predicted easypj:v1.1 would keep running before you even typed the run command, you've got 7.2's core model cold.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.3 — Deploy by Digest, Not by Hope

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Push any tag to a registry you can reach, note the digest Docker prints, then pull the SAME image using only that digest — no tag anywhere in the reference. Verify the pull succeeds with zero tag involved.

Hint: the line <tag>: digest: sha256:... that docker push prints is a complete, standalone reference — registry/repo@sha256:... is valid syntax with no tag component whatsoever.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# 1. Push and capture the digest it prints
docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1
docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1
# v1.1: digest: sha256:4be2a1c9d3f0... size: 1786   <- write this down

# 2. Remove the local copy so the pull below can't cheat off the cache
docker rmi ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1

# 3. Pull by DIGEST — notice there is no ":v1.1" anywhere
docker pull ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:4be2a1c9d3f0...
# sha256:4be2a1c9d3f0...: Pulling from you/easypj
# Status: Downloaded newer image for ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:4be2a1c9d3f0...

Check yourself: the pull succeeded with a reference that never mentioned a tag — proof the registry addresses content by digest, and tags are purely a local-index convenience layered on top. If you removed the local image first and it still resolved correctly, you've proven content-addressing to yourself, not just read about it.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.4 — Prove export Forgets How To Start

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Round-trip easypj:v1.1 through save/load, and separately through create → export → import. docker inspect the Cmd field of BOTH resulting images before running either one.

Hint: compare docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Cmd}}' on the loaded vs. the imported image before you even try docker run on either — one of the two is not null.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# Path A: save -> load (the correct way to move an image)
docker save easypj:v1.1 -o v1.1.tar
docker load -i v1.1.tar
docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Cmd}}' easypj:v1.1
# [gunicorn easypj.wsgi:app]        <- CMD survived intact

# Path B: create -> export -> import (the trap)
docker create --name tmp-easypj easypj:v1.1
docker export tmp-easypj -o v1.1-fs.tar
docker import v1.1-fs.tar easypj:flattened
docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Cmd}}' easypj:flattened
# <no value>                        <- Cmd is null, it forgot how to start

# 3. Watch the difference in person
docker run --rm easypj:flattened
# exits instantly, code 0 — nothing was ever told to run
docker rm tmp-easypj

Check yourself: the loaded image's Cmd printed the real gunicorn command; the imported image's Cmd printed nothing at all, because export only ever captured the container's FILESYSTEM, never its config. Running the flattened image exits immediately with no error — that silent, instant exit is the entire lesson of "always use save/load for image transfer."

🔬 Practice Drill 7.5 — Climb the Ladder, Verify Each Rung

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Run docker system df, then docker image prune, then docker system df again. Read the Images RECLAIMABLE delta, and confirm every named easypj tag is still present — only -a would have touched them.

Hint: plain prune only ever removes <none>:<none> dangling images — any tagged easypj image, used or not, is untouched until you add -a.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# BEFORE
docker system df
# TYPE      TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images    23      4        9.8GB     7.1GB (72%)

docker image prune
# WARNING! This will remove all dangling images.
# Are you sure? [y/N] y
# Total reclaimed space: 2.3GB

# AFTER — only the dangling slice came back
docker system df
# TYPE      TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images    16      4        7.5GB     4.8GB (64%)

docker images easypj
# every tagged easypj row is still there — prune never touched a name

Check yourself: the reclaimed 2.3GB is smaller than the full 7.1GB RECLAIMABLE figure, because that figure also counted tagged-but-unused images that only prune -a is willing to remove. Every named easypj tag surviving plain prune is the proof the cleanup ladder is genuinely graduated by blast radius, not a single all-or-nothing switch.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.6 — Rank the Fattest Layers

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Run docker history easypj:v1.1 --no-trunc, rank the THREE heaviest layers by SIZE, and name the instruction each one corresponds to.

Hint: the SIZE column is per-layer, not cumulative — sort by that column, not by the layer's position in the list.
View Solution
TERMINAL
docker history easypj:v1.1 --no-trunc
# IMAGE          CREATED BY                                          SIZE
# 3f9a12bc77de   CMD ["gunicorn" "easypj.wsgi:app"]                  0B
# <missing>      COPY . /app/ # buildkit                             500kB
# <missing>      RUN pip install -r requirements.txt                80MB   ← #1
# <missing>      COPY requirements.txt .                             200B
# <missing>      WORKDIR /app                                        0B
# <missing>      CMD ["python3"]                                     0B
# <missing>      FROM python:3.11-slim                               150MB  ← #2

Check yourself: your ranking should name the python:3.11-slim base (150MB) and the pip install layer (80MB) first — together they're well over 90% of the image's total size, and the small COPY layers barely register. Those exact two targets are what Chapter 8's multi-stage builds and slimmer base images go after.

📌 Chapter 7 Visual Summary — the full custody lifecycle
   ┌────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────────┐
   │ LIST/  │─▶│ TAG     │─▶│ PUSH/PULL  │─▶│ SAVE/  │─▶│ PRUNE +    │
   │ FILTER │  │ (free,  │  │ (digest =  │  │ LOAD   │  │ HISTORY/   │
   │ (7.1)  │  │ same ID)│  │ truth,7.3) │  │ (7.4)  │  │ INSPECT    │

In one line: Chapter 7 is the full custody lifecycle of an image: find it (7.1), name it correctly (7.2), move it to and from a registry by a digest you can trust (7.3), carry it offline intact when there is no registry at all (7.4), then keep the local store honest with a graduated cleanup ladder and an auditable history (7.5-7.6).

The takeaway: nothing here changes what is INSIDE an image — that is Chapter 8's job; Chapter 7 only ever manages what already exists.

Chapter 8 · Optimizing Docker Images — Smaller, Faster, Safer

easypj works today — as an 850 MB image carrying 120+ CVEs. Every one of those megabytes gets pulled on every deploy, cached on every node, and re-scanned in every audit; every extra package is one more square inch of attack surface. This chapter turns that working-but-fat image into a professional one: the right base, tight layers, a scan report you can actually read, and — where it fits — distroless. Problem solved here: "it runs, but it is heavy, slow to ship, and indefensible in a security review."

Image Creation, Management & Registry 20% Security 15%
🎯 Where Image Management and Security Overlap Hardest

Base image choice, layer/cache mechanics, and image scanning are all named competencies inside Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%) and Security (15%) — Chapter 8 is where those two domains overlap hardest.

  • Layers only ever grow — cleanup MUST happen in the same RUN that created the mess, or the bytes are fossilized.
  • docker scout quickview splits findings into BASE (fixed by rebuilding on a newer base) vs YOUR LAYER (fixed by bumping your own pins).
