8.1 Why Image Size Matters

Every megabyte in your image costs you: slower builds (more to process), slower deployments (more to pull), larger attack surface (more packages = more CVEs), and more disk usage on every node and registry. Target: keep production images under 200 MB.

Image Size Impact
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📊 IMAGE SIZE — WHY EVERY MB COUNTS                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Metric                │  850 MB (Bloated)  │  180 MB (Optimized)        │
  │  ──────────────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────────────────────   │
  │  Build Time            │  ~2 min             │  ~45 sec                   │
  │  Push to Registry      │  ~11 min (10 Mbps)  │  ~2.4 min                  │
  │  Pull on New Node      │  ~11 min            │  ~2.4 min ⚡ (4.6x faster)│
  │  Disk per 10 Deploys   │  8.5 GB             │  1.8 GB                    │
  │  CVEs (Vulnerabilities)│  120+               │  30-40 ✅ (3x safer)       │
  │  Attack Surface        │  Large (gcc, git..) │  Minimal                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 What Exactly Scales With Size

Size taxes every stage of the pipeline: registry storage, network transfer on every single pull (and CI pulls the image once per JOB, not once per day), node disk on every host that schedules the container, and even scanner runtime. Attack surface scales with package count more than raw bytes — every extra binary in the image is one more thing that can carry a CVE. The 200 MB target above is the point where a Django + gunicorn + psycopg2 image stops carrying anything it never actually executes.

Where the Bytes Actually Live — Layer-by-Layer Breakdown
  ┌────────────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ SINGLE-STAGE   850 MB      │   │ MULTI-STAGE    180 MB      │
  ├────────────────────────────┤   ├────────────────────────────┤
  │ python:3.11 (dev)  268 MB  │   │ python:3.11-slim   130 MB  │
  │ build tools         240 MB │   │ deps (wheels only)  38 MB  │
  │ deps (unpinned)     150 MB │   │ app code             12 MB │
  │ pip cache           180 MB │   │ — build tools: gone —      │
  │ app code             12 MB │   │ — pip cache: gone —        │
  └────────────────────────────┘   └────────────────────────────┘

  850 MB ██████████████████████████████████████████
  180 MB █████████

easypj's single-stage prototype (850 MB) shrinks by roughly 4.7× to 180 MB once the build-toolchain and pip-cache rows disappear entirely — those two rows alone (240 MB + 180 MB = 420 MB) are pure build-time weight that a multi-stage split (8.3-8.4) throws away for free. At 20 CI runs/day, that gap is the difference between pulling ~17 GB and ~3.6 GB of layers before lunch.

🔍 Beyond docker history — the dive Tool

dive <image> (a popular third-party CLI, wagoodman/dive) turns the byte breakdown above into an interactive, file-level explorer: it walks every layer and reports an efficiency score — how many of the image's bytes are actually reachable in the final filesystem versus wasted on files a later layer overwrote or deleted. docker history tells you WHICH layer is heavy; dive tells you WHICH FILES inside it are, and will even flag the exact whiteout-hidden files this chapter's Under the Hood section (①) explains.

🧳 Analogy — Airline Baggage

Every kilo you check flies on EVERY flight, and every extra item is one more thing security has to screen. Image weight works the same way: you pay the pull-time and CVE-scan cost on every single deploy, forever, for bytes you only ever packed once at build time.

🔬 easypj: a 3-line hotfix to jobpost/views.py should deploy in seconds. With an 850 MB image, that same one-line fix waits behind an ~11-minute pull — at exactly the moment you can least afford to wait.

💡 Size and CVE Count Aren't a Coincidence

Every extra package dragged in by a bigger base is one more binary Section 8.5's scanner can flag, and one more thing to patch on every rebuild — size and audit burden grow together, not separately. That's why 8.2-8.4's byte-trimming and 8.5's vulnerability count trend down together on the same image.

🧪 Practice — Name the Two Heaviest Layers

Run docker images then docker history (7.6) against any image you've built. Verify: you can name the exact Dockerfile instruction behind each of the two heaviest rows — those two instructions are exactly what 8.2's base-image swap and 8.3-8.4's layer discipline go after.

8.2 Choosing the Right Base Image

The base image is the foundation. Choose wisely — it determines your image's size, compatibility, and security posture.

ImageSizeBased OnBest ForWatch Out
Alpine~5 MBAlpine Linux (musl libc)Go apps, simple servicesmusl libc ≠ glibc — some Python packages break!
Slim~130 MBDebian (glibc, stripped)Python/Django, Node.jsBest balance for web apps ✅
Full Debian/Ubuntu~900 MBDebian/Ubuntu (full)Legacy apps, complex depsLarge, many CVEs
Distroless~20 MBDebian (no shell!)Maximum securityNo shell = harder to debug
Scratch0 MBEmptyStatic binaries (Go, Rust)No shell, no libs, no TLS certs
🏆 For easypj (Django): Use python:3.11-slim

Alpine is tempting (5 MB!) but its musl libc causes issues with many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy). Slim gives you Debian compatibility at a reasonable size (~130 MB base + ~50 MB deps/app = ~180 MB total).

The comparison above is generic; here's the same decision made concretely for a Django app like easypj, with an explicit per-base verdict:

BaseSizeVerdict for easypj
python:3.11~268 MBDev toolbox — never ship this
python:3.11-slim~130 MB✅ THE choice: glibc + apt, still compact
python:3.11-alpine~50 MB⚠️ musl: psycopg2/Pillow wheel pain
distroless~65 MB🔴 No shell — 8.6's endgame
scratch0 MBStatic binaries (Go) only — not an option for CPython
⚠️ Real-World Check: Two Numbers Above Run Bigger Than This Chapter's Rounded Teaching Figures

The ~268 MB figure for python:3.11 above is a rounded teaching number for the easypj scenario. On the real Docker Hub, the full (non-slim) python:3.11 image ships a complete Debian build toolchain — gcc, make, and friends — already baked in, not bolted on afterward, and independent measurements consistently put it around 875 MB – 1 GB uncompressed, several times heavier than the number above. Likewise, gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 specifically (the exact variant this chapter's 8.6 Dockerfile pulls) runs closer to ~65 MB than the ~20 MB shown — that lighter figure describes the generic base/static distroless variant (glibc + SSL certs + tzdata, no language runtime); adding the CPython interpreter itself is what pushes the Python-specific image heavier. The python:3.11-slim (~130 MB) and python:3.11-alpine (~50 MB) rows DO match real-world Docker Hub sizes closely. Net effect: the real gap between full and slim is closer to 6-7× than 2×, which only strengthens 8.2's verdict — slim isn't a marginal win, it's the single biggest lever in the whole chapter, exactly as 8.1's diagram and this chapter's Gotchas box both insist.

🏠 Analogy — Choosing a Venue

Full Debian is a furnished mansion — you pay for rooms you never enter. Slim is a fitted studio — everything you need, nothing you don't. Alpine is a tiny cabin with non-standard sockets — cheap to rent, but half your appliances (Python wheels) need an adapter (a compiler) before they'll even plug in.

🔬 easypj: FROM python:3.11-slim + psycopg2-binary installs from a prebuilt wheel in a clean ~40 seconds. The identical install on python:3.11-alpine wants gcc, musl-dev, and postgresql-dev plus several minutes of compiling from source — for a BIGGER effective image once those build tools are counted.

🧪 Practice — Time the Wheel vs the Compile

Time pip install psycopg2-binary inside a python:3.11-slim container, then inside a python:3.11-alpine container. Verify: slim installs a prebuilt wheel in seconds; alpine either attempts a slow source build or fails outright wanting pg_config — proving the table above, not just quoting it.

⚠️ The Tag Pins the Python Version Too

python:3.11-slim pins BOTH the OS layer and the Python minor version. A bare python:latest (or an unpinned python:3) can silently jump interpreter versions between builds — the same "unpinned tag" risk that applies to base images generally, resurfacing here specifically for the base-image decision.

📖 If You DO Use Alpine — apk --no-cache Skips the Whole Cleanup Step

Where Debian/apt needs an explicit rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same RUN (8.3) to avoid fossilizing its package index, Alpine's apk add --no-cache pkg never writes that index to disk in the first place — one flag replaces an entire cleanup instruction. Worth knowing for any OTHER service in the guide that legitimately picks alpine (a static Go binary, a tiny sidecar) — just not for easypj's Django/psycopg2 stack, where 8.2's glibc argument still wins.

8.3 Layer Optimization Techniques

Technique❌ Bad✅ Good
Chain RUN commandsRUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install pkg		RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Clean up in same layerLeave apt cache, pip cache&& rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && pip cache purge
Use .dockerignoreNo .dockerignoreExclude __pycache__, .git, env/, *.pyc
COPY specific filesCOPY . . (copies everything)COPY requirements.txt . then COPY ./easypj ./easypj
Multi-stage buildsSingle stage with build toolsBuild stage + slim runtime stage
Install-and-clean in ONE layer
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

--no-install-recommends alone roughly halves a typical apt payload by skipping "suggested" packages apt would otherwise pull in by default; combined with cleanup in the SAME RUN, this single instruction is the pattern behind every row of the table above.

🪨 Analogy — Sedimentary Rock

Each Docker layer fossilizes forever, just like a layer of sediment. Burying garbage under a new layer of soil does not remove it — the garbage truck has to leave DURING the same geological event (the same RUN instruction), or it's compressed into the rock record for good.

Before vs After: Optimized Layer Structure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🔧 BEFORE OPTIMIZATION (850 MB, 120+ CVEs)                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11            # 268 MB base, no build tools yet      │  │
  │  │ COPY . /app/                # Copies EVERYTHING (db backups, .git) │  │
  │  │ RUN apt-get update           # Creates layer with stale apt cache  │  │
  │  │ RUN apt-get install -y gcc  # Another layer, no cleanup            │  │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.txt  # pip cache bloats this layer          │  │
  │  │ CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver"]  # Dev server in prod!   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │               ✅ AFTER OPTIMIZATION (180 MB, 30-40 CVEs)                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder  # 130 MB, no build tools         │  │
  │  │ WORKDIR /app                                                        │  │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .         # Only deps list (cached!)         │  │
  │  │ RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt          │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim           # Second stage: clean              │  │
  │  │ COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local  # Only packages!    │  │
  │  │ COPY . .                        # .dockerignore filters junk      │  │
  │  │ USER app                        # Non-root security                │  │
  │  │ HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f localhost:8000/health/                     │  │
  │  │ CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]│
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔬 easypj: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt in one layer, followed by a separate RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip in the next, shrinks the final image by exactly zero bytes — the cache is fossilized in the pip layer. --no-cache-dir (or a BuildKit cache mount — RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip, full syntax in Chapter 5) is the only fix that actually works. This chapter's Under the Hood section walks the exact overlay2 mechanism behind why.

🧪 Practice — Prove Cross-Layer Deletion Is a Lie

Build one image that installs a package in layer N and rms it in layer N+1. Build a second image that installs and removes it in the SAME RUN. Compare both with docker images. Verify: only the single-RUN variant is actually smaller — docker history even shows the late rm layer as "0 B", because the bytes never left, they just became invisible in the merged view.

📖 docker build --squash — a Blunter, Riskier Alternative

The classic (non-BuildKit) builder can flatten every instruction into one final layer with docker build --squash (requires the daemon's experimental feature flag). A squashed image genuinely deletes fossilized bytes — even ones created and removed across separate RUN instructions — because the whole stack collapses into a single filesystem diff. The cost: you lose per-instruction layer caching on every future build (a one-line Dockerfile edit invalidates the WHOLE squashed layer, not just the instruction that changed), and BuildKit — the default builder since Docker 23 — does not support it at all. Multi-stage builds (8.3-8.4) get the same byte savings without that caching tax, which is why this guide reaches for multi-stage first and treats --squash as a niche, legacy-builder option.

8.4 Python/Django Specific Optimizations

Optimized Dockerfile for Django
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
# Collect static in the builder — final stage never needs the toolchain that produced it
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Copy only installed packages (not build tools!)
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Copy application code — already includes the static/ collected above
COPY --from=builder /app /app
# Security: run as non-root
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app
USER app
# No build tools, no caches, minimal attack surface!
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
💡 Django Optimization Checklist

✅ FROM python:3.11-slim (8.2's glibc-wheel argument). ✅ Use --no-cache-dir with pip. ✅ Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. ✅ Multi-stage: collect static in builder, serve from final. ✅ Remove dev dependencies for production (a separate requirements/prod.txt). ✅ Use .dockerignore for __pycache__, .git, env/.

🎸 Analogy — Touring Gear vs Rehearsal Gear

The band rehearses with spare amps, extra cables, and a sound engineer standing by (dev dependencies, gcc, pytest). The tour bus — the image you actually ship — carries only what gets played ON STAGE. Anything that only earns its keep at rehearsal stays behind in the builder stage.

📖 Three Requirements Files, Not One

Split requirements.txt into base.txt (shared), prod.txt (base + gunicorn, psycopg2-binary), and dev.txt (base + pytest, debug-toolbar, coverage) — then install ONLY prod.txt in the image. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in the ENV line above isn't a size optimization at all — it's for correct real-time log ordering (Chapter 6) — but it costs nothing to set alongside PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 since they share the same instruction.

🔬 easypj: dropping dev-only packages and moving collectstatic into the builder stage is what actually delivers the 850 MB → ~180 MB result promised back in 8.1 — measured with docker images, not assumed from a checklist.

🧪 Practice — Prove the Dev Dependencies Actually Left

Build easypj once with dev.txt installed, then again with prod.txt only. Compare sizes with docker images, then run docker run --rm easypj:prod python -c "import pytest". Verify: the prod image is measurably smaller AND the import fails — proof the ballast (and its CVEs) actually left the ship, not just that a line was deleted from a text file.

8.5 Image Scanning — Docker Scout

Docker Scout analyzes your images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs). It examines every layer, every package, and gives you actionable remediation advice.

TERMINAL
# Quick vulnerability summary
$ docker scout quickview easypj:v1
  ✓ SBOM of image already cached, 123 packages indexed
  ## Overview
  │               Analyzed Image
  ├───────────────────────────────
  │ Target   │  easypj:v1
  │     digest   │  abc12345
  │     platform │  linux/amd64
  │     vulnerabilities         │    1C     2H     7M     25L
  │     size     │  180 MB
  │     packages │  123

# Detailed CVE report
$ docker scout cves easypj:v1

# Get fix recommendations
$ docker scout recommendations easypj:v1
  Recommendation: Update base image
  Current: python:3.11-slim (Debian 12)
  Suggestion: Rebuild to get latest security patches
  Impact: Fixes 15 CVEs
🔴
Critical

Remote code execution, privilege escalation. Fix IMMEDIATELY — these can compromise your entire system. Example: CVE-2024-xxxx in libssl.

🟠
High

Can lead to data breach or denial of service. Fix within days. Example: buffer overflow in image processing library.

🟡
Medium/Low

Limited impact or requires unlikely conditions. Fix in regular update cycle. These still count as CVEs in your scan report.

📖 SBOM: Software Bill of Materials

Docker Scout generates an SBOM — a complete inventory of every package in your image, including transitive dependencies. Think of it as a nutrition label for your container. SBOMs are increasingly required for compliance (US Executive Order 14028). You can export yours: docker scout sbom easypj:v1 --format spdx.

The split, isolated
$ docker scout quickview easypj:v1.1
  Target    easypj:v1.1       1C 2H  7M 25L
  Base      python:3.11-slim  0C 1H  5M 22L

Subtract the Base row from the Target row: the 1 Critical, plus the delta on every other severity, lives entirely in your layer — bump the offending pin in requirements.txt and rebuild. Everything that appears on BOTH rows is the base's problem, fixed by pulling a fresh python:3.11-slim and rebuilding — same docker build command, a different line changed.

📖 The Real CLI Labels the Rows "Your image" / "Base image"

This chapter uses "Target" and "Base" as teaching labels for the split. The actual docker scout quickview output labels the same two rows Your image and Base image — and for images built with --provenance attestations (the default when pushing via Buildx), it can print two MORE rows, Refreshed base image and Updated base image, each showing the CVE delta you'd get by rebuilding on the current or a newer base tag, before you even run the rebuild.

🏗️ Analogy — A Building Inspection

The report separates faults in the foundation you bought (the base image) from faults in the walls you built (your own pip layer). You don't re-pour the foundation yourself — you take the builder's newer revision and rebuild on top of it.

🔬 easypj: a Critical in Django itself lands in YOUR layer — bump the pin in requirements.txt and rebuild. A Critical in zlib is the base's — pull the fresh python:3.11-slim and rebuild. Same command, different line changed.

📖 Zero CVEs Isn't the Goal

Zero CVEs is not a realistic target — new ones get published against old, unchanged packages every day. The real goal is zero UNREVIEWED criticals: every Critical and High finding triaged, and either fixed or consciously accepted with a reason.

🧪 Practice — One Minute, Three Answers

Run docker scout quickview, docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high, and docker scout recommendations against any image you've built. Verify you can state, inside one minute: (a) the critical/high count, (b) the base-vs-your-layer split, (c) the single next action to take.

⚠️ Images Don't Rot by Changing — They Rot by Standing Still

An easypj image that hasn't been rebuilt in two months can still show 15 NEW CVEs today versus its last scan — the image is byte-for-byte identical, but the CVE database learned about new vulnerabilities in the same old packages. Rescan on a SCHEDULE, not only on rebuild.

8.6 Distroless Images — The Ultimate Security

Distroless images, created by Google, contain ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies. No shell, no package manager, no curl, no utilities — nothing an attacker can use. They are the gold standard for container security.

🛡️
Why Distroless?

Every tool in your container is a weapon for an attacker. Shell = interactive access. Curl/wget = exfiltrate data. Package manager = install malware. Distroless removes ALL of these. If there's no shell, docker exec simply cannot work — blocking the most common post-exploitation vector.

🐛
How to Debug

No shell means no docker exec -it bash. Instead: (1) Use structured logging (JSON to stdout), (2) Use kubectl debug with ephemeral containers in Kubernetes, (3) Use sidecar debugging containers sharing the PID namespace, (4) Embed a health-check HTTP endpoint in your app.

📖 Distroless Isn't Only for Python

Google's gcr.io/distroless family ships a matching minimal runtime-only image for every major language, not just python3-debian12 — the same "no shell, no package manager" tradeoff this section teaches for easypj applies identically whichever language stage you're shipping.

Distroless imageRuntime it shipsTypical use case
gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12CPython interpreter onlyeasypj (this chapter)
gcr.io/distroless/java17-debian12JRE 17 onlySpring Boot / other JVM services
gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12Node.js 20 runtime onlyExpress/Node APIs
gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12glibc + SSL certs + tzdata, no language runtimestatically-compiled Go binaries needing TLS/timezone support (leaner than FROM scratch, which has neither)
gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12base plus libc/libstdc++Rust or C/C++ binaries dynamically linked against glibc
📖 Docker Hardened Images — Docker's Own Maintained Alternative to DIY Distroless

Since December 17, 2025, Docker publishes its own hardened-image catalog at docs.docker.com/dhi/ — the Community tier is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and every image ships a signed SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, and a near-zero-CVE baseline out of the box, with no scan-and-patch cycle required on your side. A Python migration follows the exact multi-stage shape this section already builds by hand — a -dev tag for the builder stage, the bare tag for the runtime stage — just pulled from Docker's own registry instead of Google's:

DHI Python — build vs runtime stage
FROM dhi.io/python:3.13-alpine3.23-dev AS builder
# ... pip install, collectstatic — same steps as the builder stage above ...

FROM dhi.io/python:3.13-alpine3.23

(dhi.io requires authenticating with a Docker account before the first pull — unlike gcr.io/distroless, it is not an anonymous public registry.) DHI doesn't replace the gcr.io/distroless approach above; it's a maintained, subscription-backed alternative to the SAME problem this chapter solves by hand — Docker owns the CVE-patching cadence and the attestation paperwork, in exchange for pulling from its own registry and, past the free Community tier, a paid Select or Enterprise plan for SLA-backed remediation (critical CVEs fixed within 7 days) and compliance variants (FIPS, STIG, CIS).

🏦 Analogy — A Bank Vault With No Doorway

Builders assembled the vault around its contents — the multi-stage COPY --from=builder equivalent — so there is no door for burglars, and no door for the locksmith either. You interact only through slots designed in advance: a published port, a stdout log stream, nothing more.

DISTROLESS DOCKERFILE for easypj
# Stage 1: Build (has all tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Distroless final (NO shell, NO package manager!)
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12
WORKDIR /app
# Copy Python packages from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
# Copy application code
COPY --from=builder /app /app
# Copy static files
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
# Set Python path
ENV PYTHONPATH=/app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Run as non-root (distroless default user)
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8000
# No bash, no sh — just the Python binary
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/python3"]
CMD ["-m", "gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
📖 nonroot Is Always UID 65532 — and Ships a :debug Twin

Across every gcr.io/distroless/* image — python3, java17, nodejs20, all of them — the nonroot user resolves to the same fixed UID/GID 65532:65532, not a name invented per language. That consistency is what makes USER nonroot:nonroot portable across the whole distroless family, but it also means any volume or bind mount the container needs to WRITE to (media uploads, a cache dir) must already be owned by 65532 on the host or in the volume — there's no shell inside the running container to chown it after the fact. For troubleshooting only, Google also publishes a -debug-suffixed tag for every distroless image (e.g. gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:debug) that bundles a busybox shell — docker run --rm -it easypj:debug sh works where the production tag's sh fails. Never ship the :debug tag: it reintroduces exactly the shell this section opened by removing — the whole point of 8.6 was that a shell is a weapon for an attacker.

FeatureStandard ImageDistroless Image
Shell (bash/sh)✅ Available❌ None — attacker can't exec
Package manager (apt/pip)✅ Available❌ None — can't install malware
Core utilities (curl, wget, netcat)✅ Available❌ None — can't exfiltrate data
Size (Python app)~180 MB (slim) / ~900 MB (full)~65 MB
CVEs30-40+~10-20 (only runtime libs)
Debuggingdocker exec -it bashkubectl debug / ephemeral containers
Best forMost production workloads — a hardened slim image is the default (8.2-8.5)Maximum-security production, regulated environments (8.6's ceiling)
⚠️ Distroless Requires Multi-Stage

You CANNOT use distroless as a single-stage build — there's no shell to run pip install. You MUST use a multi-stage build: the first stage (with shell) installs everything, the second stage (distroless) copies only the artifacts. The DCA exam may test this constraint.

⚠️ Shell Entrypoint Scripts Don't Survive the Jump to Distroless

easypj's normal docker-entrypoint.sh — the one that waits for the database, runs migrate, then execs gunicorn — is a shell script, and distroless has no /bin/sh to interpret it. Migrations have to move OUT of the entrypoint entirely: run them as a separate one-off container on the builder-stage (non-distroless) base, or as a dedicated exec-form startup step distroless CAN run directly, before the final distroless stage takes over.

🧪 Practice — Prove the Shell Is Actually Gone

Build the distroless variant above, then try docker exec -it easypj-dl sh. Verify: OCI runtime exec failed... no such file or directory — the missing shell IS the security feature, not a bug. docker logs easypj-dl still shows everything gunicorn says; only interactive exec is gone.

🔧 Under the Hood — the six mechanisms behind every trick in this chapter

8.1-8.6 taught six practical moves — clean up in the same RUN, skip Recommends, prefer slim, set an env var, read a scanner split, jump to distroless. Each one leans on a specific piece of Linux/toolchain mechanism underneath it; this section walks all six, in the same order the diagram below lists them.

 EVERY "optimization trick" above leans on ONE underlying mechanism:

   cleanup in the same RUN (8.3) ─────────▶ ① OverlayFS whiteouts, BUILD-time vs container-time
   --no-install-recommends (8.3) ─────────▶ ② apt's Depends / Recommends / Suggests graph
   slim beats alpine (8.2) ────────────────▶ ③ the ELF dynamic linker + manylinux/musllinux wheel tags
   PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 (8.4) ───────▶ ④ CPython's PEP 552 bytecode cache
   docker scout quickview's split (8.5) ──▶ ⑤ BuildKit provenance attestations
   distroless's CVE drop (8.6) ───────────▶ ⑥ the dpkg database that was never installed
🔑 None of these six are new tools to learn — they're the reasons the six tricks you already know actually work, in enough detail that you could rebuild each rule from first principles if you forgot the rule of thumb.
① OverlayFS Whiteouts — the BUILD Layer Is Not the Container's Writable Layer

8.3's claim — "cleanup MUST happen in the same RUN, or the bytes are fossilized" — and the mechanism behind it (a WHITEOUT: a character-device marker, major/minor number 0/0, written under the same name as the deleted file) are the same overlay2 primitive Chapter 18's Under the Hood section deep-dives for a running container's writable layer. The two situations look identical on the page but are NOT the same lifetime. A container has exactly ONE writable layer (its upperdir), shared by every process inside it, that is destroyed completely — whiteouts and all — the moment docker rm runs. A build has no such shared scratch space at all: BuildKit commits a brand-new, individually PERMANENT read-only layer after every single RUN/COPY/ADD instruction, and each of those layers ships inside every image built FROM this one, forever. A RUN rm -rf in a later instruction isn't cleaning up shared scratch space — it is manufacturing a new permanent layer whose entire content is a handful of whiteout markers pointing at bytes that are still sitting, undisturbed, in the permanent layer right below it.

 docker build — ONE layer PER INSTRUCTION, each PERMANENT, shipped forever
   RUN pip install -r requirements.txt   → layer N    commits ~180 MB of real files   ┐
   RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip           → layer N+1  commits ONE whiteout marker     ┘  BOTH
                                                                                            ship in
                                                                                            every
                                                                                            derived
                                                                                            image

 docker run — ONE writable layer TOTAL per container, fully EPHEMERAL
   any process inside the container writes or deletes → all of it lands in ONE upperdir
   docker rm <container>  →  that upperdir is destroyed whole, whiteouts and all — nothing shipped
PropertyContainer's writable layerA build-time image layer (here)
How many existexactly one, shared by the whole containerone PER instruction that touches the filesystem
Lifetimeephemeral — gone on docker rmpermanent — baked into the image, and every image built FROM it
What a whiteout there means"hidden until someone removes this one container""hidden in this image and every descendant, forever — the earlier layer's bytes never leave"
🔑 This is the mechanical reason 8.3's rule has no exceptions: because BuildKit commits one PERMANENT layer per instruction rather than accumulating writes into one shared scratch space, there is no later point in a multi-instruction Dockerfile where a delete can ever reach backward and shrink an already-committed layer — the only RUN that can avoid fossilizing bytes is the one that never wrote them to that layer in the first place.
② apt's Dependency Graph — Depends, Recommends, and Suggests Are Three Different Promises

8.3's --no-install-recommends flag skips a specific, named edge in Debian's own package metadata, not a vague "extra stuff" bucket. Every .deb's control stanza can declare three separate relationship fields: Depends: (hard requirement — apt refuses to install the package at all without satisfying every one of these), Recommends: (apt installs these BY DEFAULT alongside the package, on the theory that "most users would want this too" — this is the exact behavior --no-install-recommends switches off), and Suggests: (apt never auto-installs these under any default setting; they are purely informational, surfaced only if you go looking). The flag — or the equivalent persistent setting APT::Install-Recommends "false"; — tells apt's dependency resolver to compute the install set by walking ONLY the Depends graph, pruning every Recommends edge before it ever reaches the download queue.

 apt-get install libpq5   (Debian's control-file relationship graph)

   libpq5
     ├─ Depends:    libc6, ...              ← apt ALWAYS installs these — hard requirement
     ├─ Recommends: (varies by release)     ← apt installs these TOO, unless --no-install-recommends
     └─ Suggests:   (varies by release)      ← apt NEVER auto-installs these, informational only

   RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5
        walks ONLY the Depends edges ──▶ smaller install set, same package still fully functional
   RUN apt-get install -y libpq5                    (no flag)
        walks Depends AND Recommends edges ──▶ larger install set — the "roughly halves" gap in 8.3
Control fieldapt's default behaviorSkipped by --no-install-recommends?
Depends:always installed — the package won't install without itnever — it's a hard requirement, not optional
Recommends:installed by default, alongside Depends✅ yes — this is the whole effect of the flag
Suggests:never auto-installed, any wayn/a — already skipped by default
🔑 "Roughly halves a typical apt payload" (8.3) is a rule of thumb about how heavily Debian's maintainers lean on Recommends, package by package — some packages carry almost nothing there, others (anything with an optional GUI helper, docs package, or companion CLI tool) carry a lot. The flag itself is not a heuristic at all: it is a precise, deterministic instruction to prune one named edge type from apt's dependency graph, every time.
③ The ELF Dynamic Linker — the Mechanical Reason glibc Beats musl for Python C-Extensions

8.2's table says "musl libc ≠ glibc — some Python packages break." The break happens at a specific, inspectable point: every compiled binary or shared library on Linux is an ELF file, and every DYNAMICALLY linked one embeds an interpreter path in its .interp section — /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 on a glibc system, /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 on Alpine. When the kernel exec()s that file, it hands control to whichever interpreter path is embedded, and THAT program resolves the file's DT_NEEDED list of required shared libraries and symbols before your code ever runs. A Python C-extension (a .so file — psycopg2's, Pillow's, numpy's) is exactly this kind of ELF binary, and PyPI's "manylinux" wheels (tagged e.g. manylinux_2_28_x86_64) are compiled against glibc specifically, using glibc's SYMBOL VERSIONING scheme (symbols suffixed @GLIBC_2.x) — a mechanism musl's linker does not implement the same way. The mismatch isn't a missing file; it's an ELF interpreter that fundamentally cannot resolve those versioned symbols against musl's own libc.so.

 pip install psycopg2-binary   — wheel-tag resolution at install time

   pip reads the running interpreter's platform tag (via packaging.tags)
        │
        ├─ on python:3.11-slim (glibc) → looks for manylinux_2_28_x86_64 wheels
        │        found on PyPI → download prebuilt .so → done in seconds
        │
        └─ on python:3.11-alpine (musl) → looks for musllinux_1_2_x86_64 wheels
                 rarely published for C-extension-heavy packages → falls back to
                 the SOURCE distribution (sdist) → needs gcc + musl-dev + headers
                 → compiles from scratch, several minutes, only THEN installs
Aspectglibc (Debian / slim)musl (Alpine)
ELF interpreter path (.interp)/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2/lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1
Symbol versioningyes — @GLIBC_2.x suffixesno equivalent scheme
Wheel tag pip resolves tomanylinux_2_28_x86_64 (broad coverage)musllinux_1_2_x86_64 (sparse for C-extensions)
Typical install path for psycopg2/Pillow/numpyprebuilt wheel, secondssdist compile, minutes, needs a toolchain
🔑 This is exactly why 8.2's timed practice drill shows slim installing in seconds and alpine either compiling for minutes or failing outright wanting pg_config — the wheel that "just works" on slim was never going to resolve against musl's ELF interpreter, no matter how the Dockerfile is written.
④ CPython's Bytecode Cache — Why PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 Costs Nothing

8.4's checklist lists PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 as a free win, and the reason is in CPython's own import machinery (PEP 552). On every import, CPython compiles the source to bytecode in memory — that step is mandatory, there is no way to run a .py file without it. Separately, by default, CPython ALSO writes that compiled form to disk as <module>.cpython-311.pyc inside a __pycache__/ directory, tagging the file's header with the source's mtime and size (PEP 552's default "timestamp-based" mode; an optional "hash-based" mode stores a source hash instead, useful when mtimes aren't trustworthy — which is close to always true after a Docker COPY). Setting PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 sets sys.dont_write_bytecode = True, which disables ONLY that second, optional disk-write step. The in-memory compile — the part that actually costs CPU — happens exactly the same either way.

 import myapp.views                          (every time, either way)
      │
      ▼
 CPython compiles views.py → bytecode, IN MEMORY   ← mandatory, unavoidable, same cost both ways
      │
      ├─ PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE unset (default):
      │     also WRITES __pycache__/views.cpython-311.pyc to disk
      │     → becomes a real file in this build's layer diff (or a stale, un-reused one)
      │
      └─ PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1:
            skips the write entirely — sys.dont_write_bytecode = True
            → zero bytes added to any layer, zero extra runtime cost vs. the unset case
.pyc modeHeader storesRecompiles when…
Timestamp-based (default)source mtime + sizesource's mtime OR size differs from the stored value
Hash-based, checkedhash of source bytessource bytes differ — re-hashed and compared on EVERY import (slower)
Hash-based, uncheckedhash of source bytesnever re-checked — trusted blindly, fastest, used for frozen/vendored code
🔑 CPython's import machinery also catches a failed .pyc write (permission denied, read-only filesystem) and silently continues running from the in-memory compiled form rather than crashing — so the env var isn't required for CORRECTNESS even on a 19.5-style --read-only container; it just avoids paying for a disk write (and the log noise of a failed one) that was never going to survive anyway.
⑤ Build Attestations — How docker scout quickview Actually Knows Which Image Is "Base"

8.5's two-row split (Target vs Base) requires Scout to know, with certainty, exactly WHICH upstream image a given build pulled FROM — not "probably the newest python:3.11-slim," but the exact digest that was resolved at build time, which a moving tag can disagree with later. BuildKit answers this with a PROVENANCE ATTESTATION: an in-toto-formatted JSON document, generated automatically for images pushed via buildx (--provenance=true is the default for pushed images since Buildx 0.10), stored as its own entry alongside the image manifest, recording the exact base-image digest(s) that build actually resolved and pulled. Scout reads that attestation, resolves the recorded digest to that upstream image's OWN SBOM (generating or fetching one, the same INVENTORY step behind every scan), scans it independently, and computes the Base/Target split as a straightforward SET DIFFERENCE of the two SBOMs' CVE matches.

 BUILD TIME (docker buildx build --provenance=true, on by default when pushing)
   FROM python:3.11-slim  ──resolve──▶ digest sha256:aaa…
        │
        ▼
   provenance attestation (in-toto JSON) embeds: "actually built FROM sha256:aaa…"
        │  pushed as its own manifest entry, alongside the image

 SCAN TIME (docker scout quickview easypj:v1.1)
   reads the provenance attestation ──▶ resolved Base digest = sha256:aaa…
        │
        ├─▶ scans Target (easypj:v1.1)'s own SBOM  → full CVE match list
        ├─▶ scans Base (sha256:aaa…)'s SBOM         → its own CVE match list
        ▼
   Target list − Base list = "YOUR LAYER" row      Target ∩ Base = "BASE" row
PathSource of "which image is Base"Accuracy of the split
With a provenance attestationexact digest, recorded at build timeexact — matches what was actually built
Without one (older image, or built without BuildKit)Scout re-parses the FROM line from the image config's history[] and re-resolves that TAG nowapproximate — can drift if the tag moved since the original build
🔑 This is what Chapter 7's Docker Content Trust box was pointing at when it named --sbom/--provenance as the modern supply-chain answer: the attestation isn't just an audit trail, it is the literal data source 8.5's base-vs-your-layer split reads from. An unattested image doesn't lose the SPLIT feature entirely — it just falls back to a same-tag guess instead of a recorded fact.
⑥ Distroless's Missing dpkg Database — a Structural CVE Drop, Not Just a Smaller One

Chapter 21's Under the Hood section establishes that a vulnerability scanner's first step is always INVENTORY: enumerate every installed OS package by reading the package manager's own metadata — on Debian/Ubuntu, that means /var/lib/dpkg/status. A distroless image has no such file at all — not a trimmed-down one, an ABSENT one — because distroless images are never built by running apt install and then deleting things afterward; they are assembled by copying only the specific runtime library FILES a small, fixed set of packages need directly into a layer, computed ahead of time as a dependency closure. The package manager's own bookkeeping — the step that would have created and updated /var/lib/dpkg/status in the first place — simply never ran inside the image at any point in its construction.

 STANDARD slim image scan                        DISTROLESS image scan
   read /var/lib/dpkg/status                        look for /var/lib/dpkg/status
        │  found → N installed OS packages                │  ABSENT — nothing to enumerate
        ▼                                                  ▼
   match each against CVE feed                       (OS-package CVE bucket: structurally empty)
        │  → OS-package CVE bucket: N findings
        ▼
   ALSO read pip metadata (Django, psycopg2, ...)     ALSO read pip metadata (Django, psycopg2, ...)
        │  → app-package CVE bucket: M findings             │  → app-package CVE bucket: M findings
        ▼                                                    ▼
   TOTAL: N (OS) + M (app)                            TOTAL: 0 (OS, structural) + M (app) only
Layer of the stackPresent in distroless?Shows up in a CVE scan?
Debian OS packages (dpkg-tracked)❌ never installed — no dpkg database exists to track them❌ no OS-package CVE bucket at all — nothing to enumerate
glibc + the Python interpreter's own shared libraries✅ copied in deliberately — the interpreter can't run without them✅ yes — these can and do still carry CVEs
Python packages (Django, psycopg2, ...)✅ copied in via COPY --from=builder /root/.local✅ yes — pip's own package metadata is still readable
🔑 This is also the deep reason 8.6's danger box is unconditional, not a policy choice: pip install needs a package manager binary AND somewhere to record what it installed, and distroless's build process never assembled either — there is no apt/dpkg to delete, because dependency-closure assembly never copied one in to begin with. Multi-stage isn't a best practice here; it's the only way to get bytes INTO an image that was never given the tooling to install them itself.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Size is a recurring tax, not a one-time cost: it multiplies by every pull, every CI job, every node — 850MB vs 180MB is an 11-min vs 2.4-min pull at 10 Mbps.
  • python:3.11-slim is the Django default: glibc means prebuilt manylinux wheels install in seconds; alpine's musl libc forces slow, fragile source builds for the same packages.
  • Layers only ever grow — cleanup MUST happen in the same RUN that created the mess, or the bytes are fossilized.
  • Django's specific win: slim base + --no-cache-dir + no .pyc + multi-stage collectstatic + prod-only requirements = the 850MB → ~180MB result, measured not assumed.
  • docker scout quickview splits findings into BASE (fixed by rebuilding on a newer base) vs YOUR LAYER (fixed by bumping your own pins) — read the split, don't just count CVEs.
  • Distroless removes the shell and package manager entirely — a huge attack-surface win, but it also removes shell-based entrypoints and shell-based HEALTHCHECKs.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: expect items on WHY a smaller image is preferred and on distinguishing build-time vs runtime dependencies — both are graded, not just "best practice."
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Any layer's cleanup shrinks the image → Optimizing the app layer is wasted effort if the BASE image is 700MB — always attack the biggest layer first (docker history).
  • Alpine always saves space → Its "savings" often come back as gcc/musl-dev needed just to compile a wheel that slim gets prebuilt — measure the WHOLE build, not just the final base size.
  • libpq5 is safe to delete in the final stage → Deleting it breaks Django at the first database query — psycopg2 needs it at runtime.
  • A HEALTHCHECK with curl works on distroless → distroless has no shell: a HEALTHCHECK CMD using curl, or a shell ENTRYPOINT script, silently cannot run.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker history <image> | head -5 right after any build — the two heaviest rows tell you exactly where 8.2-8.4 apply next.
  • Keep separate requirements/base.txt, requirements/prod.txt, requirements/dev.txt from day one — a prod-only build is then one -r requirements/prod.txt away, no editing required.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 8)

find the fat, scan it, confirm the fix 
# Find the fat layers
docker history <image>

# CVE count, base split
docker scout quickview <image>
docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high <image>

# Suggested next fix
docker scout recommendations <image>

# Confirm size after a fix
docker images <repo>

# Prove dev deps gone
docker run --rm <image> python -c "import pytest"

🧠 Chapter 8 — DCA Practice Questions (20)

Quick recall of image-shrinking mechanics, plus scenario-based reasoning with real numbers — 20 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why is Alpine Linux NOT always the best choice for Python applications?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Alpine uses musl libc instead of glibc. Many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy) are compiled against glibc and may fail or behave unexpectedly on musl. Slim images (Debian-based) avoid these issues.

EXPLANATION

Alpine is ~5 MB — incredibly small — but the musl tradeoff means you'll spend hours debugging cryptic C-extension errors. For Django apps, python:3.11-slim is the pragmatic choice: Debian compatibility at a reasonable size.

C-extension packagepython:3.11-slim (glibc)python:3.11-alpine (musl)
psycopg2✅ prebuilt wheel, ~seconds⚠️ needs gcc + postgresql-dev, slow source build
Pillow✅ prebuilt wheel⚠️ needs jpeg-dev, zlib-dev
numpy✅ prebuilt wheel⚠️ slow source compile, bigger effective image once build tools are counted
Q2
What's the proper way to chain RUN commands to minimize layers and clean up?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg1 pkg2 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. All in one RUN — one layer, no cached package lists bloating the image.

EXPLANATION

Separate RUN commands create separate layers. Even if you rm -rf in layer 3, the files still exist in layer 2 (just "deleted" from view, via a whiteout marker). Chaining ensures the cleanup happens in the SAME layer, so the files truly never enter the image.

  ❌ SEPARATE (3 layers)                   ✅ CHAINED (1 layer)
  RUN apt-get update            L1         RUN apt-get update \
  RUN apt-get install -y pkg    L2          && apt-get install -y pkg \
  RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*  L3        && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*   L1

  lists/* hidden by a whiteout in L3,       lists/* is never committed to
  but STILL sitting inside L2 ❌             any layer at all — genuinely gone ✅
Q3
What is a distroless image and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A distroless image contains ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no utilities. It is used for maximum security: no shell means an attacker who compromises your container cannot exec into it.

EXPLANATION

Distroless images are built by Google — only your app, its runtime, and essential libraries. No shell means docker exec cannot work. Debug via logs or kubectl debug with ephemeral containers in Kubernetes.

python:3.11-slimDistroless
Shell (bash/sh)✅ present❌ none
Package manager✅ apt/pip❌ none
docker exec -it <ctr> bash✅ works❌ fails — nothing to exec into
Q4
What command scans a Docker image for known vulnerabilities?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker scout quickview <image> for a summary, docker scout cves <image> for detailed CVEs.

EXPLANATION

Docker Scout replaced docker scan, generating an SBOM and checking every package against vulnerability databases — and it splits findings into base-image vs your-layer.

  $ docker scout quickview easypj:v1
    vulnerabilities   1C   2H   7M   25L        ← summary only

  $ docker scout cves easypj:v1
    CVE-2024-xxxx  libssl  CRITICAL  fixed in 3.0.14   ← full per-CVE detail
Q5
How does a multi-stage build reduce image size?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The first stage includes build tools; the final stage copies only built artifacts. Build tools stay in the discarded first stage, slashing image size by 70-80%.

EXPLANATION

Without multi-stage: either include build tools (850 MB+) or build outside Docker (not reproducible). Multi-stage gives both a clean build environment and a slim shipped image.

  STAGE 1 "builder" (has gcc, has pip cache)   STAGE 2 "final" (ships)
  FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder             FROM python:3.11-slim
  RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt   COPY --from=builder /root/.local ./
  COPY . .                                     COPY . .
        │
        └── entire stage DISCARDED ──▶ never reaches the pushed image
Q6
Why should you use --no-cache-dir with pip install in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Pip cache stores downloaded packages. In Docker, this cache is never reused (each build is fresh, or reuses BuildKit's own cache mount instead). --no-cache-dir prevents ~100 MB waste.

EXPLANATION

Pip caches wheels in ~/.cache/pip. In a plain Docker build, that on-disk cache does not carry over between builds — it only wastes layer space in the image you ship.

Install command~/.cache/pip written to layer?Extra size
pip install -r requirements.txt✅ yes+~100-180 MB (8.1's breakdown)
pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt❌ no+0 MB
Q7
What's the size difference between python:3.11 (full) and python:3.11-slim?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

python:3.11 full is roughly double the size of python:3.11-slim — the full image includes build tools and docs not needed at runtime.

EXPLANATION

The full image includes GCC, make, git, docs — none needed at runtime. Slim keeps glibc compatibility while removing development cruft.

TagSize (8.2's table)Contains
python:3.11~268 MBGCC, make, git, docs — dev toolbox
python:3.11-slim~130 MBglibc + apt, runtime only
Q8
What Python environment variables help reduce image size?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 prevents .pyc generation. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 ensures stdout is not buffered for better Docker logging.

EXPLANATION

Python compiles .py to .pyc on first import — wasting space in immutable container filesystems. The first variable skips this.

Env varEffectWhy it matters in a container
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Skips .pyc generationFilesystem is rebuilt every deploy anyway — .pyc is pure waste

What is the Scratch base image and when is it appropriate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Scratch is completely empty (0 bytes). Only for statically-compiled binaries (Go, Rust). No shell, no libc — binary must be fully self-contained.

EXPLANATION

Go example: FROM scratch; COPY --from=builder /app/server /server; CMD ["/server"]. Python/Node/Ruby cannot use Scratch — they need an interpreter present.

LanguageStatic binary possible?Works FROM scratch?
Go (CGO_ENABLED=0)✅ yes✅ yes
Rust (musl target)✅ yes✅ yes
Python / Node / Ruby❌ needs an interpreter❌ no
Q10
Your production image has 120 CVEs. What's the fastest way to fix most of them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rebuild with an updated base image. Most CVEs come from outdated system packages in the base image. Run docker pull python:3.11-slim (get the latest) and rebuild. Then run docker scout quickview to verify the fix.

EXPLANATION

System-level CVEs (in libc, OpenSSL, etc.) come from the base image. Rebuilding with the latest base image picks up all security patches. Application-level CVEs (in pip packages) require updating requirements.txt — docker scout recommendations tells you which category each CVE falls into.

CVE sourceFastest fix
System packages in the base (libc, OpenSSL...)Rebuild on a freshly-pulled python:3.11-slim
Application-level (pip packages)Bump the pin in requirements.txt

Disk is only one of four costs — pull time, CI bandwidth, and CVE count also scale with size, and none of those are "cheap."

The size tax is paid on EVERY deploy, forever — not once at build:

slim uses glibc (Debian), so psycopg2-binary and other manylinux wheels install as prebuilt binaries in seconds; alpine's musl libc often forces a slow source compile (or fails outright without extra build tools).

The "savings" from alpine's smaller base are frequently erased by needing gcc, musl-dev, and postgresql-dev in the build stage — smaller base, bigger real cost.

Q13
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt in layer 3, followed by RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip in layer 4 — does layer 4 shrink the final image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — zero bytes recovered.

EXPLANATION

Overlay filesystems are additive; a later layer can only HIDE a file with a whiteout marker, not remove its bytes from an already-committed earlier layer. docker history even shows layer 4 as "0B" — the cache never left, it just became invisible in the merged view.

  Layer 3: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt   → commits ~180 MB (incl. cache)
  Layer 4: RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip           → writes a WHITEOUT marker only

  docker history:  Layer 4 SIZE = 0B  ← cache bytes still sit in Layer 3, merely hidden

Show Answer & Explanation

Any three of: --no-cache-dir on pip install; splitting requirements into base/prod/dev and installing prod-only; running collectstatic in a builder stage (not the final image); setting PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1.

Q16
An easypj image hasn't been rebuilt in two months, yet a scan today shows 15 new CVEs it didn't have at build time. Did the image change?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Images don't rot by changing, but they do rot in the sense of being scanned against an ever-growing database — rescanning on a SCHEDULE (not only on rebuild) is the only way to catch this.

  Build day:   easypj:v1  (bytes X)  ──scan──▶  0 new findings
  +2 months:   easypj:v1  (SAME bytes X)  ──scan──▶  15 new findings

              image never changed — the CVE DATABASE grew, not the image

docker exec -it <container> bash cannot work because there is no bash; most post-exploitation tooling (sh, curl, apt, wget) an attacker would reach for simply does not exist in the image at all.

The migration/wait logic has to move out of a shell entrypoint and into a separate step (a one-off container on the builder-stage base, or an exec-form startup distroless CAN run) before the final distroless stage can be used.

  docker-entrypoint.sh  (wait-for-db && migrate && exec gunicorn)
          │
          ▼
     needs /bin/sh to interpret it   ──▶   ❌ absent on distroless

          ▼
     FIX: run migrate as a one-off container on the builder-stage base,
          then let distroless's exec-form CMD start gunicorn directly
Q19
A HEALTHCHECK using curl -f http://localhost:8000/ worked fine on python:3.11-slim. It silently fails after switching to distroless. Why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

distroless has no curl (no shell, no coreutils, no utilities).

EXPLANATION

The fix is a probe distroless CAN run natively — python -c "import urllib.request; ..." — or moving health probing to the orchestrator entirely (the Kubernetes guide).

Basecurl present?HEALTHCHECK CMD curl works?
python:3.11-slim✅ if installed✅ yes
distroless❌ none❌ silently fails
Q20
Rank these four techniques by expected size impact for easypj, biggest first: (a) --no-cache-dir, (b) slim vs full Debian base, (c) multi-stage collectstatic, (d) removing dev-only requirements.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Roughly (b) > (d) ≈ (c) > (a) — the base image swap is the single biggest lever (268MB → 130MB before anything else changes); dropping dev requirements and moving collectstatic out of the final stage are next biggest; --no-cache-dir alone saves real but comparatively smaller MBs.

RankTechniqueImpact
1(b) slim vs full Debian basebiggest — 268MB → 130MB before anything else changes
2(d) drop dev-only requirementsremoves dev deps and their CVEs
2(c) multi-stage collectstatickeeps the static-build toolchain out of the final image
4(a) --no-cache-dirsmaller but real MBs saved
EXPLANATION

This ordering is exactly why this chapter's Gotchas box insists on attacking the BIGGEST layer first — order of operations matters.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.1 — Shrink One Real Image

⏱️ Target Time: 10 minutes
Scenario

Pick any image you built in Part 2, run docker history on it, name its two heaviest layers, then apply ONE technique from 8.2-8.4 and rebuild. Done when docker images shows a measurably smaller SIZE for the same functionality.

Hint: docker history <image> | head -5 right after the ORIGINAL build tells you exactly where to spend your one fix — the two heaviest rows are always either the base image itself or an uncleaned RUN layer (this chapter's Speed Tip).
View Solution
TERMINAL

docker history myapp:v1
# IMAGE    CREATED BY                       SIZE
# ab12cd3  RUN apt-get install -y gcc ...   240MB   ← heaviest
# ef34gh5  RUN pip install -r req.txt       150MB   ← 2nd heaviest

# Apply ONE fix from 8.2-8.4 — e.g. switch base + chain/clean the RUN
docker build -t myapp:v2 .

# AFTER — confirm the drop
docker images myapp
# REPOSITORY   TAG   SIZE
# myapp        v1    850MB
# myapp        v2    180MB   ← measurably smaller, same functionality
Before (v1)After (v2)
Heaviest layerbuild tools / an uncleaned RUNgone, or never committed at all

Check yourself: the drop has to come from the SAME two heaviest rows you named up front — if you fixed a layer that wasn't one of your two heaviest, you optimized the wrong thing (this chapter's Gotchas: always attack the biggest layer first).

9.1 Project Structure Review

The easypj project is a Django 5.2 application with a jobpost app containing 5 models: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User (via Django's auth system).

easypj Project Structure
  easypj/
  ├── manage.py                    # Django CLI entry point
  ├── requirements.txt             # Python dependencies
  ├── easypj/                      # Django project package
  │   ├── __init__.py
  │   ├── settings.py              # Django settings
  │   ├── urls.py                  # URL routing
  │   ├── wsgi.py                  # WSGI entry point
  │   └── asgi.py                  # ASGI entry point
  └── jobpost/                     # Django app (your application)
      ├── __init__.py
      ├── models.py                # Skills, Author, Location, JobPost
      ├── views.py                 # HTTP request handlers
      ├── urls.py                  # App URL routing
      ├── admin.py                 # Admin interface registration
      └── migrations/              # Database migrations
The Container's-Eye View — every file mapped to the chapter that consumes it
  easypj/
  ├── manage.py           ← exec target for migrations (6.4)
  ├── requirements.txt    ← COPYed FIRST, its own cache layer (4.4/5.3)
  ├── Dockerfile           ← this chapter's artifact
  ├── .dockerignore        ← gatekeeper of the build context (5.2)
  ├── easypj/              ← settings.py, wsgi.py — gunicorn's CMD names
  │                          the dotted path easypj.wsgi:application
  └── jobpost/             ← models.py: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost
                             (FK → User) — migrate turns these into tables
🔎 What Matters to Docker in This Tree

requirements.txt pins the three names the whole chapter depends on: Django 5.2, gunicorn, and psycopg2-binary — PostgreSQL is the only database this guide ever targets, and settings.py reads DB_HOST/DB_NAME/DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD from the environment (12-factor style), never hardcoded. wsgi.py exposes an application object — the exact dotted path (easypj.wsgi:application) the Dockerfile's gunicorn CMD names later in 9.2. The database itself is deliberately NOT in this tree at all — it runs as its own separate container (Part 4 formalizes this as a Compose service).

🏗️ Analogy — An Architect's Site Survey

Before pouring concrete (building images) you mark what exists — load-bearing walls (wsgi.py, requirements.txt) versus furniture (everything .dockerignore will keep off the truck in 9.3). Skip the survey and you find out which wall was load-bearing only after the wall — and the build — comes down.

🔬 easypj: jobpost/models.py holds Skills, Author, Location and JobPost — migrate (run via 4.7's entrypoint, or by hand in 9.5/9.6) is the step that turns those Python classes into real PostgreSQL tables at container startup. Nothing in this tree talks to a database until that command runs.

9.2 Writing the Dockerfile

Dockerfile
# === easypj Production Dockerfile ===
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Set environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings

WORKDIR /app

# Install system dependencies (if needed)
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc libpq-dev && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Python dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && \
    apt-get purge -y gcc && \
    apt-get autoremove -y

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Create non-root user
RUN addgroup --system app && \
    adduser --system --group app && \
    chown -R app:app /app
USER app

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
LineInstructionWhy This Choice
1FROM python:3.11-slimSlim = Debian-based, glibc compatibility. Alpine would break psycopg2 and Pillow C-extensions. Pinned to 3.11, not :latest.
3-5ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Stops .pyc generation in immutable image layers — saves MBs and prevents unnecessary layer deltas.
7WORKDIR /appCreates /app if missing; all subsequent commands run here. Better than RUN mkdir /app && cd /app.
10-12RUN apt-get install gcc libpq-devlibpq-dev is needed to compile psycopg2 (PostgreSQL driver). gcc is removed after pip install to keep image lean.
15COPY requirements.txt .Copied BEFORE source code — maximizes layer caching. requirements.txt rarely changes.
16-18RUN pip install --no-cache-dir--no-cache-dir prevents ~100 MB wasted pip cache. Purge gcc after install to remove build tool from final image.
21COPY . .Copies application code LAST (changes most frequently). .dockerignore filters out env files, __pycache__, .git.
24-26RUN addgroup/adduser + USER appCreates system user (no login, no home dir). Switches from root — defense-in-depth security. Must chown app files.
28EXPOSE 8000Documentation — tells readers the app listens on 8000. Does NOT publish the port; use -p 8000:8000 at runtime.
30-31CMD ["gunicorn", ...]Gunicorn = production WSGI server. NOT runserver. --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 accepts external connections. --workers 3 = 3 worker processes.
🧮 Sizing --workers Correctly — and the Container Gotcha Nobody Warns You About

Gunicorn's own docs recommend (2 × CPU cores) + 1 worker processes as a starting point — enough to keep the CPU busy while one worker blocks on I/O. The trap: if you compute that number with Python's multiprocessing.cpu_count() (or a --workers $(python -c "import multiprocessing; print(multiprocessing.cpu_count())") idiom), it reads the HOST machine's total core count — NOT the container's --cpus cgroup limit (6.6). A host with 16 cores but a container capped at --cpus=1 auto-sizes to 33 workers fighting over one CPU's worth of scheduler time, each one starved and slow. Either hardcode --workers to match the ACTUAL --cpus/resources.limits.cpu the container will run under, or size it at deploy time from an environment variable your orchestrator sets — never trust in-container CPU auto-detection to know its own cgroup limit.

💡 Why Not Alpine for Django?

Alpine is 5 MB — incredibly tempting! But it uses musl libc instead of glibc. Many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy, lxml) are pre-compiled for glibc. On Alpine, they either fail to install or crash at runtime with cryptic errors. Slim images keep glibc compatibility while stripping development cruft — the pragmatic sweet spot for Python web apps.

🎲 A Rebuilt Image Can Silently Reassign app's UID

Docker's own Dockerfile best-practices guide flags a subtlety this section's addgroup/adduser pair inherits: the UID/GID a system user gets is non-deterministic across rebuilds — the "next" free ID is picked at build time, not fixed by the Dockerfile's text, so two builds of the exact same file can hand app two different UIDs. That's invisible until something OUTSIDE the container cares about the number — a bind-mounted host directory's ownership (Part 6), or a Kubernetes securityContext.runAsUser pinning a specific UID. Pin it explicitly the moment either applies: RUN addgroup --system --gid 1000 app && adduser --system --uid 1000 --gid 1000 app. One more wrinkle straight from the same official guidance: raw useradd examples elsewhere often add a --no-log-init flag to dodge a legacy disk-exhaustion bug in /var/log/faillog — but Debian/Ubuntu's own adduser wrapper (what this Dockerfile actually calls, being python:3.11-slim) does not accept that flag at all, so don't go copying it in from a raw-useradd example you find elsewhere.

♟️ Analogy — A Chess Game's Annotated Score Sheet

Every move is written down WITH the reason it was played, not just "pawn to e4." A reviewer replays the reasoning, not merely the moves — which is exactly what the table above does for this Dockerfile: every instruction cites the chapter that decided it, so a teammate can audit the file without you in the room.

🔬 easypj: with USER app in force, a hijacked Django process cannot apt-get anything, cannot write outside /app, and cannot bind privileged port 80 — three separate attack surfaces closed by one line near the bottom of the file.

9.3 Writing .dockerignore

.dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/

# Django
media/
staticfiles/

# Virtual Environment
env/
venv/
.env

# Git
.git/
.gitignore

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# OS
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Docker
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml
EntryWhat It ExcludesWhy Exclude It
__pycache__/, *.py[cod]Python bytecode cacheGenerated at runtime — baking stale .pyc from your machine wastes space and may cause version mismatch errors.
.envLocal secrets file🛑 CRITICAL: Contains SECRET_KEY, DB password. If baked into image, it's in your registry forever — a data leak. Inject secrets at runtime instead.
media/, staticfiles/Uploaded files, collected staticGenerated content — media can be GBs of uploads. Static should be collected during build, not copied from dev machine.
env/, venv/Python virtual environmentsLocal venv has machine-specific binaries. The image creates its own Python environment during pip install.
.git/Git repository metadata.git can be hundreds of MBs of commit history — no place in production, and could leak source history.
.vscode/, .idea/IDE configurationEditor settings irrelevant to the container. Adds noise and potential local path references.
Dockerfile, .dockerignoreDocker build filesBuild instructions, not application code. Including them leaks your build configuration unnecessarily.
.DS_Store, Thumbs.dbOS metadata filesmacOS/Windows auto-generated binary junk — zero value inside a Linux container.
🛑 The .dockerignore Security Rule

If you have a .env file with secrets, ALWAYS add it to .dockerignore. A single COPY . . without protection bakes secrets into the image — visible via docker history or registry pull. Secrets belong in runtime injection (docker run -e, Docker secrets, Kubernetes Secrets), NEVER in images.

➖ Negation Patterns — and Their One Sharp Edge

A leading ! re-includes a path an earlier pattern excluded — e.g. exclude media/* wholesale but keep one seed file with !media/.gitkeep. The sharp edge, straight from Docker's own .dockerignore reference: you can not re-include a file whose PARENT DIRECTORY is itself excluded. media/ (matching the whole directory entry, not just its contents) followed by !media/keep.txt silently does nothing — the directory itself never entered the build context for the negation to act on. Exclude with media/* (the contents, not the directory) if you ever plan to negate a file back in.

🚪 Analogy — The Bouncer's List at the Build's Door

Written once, enforced identically on every single build, with no judgment calls made at 2 AM by a tired engineer. .dockerignore never gets tired, never makes an exception "just this once" for a rushed hotfix build — that's the whole point of writing the rule down instead of trusting memory.

🔬 easypj: the .env file sitting right next to manage.py holds DB_PASSWORD for local runs — precisely why it must NEVER enter the image. The container receives that same value at RUN time instead, via --env-file .env (see 9.5's two-container circuit) — same secret, delivered the safe way.
