Check the paperwork (tag exists), weigh the crate (size is in the expected ballpark), open the packing list (docker history's fat layers are the expected ones) — all BEFORE the truck (docker run) ever leaves the yard. Catching a fat, wrong, or non-deterministic build here is free; catching it in production is not.

🔬 easypj: 185 MB confirms slim base + no leftover dev deps + clean layers in one glance — a SIZE that audits four chapters of choices at once. And a second identical build finishing in under a second, with the exact same IMAGE ID, is proof the build is deterministic, not merely lucky.

9.5 Running the Container Locally

TERMINAL
# Run in detached mode with port mapping
$ docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj-container easypj:v1.0

# Verify it's running
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          COMMAND                  STATUS         PORTS
abc123def456   easypj:v1.0   "gunicorn easypj.wsgi"   Up 5 seconds   0.0.0.0:8000->8000/tcp

# Check logs
$ docker logs easypj-container
[2026-06-12 10:00:00] Starting gunicorn 21.2.0
[2026-06-12 10:00:00] Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000
[2026-06-12 10:00:00] Using worker: sync
[2026-06-12 10:00:00] Booting worker with pid: 8

# Run Django migrations inside the running container
$ docker exec easypj-container python manage.py migrate
Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions, jobpost
Running migrations:
  Applying jobpost.0001_initial... OK

# Visit http://localhost:8000 in your browser — easypj is live! 🚀

The single-container run above proves easypj starts — but production easypj always answers alongside a second container, PostgreSQL, reached over a user-defined network by name, never localhost. Here's the same image brought up next to a real database — the full local circuit a DCA practical task expects:

TERMINAL — the two-container circuit
# Create a user-defined network — the shared DNS scope
$ docker network create easypj-net

# Bring up PostgreSQL on that network FIRST
$ docker run -d --name easypj-db --network easypj-net \
    -e POSTGRES_DB=easypj -e POSTGRES_USER=easypj \
    -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass postgres:16

# Bring up easypj on the SAME network, pointed at the db BY NAME
$ docker run -d --name easypj-container --network easypj-net \
    -p 8000:8000 -e DB_HOST=easypj-db --env-file .env \
    easypj:v1.0

# Watch it come up — migrations, then gunicorn boot
$ docker logs -f easypj-container
[INFO] Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000

# The first real HTTP request, from the HOST
$ curl -I http://localhost:8000/jobs/
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
🥇 Why -e DB_HOST=easypj-db --env-file .env Is Safe to Combine

When the SAME key appears in both places, the explicit -e/--env flag always wins over --env-file, regardless of which one is written first or last on the command line. That is exactly why the run command above is safe even if a stale DB_HOST value happens to sit inside .env — the explicit -e DB_HOST=easypj-db overrides it every time. This is plain docker run behavior, distinct from Compose's own five-source precedence ladder (12.7) for environment:/env_file: keys in a compose.yaml.

🎭 Analogy — Opening Night With the Full Cast

The database is the orchestra in its own pit (a separate container), Docker's embedded DNS is the conductor's eye contact keeping everyone in time, and that final curl is the first paying customer walking through the door — the moment the whole production actually has to work, not just rehearse alone.

🔬 easypj: after migrate runs, /admin/ lists Skills, Authors, Locations, and Job Posts — those model tables now live inside the PostgreSQL container, never on your laptop's own system install. Run docker restart easypj-container and a JobPost saved through admin is still there afterward — proof the data was never the web container's to lose in the first place.

9.6 Debugging When Things Go Wrong

Every Docker + Django developer encounters these issues. Here's your troubleshooting reference — 12 common problems with their causes and exact debug commands:

#SymptomLikely CauseDebug Command
1Container exits immediatelyWrong CMD, missing file, syntax errordocker logs <id>
2Port already in useAnother process using port 8000 — often a STALE container left running from a previous docker run, not a host processdocker ps — an old container frequently still owns the port; stop/rm it, remap with docker run -p 8001:8000 ..., or fall back to lsof -i :8000 only for a genuine host-level conflict
3Module not found: 'easypj'Wrong WORKDIR or COPY pathdocker exec <id> ls /app && docker exec <id> pwd
4Django settings errorMissing DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE envdocker exec <id> env | grep DJANGO
5Database connection refusedDB_HOST pointing to localhost, or the two containers aren't on the same networkdocker network inspect easypj-net — confirms both containers are attached to the SAME network, and that DB_HOST matches the db container's NAME, not localhost
6Permission deniedRunning as non-root without chownRUN chown -R app:app /app before USER app
7Static files 404 (white page)collectstatic not run or wrong STATIC_ROOTdocker exec <id> python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
8Gunicorn workers timing outRequest taking too long, worker count too lowIncrease --timeout 120 and --workers 4
9Image build fails on pip installMissing system deps (gcc, libpq-dev)Add RUN apt-get install -y gcc libpq-dev before pip
10Container runs but health check failsWrong HEALTHCHECK endpoint or portdocker inspect <id> | grep -A10 Health
11ModuleNotFoundError for a THIRD-PARTY package (e.g. psycopg2, not your own easypj code)The package was never pinned in requirements.txt at all — pip install succeeded because it had nothing to fail ondocker exec <id> pip list | grep -i <pkg> — confirms whether it's actually installed inside the image, distinct from row 3's path/WORKDIR problem
12Container killed unexpectedly — exit code 137Kernel OOM-killer terminated it (memory limit too low, 6.6), OR docker stop's SIGKILL landed after the 10s grace period expireddocker inspect <id> | grep -A5 State — OOMKilled: true means memory pressure; false with 137 means a graceless shutdown instead
🔧 Debugging Workflow: The 3-Step Method

Step 0, if you don't have the ID handy: docker ps -a — find the container. Step 1: docker logs <id> — read what happened. Step 2: docker inspect <id> | grep -A20 State — check exit code, OOM status, error. Step 3: docker exec -it <id> bash — reproduce it live. Steps 1-3 are the same fixed protocol — logs → inspect → exec — this chapter uses everywhere, and together they resolve roughly 90% of first-week container pain: classify what's left as content, config, or wiring and the remaining 10% stops feeling random too. If a container dies too fast to exec into, hold it open with docker run -it --entrypoint bash easypj:v1.0.

The Debugging Decision Tree — stop at the FIRST answer
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 1  docker logs easypj-container                           │
│   dying words visible? ─YES─▶ fix code/config. DONE.           │
│   │ NO / unclear                                                │
│   ▼                                                              │
│ STEP 2  docker inspect easypj-container                         │
│   exit code 137?  ─YES─▶ OOM-killed, raise --memory (6.6)      │
│   │ NO                                                           │
│   ▼                                                              │
│   wrong Env / Network? ─YES─▶ fix run flags. DONE.              │
│   │ NO                                                           │
│   ▼                                                              │
│ STEP 3  docker exec -it easypj-container sh                     │
│   reproduce it live ─▶ content vs config vs wiring, found       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
✈️ Analogy — An Aircraft Accident Board, Not a Séance

Investigators read the flight recorder (logs), then the maintenance file (inspect), then walk the wreck (exec) — never the other way around. Boards publish causes BECAUSE they read instruments in a fixed order every time, not because they guess harder than everyone else.

Every row in the table above is really one of only three classes of failure: image content (something missing or wrong inside the built image), runtime config (a wrong or missing flag/env var at docker run time), or wiring (two containers that can't reach each other). Naming the class first tells you which container to even look at.

Failure ClassWhat It MeansRows From the Table AboveWhere the Fix Lives
Image contentSomething missing or wrong was baked INTO the image itself#1 wrong CMD/missing file/syntax error, #3 module not found, #7 static 404, #9 pip install fails, #11 third-party package never pinnedEdit the Dockerfile or requirements.txt, then rebuild
Runtime configA wrong or missing flag/env var at docker run time#2 port in use, #4 settings module, #6 permission denied, #8 worker timeout, #12 OOM/exit 137Fix the docker run flags (or the compose service definition)
WiringTwo containers that cannot reach each other over the network#5 database connection refused, #10 health check failsFix --network, container names, or the DNS name being dialed

🔬 easypj: a log line reading OperationalError: could not translate host name "easypj-db" reads instantly as: code fine, image fine, WIRING broken — check both containers' networks (same --network, matching names) before you touch a single line of Python.

💡 Once easypj becomes Compose's four services (Part 4), this exact ladder still runs — just as docker compose logs <service> instead of a bare docker logs. The protocol doesn't change; only the command prefix does.

9.7 The Complete easypj Dockerfile (Final Version)

After applying all optimizations from Chapters 4-8, here's the final production Dockerfile. Read it as the Parts 2-3 midterm: every single line should be traceable to a chapter's decision, with the dev-vs-prod split fully explained below.

Dockerfile (Final Optimized)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Run (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
🛠️ Why COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local Matters

Stage 1 only ever receives requirements.txt — never the application source, which is COPYed in stage 2 instead — and installs every Python package with pip install --user, which lands them all under /root/.local — nowhere else. Stage 2 copies ONLY that one directory into the final image, leaving stage 1's pip cache and any build tooling entirely behind in the discarded builder layer. That single targeted COPY --from= is what keeps the shipped runtime image at ~180 MB instead of carrying a whole build toolchain nobody at runtime will ever use.

🧑‍💻 The Dev Variant — Same Image, Different CMD

Production runs the image as-built, but local development overrides the CMD at run time instead of maintaining a second Dockerfile: docker run -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD":/app easypj:v1.0 python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 — a bind mount (Part 6) swaps in live source, and runserver replaces gunicorn for auto-reload. One image, two run commands, zero drift between what dev tests and what prod ships.

🔒 One More Hardening Step — Pin FROM by Digest, Not Just Tag

Docker's own official Dockerfile best-practices guide now recommends pinning base images to an exact content digest for supply-chain integrity, not merely a version tag: FROM python:3.11-slim@sha256:<digest> instead of just FROM python:3.11-slim. This is Chapter 7's tag-vs-digest lesson applied for real — a TAG is a free, mutable, movable pointer (the maintainer can silently repoint python:3.11-slim at a new build tomorrow), while a DIGEST is the one deploy-safe identity that can never change underneath you. docker pull and docker inspect on the currently-running base image reveal today's digest to pin; CI can then fail loudly instead of silently rebuilding on an unreviewed upstream change. A pinned digest isn't a one-time freeze either — Docker Scout ships automation that opens a pull request bumping the pinned digest whenever a new build of python:3.11-slim is published, so the image stays reviewable AND current instead of silently drifting or silently going stale.

⚠️ A Slim Base Doesn't Ship pg_isready — the Entrypoint Needs One More Package

docker-entrypoint.sh (4.7) opens with until pg_isready -h "$DB_HOST" -p 5432 -q; do ... done — but pg_isready is a PostgreSQL CLIENT-TOOLS binary, shipped in Debian's postgresql-client package, and it has nothing to do with psycopg2-binary's own bundled libpq (that wheel only supplies the Python driver's linked library, never a standalone CLI). Neither this stage nor 9.2's single-stage version ever installs it, so the very FIRST time this exact image runs, the entrypoint fails at the top of the script with pg_isready: not found — before it ever gets the chance to report a real database problem. Fix it in the RUNTIME stage specifically: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends postgresql-client && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* — installing it in the discarded builder stage instead would vanish along with everything else COPY --from=builder doesn't name (this section's own first callout, applied to a real miss).

📋 Analogy — A Home Recipe vs. a Printed Restaurant Menu Card

Same dish as the very first Dockerfile back in 4.4 — but now portioned (--workers 3), allergen-labeled (USER, the ENV block), and reproducible by any cook on any shift, not just the one who invented it.

🔬 easypj: this exact file is what every later part of this guide builds ON, not around — Compose (Part 4) wraps it, user-defined networks (Part 5) connect it to PostgreSQL, volumes (Part 6) keep its media, and CI (Part 8) builds and ships it. Nothing after Part 3 rebuilds this artifact from scratch.

9.8 docker init — Scaffolding Dockerfiles Automatically

docker init is an interactive generator run in the project directory. It detects Python, asks version/port/run-command, and generates Dockerfile, .dockerignore, compose.yaml, and README.Docker.md — a starting point, not a shipped artifact.

docker init in the easypj checkout
$ cd easypj && docker init
? What application platform does your project use?  Python
? What version of Python do you want to use?        3.11
? What port do you want your app to listen on?      8000
? What is the command you use to run your app?
  gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
✔ Created → Dockerfile  .dockerignore  compose.yaml  README.Docker.md

docker init inspects the directory (finding requirements.txt → Python template) and writes four files. The generated Dockerfile is genuinely decent: slim base, cache-mounted pip (5.7), a non-root user, requirements-first ordering. What it CANNOT know: your entrypoint needs (4.7's wait-and-migrate), collectstatic, the dev/prod requirements split (8.4), or that compose.yaml needs a postgres service with a volume — it scaffolds a generic app; you re-apply the Django decisions.

🌍 Not Just Python — docker init's Full Template List

easypj triggers the Python template because requirements.txt is the marker file docker init looks for, but per the official CLI reference the tool now ships templates for eight platforms: ASP.NET Core, Go, Java, Node, PHP with Apache, Python, Rust, and a generic "Other" fallback for anything else. Every template follows the exact same contract 9.8 just walked through for Python — a genuinely decent generic Dockerfile plus a compose.yaml, with the framework-specific 20% (migrations, static assets, a database service) left for you to add by hand, same as here. Worth knowing on the DCA: a lab task could hand you a Go or Node project instead of Django and the workflow doesn't change at all.

Aspectdocker init generates9.7 final adds
StagesSingle stageMulti-stage build+run
Base imagepython:3.11-slimSame, kept as-is
pip install--mount=cache (5.7)--user, then COPY --from=builder /root/.local
Non-root userGeneric addusersame pattern + same-layer chown -R before USER
Static filesNot generatedRUN collectstatic
EntrypointNone — bare CMDdocker-entrypoint.sh
Compose dbNo postgres servicepostgres:16 + volume
Image size~220 MB~180 MB
💡 A Tailor's Standard Pattern

Right fabric, straight seams, average measurements — it fits the mannequin perfectly. YOUR shoulders (migrations, static, PostgreSQL) still need fitting by hand. docker init reads requirements.txt to pick the Python template and version pin — an empty or missing file makes it guess wrong. It also needs Docker Desktop 4.19+ / Engine 24+, an easy miss on an older CI runner.

⚠️ Rerunning docker init Overwrites Files

Rerunning docker init OVERWRITES existing files after one confirm — never say yes in a repo holding hand-tuned, uncommitted Docker files. Keep a scratch copy of the project just for docker init experiments.

🔬 easypj: after running docker init against a scratch copy, the edit list back to the real project is short and principled — add 4.7's wait-and-migrate entrypoint, add collectstatic (multi-stage, for 9.7 parity), and point compose.yaml at a postgres:16 service with a volume. Every one of those edits cites a specific section of this guide, which is exactly the point of running the diff in the first place.

🔧 Under the Hood — six mechanisms behind this chapter's build → run → debug pipeline

9.1-9.8 taught eight practical moves — know the tree, write the Dockerfile, ignore the right files, build, run on a shared network, debug in a fixed order, ship the final multi-stage file, and let docker init scaffold the boilerplate. Each one leans on a specific piece of kernel or daemon mechanism underneath it; this section walks six of them, in the order the diagram below lists.

 EVERY move in this chapter leans on ONE underlying mechanism:

   0.0.0.0 bind + -p mapping (9.5) ────────▶ ① network namespaces + iptables DNAT
   DB_HOST=easypj-db, not localhost (9.5/9.6) ▶ ② the embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11
   0.8s rebuild, same IMAGE ID (9.4) ───────▶ ③ BuildKit's content-addressable cache
   CMD ["gunicorn", ...] exec form (9.2/9.7) ▶ ④ PID 1 & signal handling
   COPY --from=builder (9.7) ───────────────▶ ⑤ BuildKit's multi-stage DAG
   docker init "detects" Python (9.8) ──────▶ ⑥ marker-file template matching
🔑 None of these six are new tools to learn — they're the reasons the eight moves you just practiced actually work, in enough detail that you could predict a failure mode this chapter's table didn't spell out.
① Network Namespaces & iptables DNAT — Why 0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 Decides Whether -p Works

Every container gets its OWN network namespace — its own loopback interface, separate from the host's. When gunicorn binds 127.0.0.1:8000, it is only listening on ITS namespace's loopback, which nothing outside that namespace (not the host, not another container, not docker run -p) can ever reach — the bind address is not a formality, it is the actual gate. Binding 0.0.0.0:8000 listens on every interface INSIDE that namespace, including the veth pair Docker wires to the bridge network — exactly what -p 8000:8000's userland-proxy/iptables DNAT rule needs on the other end to have somewhere to deliver packets to.

 ┌─ HOST ──────────────┐        ┌─ CONTAINER NETNS ────────────────┐
 │ localhost:8000 ─────┼─iptables┼──▶ veth ──▶ 0.0.0.0:8000  OK    │
 │ (via -p mapping)    │  DNAT   │            127.0.0.1:8000  FAIL │
 └─────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────────────┘
AspectBind 127.0.0.1:8000Bind 0.0.0.0:8000
Reachable fromonly processes inside the SAME netnsevery interface in the netns, incl. the veth to the bridge
-p 8000:8000 DNAT targetno listener on the veth side → connection refusedthe veth-side listener DNAT actually delivers to
Typical symptomcurl: (56) Recv failure from the HOST, container LOOKS healthy in docker psworks from host, other containers, and -p
🔑 This single bind-address choice is 9.5's #1 first-run failure — and the same namespace isolation is WHY DB_HOST=localhost fails too: "localhost" inside easypj-container's namespace is easypj-container itself, never the easypj-db container next to it.
② The Embedded DNS Server — How DB_HOST=easypj-db Actually Resolves to an IP

9.5's two-container circuit tells easypj to reach Postgres by NAME, never by IP — that only works because every container attached to a user-defined network (like easypj-net) gets its /etc/resolv.conf rewritten by the daemon at start to point nameserver 127.0.0.11, Docker's own embedded DNS resolver. The DEFAULT bridge network (docker0) never gets this treatment — no embedded resolver, no name-based discovery, which is exactly why pre-user-defined-network Docker required fragile --link flags. When easypj's libc resolver looks up easypj-db, the query never leaves the container's own netns for the wider internet — an iptables rule redirects the 127.0.0.11:53 query straight to a resolver process the daemon runs per network, which checks that NETWORK's own service-discovery table (built from container names and --network-alias at attach time) and returns the matching container's internal IP directly.

 easypj-container (on easypj-net) resolves "easypj-db":

   getaddrinfo("easypj-db")
        │  reads /etc/resolv.conf → nameserver 127.0.0.11
        ▼
   iptables (this netns) redirects 127.0.0.11:53 ──▶ dockerd's embedded
                                                        resolver for easypj-net
        │
        ├─ name matches a container/alias on easypj-net?
        │      YES ──▶ return that container's internal IP  (easypj-db → 172.20.0.2)
        │
        └─ NO match on this network?
               forward upstream to the host's configured nameservers (or --dns)
AspectDefault bridge (docker0)User-defined bridge (easypj-net)
DNS by container name❌ not supported (only legacy --link)✅ automatic, via the embedded resolver
/etc/resolv.conf inside the containercopies the host's real nameserversnameserver 127.0.0.11 (embedded resolver)
Extra DNS namesnone--network-alias registers more names per container
Unmatched external namegoes straight to host's nameserversembedded resolver forwards it upstream for you
🔑 9.6's OperationalError: could not translate host name "easypj-db" now reads precisely: the query DID reach 127.0.0.11, and 127.0.0.11 returned NXDOMAIN — which only happens when the two containers are not on the SAME user-defined network (typo'd --network, one container still on the default bridge, or the db container never started). It is never a "DNS is down" problem — Docker's embedded resolver has no separate failure mode to have.
③ BuildKit's Content-Addressable Cache — Why a Zero-Change Rebuild Is Deterministic, Not Lucky

9.4 rebuilds with NO source changes and finishes in 0.8s with the exact same IMAGE ID — that is not luck, it is BuildKit computing a CACHE KEY for every node in its build DAG from three inputs: the instruction's own text, the content digest of anything it COPYs (hashed from the actual bytes in the build context, never from a file's mtime), and the cache key of its parent step. If all three match a step BuildKit has already executed, it reuses that exact cached layer instead of re-running the instruction — and the reuse cascades forward until it reaches the first instruction whose inputs actually changed. This is the mechanical reason 9.2 copies requirements.txt BEFORE COPY . .: requirements.txt's content hash rarely changes, so every step through pip install keeps cache-hitting even while application source underneath COPY . . changes on every commit.

 Dockerfile build DAG — each node's cache key = (instruction + input hash + parent key)

   FROM python:3.11-slim ──▶ WORKDIR /app ──▶ RUN apt-get install ──▶ COPY requirements.txt .
                                                                              │  hash unchanged
                                                                              ▼
                                                              RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
                                                                    │  same key ⇒ CACHE HIT, reused
                                                                    ▼
                                              COPY . .   ← source edited ⇒ hash changed ⇒ CACHE MISS
                                                    │        (everything from HERE down re-executes)
                                                    ▼
                                    RUN addgroup/adduser + chown ──▶ USER app ──▶ CMD [...]
Cache-key inputComputed fromChanges when…
Instruction textthe Dockerfile line + its argumentsyou edit that line itself
COPY source contentSHA-256 of the actual bytes in the build contextthe file's bytes differ — a bare touch does NOT invalidate it
Parent step's keythe previous node's own cache keyany EARLIER step in the chain already missed
🔑 One edited line in views.py invalidates COPY . . and every instruction below it, but nothing ABOVE it — which is exactly why 9.2's ordering (deps first, source last) isn't a style preference, it's the literal cache boundary between a 30-second rebuild and an 0.8-second one.
④ PID 1 & Signal Handling — Why CMD ["gunicorn", ...] Must Be Exec Form

Whatever process a Dockerfile's CMD/ENTRYPOINT ultimately execs becomes PID 1 inside the container's PID namespace, and the Linux kernel treats PID 1 specially: default signal dispositions don't apply to it the way they do to every other process — a signal only affects PID 1 if that exact process installs a handler for it. docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits (10s default, or --time), then sends SIGKILL. Written as SHELL form — CMD gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application ..., which Docker silently wraps as ["/bin/sh", "-c", "gunicorn ..."] — /bin/sh becomes PID 1 and gunicorn is only ITS child; many shells never forward SIGTERM to a child at all, so gunicorn never learns to shut down gracefully and the whole 10-second grace window is wasted before a hard SIGKILL lands mid-request. 9.2/9.7's JSON-array EXEC form — CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"] — skips the shell entirely: gunicorn's own master process IS PID 1, receives SIGTERM directly, and its built-in handler drains workers gracefully before exiting.

 SHELL form  CMD gunicorn ...            EXEC form  CMD ["gunicorn", ...]  (9.2/9.7's actual syntax)

   PID 1 = /bin/sh -c "gunicorn ..."       PID 1 = gunicorn (master process itself)
     └─ gunicorn = a CHILD process           received SIGTERM DIRECTLY
   docker stop ─▶ SIGTERM to /bin/sh       docker stop ─▶ SIGTERM to gunicorn
     sh often does NOT forward it            gunicorn's own handler: stop accepting new
     gunicorn never hears SIGTERM            requests, finish in-flight ones, exit workers
     10s grace period wasted ─▶ SIGKILL      exits cleanly, usually well under 10s
CMD formPID 1 is…SIGTERM reaches gunicorn?Graceful shutdown?
Shell — CMD gunicorn .../bin/shonly if the shell forwards it (often doesn't)usually NO — hits the SIGKILL timeout
Exec — CMD ["gunicorn", ...]gunicorn itselfdirectly, immediatelyYES — the documented behavior in 9.2/9.7
🔑 Exit code 137 = 128 + signal 9 = "killed by SIGKILL" — the same code whether the kill came from a wasted docker stop grace period (this mechanism) or the kernel's OOM-killer (6.6's --memory limit, 9.6's row 12). docker inspect <id> | grep -A5 State distinguishes the two: OOMKilled: true means memory pressure killed it; a clean false with 137 means this section's signal-forwarding gap caused an un-graceful shutdown instead.
⑤ BuildKit's Multi-Stage DAG — Why COPY --from=builder Discards Everything Else

9.7's final Dockerfile declares two FROM lines — each one starts a fresh, independently-cached stage, and BuildKit compiles both into ONE build DAG. Naming a stage (AS builder) doesn't change how it builds; it just gives that DAG node a label the SECOND stage can reference. COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local does not copy the whole builder stage or its image — it reads exactly ONE path out of that stage's final filesystem snapshot and writes only those bytes as a new layer in stage 2's own image. Every other byte stage 1 ever materialized — its own base OS layer, pip's download cache, the full requirements.txt COPY, any build tooling — exists ONLY inside the discarded builder stage, is never referenced by stage 2's manifest, and becomes eligible for docker builder prune the moment the build finishes.

 Stage 1 "builder"                              Stage 2 (final, untagged AS)
   FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder               FROM python:3.11-slim
   WORKDIR /app                                   WORKDIR /app
   COPY requirements.txt .                         ENV ... DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=...
   RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt      COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local ◀┐
        → /root/.local (~180 MB incl. pip cache,    ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH                │
          any build tooling)                        COPY . .                                        │
   ─────────── DISCARDED, never tagged ──────────   RUN collectstatic / adduser / USER app          │
   docker builder prune reclaims this later         EXPOSE / HEALTHCHECK / ENTRYPOINT / CMD         │
                                                     ▲── the ONE path actually copied across ────────┘
What exists in Stage 1 (builder)Copied into Stage 2's image?
Stage 1's own base OS layerNO — stage 2 has its own separate base layer
pip's download/build cacheNO — never referenced by COPY --from
Build tooling (gcc, headers, if any)NO
/root/.local (the installed packages)YES — the one path 9.7 names
🔑 This is the mechanical reason 9.7's stage-2 image lands near ~180 MB instead of carrying a whole build toolchain: multi-stage isn't "smaller because we tried harder," it's structurally impossible for the final manifest to reference bytes that no COPY --from instruction ever named.
⑥ docker init's Template Matching — How a Bare Directory Becomes "Python" With the Right Flags

docker init is a Go binary bundled with the Docker CLI — it never runs your project's code or imports it. It picks a template by pattern-matching a FIXED list of marker files against the target directory: requirements.txt/pyproject.toml/Pipfile signals Python, package.json signals Node, go.mod signals Go, and so on. Once a match is found, it loads that language's bundled, hand-written Dockerfile TEMPLATE — it does not generate the Dockerfile by parsing your source — and substitutes your interactive answers (Python version, port, run command) directly into that template's placeholders. This is exactly why it can produce a solid slim-base, cache-mounted-pip skeleton (things a fixed template always gets right) while having zero way to know your app is Django specifically, needs a WSGI dotted path, or has a collectstatic step (things that require actually reading and understanding your source, which it never does).

 $ docker init   (inside the easypj checkout)

   scan directory for marker files:
     requirements.txt present?  ──YES──▶ load the bundled PYTHON template
     package.json / go.mod / Cargo.toml / Gemfile.lock? ──▶ (not checked further once matched)
        │
        ▼
   ask interactive questions (version / port / run command)
        │
        ▼
   substitute answers into the TEMPLATE's placeholders (no parsing of your .py files at all)
        │
        ▼
   write Dockerfile · .dockerignore · compose.yaml · README.Docker.md
docker init CAN determineIt CANNOT determine (9.8's table, "your judgment")
Language/platform, from a marker file's presenceWhich web framework — Django vs Flask vs FastAPI
Version/port/run command — FROM your typed answersThe correct WSGI dotted path or entrypoint script
A generic non-root user + cache-mounted pip patternWhether migrations or collectstatic must run first
A generic compose.yaml service for the app itselfWhether a postgres/redis service belongs in it
🔑 This is also why 9.8's warning box is unconditional: rerunning docker init doesn't MERGE your hand-tuned edits with a fresh scan — it re-runs the identical marker-match-and-substitute process from scratch and overwrites the file, because the tool never read your customizations in the first place; it only ever read the marker file and your typed answers.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Know the tree BEFORE touching Docker: wsgi.py's dotted path, requirements.txt's real dependencies, and the env-driven DB settings are what the Dockerfile depends on.
  • 9.2 and 9.7's Dockerfiles are built from named decisions, not habit — slim base (8.2), requirements-first COPY (5.3), same-layer cleanup (8.3), non-root USER (4.6).
  • .dockerignore does three jobs at once: smaller/faster build context, stable cache, and keeping secrets (.env) out of any shippable layer.
  • Verify a build BEFORE running it: tag exists, size is in the expected ballpark, history's fat layers are the expected ones.
  • A real run needs a user-defined network, container-name DNS (never localhost), and gunicorn bound to 0.0.0.0.
  • 9.6's triage order is fixed, not improvised: logs (dying words) → inspect (exit code + config) → exec (test the hypothesis), every time.
  • The final multi-stage Dockerfile (9.7) and docker init's scaffold (9.8) encode the SAME lessons — one hand-built, one auto-generated and then hand-corrected.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: 9.1-9.8's full build→run→debug arc rehearses a real DCA practical task — Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%) tested as one continuous exercise, not isolated commands.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Django DEBUG=True in production → Always set DEBUG=False via environment variable. DEBUG=True exposes sensitive info.
  • Binding to 127.0.0.1 inside container → Gunicorn must bind to 0.0.0.0:8000, not 127.0.0.1, or the port won't be reachable.
  • Forgetting collectstatic → Django won't serve static files without running collectstatic during the build.
  • Hardcoded DB credentials in settings.py → They break portability — the container must read them from the ENVIRONMENT.
  • USER can go anywhere in the Dockerfile → It must be set AFTER installs but BEFORE CMD — reversed, pip fails on permissions, or the image ships running as root.
  • .dockerignore works from any directory → It must live in the CONTEXT ROOT — one directory off and it is silently ignored with no warning.
  • A successful docker build means the app works → Build success only proves the image COMPILED. Imports, settings, and DB wiring are RUNTIME facts — that's exactly what 9.5 and 9.6 exist to test.
  • DB_HOST=localhost works once containers share a network → It never will — "localhost" inside a container is always THAT container. DB_HOST must be the database container's NAME on the shared user-defined network.
  • The entrypoint script "just works" once it's COPYed in → It must be chmod +x BEFORE the COPY (git preserves the executable bit) — "permission denied" at startup is that missing bit, not a Docker mystery.
  • A container that dies too fast to exec into can't be debugged → Hold it open with docker run -it --entrypoint bash easypj:v1.0 — an autopsy room where the body can't vanish before you can look at it.
  • Rerunning docker init merges with my hand-tuned files → It doesn't — it OVERWRITES existing files after one confirm. Never say yes in a repo holding hand-tuned, uncommitted Docker files; keep a scratch copy just for docker init experiments.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker build -t easypj:v1.0 . && docker history easypj:v1.0 | head -4 — build and sanity-check layer sizes in one line.
  • docker logs -f --since 10m <container> for intermittent failures instead of re-running from scratch.
  • Keep a scratch copy of the project just for docker init experiments — never run it against uncommitted hand-tuned files.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 9)

build, network, run & debug easypj end to end 
# Produce the artifact
docker build -t easypj:v1.0 .

# Shared DNS scope
docker network create easypj-net

docker run -d --network easypj-net ... postgres:16
docker run -d --network easypj-net -p 8000:8000 ... easypj:v1.0

# Step 1, always
docker logs -f <container>

# Step 2: exit code, env
docker inspect <container>

# Step 3: reproduce live
docker exec -it <container> sh

# Scaffold, then audit
docker init

🧠 Chapter 9 — DCA Practice Questions (18)

Quick recall of the end-to-end containerization workflow — 18 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What is the purpose of PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Prevents Python from writing .pyc bytecode files to disk. In a Docker container, these cached files are unnecessary (the container is ephemeral) and waste space. Saves several MBs in the final image.

EXPLANATION

Python normally compiles .py to .pyc on first import and stores them in __pycache__/. In a Docker image, these files add MBs of bloat, are never reused across container instances, and create unnecessary layer deltas.

BehaviorWithout the ENV varWith PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
On every importwrites __pycache__/*.pyc into the image layerno bytecode files ever written
Final image size+ a few MB of stale .pyc baked into a read-only layer0 extra bytes
Q2
Why create a non-root user in your Dockerfile instead of running as root?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Running as root is a security risk — if an attacker exploits your app, they get root access inside the container. A non-root user limits the damage. Create with RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app then USER app.

EXPLANATION

Docker containers share the host kernel. A root user inside a container has UID 0 — the same as host root. Running as non-root is defense-in-depth: even if your app is compromised, the attacker starts with minimal privileges.

Root Dockerfile (no USER)With USER app
whoami inside containerrootapp
id -u0non-zero (e.g. 101)
Blast radius if compromisedfull root inside the containerno write outside /app, no apt-get, no privileged ports
Q3
What does the HEALTHCHECK instruction do in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It defines a command that Docker runs periodically to check if the container is healthy. The exit code determines health: 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy. Docker reports the status in docker ps.

EXPLANATION

Without HEALTHCHECK, Docker only knows if the process is running — not if it's actually working. A Django app might have gunicorn running but be stuck in a deadlock. HEALTHCHECK catches this.

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/ || exit 1
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   STATUS
abc123def456   Up 2 minutes (healthy)
Q4
Why should .env be in .dockerignore for a Django project?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

.env holds SECRET_KEY, DB passwords, and other secrets. If it's copied into the image via COPY . ., it's now baked into every layer — visible via docker history and accessible to anyone with pull access on the registry.

EXPLANATION

This is a real-world security incident waiting to happen. Always exclude secrets, media uploads, and any stateful/sensitive data from Docker images — inject them at runtime instead.

.env NOT in .dockerignore.env in .dockerignore
COPY . .bakes SECRET_KEY + DB password into a layersecret never enters the build context
docker historysecret recoverable from any pulled imagenothing to recover
Q5
How do you run Django database migrations inside a running container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec easypj-container python manage.py migrate. This runs the migration inside the already-running container where Django and all dependencies are available.

EXPLANATION

Migrations must run inside the container because it has the exact Python version, dependencies, and database network access. In production, migrations are often run as an init container or a one-shot Job — never baked into the CMD.

$ docker exec easypj-container python manage.py migrate
Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions, jobpost
Running migrations:
  Applying jobpost.0001_initial... OK
Q6
Your container runs but you get "Connection refused" when accessing localhost:8000. Why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The app inside the container might be listening on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0. 127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from within the container's own network namespace — not from the host. Always bind to 0.0.0.0 in containerized apps.

EXPLANATION

This is the #1 Docker networking gotcha. Since the container has its own network namespace, the host is external to it. Gunicorn's default is 127.0.0.1:8000 — always override with --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 in Docker.

  HOST  curl :8000 ──iptables DNAT──▶ veth ──▶ 0.0.0.0:8000   ✅ reachable
                                              ╲─▶ 127.0.0.1:8000  ❌ own netns only
Q7
Why use gunicorn instead of Django's manage.py runserver in production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

runserver is single-threaded, not designed for production, and explicitly warns "DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION." Gunicorn is a production WSGI server: multi-worker, handles concurrent requests, battle-tested.

EXPLANATION

Gunicorn uses a pre-fork worker model: one master + N worker processes for true concurrency, with proper timeout/keepalive handling that runserver lacks.

Aspectmanage.py runservergunicorn
Worker modelsingle-threaded, dev-onlypre-fork, N worker processes
Concurrencyone request at a timetrue concurrent requests
Production-ready❌ Django docs: "DO NOT USE"✅ battle-tested WSGI server
Q8
What command shows what's happening inside a container that's failing to start?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs <container-id> shows stdout/stderr from the container. Even if the container has exited, logs persist. This is the first debugging step for any container issue.

EXPLANATION

For containers that exit instantly, use docker ps -a to find the exited container ID, then docker logs <id>. Also check docker inspect <id> | grep -A5 State for exit codes.

$ docker ps -a
CONTAINER ID   STATUS
abc123def456   Exited (1) 5 seconds ago

$ docker logs abc123def456
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'easypj.wgsi'
Q9
What does --no-install-recommends do in apt-get?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It tells apt-get to install only the explicitly requested packages, NOT their "recommended" packages. This can save 50-200 MB in the final image.

EXPLANATION

Without --no-install-recommends, a simple install pulls in documentation, man pages, and optional libs. Always combine with rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* to clean the package index in the same layer.

Without --no-install-recommendsWith it
apt-get install gcc libpq-devpulls docs, man pages, optional libs tooonly the two named packages
Typical size cost+50-200 MBbaseline
Q10
What's the difference between what docker init generates and the 9.7 final Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker init writes a decent single-stage Dockerfile with a cache-mounted pip install and a generic non-root user, but it never generates an entrypoint script, collectstatic, or a postgres service in compose.yaml. The 9.7 version adds multi-stage, a same-layer chown -R before USER, collectstatic, and a full entrypoint.

EXPLANATION

docker init gets you 80% of the way for a generic Python app; the Django-specific 20% — migrations, static files, PostgreSQL wiring — is the judgment this whole guide trains.

Dimensiondocker init generates9.7 final Dockerfile
Stagessingle-stagemulti-stage (builder + runtime)
Non-root usergenericsame pattern, same-layer chown -R app:app /app before USER
Entrypoint / collectstaticnonefull entrypoint script + collectstatic
compose.yaml databaseno postgres servicepostgres service wired in
Q11
Before writing any Dockerfile line, what two files in the easypj tree does 9.1 say the container story most depends on?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

requirements.txt (pins Django, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary) and easypj/wsgi.py (exposes the application object gunicorn's CMD names by dotted path).

EXPLANATION

Everything downstream — base image choice, the CMD line, whether the app even imports — traces back to these two files being correct and present in the build context.

  easypj/
  ├── requirements.txt   ← pins Django, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary
  └── easypj/wsgi.py     ← exposes `application`, named by gunicorn's CMD
                            (the dotted path easypj.wsgi:application)
Q12
Where does easypj's PostgreSQL database live relative to the application's own container or tree?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In its OWN separate container — it is never part of the easypj image or tree.

EXPLANATION

settings.py reads DB_HOST/DB_NAME/DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD from the environment (12-factor style); Part 4 formalizes the database as a Compose service, but even in a manual docker run walkthrough it is always a second, independent container.

  ┌─ easypj-container ────────┐        ┌─ easypj-db (postgres:16) ──┐
  │ Django + gunicorn          │──DNS──▶│ PostgreSQL                  │
  │ NOT part of the DB's tree  │        │ its OWN separate container  │
  └────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
Q13
In a Dockerfile that creates a non-root user with RUN adduser ... && chown -R app:app /app followed by USER app, what breaks if you reverse the order and set USER app BEFORE those setup steps?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The adduser/chown steps themselves need root to run — dropping to a non-root USER first makes chown fail on permissions, or the build silently completes with the wrong owner on /app.

EXPLANATION

Installs and file-ownership setup need root; everything actually EXECUTED at runtime (including CMD) should not — get the order backwards and you either break the build or ship a container that quietly still runs as root.

# CORRECT — root does the setup, THEN drops privilege
RUN adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app

# WRONG — chown has no permission once already non-root
USER app
RUN adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app   # ❌ permission denied
Q14
Name the three separate jobs a correct .dockerignore does for easypj, per 9.3.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Speed — a smaller build context transfers faster. (2) Cache stability — host junk like __pycache__ can't invalidate layers. (3) Secret hygiene — .env (holding DB_PASSWORD) never enters a pullable image layer.

EXPLANATION

A single missing entry (forgetting .env, say) can fossilize a secret into every image ever pushed from that Dockerfile — one dotfile, three protections, is .dockerignore's whole reason to exist.

#JobExample
1Speedsmaller build context transfers faster
2Cache stability__pycache__ can't invalidate layers
3Secret hygiene.env never enters a pullable layer
Q15
After docker build -t easypj:v1.0 . succeeds, what three things does 9.4 say to check BEFORE ever running the container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The tag exists (docker images), the SIZE is in the expected ~180 MB range (not 850 MB), and docker history shows the expected fat layers (pip install, base image).

EXPLANATION

A surprising SIZE is the cheapest possible bug report — it means .dockerignore or the slim base didn't apply, and it's cheaper to catch here than after a failed run.

CheckCommandExpect
Tag existsdocker imageseasypj:v1.0 listed
Size sanedocker images SIZE column~180 MB, not 850 MB
Layer breakdowndocker historyonly the expected fat layers (pip install, base image)
Q16
Why specifically does DB_HOST=localhost never work, even once easypj and PostgreSQL share a user-defined network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because "localhost" inside a container always resolves to THAT container's own network namespace — never a sibling container, no matter what network they share.

EXPLANATION

easypj and easypj-db must be reached by NAME — Docker's embedded DNS resolves the database container's NAME to its IP on the shared network — "localhost" can never do that job, on any network topology.

  easypj-container's "localhost"  =  easypj-container ITSELF
  easypj-db's "localhost"          =  easypj-db ITSELF
  → DB_HOST=localhost always points a container at its own empty loopback,
    never at a sibling container — regardless of shared network.
Q17
Per 9.6's debugging protocol, why is docker logs the FIRST command against a container that "won't start" — not docker inspect?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because a container that "won't start" is almost always a process that DID start and then printed its dying words before exiting — logs is the cheapest, fastest signal.

EXPLANATION

inspect (exit code, env, networks) and exec (live reproduction) are only needed when logs are silent or ambiguous — the protocol is ordered cheapest-and-most-likely-to-answer first, not alphabetically or by habit.

OrderCommandAnswers
1stdocker logswhat did the process print before dying? (cheapest, usually enough)
2nddocker inspectexit code, env, networks — when logs are silent
3rddocker execlive reproduction — when logs+inspect are ambiguous
Q18
In the final multi-stage Dockerfile, what does copying ONLY the installed-packages directory from the builder stage into the runtime stage accomplish that a single-stage build could not?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It brings ONLY the installed Python packages into the final image, leaving the builder stage's pip cache, build tools, and full source checkout entirely behind in the discarded builder layer.

EXPLANATION

Isolating installed packages to one directory in the builder stage, then copying just that directory (plus the --chowned app code) into the runtime stage, is what keeps the final image at ~180 MB instead of carrying the builder's whole toolchain. This is a bigger win than 9.2's same-layer apt-get purge -y gcc alone: that trick already got the single-stage Dockerfile down to 185 MB (9.4) by removing the COMPILER, but the pip cache and every earlier layer's fossilized bytes were still in the image — multi-stage discards the builder's entire filesystem, cache included, which is the extra margin below.

Naive single-stage (no cleanup at all)Multi-stage (COPY --from=builder)
Final image containspip cache + build tools (gcc) + full source checkoutonly the installed packages dir + --chowned app code
Typical size~850 MB~180 MB

🔬 Practice Drill 9.1 — Sabotage On Purpose, Then Diagnose By the Book

⏱️ Target Time: 15 minutes
Scenario

From a clean checkout, build easypj:v1.0 and bring up the two-container circuit from 9.5. Then break it on purpose, three separate ways, one at a time: (1) omit -e DB_HOST=easypj-db on the second run, (2) run easypj-container on a DIFFERENT network than easypj-db, and (3) override the entrypoint to run gunicorn directly against a typo'd module path. Done when 9.6's table names the correct culprit for each, using only docker logs, in under a minute per scenario.

Hint: all three break DIFFERENTLY on purpose — a missing DB_HOST still resolves to SOMETHING (a wrong default), a wrong network fails at DNS resolution, and a typo'd module fails before gunicorn's master process even forks a worker. Matching the SHAPE of the error in docker logs to the right class — content, config, or wiring — without guessing is the actual skill this drill rehearses.
View Solution
TERMINAL — three sabotaged runs
# 1. Missing DB_HOST — omit the -e flag entirely
$ docker run -d --name easypj-c1 --network easypj-net -p 8000:8000 \
    --env-file .env easypj:v1.0
$ docker logs easypj-c1
# django.db.utils.OperationalError: connection to server at "localhost" ... failed
# culprit: DB_HOST never set, Django fell back to a wrong default — CONFIG class

# 2. Wrong network — db and web can't see each other at all
$ docker network create wrong-net
$ docker run -d --name easypj-c2 --network wrong-net -p 8001:8000 \
    -e DB_HOST=easypj-db --env-file .env easypj:v1.0
$ docker logs easypj-c2
# OperationalError: could not translate host name "easypj-db" to address
# culprit: DNS can't resolve a name that isn't on the SAME network — WIRING class

# 3. Typo'd module — bypass the entrypoint to isolate the CMD itself
$ docker run --rm --network easypj-net -e DB_HOST=easypj-db --env-file .env \
    --entrypoint gunicorn easypj:v1.0 easypj.wgsi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
$ docker logs
# ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'easypj.wgsi'
# culprit: a one-letter typo (wgsi vs wsgi) — CONTENT class

Check yourself: if any of the three took longer than a minute to name, re-read docker logs' FIRST line before anything else — every one of these errors names its own cause in plain English; the skill is trusting that line instead of reaching for docker inspect or exec first.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.2 — Prove Root Is Gone

⏱️ Target Time: 3 minutes
Scenario

Build easypj:v1.0, then run docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 whoami and docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 id -u. Done when both report the non-root app user and a non-zero UID.

Hint: USER app in the Dockerfile only changes who future instructions execute as — running whoami inside the actual container proves it took effect at runtime, not just that the line exists in the file.
View Solution
TERMINAL
$ docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 whoami
app

$ docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 id -u
101

Check yourself: if either command prints root or 0, walk the Dockerfile top to bottom — either USER app is missing entirely, or it was placed BEFORE a later instruction that needed root (9.2's ordering gotcha), silently un-dropping the privilege you thought you'd already removed.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.3 — Measure the .dockerignore Win

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Time the build context with docker build . 2>&1 | grep "transferring context" BEFORE and AFTER adding .dockerignore, then run docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 ls -a /app. Done when the context shrinks to roughly 1 MB and no .env, env/, or .git appears inside the image's /app.

Hint: a fat "transferring context" line almost always means a stray .git/ or local virtual environment is riding along with every single build — .dockerignore is the ONLY thing standing between your laptop's junk drawer and the image.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# BEFORE adding .dockerignore
$ docker build . 2>&1 | grep "transferring context"
 => => transferring context: 14.8MB                     0.6s

# AFTER adding .dockerignore
$ docker build . 2>&1 | grep "transferring context"
 => => transferring context: 0.9MB                      0.1s

# Confirm nothing sensitive made it in
$ docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 ls -a /app
.  ..  manage.py  requirements.txt  easypj  jobpost
# no .env, no env/, no .git — all correctly excluded

Check yourself: the context drop should be roughly the size of your local .git/ plus any virtual environment — if it barely moved, .dockerignore is probably sitting one directory away from the actual build context root (9.3's gotcha).

🔬 Practice Drill 9.4 — Prove Build Determinism

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Run the 9.4 build once, note the IMAGE ID from docker images easypj, then rebuild with ZERO source changes. Done when the second build reports every step CACHED in about a second and produces the exact same IMAGE ID.

Hint: any step reported as re-run (not CACHED) on an unchanged tree means something upstream of it changed — usually a file .dockerignore should have excluded (like a timestamp-touched log) invalidating the layer cache.
View Solution
TERMINAL
$ docker build -t easypj:v1.0 . && docker images easypj
# easypj   v1.0   abc123def456   ...   185MB

# Rebuild — nothing changed on disk
$ docker build -t easypj:v1.0 .
[+] Building 0.8s (11/11) FINISHED
 => CACHED [1/6] FROM python:3.11-slim                  0.0s
 => CACHED [2/6] WORKDIR /app                            0.0s
 => CACHED [3/6] RUN apt-get update && apt-get install... 0.0s
 => CACHED [4/6] COPY requirements.txt .                 0.0s
 => CACHED [5/6] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r req.txt 0.0s
 => CACHED [6/6] COPY . .                                0.0s

$ docker images easypj
# easypj   v1.0   abc123def456   ...   185MB   <- same IMAGE ID

Check yourself: the SAME IMAGE ID on both builds is the whole proof — Docker didn't rebuild anything because nothing in the build context or Dockerfile actually changed, which is exactly what layer caching (5.3) promises.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.5 — Full Circuit With a Real Database

⏱️ Target Time: 12 minutes
Scenario

Bring up the full two-container circuit from 9.5 (easypj-net, easypj-db, easypj-container), create a Django superuser, and log in at /admin/. Done when a JobPost you save through admin survives docker restart easypj-container — proof state lives in the database container, not the app container.

Hint: docker exec easypj-container python manage.py createsuperuser runs interactively inside the already-running web container — it needs Django and the DB connection, not a shell you open separately.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# 1. Bring up the circuit (9.5)
docker network create easypj-net
docker run -d --name easypj-db --network easypj-net \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=easypj -e POSTGRES_USER=easypj \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass postgres:16
docker run -d --name easypj-container --network easypj-net \
  -p 8000:8000 -e DB_HOST=easypj-db --env-file .env easypj:v1.0

# 2. Create an admin login and save a JobPost via /admin/
docker exec -it easypj-container python manage.py createsuperuser

# 3. Restart the WEB container only — the database container is untouched
docker restart easypj-container

# 4. Log back in at /admin/ — the JobPost is still there

Check yourself: if the JobPost is GONE after the restart, the app is almost certainly writing to SQLite inside its own writable layer instead of PostgreSQL — check DB_HOST reached easypj-db and not a fallback default (9.1's env-driven settings gotcha).

🔬 Practice Drill 9.6 — Verify the Tree Before Touching Docker

⏱️ Target Time: 2 minutes
Scenario

Before writing or building anything, run python -c "import easypj.wsgi" from inside your easypj checkout, then open requirements.txt. Done when the import succeeds with no traceback AND the file pins all three names the rest of this chapter depends on: Django, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary.

Hint: this check costs seconds and catches an entire class of mistakes — a broken wsgi.py import or a missing dependency pin — BEFORE you spend 40+ seconds on a Dockerfile build that would only fail for the exact same reason, just later and with a noisier error.
View Solution
TERMINAL
$ python -c "import easypj.wsgi"
# no output, no traceback — the import succeeded

$ cat requirements.txt
Django==5.2
gunicorn==21.2.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.9

Check yourself: if the import raises ModuleNotFoundError or ImportError, the Dockerfile you are about to write would fail at the exact same line inside docker run, just after paying the full build cost first — this drill exists to make that failure cheap instead of expensive.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.7 — Scan the Final Image and Prove Root Is Still Gone

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Build the 9.7 final multi-stage Dockerfile, rerun the 9.5 two-container circuit against it, then run docker scout quickview easypj:v1.0 and docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 whoami. Done when the image is roughly ~180 MB, the CVE count is comfortably under 50, and whoami reports the non-root app user — the multi-stage build didn't just shrink the image, it kept every earlier chapter's security decision intact.

Hint: a fat CVE count almost always traces back to the BASE image (8.2's territory — rebuild on a newer python:3.11-slim tag), not to easypj's own thin application layer — docker scout quickview's summary line tells you which bucket to look in before you go hunting.
View Solution
TERMINAL
$ docker build -t easypj:v1.0 .   # the 9.7 multi-stage file
$ docker images easypj
# easypj   v1.0   ...   ~180MB

$ docker scout quickview easypj:v1.0
#   Target      │  0C  │  2H  │ 14M  │ 21L
#   digest xxxx │
#   Base image  python:3.11-slim  is out of date  →  33 vulnerabilities  (upgrade available)

$ docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 whoami
app

Check yourself: if the CVE count is high AND docker scout quickview attributes most of it to the base image line, that is 8.2's lesson repeating itself — pull a fresher python:3.11-slim tag and rebuild before assuming anything in easypj's own Dockerfile is the problem.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.8 — Diff docker init Against the 9.7 Final Dockerfile

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Run docker init in a SCRATCH copy of the easypj checkout (never the real one — see the gotcha below), then diff its generated Dockerfile against 9.7's final version line by line. Done when you can defend every single difference out loud — which lines docker init got right unassisted (you should spot the pip cache mount from 5.7 among them), and which Django-specific lines it could never have known to write.

Hint: 9.8's table already lists the eight dimensions that differ (stages, base image, pip install, non-root user, static files, entrypoint, compose db, image size) — use it as your diff checklist instead of eyeballing two Dockerfiles side by side from scratch.
View Solution
TERMINAL
# 1. Scratch copy ONLY — docker init overwrites files on confirm
$ cp -r easypj easypj-scratch && cd easypj-scratch
$ docker init
# Created -> Dockerfile  .dockerignore  compose.yaml  README.Docker.md

# 2. Diff against the real, hand-tuned Dockerfile
$ diff Dockerfile ../easypj/Dockerfile
# single-stage vs multi-stage, no ENTRYPOINT line, no collectstatic RUN,
# but --mount=type=cache for pip is ALREADY there — docker init learned that one

Check yourself: the edit list back to production should be SHORT and PRINCIPLED — add 4.7's entrypoint, add collectstatic, point compose.yaml at postgres:16 with a volume. If your list is longer than that, you're re-deriving decisions docker init already got right instead of building on top of them.

   │ TREE   │▶│ DOCKERFILE │▶│ .docker │▶│ BUILD  │▶│ RUN +   │▶│ DEBUG +   │
   │ (9.1)  │ │ (9.2)      │ │ ignore  │ │ VERIFY │ │ VERIFY  │ │ FINAL FILE│

In one line: Chapter 9 takes easypj from a bare project tree to a verified, running, debuggable container and finally to the exact multi-stage Dockerfile every later part in this guide assumes exists. Nothing here is a new Docker idea — 9.1-9.8 are Chapters 4 through 8's decisions, applied in order, on one real app, with a verification step after every single one.

The takeaway: that discipline — build, then PROVE it, before moving on — is the habit Part 3 exists to install.

🏗️ Part 3 · Recap · Complete

Docker Images — Managed, Shrunk, Shipped

You started Part 3 already able to build and run a container, but treating the image itself as a disposable byproduct. Now you own its full custody lifecycle — list, tag, push, pull, save, load, and prune with intent — know exactly how to make it smaller and safer (right base image, same-layer cleanup, a docker scout scan you can actually read), and proved every bit of it by taking easypj from a bare project tree to a verified, network-reachable, debuggable container.

🔑 Part 3 — Key Takeaways

  • An image has exactly one real identity — the IMAGE ID (and the DIGEST once pushed); tags are free, disposable pointers, and the cleanup ladder runs prune → prune -a → system prune -a --volumes, ranked by blast radius (Ch 7).
  • Size is a recurring tax, not a one-time cost — the base image is the biggest lever (slim over alpine, for glibc-compatible wheels), then same-layer cleanup and multi-stage builds, verified with a docker scout scan that splits CVEs into base vs. your-layer (Ch 8).
  • Applied end to end on easypj: tree → Dockerfile → .dockerignore → build+verify → run+verify (user-defined network, bind 0.0.0.0) → debug by fixed protocol — logs, then inspect, then exec, never by guessing (Ch 9).
  • 🎯 Exam: Chapters 7-8 together ARE the DCA's Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%) domain — this Part is core content, not background reading.
  • 🔑 docker tag · push/pull · save/load · image prune · history · scout quickview
📌 Part 3 Visual Summary — own it, shrink it, prove it
   🖼️  OWN IT (Ch 7)                                                  custody: list → tag → push/pull → save/load → prune
   list/filter ─▶ tag (free ptr) ─▶ push/pull (digest=truth) ─▶ save/load ─▶ prune + history
                                                                                    │
                                                                                    ▼
   📏 SHRINK IT (Ch 8)                                                same image, now smaller & scanned
   why size matters ─▶ pick base (slim) ─▶ layer + Django trim ─▶ scout scan ─▶ distroless (optional)

   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   one image: owned, shrunk, and proven end-to-end — that's Part 3. 📦

In words: Chapter 7 gives you full custody of an image that already exists — list and filter it, tag it (a free, disposable pointer, unlike the one real ID/digest underneath), move it to and from a registry, carry it offline via save/load when there's no registry at all, and keep the local store honest with a graduated prune ladder and an auditable docker history.

Chapter 8 turns that owned image into a lean one: size is a recurring tax paid on every pull, every CI job, every node — so you attack the base image first, add same-layer cleanup and multi-stage builds, and confirm the result with a docker scout scan that separates what the base image owes you from what your own layer owes you, with distroless as the ceiling for teams willing to trade shell-based debugging for the smallest possible attack surface.

Chapter 9 spends that whole toolkit on one real app: easypj goes from a bare project tree to a Dockerfile you can trace line-by-line back to earlier chapters' decisions, a working .dockerignore, a build you verify by size and history before you ever run it, a run on a user-defined network bound to 0.0.0.0, and a debugging protocol — logs, then inspect, then exec — never panic.

The one idea to keep: an image isn't a black box you build once and forget — it's something you own (custody), shrink (optimize), and prove (verify), and Chapter 9 showed all three habits compounding into one production-ready Dockerfile.

Chapter 10 · Docker Compose Fundamentals

Docker Compose is how you run MULTIPLE containers as a single application. Instead of remembering 4+ docker run commands, you declare everything in one YAML file and start it with one command. This is the foundation of modern containerized development.
