10.1 What is Docker Compose?

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. You write a compose.yaml (or docker-compose.yml) file that describes all your services, networks, and volumes — then start everything with docker compose up.

Real-world use case: easypj needs 4 services to run — Django (app), PostgreSQL (database), Redis (cache), and Nginx (reverse proxy). Without Compose, you'd run 4 separate docker run commands, manually create a network, and manage startup order. With Compose: one file, one command.

Docker Compose — One Command, Four Containers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🎼 docker compose up — THE MAGIC                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                                         │
  │  │  compose.yaml               │     ONE COMMAND:                        │
  │  │                             │     $ docker compose up -d              │
  │  │  services:                  │                                         │
  │  │    django:   build: .       │         │                               │
  │  │    postgres: image: pg:15   │         │                               │
  │  │    redis:    image: redis:7 │         ▼                               │
  │  │    nginx:    image: nginx   │                                         │
  │  └─────────────┬───────────────┘                                         │
  │                │                                                         │
  │                ▼                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                    🐳 DOCKER HOST                                │    │
  │  │                                                                  │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐        │    │
  │  │  │ 🐍 Django │  │ 🐘 Postgres│ │ 🔴 Redis  │  │ 🟢 Nginx  │        │    │
  │  │  │  :8000   │  │  :5432   │  │  :6379   │  │  :80     │        │    │
  │  │  │          │  │          │  │          │  │          │        │    │
  │  │  │ easypj   │  │ easypj_db│  │ cache    │  │ reverse  │        │    │
  │  │  │ app      │  │ data 📂  │  │ backend  │  │ proxy    │        │    │
  │  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘        │    │
  │  │       └─────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┘              │    │
  │  │                        │                                        │    │
  │  │           easypj_default (auto-created network)                 │    │
  │  │           DNS: "django", "postgres", "redis", "nginx"           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🌐 Browser → http://localhost:80 → nginx → django:8000 → postgres:5432 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
Declarative Configuration

Compose files are declarative — you describe the DESIRED state (4 containers, specific images, ports, volumes), and Docker figures out HOW to achieve it. This is the same philosophy as Kubernetes and Terraform.

🔄
Infrastructure as Code

Your compose.yaml lives in Git alongside your source code. Anyone on your team can clone the repo and run docker compose up — they get the EXACT same environment. No more "works on my machine" issues.

🏃
Level 1
docker run

One container per command. Manual networking. Shell scripts for startup order.

⚠️ Works but fragile
🎼
Level 2
docker compose

Multiple containers from one YAML file. Auto DNS networking. One command: up.

✅ Dev & single-server prod
☸️
Level 3
Kubernetes

Multi-node orchestration. Auto-scaling, rolling updates, self-healing. Cloud-native.

🏆 Production at scale
💡 The Cooking Analogy

docker run is cooking each dish by shouting instructions; compose.yaml is the printed menu the kitchen executes as one order. In the MAGIC diagram above, the YAML box is the menu; the four containers on the host are the dishes arriving together.

10.2 Docker Compose vs docker run

Why use Compose when you can just run docker run four times? Because Compose handles networking, startup order, configuration, and teardown automatically:

Aspectdocker rundocker compose
Containers per command1 container per commandMultiple in one file ✅
NetworkingManual (docker network create)Auto-created DNS network ✅
Startup OrderManual (wait + run sequence)depends_on + health checks ✅
ConfigurationCLI flags onlyDeclarative YAML file ✅
ReproducibilityShell script dependentcompose.yaml = single source ✅
Tear Downdocker rm for each containerdocker compose down (all at once) ✅
Environment Vars-e flag per container.env file + env_file key ✅
Volumes-v flag per mountvolumes: section (declarative) ✅
Team SharingShare shell scriptsShare compose.yaml (Git) ✅
Production Ready❌ No⚠️ Dev only (use K8s/Swarm for prod)
💡 The Namespacing Bonus

docker run state lives in your shell history; Compose state lives in a versioned file. Compose also NAMESPACES everything: the project name prefixes containers (easypj-django-1), networks (easypj_default) and volumes — stacks never collide.

10.3 Installing Docker Compose

Docker Compose v2 is now built into Docker Desktop and available as docker compose (note: no hyphen!). On Linux, it's a plugin installed separately:

TERMINAL
# Docker Desktop (Windows/macOS): Already included — just use:
$ docker compose version
Docker Compose version v2.27.0

# Linux: Install as plugin
$ sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-compose-plugin
# OR download binary:
$ sudo curl -SL "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/latest/download/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
$ sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# Verify installation
$ docker compose version
$ docker-compose --version  # legacy (v1) syntax — still works
📖 Compose v1 vs v2

Compose v1 (docker-compose with hyphen) was a standalone Python script. Compose v2 (docker compose without hyphen) is a Docker CLI plugin written in Go — faster, better integrated, and actively maintained. Always use v2 for new projects. The v1 syntax (docker-compose up) still works for backward compatibility, but treat it as end-of-life and retire it on sight.

10.4 The compose.yaml File Structure

A compose.yaml file has 6 top-level sections. Here's the complete anatomy — every key you'll encounter on the DCA exam:

compose.yaml Anatomy — Every Key Explained
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📋 compose.yaml ANATOMY                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ services:              ← CONTAINERS: your app stack               │   │
  │  │   django:              ← Service name (becomes DNS hostname!)     │   │
  │  │     build: .           ← Build from Dockerfile in current dir     │   │
  │  │     image: easypj:v1   ← OR use pre-built image                   │   │
  │  │     ports:             ← Port mapping (HOST:CONTAINER)            │   │
  │  │       - "8000:8000"    ← Host 8000 → Container 8000               │   │
  │  │     environment:       ← Environment variables                    │   │
  │  │       - DEBUG=False    ← (use .env file for secrets!)             │   │
  │  │     volumes:           ← Mount storage                            │   │
  │  │       - ./src:/app     ← Bind mount (dev)                         │   │
  │  │       - static:/static ← Named volume (prod)                      │   │
  │  │     depends_on:        ← Startup order (NOT readiness!)           │   │
  │  │       postgres:        ← Wait for postgres container to START     │   │
  │  │         condition:     ← v2.1+: can wait for health check         │   │
  │  │           service_healthy                                        │   │
  │  │     healthcheck:       ← Container health monitoring              │   │
  │  │       test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/"]        │   │
  │  │       interval: 30s    ← Check every 30 seconds                   │   │
  │  │       retries: 3       ← 3 failures = unhealthy                   │   │
  │  │     restart: always    ← Restart policy                           │   │
  │  │     networks:          ← Which networks to join                   │   │
  │  │       - backend        ← Django on backend network                │   │
  │  │       - frontend       ← Django also on frontend (for nginx)      │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ networks:              ← CUSTOM NETWORKS                           │   │
  │  │   backend:             ← Internal network (DB, Redis, Django)      │   │
  │  │     driver: bridge     ← Network driver                            │   │
  │  │   frontend:            ← External network (Nginx, Django)          │   │
  │  │     driver: bridge     ← Standard bridge network                   │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ volumes:               ← NAMED VOLUMES                             │   │
  │  │   postgres_data:       ← Persists DB data across restarts          │   │
  │  │   static:              ← Persists collected static files           │   │
  │  │   media:               ← Persists user uploads                     │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ secrets:               ← SWARM SECRETS (encrypted at rest)         │   │
  │  │   db_password:         ← Sensitive data — never in plain text!     │   │
  │  │     external: true     ← Pre-created: docker secret create        │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ configs:               ← CONFIGURATION FILES (Swarm)               │   │
  │  │   nginx_conf:          ← Nginx configuration as config object      │   │
  │  │     file: ./nginx.conf ← Source file on host                       │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳
services

The containers that make up your app. Each service runs one image. Service names become DNS hostnames on the Compose network — Django can reach PostgreSQL at postgres:5432.

🌐
networks

Custom networks for isolation. The backend network connects Django + DB + Redis (internal). The frontend network connects Nginx + Django (external-facing).

💾
volumes

Named volumes persist data. Without volumes, PostgreSQL data disappears on docker compose down. Named volumes survive container restarts, recreations, and teardowns.

🔐
configs & secrets

Swarm-only features for secure configuration management. Secrets are encrypted at rest and only mounted into authorized services. For non-Swarm: use .env files + env_file.

🔧 Under the Hood — how docker compose up actually talks to Docker

Compose v2 is NOT a second daemon. It is a CLI plugin (10.3) that parses and merges your YAML into an in-memory PROJECT model, then drives the exact same Docker Engine API that docker run drives — there is no compose-specific container runtime underneath.

 compose.yaml + .env
      │ (1) parse, merge, interpolate ${VARS}
      ▼
 in-memory PROJECT MODEL (services/networks/volumes resolved)
      │ (2) diff against what is already running
      ▼
 Docker Engine API (same socket docker run/network/volume use)
      │ (3) create network → create volume → create/start each
      │     container, LABELED:
      │       com.docker.compose.project=easypj
      │       com.docker.compose.service=django
      │       com.docker.compose.config-hash=<sha>
      ▼
 running containers — identical to docker run output except
 for those labels, which is how compose ps / compose down
 know which containers belong to THIS project.
🔑 Those config-hash labels are why re-running docker compose up is safe: Compose hashes each service's rendered config and only recreates containers whose hash changed — untouched services are left running exactly as they were.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Compose declares desired state for a multi-container app on ONE host; up/down reconcile and remove that state as a unit.
  • Compose v2 is a CLI plugin (docker compose, space) that speaks the same Engine API as docker run — v1 (docker-compose, hyphen) is end-of-life; retire it on sight.
  • Every Compose-managed object carries com.docker.compose.* labels (project/service/config-hash) — that's the whole mechanism behind compose ps, compose down, and safe re-up.
  • Four top-level keys matter: services, networks, volumes, secrets/configs — every service key maps 1:1 to a docker run flag (ports→-p, environment→-e, volumes→-v, restart→--restart).
  • The service NAME is the DNS hostname on the project's network — the single most load-bearing line in any compose.yaml.
  • depends_on orders container STARTUP only; it does not wait for readiness unless paired with condition: service_healthy (Chapter 12).
  • The project name namespaces everything it creates (containers like easypj-django-1, networks like easypj_default) so stacks never collide.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • depends_on without healthcheck condition → depends_on only waits for container START, not READY. Use condition: service_healthy.
  • Hardcoding credentials in compose.yaml → Use .env file or Docker secrets for credentials. compose.yaml should reference vars.
  • Forgetting networks in compose → Services on different custom networks can't communicate. Use a shared network.
  • Confusing docker-compose (v1, EOL) with docker compose (v2) → The commands mostly translate, but the v1 binary may not even be installed on a fresh machine.
  • Manually docker run-ing a container "into" a Compose project → docker compose down only removes what the file declares, so the manual container lingers and confuses compose ps.
  • Publishing a service's port "just for convenience" → Compose's default posture is backend-internal, not published; every published port should be a deliberate decision.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker compose version immediately after any install — confirm the v2 plugin answered before typing anything else.
  • ls ~/.docker/cli-plugins/ (or the Linux package path) to see exactly which binary docker compose resolves to when something looks off.
  • Alias dc to docker compose once — every command in this guide from here on gets shorter.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 10)

the Chapter 10 cheat-card 
docker compose version              # confirm the v2 plugin exists
docker-compose version              # v1 relic — should error/EOL
docker compose up -d                # create + start every service
docker compose up                   # foreground, multiplexed logs
docker compose down                 # stop + remove the whole stack
docker compose config               # print the merged, resolved YAML

🧠 Chapter 10 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From "what is Compose" to the depends_on readiness gap — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What problem does Docker Compose solve for easypj that Chapter 3's docker run could not?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Chapter 3 ran ONE container. easypj is FOUR (django, postgres, redis, nginx) that must share a network, start in order, and be torn down together — Compose replaces a page of docker run flags with one file and one command, docker compose up -d.

EXPLANATION

This is the exact WHY stated at the top of Chapter 10 — the "five terminals and a wiki page" problem.

Q2
In 10.1's "ONE COMMAND, 4 CONTAINERS" diagram, what creates easypj_default, and who resolves names like "postgres" on it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose up auto-creates the project's default network; its embedded DNS server resolves each service NAME to that service's container IP — no IPs are ever hardcoded.

EXPLANATION

compose.yaml → docker compose up → 🐳 DOCKER HOST (auto network, DNS by name: django, postgres, redis, nginx).

Q3
Fill in the missing cells: Networking, Startup Order, and Team Sharing for docker run vs docker compose.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Networking: Manual (docker network create) → Auto-created DNS network. Startup Order: Manual (wait + run sequence) → depends_on + health checks. Team Sharing: Share shell scripts → Share compose.yaml (git).

EXPLANATION

These three rows are exactly why a teammate cloning easypj gets the SAME stack instead of a README to interpret.

Q4
Why are docker-compose (hyphen) tutorials "v1 era," and what command proves which one YOUR machine runs?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

v2 replaced the standalone Python docker-compose binary with a Go CLI plugin invoked as docker compose (space). Run docker compose version (expect v2.x) versus docker-compose version (v1 relic, may not even resolve on a fresh install).

EXPLANATION

10.3 calls v1 "end-of-life and should be retired on sight" — the hyphen is the tell.

Q5
Trace the resolution chain from typing docker compose up to the binary that actually executes it.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose up → /usr/bin/docker (the docker CLI, "compose" isn't a built-in verb so it searches cli-plugins) → ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose (or the Linux package path) → found → exec the plugin binary, forward all remaining args.

EXPLANATION

This is also how docker buildx and other third-party subcommands plug in, with zero core CLI changes.

Q6
Name the four top-level compose.yaml keys and one docker run concept each replaces.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

services (one block per docker run invocation), networks (docker network create), volumes (docker volume create / -v), secrets/configs (sensitive files/values — real Docker secrets need Swarm, Part 10).

EXPLANATION

Straight from 10.4's anatomy diagram.

Q7
Why does the service NAME matter more than nearly any other line in the file?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It becomes the DNS hostname on the project network — e.g. nginx.conf can say proxy_pass http://django:8000 and never know or care about an IP address.

EXPLANATION

10.4 calls this "the single most load-bearing line."

Q8
What is the difference between bare depends_on: [postgres] and depends_on with condition: service_healthy?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Bare depends_on waits only for the postgres CONTAINER PROCESS to start; condition: service_healthy waits for postgres's own healthcheck to report healthy — i.e. actually ready for queries.

EXPLANATION

10.4's closing gotcha; Chapter 11 and Chapter 12's 12.4 are where this distinction gets used for real.

Q9
Give two concrete costs of "I'll just keep using docker run scripts" versus committing a compose.yaml.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Reproducibility — a shell script silently drifts from what was actually run; compose.yaml is a single versioned source of truth. (2) Team Sharing — onboarding means handing over 12 docker run lines to interpret, versus git clone && docker compose up.

EXPLANATION

Both rows come directly from 10.2's 10-dimension comparison table.

Q10
What one-sentence gotcha closes 10.4, and why does it matter for Chapter 11's django+postgres pairing?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

"depends_on orders STARTUP only — it never waits for readiness unless you add condition: service_healthy." It matters because Chapter 11 pairs django with postgres and needs exactly that gate so gunicorn doesn't query a postgres still running initdb.

EXPLANATION

This is the thread Chapter 11 immediately pulls on.

11.1 Planning the easypj Stack

The easypj project needs 4 services to run in production-like mode: Django (application), PostgreSQL (relational database), Redis (cache/sessions), and Nginx (reverse proxy + static files). Here's how they connect:

easypj Compose Stack — 4 Services Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🏗️ easypj DOCKER COMPOSE STACK                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                    🌐 EXTERNAL TRAFFIC                             │   │
  │  │                    http://localhost:80                             │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                   │                                      │
  │                                   ▼                                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  🟢 NGINX (port 80 → django:8000)                               │    │
  │  │  Serves: /static/* (from static volume)                         │    │
  │  │  Proxies: /* → django:8000 (all requests to Django)             │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                     │                                    │
  │                  ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐                │
  │                  ▼                                      ▼                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  🐍 DJANGO (port 8000)        │  │  🔴 REDIS (port 6379)         │  │
  │  │  • easypj project             │  │  • Django cache backend       │  │
  │  │  • jobpost app (5 models)     │  │  • Celery message broker      │  │
  │  │  • Gunicorn WSGI server       │  │  • Session storage            │  │
  │  └──────────────┬────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                 │                                                       │
  │                 ▼                                                       │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐                                      │
  │  │  🐘 POSTGRESQL (port 5432)    │                                      │
  │  │  • Database: easypj           │  💾 Volume: postgres_data            │
  │  │  • All Django model data      │     /var/lib/postgresql/data         │
  │  │  • User accounts & auth       │     PERSISTENT across restarts!      │
  │  │  • Job posts, skills, etc.    │                                      │
  │  └───────────────────────────────┘                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NETWORKS: frontend (nginx+django) + backend (django+postgres+redis)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ServiceImage sourceVolume?Networks
djangobuild: .no (stateless)backend, frontend
postgresimage: postgres:15yes (postgres_data)backend only
redisimage: redis:7-alpinenobackend only
nginximage: nginx:alpineno (mounts static:ro)frontend only
💡 Decide These Three Columns Before Writing Any YAML

Only postgres gets a persistent volume — django, redis, and nginx are stateless or read-only mounts. Only nginx exposes a host port (80); postgres and redis stay backend-internal by default. Getting this table right up front is what makes 11.2-11.3's YAML unsurprising.

11.2 compose.yaml — Django + PostgreSQL Service

Start with the two core services. Django needs PostgreSQL to be running first — depends_on handles this:

compose.yaml (Django + Postgres)
services:
  # ─── PostgreSQL Database ───
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: easypj_db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: easypj
      POSTGRES_USER: easypj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"           # Expose for external tools (DBeaver, pgAdmin)
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypj"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend

  # ─── Django Application ───
  django:
    build: .                   # Builds from Dockerfile in current dir
    container_name: easypj_app
    command: gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://easypj_user:${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/easypj
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/static
      - media_volume:/app/media
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy  # Wait for health check, not just "started"!
    networks:
      - backend
      - frontend

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  static_volume:
  media_volume:

networks:
  backend:
    driver: bridge
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
⚠️ depends_on ≠ Ready

depends_on without condition: service_healthy only waits for the container to START — not for PostgreSQL to be ready to accept connections. Always add a healthcheck to PostgreSQL and use condition: service_healthy in depends_on. Otherwise Django may try to connect before PostgreSQL is initialized, causing a crash loop.

🔧 Under the Hood — why POSTGRES_PASSWORD only matters on the FIRST boot

The official postgres image's entrypoint script checks whether PGDATA (the volume mount, /var/lib/postgresql/data) already contains a data directory. Only on an EMPTY volume does it run initdb and consume POSTGRES_DB/POSTGRES_USER/POSTGRES_PASSWORD to create the role and database; on every later boot it just starts postgres against the existing files and ignores those variables.

 postgres_data volume EMPTY?
      │
      ├─ yes ─▶ entrypoint runs initdb ─▶ creates role/db from
      │          POSTGRES_* env vars ─▶ writes data files
      │
      └─ no ──▶ entrypoint SKIPS initdb ─▶ starts postgres
                 directly against existing files ─▶ POSTGRES_*
                 vars ignored entirely
🔑 This is exactly why the depends_on gotcha above holds: the credential now lives INSIDE the volume's data files, not in the environment — changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env after the first boot changes nothing until you either drop the volume (losing all data) or connect with psql and run ALTER ROLE yourself.

11.3 Adding Redis & Nginx Services

Redis provides caching and session storage. Nginx serves as the reverse proxy — handling static files directly and proxying all other requests to Django:

compose.yaml (Full 4-Service Stack)
  # ─── Redis Cache ───
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: easypj_redis
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

  # ─── Nginx Reverse Proxy ───
  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    container_name: easypj_nginx
    ports:
      - "80:80"                # Expose to host — access at http://localhost
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro  # Custom config
      - static_volume:/static:ro                         # Serve static files
      - media_volume:/media:ro                           # Serve media files
    depends_on:
      - django
    networks:
      - frontend
nginx.conf
upstream django_app {
    server django:8000;           # Compose DNS resolves "django" to container IP
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name localhost;

    # Static files — Nginx serves directly (FAST)
    location /static/ {
        alias /static/;
        expires 30d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }

    # Media files — uploaded by users
    location /media/ {
        alias /media/;
    }

    # Everything else → Django
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://django_app;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
🏆 The Power of Compose DNS

Notice server django:8000; in nginx.conf — this works because Compose creates a DNS network where django resolves to the Django container's IP. No hardcoded IPs. No port mapping needed between services — they communicate directly on the internal network. This is the magic that makes Compose files portable across machines.

Redis carries two distinct jobs for easypj, each on its own logical database index: the Django cache backend at redis://redis:6379/1, and the Celery message broker at redis://redis:6379/0 — one container, two DB indexes, no persistence needed for either.

Request Path — /jobs/ vs a static file
  /jobs/  ──▶ nginx :80 ──▶ proxy_pass ──▶ django:8000
                                         (appears in django's logs)
  /static/... ──▶ nginx :80 ──▶ alias /static/ (served from the
                              `static` volume — ONLY in nginx's logs)

11.4 Environment Variables & Secrets in Compose

Never put secrets in compose.yaml. Use a .env file (gitignored) and reference variables with ${VAR} syntax:

.env
# easypj environment variables — NEVER commit this file!
DB_PASSWORD=super_secret_db_password_123
SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123xyz789
DEBUG=False
ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1
REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
🛑 The .env Security Rule

ALWAYS add .env to .gitignore. A committed .env file with database passwords is one of the most common security incidents in Docker projects. Provide a .env.example file instead — with placeholder values — so new developers know what variables to set.

.env feeds two distinct mechanisms, and it matters which one carries a secret: (1) ${VAR} interpolation substituted into compose.yaml at parse time, and (2) env_file: injecting variables into the container at runtime. SECRET_KEY travels via env_file into the container environment, read by os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] — it never appears in compose.yaml itself.

11.5 Running the Full easypj Stack

TERMINAL
# Start everything in detached mode
$ docker compose up -d
[+] Running 5/5

 ✔ Network easypj_frontend   Created    0.1s
 ✔ Container easypj_redis    Started    0.8s
 ✔ Container easypj_db       Healthy    3.2s
 ✔ Container easypj_app      Started    2.1s
 ✔ Container easypj_nginx    Started    0.5s

# See all services
$ docker compose ps
NAME            IMAGE              STATUS                    PORTS
easypj_nginx    nginx:alpine       Up 30 seconds             0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp
easypj_app      easypj-compose     Up 30 seconds             8000/tcp
easypj_db       postgres:15-alpine Up 30 seconds (healthy)   0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp
easypj_redis    redis:7-alpine     Up 30 seconds (healthy)   0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp

# Run migrations (inside the django container)
$ docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate
Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions, jobpost
Running migrations:
  Applying jobpost.0001_initial... OK

# Follow all service logs
$ docker compose logs -f

# Follow only django logs
$ docker compose logs -f django

# Stop everything (preserves volumes)
$ docker compose down
# To also DELETE database data:
$ docker compose down -v

A cold-start verification is six commands in order: up -d (build+create+start) → ps (postgres healthy, 4 running) → exec migrate (schema applied) → exec createsuperuser (admin access exists) → logs -f django (gunicorn listening) → curl -I /jobs/ (200 OK end to end).

11.6 Development Workflow with Docker Compose

Compose isn't just for running stacks — it's your daily development driver. Here's the workflow that replaces python manage.py runserver with a full production-like environment:

Development Workflow with Compose
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔄 COMPOSE DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │  ✏️ Edit  │───▶│  👀 Watch │───▶│  🔄 Sync │───▶│  🧪 Test  │          │
  │  │  Code    │    │  Changes │    │  to      │    │  Results  │          │
  │  │          │    │          │    │  Container│    │          │          │
  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. Edit views.py          3. Changes sync instantly to container       │
  │  2. Compose watch detects   4. Browser refresh → see changes!            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OR with bind mounts (traditional approach):                             │
  │  volumes: - .:/app  →  changes reflect immediately (no rebuild needed)  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Running tests:                                                          │
  │  $ docker compose run django python manage.py test jobpost               │
  │  $ docker compose run django pytest                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Debugging:                                                              │
  │  $ docker compose exec django bash              # Interactive shell      │
  │  $ docker compose exec django python manage.py shell  # Django shell    │
  │  $ docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj_user easypj  # DB shell  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏆 The Compose Development Advantage

Instead of installing PostgreSQL, Redis, and configuring them locally, you get a production-like environment with ONE command. Your entire team runs the same stack. No more "it works on my machine but not in staging" — your dev environment IS your staging environment, just with debug mode and volume mounts. This is the modern development workflow that the DCA exam expects you to understand.

There are two distinct hot-reload routes, and only one handles a changed requirements.txt: a bind mount (.:/app) plus a reloading dev server (runserver) syncs code instantly but does nothing for dependency changes; docker compose watch's develop.watch can also rebuild when requirements.txt or the Dockerfile changes — the bind-mount route cannot. Chapter 12 covers the full watch mechanics.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Plan first: build for django, pull for postgres/redis/nginx; only postgres gets a persistent volume (postgres_data).
  • postgres/redis stay backend-only; only nginx exposes a host port (80) — the frontend/backend network split from 11.1.
  • condition: service_healthy + pg_isready is what makes django wait for a database that can actually answer, not just exist.
  • POSTGRES_* env vars are read once, only when the data volume is empty — never assume changing .env changes a live database.
  • .env feeds two distinct mechanisms: ${} interpolation into compose.yaml, and env_file injection into the container.
  • The daily verb set is up -d / ps / exec ... migrate / logs -f — four commands cover cold start through verification.
  • down -v deletes named volumes too; that's the whole difference between "restart the stack" and "drop the database."
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Exposing postgres or redis with ports: "for convenience" → Backend-internal is the default posture from 11.1's plan.
  • Expecting a changed POSTGRES_PASSWORD to take effect on an existing volume → It won't, without a volume reset or ALTER ROLE.
  • Editing nginx.conf on the host and expecting nginx to reload it automatically → Needs nginx -s reload or a service restart.
  • Relying on gunicorn's default behavior for hot reload in dev → It does not reload; use runserver or gunicorn --reload instead.
  • Running down -v when you meant plain down → The extra flag silently takes the database with it.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj_user easypj then \dt for a 10-second schema sanity check.
  • docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost for a clean, disposable test run that leaves nothing in docker ps -a.
  • Compare docker compose logs nginx against logs django side by side to separate static-file hits from real app requests.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 11)

the Chapter 11 cheat-card 
docker compose up -d                                   # boot the full stack
docker compose ps                                       # postgres healthy? 4 running?
docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate     # apply jobpost's schema
docker compose exec django python manage.py createsuperuser  # admin access
docker compose logs -f django                            # confirm gunicorn is listening
docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj_user easypj    # \dt to see jobpost tables
docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost  # one-shot, self-cleaning tests
docker compose down -v                                    # DANGER: also deletes volumes

🧠 Chapter 11 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

Building easypj's real compose.yaml, service by service — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
For each of easypj's 4 services, is it built or pulled, does it get a persistent volume, and which network(s) is it on?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

django: build: ., no volume (stateless), backend+frontend. postgres: image postgres:15, volume postgres_data, backend only. redis: image redis:7-alpine, no volume, backend only. nginx: image nginx:alpine, no volume (mounts static:ro), frontend only.

EXPLANATION

This table IS 11.1's planning diagram in tabular form — decide these three columns before writing any YAML.

Q2
Why does postgres get a pg_isready healthcheck, and what does condition: service_healthy change about django's startup?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

pg_isready confirms postgres can actually accept connections, not just that the process exists; service_healthy makes django's depends_on wait for that healthy state instead of merely "container started" — closing Chapter 10's gotcha for real.

EXPLANATION

Without it, Django tries to connect immediately, PostgreSQL isn't ready, Django crashes, Docker restarts it, and it crashes again — a classic crash loop.

Q3
What is the gunicorn command 11.2 uses to serve easypj, and why does it bind 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3; binding 0.0.0.0 is required so the process accepts connections arriving from OTHER containers (nginx), not only from inside its own process.

EXPLANATION

11.3's nginx upstream depends on this bind address — the same 0.0.0.0 lesson from Chapter 9.5.

Q4
In nginx.conf, what does server django:8000; resolve to, and why does it work without an IP address?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It resolves via Compose's embedded DNS to whichever container is currently named "django" on the frontend network — the service name is the hostname, so nginx never hardcodes an IP.

EXPLANATION

This reuses Chapter 10's DNS-hostname takeaway on a real config file.

Q5
Draw the request path for a browser hitting http://localhost/jobs/ versus /static/admin/css/base.css.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/jobs/ → nginx :80 → proxy_pass → django:8000 (appears in django's logs). /static/... → nginx :80 → alias /static/ (served from the static volume — ONLY in nginx's logs).

EXPLANATION

11.3's PRACTICE step verifies exactly this split by comparing docker compose logs nginx vs logs django.

Q6
Name Redis's two jobs in easypj and the two logical databases they use.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Django cache backend at redis://redis:6379/1 and the Celery message broker at redis://redis:6379/0 — one container, two DB indexes, no persistence needed for either.

EXPLANATION

From 11.3's easypj example.

Q7
What are the two distinct mechanisms .env feeds in Compose, and which one carries SECRET_KEY to Django?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) ${VAR} interpolation substituted into compose.yaml at parse time, and (2) env_file: injecting variables into the container at runtime; SECRET_KEY travels via env_file into the container environment, read by os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] — it never appears in compose.yaml itself.

EXPLANATION

11.4 names both mechanisms explicitly.

Q8
List the six commands of a cold-start verification, in order, and what each one proves.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

up -d (build+create+start) → ps (postgres healthy, 4 running) → exec migrate (schema applied) → exec createsuperuser (admin access exists) → logs -f django (gunicorn listening) → curl -I /jobs/ (200 OK end to end).

EXPLANATION

This is 11.5's full TERMINAL sequence.

Q9
You run docker compose down then up -d again — does your superuser survive? What if you'd run down -v instead?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Plain down keeps volumes, so postgres_data (and your superuser row) survives intact; down -v deletes named volumes too, wiping postgres_data and the database with it.

EXPLANATION

11.5's closing gotcha, verified by its own PRACTICE step.

Q10
What's the difference between the two hot-reload routes in 11.6, and which one also handles a changed requirements.txt?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A bind mount (.:/app) plus a reloading dev server (runserver) syncs code instantly but does nothing for dependency changes; docker compose watch's develop.watch can also rebuild when requirements.txt or the Dockerfile changes — the bind-mount route cannot.

EXPLANATION

11.6 names both routes and defers the full watch mechanics to Chapter 12.5.

Chapter 12 · Docker Compose Advanced Features

One compose.yaml now has three masters — your laptop, CI, and something production-like — and they disagree about ports, mounts, and debug flags. Now that you can build a full stack (Chapter 11), this chapter adds the machinery that keeps ONE source of truth serving all three: profiles for environment-specific services, multiple Compose files for dev/prod overrides, deep networking control, proper health-check-gated startup ordering, hot reload with watch mode, scaling, and validating exactly what the engine will run.

12.1 Compose Profiles — Environment-Specific Services

Not all services need to run in every environment. Profiles let you tag services and include them only when a specific profile is active:

compose.yaml (with profiles)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    # No profile = always runs (default profile)

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    # No profile = always runs

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    # No profile = always runs

  # Dev-only tools
  pgadmin:
    image: dpage/pgadmin4
    profiles: ["dev", "debug"]    # Only in dev/debug profiles
    ports: ["5050:80"]

  # Debugging tools
  mailhog:
    image: mailhog/mailhog
    profiles: ["debug"]           # Only in debug profile
    ports: ["8025:8025"]

  # Production monitoring
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus
    profiles: ["prod"]            # Only in prod profile
    ports: ["9090:9090"]

# Start normally (only services without profiles):
$ docker compose up -d

# Start with dev tools:
$ docker compose --profile dev up -d

# Start with everything:
$ docker compose --profile dev --profile debug --profile prod up -d
💡 When to Use Profiles

Use profiles for: debugging tools (MailHog, pgAdmin), optional monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana), test runners (Selenium, Cypress), and expensive services (Elasticsearch) that not every developer needs. Don't use profiles for core application services — those should always run.

A leaner, network-scoped version of the pattern — bind pgadmin to localhost only and keep it on the backend network so it never gets a public IP by accident:

compose.yaml (profile-tagged service, network-scoped)
pgadmin:
  image: dpage/pgadmin4
  ports: ["127.0.0.1:5050:80"]  # localhost only, never 0.0.0.0
  profiles: ["debug"]
  networks: [backend]
💡 The Theatre Lighting Analogy

Every lamp is wired (declared) whether or not tonight's show uses it. --profile picks the lighting preset — the wiring never changes. easypj: pgadmin sits under profile debug — daily up boots 4 services; docker compose --profile debug up -d adds the DB GUI on :5050 when you need to eyeball jobpost rows.

12.2 Compose Overrides — Multiple Compose Files

Compose automatically merges compose.override.yaml with compose.yaml. This lets you define a base configuration and layer environment-specific overrides:

compose.yaml (Base)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  postgres_data:
compose.override.yaml (Dev Overrides — AUTO-MERGED)
services:
  django:
    environment:
      - DEBUG=True             # Override: enable debug in dev
    volumes:
      - .:/app                 # Add: bind mount for hot reload
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000  # Override CMD
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"            # Add: expose port for direct access
  postgres:
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"            # Add: expose DB for local tools
📖 Merge Rules

Compose merges multiple files left-to-right. Later files override earlier ones. For single-value keys (image, command), the last value wins. For list keys written as a plain YAML sequence (ports, volumes), a later file's list REPLACES the earlier one wholesale — not appended. For mapping keys (environment as key:value, labels, deploy), keys are merged and later values override. Use docker compose config to see the merged result without starting anything.

Explicit -f lists work the same way for a third file — a production layer that swaps in gunicorn and drops the source mount entirely:

The Three-File Layout
compose.yaml           # base: services, networks, volumes
compose.override.yaml  # dev: mount .:/app, runserver,
                        #      DEBUG=True, ports 8000:8000
compose.prod.yaml      # prod: gunicorn, restart: always,
                        #      no source mount, no 8000 exposed
$ docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d
💡 The Blueprint Analogy

The base file is the house blueprint; overrides are transparent sheets laid on top — dev's sheet draws a workbench in the living room, prod's sheet bolts the doors. The bottom blueprint never changes. easypj: the dev override swaps command to runserver and mounts the source; the prod file swaps in the gunicorn command and drops the mount so the image's COPY'd code is what actually runs.

🔧 Under the Hood — how Compose actually MERGES multiple -f files

docker compose -f a.yml -f b.yml config does not just concatenate the files — each YAML type merges by a different rule: scalars (strings/numbers/booleans) in a LATER file REPLACE the earlier value; maps (environment as key: value, labels) are merged key-by-key; sequences written as a plain YAML list (a service's ports: or volumes:) are REPLACED wholesale by a later file's list, not appended to it.

 compose.yaml:       command: gunicorn ...            (scalar)
 compose.prod.yaml:  command: gunicorn --workers 4    ← REPLACES
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 compose.yaml:       environment: {DEBUG: "True"}        (map)
 compose.override:   environment: {LOG_LEVEL: info}   ← MERGES
 result:              {DEBUG: "True", LOG_LEVEL: info}
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 compose.yaml:       ports: ["8000:8000"]               (list)
 compose.prod.yaml:  ports: []                        ← REPLACES
 result:              ports: []   (nothing published at all)
🔑 This is exactly why 12.7's rule — "always confirm with docker compose config" — is not optional caution. It is the only way to know which merge rule applied to a given key without memorizing the entire compose-spec merge algorithm.

12.3 Compose Networking Deep Dive

Understanding Compose networking is critical for the DCA exam. Each Compose project gets its own isolated network with built-in DNS:

Compose Networking — 4 Services Connected
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 🌐 DOCKER COMPOSE NETWORKING                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Network: easypj_default (auto-created by compose)                       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │                                                                     │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐       │  │
  │  │  │   nginx      │────▶│   django     │────▶│  postgres    │       │  │
  │  │  │  (port 80)   │     │  (port 8000) │     │  (port 5432) │       │  │
  │  │  │              │     │              │     │              │       │  │
  │  │  │  DNS: nginx  │     │  DNS: django │     │ DNS: postgres│       │  │
  │  │  │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │       │  │
  │  │  │  80:80       │     │  (internal)  │     │  (internal)  │       │  │
  │  │  └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘       │  │
  │  │         │                   │                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    ┌──────────────┘                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
  │  │         │    │  docker exec django ping postgres   │                │  │
  │  │         │    │  → resolves! ✅                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
  │  │         ▼    ▼                                    │                │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐                                 │                │  │
  │  │  │    redis     │◀────────────────────────────────┘                │  │
  │  │  │  (port 6379) │   docker exec django redis-cli -h redis ping    │  │
  │  │  │              │   → PONG ✅                                      │  │
  │  │  │  DNS: redis  │                                                  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────┘                                                  │  │
  │  │                                                                     │  │
  │  │  EXTERNAL: curl http://localhost:80 → nginx → django                │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 Each service can reach any other service by its SERVICE NAME!        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Network Isolation

Each Compose project gets its own default network (named {project}_default). Services in different projects CANNOT communicate by default — they're on separate networks. To connect services across projects, use external: true networks: create a network with docker network create shared, then reference it in both compose files as networks: shared: external: true.

The diagram above is what Compose gives you by DEFAULT when no networks: key is declared at all — one open-plan room where everyone answers to their NAME and can walk to anyone else's desk. easypj never actually ships this flat layout: Chapter 11's frontend/backend split (11.1-11.3) already built the walls — postgres sits in a windowless back office only django has a door to. internal: true is what removes that office's street exit too, so it can't even reach the internet.

💡 The Windowless Office

A network with no internal: flag still lets its services reach the internet (and, via published ports, the host). internal: true removes ALL outside routing — services on it can only reach each other, matching postgres/redis's backend-isolation pattern. Chapter 14 goes one layer deeper into the network model that makes those walls work.

12.4 depends_on with Health Checks

The #1 Compose gotcha: depends_on without health checks. Let's fix it properly:

compose.yaml (Health Checks Done Right)
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s   # Grace period before checking starts

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  django:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy    # Wait for postgres to be READY
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy    # Wait for redis to be READY
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health/"]
      interval: 30s
      retries: 3
💡 Two More Healthcheck Fields That Matter for Slow-Booting Services

start_period gives a grace window where failures don't count toward retries — useful while django runs migrate before its own healthcheck can pass. start_interval sets a FASTER probe cadence during that same window, so the grace period doesn't cost a full interval per attempt. disable: true turns off a HEALTHCHECK baked into a base image without forking the Dockerfile.

💡 The "OPEN" Sign Analogy

A container that started but isn't ready is a shop with the lights on and the till not counted. The healthcheck is the OPEN sign the shopkeeper flips — service_healthy means "queue outside until the sign flips". easypj: without the gate, gunicorn boots first and Django's first query hits a postgres still running initdb → connection refused → crash loop. With pg_isready gating, cold starts are boring — which is the goal.

12.5 docker compose watch — Hot Reload

Compose v2.22+ introduced watch — automatic file sync and rebuild during development. No more manual rebuilds:

compose.yaml (watch config)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync          # Copy changed files into container
          path: ./easypj
          target: /app/easypj
        - action: sync
          path: ./jobpost
          target: /app/jobpost
        - action: rebuild       # Rebuild image when deps change
          path: requirements.txt
        - action: restart       # Restart container when config changes
          path: compose.yaml
💡 Watch Actions

sync: copies changed files into the running container (fast, no rebuild). rebuild: rebuilds the image when Dockerfile or dependencies change. restart: restarts the container (good for config changes). sync+restart: copies files AND restarts the container (for compiled languages). Run with docker compose watch instead of docker compose up.

The full easypj watch block also distinguishes sync from sync+restart — a plain file copy versus a copy that also bounces the process, which matters when the changed file is read only at process startup:

compose.yaml (develop.watch, full easypj block)
django:
  develop:
    watch:
      - action: sync            # .py, templates → copy in
        path: .
        target: /app
        ignore: [".git/", "*.pyc"]
      - action: rebuild         # deps changed → new image
        path: requirements.txt
      - action: sync+restart    # config → restart process
        path: easypj/settings.py
        target: /app/easypj/settings.py
💡 Three Severities of Edits

Three severities of edits to a play mid-run: sync = slip the actor a corrected line; sync+restart = redo the scene; rebuild = new script, restage the whole play. easypj: views.py edits sync in a blink; touching requirements.txt correctly forces the pip-layer rebuild — watch knows the difference so you don't have to. Synced files land in the container's writable layer — a rebuild discards them; your disk copy (the source of the sync) is the only durable one, by design.

12.6 Scaling Services with Compose

Need more Django workers? Compose can scale services to multiple replicas — all on one host:

TERMINAL
# Scale django to 3 replicas
$ docker compose up -d --scale django=3
[+] Running 5/5
 ✔ Container easypj-postgres-1  Running
 ✔ Container easypj-redis-1     Running
 ✔ Container easypj-django-1    Started
 ✔ Container easypj-django-2    Started   # New replica!
 ✔ Container easypj-django-3    Started   # New replica!
 ✔ Container easypj-nginx-1     Running

# Nginx automatically load-balances across all 3 django replicas
# because upstream django_app { server django:8000; } resolves to all 3 IPs!
3 Django Replicas Behind Nginx
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📊 SCALING WITH COMPOSE                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │                        🌐 http://localhost:80                             │
  │                               │                                          │
  │                               ▼                                          │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────┐                             │
  │                    │    🟢 NGINX (:80)    │                             │
  │                    │   upstream django {  │                             │
  │                    │     server django:8000 ← resolves to ALL 3 IPs!    │
  │                    │   }                  │                             │
  │                    └──┬────────┬──────────┘                             │
  │                       │        │        │                                │
  │              ┌────────▼──┐ ┌───▼─────┐ ┌─▼──────────┐                  │
  │              │ 🐍 Django  │ │ 🐍 Django│ │ 🐍 Django   │                  │
  │              │ Replica 1  │ │ Replica 2│ │ Replica 3   │                  │
  │              └────────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────────┘                  │
  │                       │        │        │                                │
  │                       └────────┼────────┘                                │
  │                                ▼                                         │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────┐                             │
  │                    │  🐘 PostgreSQL       │                             │
  │                    └──────────────────────┘                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️ All on ONE host — for multi-host scaling, use Kubernetes/Swarm      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Compose Scaling Limitations

Compose scaling runs all replicas on ONE host. For true horizontal scaling across multiple servers, you need Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. Compose is perfect for development, CI/CD, and single-server production — but not for multi-node clusters. Also: if you scale a service with port mappings (like "8000:8000"), only ONE replica can bind to the host port — remove the port mapping and let Nginx handle routing.

Put next to Swarm and Kubernetes, --scale's entire row is exactly one host with no self-healing — the other two columns are what Part 10 (Swarm) and the Kubernetes guide add once one host stops being enough:

DimensionComposeSwarmKubernetes
Max hosts1 (this host)N (swarm nodes)N (cluster)
Scale command--scale svc=3service scalekubectl / HPA
Auto-scalingnone, manualnone, manualHPA (automatic)
Failed replicastays deadrescheduledrescheduled
Cross-host LBn/a (1 host)routing meshService / LB
💡 Compose Has No Scheduler At All

--scale launches N containers once and stops; if host capacity runs out mid-scale the command just errors, unlike Swarm/K8s, which hold a desired-replica-count and keep retrying in the background.

Two syntaxes cap the same resource goal — a plain attribute for a bare docker compose up, or a deploy: block that only takes effect under docker stack deploy (Swarm mode):

NeedPlain attributedeploy: (Swarm)
Hard mem capmem_limit: 512mlimits.memory: 512M
Soft mem targetmem_reservation: 256mreservations.memory
CPU sharecpus: "0.50"limits.cpus: "0.50"

12.7 Validating & Debugging Compose Files

Debug any "compose does something weird" in one move: render the merged truth and read what the engine actually saw. docker compose config parses ALL -f files, applies override merging, resolves profiles, and substitutes every ${VAR} — its output is the ONLY file the engine acts on.

Interpolation grammar
${VAR}                              # empty string if VAR is unset
${VAR:-8000}                        # default 8000 if VAR is unset/empty
${VAR:?msg}                         # abort `up` loudly with msg if VAR is unset

# easypj examples:
SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY:?set it in .env}   # prod fails fast instead of running empty
PORT=${PORT:-8000}                          # a fresh clone boots with zero setup

Env values can come from five places, and only the highest-precedence source wins per variable:

PrecedenceSourceExample
1 (highest)shell env of the compose commandexport DEBUG=True
2--env-file FILE flag--env-file .env.prod
3.env beside compose.yamlPOSTGRES_PASSWORD=…
4env_file: inside the serviceruntime-only vars
5 (lowest)ENV in the image's Dockerfilelast-resort defaults

YAML's own grammar hides a few traps that silently change what a value means:

TrapWhat YAML doesFix
TAB indentationhard parse errorspaces, always
ports: [22:22]parsed as a sexagesimal numberquote "22:22"
DEBUG: falseboolean, not stringquote "false"
COUNTRY: NOYAML 1.1 → boolean falsequote "NO"
💡 The Pharmacist's Final Prescription

compose config is asking the pharmacist to print the FINAL prescription after every doctor's note was merged — you argue with that paper, not with the sticky notes (-f files). Use docker compose config --services to list only service names, or docker compose config --volumes for volumes — quick sanity lists without reading the whole merged file.

🛑 compose config Prints Resolved Secrets in Plain Text

docker compose config prints RESOLVED secrets in plain text — pipe it to your eyes, never into a ticket or a commit. The healthcheck command also runs INSIDE the container — curl/pg_isready must exist in that image, or the check fails forever and the stack never starts.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • profiles = conditional stack membership; untagged services always run, tagged ones need --profile (or COMPOSE_PROFILES).
  • compose.override.yaml auto-loads; explicit -f lists load left-to-right, later files winning per the merge rules (scalars replace, maps merge, lists replace).
  • the project's default network gives every service DNS-by-name; internal: true removes any route out of the host entirely.
  • started != healthy; service_healthy gates real readiness across all three tiers — postgres, redis, and django's own healthcheck.
  • watch routes: sync (code), rebuild (deps/Dockerfile changed), sync+restart (config changed) — three severities, one tool.
  • --scale needs a stateless service with NO fixed host port; Compose scaling is single-host, manual, with no self-healing.
  • docker compose config is the one command that prints what the engine will actually run — the final word in any dispute.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • An unprofiled service listing depends_on: a profiled one → The default `up` breaks outright — dependencies must share the same profile(s).
  • Deploying to a server without explicit -f flags → compose.override.yaml auto-loads and can silently ship runserver + DEBUG=True to production.
  • A healthcheck test: that assumes curl/pg_isready exist → The command runs INSIDE the container — if it's not in that image, the check fails forever and the stack never starts.
  • Running --scale django=3 while ports: "8000:8000" is still set → Replica 2 dies with "port is already allocated" — remove the fixed port mapping first.
  • Leaving ports: 22:22, DEBUG: false, or COUNTRY: NO unquoted → YAML silently reinterprets them as a sexagesimal number or a boolean — always quote such values as strings.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker compose config --services / --volumes for a quick sanity list without reading the whole merged file.
  • ${VAR:?msg} on any secret that must never silently boot empty in production.
  • docker compose ps (health column) to read a service's actual health state instead of guessing from raw logs.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 12)

the Chapter 12 cheat-card 
docker compose --profile debug up -d                          # include profiled services
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d     # explicit merge, prod
docker compose config                                          # merged, interpolated truth
docker compose config --services                              # quick service sanity list
docker compose up -d --scale django=3                          # N replicas, one host
docker compose watch                                           # sync/rebuild/sync+restart loop
docker compose ps                                              # health column, per-service

Q7
Why does scaling django to 3 replicas REQUIRE removing its ports: "8000:8000" line first?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Three containers cannot all bind the same host port; a scaled service must rely on the internal network plus nginx's DNS-based upstream instead of a fixed host port mapping.

EXPLANATION

This is 12.6's scaling diagram and closing gotcha.

Q8
Per 12.6's scaling-ceiling table, what happens to a failed replica under Compose versus Swarm/Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose: the replica "stays dead," no rescheduling. Swarm/K8s: the replica is automatically rescheduled to restore the desired count.

EXPLANATION

This is the exact row-by-row contrast in 12.6's scaling-ceiling table.

Q9
What's the difference between ${VAR:-8000} and ${VAR:?msg}, and which one should guard SECRET_KEY in prod?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

:-default substitutes a default when VAR is unset/empty (dev ergonomics); :?msg aborts up loudly with msg when VAR is unset — SECRET_KEY should use :?msg so prod never boots with a blank key.

EXPLANATION

This is 12.7's interpolation grammar and easypj example.

Q10
Name the three YAML traps from 12.7's table and the fix for each.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

TAB indentation (hard parse error) → use spaces, always. ports: [22:22] (parsed as a sexagesimal number) → quote "22:22". DEBUG: false / COUNTRY: NO (YAML booleans) → quote them as strings, "false"/"NO".

EXPLANATION

This is 12.7's top-YAML-traps table, reproduced exactly.

🎼 Part 4 · Recap · Complete

Compose — One File, Every Environment

You started this Part remembering a handful of docker run flags for one container; now you can read and write a full compose.yaml, wire a real 4-service stack (Django + PostgreSQL + Redis + Nginx) with healthcheck-gated startup, and keep that one file honest across dev, CI, and production with profiles, overrides, and docker compose config. Compose stopped being a shortcut and became the single source of truth for the whole stack.

🔑 Part 4 — Key Takeaways

  • Compose declares desired state for a multi-container app on one host — the service NAME is the DNS hostname, and docker compose up/down reconcile or remove that state as a unit (Ch 10).
  • depends_on orders startup, not readiness — only condition: service_healthy paired with a real healthcheck (e.g. pg_isready) makes a dependent service wait for "ready," not just "started" (Ch 10 names the gap; Ch 11-12 close it).
  • Plan before YAML: the easypj stack wires django + postgres + redis + nginx across a frontend/backend network split — only postgres gets a persistent volume, only nginx exposes a host port (Ch 11).
  • Secrets live in .env, never in compose.yaml — ${VAR} interpolation resolves at parse time, env_file injects at runtime, and POSTGRES_* vars are only read once, on an empty volume (Ch 11).
  • One base file, many shapes: profiles gate optional services (pgadmin, prometheus) behind --profile, and -f overrides merge scalars-replace / maps-merge / lists-replace to serve dev, CI, and prod from one source of truth (Ch 12).
  • compose watch picks the right severity per change — sync (code), rebuild (deps/Dockerfile), sync+restart (config) — and --scale proves Compose's ceiling: one host, no self-healing, no auto-scaling (Ch 12).
  • 🎯 Exam: Orchestration is DCA's heaviest domain at 25%, and Chapters 10-12 ARE that domain's hands-on core — compose.yaml anatomy, a real multi-service stack, and profiles/overrides/health-gating/watch/scale.
  • 🔑 docker compose up -d · ps · exec ... migrate · logs -f · --profile · -f a.yml -f b.yml · config · watch · --scale svc=N

In words: Chapter 10 gave you the grammar — every top-level compose.yaml key (services, networks, volumes, secrets/configs) and how each service key maps back to a docker run flag you already knew. Chapter 11 wrote the actual sentence: the real easypj stack, planned service-by-service (image source, state, network placement) before a line of YAML, wired so nginx fronts django, django waits for a postgres that's service_healthy — not merely started — and redis serves as both cache and Celery broker.

Chapter 12 then took that one file and made it survive three different audiences without forking it: profiles hide optional services (pgadmin, mailhog, prometheus) behind --profile, override files layer dev/CI/prod configuration on top of the same base (scalars replace, maps merge, lists replace), and docker compose watch picks sync / rebuild / sync+restart by how deep a change reaches. When any of that gets confusing, docker compose config prints the merged, interpolated truth — the only file the engine ever actually runs.

The one idea to keep: Compose is one declarative file describing desired state for a whole stack, plus a small set of guardrails (health checks, profiles, overrides) that keep dev, CI, and production all pointing at that same one file instead of drifting into three. Master this and the deeper networking and storage chapters ahead are just filling in details this Part already sketched.

Chapter 13 · Docker Networking Fundamentals

Networking is how containers communicate — with each other, with the host, and with the outside world. Compose "just worked" in Chapters 10-11 — nginx found django, django found postgres — and you deserve to know why. This chapter opens the hood: the Container Network Model, all 5 network drivers, the docker0 bridge in depth, and the embedded DNS server that makes automatic service discovery possible.

13.1 How Docker Networking Works

Docker networking is built on the Container Network Model (CNM) — a specification that defines how containers connect to networks. The CNM has three components:

🏖️
Sandbox

An isolated network stack: its own interfaces, routing table, and DNS config. Each container gets its own sandbox via Linux network namespaces.

🔌
Endpoint

A virtual network interface (veth pair) connecting a sandbox to a network. Think of it as a network cable plugged into the container.

🌐
Network

A collection of endpoints that can communicate. Implemented as a Linux bridge, overlay, or other driver. The docker0 bridge is the default network.

CNM Architecture — How Containers Connect
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🏗️ CONTAINER NETWORK MODEL (CNM)                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                         DOCKER HOST                                │   │
  │  │                                                                   │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐       │   │
  │  │  │ Container C1 │    │ Container C2 │    │ Container C3 │       │   │
  │  │  │ ┌──────────┐ │    │ ┌──────────┐ │    │ ┌──────────┐ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ SANDBOX  │ │    │ │ SANDBOX  │ │    │ │ SANDBOX  │ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ eth0     │ │    │ │ eth0     │ │    │ │ eth0     │ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ 172.17.0.2│    │ │172.17.0.3│    │ │172.17.0.4│ │       │   │
  │  │  │ └────┬─────┘ │    │ └────┬─────┘ │    │ └────┬─────┘ │       │   │
  │  │  └──────┼───────┘    └──────┼───────┘    └──────┼───────┘       │   │
  │  │         │                   │                    │                │   │
  │  │         │    ENDPOINT       │    ENDPOINT        │    ENDPOINT    │   │
  │  │         │  (veth pair)      │  (veth pair)       │  (veth pair)   │   │
  │  │         │                   │                    │                │   │
  │  │         ▼                   ▼                    ▼                │   │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │              NETWORK: docker0 BRIDGE (172.17.0.0/16)       │  │   │
  │  │  │              + Embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11                  │  │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  │                             │ NAT (iptables)                       │   │
  │  │                             ▼                                      │   │
  │  │                     ┌──────────────┐                              │   │
  │  │                     │ eth0 (host)  │──▶ Internet / LAN             │   │
  │  │                     │ 192.168.1.100│                              │   │
  │  │                     └──────────────┘                              │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Hotel Wiring Analogy

Think of a hotel: the sandbox is a room's own wall sockets, the endpoint is the cable running from the room to the patch panel, and the network is the patch panel itself — the diagram above is that wiring closet, drawn out. Run docker exec easypj-web ip addr and you'll see eth0@ifXX — the veth's inside end; ip link on the host shows its twin attached to the bridge.

📖 A Container Can Hold Many Endpoints, But Only One Sandbox

A container can be multi-homed — attached to several networks, each with its own endpoint (veth pair) — but it always has exactly ONE sandbox (network namespace). Multi-homed, never multi-brained. Try it: run both commands above and match the ifXX index across host and container — the numbers pair up, proving you've traced one endpoint end to end.

13.2 Network Drivers Overview

Docker provides 5 network drivers, each with different isolation and connectivity characteristics. Choosing the right driver is a key DCA exam topic:

5 Network Drivers Visualized

DriverIsolationMulti-HostPerformanceUse Case
bridge✅ Good❌ No🟡 MediumDefault, most single-host apps
host❌ None❌ No🟢 MaxHigh-perf, no isolation needed
none✅ Max❌ NoN/ASecurity-sensitive, no network needed
