💡 The Housing Analogy

Picture five housing options for the same tenant: bridge = an apartment with a shared front desk (NAT), host = living in the lobby (no walls at all), none = a bunker (zero connectivity), overlay = sister buildings joined by a private skybridge (multi-host), and macvlan = your own street address (a real LAN IP). All five are drawn above — same containers, different walls.

📖 What docker network ls Shows on a Fresh Engine

Run docker network ls on a freshly installed engine and you'll see exactly three networks: bridge, host, and none. The other drivers — overlay, macvlan/ipvlan — only appear once YOU explicitly create a network using them.

13.3 Bridge Networks — The Default

When you install Docker, it creates a default bridge network called bridge (using the docker0 Linux bridge). All containers join this network unless you specify otherwise. Bridge networks provide NAT-based connectivity with port mapping for external access:

Bridge Network Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🌉 BRIDGE NETWORK ARCHITECTURE                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  EXTERNAL WORLD (Internet / LAN)                                         │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │       │  curl http://host:8080                                           │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                         HOST (192.168.1.100)                       │   │
  │  │                                                                   │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐   │   │
  │  │  │  eth0 (physical) │         │       docker0 bridge          │   │   │
  │  │  │  192.168.1.100   │  NAT    │       172.17.0.1              │   │   │
  │  │  └────────┬─────────┘◀────────│                               │   │   │
  │  │           │                   │  -p 8080:80 → routes to C2:80│   │   │
  │  │           │     ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐                │   │   │
  │  │           │     ▼             ▼             ▼                │   │   │
  │  │           │  ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │  C1  │    │  C2  │    │  C3  │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │.0.2  │    │.0.3  │    │.0.4  │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │easypj│   │nginx │    │redis │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │:8000 │    │:80   │    │:6379 │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘               │   │   │
  │  │           │                                                  │   │   │
  │  │           │  DNS: C1 can ping "nginx" → resolves to .0.3    │   │   │
  │  │           │  DNS: C1 can ping "redis" → resolves to .0.4    │   │   │
  │  │           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Precision Check — Read the Diagram's DNS Lines Carefully

The two "DNS" lines drawn on the diagram above describe a user-defined bridge, not the plain docker0 default. On the actual DEFAULT bridge, C1 pinging "nginx" or "redis" by NAME fails — docker0 has no embedded DNS at all. Pinging by IP (172.17.0.3) works fine either way. Only a user-defined bridge (created with docker network create) wires up the embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 that lets containers resolve each other by name — see 13.4/13.5.

📖 Custom Bridge vs Default Bridge

The default bridge network does NOT provide automatic DNS resolution between containers — you need --link (legacy, deprecated). Custom bridge networks (created with docker network create) DO provide automatic DNS. Always create custom bridge networks for your applications — never rely on the default bridge for multi-container communication.

💡 Isolation Is Per-Bridge, Not Per-Host

Two containers on two DIFFERENT bridge networks cannot communicate at all — not even by IP — regardless of whether they're on the same Docker host. Isolation is enforced per-bridge via the DOCKER-ISOLATION iptables chains, which apply to every bridge Docker manages, docker0 included.

13.4 docker network Commands

These are your daily networking commands. Every DCA candidate must know them:

TERMINAL
# List all networks
$ docker network ls
NETWORK ID     NAME              DRIVER    SCOPE
abc123def456   bridge            bridge    local
def456ghi789   host              host      local
ghi789jkl012   none              null      local
jkl012mno345   easypj_backend    bridge    local

# Create a custom bridge network
$ docker network create --driver bridge easypj-net

# Inspect network details (subnets, connected containers, IPs)
$ docker network inspect easypj-net

# Connect a running container to a network
$ docker network connect easypj-net easypj-container

# Disconnect a container from a network
$ docker network disconnect easypj-net easypj-container

# Remove a network (must have no connected containers)
$ docker network rm easypj-net

# Remove all unused networks
$ docker network prune
💡 The Patch-Panel Analogy

Network lifecycle operations are patch-panel operations: create = mount a new panel, connect = plug a cable in, inspect = read the port labels, prune = rip out panels with no cables left in them. connect/disconnect operate on RUNNING containers live — a new veth (eth1) appears inside, no restart required.

Network Lifecycle — Four States
  CREATED  (docker network create, 0 endpoints, no traffic)
     │  docker run --network=... / docker network connect
     ▼
  CONNECTED  (≥1 container attached, veth live, DNS active)
     │  docker network disconnect (or the last container exits)
     ▼
  DISCONNECTED  (0 endpoints again — same state as CREATED)
     │  docker network rm (refuses if any endpoint remains)
     ▼
  REMOVED  (object gone; docker network ls no longer lists it)

  ↺ CONNECTED can also loop straight back to CONNECTED — connect
    another container without passing through DISCONNECTED.
💡 Disconnecting Never Stops a Container

Disconnecting a container from a network never stops it — it only removes that one interface (eth1, etc). A container only goes fully network-less if you disconnect its LAST network, and even DNS lookups inside it start failing at that point.

13.5 Container DNS & Service Discovery

Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container. This DNS resolves container names to IP addresses — enabling automatic service discovery without hardcoded IPs:

DNS Resolution Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔍 DOCKER DNS RESOLUTION                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Container django wants to connect to postgres:                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────┐    ① DNS query         ┌──────────────────────┐       │
  │  │   django    │──────────────────────▶ │  Docker DNS Server    │       │
  │  │ 172.17.0.2  │    "Where is postgres?"│  127.0.0.11:53        │       │
  │  │             │◀────────────────────── │                       │       │
  │  └─────────────┘    ② DNS response       │  Container Registry:  │       │
  │                      "postgres = .0.3"   │  ├ nginx   → 172.17.0.4      │
  │                                          │  ├ postgres→ 172.17.0.3      │
  │  ┌─────────────┐    ③ Connect             │  └ redis   → 172.17.0.5      │
  │  │  postgres   │◀──────────────────────  └──────────────────────┘       │
  │  │ 172.17.0.3  │    TCP 172.17.0.3:5432                                  │
  │  └─────────────┘                                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  --network-alias adds extra names:                                       │
  │  docker run --network-alias db --network-alias database postgres         │
  │  Now BOTH "db" and "database" resolve to the postgres container!         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Avoid --link (Legacy)

The --link flag was Docker's original service discovery mechanism — it injected environment variables and /etc/hosts entries. It's deprecated and should never be used in new projects. Use custom networks with automatic DNS instead: containers on the same custom network can resolve each other by name with zero configuration.

💡 The Receptionist Analogy

The embedded DNS is the office receptionist: colleagues are known by first name (container names), departments are known by role (--network-alias), and unknown visitors get pointed to the city directory (upstream DNS forwarding).

📖 Verify It Yourself

docker exec easypj-web cat /etc/resolv.conf shows nameserver 127.0.0.11; then run nslookup postgres from inside the container — it returns an answer inside the network's own subnet, proof the embedded resolver (not your host's DNS) answered the query. A concrete easypj example: --network-alias db on the postgres container lets old config expecting HOST="db" and new config using HOST="postgres" both resolve to the SAME container.

🔧 Under the Hood — why docker0 never got DNS

docker0 is a Linux bridge device created once at dockerd startup; every container's veth peer attaches to it as a bridge port. A user-defined bridge is just ANOTHER Linux bridge created on demand by docker network create, but wired to a daemon subsystem docker0 was never retrofitted with: an embedded DNS process reachable at 127.0.0.11:53 inside every container's namespace (via an iptables DNAT rule dockerd installs per-container). docker0 predates that feature — Docker's earliest releases had exactly one flat bridge and no DNS to embed — and was left alone for backward compatibility while new bridges got name resolution on top. The DOCKER-ISOLATION iptables chains that block traffic between DIFFERENT bridges, by contrast, apply to EVERY bridge dockerd manages, docker0 included — isolation was never a user-defined-only feature.

 dockerd starts
    │
    ├─▶ creates docker0 (Linux bridge) ── no DNS (legacy default)
    │                                      still isolated from
    │                                      every OTHER bridge
    └─▶ `docker network create X` ──▶ new bridge "br-xxxx"
                                       ├─ iptables DNAT:
                                       │  127.0.0.11:53 → embedded DNS
                                       └─ DOCKER-ISOLATION rule vs
                                          every OTHER bridge
🔑 It isn't that docker0 is "broken" — it only missed the DNS upgrade; per-bridge isolation has always applied to it too.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • CNM = sandbox (netns) + endpoint (veth) + network (bridge or driver) — every Docker network is built from these three nouns.
  • 5 drivers cover every case: bridge (default), host (no isolation), none (loopback only), overlay (multi-host), macvlan/ipvlan (real LAN IP).
  • docker0 has NO embedded DNS — only user-defined bridges get 127.0.0.11 name resolution.
  • The full network lifecycle is create → connect → inspect → disconnect → rm, with prune sweeping anything at zero endpoints.
  • network connect/disconnect operate on RUNNING containers live — no restart required.
  • Container names, compose service names, and every --network-alias are ALL answered by the embedded DNS; unknown names are forwarded upstream.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: driver selection and DNS behavior are directly graded exam competencies, not just background reading.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Expecting -p to work with --network host → --network host silently ignores -p — there is no NAT layer left for it to configure.
  • Assuming containers on the default docker0 bridge can resolve each other by name → They cannot — the default bridge has no embedded DNS. This is the single most common beginner "networking is broken" report.
  • Running docker network rm on a network with attached containers → It refuses ("has active endpoints") — disconnect or remove the containers first.
  • Assuming two containers on different bridges can talk if they know each other's name → They can't talk at all, even by IP — isolation is per-bridge, not per-host.
  • Following a tutorial that uses --link → --link predates user-defined networks entirely; its presence is itself evidence the material is old.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker network inspect NET --format '{{json .Containers}}' for a fast attached-container list without wading through the full JSON dump.
  • Default every docker network create to an explicit --subnet from day one — re-subnetting later means recreating the network from scratch.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 13)

the Chapter 13 cheat-card 
docker network ls                                 # bridge/host/none + yours
docker network create --driver bridge X            # new bridge network
docker network inspect X                            # subnet, gateway, members
docker network connect X container                  # live-attach, running
docker network disconnect X container                # live-detach, keeps running
docker network rm X                                  # fails if endpoints remain
docker network prune                                 # remove every unused net
docker exec CONTAINER cat /etc/resolv.conf           # confirm 127.0.0.11

🧠 Chapter 13 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the three CNM nouns to why --link is legacy — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What are the three nouns of the Container Network Model (CNM), and what real object does each map to?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Sandbox = the container's network namespace; Endpoint = one veth pair (one end becomes eth0 inside the sandbox); Network = the virtual switch a driver implements.

SANDBOX (netns) ══ENDPOINT(veth)══▶ NETWORK (bridge/driver)
one per container    one per network JOINED    one per docker network
EXPLANATION

This is 13.1's wiring-closet model — a container can hold many endpoints but exactly one sandbox.

Q2
How would you prove, from the host AND from inside a container, that one specific veth pair connects them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Inside: docker exec CONTAINER ip addr shows eth0@ifXX. On the host: ip link lists a matching vethXXXXX@ifYY attached to the bridge — the ifXX/ifYY indices identify the two ends of the SAME pair.

EXPLANATION

This is exactly 13.1's PRACTICE lab — tracing one endpoint end to end.

Q3
Which driver fits (a) a latency-critical metrics agent, (b) a 3-node Swarm cluster, (c) a legacy scanner needing a real LAN IP, (d) a security-sensitive container with no network at all?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(a) host (b) overlay (c) macvlan (d) none.

Driver  | Isolation | Multi-Host | Performance
host    | None      | No         | Max
overlay | Good      | Yes        | Medium
macvlan | Good      | No         | High
none    | Max       | No         | N/A
EXPLANATION

The 13.2 selection table maps one dominant need to one driver each — memorize the mapping, not just the names.

Q4
Two running containers both know each other's name, yet ping other-container fails with "bad address." Most likely cause and fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both are on the DEFAULT docker0 bridge, which has no embedded DNS. Fix: create a user-defined bridge and run both containers on it.

EXPLANATION

13.3's single most-asked interview scenario.

Q5
In one sentence each — what happens to (a) an inbound packet hitting a published port, and (b) an outbound packet leaving a container for the internet?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(a) DNAT rewrites the destination from host:port to container-IP:port before routing. (b) MASQUERADE (SNAT) rewrites the container's source IP to the host's outbound IP so replies can find their way back.

EXPLANATION

13.3's TECH block — the two halves of every bridge-network conversation with the outside world.

Q6
List, in order, the four states a Docker network passes through from creation to deletion, and what drives each transition.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CREATED —(run --network / network connect)—▶ CONNECTED —(disconnect, or last container exits)—▶ DISCONNECTED —(network rm)—▶ REMOVED. CONNECTED can also loop straight back to CONNECTED by attaching another container.

EXPLANATION

13.4's lifecycle diagram — docker compose down then up -d cycles easypj-net through all four states.

Q7
If you disconnect a container from its ONLY remaining network, does the container stop? What actually breaks?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — it keeps running, fully network-isolated (loopback only); DNS lookups and outbound connections stop working until it's reconnected.

EXPLANATION

13.4's 💡 callout — disconnecting never stops a container, it only removes an interface.

Q8
Walk through what happens, step by step, when a container asks "who is postgres?"
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/etc/resolv.conf points at 127.0.0.11 → the embedded DNS (dockerd) checks its per-network table → if "postgres" is a known name on THIS network it answers with the container's IP; otherwise the query is forwarded upstream.

EXPLANATION

13.5's DNS-lookup diagram, restated as prose.

Q9
Give a concrete easypj example of --network-alias solving a real naming problem.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--network-alias db on the postgres container lets old config expecting HOST="db" and new config using HOST="postgres" both resolve to the SAME container.

EXPLANATION

13.5 — one container, two names, zero code changes.

Q10
Why should a Docker tutorial that still uses --link be treated as outdated?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--link predates user-defined networks and their embedded DNS entirely; everything it did is now handled better, and by default, by a user-defined bridge — its presence is itself evidence the material is old.

EXPLANATION

13.5's closing gotcha.

🔬 Practice Drill 13.1 — Named Bridge vs Default Bridge (10 min)

Create a user-defined bridge, run two alpine containers on it, ping one from the other BY NAME (works). Then run a THIRD alpine on the default bridge and try to ping either of the first two, by name and by IP (both fail). Verify: you can state in one sentence why the third container failed differently from a plain DNS miss.

📌 Chapter 13 Visual Summary — CNM, five drivers, one DNS fork
  ┌──────────────────── CHAPTER 13 — THE WHOLE PICTURE ───────────────────┐
  │  CNM: SANDBOX(netns) ══ENDPOINT(veth)══▶ NETWORK (one of 5 drivers)   │
  │                                                │                     │
  │                       ┌────────────────────────┼───────────────┐     │
  │                       ▼                        ▼               ▼     │
  │              docker0 (default)        user-defined bridge   host/none/│
  │              NAT, NO DNS               NAT + DNS @127.0.0.11 overlay/ │
  │                                                │              macvlan │
  │                                  create→connect→inspect→disconnect→rm │
  │                                  (13.4 lifecycle — all of it, live)   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In one line: Every Docker network, regardless of which of the five drivers backs it, is built from the same three CNM nouns: a sandbox (the container's private namespace), an endpoint (the veth pair connecting it), and a network (the virtual switch a driver implements). The fork that causes the most beginner pain is docker0 vs a user-defined bridge — identical NAT behavior, but only the user-defined one wires up the embedded 127.0.0.11 DNS server that lets containers find each other by name.

The takeaway: every action on a network — create, connect, inspect, disconnect, remove — happens live, on running containers, which is exactly why Chapter 14 can wire and rewire easypj's topology without ever restarting the stack.

Chapter 14 · Networking easypj Containers

Let's apply networking concepts to the easypj stack. We'll design a two-network architecture — backend for internal services and frontend for external access — then implement it with Docker networks and Compose. Theory becomes architecture here: Chapter 13's bridges and DNS get applied on purpose, so that "my stack works, but every service is one -p flag away from the public internet" stops being true.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~90-105 min 🌐 Network 🎯 DCA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Attach containers to one or two networks, at run time and live, and prove reachability with ping in both directions (14.3)
  • ✅ Explain precisely what EXPOSE does (metadata only) versus what -p does (a real DNAT rule) (14.4)
  • ✅ Choose the right publish syntax for a given exposure need — loopback-only, all-EXPOSEd, UDP, container-to-container (14.4)
  • ✅ Encode the entire two-network design as a compose.yaml networks: section, including internal: true (14.5)

Networking 15%
🎯 A Direct, Hands-On Application of the Networking Domain

This chapter is a direct, hands-on application of the DCA "Networking" domain to a real multi-service stack — subnet planning, publish semantics, and compose network placement all appear on the exam in exactly this shape.

  • Why this chapter exists: Chapter 13 taught bridges and DNS in the abstract; here they get applied to easypj on purpose — a backend network the internet can never reach, a frontend network nginx guards, and a database with NO published port.
  • The load-bearing line: django is the ONLY dual-homed service — the blast radius of a compromised nginx has to stop at django, never reach postgres directly.

14.1 Network Design for easypj Stack

🎯 Goal: place easypj's four services on two networks so the blast radius of a compromised nginx is one hop — not the database. Security best practice: separate your services into network zones. The database and cache should be on an internal network — not directly accessible from outside. Only Nginx and Django need to be on the frontend network:

easypj Two-Network Architecture

  │               🔒 easypj TWO-NETWORK DESIGN                                │
  │                                                                          │

  │  │    frontend NETWORK           │    │    backend NETWORK             │  │

🏦
The Bank-Branch Analogy

A bank branch: frontend is the customer hall, django the teller window, backend the vault corridor. The teller works both zones; customers never enter the corridor; the vault has no street door AT ALL (no ports:).

🔬
easypj in Practice

JobPost rows and User password hashes — everything valuable lives in postgres, and postgres is reachable ONLY as postgres:5432 from backend members. No -p, no exposure, ever.

🧪 Practice — Verify Isolation Live

From nginx, try wget -qO- postgres:5432; repeat from django. Verify: nginx cannot even RESOLVE the name (different network); django connects. Two networks, one dual-homed app tier, zero published DB ports — this diagram is the reference posture for every later Part of the guide.

⚠️ "It's Just Dev" Is How Breaches Start

"It's just dev" is how port 5432 ends up bound to 0.0.0.0 — design the isolation BEFORE the first up, not after the first breach.

14.2 Creating Custom Networks for easypj

🎯 Goal: create both easypj networks and read an inspect output like a map.

TERMINAL
# Create backend network (internal — DB and cache)
$ docker network create --driver bridge easypj-backend
abc123def456

# Create frontend network (external-facing)
$ docker network create --driver bridge easypj-frontend
def456ghi789

# Verify networks
$ docker network ls | grep easypj
abc123def456   easypj-backend    bridge    local
def456ghi789   easypj-frontend   bridge    local

# Inspect backend network
$ docker network inspect easypj-backend
[
    {
        "Name": "easypj-backend",
        "Driver": "bridge",
        "Subnet": "172.20.0.0/16",
        "Gateway": "172.20.0.1",
        "Containers": {}       # No containers connected yet
    }
]
📖 Prefer Explicit Subnets on the Exam

Without --subnet, dockerd allocates the next free pool from its default-address-pools — that's what produced the auto-assigned 172.20.0.0/16 above. Explicit subnets buy stable firewall rules and no collisions with the office VPN's ranges: docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/24 --gateway 172.28.0.1 easypj-backend. Naming the corridors before moving furniture beats letting every docker run improvise its own hallway.

🧪 Practice — Create & Inspect Both

Create both networks, then docker network ls and inspect each. Verify: driver bridge, distinct subnets, empty Containers — and you can say which subnet is backend. Networks are cheap — name them like you mean it.

⚠️ Subnet Collisions Blackhole Traffic

A subnet overlapping your VPN or LAN silently blackholes traffic — the #1 "Docker broke my VPN" cause. Pick ranges like 172.28.x.x deliberately.

14.3 Connecting Containers to Networks

🎯 Goal: attach each easypj container to its planned network(s) — at run time and live — and prove the wiring in both directions.

TERMINAL
# Start PostgreSQL on backend only
$ docker run -d --name easypj-db \
    --network easypj-backend \
    -e POSTGRES_DB=easypj \
    postgres:15-alpine

# Start Redis on backend only
$ docker run -d --name easypj-redis \
    --network easypj-backend \
    redis:7-alpine

# Start Django on backend first, then connect to frontend
$ docker run -d --name easypj-app \
    --network easypj-backend \
    easypj:v1.0
$ docker network connect easypj-frontend easypj-app

# Start Nginx on frontend only
$ docker run -d --name easypj-nginx \
    --network easypj-frontend \
    -p 80:80 \
    nginx:alpine

# Verify connectivity
$ docker exec easypj-app ping easypj-db      # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec easypj-app ping easypj-redis   # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec easypj-app ping easypj-nginx   # Works! (same frontend network)
$ docker exec easypj-db ping easypj-app      # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec easypj-db ping easypj-nginx    # FAILS! (different networks)
🔑 Issuing Keycards

Issuing keycards: django gets two (both corridors), nginx one, postgres one — and the ping test is walking each corridor rattling every door. --network at run time attaches the FIRST network; further ones need docker network connect (live — adds eth1). The failing third ping is the design working: nginx and postgres share no network, so not even DNS crosses.

⚠️ docker run Only Accepts ONE --network Flag

docker run accepts only ONE --network flag — the "django on both" step MUST be a separate connect. Compose does this for you automatically (14.5); the raw CLI makes you feel it.

14.4 Port Publishing & Exposure

The distinction between EXPOSE and publish (-p) is one of the most tested DCA topics:

MechanismSyntaxWhat It DoesRequired for External Access?
EXPOSE (Dockerfile)EXPOSE 8000Documentation only — metadata saying "this container listens on 8000"❌ No — does NOT publish ports
-p (short publish)-p 8000:8000Maps host port 8000 to container port 8000✅ Yes
-P (publish all)-PPublishes ALL EXPOSEd ports to random host ports✅ Yes
--publish (long syntax)--publish mode=host,target=80,published=8080Full control: mode (host/ingress), protocol (tcp/udp)✅ Yes
⚠️ EXPOSE Does NOT Publish Ports!

This is the most common Docker networking misconception. EXPOSE 8000 in a Dockerfile is purely documentation — like a comment. It does NOT make the port accessible from the host. Only -p or -P in docker run actually publishes ports. The DCA exam will test this distinction.

NeedFlagResult
Laptop dev-p 8000:8000host:8000 → app
Loopback only-p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000not LAN-visible
Random host port-p 8000ephemeral high port
All EXPOSEd ports-Pquick demos
Container→container(no flag at all)DNS + port
UDP service-p 514:514/udpprotocol explicit
EXPOSE vs -p — What Each Actually Touches
    EXPOSE 8000 in Dockerfile          (easypj's Django port)
       └─▶ stored in image JSON (Config.ExposedPorts) ─▶ done.
           no daemon action, no kernel rule, ever fires.

    -p 8000:8000 in `docker run` / compose `ports:`
       └─▶ dockerd creates the container ─▶ writes an iptables
           nat-table DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain ─▶ reachable
           from outside (full packet path: Chapter 15.6)
💡 A Sticker Never Rang Anything

EXPOSE is the "doorbell here" sticker printed on the blueprint; -p actually wires the doorbell to the street. A sticker never rang anything. easypj: nginx gets -p 80:80 — the ONLY publish in the entire stack; django, postgres and redis rely purely on container-to-container DNS.

💡 EXPOSE's Only Runtime Effect

EXPOSE's only runtime effect is enabling -P (capital): with zero EXPOSE lines, docker run -P publishes nothing — it just reads the image's ExposedPorts list and maps each one to a random host port. It invents nothing on its own.

⚠️ 0.0.0.0 Is LAN-Visible

-p 8000:8000 binds 0.0.0.0 — your "local dev" is LAN-visible at the coffee shop; the 127.0.0.1: prefix is one keystroke of paranoia that pays for itself.

14.5 Service Discovery in Compose

Compose's networking is where its real power shines. Unlike raw docker run, Compose automatically creates a custom bridge network and registers every service name as a DNS entry — zero configuration needed:

compose.yaml (network config)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    networks:
      - backend
      - frontend
    environment:
      # Service name "postgres" → resolves via Compose DNS!
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@postgres:5432/easypj
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    networks:
      - backend       # Only on internal network

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks:
      - backend       # Only on internal network

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    networks:
      - frontend      # Only on external-facing network
    # nginx.conf: upstream django { server django:8000; }
    # Compose DNS resolves "django" to the container IP!

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true    # No internet access for backend services
🏆 Compose DNS vs Manual Networking

With manual docker run: create networks → specify --network on every container → manually verify connectivity. With Compose: write service names → they become DNS hostnames → docker compose up → everything just works. This is why Compose is the default development tool — it eliminates networking boilerplate entirely.

🔌 One File, Same Wiring

Compose creates real networks named <project>_frontend and <project>_backend and registers every joined service in the embedded DNS of each network it joins — DATABASE_URL uses the service name: postgres://easypj_user:pg-pass@postgres:5432/easypj. 14.3 wired the stack by hand, cable by cable; this file is the same wiring as a printed patch-panel chart — applied with one up, reproducible forever. The manual demo (14.3) and this YAML produce the SAME three ping results — nginx→django yes, django→postgres yes, nginx→postgres refused.

🧪 Practice — Reproduce 14.3 With Zero Manual Connects

docker compose up -d, then re-run 14.3's three pings via compose exec. Verify: identical outcomes with zero manual connects — the file did the wiring. Service name = one DNS record per joined network; networks: is the placement column of your architecture diagram.

🔧 Under the Hood — what internal: true actually removes

A normal user-defined bridge gets a MASQUERADE (SNAT) rule in the nat POSTROUTING chain, letting its containers reach the internet through the host's default route. When a compose network is declared internal: true, dockerd creates the bridge WITHOUT that MASQUERADE rule and without a route out of the bridge's subnet at all — it isn't just firewalled, there is structurally no path out. That is why postgres and redis on easypj-backend can't reach PyPI or any external host even if a misconfigured process tried.

 normal user-defined bridge:              internal: true bridge:
 container─▶bridge─▶MASQUERADE─▶eth0        container─▶bridge─▶(no route out)
 ─▶ internet                                 ✗ no MASQUERADE rule installed
🔑 internal: true is a routing decision, not a rule you could accidentally bypass from inside the container — that's why django, not postgres, has to be the dual-homed service if backend members ever need real internet access.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Two networks, one dual-homed service (django) = the smallest blast radius for a compromised edge container (nginx).
  • Explicit --subnet/--gateway beats auto-allocation — stable firewall rules, no VPN/LAN collisions.
  • docker run accepts only ONE --network flag; a second attachment is always a live docker network connect.
  • EXPOSE is metadata (Config.ExposedPorts) — it opens nothing; only -p/-P/compose ports: create real DNAT rules.
  • internal: true removes BOTH inbound reachability AND outbound routing — decide which service needs real internet access before flagging a network internal.
  • Compose creates real, inspectable networks named <project>_<name> and registers every joined service in each network's DNS.
  • DCA relevance: subnet planning, publish-syntax variants, and compose networks: topology are all directly examinable.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Leaving a dev database's port bound to 0.0.0.0 "just for now" → Design network isolation before the first up, not after an incident — bind loopback-only or don't publish DB ports at all.
  • Letting Docker auto-allocate a network's subnet → Pin an explicit --subnet like 172.28.0.0/24 — auto-allocated pools can collide with your VPN or office LAN and silently blackhole traffic.
  • Assuming internal: true only blocks inbound traffic → It removes outbound routing too — no MASQUERADE rule, no path out — which is exactly why django, not postgres, is the dual-homed service.
  • Trying docker run --network net1,net2 for two networks → docker run --network accepts only ONE value — the second attachment is always a live docker network connect.
  • Publishing with -p 8000:8000 for "local-only" dev testing → -p 8000:8000 binds 0.0.0.0 (LAN-visible); use -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 for genuinely loopback-only access.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker compose config renders the fully-resolved networks: section — read it once before up to catch topology mistakes on paper.
  • Bind dev-only debug ports as -p 127.0.0.1:PORT:PORT by muscle memory; typing the loopback prefix costs less than a LAN leak.
  • docker network inspect -f '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}' NETWORK for a quick container list without parsing the full JSON.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 14)

the Chapter 14 cheat-card 
docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/24 \
    --gateway 172.28.0.1 easypj-backend               # explicit subnet
docker network create easypj-frontend                  # auto-allocated is fine here
docker run -d --name postgres --network easypj-backend \
    postgres:15                                         # first network at birth
docker network connect easypj-frontend django           # 2nd network, live
docker exec nginx ping -c1 postgres                      # expect: fails
docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.ExposedPorts}}' easypj:v1  # EXPOSE is metadata only
docker compose config --format json | jq .networks       # fully-resolved topology

🧠 Chapter 14 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the two-network design to encoding it as compose.yaml — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why is django the ONLY dual-homed service in easypj's design, and what would break if nginx were dual-homed instead?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

django must reach both nginx (frontend, to serve responses) and postgres/redis (backend, to serve data); if nginx were also on backend it could reach postgres directly, defeating the entire isolation design. internet──▶[nginx]──▶[django]──▶[postgres]/[redis], frontend then backend (no ports:).

EXPLANATION

14.1's two-network diagram — the blast radius of a compromised nginx must stop at django.

Q2
What TWO things does internal: true remove from a compose network, not just one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both inbound reachability from other networks AND outbound routing to the internet — there is no MASQUERADE rule and no default route out, so there's structurally no path, not just a firewalled one.

EXPLANATION

Ties 14.1's design to this chapter's Under the Hood deep-dive in 14.5.

Q3
Why does easypj-backend use an explicit --subnet (172.28.0.0/24) instead of Docker's auto-allocated pool?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Auto-allocated pools can collide with a VPN or office LAN range, silently blackholing traffic — the #1 "Docker broke my VPN" cause; explicit subnets are deliberate and auditable.

EXPLANATION

14.2's gotcha, restated as a why-question.

Q4
django needs to join TWO networks. Why can't one docker run --network do that, and what's the real two-step sequence?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --network accepts only one value. Sequence: docker run --network easypj-backend --name django ... followed by a live docker network connect easypj-frontend django.

EXPLANATION

14.3 — the raw CLI makes you feel a step Compose normally hides.

Q5
From nginx, wget -qO- postgres:5432 fails even though nginx knows the string "postgres." Why, precisely?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

nginx and postgres share no network, so nginx can't even RESOLVE the name — it's a resolution failure ("bad address"), not a connection refusal.

EXPLANATION

14.3's third ping — the design working exactly as intended.

Q6
A Dockerfile has EXPOSE 8000 and the container runs with no -p flag at all. Can a LAN machine reach port 8000? Can another container on the same Docker network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

LAN: no — EXPOSE is metadata only, it opens nothing. Same network: yes — container-to-container traffic needs neither EXPOSE nor -p, only the DNS name and the actual listening port.

EXPLANATION

14.4's publish-scenario table, condensed: laptop dev → -p 8000:8000; loopback only → -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000; container→container → no flag at all.

Q7
What is the concrete difference between -p 8000:8000 and -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The first binds 0.0.0.0 — reachable from the LAN (or the internet, if the host is public); the second binds only loopback — reachable only from the host itself.

EXPLANATION

14.4's closing gotcha.

Q8
An image has zero EXPOSE lines. What does docker run -P do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing — -P only maps ports already listed in the image's ExposedPorts; with zero EXPOSE lines there is nothing for it to publish.

EXPLANATION

14.4's 💡 callout.

Q9
Translate easypj's 14.1 design into the compose.yaml networks: keys each service needs.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

nginx: [frontend]; django: [frontend, backend]; postgres: [backend]; redis: [backend]; top-level: frontend: {}, backend: {internal: true}.

EXPLANATION

14.5's networks: section, restated as a mapping.

Q10
After docker compose up -d, which three exec-based ping tests prove the design works, and what result does each expect?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

nginx→django (works), django→postgres (works), nginx→postgres (fails/refused) — the third one failing IS the success condition.

EXPLANATION

14.5 reproducing 14.3's manual results with zero manual connects.

🔬 Practice Drill 14.1 — By Hand, Then By Compose (15 min)

Stand up easypj's two networks by hand (14.2-14.3), then bring up the SAME stack via docker compose up -d using the compose.yaml from 14.5, and diff the two docker network inspect outputs. Verify: same subnets, same isolation, same three ping outcomes — only the amount of typing changed.

📌 Chapter 14 Visual Summary — easypj's real topology
  ┌──────────────────── CHAPTER 14 — EASYPJ'S REAL TOPOLOGY ──────────────┐
  │  internet ──▶ [nginx :80] ──▶ [django] ──▶ [postgres] (no ports:)     │
  │               frontend net    dual-homed  └──▶ [redis]  (no ports:)  │
  │                                            backend net (internal:true)│

In one line: Chapter 14 turns Chapter 13's vocabulary into a real, defensible topology: two networks, one dual-homed app tier, and databases with zero published ports. EXPOSE never opens anything by itself — only -p, -P, or compose's ports: key create the iptables rules that make a container reachable from outside — and internal: true removes both the inbound AND the outbound path for the tier that holds the data.

The takeaway: this exact posture is what every later Part of the guide assumes is already standing.

15.1 Host Networking

Host networking removes Docker's network virtualization entirely — the container uses the host's network stack directly. No bridge, no NAT, no port mapping needed:

AspectBridge NetworkHost Network
Network isolation✅ Full isolation❌ No isolation — shares host stack
Port mapping-p 8080:80 requiredNot needed — container uses host ports directly
Performance🟡 Slight NAT overhead🟢 Bare-metal speed (no translation)
Port conflicts✅ Can't conflict (different namespace)❌ WILL conflict if host uses same port
Use caseStandard applicationsHigh-throughput network apps, monitoring agents
⚠️ Host Networking Caveats

Only works on Linux. On Docker Desktop (Windows/macOS), host networking uses the VM's network, not your laptop's. The container can bind to privileged ports (<1024). Multiple containers using host networking CANNOT use the same port — they'll conflict. Use only when you absolutely need bare-metal network performance and can accept zero isolation.

Bridge Path vs Host Path — Where the Hops Go
  BRIDGE (default, needs -p 8080:80)
  client ─▶ host eth0:8080 ─▶ NAT/DNAT ─▶ docker0 bridge ─▶
    veth pair ─▶ container eth0 (172.17.0.x) ─▶ app :80
  3 translation hops; container gets its OWN IP + port table

  HOST (--network host, -p has no effect)
  client ─▶ host eth0:80 ─▶ app :80 (same netns as the host)
  0 translation hops; container has the HOST's IP and the
  HOST's port table — binding :80 in the container binds :80
  on the host, port conflicts and all
💡 The Hotel Room Analogy

Bridge = your own hotel room with mail forwarding — private, isolated, reachable only through the front desk's port map. Host = sleeping in the lobby. Fastest path to the front door, zero privacy, and only ONE guest can claim the sofa — one owner per host port.

📖 easypj Never Uses Host Mode — Here's Why

Host networking is never appropriate for django or postgres — but it's a plausible choice for a node-exporter-style metrics agent that must see the host's real interfaces to be useful at all. Compose spells this network_mode: host (not networks:) — the moment it's set, ports: on that service does nothing, and Compose logs a warning saying so, which is the fastest way to confirm host mode is actually active.

🧪 Practice

docker run --rm --network host alpine ip addr, then compare with the host's own ip addr. Verify: IDENTICAL interface lists — the isolation is simply gone.

15.2 Macvlan / IPvlan Networking

Macvlan gives each container its own MAC address and IP on the physical network — the container appears as a separate physical device. IPvlan shares the host's MAC but gives containers unique IPs:

Macvlan vs IPvlan
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔌 MACVLAN vs IPVLAN                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MACVLAN: Each container has OWN MAC address                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Physical Switch: 192.168.1.0/24                                    │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                     │   │
  │  │  │  Host    │   │ Container│   │ Container│                     │   │
  │  │  │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: cc:dd│   │MAC: ee:ff│                     │   │
  │  │  │IP: .100  │   │IP: .101  │   │IP: .102  │                     │   │
  │  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                     │   │
  │  │  ⚠️ Some cloud providers block multiple MACs per port!            │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  IPVLAN: Containers share host MAC, unique IPs                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Physical Switch: 192.168.1.0/24                                    │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                     │   │
  │  │  │  Host    │   │ Container│   │ Container│                     │   │
  │  │  │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: aa:bb│  ← Same MAC!         │   │
  │  │  │IP: .100  │   │IP: .101  │   │IP: .102  │                     │   │
  │  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                     │   │
  │  │  ✅ Works in cloud environments (no MAC restrictions)              │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Macvlan / IPvlan — Where They Attach on the LAN
  physical LAN 192.168.1.0/24 ── switch ── router
                     │
                 host eth0
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
    MACVLAN sub-ifs          IPVLAN L2 sub-ifs
    C1 .50  MAC aa:aa        C1 .50 ┐ share the
    C2 .51  MAC bb:bb        C2 .51 ┘ host's MAC
    (a MAC per container:    (one MAC on the wire:
     switch sees them all)    port-security friendly)

Both drivers bond container sub-interfaces to the parent NIC (-o parent=eth0), skipping bridge and NAT entirely — DHCP servers, printers and legacy scanners see a first-class LAN citizen. Macvlan mints one MAC per container; ipvlan reuses the host's MAC and differs only at L3.

💡 Houses vs Apartments

Macvlan = each container gets its own house on the street (own mailbox, own nameplate). IPvlan = apartments in the host's building — one street door (MAC), many unit numbers (IPs).

📖 easypj: Not the Web Stack

Macvlan/ipvlan are not for django/postgres/redis/nginx — but a legacy license server or an IoT integration that must ARP on the real LAN is the genuine use case. Practice: create a macvlan network with your LAN's subnet and -o parent=eth0, run alpine with --ip, then ping it from ANOTHER machine. Verify: an outside device reaches a container with no -p anywhere in sight.

⚠️ The Host Can't Reach Its Own Macvlan Containers

A kernel hairpin restriction blocks the host itself from reaching containers on a macvlan network it created — plan a macvlan shim interface, or simply accept host-blindness as the trade-off. Pick ipvlan instead when switches or wifi filter by MAC count.

15.3 Overlay Networking (Swarm)

Overlay networks connect containers across multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN tunneling. This is the foundation of Docker Swarm's multi-host networking:

TERMINAL
# Initialize Swarm (required for overlay)
$ docker swarm init

# Create an encrypted overlay network
$ docker network create --driver overlay \
    --opt encrypted \
    --subnet 10.0.9.0/24 \
    easypj-net

# Deploy services that communicate across hosts
$ docker service create --name django \
    --network easypj-net \
    --replicas 3 \
    easypj:v1.0

# Containers on different hosts can now communicate:
# django.1 on node-1 can ping django.2 on node-2
# All service names resolve via Swarm's built-in DNS
Overlay Network — 3 Swarm Nodes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    ☁️ OVERLAY NETWORK (VXLAN)                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐      │
  │  │   🐝 Manager     │  │   🐝 Worker 1    │  │   🐝 Worker 2    │      │
  │  │   10.0.0.1       │  │   10.0.0.2       │  │   10.0.0.3       │      │
  │  │                  │  │                  │  │                  │      │
  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │      │
  │  │  │ C1 │ │ C2 │  │  │  │ C3 │ │ C4 │  │  │  │ C5 │ │ C6 │  │      │
  │  │  │.0.4│ │.0.5│  │  │  │.0.6│ │.0.7│  │  │  │.0.8│ │.0.9│  │      │
  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │      │
  │  │                 │  │                 │  │                 │      │
  │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │      │
  │  └───────┬─────────┘  └───────┬─────────┘  └───────┬─────────┘      │
  │          │                    │                    │                 │
  │          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘                 │
  │                               │                                      │
  │                    Physical Network (underlay)                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Container C1 on Node-1 pings Container C6 on Node-3:                   │
  │  C1 → VXLAN encapsulate → UDP → Node-3 → VXLAN decapsulate → C6 ✅     │
  │  All containers see each other as if on the same local network!         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
easypj on a 3-Node Overlay
  overlay easypj-net 10.0.9.0/24 (VXLAN)
  ┌── node1 ───┐   ┌── node2 ───┐   ┌── node3 ───┐
  │ [django]   │   │ [django]   │   │ [postgres] │
  │  10.0.9.3  │   │  10.0.9.4  │   │  10.0.9.5  │
  └────╥───────┘   └────╥───────┘   └────╥───────┘
       ╚═══ UDP 4789 ═══╩═ VXLAN tunnels ╝
       (containers' L2 frames ride inside UDP packets)

VXLAN wraps container Ethernet frames in UDP/4789 packets between nodes; each node's kernel unwraps and delivers as if one switch spanned the cluster. Needs Swarm mode (Part 10) for the control plane; --opt encrypted adds IPsec between nodes.

💡 The Pneumatic Tube Analogy

Sister office buildings with a pneumatic tube system: interoffice envelopes (frames) ride inside courier capsules (UDP packets); staff just write room numbers (10.0.9.x) and never see the tubes.

📖 easypj on a 3-Node Swarm

django on node1 dials postgres:5432 exactly as it did in Compose — the connection string never learns the database moved machines. Practice: docker swarm init, join a second node, create an attachable overlay, run alpine on each, ping across. Verify: tcpdump on eth0 shows UDP 4789 while the ping runs.

⚠️ Overlays Need Three Ports Open — Not Just VXLAN

Overlays need 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp AND 4789/udp open between EVERY node — one blocked port in a cloud security group and "overlay is broken" tickets follow.

15.4 Network Troubleshooting Tools

When containers can't communicate, these are your diagnostic tools:

TERMINAL
# 1. Check if containers are on the same network
$ docker inspect container1 | grep -A20 Networks
$ docker inspect container2 | grep -A20 Networks

# 2. Test DNS resolution inside a container
$ docker exec container1 nslookup container2
$ docker exec container1 ping container2

# 3. Check network configuration
$ docker network inspect easypj-backend

# 4. Test port connectivity
$ docker exec container1 nc -zv container2 5432

# 5. View iptables rules (NAT and port mapping)
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L -n | grep DOCKER

# 6. Run a temporary debug container on the same network
$ docker run --rm -it --network easypj-backend alpine sh
# Now you can ping, nslookup, curl from within the network
The 4-Rung Debugging Ladder
  # 1. Is the target on the network I think it is?
  $ docker network inspect easypj-backend | grep -A3 Name

  # 2. Does DNS resolve from the source's viewpoint?
  $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend alpine \
      nslookup postgres

  # 3. Is the PORT open (not just the host alive)?
  $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend \
      nicolaka/netshoot nc -zv postgres 5432

  # 4. Full toolbox INSIDE the source's own netns:
  $ docker run --rm -it --network container:django \
      nicolaka/netshoot        # tcpdump, dig, ss, curl, iperf

Rung 4's --network container:django joins django's OWN network namespace — you see its eth0, its resolv.conf, its routes, without installing one tool into the app image.

💡 The Plumber's Ladder Analogy

Check the house is on the street (inspect), the address resolves (nslookup), the tap opens (nc -zv), then put your ear on THIS house's pipes (netshoot inside the same netns).

📖 easypj: A Classic Finding

Rung 2 fails because django ran with --network easypj-frontend only; one docker network connect easypj-backend django later, rungs 2-4 go green. Practice: break the stack on purpose (disconnect django from backend), walk the ladder, fix, re-walk. Verify: you can name WHICH rung failed and why — that sentence is the skill.

⚠️ A New Container Is Not the Source's Netns

A NEW container on the same network is NOT the same as the source's netns — a wrong resolv.conf or per-container rules only show up via --network container:<name> (rung 4).

15.5 Network Security Basics

🔒
Use Internal Networks

Create networks with --internal flag to prevent containers from accessing the internet: docker network create --internal secure-net. Containers can talk to each other but NOT to the outside world. Perfect for databases and caches.

📋
Encrypt Overlay Traffic

For Swarm overlay networks, add --opt encrypted to enable IPSec encryption of all container-to-container traffic. Without this, VXLAN traffic between hosts is unencrypted by default.

🚫
Limit Published Ports

Only publish ports that need external access. Never publish database ports (5432, 3306, 27017) to 0.0.0.0. If you must publish, bind to localhost: -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432.

🔍
Network Segmentation

Place services on different networks based on their security zone. Frontend (Nginx) on one network, backend (Django+DB+Redis) on another. Only the application layer bridges them — not the database directly.

Docker networking is default-ALLOW inside a network and default-DENY across networks — segmentation IS the firewall. Here's the full 10-rule default-deny checklist for shipping easypj:

✅ 10-Rule Default-Deny Network Security Checklist
  • 1 — Publish NOTHING but the edge (nginx :80/:443)
  • 2 — DB/cache on internal: true networks — no NAT either way
  • 3 — Bind dev-only ports to 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0
  • 4 — One network per trust zone; dual-home only the app tier
  • 5 — Never --network host for internet-facing services
  • 6 — Encrypt overlays that cross datacenters (--opt encrypted)
  • 7 — icc=false on the default bridge — or don't use it
  • 8 — Explicit subnets — auditable firewall rules, no VPN wars
  • 9 — Re-scan docker ps for 0.0.0.0 leaks after every change
  • 10 — Know -p bypasses ufw (15.6) — audit the DOCKER chain too
💡 The Castle Design Analogy

One gate (nginx), an inner keep with no outside door (internal: true), separate courtyards per trust zone — and rule 10 is checking the tunnel the drawbridge keeper (iptables) dug without telling the guards (ufw).

📖 easypj Already Scores 3 of 10

The Chapter 14 design already scores rules 1, 2 and 4; adding 127.0.0.1 binds for dev tools and explicit subnets completes the posture in one afternoon. Practice: run docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}' on your stack. Verify: exactly ONE 0.0.0.0 entry (nginx) — any other line is a checklist violation with your name on it.

15.6 How -p Really Works — NAT, iptables & the Published-Port Path

-p writes iptables rules, not proxies: a nat-table DNAT in the DOCKER chain rewrites the destination BEFORE routing. docker-proxy (one process per published port) survives only as a userland fallback for localhost and hairpin traffic. ufw's INPUT rules never match because DNATed traffic traverses FORWARD, not INPUT — the one hook Docker guarantees you is the DOCKER-USER chain.

The Published-Port Path
  client:54321 ─▶ host eth0 :8000
    ─▶ nat PREROUTING ─▶ DOCKER chain
         match tcp dpt:8000 → DNAT to 172.18.0.4:8000
    ─▶ FORWARD (DOCKER-USER first, then DOCKER)
    ─▶ bridge ─▶ veth ─▶ container eth0 ─▶ gunicorn :8000
  reply: conntrack rewrites the source back — the client
  never sees 172.18.0.4
💡 The Mailroom Analogy

The mailroom rewrites the envelope's address (DNAT) at the loading dock BEFORE the receptionist (INPUT/ufw) ever sees it — complaining to the receptionist about deliveries she never handles is the whole "ufw doesn't block Docker" bug.

📖 easypj: See It With Your Own Eyes

-p 5432:5432 "just to debug" DNATs the whole internet to PostgreSQL even with ufw deny 5432 active. The fix is binding scope: -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 makes the DNAT rule itself match only loopback destinations.

TERMINAL
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n | grep 5432
  DNAT tcp -- 0.0.0.0/0 ... dpt:5432 to:172.18.0.3:5432
$ ps aux | grep docker-proxy    # one per published port
🧪 Practice

Publish nginx as -p 8080:80, add ufw deny 8080, curl from another machine (still answers!); re-run with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80. Verify: LAN curl now refused, localhost fine — and the iptables line shows the 127.0.0.1 match.

⚠️ No Address Means Every Interface

-p with no address means 0.0.0.0 AND [::] — the port answers on every interface the host owns, cloud-public IP included.

🔧 Under the Hood — the firewall chain order Docker actually uses

Inbound traffic to a published port does not hit iptables' INPUT chain at all — it is DNATed in the nat table's DOCKER chain and then evaluated in the filter table's FORWARD chain, in a fixed order: DOCKER-USER first (a chain Docker guarantees it will never flush or manage — the one stable hook for your own rules), then DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2 (blocking cross-bridge traffic by default, rewritten on every daemon restart), then DOCKER (the per-container ACCEPT rules Docker manages itself). This ordering is WHY 15.5's checklist rule about auditing DOCKER-USER matters, and why 15.6's ufw story happens at all.

 nat:PREROUTING ─▶ DOCKER (DNAT rewrite) ─▶ filter:FORWARD
      │
      ▼
 filter:DOCKER-USER    (empty by default — YOUR rules survive here)
      │
      ▼
 filter:DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2   (blocks cross-bridge traffic)
      │
      ▼
 filter:DOCKER   (per-container ACCEPT rules Docker manages)
      │
      ▼
 destination container
🔑 Recap: if you want a firewall rule Docker will never silently delete out from under you, DOCKER-USER is the only chain built for that purpose.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • --network host deletes the sandbox boundary entirely — native speed, zero isolation, one owner per host port.
  • Macvlan mints one MAC per container; ipvlan shares the host's MAC and differs only at L3 — pick ipvlan when switches or wifi filter by MAC count.
  • Overlay tunnels container frames inside VXLAN (UDP/4789) between Swarm nodes; --opt encrypted adds IPsec on top.
  • The 4-rung ladder (inspect → nslookup → nc -zv → netshoot-in-netns) diagnoses the large majority of connectivity tickets without guesswork.
  • -p writes a real iptables DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain — docker-proxy is only a niche fallback for loopback/hairpin cases, not the common path.
  • ufw/firewalld INPUT rules never see published-port traffic because DNATed packets traverse FORWARD, not INPUT.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: driver trade-offs, Swarm overlay basics, and the DNAT mental model are all directly examinable.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Testing --network host on Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) to validate Linux host-mode behavior → Desktop's host mode attaches to the hidden VM's network, not your physical laptop's — "only works on the Linux server" is the tell.
  • Expecting the Docker host itself to reach containers on a macvlan network → A kernel hairpin restriction blocks it — plan a macvlan shim interface or accept host-blindness.
  • Assuming an overlay only needs VXLAN's UDP/4789 open → Swarm's control plane also needs 2377/tcp and 7946/tcp+udp between EVERY node — miss one in a cloud security group and "overlay is broken" tickets follow.
  • Publishing with -p 5432:5432 and assuming it only binds IPv4 → No address means 0.0.0.0 AND [::] — the port answers on every interface the host owns, including a cloud-public IP.
  • Hand-editing iptables rules outside DOCKER-USER to "fix" Docker's firewall behavior → Docker rewrites its own chains on every daemon restart — only DOCKER-USER survives; encode policy in networks and daemon.json instead.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Keep nicolaka/netshoot pulled locally — it's the one image worth caching before you need it at 2 a.m.
  • iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n | grep <port> answers "is this actually published, and to where" faster than re-reading compose files.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 15)

the Chapter 15 cheat-card 
docker run --rm --network host alpine ip addr        # host mode has zero isolation
docker network create -d macvlan --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 \
    -o parent=eth0 lanX                                # macvlan on the real LAN
docker swarm init && docker network create -d overlay \
    --attachable easypj-net                             # attachable overlay
docker run --rm --network easypj-backend alpine nslookup postgres  # rung 2
docker run --rm --network easypj-backend nicolaka/netshoot \
    nc -zv postgres 5432                                # rung 3
docker run --rm -it --network container:django nicolaka/netshoot  # rung 4
sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n                       # the real DNAT rules
docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}'               # scan for 0.0.0.0 leaks

🧠 Chapter 15 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From host mode's zero isolation to the iptables truth behind -p — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
List three concrete differences between bridge and host networking, and explain why testing "host mode" on Docker Desktop for Mac doesn't prove what you think it proves.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Isolation (own netns vs none), port mapping (-p required vs ignored), performance (NAT overhead vs native). On Desktop, host mode attaches to the HIDDEN Linux VM's network, not your Mac/Windows interfaces.

| dimension | bridge              | host              |
| isolation | own netns, own IP   | NONE              |
| port map  | -p required (NAT)   | -p IGNORED        |
EXPLANATION

15.1's bridge-vs-host table plus its Desktop gotcha.

Q2
You run a container with --network host -p 9000:80. What actually happens to the -p flag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It's silently ignored — there is no NAT/sandbox layer for -p to configure; the app binds directly to the host's own port 80, not 9000.

EXPLANATION

15.1's core trap.

Q3
What ONE criterion decides macvlan vs ipvlan, and why can't the Docker HOST reach a container on a macvlan network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

MAC count — macvlan gives each container its own MAC (real LAN citizen); ipvlan shares the host's MAC. The host can't reach its own macvlan containers due to a kernel hairpin restriction.

EXPLANATION

15.2's criterion plus its closing gotcha.

Q4
How do two containers on DIFFERENT hosts share one subnet under an overlay network, which ports must be open between nodes, and what does --opt encrypted add?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Container frames are wrapped in UDP/4789 (VXLAN) packets between nodes; Swarm's control plane also needs 2377/tcp and 7946/tcp+udp. --opt encrypted adds IPsec between the nodes.

node1[django]═╗           ╔═[django]node2   ╔═[postgres]node3
       UDP 4789 tunnels (VXLAN) ═════════════╝
EXPLANATION

15.3's diagram and required-ports list.

Q5
Put these in the correct debugging order and say what each rung answers: nc -zv, network inspect, netshoot-in-netns, nslookup.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1) network inspect — is the target on the network I think it is; 2) nslookup — does DNS resolve from the source's viewpoint; 3) nc -zv — is the port actually open; 4) netshoot in the source's netns — full toolbox from the exact failing vantage point.

EXPLANATION

15.4's 4-rung ladder.

Q6
What does --network container:django actually do, and why is it more revealing than running netshoot on the SAME Docker network as django?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It joins netshoot to django's OWN network namespace (same eth0, same resolv.conf, same routes) instead of giving it a fresh namespace on the same network — so it sees exactly what django sees, quirks included.

EXPLANATION

15.4's rung 4.

Q7
Pick three rules from the security checklist and say what concrete easypj mistake each prevents.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rule 1 (publish only the edge) prevents postgres/redis ports leaking to 0.0.0.0; Rule 2 (internal: true on DB/cache) prevents any outbound path from the vault tier; Rule 3 (bind dev ports to 127.0.0.1) prevents a "just for debugging" -p from being LAN-visible at a coffee shop.

EXPLANATION

15.5's 10-rule checklist, applied.

Q8
Trace one inbound packet to a published port from the wire to the application, and explain why ufw deny <port> does not stop it.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

client → host eth0 → nat:PREROUTING → DOCKER chain (DNAT rewrite) → filter:FORWARD → bridge → veth → container eth0 → app. ufw's rules live in INPUT; DNATed traffic to a container traverses FORWARD instead, so ufw never sees it.

client:54321─▶eth0:8000─▶PREROUTING─▶DOCKER(DNAT)─▶FORWARD─▶container
EXPLANATION

15.6's packet-path diagram, restated.

Q9
How does adding 127.0.0.1: to a -p flag change the actual iptables rule created?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The DNAT rule's destination-address match narrows from 0.0.0.0/0 (any interface) to loopback only — packets arriving on any OTHER interface never match, so they're never DNATed to the container.

EXPLANATION

15.6's binding-scope mechanics.

Q10
If you want a custom firewall rule Docker will never silently delete, which iptables chain should you use, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DOCKER-USER — Docker guarantees it never flushes or manages that chain itself, unlike DOCKER and DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2, which it rewrites on every daemon restart.

EXPLANATION

This chapter's Under the Hood deep-dive (15.6).

Publish nginx with -p 8080:80, add ufw deny 8080, curl it from another machine (still answers!), then re-publish as -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 and repeat. Verify: LAN curl is now refused, localhost still works, and you can point at the exact iptables line that changed.

In one line: Chapter 15 is everything that departs from Chapter 14's default bridge path: host mode trades all isolation for native speed, macvlan/ipvlan hand a container a first-class spot on the physical LAN, and overlay stretches one virtual switch across Swarm nodes over VXLAN.

The takeaway: the chapter's real payoff is operational — a fixed four-rung debugging ladder that turns "the network is broken" into a rung number, and the iptables truth that -p is a kernel DNAT rule living in the DOCKER chain, which is exactly why a host-level firewall like ufw can look perfectly configured and still never see the traffic it thinks it's blocking.

🌐 Part 5 · Recap · Complete

Docker Networking — What You Now Know

You started only knowing that -p "publishes a port"; now you can name the three CNM nouns behind every network, design a two-network topology that keeps a database off the internet, and pick — and defend — host, macvlan/ipvlan, or overlay when bridge isn't the right answer. That's the difference between a container that happens to talk to another one and a network you actually designed.

🔑 Part 5 — Key Takeaways

  • Every Docker network is built from the same three CNM nouns — sandbox (netns), endpoint (veth), network (the driver's virtual switch) — regardless of which of the five drivers backs it (Ch 13).
  • The default docker0 bridge has NO embedded DNS; only a user-defined bridge gets the 127.0.0.11 resolver, which is why "ping by name" fails on docker0 and works everywhere else (Ch 13).
  • Two networks, one dual-homed service beats one flat network — easypj's nginx→frontend, django→both, postgres/redis→backend(internal) design keeps a compromised edge container from ever reaching the data tier (Ch 14).
  • EXPOSE is metadata, not a firewall rule — only -p, -P, or compose's ports: key write the real iptables DNAT rules that make a container reachable from outside (Ch 14).
  • internal: true removes BOTH directions — no inbound reachability and no outbound route (no MASQUERADE) — not just a firewalled network but a structurally cut-off one (Ch 14).
  • Driver choice is a trade-off, not a default: host trades all isolation for native speed, macvlan/ipvlan hand a container a first-class LAN identity, overlay tunnels frames over VXLAN across Swarm nodes (Ch 15).
  • The 4-rung debugging ladder — inspect → nslookup → nc -zv → netshoot-in-netns — turns "the network is broken" into a specific rung, and a fact worth remembering forever: ufw/firewalld INPUT rules never see published-port traffic, because DNATed packets ride FORWARD (Ch 15).
📌 Part 5 Visual Summary — from CNM nouns to a defended, debuggable topology
   🌐 CNM: sandbox ══endpoint══▶ network — one of 5 drivers                       (Ch 13: the model)
                                          │
        docker0 (default): NAT, NO DNS   │   user-defined bridge: NAT + DNS @127.0.0.11
                                          ▼
   internet ──▶ 🌍 [nginx :80] ──frontend──▶ 🐍 [django] ──backend (internal:true)──▶ 🗄️ [postgres] [redis]
                                 (dual-homed, only crosser)      no ports: published anywhere        (Ch 14: the design)
   EXPOSE = metadata only, opens nothing   │   -p / -P / ports: = the real iptables DNAT rule
                                          ▼
   🛣️ host: 0 hops, 0 isolation   │   🔌 macvlan/ipvlan: real LAN IP   │   🌐 overlay: VXLAN/4789 across Swarm nodes   (Ch 15: beyond default)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   when it breaks: inspect ─▶ nslookup ─▶ nc -zv ─▶ netshoot-in-netns — and remember, ufw's INPUT chain never sees DNATed FORWARD traffic. 🔌

In words: Chapter 13 gave you the vocabulary: every network, no matter which of the five drivers backs it, is just a sandbox joined to a network through an endpoint — and the one fork that trips up beginners is that the default docker0 bridge does NAT but never DNS, while any user-defined bridge gets both. Chapter 14 put that vocabulary to work on a real app: easypj splits into a frontend network the internet can reach and a backend network flagged internal: true, with django as the single dual-homed bridge between them and EXPOSE doing nothing on its own — only -p/-P/ports: actually open a path in.

Chapter 15 then covered what happens when the default bridge path isn't the right tool: --network host for native speed at the cost of all isolation, macvlan/ipvlan for a container that needs to look like a real device on the LAN, and overlay for stretching one virtual switch across Swarm nodes over VXLAN. It closed with the operational payoff of the whole Part — a fixed four-rung ladder for diagnosing connectivity failures, and the iptables truth that -p is a kernel DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain, which is exactly why a host firewall's INPUT rules can look perfectly configured and still never see the traffic they think they're blocking.

The one idea to keep: Docker networking is never "does it connect" — it's "who is allowed to connect to whom, on purpose." Every chapter in this Part is really one continuous design decision: three nouns become five drivers, five drivers become a two-network blast-radius design, and that design becomes something you can prove, debug, and defend down to the exact iptables chain.

Chapter 16 · Docker Storage Fundamentals

Containers are ephemeral by design — when you delete a container, everything inside it disappears. Storage volumes solve this by separating data from the container lifecycle. Master volumes, and your data survives anything. Skip this chapter and easypj's PostgreSQL data, and every user upload, evaporates on the next docker compose down.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~60-75 min 💾 Storage 🎯 DCA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ State exactly what survives and what dies when a container is removed (16.1)
  • ✅ Name Docker's four mount types — volume, bind mount, tmpfs, npipe — and pick the correct one from a need, not a guess (16.2)
  • ✅ Explain why a volume's lifecycle is independent of any container that mounts it, and create one with docker volume create (16.3)
  • ✅ Run all five docker volume subcommands (create, ls, inspect, rm, prune) and read their output correctly (16.4)
  • ✅ Tell an anonymous volume from a named one, and explain why only named volumes are safe to rely on long-term (16.3-16.4)
  • ✅ Read a docker volume inspect Mountpoint and locate a volume's real files on the host filesystem (16.4)
🎓 DCA Relevance
Storage & Volumes 10%
🎯 A Core Chapter, Not Supplementary Background

Every container you have run so far dies with its data intact only by accident — kill it and whatever it wrote is gone. Chapter 16 replaces that accident with a deliberate choice: volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs, each solving a different persistence problem. Chapter 16 is graded directly under the Storage & Volumes domain (10%) — volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs is exam content, not just production hygiene.

  • Why this chapter exists: containers are cattle, disposable by design — but your data is precious. Volumes are the "collar" that survives the animal.
  • The load-bearing line: a volume's lifecycle is COMPLETELY separate from any container that mounts it — only docker volume rm deletes one.

16.1 The Ephemeral Container Problem

Containers are designed to be disposable. docker rm deletes everything — the writable layer, all files, all data. For stateless apps, this is fine. But what about your PostgreSQL database? Your users' uploaded files? That data must survive container deletion.

The Ephemeral Container Problem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              💾 THE EPHEMERAL CONTAINER PROBLEM                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT VOLUMES (Data dies with container):                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
  │  │ Container: postgres │     │ Container: DELETED  │                     │
  │  │ ┌─────────────────┐ │     │                     │                     │
  │  │ │ /var/lib/       │ │     │  💀 DB GONE!        │                     │
  │  │ │   postgresql/   │ │ ──▶ │  💀 Users GONE!     │                     │
  │  │ │   data/         │ │ rm  │  💀 Orders GONE!    │                     │
  │  │ │   (20 GB DB)    │ │     │  💀 Everything!     │                     │

  │  └─────────────────────┘                                                │
  │                                                                          │

  │  │ │   data/         │ │   rm    │                     │                │
  │  │ └───────┬─────────┘ │         └─────────────────────┘                │
  │  └─────────┼───────────┘                                               │
  │            │ mount                                                      │
  │            ▼                                                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐                │
  │  │ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │────────▶│ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │                │
  │  │ /var/lib/docker/    │  new    │ STILL HERE! ✅      │                │
  │  │ volumes/pg_data/    │  cont.  │ Mount to new        │                │
  │  │ (20 GB, persistent) │         │ container!          │                │
  │  └─────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────┘                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 "Cattle, Not Pets" — With a Volume Collar

Containers are cattle (disposable), but your data is precious. Volumes are the "collar" that survives the animal. You can delete and recreate containers freely — as long as they reattach to the same volume, the data is safe. This is the fundamental storage pattern of containerized applications.

💀
Level 0
No Persistence

Data lives in container writable layer. docker rm = everything gone.

❌ Data loss guaranteed
📁
Level 1
Bind Mounts

Host directory mounted into container. Survives deletion but host-dependent.

⚠️ Dev only, fragile
📦
Level 2
Named Volumes

Docker-managed, portable, driver plugins. Independent lifecycle.

✅ Production standard
☁️
Level 3
Cloud Drivers

EBS, Azure Disk, NFS. Multi-host, auto-backup, enterprise-grade.

🏆 Enterprise production
💡 A Hotel Room vs a Safety-Deposit Box

Whatever you leave in the room (the writable layer) gets cleared at checkout (docker rm); the box (the volume) sits in the vault regardless of which room you book next — same building, independent lifecycle.

easypj lab: run docker run postgres with no -v, insert one row, docker rm -f it, then start a fresh postgres container and check docker volume ls — nothing there. The 20 GB dataset the diagram warns about was never anything but container-local. Verify it yourself: the row is gone — you just reproduced the top half of the diagram with your own data.
