TypePersists?SpeedUse Case
Volume✅ YesFastDB data, uploads, production
Bind Mount✅ YesFastDev hot-reload, config files
tmpfs❌ No (RAM)🚀 FastestSecrets, temp files, cache
npipeN/AN/AWindows container IPC
NeedPick this mount type
Survive restart, don't care where on diskvolume
Edit code live from your host editorbind mount
Secret that must never touch disktmpfs
💡 Three Storage Units, Three Real Choices

Renting a Docker-managed storage unit (volume) vs using your own garage (bind mount) vs a whiteboard wiped nightly (tmpfs) — each box in the diagram above is one of those three real-world containers for your stuff. Only the first three ever hold application data; npipe never does — it's Windows IPC plumbing, not a data store.

easypj: postgres data → volume; ./app:/app while coding → bind mount; a decrypted API key for one request → tmpfs. For each easypj directory (media/, static/, your working copy, a decrypted secret), name its mount type using ONLY the decision table above.

16.3 Docker Volumes — The Recommended Way

Volumes are Docker-managed directories stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/. They're the recommended way for persistent data because Docker handles: creation, mounting, permissions, backup, and driver plugins. Volumes exist independently of containers:

Volume Lifecycle — Independent of Containers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 VOLUME LIFECYCLE                                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────┐   create    ┌─────────┐   mount    ┌─────────┐            │
  │  │ Nothing │────────────▶│ 📦Volume│──────────▶│Container│            │
  │  │         │             │ (empty) │            │ uses it │            │
  │  └─────────┘             └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘            │
  │                               │                      │                  │
  │                               │   Container writes   │                  │
  │                               │◄─────────────────────┘                  │
  │                               │                                         │
  │                               │   Container deleted                     │
  │                               │   ┌─────────┐                          │
  │                               │   │Container│ 💀                       │
  │                               │   │ DELETED │                          │
  │                               │   └─────────┘                          │
  │                               │                                         │
  │                               ▼                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐                          │
  │  │ 📦 Volume STILL EXISTS with all data!   │                          │
  │  │ docker volume ls → my-volume            │                          │
  │  │ docker run -v my-volume:/data new-img   │◀── Remount!             │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 KEY INSIGHT: Volume lifecycle is COMPLETELY separate from container! │
  │     docker volume rm my-volume ← ONLY way to delete the volume.         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 A Shared Storage Locker With Its Own Key

Not tied to any one tenant: tenants (containers) move in and out, the locker (volume) and its contents outlast every one of them — exactly the "STILL EXISTS" box the diagram ends on. A volume can also be created implicitly by the first -v that references it.

easypj: docker volume create pgdata, mount it into postgres, docker rm -f the container, then docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres again — same rows, new container. Try it yourself: docker volume create test, run alpine with -v test:/data, write a file, remove the container, run a SECOND alpine with the same volume. Verify: cat /data/file in container #2 prints what container #1 wrote.

⚠️ Anonymous Volumes Are Just As Persistent — Just Harder to Find

An anonymous volume (-v /data, no name) is just as persistent as a named one, but nearly impossible to find later — it only gets a long hash, never a human-readable name. Always name volumes you intend to keep.

16.4 docker volume Commands

Five subcommands cover the entire volume lifecycle from the CLI — create, ls, inspect, rm, and prune:

TERMINAL
# List all volumes
$ docker volume ls
DRIVER    VOLUME NAME
local     postgres_data
local     static_volume
local     media_volume

# Create a new volume
$ docker volume create easypj-logs

# Inspect volume details (mountpoint, driver, labels)
$ docker volume inspect postgres_data
[
    {
        "Name": "postgres_data",
        "Driver": "local",
        "Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres_data/_data"
    }
]

# Remove a volume (must not be in use)
$ docker volume rm easypj-logs

# Remove all unused volumes
$ docker volume prune
WARNING! This will remove all local volumes not used by at least one container.
Are you sure? [y/N] y
Total reclaimed space: 2.5 GB

inspect is the command that matters most: it prints the real Mountpoint on the host — the ONE place you can ls a volume's contents without going through a container at all. On the exam and in the field: create, inspect, and remove a throwaway volume, noting the Mountpoint path each time — docker volume ls should return empty after rm, with no orphaned entry left behind.

Volume State Lifecycle — the Four States a Volume Passes Through
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🔄 VOLUME STATE LIFECYCLE                        │
  │                                                                    │
  │   CREATED    (docker volume create, or auto via first -v, empty) │
  │      │  docker run -v name:/path ... (mount into a container)    │
  │      ▼                                                            │
  │   MOUNTED    (≥1 container has it attached, data can change)     │
  │      │  docker rm the container(s) that had it mounted           │
  │      ▼                                                            │
  │   UNMOUNTED  (0 containers attached — data is UNTOUCHED)         │
  │      │  docker volume rm name (refuses if still mounted)         │
  │      ▼                                                            │
  │   REMOVED    (data deleted from /var/lib/docker/volumes/, gone)  │
  │                                                                    │
  │   ↺ UNMOUNTED loops straight back to MOUNTED any time — that     │
  │     loop is the whole point: data outlives any one container.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 "Mounted" Tracks Attachment, Not Running State

A volume can be MOUNTED into a STOPPED container — "mounted" tracks attachment, not whether the container is running. That is why docker volume rm refuses even for a volume attached only to a container you have not started in weeks. In easypj, postgres_data lives almost entirely in the MOUNTED ⇄ UNMOUNTED loop — it should never see REMOVED.

🔧 Under the Hood — how the daemon actually tracks a volume

Every named volume is really two things on disk: a metadata record the daemon keeps (which driver owns it, when it was created, which containers currently reference it) and the data directory itself, always at /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data for the local driver. docker volume inspect (16.4) prints exactly that Mountpoint because there is no path translation left to hide.

 Container mount request: -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      │
      ▼
 dockerd's volume subsystem
      │  1. look up "pgdata" in its local metadata store
      │  2. if missing, driver="local" creates it right here:
      ▼
 /var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data   (the real files live here)
      │
      ▼
 bind-mounted into the container's mount namespace at
 /var/lib/postgresql/data — the container's kernel-level view
 IS this host directory, not a copy of it.
🔑 Bind mounts skip the metadata step entirely — the kernel just maps a host path directly into the container's mount namespace, which is why docker volume ls never lists bind mounts: they were never Docker-managed objects to begin with.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Containers are disposable compute; anything that must outlive one belongs in a volume, never in the writable layer.
  • Docker has four mount types — volume, bind mount, tmpfs, npipe — and only the first three ever hold real application data.
  • A volume's lifecycle is independent of any container: create, mount, unmount, remount, and only docker volume rm deletes it.
  • Anonymous volumes persist exactly like named ones but are nearly impossible to find again — name everything you intend to keep.
  • docker volume inspect is your window into the host filesystem — the Mountpoint is a real, ls-able path.
  • docker volume prune deletes EVERY unused local volume, not a curated subset — read its warning before confirming.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming docker compose down deletes named volumes → docker compose down -v deletes named volumes; plain down does not — one flag is the entire difference between safe and gone.
  • Bind-mounting a directory and expecting it to "just work" across machines → Bind mounts inherit host file permissions/UID exactly — the #1 source of "permission denied" errors inside a container.
  • Treating an anonymous volume as "gone" once its container is removed → An anonymous volume (-v /data, no name) still needs docker volume rm <hash> to clean up — it just never gets an easy name.
  • Backing up a volume while its container is actively writing to it → Stop the container first or use database-native backup tools (pg_dump) — a tar snapshot of a live write is not consistent.
  • Expecting docker volume rm to work on an in-use volume → Docker refuses to delete volumes still attached to any container, running or stopped.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker volume inspect <name> -f '{{.Mountpoint}}' prints just the path — skip reading the full JSON blob by eye.
  • docker volume ls -f dangling=true lists only unused volumes BEFORE you prune, so you know exactly what is about to be deleted.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 16)

the Chapter 16 cheat-card 
docker volume create pgdata          # make a named volume
docker volume ls                     # list all volumes
docker volume inspect pgdata         # show driver + Mountpoint
docker volume rm pgdata              # delete (fails if in use)
docker volume prune                  # delete ALL unused volumes
docker run -v pgdata:/data alpine    # mount a named volume
docker run -v /data alpine           # mount an ANONYMOUS volume
docker run -v "$(pwd)":/app alpine   # bind mount (host path=source)
docker run --rm -v appdata:/src -v $(pwd):/dst alpine tar czf /dst/backup.tar.gz -C /src .  # backup a volume
docker run --rm -v appdata:/dst -v $(pwd):/src alpine tar xzf /src/backup.tar.gz -C /dst    # restore a volume

🧠 Chapter 16 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the ephemeral-container problem to picking the right mount type on sight — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
You run a postgres container with no -v flag, insert rows, then docker rm -f it. Are the rows recoverable?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No. With no volume, PostgreSQL's data directory lives only in the container's writable layer, which docker rm deletes along with the container.

EXPLANATION

This is the WITHOUT VOLUMES half of 16.1's diagram — nothing outside the container's storage-driver layer ever held the data, so there is nothing left to recover.

Q2
What are Docker's four mount types, and which of them never holds application data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

volume, bind mount, tmpfs, and npipe. npipe never holds application data — it is Windows-only IPC plumbing, not storage.

EXPLANATION

Type / Persists / Speed / Typical use — volume: Yes, Fast, DB data & uploads; bind: Yes, Fast, dev hot-reload & config; tmpfs: No, Fastest, secrets & temp files; npipe: N/A, N/A, Windows daemon IPC.

Q3
Why is a bind mount the wrong default for a database's data directory even though it also "persists"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It works, but it ties the container to the host's exact filesystem layout and inherits host file permissions/UID exactly — the #1 cause of container permission errors.

EXPLANATION

16.2's decision table routes "survive restart, don't care where on disk" to a volume specifically because Docker manages the path and permissions for you.

Q4
You mount the same named volume into two different containers, one after the other. What does the second container see?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Whatever the first container wrote — the volume's data is independent of both containers.

EXPLANATION

This is 16.3's VOLUME LIFECYCLE diagram in miniature: create → mount → write → rm container → STILL EXISTS → remount. The volume never re-enters existence; it simply never left.

Q5
What is the difference between a named volume and an anonymous volume, in terms of what happens to your data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing — both persist identically. The only difference is that a named volume has a human-readable name; an anonymous one only has a long hash.

EXPLANATION

16.3's gotcha exists precisely because anonymous volumes are just as durable as named ones, only harder to manage.

Q6
What does docker volume inspect pgdata show that docker volume ls does not?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The Mountpoint — the real host path (/var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data) where the volume's files actually live, plus driver and label metadata.

EXPLANATION

ls only lists names and drivers; inspect lets you ls the real files from the host directly, no container needed.

Q7
Does plain docker compose down delete named volumes defined under a compose file's top-level volumes: key?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No. Named volumes survive; only containers and the default network are removed.

EXPLANATION

16.1's closing gotcha is exactly this — docker compose down -v is the one-flag difference that deletes them.

Q8
A volume is currently mounted only into a container you stopped (not removed) three weeks ago. Can you docker volume rm it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — Docker refuses because the volume is still "mounted" (attached), even though the container is not running.

EXPLANATION

16.4's state diagram tracks MOUNTED vs UNMOUNTED by attachment, not by running state — remove the container first.

Q9
What does docker volume prune actually delete?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

EVERY volume with zero containers currently referencing it — not a curated guess, all of them.

EXPLANATION

16.4's gotcha warns exactly about this — a volume you meant to keep but forgot to attach anywhere is fair game.

Q10
You need a directory that changes as fast as possible and must NEVER touch disk, even briefly. Which mount type do you reach for, and why not a volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

tmpfs — it is backed by RAM only. A volume still round-trips through the storage driver to real disk (or the VM disk on Desktop), which tmpfs skips entirely.

EXPLANATION

16.2's four-way comparison marks tmpfs as the only type explicitly "never on disk."

🔬 Practice Drill 16.1 — Remount and Verify (5 min)

Create a volume named drillvol, run alpine with it mounted at /data, write one file, remove the container, then run a SECOND alpine with the same volume mounted. cat the file. Stop the clock the moment you see its contents print — that's the volume lifecycle from 16.3 in five minutes flat.

  │                                                              │

In one line: Chapter 16 draws one hard line: a container's writable layer dies with docker rm, full stop, but a volume is a separate Docker-managed object whose lifecycle you control explicitly with docker volume create/rm. Bind mounts and tmpfs round out the other two real choices — host-path-managed persistence and RAM-only non-persistence — while npipe is Windows plumbing, not a data store.

The takeaway: Chapter 17 spends its entire length deciding which of these four every easypj directory gets.

Chapter 16 gave you four mount types in the abstract; this chapter decides which easypj directory gets which one, and proves each choice under real failure. We'll configure volumes for PostgreSQL data, Django media/uploads, and static files, wire up a dev-only bind mount, reach for tmpfs exactly once, and build — then actually test — a backup and restore strategy for production.

17.1 What Needs to Persist in easypj?

Name the four easypj data categories and the ONE question that decides each one's mount type: would losing it on the next docker rm be a data-loss incident (DB rows, user uploads) or just a rebuild step (collectstatic output, cached logs)? Only the first kind is non-negotiable.

🐘
PostgreSQL Data

/var/lib/postgresql/data — The database itself. All your models (Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, Users). This MUST persist — losing it means losing all data.

📸
Django Media Files

/app/media — User-uploaded files (resumes, profile pictures, job attachments). Must persist across deployments.

🎨
Django Static Files

/app/static — CSS, JS, images collected by collectstatic. Shared between Django (writes) and Nginx (reads).

📋
Application Logs

Optional: persist logs to a volume for debugging. Usually sent to stdout for Docker logging, but can be volume-mounted for log aggregation tools.

DataMust persist?Where
PostgreSQL data dir✅ Yes, alwaysNamed volume (17.2)
Django media uploads✅ Yes, alwaysNamed volume (17.3)
Django static files⚠️ RebuildableNamed volume (17.3, for convenience)
Application logsUsuallyVolume or log driver
easypj Containers → Persistent Paths
  postgres ─▶ postgres_data  ─▶ /var/lib/postgresql/data
    (rows: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, User — 17.2)
  django   ─▶ media_volume   ─▶ /app/media   (uploads, 17.3)
  django   ─▶ static_volume  ─▶ /app/static  (generated, 17.3)
  nginx    ─▶ static_volume  ─▶ /app/static  (:ro, reads only)
  redis    ─▶ (none — cache only, nothing here worth keeping)
💡 Redis Has No Volume, On Purpose

The table above already marks cache data as disposable — giving redis a volume would just be extra disk I/O for data you already decided to lose. Sorting moving boxes: "irreplaceable" (family photos → DB rows, uploads) vs "can be bought again" (furniture from a catalog → generated static files).

🧪 Practice — Map Every Path

List every path easypj writes to at runtime and mark each irreplaceable or rebuildable. Verify: your list matches the four rows in the table above. Delete static_volume and one collectstatic rebuilds it; delete postgres_data and every JobPost, Skills, Author, Location, and User row is gone with no rebuild possible.

⚠️ Logs Feel Disposable Until an Incident Review Needs Them

Application logs feel disposable until an incident review needs last week's — decide log retention on purpose, not by accident (17.6-17.7 apply the same "actually prove it works" discipline to backups).

17.2 Volume Setup for PostgreSQL

postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data is the ONE mount that matters — that path is where postgres's own data files live; everything else in the container is disposable image content, rebuildable from postgres:15-alpine at any time.

compose.yaml (PostgreSQL Volume)
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # Named volume = data survives!
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: easypj
      POSTGRES_USER: easypj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

volumes:
  postgres_data:    # Top-level declaration = named volume = persists forever
Backup & Restore
# Backup: compress volume contents to a tar.gz on host
$ docker run --rm \
    -v postgres_data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/postgres_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore: extract backup into volume
$ docker run --rm \
    -v postgres_data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar xzf /backup/postgres_backup_20260612.tar.gz -C /data

# Better: pg_dump for database-level backup
$ docker exec easypj_db pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj > backup.sql
💡 The Filing Cabinet, Not the Clerk

The volume is the filing cabinet; the postgres container is just this month's clerk operating it — replace the clerk (docker rm db), hire a new one, cabinet untouched.

🧪 Practice — Prove It Survives a Restart

easypj: after this change, docker compose down && docker compose up -d restarts the whole stack — Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User rows survive untouched. Run docker compose down, docker compose up -d, then docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj_user -d easypj -c "SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_jobpost;". Verify: the count matches what it was before you brought the stack down.

🔧 Under the Hood — how Compose actually names the volume on disk

When compose.yaml declares a service volume as postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data, "postgres_data" is not the final volume name on disk — Compose prefixes it with the PROJECT name (the directory name, or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME/-p override) unless the top-level volumes: entry sets name: explicitly. This is exactly the gotcha below: two unrelated projects both naming a volume postgres_data never collide, because they resolve to different real names.

 compose.yaml (project dir: "easypj")
      service volume ref: postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
                  │
                  ▼
      Compose resolves the top-level `volumes:` entry
                  │
      ┌───────────┴────────────────┐
      │ no `name:` override        │  `name: postgres_data` set
      ▼                             ▼
real volume = "easypj_postgres_data"  real volume = "postgres_data"
(docker volume ls shows THIS)         (docker volume ls shows THIS)
🔑 Either way, docker compose down (no -v) never touches the volume object regardless of its resolved name — the prefixing only affects how you would reference it with plain docker volume commands OUTSIDE of Compose.

17.3 Volume Setup for Django Media & Static

Give Django media uploads and collected static files the same durability postgres just got — without conflating them. static_volume is mounted :ro into nginx — nginx only ever READS what collectstatic wrote into the SAME volume from the django container; two services, one volume, one direction.

compose.yaml (All Volumes)
services:
  django:
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/static     # collectstatic writes here
      - media_volume:/app/media       # User uploads stored here

  nginx:
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/static:ro      # Read-only — Nginx only serves
      - media_volume:/media:ro        # Read-only — Nginx only serves
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro

volumes:
  postgres_data:    # DB data — most critical
  static_volume:    # Shared between Django and Nginx
  media_volume:     # Shared between Django and Nginx
💡 A Shared Print Tray

Django prints (writes) pages into the tray, nginx only ever picks pages up (reads) — the :ro flag is the label on nginx's side saying "no writing here".

🧪 Practice — Find an Upload on the Host

easypj: a user's uploaded resume PDF lands in media_volume via a FileField; nginx never touches media — Django (or a signed URL) serves that path directly. Upload a file through easypj's admin, docker volume inspect media_volume for its Mountpoint, sudo ls it on the host. Verify: the uploaded filename appears there.

⚠️ Skipping :ro Doesn't Break Anything Today

Three named volumes now cover DB rows, user uploads, and generated static assets — none of it lives in a container. But skipping :ro on nginx's static mount doesn't break anything today; it lets a compromised nginx write into a path Django trusts. Least privilege, even on volumes.

17.4 Bind Mounts for Development

Bind mounts let you mount your source code into the container — edit files on your host, changes reflect instantly. Essential for development, NEVER for production. Get live code reload in dev without ever baking that habit into the production image:

compose.override.yaml (Dev Only)
services:
  django:
    volumes:
      - .:/app                      # Bind mount: live code reload!
      - static_volume:/app/static
      - media_volume:/app/media
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
⚠️ Bind Mounts: Dev Only

Never use bind mounts in production. They: (1) tie your container to a specific host directory, (2) may expose sensitive files (.git, .env), (3) have host-specific permission models, (4) can't be migrated with the container. Production uses volumes or copies all code into the image at build time.

💡 A Whiteboard Clipped Over the Framed Poster

Erase and redraw all day (bind mount), then unclip it (deploy without the override) and the original poster (production image) is untouched. compose.override.yaml auto-merges over compose.yaml on plain docker compose up — the bind mount and dev command apply locally, never in a prod build where this file is intentionally absent.

🧪 Practice — Edit, Refresh, No Rebuild

easypj: edit views.py in your editor, runserver inside the container sees the change immediately — no rebuild, no docker cp, because .:/app IS your working directory. With the override active, change a Django template's text, refresh the browser. Verify: the new text appears with no docker compose build in between.

⚠️ The #1 "Why Can't I Edit This" Bug

Bind mounts trade isolation for iteration speed — the right trade in dev, the wrong one in prod. On Linux, files the container writes appear owned by the CONTAINER's UID on your host — mismatched UIDs between image and host user are the #1 "why can't I edit this" bug.

17.5 tmpfs Mounts — In-Memory Storage

Decide, without hesitating, when tmpfs beats a volume for one specific easypj value. tmpfs is a RAM-backed filesystem the KERNEL exposes — it never touches the storage driver or the host disk at all; --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m caps it so one runaway write can't exhaust host memory.

Use CaseCommandWhy
Temp files--tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=128mFaster than disk, auto-cleaned
Secrets at runtime--tmpfs /run/secrets:ro,size=1mNever touches disk — zero trace after stop
Django cache--tmpfs /app/cache:rw,size=256mRAM-speed cache, volatile (use Redis for production)
tmpfs use caseLimitation
Decrypted DB creds for one processGone on container stop
Session cache faster than a volumeCapped by --tmpfs-size
Scratch space for image processingCounts against host RAM
Mount typeBacking storeLinux hostDesktop VM
tmpfsRAM (kernel), no diskFastestFastest
volumeHost/VM disk, overlay2Near-nativeNear-native
bind mountHost disk, directNear-native5-20x slower
💡 A Whiteboard, Not a Notebook

Fast to write on, but wiped the instant the room (container) is vacated — nothing written there was ever meant to be found later. easypj: /run/secrets (tmpfs) and postgres_data (volume) never feel this gap; a .:/app bind mount (17.4) is exactly where Desktop's per-file overhead shows up during pip installs.

🧪 Practice — Confirm the Filesystem Type

easypj: mounting --tmpfs /run/secrets:size=1m for a decrypted DATABASE_URL keeps it out of both the image layer and any volume backup that might leak it. Run docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=16m alpine df -h /tmp. Verify: /tmp shows filesystem type tmpfs sized 16m, not the container's overlay root.

💡 The Desktop Workaround

On Docker Desktop, some teams dodge the bind-mount penalty by mounting the repo once, then copying it into a named volume before running tests or builds — trading one slow copy for a fast volume for the rest of the run.

⚠️ tmpfs on Docker Desktop for Windows Isn't Native

tmpfs trades persistence for speed and secrecy — perfect for secrets and scratch space, wrong for anything easypj needs tomorrow. tmpfs on Docker Desktop for Windows isn't native Linux tmpfs — it's backed by the Desktop VM's RAM, not the host you think you have. And tmpfs is RAM-only: data is lost on container stop AND host reboot, always — it never "just" survives a restart.

17.6 Backup & Restore Strategies

pg_dump produces a logical, version-portable SQL dump — unlike a raw tar of the data directory, this restores cleanly onto a DIFFERENT postgres minor version and can target a brand-new, empty database.

TERMINAL
# ─── Strategy 1: Volume-level backup ───
$ docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/all_volumes.tar.gz -C /data .

# ─── Strategy 2: Database-level (pg_dump) ───
$ docker exec easypj_db pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj > backup.sql
$ docker exec -i easypj_db psql -U easypj_user easypj < backup.sql

# ─── Strategy 3: Media files only ───
$ docker run --rm -v media_volume:/media -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/media.tar.gz -C /media .

# ─── Automated nightly backup (cron on host) ───
# 0 2 * * * docker exec easypj_db pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj > /backups/easypj_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).sql
pg_dump — Full Cycle
$ docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj \
    > easypj_backup.sql
$ ls -lh easypj_backup.sql
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 42K easypj_backup.sql
$ docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U easypj_user easypj \
    < easypj_backup.sql
💡 A Recipe Card vs a Frozen Dish

The tar backup is the frozen meal — only reheats in an identical oven; the pg_dump SQL is the recipe — any working kitchen can cook it. easypj: pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj captures every row across Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User in one portable .sql file you can commit to encrypted backup storage.

🧪 Practice — Dump, Drop, Restore

Dump easypj, drop and recreate the database, restore the dump. Verify: SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_jobpost; returns the same number as before the drop.

⚠️ The -T Flag You'll Forget Once

psql < dump.sql needs -T on docker compose exec (disable pseudo-TTY) or the piped stdin silently fails. Tar the volume for fast whole-disk snapshots; pg_dump for portable, restorable, version-safe database backups.

17.7 Automated Backups — cron + pg_dump Pattern

Stand up an automated, retained, and PROVEN-restorable backup for easypj's PostgreSQL data. Two valid schedulers: host cron calling docker exec postgres pg_dump ... from outside, or a sidecar service in compose.yaml running its own loop over the compose network — the sidecar deploys with the stack, host cron does not. Either way, pg_dump streams SQL to stdout; piping through gzip before it touches disk keeps a growing jobpost database's backups small.

⏰
Host Cron

Lives outside compose entirely. Calls docker exec postgres pg_dump ... on a schedule. Must be set up separately on every host that runs the stack.

🚢
Sidecar Service

A db-backup service defined right in compose.yaml. Travels WITH the stack wherever it's deployed — no per-host setup needed.

compose.yaml (db-backup sidecar)
services:
  db-backup:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    depends_on: [postgres]
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ./backups:/backups
    entrypoint: >
      sh -c "while true; do
      pg_dump -h postgres -U easypj_user easypj |
      gzip > /backups/easypj_$(date +%F_%H%M).sql.gz;
      find /backups -name '*.sql.gz' -mtime +7 -delete;
      sleep 86400; done"
💡 A Fire Drill, Not a Fire Extinguisher on the Wall

An extinguisher (backup file) never test-fired might be empty. The RESTORE drill is pulling the pin once a month on purpose, on a THROWAWAY building, to prove it still sprays.

🧪 Practice — Run It, Then Restore It

easypj: the service above dumps the easypj database (Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User tables) daily, gzips it into ./backups on the host, and prunes anything past 7 days with find -mtime +7 — a three-line retention policy. Run db-backup once by hand (docker compose run --rm db-backup), then RESTORE it into a fresh container: gunzip -c backups/latest.sql.gz | docker exec -i newpg psql -U easypj_user easypj. Verify: SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_jobpost; matches the original database.

🛑 Same-Host Backups Are Not Disaster Recovery

Schedule the dump, compress it, prune old copies, and — the step everyone skips — actually restore one on a recurring basis. A backup volume on the SAME Docker host as the database is not disaster recovery — one disk failure takes both; ship backups off-host (S3, another server) for real DR.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Sort data first, mount second: irreplaceable data (DB rows, user uploads) always gets a volume; rebuildable output (static files) gets one too, but for convenience, not survival.
  • postgres_data mounts onto exactly one path that matters: /var/lib/postgresql/data — everything else in that container is disposable image content.
  • static_volume is shared between django (writes) and nginx (reads :ro) — one volume, one direction, least privilege enforced by the mount flag itself.
  • Bind mounts are a dev-only convenience (compose.override.yaml); they never belong in the production image or a prod compose file.
  • tmpfs is for the one class of data that must never survive even briefly on disk — decrypted secrets, not application state.
  • pg_dump produces a portable, version-safe SQL backup; a raw tar of the volume only reheats on an identical postgres version.
  • An untested backup is not a backup — schedule the restore drill, not just the dump.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming your named volume postgres_data is literally called that on disk → Compose prefixes it with the project name (e.g. easypj_postgres_data) unless you set name: explicitly under the top-level volumes: key.
  • Expecting tmpfs data to survive a container restart → tmpfs is RAM-only — data is lost on container stop AND host reboot, by design.
  • Assuming a file a bind-mounted container writes keeps YOUR host user's ownership → It appears owned by the CONTAINER's UID on the host — mismatched UIDs are the #1 dev bind-mount bug.
  • Piping psql < dump.sql straight through docker compose exec → Add -T to disable the pseudo-TTY exec allocates by default, or piped stdin silently fails.
  • Treating a daily backup in ./backups on the same Docker host as disaster recovery → One disk failure destroys the live database AND every local backup — ship backups off-host (S3, another server) for real DR.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump ... — add -T up front for any piped exec, not just restores, to avoid TTY surprises.
  • Alias a one-line backup: alias pjbackup='docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj | gzip > backup_$(date +%F).sql.gz'
  • docker system df -v before deciding what to prune — see exactly how much each volume is costing you on disk.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 17)

the Chapter 17 cheat-card 
docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj > b.sql       # backup
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U easypj_user easypj < b.sql       # restore
docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .                        # raw tar backup
docker volume inspect media_volume -f '{{.Mountpoint}}'                  # find uploads on host
docker compose run --rm db-backup                                        # run backup sidecar once
docker volume ls                                                         # check real (prefixed) volume names
docker compose up -d                                                     # applies override automatically
docker compose down -v                                                   # DANGER: also deletes volumes

🧠 Chapter 17 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From sorting irreplaceable vs rebuildable data to a proven, off-host-worthy restore — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Which easypj data path is non-negotiable to persist, and which is merely convenient?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

PostgreSQL's data directory is non-negotiable — losing it loses every Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User row. Django's collected static files are convenient — losing them costs one collectstatic re-run.

EXPLANATION

17.1's data map draws exactly this line: postgres data dir = yes, always; static_volume (generated) = rebuildable.

Q2
What single path does the postgres_data volume mount onto, and why does nothing else in that container need a volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/var/lib/postgresql/data. Everything else in the postgres container is image content, rebuildable from postgres:15-alpine at any time.

EXPLANATION

17.2's compose.yaml mounts exactly this one path — mounting more would just be unnecessary extra durability.

Q3
Why is static_volume mounted :ro into nginx but read-write into django?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Django is the only service that WRITES static files (via collectstatic); nginx only ever needs to READ them to serve.

EXPLANATION

django (write) ──▶ static_volume (volume) ──▶ nginx (:ro, read-only). 17.3's gotcha calls this out directly — skipping :ro doesn't break anything today but violates least privilege if nginx is ever compromised.

Q4
You edit a Django template on your host while the dev container runs with a bind mount active. Do you need to rebuild the image to see the change?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — the bind mount means the container's /app IS your working directory; runserver picks it up immediately.

EXPLANATION

17.4's compose.override.yaml example is precisely this — .:/app plus runserver, no docker cp, no rebuild.

Q5
A file the container wrote through a bind mount now appears owned by a strange numeric UID on your host. What caused it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container process's UID (not necessarily matching your host user's UID) wrote the file directly onto the host path.

EXPLANATION

17.4's gotcha names this the #1 "why can't I edit this" bug — bind mounts inherit host permissions exactly, in both directions.

Q6
Why keep a decrypted DATABASE_URL in a tmpfs mount instead of a named volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

tmpfs never touches disk or the storage driver, so the decrypted value cannot leak into a volume backup or an image layer; it disappears the moment the container stops.

EXPLANATION

17.5 makes this exact case for /run/secrets.

Q7
What can a pg_dump backup do that a raw tar of postgres_data cannot?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Restore cleanly onto a DIFFERENT postgres minor version, or into a brand-new empty database — the tar only reheats on an identical setup.

EXPLANATION

17.6's recipe-card-vs-frozen-meal analogy is built on exactly this distinction.

Q8
Your psql < dump.sql restore through docker compose exec hangs or silently does nothing. What flag did you forget?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-T, to disable the pseudo-TTY that exec allocates by default — piped stdin needs it disabled.

EXPLANATION

17.6's gotcha names this exact failure mode.

Q9
What is the difference between scheduling backups with host cron versus a db-backup sidecar service in compose.yaml?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A sidecar deploys and travels WITH the compose stack; host cron lives outside it and must be set up separately per host.

EXPLANATION

17.7 lists both as valid, but only the sidecar is guaranteed present wherever the stack is deployed.

Q10
Why is a daily easypj backup sitting only in ./backups on the SAME Docker host not real disaster recovery?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

One disk failure destroys the live database AND every local backup at once — they share the same failure domain.

EXPLANATION

17.7's closing gotcha requires shipping backups off-host (S3, another server) for that reason.

docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U easypj_user easypj > drill.sql, drop and recreate the easypj database, restore drill.sql, then re-run 17.6's row-count query: SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_jobpost;. Stop the clock once the count matches.

In one line: Chapter 17 turned Chapter 16's four abstract mount types into seven concrete decisions for easypj: the database and user uploads get durable named volumes (17.2-17.3), static files get a volume shared read-only with nginx (17.3), dev convenience gets a bind mount that never reaches production (17.4), one decrypted secret gets tmpfs (17.5), and backups move from a raw tar to a portable pg_dump cycle (17.6) that's actually automated and proven restorable (17.7).

The takeaway: "it's backed up" only counts once you've restored it — 17.7 insists on that proof before the chapter closes.

Beyond basic volumes: understand how Docker manages image layers with storage drivers, use volume plugins for cloud storage, configure NFS volumes for multi-host data sharing, and peek inside the union filesystem that makes Docker images work.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~60-75 min 💾 Storage 🎯 DCA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Choose local vs nfs vs a cloud volume driver based on whether storage must be reachable from more than one host

Storage & Volumes 10% Installation & Configuration 15%
🎯 Graded Under Two Domains at Once

Storage drivers are listed explicitly under BOTH the Storage & Volumes domain (10%, "storage drivers") and the Installation & Configuration domain (15%, "daemon configuration, storage drivers") — Chapter 18 is graded twice over.

  • Why this chapter exists: Volumes (Chapters 16-17) solved DATA persistence; this chapter opens the box underneath — how Docker itself stores image layers and a container's writable layer on disk.
  • Skip it and two real incidents have no explanation: a host filesystem change wiping every image, and one file edit taking seconds instead of milliseconds — both trace to the mechanics here.

🧭 Section Map

18.1 storage drivers (image/container layers) → 18.2 volume drivers (local/nfs/cloud) → 18.3 NFS volumes in practice → 18.4 overlay2 internals and copy-on-write — each section answers "what's on disk and who controls it" one layer deeper than the last.

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway

18.1 Storage Drivers (Overlay2, aufs, etc.)

A storage driver manages how image layers and the container's writable layer are stored on disk. Docker supports several — overlay2 is the default and recommended for all modern Linux systems:

DriverStatusFilesystemNotes
overlay2✅ Defaultext4, xfsBest performance, recommended for all modern kernels
aufs⚠️ Legacyext4, xfsOriginal Docker driver, deprecated
devicemapper⚠️ Legacydirect-lvmRHEL/CentOS 7 default, replaced by overlay2
btrfs/zfs🔧 Nichebtrfs, zfsAdvanced features (snapshots, compression)
vfs🐌 TestingAnyNo copy-on-write — full copy per layer. Testing only.
TERMINAL
# Check which storage driver is in use
$ docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
Storage Driver: overlay2
🗄️
Storage Driver

Manages IMAGE LAYERS and the container's own writable layer — overlay2 uses the kernel's native OverlayFS directly, no extra kernel module to install or maintain.

💾
Volume Driver

Manages where a VOLUME's data physically lives (local/nfs/cloud) — completely orthogonal to the storage driver. Changing one never touches the other (18.2).

💡 The Warehouse-and-Locker-Room Analogy

The storage driver is the warehouse's shelving system; volumes are a separate locker room down the hall — reshelving the warehouse (changing storage drivers) never touches what's in the lockers. Whichever driver is active, easypj's postgres_data named volume is completely unaffected; only easypj's own IMAGE layers and its container's writable layer go through it.

🧪 Quick Check

Run docker info | grep "Storage Driver". Verify it prints overlay2 on any current Docker install — anything else is worth investigating, not assuming.

18.2 Volume Drivers & Plugins

A volume driver decides WHERE volume data physically lives — swap the driver and the container-side mount point and your application code never change, only the backing plugin:

DriverTypePersistenceBest For
localBuilt-inSingle hostDefault, most applications
NFSBuilt-in (local with opts)Multi-hostShared storage across hosts
AWS EBSCloud pluginAZ-specificEC2 instances, high IOPS
Azure DiskCloud pluginZone-specificAzure VMs, managed disks
GCE Persistent DiskCloud pluginZone-specificGCP instances
Volume Driver Topology — local vs NFS vs Cloud
  LOCAL: Host A [ vol ] — only Host A's containers ever see it
         Host B [ vol ] — a DIFFERENT volume, same name, no link

  NFS:   Host A ─┐
         Host B ─┼─▶ NFS server ─▶ ONE shared export
         Host C ─┘    (every host mounts the SAME data)

  CLOUD: Host A ─▶ EBS / Azure Disk / GCE PD (block volume)
         Host B    ✗ cannot also attach it — single-AZ, usually
                     single-node, cloud block storage
⚠️ The Swarm Trap

Naive docker service create --mount source=postgres_data on Swarm is a trap: Swarm may reschedule the postgres task onto a DIFFERENT node, where "postgres_data" is a brand-new, EMPTY local volume — not the one with your data. A local volume is invisible to every OTHER host; moving a container to a new node does NOT move its data with it.

easypj's real trade-off: single-host deploys use local for postgres_data with zero config; a multi-host Swarm deploy of easypj (Part 10) needs nfs or a cloud driver so ANY node can mount the database — that's exactly what 18.3 sets up.

18.3 NFS Volumes in Docker

NFS volumes turn Docker's single-host local driver into a shared, multi-host-reachable one — only the volume's creation flags differ, not your application code:

TERMINAL
# Create an NFS volume
$ docker volume create \
    --driver local \
    --opt type=nfs \
    --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw,nfsvers=4 \
    --opt device=:/exports/easypj_data \
    nfs_shared_volume

# Use it like any other volume
$ docker run -d --name easypj-app \
    -v nfs_shared_volume:/app/data \
    easypj:v1.0

# In compose.yaml:
volumes:
  shared_data:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: nfs
      o: "addr=192.168.1.100,rw,nfsvers=4"
      device: ":/exports/easypj_data"
🔗
Same Shelf, Shared Wall

A shelving unit (local driver) bolted to a wall that happens to be a shared warehouse's wall (the NFS server) — any other room (Docker host) with a door to that warehouse reaches the identical shelf.

🏥
easypj HA Failover

Two easypj web nodes on separate hosts both mount nfs_pgdata; whichever node currently runs the db container, the SAME PostgreSQL files back it — the basis for HA failover.

⚠️ Benchmark Before You Trust It

NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem call — a chatty database on NFS is often SLOWER than expected. Databases also need consistent, low-latency I/O with reliable file locking, which NFS has historically struggled to guarantee; PostgreSQL and MySQL explicitly warn against NFS for data directories. Benchmark before trusting it under production write load.

18.4 Container Filesystem Internals

The Overlay2 filesystem is how Docker creates the illusion of a single unified filesystem from multiple image layers. Understanding it helps debug storage issues:

Overlay2 — Union Filesystem Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  📚 OVERLAY2 FILESYSTEM — HOW IT WORKS                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  What the CONTAINER sees:                   What's REALLY on disk:        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────┐                ┌───────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ /app/                 │                │  ┌─────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │ ├── manage.py  (R/W) │                │  │ UpperDir (R/W)       │  │  │
  │  │ ├── easypj/    (R/W) │                │  │ Container's changes  │  │  │
  │  │ ├── jobpost/   (R/W) │                │  │ (writable layer)     │  │  │
  │  │ ├── bin/python (R/O)│                │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │  │ └── lib/       (R/O)│                │             │             │  │
  │  └───────────────────────┘                │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │                                          │  │ LowerDir (R/O)      │  │  │
  │  The container sees ONE                  │  │ Layer 5: COPY . .   │  │  │
  │  unified filesystem — but                │  │ Layer 4: pip install│  │  │
  │  behind the scenes, Overlay2             │  │ Layer 3: COPY reqs  │  │  │
  │  merges multiple layers                  │  │ Layer 2: WORKDIR    │  │  │
  │  using Copy-on-Write.                    │  │ Layer 1: FROM slim  │  │  │
  │                                          │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │  Copy-on-Write:                          │             │             │  │
  │  Write to a file → copy from             │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │  LowerDir to UpperDir first.             │  │ WorkDir (internal)  │  │  │
  │  Read: if in UpperDir, use it.           │  │ Merge scratch space │  │  │
  │  If not, read from LowerDir.            │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │                                          │             │             │  │
  │                                          │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │                                          │  │ Merged View         │  │  │
  │                                          │  │ (what container     │  │  │
  │                                          │  │  actually sees)     │  │  │
  │                                          │  └─────────────────────┘  │  │
  │                                          └───────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Copy-Up Cost Scales With FILE Size

Editing an existing file triggers copy-up: the WHOLE file copies from its LowerDir into UpperDir first, THEN the write applies — never in place. Appending one byte to a 2 GB log file copies all 2 GB into UpperDir first; that's a real, measurable latency spike, not a rounding error.

TERMINAL
# Exec into a running container, edit a file that shipped in the image
$ docker exec -it easypj-app sh
$ echo "x" >> /app/manage.py
$ exit

# From the host, see what overlay2 recorded
$ docker diff easypj-app
C /app/manage.py

Verify: manage.py is listed with a C (changed) — that line lives only in UpperDir until the container is removed.

🔧 Under the Hood — how overlay2 represents a DELETED file

Copy-on-write (above) explains how EDITS land in UpperDir, but deletion is trickier: overlay2 cannot remove a file from a read-only LowerDir. Instead, deleting a file that exists in any LowerDir makes overlay2 create a WHITEOUT — a character device file (major/minor number 0/0) with the same name, in UpperDir. The kernel's overlay driver treats any whiteout as "this file does not exist in the merged view," even though the original bytes still sit untouched in the image layer below.

 rm /app/old_config.py  (file exists in a LowerDir, image layer)
      │
      ▼
 overlay2 CANNOT touch the read-only LowerDir
      │
      ▼
 creates a WHITEOUT marker in UpperDir: c000 old_config.py
      │
      ▼
 MergedDir view: old_config.py appears GONE
 (the real bytes are still in the LowerDir, completely untouched)
🔑 This is why docker diff reports a deleted file as D — it is reading the whiteout marker in UpperDir, not scanning for absence. It also explains why deleting a huge file INSIDE a container does not shrink the underlying image at all: the bytes never leave the LowerDir; only a tiny whiteout marker was added.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A storage driver manages image layers + the container's writable layer; a volume driver manages where VOLUME data physically lives — the two are completely orthogonal.
  • overlay2 is the default since Docker 18.09 because it uses the kernel's native OverlayFS, no extra kernel module required.
  • Changing storage drivers wipes ALL local images/containers; named volumes under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ are untouched by the change.
  • local covers single-host easypj completely; multi-host orchestration (Swarm/K8s) is the only reason to reach for nfs or a cloud volume driver.
  • A local volume is invisible to every other Docker host — moving a container to a new node does NOT bring its data with it.
  • overlay2's MergedDir = LowerDir(s) [read-only] + UpperDir [writable] + WorkDir [internal scratch] — deletions become whiteout markers, not real removal from the image.
  • Copy-up cost scales with FILE size, not edit size — appending one byte to a multi-GB file still copies the whole file first.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Treating a storage-driver switch as a routine config tweak → It deletes every local image and container; plan a re-pull, don't discover this in production.
  • Trusting docker service create --mount source=postgres_data by name alone on Swarm → If the task lands on a node that's never seen that volume name before, it silently creates a brand-new EMPTY local volume.
  • Assuming NFS "just works" for a chatty database → NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem call — benchmark before trusting it under write load.
  • Deleting a large file inside a container to reclaim host disk space → The bytes remain in the image's LowerDir; only a tiny whiteout marker is added — nothing is reclaimed.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker info | grep "Storage Driver" — the fastest way to confirm overlay2 (or catch a legacy driver) without digging through JSON.
  • docker diff <container> before assuming a file is gone for good — D means whiteout, not "unrecoverable from the image."

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 18)

the Chapter 18 cheat-card 
docker info | grep "Storage Driver"                     # confirm overlay2 is active
docker info | grep -A3 "Plugins"                         # list available volume drivers
docker volume create --driver local \
  --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=HOST,rw \
  --opt device=:/export/path nfsvol                       # NFS-backed volume
docker diff <container>                                  # A/C/D changes vs image
docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <ctr>           # raw LowerDir/UpperDir paths

🧠 Chapter 18 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

Storage drivers, volume drivers, NFS, and overlay2 internals — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What does a storage driver manage that a volume driver does not?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A storage driver manages IMAGE layers and the container's own writable layer; a volume driver manages where a VOLUME's data physically lives. They never overlap.

EXPLANATION

18.1's warehouse-shelving-vs-locker-room analogy makes this split explicit.

Q2
Why did overlay2 replace aufs and devicemapper as the default?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It uses the kernel's native OverlayFS directly — no extra kernel module to install or maintain.

EXPLANATION

18.1's table marks aufs/devicemapper as legacy paths tied to older kernels or specific distros.

Q3
You switch your daemon's storage driver from overlay2 to something else. What happens to your images, and what happens to your named volumes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

All local images and containers are wiped (each driver keeps its own layout); named volumes under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ are completely untouched.

EXPLANATION

18.1's closing gotcha states this split exactly — volumes bypass the storage driver entirely.

Q4
A Swarm service uses --mount source=postgres_data with the default local volume driver, and the scheduler reschedules the task onto a brand-new node. What data does the task see?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An empty volume — local volumes are per-host; the new node has never created a "postgres_data" volume before.

EXPLANATION

18.2's gotcha calls this out as a real trap for naive Swarm deployments.

Q5
What does --opt type=nfs change about a volume created with --driver local?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It tells the local driver to back the volume with a remote NFS export instead of local disk — no separate plugin install needed for basic NFS shares.

EXPLANATION

18.3's terminal example shows exactly this flag combination creating nfs_shared_volume.

Q6
Why might a chatty database perform WORSE on an NFS volume than expected, even though NFS "works"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem call — something a local disk-backed volume never incurs.

EXPLANATION

18.3's closing gotcha explicitly warns to benchmark before trusting NFS under production write load.

Q7
In the overlay2 model, which directory is writable, and which directories are shared read-only across every container from the same image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

UpperDir is the one writable layer, private to that container. Every LowerDir is read-only and shared by ALL containers started from that image.

EXPLANATION

18.4's layers diagram stacks the LowerDirs under one UpperDir.

UpperDir (writable, private to one container)
     │
LowerDir N...1 (read-only, shared by every container from this image)
Q8
You append one byte to a 2 GB log file inside a running container. Roughly how much data does copy-on-write actually copy?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The entire 2 GB — copy-up cost scales with FILE size, not edit size; the whole file moves into UpperDir before the byte is appended.

EXPLANATION

18.4's closing gotcha names this exact scenario as a real, measurable latency spike.

Q9
You rm a file inside a container that originally shipped in the base image. Does this shrink the image on disk?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No. overlay2 cannot modify the read-only LowerDir; it adds a whiteout marker in UpperDir instead. The original bytes remain in the image layer.

EXPLANATION

This chapter's Under the Hood section walks through this exact whiteout mechanism.

rm file (exists in LowerDir) → whiteout added to UpperDir →
MergedDir shows it gone, LowerDir bytes completely untouched
Q10
What does docker diff <container> report for a file that was deleted inside the container versus one that was only edited?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A deleted file shows D; an edited file shows C (changed). Both are reads of UpperDir — D reflects a whiteout marker, C reflects a copied-up, modified file.

EXPLANATION

18.4's practice drill uses docker diff to observe the C case directly; the Under the Hood section extends it to the D case.

🔬 Practice Drill 18.1 — Find the Whiteout (10 min)

docker exec into any running container, delete a file that shipped in the image, then run docker diff and docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' on it. Find the whiteout's effect in the diff output. Stop the clock once you can explain, out loud, why the image itself did not shrink.

In one line: Chapter 18 opens the box that Chapters 16-17 left closed: overlay2 is the storage driver managing every image layer and each container's private, copy-on-write UpperDir, while a completely separate volume driver (local by default, nfs or cloud for multi-host) decides where a named volume's actual bytes live.

The takeaway: the two never overlap — changing one never touches the other — which is exactly why postgres_data survived every experiment in Chapter 17 regardless of what the storage driver was doing underneath it.

You started this Part with every container's data one docker rm away from gone. Now you can name all four mount types on sight, assign every easypj path — database, uploads, static files, secrets — to the right one, back it up and actually restore it, and explain exactly what overlay2 and a volume driver are each doing underneath. 🔑 Part 6 — Key Takeaways

  • Containers are disposable; volumes are not — a volume's lifecycle is completely independent of any container that mounts it, and only docker volume rm ever deletes one (Ch 16).
  • Every easypj path gets sorted before it gets mounted: postgres_data and media_volume are non-negotiable, static_volume is shared read-only with nginx, bind mounts stay dev-only, tmpfs holds one class of decrypted secret, and a backup isn't a backup until it's been restored (Ch 17).
  • Two drivers sit underneath every volume, and they're orthogonal: overlay2 (storage driver) manages image layers and each container's copy-on-write writable layer, while a separate volume driver — local, nfs, or cloud — decides where a volume's actual bytes live (Ch 18).
  • 🎯 Exam: Storage & Volumes is 10% of the DCA on its own, and storage drivers are graded again under Installation & Configuration (15%) — Part 6 counts twice.

   📦 postgres_data ─┐
      media_volume  ─┼─▶ easypj's real assignments  ──pg_dump──▶ gzip ──▶ TESTED restore   (Ch 17)
      static_volume ─┘   (:ro into nginx; bind mount & tmpfs stay dev-only / secrets-only)
                        │

   name it, mount it, back it up, prove the restore — that's Part 6 in one line. 💾

In words: Chapter 16 draws the line the rest of Part 6 stands on: a container's writable layer dies with docker rm, full stop, but a named volume is a separate Docker-managed object you control explicitly — create, mount, unmount, remount, and only docker volume rm deletes it. Chapter 17 turns that abstraction into concrete decisions for easypj: postgres_data and media_volume are non-negotiable named volumes, static_volume is shared read-only into nginx, a bind mount buys live reload in dev only, tmpfs holds one class of decrypted secret, and pg_dump backups are scheduled AND proven restorable.

Chapter 18 then opens the box underneath every one of those volumes: overlay2, the default storage driver, manages image layers and each container's copy-on-write writable layer — completely separate from the volume driver (local by default, nfs or a cloud plugin once more than one host needs the same data) that decides where a volume's actual bytes live. Edits copy-up a whole file before writing; deletes leave a whiteout marker instead of touching the read-only layer below — and none of that machinery ever reaches into /var/lib/docker/volumes/.

The one idea to keep: nothing you care about should ever live only in a container's writable layer. Name it, mount it, back it up, and prove the restore — everything else in Part 6 is detail on top of that one rule.

Chapter 19 · Container Security Fundamentals

Containers share the host kernel — which means a compromised container can potentially compromise the host. A container is not a security boundary by default; it is a shared-kernel process wearing isolation. This chapter builds the defense-in-depth model — namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, non-root users, and a read-only root filesystem — that stands between "one RCE in a Django upload handler" and "the whole host is owned."

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🔐 Security 🎯 DCA 15%

  • ✅ Run easypj as a non-root user via USER in the Dockerfile or --user, and verify it with docker exec ... id (19.3)
  • ✅ Apply --cap-drop ALL / --cap-add correctly, and explain why CAP_SYS_ADMIN is treated as near-root (19.4)
  • ✅ Run easypj with --read-only plus the right --tmpfs mounts without breaking app writes (19.5)
  • ✅ Explain what the default seccomp profile blocks and read an AppArmor denial out of the audit log (19.6)
  • ✅ Identify --privileged and seccomp=unconfined on sight as the anti-patterns that erase every other control in this chapter
🎓 DCA Relevance
Security 15%
🎯 The Security Domain's Core Chapter

This chapter underlies the Security domain directly (15%) — non-root users and capabilities are examined directly on the DCA. Chapter 20 applies these primitives to easypj's whole stack; Chapter 21 measures the result.

  • Why this chapter exists: "my container runs as root with full capabilities, and one RCE in Django would own the whole host" — this chapter is the fix, one independent layer at a time.
  • The load-bearing line: defense-in-depth means an attacker who escapes one layer (namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, read-only rootfs) still faces the other nine — no single failure is game over.
