19.1 Why Container Security Matters

Containers are NOT virtual machines. They share the host kernel — a kernel exploit in a container can affect the ENTIRE host and all other containers. Real-world risks include cryptojacking (stealing CPU for crypto mining), data exfiltration, and container breakout (escaping to the host). Security is not optional — it's the foundation of containerized production.

Three container-specific attack classes cover almost every real incident: breakout (a root container plus a host mount adds up to host takeover), supply chain (an unpinned base image ships a backdoored library you never wrote), and runtime abuse (a popped Django worker mines crypto or exfiltrates the database). A single RCE in a JobPost upload handler, running in a root container with the Docker socket mounted, is not "one app hacked" — it is the whole host and every other container compromised.

⚠️
Shared Kernel Risk

Unlike VMs (each has its own kernel), containers share the host kernel. A kernel vulnerability exploited inside a container can compromise the entire host and all other containers.

🔓
Container Breakout

If a process escapes the container's namespace isolation, it gains access to the host. This is the worst-case scenario — full host compromise from inside a container.

📦
Supply Chain Attacks

Pulling a malicious base image from a public registry can give attackers a foothold. Always use trusted images, scan for CVEs, and verify signatures with Docker Content Trust.

🔓
Level 0
Default Container

Runs as root. All capabilities. Writable rootfs. No scanning.

❌ Vulnerable
👤
Level 1
Non-Root + Cap Drop

USER app. --cap-drop ALL. Basic hardening applied.

⚠️ Improved
📖
Level 2
Read-Only + Seccomp

--read-only + custom seccomp. Immutable infrastructure.

✅ Hardened
🛡️
Level 3
Full Defense-in-Depth

All 10 layers. DCT, scanning, userns-remap, CIS compliance.

🏆 Production-grade
💡 The Apartment Building Analogy

Containers sharing one kernel are like apartments sharing one foundation: a fire in one unit (a kernel-level compromise) threatens the whole building, unlike detached houses (VMs) with separate foundations. Run docker scout quickview (or trivy) on your base image — it lists the CVEs you inherited for free, the supply-chain surface you didn't write but still ship.

19.2 Docker Security Architecture — The Onion of Defense

Docker secures containers with multiple independent layers. Even if an attacker bypasses one layer, the next ones still protect the system:

10 Layers of Docker Security
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🔐 DOCKER SECURITY — ONION OF DEFENSE                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │                           ┌───────────┐                                  │
  │                           │  🐳 Your   │                                 │
  │                           │ Container │                                 │
  │                           └─────┬─────┘                                 │
  │                                 │                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  LAYER 1: User Namespace     │  🔑 USER instruction / --user    │    │
  │  │  (uid=1000, not root!)       │  docker run --user 1000:1000      │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 2: Capabilities       │  🎯 Drop all, add back only needed│    │
  │  │  (not full root!)            │  --cap-drop ALL                   │    │
  │  │                              │  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE       │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 3: Seccomp Profile    │  🚫 Block dangerous syscalls      │    │
  │  │  (system call filter)        │  ~44 blocked of ~350+ possible    │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 4: AppArmor/SELinux   │  📋 Mandatory Access Control      │    │
  │  │  (per-process profiles)      │  Limit file access per container  │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 5: Cgroups            │  💪 Limit CPU, RAM, disk I/O     │    │
  │  │  (resource limits)           │  --memory=512m --cpus=1.5         │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 6: Read-Only Root FS  │  📖 --read-only (immutable!)      │    │
  │  │  (no writes to root)         │  + tmpfs for /tmp, /run           │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 7: Network Isolation  │  🌐 No port exposure unless -p    │    │
  │  │  (bridge/internal networks)   │  Internal-only networks           │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 8: Image Scanning     │  🔍 docker scout quickview         │    │
  │  │  (CVE detection)             │  Trivy, Snyk, Grype                │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 9: Content Trust      │  ✍️ Docker Content Trust (DCT)     │    │
  │  │  (image signing)             │  DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1            │    │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
  │  │  LAYER 10: Host Security     │  🖥️ Docker Bench Security          │    │
  │  │  (daemon config, CIS)        │  Secure daemon.json config         │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🏆 Even if attacker escapes one layer, 9 more to go!                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The four load-bearing layers of the onion, from the inside out: namespaces control what a container can SEE (PID/NET/MNT/USER…), capabilities control which of root's powers it KEEPS (drop the rest), seccomp controls which SYSCALLS it may call (~44 blocked by default), and AppArmor controls which FILES and operations its profile permits. For easypj's web tier, that means: drop all capabilities, keep the default seccomp profile, run as uid 1000, mount the rootfs read-only — that alone removes most of the breakout surface.

💡 The Onion IS the Analogy

An attacker peeling one layer still faces nine more, each a different lock needing a different key — no single failure is game over. Run docker inspect on a default container and check its CapAdd/CapDrop/SecurityOpt/Privileged fields: by default caps are the standard set and Privileged is false.

⚠️ The One Flag That Erases the Onion

--privileged collapses the ENTIRE onion at once — all capabilities, all devices, no seccomp. Security is layered, not a single switch; namespaces + capabilities + seccomp + AppArmor + non-root + read-only compound their protection, and --privileged is the anti-pattern the whole diagram exists to prevent.

19.3 Running as Non-Root User

By default, Docker containers run as root (UID 0). If an attacker compromises your app, they have root inside the container — and potentially on the host. Running as non-root is the single most impactful security measure:

Dockerfile (Non-Root User)
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Create a system user (no login, no home directory)
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . .

# Switch to non-root user
USER app

CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

# Or override at runtime:
# docker run --user 1000:1000 easypj:v1
⚠️ Root by Default

Unless you explicitly set USER in your Dockerfile or use --user at runtime, the container process runs as UID 0 (root). This means: (1) the process can modify any file, (2) can bind to privileged ports (<1024), (3) can install packages, (4) can change kernel parameters if capabilities allow it. Always run as non-root.

The Dockerfile pattern is a visitor badge, not a master key: create the user, COPY --chown=app:app so it owns what it needs, then USER app so it can do its job without being able to open the server room even if it wanders off. A breakout as uid "app" lands with no host root, no ability to load kernel modules, and no write access to system paths.

🔬 easypj in Practice

With USER app set, gunicorn runs as uid "app" instead of root. Verify with docker exec <ctr> id — the uid should NOT be 0 (e.g. uid=100(app)) — then try to write /etc/passwd inside the container and confirm you get "permission denied."

19.4 Linux Capabilities

Traditionally, root has all power. Linux capabilities split root's power into fine-grained permissions. Docker gives containers a default set — drop ALL and add back only what you need:

CapabilityAllowsRiskWhen Needed
NET_BIND_SERVICEBind to ports < 1024LowWeb servers binding to port 80/443
CHOWNChange file ownershipLowAlmost always needed
SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, many admin ops🔴 Critical — ≈ root!Almost never — avoid!
SYS_PTRACEDebug other processesMediumDebugging tools (strace, gdb)
NET_RAWRaw sockets (ping)MediumNetwork diagnostic tools
TERMINAL
# Run with minimal capabilities
$ docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE --cap-add CHOWN easypj:v1

# Check current capabilities
$ docker run --rm alpine capsh --print

Instead of one master key (root), Linux capabilities hand out a ring of labeled keys — hand out only "bind low port" and take back the rest, especially the "does everything" master, SYS_ADMIN. easypj's gunicorn binds :8000 (>1024) behind nginx, so easypj needs zero added capabilities: --cap-drop ALL alone and it still runs fine.

🔬 Prove Capabilities Are Actually Enforced

Run easypj with --cap-drop ALL — the app still serves requests. Then --cap-drop ALL a container that pings and watch ping fail because NET_RAW is gone. That contrast is the proof capabilities are a real kernel-enforced boundary, not a cosmetic flag.

🛑 --privileged Is Not "All Capabilities"

--privileged is NOT the same as --cap-add ALL — it is capabilities PLUS device access PLUS no seccomp filter, all at once. Even --cap-add ALL alone is safer than --privileged.

19.5 Read-Only Root Filesystem

A read-only root filesystem prevents an attacker from modifying binaries, installing malware, or tampering with configuration files. Only explicitly mounted volumes and tmpfs directories are writable:

TERMINAL
# Run with read-only root filesystem
$ docker run --read-only \
    --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid \
    --tmpfs /run:rw,noexec,nosuid \
    -v static_volume:/app/static \
    easypj:v1

# Django needs writable /tmp for:
# - Gunicorn socket files
# - File uploads temp storage (before moving to media/)
# - Session files (if using file-based sessions)

Think of a hotel room bolted shut except for one labeled scratchpad (tmpfs): guests can jot a note, but they cannot repaint the walls or hide anything for the next occupant. Django and gunicorn need /tmp for sockets and in-progress uploads — those go on tmpfs, media persists on a named volume, and the rest of the filesystem is frozen against tampering.

🔬 Prove the Read-Only Boundary

Run easypj with --read-only and no tmpfs — watch it fail writing /tmp. Add --tmpfs /tmp and it starts. Verify: touch /etc/x inside is denied while touch /tmp/x works — that split is the whole point of the flag.

19.6 Seccomp & AppArmor in Practice

Docker's default seccomp profile blocks roughly 44 dangerous syscalls out of 350+ possible ones — things like mount, reboot, and kexec_load — while allowing the ~300 syscalls a normal application actually needs. A custom profile is just JSON (a defaultAction plus a syscalls allow-list) passed with --security-opt seccomp=profile.json. AppArmor's docker-default profile runs independently alongside seccomp, confining file access and capabilities per container process.

🚫
Seccomp — the Syscall Bouncer

Seccomp is the bouncer checking each SYSCALL against a guest list at the kernel door. It filters at the kernel level, before the syscall executes — a denial is a kernel EPERM, not something Docker or your app decided at runtime.

📋
AppArmor — the Room Access List

AppArmor is building security deciding which ROOMS (files) a guest may enter once already inside. Its docker-default profile independently confines file/network/capability access per container.

TERMINAL
# Inspect and apply seccomp / AppArmor
$ docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status  # 2 = filtered
$ docker run --security-opt seccomp=custom.json easypj:v1
$ docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-default easypj:v1

# denials appear as EPERM in the app; on the host:
$ dmesg | grep -i apparmor    # DENIED audit lines

The default profiles are enough for Django + gunicorn — easypj never calls mount() or reboot(), so keep the defaults on and only write a custom profile if a specific library needs a syscall the default rightly blocks.

🔬 Prove the Filter Is Actually Attached

Run one container with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined and one without; compare grep Seccomp /proc/1/status on each. Verify: 0 (unconfined) vs 2 (filtered) — proof the profile is really attached, not just assumed.

🛑 seccomp=unconfined Is a Confession, Not a Fix

--security-opt seccomp=unconfined and --privileged both strip the seccomp filter entirely. A container that "only works" unconfined is telling you it is doing something the default profile rightly blocks — treat that as a signal to investigate, not a reason to ship it that way.

🔧 Under the Hood — how the onion is actually enforced by the kernel

Every layer in 19.2's onion is a real Linux kernel mechanism, not a Docker invention. docker run translates your flags into an OCI runtime spec that runc hands to the kernel in one sequence, before your process ever executes. NAMESPACES are created with clone()/unshare() using flags like CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWUSER — this is what 19.2's "what a container can SEE" actually is. CAPABILITIES are a set of bitmasks (permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding, ambient) that runc sets on the container's init process via capset() before exec — --cap-drop ALL simply clears bits instead of leaving Docker's default subset in place. SECCOMP is a BPF program attached with the seccomp() syscall; the KERNEL evaluates it on every syscall the process makes for the rest of its life — a denial is a kernel-level EPERM, not something Docker or your app decided at runtime. AppArmor/SELinux is a separate Linux Security Module hooked into the same syscall path, checking file/network/capability access against a loaded profile — it runs alongside seccomp, not instead of it.

 docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only \
            --security-opt seccomp=default.json easypj:v1
                    │
                    ▼
 containerd + runc build an OCI spec: namespace list,
 capability bitmask, seccomp BPF program, mount list
                    │
                    ▼
 KERNEL: clone() w/ ns flags + capset() bitmask + seccomp() BPF
                    │
                    ▼
 gunicorn (PID 1 inside): every syscall it makes is now checked
 against BOTH the capability set AND the seccomp filter
🔑 This is exactly why --privileged is so total: it sets the capability bitmask to all-1s, attaches NO seccomp filter, and grants raw device access — three independent kernel controls erased by one flag, which is why 19.2/19.4 call it the onion's single point of failure.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Containers share the host kernel — a breakout is a HOST compromise, not just an app compromise (19.1).
  • Three attack classes: breakout (over-privileged container), supply chain (malicious/vulnerable base image), runtime abuse (a popped app mining crypto or exfiltrating data) (19.1).
  • The security onion is 10 independent layers — namespaces, caps, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, cgroups, read-only rootfs, network isolation, image scanning, content trust, host/CIS hardening; one failed layer still leaves nine more (19.2).
  • USER app (non-root) is the single highest-value, one-line fix — a breakout as uid 1000 is not host root (19.3).
  • --cap-drop ALL then add back only what's proven necessary — easypj's web tier needs zero added capabilities (19.4).
  • --read-only + narrow --tmpfs mounts make the filesystem an explicit allow-list of writable paths, not a free-for-all (19.5).
  • Default seccomp blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls; AppArmor's docker-default independently confines file/capability access; denials surface as EPERM and in the host audit log (19.6).
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Root in a container = limited, "it's isolated anyway" → Root in container IS root on host (unless user namespaces are remapped) — always use USER, never assume namespace isolation alone protects you.
  • --privileged "just to unblock a stuck build" → It is NOT "all capabilities" — it sets caps to all-1s, disables seccomp, AND grants raw device access simultaneously, erasing the whole onion in one flag.
  • Switching to USER app and assuming every write still works → It breaks writes to paths the new user doesn't own (/app/static, /app/media, bind mounts) — chown them first (COPY --chown=app:app), don't abandon USER.
  • Enabling --read-only without enumerating writable paths first → A missing tmpfs path (/tmp, /run) crashes the app on boot instead of degrading gracefully — list the real writable paths before you flip the flag.
  • --security-opt seccomp=unconfined "just to make a library work" → It silently strips the syscall filter entirely — a container that "only works" unconfined is telling you it needs a syscall the default profile rightly blocks.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker inspect <ctr> --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' — a one-line sanity check that a container is NOT privileged.
  • docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status — 2 means filtered, 0 means unconfined; a 5-second proof the flag applied.
  • dmesg | grep -i apparmor right after a mysterious permission error — a silent AppArmor DENY often looks like an app bug.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 19)

the Chapter 19 cheat-card 
docker inspect <c> --format '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}} {{.HostConfig.CapDrop}}'  # what caps were added/dropped
docker run --user 1000:1000 easypj:v1                  # force non-root
docker run --cap-drop ALL easypj:v1                     # drop every capability
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run easypj:v1  # immutable rootfs + writable exceptions
docker run --security-opt seccomp=unconfined ...        # DANGER, testing only
docker exec <ctr> id                                    # verify uid != 0
dmesg | grep -i apparmor                                 # AppArmor DENY lines
docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status       # 2 = filtered

🧠 Chapter 19 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the shared-kernel threat model to proving seccomp is really attached — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why does a shared kernel make container security fundamentally different from VM security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A container is a process on the HOST kernel; a breakout escapes directly to the host, unlike a VM's separate kernel behind a hypervisor boundary.

EXPLANATION

This is why 19.2's namespaces/capabilities/seccomp exist as SOFTWARE boundaries — there is no hardware isolation backing them up, which is the entire reason defense-in-depth (not a single switch) is the chapter's model.

Q2
List the three container-specific attack classes from 19.1 and give one easypj example of each.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Breakout (root container + host mount → host takeover), supply chain (unpinned base image ships a backdoored lib), runtime abuse (a popped Django worker mines crypto or exfiltrates the database).

EXPLANATION

Each needs a different defense: breakout is closed by 19.3-19.6's hardening, supply chain is Chapter 21's image-scanning territory — security is not one problem with one fix.

Q3
List, inner to outer, the 10 layers of 19.2's security onion.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) user namespace/non-root, (2) capabilities, (3) seccomp, (4) AppArmor/SELinux, (5) cgroups, (6) read-only rootfs, (7) network isolation, (8) image scanning, (9) content trust, (10) host/CIS hardening.

EXPLANATION

🐳 container → 1 userns → 2 caps → 3 seccomp → 4 AppArmor → 5 cgroups → 6 read-only → 7 network → 8 scan → 9 trust → 10 host/CIS — each ring is independent of the others, which is exactly what makes it defense-in-depth rather than a single point of failure.

Q4
What single Dockerfile line converts a root container into an unprivileged one, and why does it matter?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

USER app (after creating the user in the Dockerfile). A breakout as root is host root; a breakout as uid 1000 is not.

EXPLANATION

It's the highest payoff-per-line change in the whole chapter — one word in the Dockerfile closes the single most dangerous default in Docker.

Q5
You add USER app to easypj's Dockerfile and the container now crashes writing to /app/media. What happened, and the fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The app user doesn't own /app/media. Fix: COPY --chown=app:app in the build, or chown the mounted volume.

EXPLANATION

This is 19.3's own closing gotcha — non-root breaks any writable path the new user doesn't already own, so switching users always needs a matching chown pass.

Q6
What does --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE do, and why does easypj's gunicorn setup not even need the add-back?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Drops all ~40 Linux capabilities, then re-adds only the power to bind ports <1024. easypj's gunicorn binds :8000 (>1024) behind nginx, so it runs fine with ZERO added capabilities.

EXPLANATION

NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind <1024, rarely needed by the app tier), SYS_ADMIN (≈ root, never add to the app), NET_RAW (ping/raw sockets — drop it, it blocks spoofing) — 19.4's table of what to keep versus what to drop.

Q7
Why does --privileged collapse the ENTIRE onion at once rather than just one layer?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It sets capabilities to all-1s, disables seccomp filtering, AND grants device access simultaneously — three layers gone in one flag.

EXPLANATION

This is exactly why 19.2 and 19.4 call it the anti-pattern the whole onion diagram exists to prevent — no other single flag erases that many independent controls at once.

Q8
A container runs with --read-only and no tmpfs mounts. What happens when gunicorn tries to write a WSGI socket to /tmp, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The write fails (read-only filesystem) and the app crashes on boot. Fix: add --tmpfs /tmp (and /run if used).

EXPLANATION

19.5's gotcha: enumerate real writable paths instead of abandoning --read-only altogether — the fix is a narrow allow-list, not giving up on immutability.

Q9
Roughly how many syscalls does Docker's default seccomp profile block, and what shows up when a blocked one is attempted?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

~44 dangerous syscalls (mount, reboot, kexec_load, etc.) out of ~350+; a blocked call surfaces as EPERM in the app and can appear in the host's audit log.

EXPLANATION

19.6 covers this directly — seccomp filtering happens at the kernel level, before the syscall executes, so the denial looks like a permission error to your application code.

Q10
How do you PROVE, from inside a running container, that seccomp filtering is actually attached rather than assumed?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

grep Seccomp /proc/1/status — 2 means filtered (SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER), 0 means unconfined/disabled.

EXPLANATION

19.6's speed-tip habit: never trust a security flag without a kernel-reported check — the same discipline as verifying uid != 0 after adding USER.

🔬 Practice Drill 19.1 — Harden a Container in 10 Minutes

Take any easypj container started with plain defaults. In 10 minutes: (1) docker inspect it and record Privileged/CapAdd/CapDrop. (2) re-run it with --user 1000:1000 --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run. (3) confirm it still serves a request. (4) docker exec ... id and confirm uid != 0. All four steps passing with the app still healthy IS this chapter.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

In one line: a default container is root, fully capped, unfiltered, and writable everywhere (19.1); the security onion names ten independent layers standing between an attacker and the host (19.2); and 19.3-19.6 make four of the highest-value layers concrete on easypj — non-root, dropped capabilities, seccomp/AppArmor, and a read-only filesystem — so a single RCE stops meaning "game over" and starts meaning "an unprivileged process that can't write, can't call dangerous syscalls, and can't escalate."

20.1 Security Hardening Checklist for easypj

The high-value controls, in priority order: pin base image tags (not :latest), run non-root, --cap-drop ALL, read-only rootfs + tmpfs, scan images (Scout/Trivy), secrets NOT in ENV, resource limits (--memory/--cpus), health checks, Content Trust, and keep the Engine patched. Each item maps to a layer of the security onion Chapter 19 named.

#Security MeasureImplementation
1Specific base image tagFROM python:3.11-slim (not :latest)
2Run as non-rootUSER app after groupadd/adduser --system
3Drop capabilities--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE
4Read-only rootfs--read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run
5Scan for CVEsdocker scout quickview easypj:v1
6No secrets in ENVUse Docker secrets or .env file (gitignored)
7Resource limits--memory=512m --cpus=1
8Health checksHEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/
9Content TrustDOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
10Keep updatedRegularly rebuild with latest base image
easypj Hardening Checklist — Applied
  [ ] base image pinned (python:3.12-slim, not :latest)
  [ ] USER app (non-root)          [ ] --cap-drop ALL
  [ ] --read-only + tmpfs /tmp     [ ] --memory / --cpus set
  [ ] secrets via file, not ENV    [ ] HEALTHCHECK defined
  [ ] image scanned, 0 criticals   [ ] Engine + base patched
  [ ] Content Trust (DCT) enabled
💡 The Pre-Flight Checklist Analogy

Pilots do not "remember" to lower the landing gear — they READ the checklist every time. Hardening easypj is the same discipline: a list you run on every deploy, not a thing you recall from memory under pressure.

TERMINAL (hardened easypj run)
# The checklist rendered as flags on ONE command — this is what "hardened" looks like:
$ docker run -d --name easypj_web \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run \        # item 4: read-only rootfs
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \    # item 3: drop capabilities
  --memory=512m --cpus=1 \                        # item 7: resource limits
  --health-cmd="curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1" \  # item 8
  --health-interval=30s --health-retries=3 \
  easypj:v1.2.3                                    # item 1: pinned tag, not :latest
# (USER app is baked into the image — item 2; scan + DCT are pre/post-run steps 5 & 9)
⚠️ :latest Is Not a Version

An unpinned :latest base silently changes underneath you between builds — an unreviewed dependency upgrade shipping on every deploy. Pin the tag before you do anything else on this checklist.

20.2 Secrets Management

Environment variables in Dockerfiles and docker inspect are visible to anyone with Docker access. Secrets must be handled differently:

Swarm Secrets (Production)
# Create a secret
$ echo "super-secret-django-key" | docker secret create django_secret_key -

# Use in compose (Swarm mode):
services:
  django:
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
    environment:
      - SECRET_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/django_secret_key

secrets:
  django_secret_key:
    external: true

# For non-Swarm: use .env file (gitignored!)
# .env:
# DB_PASSWORD=secure_password_here
# SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-xyz
💡 The Sealed Envelope Analogy

An ENV secret is a password on a sticky note on the monitor — anyone glancing sees it. A mounted secret file is the password in a sealed envelope, handed only to the one process that needs it.

compose.yaml (file-based secret for easypj)
services:
  web:
    environment:
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets:
      - db_password
secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt   # gitignored

Django reads SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD from files at /run/secrets/*; docker inspect web shows only the FILE PATH, never the secret value.

🚨
ENV Vars (Leaky)

Visible in docker inspect, /proc/1/environ, and child processes. Baked into image layers if set via Dockerfile ENV — persists even after the Dockerfile is deleted.

🔒
Mounted Secret Files

Swarm secrets are encrypted at rest and in transit, mounted only as files under /run/secrets/ — invisible to docker inspect and env, and only available to services explicitly granted access.

🛑 A Deleted File Is Not a Deleted Secret

A Dockerfile that does ARG DB_PASSWORD then RUN echo $DB_PASSWORD > /tmp/x && rm /tmp/x in one layer has NOT removed the secret — the ARG value and everything the RUN step touched are baked into that layer's diff. Deleting the file in the same layer removes it from the final filesystem view, but the value can still be extracted from layer history and the build cache. Use --mount=type=secret build secrets instead — they never write the secret into a layer at all.

20.3 Securing the Docker Daemon

The Docker daemon runs as root. Its socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is equivalent to root access. Never expose it without TLS:

daemon.json
{
  "icc": false,                  // Disable inter-container communication
  "userns-remap": "default",     // User namespace remapping
  "live-restore": true,          // Keep containers alive during daemon downtime
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  },
  "no-new-privileges": true     // Prevent privilege escalation
}
💡 The Master Key Analogy

docker.sock is the master key to the whole building. A container with the socket mounted is a tenant holding that master key — polite until it is not, then every door is already open.

🔧 Under the Hood — userns-remap and why docker.sock is really root

20.3's userns-remap setting doesn't touch the container process at all — it changes what UID 0 INSIDE a container maps to OUTSIDE it. The daemon reads ranges from /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid (e.g. dockremap:231072:65536) and asks the kernel to remap the container's entire UID/GID space into that unprivileged host range. Root inside becomes uid 231072 on the host — a kernel exploit that would normally hand over host root instead hands over an ordinary, powerless host account.

docker.sock is dangerous for an unrelated reason: it is a Unix domain socket owned by root, and the DAEMON listening on it runs as root by default. Anyone who can write to that socket is not calling a sandboxed API — they are handing arbitrary container specs (including --privileged, -v /:/host) to a root process that will execute them without question.

 WHY MOUNTING docker.sock = HANDING OVER HOST ROOT
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  container WITH docker.sock mounted                              │
 │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
 │  │ curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \                   │ │
 │  │   -d '{"Image":"alpine","HostConfig":{"Privileged":true,    │ │
 │  │        "Binds":["/:/host"]}}' http://localhost/containers/  │ │
 │  │   create                                                    │ │
 │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
 │                     │  daemon (ROOT) obeys — it cannot tell a    │
 │                     │  "friendly" caller from a hostile one      │
 │                     ▼                                            │
 │           a NEW privileged container with the WHOLE host         │
 │           filesystem bind-mounted at /host — game over           │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ userns-remap and "mount docker.sock into a container" are opposite instincts: one shrinks what root can do, the other hands root out to whoever asks nicely.

20.4 Image Signing & Content Trust

Docker Content Trust (DCT) uses Notary to sign and verify images, ensuring you're running exactly what the publisher intended:

TERMINAL
# Enable Content Trust
$ export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

# Pull only signed images
$ docker pull easypj:v1         # Fails if unsigned!

# Sign and push (requires signing key)
$ docker trust signer add --key cert.pem alice registry.example.com
$ docker trust sign registry.example.com/easypj:v1

# Verify image signature
$ docker trust inspect easypj:v1
💡 The Wax Seal Analogy

DCT is a wax seal on a letter: the recipient (pull) checks the seal is intact and yours before trusting the contents; a broken or missing seal means reject, do not open.

TERMINAL (sign + enforce for easypj)
$ export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
$ docker push easypj/web:v1.2.3     # prompts for signing key
$ docker trust inspect easypj/web:v1.2.3 --pretty
$ docker pull easypj/web:v1.2.3     # verifies before pulling
$ docker pull easypj/web:tampered   # ERROR: no valid trust data

On production hosts running with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1, a compromised registry serving a swapped easypj image is rejected at pull time instead of silently deployed.

20.5 Podman vs Docker — Rootless Containers

Podman is daemonless and rootless by default: containers run as your user via user namespaces, so "root" inside maps to your unprivileged UID outside — no root daemon, no socket to steal. Docker offers rootless mode too (dockerd as a non-root user). The CLIs are near-identical (alias docker=podman often just works).

AspectDockerPodman
ArchitectureClient-server (dockerd daemon)Daemonless (fork-exec model)
Root required?Daemon runs as rootRootless by default ✅
CLI compatibilitydocker runpodman run (alias docker=podman)
Compose supportdocker compose (built-in)podman-compose (separate)
KubernetesDocker Desktop K8spodman play kube (built-in)
Best forDevelopment, Docker ecosystemSecurity-focused, RHEL environments
Who Actually Launches the Container?
  DOCKER (root daemon mediates every container):
  ┌────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌────────────┐
  │ docker │──▶│ dockerd │──▶│ easypj web │
  │  CLI   │   │  (root) │   │   (root)   │
  └────────┘   └─────────┘   └────────────┘
        │ docker.sock = root-equiv access

  PODMAN (client forks the container itself, no daemon):
  ┌────────┐                        ┌─────────────────┐
  │ podman │──no-daemon,no-socket──▶│    easypj web   │
  │  CLI   │                        │ (you, not root) │
  └────────┘                        └─────────────────┘
Security DimensionDockerPodman
Daemonroot daemon (dockerd)none (fork/exec model)
Default userrootrootless
Socket riskdocker.sock = root-equivalent accessno daemon socket to steal
Systemd unitsgenerated via the daemonnative podman generate systemd
Composedocker compose (built-in)podman-compose / Quadlet
💡 The Valet Analogy

Docker's default is a valet (the root daemon) who parks everyone's car with the master key; rootless/Podman gives each driver their own limited key — no central master to hijack. Under the hood, rootless (Podman or Docker) leans on Linux user namespaces plus newuidmap/newgidmap to remap container UID 0 to your real UID, and slirp4netns/pasta for networking — a rootful daemon gets real bridges and raw sockets that rootless simply cannot.

⚠️ Rootless Isn't Always Drop-In

Rootless containers cannot bind ports below 1024 without extra configuration, and some volume/network features differ — test easypj under rootless before assuming drop-in parity.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The hardening checklist is ordered by payoff: pin the base image, de-root, de-cap, freeze the filesystem, scan, limit resources, add health checks, sign, and keep the Engine patched.
  • ENV vars leak — they show in docker inspect, /proc/1/environ, and child processes; secrets belong in mounted files (or Vault/Secrets Manager), never ENV or a Dockerfile layer.
  • A secret ARG/ENV baked into an early build stage persists in that layer forever, even if a later stage unsets it — use --mount=type=secret build secrets instead.
  • docker.sock is root-equivalent — mounting it into any container hands that container the power to create a --privileged container with the host filesystem bind-mounted.
  • userns-remap, no-new-privileges, and icc: false are three daemon.json settings that shrink what a compromised container (or its root) can actually do.
  • Docker Content Trust (DCT) makes pull also mean "verify this tag was signed by us and untampered" — but it only protects tags you actually signed.
  • Rootless containers (Podman, or Docker's rootless mode) remove the root daemon and the root-equivalent socket entirely — a strictly smaller attack surface for CI and multi-tenant hosts.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Leaving the base image tag as :latest → Pin a specific tag — :latest silently changes between builds, shipping an unreviewed dependency upgrade on every deploy.
  • Believing a secret is gone because a later build stage deletes the file it was written to → Any ARG/ENV baked into an earlier stage's layer persists in image history forever — use --mount=type=secret build secrets instead.
  • Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container "just for convenience" (e.g. a CI job that needs Docker) → That mount is functionally --privileged for the WHOLE HOST — the single most dangerous flag in common CI use.
  • Assuming DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 makes an unsigned :latest tag safe to pull → DCT only protects tags you actually signed — an unsigned tag simply fails the pull, and losing the root signing key means you can never sign that repo again.
  • Assuming rootless Podman is a zero-friction, drop-in replacement for Docker → Rootless containers can't bind ports below 1024 without extra config, and some volume/network features differ — test easypj under it before assuming parity.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker inspect <container> | grep -i -A2 env right after any incident — the fastest way to see exactly what secrets an image or container exposed.
  • Grep your Dockerfiles for ENV.*(SECRET|PASSWORD|KEY|TOKEN) in CI — the fastest way to catch a baked-in secret before it ships.
  • docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}' shows userns-remap and seccomp status on a host in one line.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 20)

the Chapter 20 cheat-card 
docker inspect web --format '{{.Config.Env}}'   # what ENV actually ships
docker secret create db_password ./secret.txt   # Swarm: encrypted secret
docker service create --secret db_password ...  # mount it at runtime
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1                    # sign on push, verify on pull
docker trust inspect easypj/web:v1 --pretty      # who signed this tag
podman run --rm easypj:v1                        # rootless, no daemon
docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'      # userns-remap/seccomp status

🧠 Chapter 20 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the ordered checklist to rootless Podman — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
List the hardening checklist's first four items in priority order — why does pinning come before scanning?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Pin the base tag (not :latest), run non-root, --cap-drop ALL, then read-only rootfs + tmpfs.

EXPLANATION

Pinning comes first because you cannot meaningfully scan or reason about an image whose base silently changes underneath you between builds (20.1).

Q2
Why does docker inspect web leak SECRET_KEY if it's passed as an ENV var, and what replaces it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENV vars are stored in the container's config and shown verbatim by docker inspect and readable from /proc/1/environ. Replace with a mounted secret file (a Swarm secret, or a plain file volume) that Django reads at startup.

EXPLANATION

ENV SECRET_KEY=abc123 is visible in docker inspect in plain text; /run/secrets/secret_key shows only the file path — the value itself never appears in inspect output (20.2).

Q3
A Dockerfile runs ARG DB_PASSWORD then RUN echo $DB_PASSWORD > /tmp/x && rm /tmp/x in one layer, believing the secret is gone. Is it actually gone?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — the ARG value and everything the RUN step touched are baked into that layer's diff; deleting the file in the SAME layer removes it from the final filesystem view, but the value can still be extracted from layer history and the build cache.

EXPLANATION

Use --mount=type=secret build secrets instead, which never write the secret into a layer at all (20.2).

Q4
Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container functionally equivalent to giving it --privileged on the whole HOST, not just itself?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The socket is the daemon's API, and the daemon runs as root. A container with the socket can ask the daemon to create a NEW container with --privileged and -v /:/host, and the root daemon will comply.

EXPLANATION

The daemon cannot distinguish a friendly caller from a hostile one — any process that can write to the socket effectively controls the host (20.3).

Q5
Name three daemon.json keys that hardening changes and what each one does.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

userns-remap (remaps container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID), no-new-privileges (blocks privilege escalation via setuid binaries), and icc: false (disables default inter-container communication on the default bridge network).

EXPLANATION

Each shrinks a different slice of what a compromised container — or a compromised root process inside it — can actually do to the host (20.3).

Q6
What does Docker Content Trust actually verify on docker pull, and what happens if you pull a tag you never signed?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It verifies the image manifest was signed by a trusted key (via Notary) and matches what was pushed — untampered and authentic. Pulling an unsigned or tampered tag with DCT enabled FAILS with a trust-data error rather than silently pulling it.

EXPLANATION

This is the whole point of DCT: pull stops meaning "download whatever the registry currently serves" and starts meaning "download and cryptographically verify" (20.4).

Q7
Your team loses the Content Trust root signing key. What is the practical consequence for that repository?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

You can never sign new releases of that repository under the old key/trust data again.

EXPLANATION

It is not a "reset password" situation — this is why 20.4 treats the root key as something to protect as carefully as the docker.sock socket itself (20.4).

Q8
Compare Docker's default architecture to Podman's for ONE security property: what happens to "root inside the container" in each?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker (root daemon): root inside the container typically IS root outside unless userns-remap is enabled. Podman (rootless by default): root inside maps to YOUR unprivileged UID outside via user namespaces — there is no root daemon to escalate to.

EXPLANATION

DOCKER: CLI → dockerd (root) → easypj web (root). PODMAN: CLI → easypj web (you, not root) — no daemon in the chain at all (20.5).

Q9
Why does 20.3 call docker.sock "the crown jewel" rather than just another dangerous flag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Every other control in Chapters 19-20 — non-root, cap-drop, read-only, secrets — can be bypassed in one step if a container also holds the socket.

EXPLANATION

The socket is root-equivalent access that overrides everything else on the host; hardening every other surface still fails if the socket is exposed (20.3).

Q10
Put the ordered hardening checklist, secrets handling, daemon lockdown, signing, and rootless together — what is the ONE thing NONE of them prove, and which chapter does?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

None of Chapter 20's measures prove whether the hardening actually worked or whether new CVEs have appeared since the image was built.

EXPLANATION

That verification, scanning, and CIS scoring is Chapter 21's job — Chapter 20 builds the hardened stack, Chapter 21 measures it (20.1-20.5 → Ch21).

🔬 Practice Drill 20.1 — ENV vs Mounted Secret (15 min)

Take easypj's current DB_PASSWORD, passed today as an ENV var. In 15 minutes: (1) docker inspect | grep -i password and confirm it's visible in plain text. (2) Switch to a mounted secret file per 20.2's compose snippet. (3) Re-run inspect and confirm the value no longer appears — only the file path does.

In one line: Chapter 20 takes every primitive Chapter 19 named and turns it into things you actually DO to easypj: an ordered checklist you run on every deploy (20.1), secrets that live in mounted files instead of a leaky ENV var or a baked-in layer (20.2), a daemon whose root socket is guarded and whose config actively shrinks what a compromised root process can do (20.3), image signing that makes "pull" mean "verify" (20.4), and a rootless option that removes the root daemon altogether for the highest-risk hosts (20.5).

The takeaway: what none of this chapter can tell you is whether it actually worked — that measurement is Chapter 21.

Chapter 21 · Docker Security Scanning & Compliance

Hardening you cannot measure is faith, not security. This chapter is the instrumentation layer: scanning images for CVEs with Docker Scout and Trivy, auditing the host against the CIS Docker Benchmark with Docker Bench Security, generating an SBOM of everything you ship, and wiring all of it into CI — so you can prove, on every build, that easypj has no known critical vulnerabilities and follows the benchmark.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2h 🔍 Scanning 🎯 DCA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Run docker scout quickview/cves/recommendations/compare on easypj and act on each command's output (21.1)
  • ✅ Run Docker Bench Security against a host and map its PASS/WARN output back to a concrete daemon.json or run-flag fix (21.2)
  • ✅ Scan easypj with Trivy and wire --exit-code into a CI gate (21.3)
  • ✅ Generate an SBOM for easypj (SPDX or CycloneDX) and use it to answer "are we affected by CVE-X?" without a rebuild (21.4)
  • ✅ Explain what the CIS Docker Benchmark covers and which of its checks are image-level versus host-wide (21.5)
  • ✅ Explain why a clean scan is a point-in-time result and must be re-run on every build, not trusted forever

🎯 Security's Measurable Half

This chapter IS the measurable half of the Security domain (15%) — Docker Scout and vulnerability scanning are graded directly; it closes out Chapters 19-20's hardening with proof.

  • Why this chapter exists: hardening you cannot measure is faith, not security — this chapter is the instrumentation that proves it, on every build.
  • The load-bearing line: a clean scan is a POINT-IN-TIME result; new CVEs land daily, so re-scan on every build and on a schedule, not once.

21.1 Docker Scout Deep Dive

Docker Scout analyzes an image's SBOM against multiple CVE databases and turns "is my image safe?" into a measured, diffable number. quickview gives a severity summary, cves lists every finding, recommendations suggests concrete fixes (usually a base-image bump), and compare diffs two tags to prove a fix actually worked. It runs locally and in CI, and can fail a build against a policy.

💡 The Home Inspector Analogy

Docker Scout is a home inspector for your image: quickview is the one-page summary, cves is the full defect list, recommendations is "replace this old water heater," and compare is "before vs after the repairs."

🔍
quickview

The one-page severity summary — Critical/High/Medium/Low counts. Run this before every push.

📋
cves

The full defect list — every CVE found, filterable with --only-severity critical,high.

🛠️
recommendations

The fix — usually a specific base-image bump that clears the most CVEs at once.

⚖️
compare

The proof — diffs two tags to confirm a fix actually reduced the vulnerability count.

TERMINAL
# Quick vulnerability summary
$ docker scout quickview easypj:v1
  Critical 0  High 3  Medium 12  Low 20

# Detailed CVE report with severity
$ docker scout cves easypj:v1
$ docker scout cves easypj:v1 --only-severity critical,high

# Get fix recommendations
$ docker scout recommendations easypj:v1
  → Update base image python:3.11-slim (fixes 12 CVEs)
  → Update package libssl3 (fixes CVE-2024-xxx)

# Compare two images
$ docker scout compare easypj:v1 easypj:v2
$ docker scout compare easypj:v1 --to easypj:v2

# CI/CD integration (GitHub Actions)
- uses: docker/scout-action@v1
  with:
    image: easypj:${{ github.sha }}
🔬 easypj in Practice

quickview flags 3 highs from an old base image; recommendations says bump python:3.12-slim to its latest patch, which docker scout compare then confirms cleared them — the whole find → explain → fix → prove loop in one image.

⚠️ A Clean Scan Is a Point-in-Time Result

New CVEs land daily. A clean docker scout quickview on Monday is not a guarantee of a clean scan on Friday — re-scan on every build and on a schedule, not once.

21.2 Docker Bench Security

Docker Bench Security runs automated checks against the CIS Docker Benchmark — the industry standard for Docker security configuration. It is shipped as a container that checks host config, daemon.json, image, and runtime settings, emitting [PASS]/[WARN]/[INFO] per check. Because it reads real host paths, it needs several host mounts plus --pid host --net host to inspect the actual daemon — not the sandboxed view a normal container gets.

💡 The Code-Compliance Inspector Analogy

Docker Bench Security is a code-compliance inspector walking your building with the official checklist, ticking each rule PASS or WARN — the CIS Benchmark is the building code, and the bench script is the inspector applying it.

Docker Bench Security — Auditing the Host
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOST                                                          │
  │  /var/lib   /etc   docker.sock   --pid host   --net host       │
  │       │       │         │             │             │          │
  │       └───────┴─────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘          │
  │                          │                                      │
  │                          ▼                                      │
  │            docker/docker-bench-security (container)             │
  │                          │                                      │
  │                          ▼                                      │
  │          CIS Docker Benchmark checks, one by one                │
  │             [PASS] / [WARN] / [INFO]  per check                 │
  │                          │                                      │
  │                          ▼                                      │
  │            Score: 23 PASS, 5 WARN, 0 FAIL                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TERMINAL
$ docker run --rm --pid host --net host --cap-add audit_control \
    -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -v /etc:/etc docker/docker-bench-security

[INFO] 1 - Host Configuration
[PASS] 1.1.1 Ensure a separate partition for containers
[WARN] 1.1.2 Ensure only trusted users control Docker daemon
[PASS] 1.2.1 Ensure auditing is configured for Docker files

[INFO] 2 - Docker Daemon Configuration
[WARN] 2.1 Restrict network traffic between containers (icc)
[WARN] 2.5 Ensure aufs storage driver is not used
[PASS] 2.11 Ensure authorization for Docker client commands

Score: 23 PASS, 5 WARN, 0 FAIL
🔬 easypj in Practice

The bench WARNs that icc (inter-container communication) is enabled — feeding the exact daemon.json fix ("icc": false) already recommended in Chapter 20.3, now surfaced as a measured finding instead of a suggestion.

⚠️ Treat It as a One-Off Audit Tool

Docker Bench itself needs docker.sock and host mounts to run — the same root-equivalent access pattern Chapter 20 warns about. Run it as a trusted, one-off audit, not a long-lived container, and remove it after.

21.3 Trivy — Open Source Vulnerability Scanner

Trivy (Aqua Security) scans images, filesystems, and infrastructure-as-code for CVEs and misconfigurations. trivy image reports OS and language-package vulnerabilities; trivy fs scans a source tree before it is ever built; --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH fails a CI job on serious findings.

💡 The Free Metal Detector Analogy

Trivy is a free, open-source metal detector you can run anywhere — on the finished image, on the raw source, or wired to the CI gate — no vendor account required.

Trivy as a CI Gate
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  docker build ──▶ trivy image --exit-code 1                      │
  │                    --severity CRITICAL,HIGH easypj:v1             │
  │                          │                                        │
  │              ┌───────────┴────────────┐                           │
  │              ▼                        ▼                           │
  │        exit 0 (clean)         exit 1 (High/Critical found)        │
  │              │                        │                           │
  │              ▼                        ▼                           │
  │      pipeline continues        pipeline FAILS — image never ships │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TERMINAL
# Scan a Docker image
$ trivy image easypj:v1
  Total: 15 (HIGH: 3, CRITICAL: 0)

# Scan filesystem (Dockerfile, configs)
$ trivy fs /path/to/project
$ trivy fs --scanners vuln,misconfig .

# Scan with severity filter
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL easypj:v1

# CI-friendly output (exit 1 if vulns found)
$ trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL easypj:v1
🔬 easypj in Practice

The same 3 highs Scout found in 21.1 appear in Trivy with fix versions; CI runs trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL so a critical CVE hard-fails the easypj pipeline.

⚠️ The Vulnerability DB Is Cached Locally

Trivy caches its vuln DB; in air-gapped or CI runs, update or mount the DB explicitly, or you scan against a stale database and miss fresh CVEs.

21.4 SBOM — Software Bill of Materials

An SBOM is a complete inventory of every component in your image — like a nutrition label for containers. It is a machine-readable list of every component and exact version shipped; feed it to Grype to match against CVEs, and when the next Log4j-style bug drops, you grep the SBOM instead of rebuilding and rescanning everything.

💡 The Ingredients Label Analogy

An SBOM is the ingredients label on the package: when a recall hits "batch of ingredient X," you read labels to find affected products — you do not re-cook every meal to check.

TERMINAL
# Generate SBOM with Docker
$ docker sbom easypj:v1
NAME                VERSION        TYPE
Django              5.2.0          python
gunicorn            21.2.0         python
psycopg2            2.9.9          python
Pillow              10.3.0         python

# Export in different formats
$ docker sbom --format spdx-json easypj:v1 > sbom.json
$ docker sbom --format cyclonedx easypj:v1 > sbom.xml
$ docker sbom easypj:v1 -o spdx-json > easypj.sbom.json

# Alternative: Syft (Anchore)
$ syft easypj:v1 -o spdx-json
$ syft easypj:v1 -o cyclonedx-json > easypj.cdx.json

# Match the SBOM against CVEs with Grype — no rebuild needed
$ grype sbom:easypj.sbom.json
$ grep -i "django" easypj.sbom.json    # which version do we ship?
DimensionSPDXCycloneDX
StewardLinux Foundation (ISO 5962)OWASP Foundation
Born fromLicense / provenance trackingAppSec / CVE tracking
Toolingsyft -o spdx-jsonsyft -o cyclonedx-json
easypj useLicense audit of dependenciesFeeds Grype's CVE match
💡 One Nuance the Terminal Doesn't Show

CycloneDX has native VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) support, letting you attach "CVE-X is present but NOT exploitable here" statements that Grype can honor — SPDX only gained comparable VEX linkage in its 3.0 spec.

🔬 easypj in Practice

The SBOM lists Django 5.x, psycopg, gunicorn and every OS lib with exact versions; a new psycopg CVE is answered by grepping the file — no rebuild required. The versions match pip freeze inside the container.

⚠️ An SBOM Is a Snapshot of One Build

Regenerate it per image tag, and store it as a build artifact — a stale SBOM answers the wrong version's question.

🔧 Under the Hood — how a scanner turns image layers into a CVE list

Scout, Trivy, and Grype all do fundamentally the same three-step job (21.1, 21.3, 21.4), even though their UIs differ:

  • INVENTORY — unpack every image layer and read each package manager's own metadata: dpkg's /var/lib/dpkg/status, apt's equivalents, Python's installed-package metadata (the same data pip freeze reads), any lockfile present. This list of {name, version, ecosystem} tuples IS the SBOM (21.4) — scanning and SBOM generation are the same first step.
  • IDENTIFY — each package is turned into a standard identifier: a CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) or a PURL (Package URL, e.g. pkg:pypi/django@5.2.5) — because CVE databases (NVD, OSV, distro security trackers) are indexed by these, not by free-text names.
  • MATCH — the identifiers are looked up against a downloaded CVE feed. A hit means "this exact version range is listed against this CVE"; the severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) comes from the feed's CVSS score, not from the scanner itself.
 easypj:v1 layers  ──▶ dpkg/pip package metadata (= the SBOM)
      │
      ▼
 pkg:pypi/django@5.2.5, pkg:deb/openssl@3.0.2...
      │
      ▼
 match against CVE feed (NVD/OSV/distro trackers)
      │
      ▼
 Critical 0  High 3  Medium 12  Low 20  (21.1's output)
🔑 This is WHY an SBOM answers "are we affected by CVE-X" without a rebuild (21.4): the inventory step already happened, so a new CVE just needs a MATCH against data you already have, not a new scan.

21.5 CIS Docker Benchmark Overview

The CIS Docker Benchmark is a consensus security-configuration standard grouped into sections: host configuration, Docker daemon configuration, daemon files/permissions, container images, container runtime, and operations. Docker Bench Security automates most checks — the benchmark is the WHAT, the bench script is the HOW-to-measure.

💡 The Building Code Analogy

CIS is the published building code; Docker Bench is the inspector who walks the site with that code in hand. You can read the code yourself, but the inspector makes it a checklist.

CategoryChecksExamples
Host ConfigurationSeparate partition, trusted users, auditingEnsure /var/lib/docker is on separate partition
Docker DaemonNetwork rules, logging, authorizationEnsure swarm mode is not used unless needed
Container ImagesTrusted base images, scanning, minimalUse specific tags, not :latest
Container RuntimeNon-root, read-only, resource limitsContainers should not run as root
Swarm ConfigurationSecrets, encryption, manager nodesEncrypt data exchanged between nodes
CIS SectionExample CheckLevel
Host configAudit the docker daemon & its filesHost-wide
Daemon configicc=false, no-new-privileges, live-restoreHost-wide
ImagesNon-root USER, no secrets in layersImage-level
Runtime--cap-drop, --read-only, --memory limitsImage / runtime-level
🔬 easypj in Practice

Nearly every easypj control so far — non-root, cap-drop, read-only, memory limits, hardened daemon.json — is a specific CIS line item; the benchmark is a rollup of Chapters 19-21.

⚠️ CIS Is Guidance, Not Law

Some checks (e.g. auditd rules, AppArmor) are host-wide and cannot be satisfied from a Dockerfile alone — hardening spans the host, not just the image.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Docker Scout gives quickview (triage), cves (the full list), recommendations (the fix), and compare (before vs after) — one tool covering the whole find-explain-fix loop (21.1).
  • Docker Bench Security automates the CIS Docker Benchmark into a PASS/WARN/INFO report — CIS is the standard, Bench is the meter (21.2, 21.5).
  • Trivy is a free, open-source, CI-friendly alternative to Scout — --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH makes it a real CI gate (21.3).
  • An SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) is the durable inventory of exactly what shipped — the fastest path from "is CVE-X in our stack?" to a yes/no answer, without a rebuild (21.4).
  • Scanning and SBOM generation are the same first step: unpack layers, read package-manager metadata, identify packages by CPE/PURL, then match against a CVE feed.
  • A clean scan is a POINT-IN-TIME result — new CVEs land daily, so re-scan on every build and on a schedule, not once (21.1).
  • CIS is guidance, not law — some checks (auditd rules, AppArmor) are host-wide and cannot be satisfied from a Dockerfile alone; hardening spans the host, not just the image (21.5).
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Treating a clean scan as a permanent, one-time result → CVE databases update daily — yesterday's clean image can be today's critical finding, so re-scan on every build.
  • Running Docker Bench Security as a long-lived container → It needs docker.sock and host mounts to run — treat it as a trusted, one-off audit tool and remove it after.
  • Assuming Trivy's local vulnerability DB is always current → In air-gapped or CI runs, update or mount the DB explicitly, or you scan against a stale database and miss fresh CVEs.
  • Treating an SBOM as valid forever → An SBOM is a snapshot of ONE build — regenerate it per image tag and store it as a build artifact.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker scout quickview before every push — a 5-second severity summary beats finding out from an auditor.
  • trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 as your first CI security gate — free, fast, and scriptable.
  • Keep the last build's SBOM alongside the image tag — the next Log4j-style CVE is a grep, not a rebuild-and-rescan.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 21)

the Chapter 21 cheat-card 
docker scout quickview easypj:v1               # severity summary
docker scout cves easypj:v1 --only-severity critical,high
docker scout compare easypj:v1 --to easypj:v2   # before vs after
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH easypj:v1
docker sbom easypj:v1 -o spdx-json > easypj.sbom.json
grype sbom:easypj.sbom.json                     # CVEs from the SBOM
docker run --rm --net host --pid host --cap-add audit_control \
  -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /etc:/etc \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  docker/docker-bench-security                  # CIS host audit

🧠 Chapter 21 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From Scout's find-explain-fix-prove loop to why CIS is "guidance, not law" — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What do docker scout quickview, cves, recommendations, and compare each answer?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

quickview: how bad is it (severity counts). cves: exactly which CVEs. recommendations: what to change (e.g. a newer base tag). compare: did the fix actually help, tag vs tag.

EXPLANATION

Together the four subcommands form one continuous loop — triage, detail, fix, and verify — covering the entire find→explain→fix→prove cycle from a single tool (21.1).

Q2
Why is a clean docker scout quickview on Monday not a guarantee of a clean scan on Friday?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CVE databases are updated continuously as new vulnerabilities are disclosed; a scan is a snapshot against the feed at that moment, so the same unchanged image can score differently a few days later.

EXPLANATION

This is 21.1's closing gotcha and the reason "shift-left" scanning must be a recurring gate in CI, not a one-time check performed at release.

Q3
What is Docker Bench Security actually checking, and why does it need --pid host --net host plus several host mounts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It audits the HOST's Docker configuration (daemon.json, filesystem permissions, running containers) against the CIS Docker Benchmark, so it needs visibility into the real host process tree, network namespace, and files — those flags and mounts are what give it that visibility.

EXPLANATION

Without host-level access the bench script would only see its own isolated container, not the daemon it's supposed to audit (21.2).

Q4
A Docker Bench run reports [WARN] 2.1 - Restrict network traffic between containers (icc). What is the concrete fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Set "icc": false in daemon.json and restart the daemon.

EXPLANATION

This is the exact fix already covered in Chapter 20.3, now surfaced as a measured finding instead of a recommendation — Docker Bench turns hardening advice into a graded checklist item (21.2).

Q5
Compare Trivy and Docker Scout on ONE dimension: what do you need to use each, and why might a team run both?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Scout is bundled with the Docker CLI/Hub and needs no extra install; Trivy is standalone open source with no vendor account required.

EXPLANATION

Teams often run both because they draw from overlapping-but-not-identical CVE sources, catching more than either alone (21.1, 21.3).

Q6
What exit code does trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH easypj:v1 return when the image is clean versus when it has a High finding, and why does that matter for CI?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Exit 0 when clean, exit 1 when a High/Critical exists.

EXPLANATION

A non-zero exit is what lets a CI pipeline actually FAIL the build instead of just printing a warning nobody reads (21.3).

Q7
What is an SBOM, and how does it let you answer "are we affected by the newest CVE?" without touching the image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Software Bill of Materials — a machine-readable list of every component + exact version shipped.

EXPLANATION

Since the CVE matching step (see Under the Hood) just needs identifiers, you grep/feed the EXISTING SBOM against the new CVE instead of re-unpacking and re-scanning the image: new CVE announced → grep easypj.sbom.json → yes/no, instant (21.4).

Q8
Your team needs to attach a "CVE-X is present but not exploitable in our deployment" statement that a scanner can honor. Which SBOM format natively supports this, and what is the mechanism called?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CycloneDX, via native VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) support.

EXPLANATION

SPDX only gained comparable VEX linkage in its 3.0 spec — CycloneDX has had it natively for longer, which is why AppSec-focused pipelines often prefer it over SPDX for this specific use case (21.4).

Q9
List three CIS Docker Benchmark sections and one example check from each, and say which are image-level versus host-wide.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Host config → audit the daemon & its files (host-wide). Daemon config → icc=false, no-new-privileges (host-wide). Images → non-root USER, no secrets in layers (image-level).

EXPLANATION

The split matters operationally: image-level checks can be fixed in the Dockerfile, but host-wide checks require daemon.json or host configuration changes that no image rebuild can satisfy (21.5).

Q10
Why does 21.5 say CIS is "guidance, not law," and give one example of a check no Dockerfile change alone can satisfy?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Some CIS checks require host-level configuration (auditd rules, AppArmor profile loading) that no image build can set.

EXPLANATION

Hardening spans the host as well as the image, which is why Chapter 20's daemon.json work and Chapter 21's scanning are BOTH necessary, not either/or (21.5).

🔬 Practice Drill 21.1 — Scan, Bump, Prove (15 min)

Run docker scout quickview easypj:v1, note the High/Critical count, bump the base image one patch version, rebuild, and docker scout compare old vs new. Then generate an SBOM and grep -i django it to confirm the version matches pip freeze inside the container. Done when the comparison shows the high-severity count dropped and the SBOM's Django version matches the running container exactly.

In one line: Chapter 21 is Part 7's proof layer — Docker Scout and Trivy turn "is easypj's image safe?" into a diffable severity count (21.1, 21.3), Docker Bench turns "is the host configured safely?" into a PASS/WARN report against the CIS Benchmark (21.2, 21.5), and an SBOM turns "what exactly did we ship?" into a durable inventory that answers the next CVE without a rebuild (21.4).

The takeaway: none of it is a one-time check — re-scanning on every build is what keeps Chapters 19-20's hardening honest as new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

🔐 Part 7 · Recap · Complete

Docker Security — From Root-by-Default to Provably Hardened

You started this part with a container that ran as root, held every capability, filtered nothing, and wrote anywhere — the insecure default. Now you can apply the ten-layer security onion to any easypj container, harden the whole stack from Dockerfile to daemon, and prove the hardening actually worked with a scan report and an SBOM instead of a guess.

🔑 Part 7 — Key Takeaways

  • A default container is root, fully capped, unfiltered, and writable everywhere — because containers share the host kernel, a breakout is a host compromise, not just an app compromise (Ch 19).
  • Defense-in-depth, not one switch: the 10-layer security onion (non-root, capabilities, seccomp/AppArmor, read-only rootfs, cgroups, network isolation, scanning, content trust, host/CIS hardening) means one failed layer still leaves nine (Ch 19).
  • USER app, --cap-drop ALL, seccomp/AppArmor, and --read-only + --tmpfs turn those layers into four concrete, one-command wins on easypj (Ch 19).
  • Chapter 19's primitives become an ordered whole-stack checklist — pin the base image, de-root, de-cap, freeze the filesystem, scan, limit, health-check, sign, patch — plus secrets in mounted files (never ENV), a guarded docker.sock, and a rootless option (Ch 20).
  • Hardening you can't measure is faith, not security: Docker Scout/Trivy scan images for CVEs, Docker Bench Security audits the host against the CIS Benchmark, and an SBOM is a durable inventory that answers the next CVE without a rebuild (Ch 21).
  • 🎯 Exam: Security is 15% of the DCA blueprint — non-root users, capabilities, and docker.sock exposure are examined directly.
  • 🔑 docker inspect --format · docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs · docker scout quickview · trivy image --exit-code 1 · docker-bench-security

                    │
                    ▼
   🧅 THE ONION, APPLIED    👤 non-root → 🎯 cap-drop ALL → 🚫 seccomp/AppArmor → 📖 read-only+tmpfs
                    │                                                          (Ch 19: 4 layers made real)
                    ▼
   📋 THE STACK, HARDENED   pin image → secrets in files → docker.sock guarded →
                             userns-remap/no-new-privileges → ✍️ DCT signing → 🚫 rootless option
                    │                                                        (Ch 20: whole-stack checklist)
                    ▼
   🔍 PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED    🩺 Scout/Trivy scan (CVEs) → Docker Bench (CIS PASS/WARN) → 📋 SBOM (inventory)
                    │                                                                   (Ch 21: measure it)
                    ▼
   🔒 PRODUCTION-GRADE easypj   unprivileged · capped · filtered · scanned · signed · re-checked every build
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   security isn't a flag you flip once — it's layers you apply, then prove, on every single deploy. 🔐

In words: Chapter 19 starts from the uncomfortable default: a container is root, holds every capability, runs unfiltered, and can write anywhere. The fix isn't one switch — it's ten independent layers (the "security onion"), four of which you made concrete on easypj: USER app for non-root, --cap-drop ALL for capabilities, seccomp/AppArmor for syscall and file confinement, and --read-only + --tmpfs for an immutable filesystem.

Chapter 20 turns those primitives into what you actually DO on every deploy: an ordered, whole-stack checklist (pin the base image, de-root, de-cap, freeze the filesystem, scan, limit resources, health-check, sign, patch), secrets that live in mounted files or a vault instead of a leaky ENV var, a daemon whose docker.sock is guarded and whose userns-remap / no-new-privileges / icc: false settings shrink what a compromised root process can do, Docker Content Trust so a pull also means "verify," and a rootless option that removes the root daemon entirely. Chapter 21 then answers the question none of that can answer on its own — did it work? — with Docker Scout and Trivy scanning images for CVEs, Docker Bench Security auditing the host against the CIS Benchmark as a PASS/WARN report, and an SBOM giving a durable inventory that answers the next CVE disclosure without a rebuild.

The one idea to keep: hardening is a set of independent layers you apply (Ch 19-20), not a single flag — and every one of those layers is a point-in-time claim that only stays true if you re-scan and re-audit on every build (Ch 21). Skip the proof step and Chapters 19-20 are faith, not security.

Chapter 22 · Docker in CI/CD Pipelines

CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) automates building, testing, and deploying your application. The "works on my machine" problem returns with a vengeance in CI — different runners, different tool versions, flaky tests — so this chapter makes Docker the constant: build, test, scan and push easypj inside containers on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, and Docker Build Cloud, so every stage runs in an identical environment.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3-3.5 hrs 🚀 CI/CD

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain why every stage of a CI/CD pipeline should run inside a container, and practice "build once, promote by tag"
  • ✅ Write a GitHub Actions workflow that logs in, tags, builds and pushes easypj using docker/login-action, docker/metadata-action and docker/build-push-action
  • ✅ Write a GitLab CI pipeline for easypj and justify a dind vs docker.sock choice for the build job
  • ✅ Write a Jenkins declarative pipeline that uses the Docker Pipeline plugin with credentials from Jenkins' store, never hardcoded in the Jenkinsfile
  • ✅ Decide when to offload easypj builds to Docker Build Cloud for a shared cache and multi-arch (amd64+arm64) speed
  • ✅ Choose a CI build strategy — dind, socket mount, or rootless kaniko/buildah — by weighing isolation against root-on-host risk
🎓 DCA Relevance
Image Creation, Management & Registry background
🎯 Not Graded Directly, But the Engine Behind Chapter 23

The DCA exam does not examine specific CI/CD platforms, so this chapter isn't a graded domain on its own — but it builds the production muscle that makes the graded Image Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%, Chapter 23) matter in the first place. You can't "promote by tag" an image you never learned to build inside a real pipeline.

  • Why this chapter exists: different CI runners, different tool versions, flaky tests — Docker makes every pipeline stage run in an identical container, eliminating "works on my machine" for good.
  • The load-bearing line: build once, promote by tag — bake the image ONE time, then run test/scan/push/deploy against that exact same artifact.

22.1 Why Docker in CI/CD?

Traditional CI/CD: "It builds on my machine but not on the CI server." With Docker, the CI runner uses the EXACT same image as production. Every step — build, test, scan, deploy — runs in an identical container environment:

Why Docker Belongs in CI/CD

Docker gives every pipeline a consistent build environment, kills "works on my machine" inside the CI runner itself, lets tests run in parallel inside isolated containers, and turns easy artifact management into a non-problem — the image itself IS the artifact.

🎯
The Goal

Explain why every stage in the pipeline diagram above — build, test, scan, push, deploy — runs inside a container. The image built in stage 2 IS the artifact that flows through the rest: the exact bytes tested are the exact bytes deployed, eliminating environment drift between CI and prod.

the artifact is the image
build  → easypj:ci-<sha>   # one immutable artifact
test   → run tests IN that image
scan   → Scout/Trivy that same image
push   → retag ci-<sha> → v1.2.3   # rebuild NOTHING
deploy → pull v1.2.3 to prod
