💡 The Factory Conveyor Analogy

A factory conveyor is the diagram above: the same part is stamped, inspected, and boxed at stations that never touch the part with bare hands — every station is a sealed, identical booth (container). ⚠️ Gotcha: rebuilding at the deploy stage — instead of retagging the already-tested image — reintroduces drift; you would ship an image nobody actually tested. Build once, promote by tag.

22.2 GitHub Actions + Docker

The official Docker GitHub Actions do the heavy lifting: docker/login-action authenticates to the registry, docker/metadata-action derives tags and labels from git refs, and docker/build-push-action builds (with buildx cache) and pushes. Secrets come from GitHub Actions secrets, never hardcoded:

.github/workflows/docker.yml
# name: Build and Push easypj

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Login to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Login to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Docker metadata — tags and labels from git refs
      - name: Docker metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          tags: |
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha,prefix=,format=short

      # Build and push, cached via GitHub Actions cache
      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
💡 Prebuilt LEGO Modules for the Pipeline

You snap login + metadata + build-push together instead of hand-writing docker CLI in shell — fewer sharp edges, tested by millions of workflows. A push to main builds easypj/web tagged with both the SHA and the branch, scans it, and pushes — with GHA layer caching so unchanged pip layers are never rebuilt.

⚠️ Secrets Belong in GitHub Actions Secrets, Never in the YAML

The workflow YAML lives in the repository, readable by anyone with repo access. GitHub Actions secrets are encrypted and injected only at run time — never displayed in logs or diffs. Registry creds MUST come from ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}, never typed directly into docker.yml.

22.3 GitLab CI + Docker

GitLab CI runs each job in a container. To build images you either run docker:dind as a privileged service (a full Docker daemon inside the job) or bind the host's docker.sock. dind is isolated but needs --privileged; the socket bind is lighter but gives the job root on the runner (see 22.6):

.gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - push

variables:
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

build:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind          # Docker-in-Docker
  script:
    - docker build -t $IMAGE .
    - docker save $IMAGE > image.tar
  artifacts:
    paths: [image.tar]

test:
  stage: test
  image: docker:latest
  services: [docker:dind]
  script:
    - docker load < image.tar
    - docker run --rm $IMAGE python manage.py test

push:
  stage: push
  image: docker:latest
  services: [docker:dind]
  script:
    - docker load < image.tar
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker push $IMAGE

easypj in practice: the GitLab pipeline builds easypj:ci-<sha> in a dind service, runs docker compose run tests, then pushes — all inside ephemeral job containers that vanish after the run.

💡 The Forge Analogy

dind is bringing your own portable forge to the job site — heavy, but yours. The socket bind is borrowing the landlord's master forge — convenient, until the job burns the building down.

⚠️ dind Needs --privileged

dind requires --privileged, which disables the seccomp/capability protections Part 7 spent a whole part establishing for that job. Isolate dind runners and never reuse them for untrusted code.

22.4 Jenkins + Docker

Jenkins runs stages on agents; the Docker Pipeline plugin adds docker.build(), .push(), and docker.image().inside {} to run steps inside a container. Agents need Docker access (a dind sidecar or a mounted socket) with the same trade-off as every other CI system:

Jenkinsfile
pipeline {
    agent any
    environment {
        IMAGE = "ghcr.io/org/easypj:${GIT_COMMIT.take(7)}"
    }
    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.build(IMAGE)
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.image(IMAGE).inside {
                        sh 'python manage.py test'
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Push') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.withRegistry('https://ghcr.io', 'github-token') {
                        docker.image(IMAGE).push()
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

easypj in practice: Jenkins builds easypj:ci-<commit>, runs the Django test suite via img.inside { sh 'python manage.py test' }, and pushes only if the stage is green.

💡 The Veteran Foreman Analogy

Jenkins is the veteran foreman with a huge plugin toolbox; the Docker Pipeline plugin is the attachment that lets the foreman hand each task to a sealed container crew.

⚠️ Credentials Live in Jenkins' Credential Store

docker.withRegistry credential IDs live in Jenkins' credential store, referenced by ID — never written into the pipeline script itself. The Jenkinsfile is typically versioned in the same repo as the app; a hardcoded password there leaks to everyone with repo read access.

22.5 Docker Build Cloud

Docker Build Cloud offloads builds to cloud infrastructure — faster builds, shared cache across your team, and no drain on your local machine:

TERMINAL
# Create a cloud builder
$ docker buildx create --name cloud-builder --use --driver cloud org/builder-name

# Build in the cloud — same syntax!
$ docker buildx build --builder cloud-builder -t easypj:v1 --push .

# Benefits:
# - Builds run on cloud VMs (faster CPUs, more RAM)
# - Cache shared across your entire team
# - Local machine stays free for coding
TERMINAL — multi-arch
# Register a cloud builder for easypj
$ docker buildx create --driver cloud easypj/builder

# amd64 + arm64 in one command, built remotely and in parallel
$ docker buildx build --builder cloud-easypj-builder \
    --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -t easypj/web:v1 --push .

easypj in practice: the slow pip-install layer, cached in Build Cloud from the last run, is reused so a one-line code change rebuilds easypj in seconds instead of minutes — on CI runners that stay small.

💡 The Shared Industrial Kitchen Analogy

A shared industrial kitchen instead of everyone cooking on a camping stove: bigger burners, and the prep one cook did (cache) is ready for the next — nobody re-chops the same onions.

⚠️ The Build Context Uploads Too

The build CONTEXT is uploaded to the cloud — a fat context (node_modules, .git, media) is slow and may leak files. Tighten .dockerignore before pointing builds at the cloud.

22.6 dind vs Socket Mount — Choosing a CI Build Strategy

Building images in CI needs a Docker engine SOMEWHERE — there are three ways to get one. docker:dind --privileged gives an isolated daemon, but privileged is risky. -v /var/run/docker.sock:... is light, but hands the job ROOT on the runner host. Rootless builders (kaniko, buildah) need no daemon and no privilege at all. Choose by trust level of the code and the runner's blast radius:

StrategyIsolationHost riskNeeds
docker:dindhighprivileged job--privileged service
socket mountlowROOT on runnerdocker.sock bind
kaniko/buildahhighnone (rootless)no daemon
💡 The 3D Printer Analogy

dind is your own locked workshop trucked in — heavy, self-contained. Socket mount is a key to the landlord's workshop — convenient, but they can burn the block. kaniko/buildah is a portable 3D printer that needs no workshop at all.

easypj in practice: on a shared runner, easypj images are built with kaniko — no daemon, no privilege, no socket — so a poisoned dependency in a build cannot escalate to the runner host or other tenants.

🔧 Under the Hood — why a docker.sock mount is equivalent to root

The docker CLI is a thin client: every command, including docker build, is just an HTTP request sent over a Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) to the dockerd API. There is no extra authorization layer on top of the socket — the ability to WRITE to that socket file IS the authorization. Whoever can talk to it can ask dockerd to do anything the engine can do, including starting a --privileged container that bind-mounts the host's / and chroots into it. That is also why membership in the local docker group has always been documented as root-equivalent, and why this section calls a CI socket mount "ROOT on the runner," not just "convenient."

 CI job container
   │  docker build ...   (an HTTP-over-Unix-socket API call — no more)
   ▼
 /var/run/docker.sock  — no auth beyond "can this process write here?"
   │
   ▼
 dockerd  (runs as root on the HOST, not in any job's container)
   │  can start --privileged containers, mount host paths, etc.
   ▼
 HOST KERNEL — anything dockerd can do, the CI job can now request.
🔑 Writing to docker.sock is dockerd's ONLY authorization check, and dockerd runs as root on the host — that's exactly why a CI socket mount is "ROOT on the runner," not merely "convenient." A "just this once" docker.sock mount tends to survive into production runners — treat it as a permanent decision, not a temporary hack.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Build once, promote by tag: bake the image ONE time, then run test/scan/push/deploy against that exact same artifact.
  • GitHub Actions: login-action + metadata-action + build-push-action = authenticate, derive tags, build (cached) and push.
  • GitLab CI jobs are themselves containers; get Docker access via dind (isolated, privileged) or a docker.sock bind (light, risky).
  • Jenkins' Docker Pipeline plugin (docker.build(), .push()) reads registry creds from Jenkins' credential store, never from the Jenkinsfile text.
  • Docker Build Cloud gives a team a shared, persistent build cache and painless multi-arch builds without bigger local machines.
  • Three CI build strategies trade isolation for convenience: dind (privileged), socket mount (root on host), kaniko/buildah (rootless, no daemon).
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: not a graded topic itself, but Image Creation & Registry (20%) assumes you can reliably produce the images it tests you on — this chapter is how that production actually runs.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Using :latest in CI/CD pipelines → Never use :latest in pipelines. Tag with the commit SHA or semver for traceability.
  • Skipping the vulnerability scan before push → Always scan BEFORE pushing to the registry. Block the pipeline on critical CVEs.
  • Rebuilding the image at the deploy stage → Retag the already-tested image instead. Rebuilding silently reintroduces environment drift — you'd ship bytes nobody tested.
  • Hardcoding registry passwords in workflow YAML or a Jenkinsfile → Use secrets (GitHub Actions secrets, Jenkins' credential store) — plaintext creds in pipeline-as-code leak to anyone with repo read access.
  • Assuming docker:dind is fully safe because it's "isolated" → dind still needs --privileged, which disables Part 7's seccomp/capability protections — isolate dind runners from untrusted code.
  • Skipping .dockerignore before using Docker Build Cloud → Tighten .dockerignore first — the whole build context uploads to the cloud, which is slow and can leak files.
  • Treating a docker.sock mount as a temporary CI hack → Treat it as a permanent decision — "just this once" socket mounts tend to survive into production runners, handing every pipeline root on the host.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Cache dependency layers with cache-from/to: type=gha (GitHub Actions) or Build Cloud's shared cache instead of reinstalling pip packages on every run.
  • Prefer docker buildx build --builder cloud-... for multi-arch images over emulated (QEMU) builds — remote native builders are dramatically faster.
  • docker scout quickview IMAGE && docker push IMAGE — one-liner scan-then-push gate before anything reaches the registry.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 22)

docker build -t easypj:ci-$SHA .                        # tag by git SHA
docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:ci-$SHA        # confirm Image ID
docker buildx create --driver cloud ORG/BUILDER         # register cloud builder
docker buildx build --builder cloud-ORG-BUILDER \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v1 --push .
docker push easypj:ci-$SHA                               # push the tested image
# GitLab dind service:   services: [ docker:27-dind ]
# Jenkins build+push:    docker.build("easypj:ci-${env.GIT_COMMIT}")

🧠 Chapter 22 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the pipeline diagram's "why a container per stage" to picking a CI build strategy by blast radius — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In the 22.1 pipeline diagram, why does EVERY stage (build, test, scan, push, deploy, smoke, monitor, rollback) run in a Docker container instead of directly on the runner?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

So every stage executes in an IDENTICAL environment, and so the image built in stage 2 is the same artifact tested, scanned, and deployed later — no "works in build, breaks in deploy" gap.

EXPLANATION

The diagram's own key line spells this out: "EVERY step runs in a Docker container → IDENTICAL environment." A bare-metal runner step would reintroduce the "works on my machine" problem this chapter exists to kill.

Q2
What does "build once, promote by tag" mean, and what breaks it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Build the image exactly once (e.g. easypj:ci-<sha>), then reuse that SAME image for test, scan, and every deploy target by adding/moving tags — never running docker build again to move it forward. Rebuilding at any later stage breaks it.

EXPLANATION

A second build can pull a different base-image digest or dependency version even from an unchanged Dockerfile, producing bytes nobody actually tested. Chapter 23 restates this as "promote by retagging the tested digest, never rebuild."

Q3
Match each GitHub Action to its job in the easypj workflow.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
ActionJob
docker/login-action@v3authenticate to the registry
docker/metadata-action@v5derive tags + labels from git refs
docker/build-push-action@v5build (with buildx cache) + push
EXPLANATION

These are official, widely-used actions that replace hand-rolled docker login/build/push shell steps with tested, declarative YAML — fewer places for a typo to leak a credential or mistag an image.

Q4
Why must the registry username/password in 22.2's workflow come from ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }} / secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN rather than being typed directly into docker.yml?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because the workflow YAML lives in the repository, readable by anyone with repo access; GitHub Actions secrets are encrypted and injected only at run time, never displayed in logs or diffs.

EXPLANATION

This is the same discipline 22.4 requires for Jenkins credentials — plaintext creds in pipeline-as-code is one of the most common real-world leak vectors.

Q5
Compare dind and docker.sock-mount as GitLab CI build strategies, and say which one 22.6 recommends for a shared runner.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
StrategyIsolationHost riskNeeds
dindhighprivileged job--privileged service
socket mountlowROOT on runnerdocker.sock bind

Recommended for a shared/multi-tenant runner: neither — use a rootless builder (kaniko/buildah, per 22.6).

EXPLANATION

dind isolates but disables Part 7's protections via --privileged; the socket mount is faster to set up but hands the job root on the host — acceptable only on trusted, single-tenant runners.

Q6
In the Jenkins pipeline from 22.4, where do registry credentials come from, and why not a plaintext password in the Jenkinsfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

From Jenkins' own credential store, referenced by ID (e.g. docker.withRegistry('', 'registry-creds')) — never written into the pipeline script itself.

EXPLANATION

The Jenkinsfile is typically versioned in the same repo as the app; a hardcoded password there is readable by anyone with repo access, exactly like the GitHub Actions case.

Q7
What two problems does Docker Build Cloud solve for a team building easypj, and what's the context-upload gotcha?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Slow local/CI builds — remote, beefier builders finish faster. (2) Duplicated work — a persistent, TEAM-SHARED cache means one teammate's cached layers speed up everyone's builds. Gotcha: the whole build CONTEXT uploads to the cloud, so a fat context (missing .dockerignore entries) is slow and can leak files.

EXPLANATION

22.5's pip-install-layer example shows this directly — a cached dependency layer from a prior run turns a one-line code change into a seconds-long rebuild instead of minutes.

Q8
List 22.6's three CI build strategies from HIGHEST to LOWEST isolation, and name the one true "no daemon, no privilege" option.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kaniko/buildah (rootless) and dind (privileged) both give high isolation; socket mount gives low isolation. Only kaniko/buildah need neither a daemon nor elevated privilege.

EXPLANATION

dind's isolation costs a privileged service; kaniko/buildah get similar or better isolation with NO daemon and NO privilege at all, which is why 22.6 calls them the rootless escape hatch for shared runners.

Q9
Using the Under-the-Hood diagram from 22.6, explain in one sentence why mounting docker.sock into a CI job is described as handing it "ROOT on the runner."
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because writing to docker.sock is the ONLY authorization check dockerd applies, and dockerd itself runs as root on the host — so any process that can reach the socket can ask the root daemon to do anything, including mounting the host filesystem.

EXPLANATION

This is exactly the mechanism 22.6's table summarizes as "socket mount | low isolation | ROOT on runner."

Q10
A shared runner builds untrusted third-party pull-request code for easypj. Which build strategy from 22.6 should it use, and why is dind not a safe enough answer here either?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kaniko or buildah — the only strategies that need neither a Docker daemon nor elevated privilege. dind still requires --privileged, which is a real host escape surface even though it is more isolated than a socket mount.

EXPLANATION

22.6's own guidance is to choose "by trust level of the code and the runner's blast radius" — untrusted PR code is exactly the case that justifies the rootless-but-slower option.

               │

In one line: Chapter 22 automates what Parts 1-7 did by hand: one docker build produces the ONE image that flows, untouched, through test, scan and deploy, on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins, optionally offloaded to Docker Build Cloud for speed and a shared cache.

The takeaway: every platform still has to answer the same underlying question — how does the CI job get Docker access, and at what cost — dind (isolated, but privileged), a docker.sock mount (fast, but root on the runner host), or a rootless builder like kaniko/buildah (neither)? That choice, not the YAML syntax, is the real decision this chapter teaches.

Chapter 23 · Docker Image Versioning & Promotion

A pile of images called :latest is an outage waiting to happen — you cannot say what is running or roll back to what worked. This chapter imposes discipline: deterministic tags, promotion by RETAGGING the tested image across environments, registry topology, and signing in the pipeline. The question it answers: "which exact easypj image is in production, and how do I promote or roll back without rebuilding?"

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5-3 hrs 🏷️ Versioning 🎯 DCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Choose between immutable tags (git SHA, semver, combined) and moving tags (:latest, branch names) for the right situation
  • ✅ Promote an easypj image dev → staging → production by RETAGGING one tested digest, never rebuilding
  • ✅ Design a registry topology for easypj (single vs split dev/prod, pull-through mirrors) with a retention policy that won't delete your emergency rollback tag
  • ✅ Sign easypj images in CI with Docker Content Trust and enforce signed-only pulls on deploy hosts
  • ✅ Answer "which exact image is running in production?" using tags plus digest comparison, not guesswork
🎓 DCA Relevance
Image Creation, Management & Registry 20%
🎯 Graded Material, Not Just Best Practice

Image tagging, versioning, and promotion appear by name under the Image Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%) in this guide's DCA domain map — study this chapter as exam content, not just best practice. Tagging and promotion are explicit exam topics, and the registry design here builds directly on the registries Chapters 2 and 7 already introduced.

  • Why this chapter exists: a pile of images called :latest is an outage waiting to happen — nobody can say what's running or roll back to what worked.
  • The load-bearing line: promotion means RETAGGING one tested digest across environments — the moment you rebuild to "promote," you've shipped an image nobody tested.

🧭 Section Map

23.1 tagging strategies → 23.2 promotion by retagging → 23.3 registry topology & retention → 23.4 signing with Docker Content Trust in CI — a straight line from "name the image" to "prove which name can be trusted."

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway
23.1 Image Tagging Strategies for CI/CDHow do I name an image so it's identifiable and reproducible?Immutable SHA/semver/combined tags for anything deployed; moving tags stay local.
23.2 Image Promotion Across EnvironmentsHow does an image move dev → staging → production?Retag the tested digest; never rebuild to promote.
23.3 Registry StrategiesWhere do images live, and for how long?Split dev/prod registries, mirror upstream, bound retention — exempt release tags.
23.4 Docker Content Trust in CI/CDHow do I prove an image came from the pipeline?Sign on push, enforce on pull — the pipeline becomes the only path to prod.

23.1 Image Tagging Strategies for CI/CD

Tags are pointers, not versions — pick a scheme that makes every easypj image identifiable and reproducible. The five schemes below cover the spectrum from CI-only traceability to human-readable releases:

StrategyExampleProsCons
Git commit SHAeasypj:abc1234Immutable, traceable to codeNot human-readable
Semantic versioneasypj:1.2.3Human-readable, follows semverManual process or CI automation needed
Branch-basedeasypj:main, :developSimple, automaticMutable — tag moves with each push
Environmenteasypj:staging, :productionClear intentMutable, not tied to specific version
Combinedeasypj:1.2.3-abc1234Best of both — version + traceabilityLongest tag name
🏆 Best Practice

Use multiple tags: easypj:1.2.3 (semver, mutable for this version), easypj:abc1234 (git SHA, immutable), easypj:production (what's currently in prod). The git SHA tag is your "fingerprint" — it uniquely identifies exactly which code produced this image.

Decision Diagram — Which Tag Scheme, When?
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ What is this build FOR?                                      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CI job / every commit   ──▶ easypj:ci-<sha>   (traceable)    │
  │ dev / feature branch    ──▶ easypj:main/:dev  (moving, ok)   │
  │ public release          ──▶ easypj:1.2.3      (semver)       │
  │ production deploy       ──▶ easypj:1.2.3-<sha> (both, exact) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Fingerprint vs. Nickname Analogy

A SHA tag is a fingerprint — unique, permanent, and useless to memorize. :latest is a nickname that points at whoever answers today — fine for a chat, useless for a subpoena. CI tags every build easypj:ci-<sha>; on release it's retagged easypj:1.2.3-<sha>, so production runs a tag that names both the human version AND the exact commit.

⚠️ CI Gotcha — Tags Can't Contain "/"

Docker tags cannot contain a / character — it's reserved for the repository path. A branch named feature/new-search cannot become easypj:feature/new-search; CI must sanitize it to easypj:feature-new-search before docker build -t, or the push fails.

Practice: build easypj and tag it three ways (SHA, semver, combined) pointing at the same image, then run docker images — you'll see three tags sharing ONE Image ID, proving tags are just labels on one artifact.

23.2 Image Promotion Across Environments

Never rebuild for different environments — promote the EXACT same image. The image that passed tests IS the artifact; promotion just adds an environment tag or registry reference to that SAME digest:

Image Promotion Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🏷️ IMAGE PROMOTION PIPELINE                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Build ONCE → Promote (retag) → Deploy everywhere:                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┐    retag    ┌──────────────┐    retag    ┌──────────┐ │
  │  │ easypj:abc123│───────────▶│ easypj:dev   │───────────▶│easypj:   │ │
  │  │ (immutable)  │    pass     │              │    pass    │ staging  │ │
  │  └──────────────┘    tests    └──────────────┘    scans   └────┬─────┘ │
  │                                                                │       │
  │                                                         retag  │       │
  │                                                                ▼       │
  │                                                         ┌──────────┐  │
  │                                                         │easypj:   │  │
  │                                                         │production│  │
  │                                                         └──────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 SAME image ID throughout — only the TAG changes!                     │
  │     docker tag easypj:abc1234 easypj:production                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Passport Analogy

A passport gets stamps at each border: same person (same digest) admitted to each country (environment) — you do not issue a brand-new person at every crossing. Gates (tests, scans, approvals) decide whether the passport gets the next stamp, but the bytes never change.

Promote by Digest
# build easypj@sha256:abc → test+scan (gate) → tag :staging
# → smoke (gate) → tag :production   [same digest throughout]

# in practice:
$ docker tag easypj@sha256:abc easypj:production
$ docker push easypj:production
$ docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:staging easypj:production
# both print the SAME Image ID — zero chance of a surprise rebuild
⚠️ The Classic Anti-Pattern

Running docker build at the promotion step is the classic anti-pattern — it silently produces a DIFFERENT image than the one you tested, even if the Dockerfile text didn't change (a base image could have updated, or a package resolver could pick different versions). Retag the digest; never rebuild to promote.

Practice: build once, promote by retagging staging → production, and compare Image IDs with docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' — staging and production tags should share one identical Image ID.

🔧 Under the Hood — tags are pointers, digests are identity

A Docker "tag" (easypj:1.2.3) is nothing but a human-readable label a registry maps to a content digest — a sha256 hash computed from the image's manifest (which itself references the config and every layer's digest). docker tag never copies bytes; it just writes a new pointer in the local image store, which is why 23.1's practice step shows THREE tags sharing ONE Image ID. Pushing multiple tags pushes the same layers once and updates multiple pointers in the registry. Because the digest is a hash OF the content, it cannot be forged to match different bytes — which is exactly the property 23.2's "promote by digest" and 23.4's signing both depend on.

 easypj:ci-abc1234    ─┐
 easypj:1.2.3-abc1234 ├──▶ sha256:9f8e7d... (ONE manifest, ONE set of layers)
 easypj:production    ─┘

 Retagging = adding/moving a pointer above.
 Rebuilding = a NEW digest, even if the Dockerfile text didn't change.
🔑 This is why comparing docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' across two tags is the real verification step — matching IDs prove no rebuild snuck into the promotion path, regardless of what the tag names say.

23.3 Registry Strategies

Organize registries for your deployment topology — findable, secure, and not infinite:

📦
Single Registry, Multiple Repos

One registry (ECR, GHCR) with repos per environment. Simpler to manage. Example: ecr/team/easypj-dev, ecr/team/easypj-prod.

🌐
Multi-Registry

Dev images on Docker Hub, production on ECR. Better separation of concerns. Staging registry can mirror production. Adds complexity.

easypj Registry Topology
  CI ──push──▶ dev registry (Docker Hub)
                    │ promote (retag, copy)
                    ▼
  prod pull ◀── private prod registry (ECR/GHCR)
  base images ◀── pull-through mirror (cache)
DimensionDocker HubECR / GHCRPull mirror
Costfree / paid tierpay-per-GBbandwidth only
Accessorg + publicIAM / SSOupstream's ACL
Retentionno auto-expirylifecycle ruleTTL / space cap
easypj roleCI pushes hereprod pulls onlycaches base images
📖 Why the Mirror Row Matters

Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls (100/6hr) and free authenticated accounts (200/6hr) — a CI fleet pulling python:3.12-slim on every easypj build can hit that ceiling fast. A pull-through mirror absorbs the repeats as one cached hit, cutting bandwidth and dodging the limit entirely.

⚠️ Retention Cuts Both Ways

No retention policy means a registry that grows without limit. But retention that's too aggressive can delete the exact old tag you need for an emergency rollback — always exempt release/rollback tags from cleanup rules.

Practice: configure a pull-through mirror and pull a base image twice — the second pull should be served from the mirror cache (faster, no upstream hit); confirm in the mirror's logs.

23.4 Docker Content Trust in CI/CD

Set DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 in the pipeline so the push step signs the tag; deployment hosts pull with DCT on and reject anything unsigned. Signing keys are injected as CI secrets (a delegation key, NOT the root key), and the root key stays offline:

CI/CD Sign + Verify
# In CI pipeline — after build, before deploy:
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_REPOSITORY_PASSPHRASE="$SIGNING_KEY_PASSPHRASE"

# Push with signing
docker push ghcr.io/org/easypj:$TAG   # Auto-signs with DCT enabled

# In deployment — before kubectl apply:
docker pull ghcr.io/org/easypj:$TAG   # Verifies signature, fails if unsigned!
💡 The Notary Analogy

The pipeline is a notary that stamps every release document; production refuses to act on any document without the notary's seal — and the notary's master stamp (the root key) lives in a vault, not the office. Only the CI pipeline holds the delegation signing key, so a developer pushing an unsigned easypj image by hand cannot get it deployed — prod's DCT-on pull rejects it.

Sign in CI, Verify on Deploy
# CI (push step)
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_REPOSITORY_PASSPHRASE=$CI_SIGN_KEY
docker push easypj/web:1.2.3        # signs on push

# deploy host
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
docker pull easypj/web:1.2.3        # refuses if unsigned/altered
🛑 Guard Signing Keys Like Production Creds

A leaked DELEGATION key lets an attacker sign malicious images that still pass Content Trust verification — but you can rotate a delegation key away. A leaked ROOT key compromises the entire trust chain permanently. Keep the root key offline and rotate delegation keys regularly.

Practice: sign a tag in a pipeline job, then push an unsigned tag manually and try to pull both with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 — the CI-signed tag should pull; the hand-pushed one should be refused.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Tags are named pointers; digests (sha256:...) are the actual content identity — many tags can share one digest.
  • :latest is not "the newest build," it is just wherever that tag was last pushed — possibly an old or broken image.
  • Promotion = retagging the ALREADY-tested digest across environments; running docker build at the promotion step is the anti-pattern this chapter warns against repeatedly.
  • Split dev/prod registries create a real security boundary; a pull-through mirror cuts bandwidth and dodges Docker Hub's anonymous/free pull-rate limits.
  • Retention policies must exempt release tags, or automated cleanup can delete the one image you need for a rollback.
  • Docker Content Trust signs on push and can block unsigned pulls on deploy hosts, making the CI pipeline the only path to prod.
  • 🎯 DCA relevance: this is graded material — the exam expects you to know tagging strategy and promotion, not just registry commands.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Tags are mutable, so they're fine for security or audit trails → Never rely on tags for security or audit. Use digests (sha256:...) for true immutability.
  • Semantic versioning in tags is optional → Always use semver (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for production image tags — it's what makes a release human-readable AND comparable.
  • A branch name can be used as-is for a Docker tag → Docker tags cannot contain a "/" — sanitize "feature/new-search" to "feature-new-search" before docker build -t, or the push fails.
  • Rebuilding an image counts as "promoting" it → Rebuilding silently produces a DIFFERENT image than the one that passed tests — retag the tested digest instead, never rebuild.
  • No registry retention policy is a safe default → No retention = unbounded registry growth; an overly aggressive one can delete the exact old tag an incident needs — exempt release tags either way.
  • A leaked CI signing key is a minor incident → A leaked delegation key lets an attacker sign malicious images that still pass Content Trust verification — guard it like a production credential and keep the root key offline.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' to compare two tags' Image IDs directly instead of trusting tag names alone.
  • Point CI's base-image pulls at a pull-through mirror to avoid Docker Hub's 100/6hr (anonymous) or 200/6hr (free auth) limits.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 23)

the Chapter 23 cheat-card 
docker tag easypj:ci-$SHA easypj:1.2.3-$SHA         # add a pointer, no rebuild
docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:1.2.3      # read the local Image ID
docker tag easypj@sha256:abc easypj:production       # promote by digest
DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker push easypj/web:1.2.3  # sign on push
DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull easypj/web:1.2.3  # refuse unsigned
docker images easypj                                  # all tags, one ID

🧠 Chapter 23 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From tag hygiene to signed promotion pipelines — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why is deploying production from :latest risky, per 23.1?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

:latest is just a default/moving tag, not a guarantee of "newest" — it points wherever it was last pushed, which could be an old or even broken build.

EXPLANATION

23.1's gotcha states this directly; moving tags are fine for local convenience but ambiguous for anything deployed.

Q2
Compare the five tagging schemes from 23.1.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
SchemeExampleBest for
git SHAeasypj:abc1234CI builds, exact traceability
semvereasypj:1.2.3public/human releases
brancheasypj:main / :developmoving, dev convenience only
environmenteasypj:staging / :productionclear intent, mutable pointer to what's deployed
combinedeasypj:1.2.3-abc1234production deploys (both)
EXPLANATION

Matches 23.1's table exactly — CI commits get SHA tags, releases get semver, environment tags mark what's currently deployed where, and prod gets combined so it is both human-readable and exactly traceable.

Q3
Walk through promoting an easypj image from staging to production WITHOUT rebuilding — what commands, what do you verify?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker tag easypj@sha256:<digest> easypj:production then push; verify with docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' that staging and production tags report the identical Image ID.

EXPLANATION

This is 23.2's core practice step — promotion moves a pointer, and the verification step proves no rebuild occurred.

Q4
Why does running docker build at the promotion step count as an anti-pattern rather than just "extra safety"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A fresh build can silently pull a different base-image digest or dependency version, producing an image that is NOT what passed tests/scans in the earlier stage — you would ship an image nobody tested.

EXPLANATION

23.2 calls this out explicitly: "docker build at the promotion step... silently produces a DIFFERENT image."

Q5
Compare single-registry and split dev/prod registry topologies for easypj.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
DimensionSingle registrySplit dev/prod
Setupsimplertwo registries to manage
Securityone trust boundarydev/prod separated
easypj usefine for small teamsCI pushes dev, prod pulls only from the private one
EXPLANATION

23.3 recommends splitting when a security boundary between "anyone can push here" (dev) and "only vetted images land here" (prod) matters.

Q6
What concrete problem does a pull-through mirror solve for a CI fleet that builds easypj constantly?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It caches upstream base images (e.g. python:3.12-slim) locally, so repeated pulls hit the mirror instead of the public registry — avoiding Docker Hub's 100/6hr (anon) or 200/6hr (free auth) rate limits and cutting bandwidth.

EXPLANATION

23.3's callout states this exact numeric limit and names it as the reason the mirror row matters for a CI fleet.

Q7
Why must a retention policy exempt release tags?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because automated cleanup that is too aggressive can delete the exact old tag you need to roll back to during an incident — retention should be bounded but release/rollback tags kept.

EXPLANATION

23.3's gotcha pairs both failure modes: no retention (unbounded growth) and over-aggressive retention (losing a needed rollback target) — the fix is exempting release tags.

Q8
What does setting DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 do differently on a push versus a pull?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

On push, it SIGNS the tag using the configured signing key. On pull, it REFUSES to pull anything unsigned or altered since it was signed.

EXPLANATION

23.4's CI/deploy-host code block shows exactly this split — sign in the CI push step, enforce on the deploy host's pull.

Q9
Why should the root Content Trust signing key stay offline while CI only holds a delegation key?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because CI secrets can leak; a leaked DELEGATION key only lets an attacker sign images (which you can rotate away), while a leaked ROOT key compromises the entire trust chain permanently.

EXPLANATION

23.4's gotcha: "guard signing keys like production creds... keep the ROOT key offline and rotate delegations."

Q10
CI tries to build a branch named feature/new-search as easypj:feature/new-search. What happens, and what's the fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The docker build -t / push fails because Docker tags cannot contain a "/" (it is reserved for the repository path). CI sanitizes the branch name first, e.g. to easypj:feature-new-search.

EXPLANATION

This is the CI gotcha called out directly under 23.1's tagging diagram.

📌 Chapter 23 Visual Summary — one digest, many pointers
  one digest ── tag:ci-<sha> ── tag:1.2.3-<sha> ── tag:production
                    (all three point at the SAME sha256 manifest)
  dev registry (CI pushes) ──promote(retag)──▶ prod registry (pulls only)
                                                    ▲
                                        signed on push (DCT) │ enforced
                                        on pull (DCT) — unsigned refused

In one line: Chapter 23 replaces "which image is live?" guesswork with discipline: tag deterministically (SHA for traceability, semver for releases, combined for prod), promote by retagging one tested digest through dev → staging → production instead of rebuilding at every hop, keep dev and prod registries separated with sane retention, and sign in CI so Docker Content Trust makes the pipeline the only route an image can take to production.

The takeaway: a tag is a label you can move; a digest is an identity you cannot fake — every mechanism in this chapter (promotion, retention, signing) exists to pin real deployments to the digest, not the label.

Chapter 24 · Container Testing Strategies

A green unit-test suite that never touched a real database or the actual image proves little about what you ship. Testing containers requires a layered approach — from fast unit tests inside a throwaway container, to integration tests against a real PostgreSQL, to full-stack end-to-end runs, to image-level checks that inspect the built artifact and the Dockerfile itself. This chapter closes the gap between "tests pass" and "the container still breaks in prod on a missing file, a bad env var, or a real database it never saw" — so the thing you deploy is the thing you actually tested.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5-3 hrs 🧪 Testing

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Place unit, integration, e2e, and image tests on the container testing pyramid and explain why the count shrinks as you climb
  • ✅ Run the easypj test suite inside a disposable container wired to real PostgreSQL with docker compose run --rm, gating CI on the exit code
  • ✅ Spin up a throwaway, version-matched PostgreSQL container per test run with Testcontainers instead of a shared test database
  • ✅ Write container-structure-test specs that assert facts about the BUILT image (files, command output, metadata like non-root USER)
  • ✅ Lint the easypj Dockerfile with Hadolint and fix its top warnings before they become production incidents
  • ✅ Recognize an "ice-cream cone" test shape (mostly slow e2e) as a CI-time smell and correct it
🎓 DCA Relevance
Image Creation, Management & Registry background
🎯 Not Graded Directly, But Proves the Shipped Image Actually Works

The DCA exam does not examine container testing methodology as its own topic — this chapter isn't a graded domain on its own — but Hadolint and container-structure-test operationalize the exact Dockerfile and image best practices the graded Image Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%) does test you on. A clean structure-test run and a clean Hadolint pass are the proof that Chapter 23's promoted digest is actually sound.

  • Why this chapter exists: a green test suite that never touched a real database or the actual built image proves little about what you ship — this chapter layers unit, integration, e2e, and image-level checks so the thing you deploy is the thing you tested.
  • The load-bearing line: image tests (structure tests + Hadolint) wrap every layer of the pyramid — they check the artifact itself, independent of whether the application tests ever ran.

🧭 Section Map

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway

24.1 Testing Pyramid for Containers

Bottom-up: many fast unit tests (Django view/model logic run inside a container), fewer integration tests (the app container plus a full real PostgreSQL), fewer still end-to-end tests (the whole Compose stack), and cross-cutting image tests (structure tests, vulnerability scans, linting) that wrap every layer. Higher up the pyramid means more realistic, slower, and fewer in number — that trade-off is deliberate, not a compromise.

Container Testing Pyramid
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🧪 CONTAINER TESTING PYRAMID                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │                          ┌─────┐                                         │
  │                          │ E2E │  ← docker compose full stack            │
  │                          │     │     Selenium/Cypress tests              │
  │                         ┌┴─────┴┐                                        │
  │                         │Integration│ ← docker compose run django test   │
  │                         │  Tests    │    Testcontainers (real DB)        │
  │                        ┌┴───────────┴┐                                   │
  │                        │     Unit      │ ← docker run pytest             │
  │                        │     Tests     │    Fast, isolated, many         │
  │                        └───────────────┘                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🖼️  IMAGE TESTS wrap ALL THREE layers above — structure tests +          │
  │      Hadolint check the artifact itself, whether app tests ran or not   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 More tests at bottom (faster, cheaper), fewer at top (slower, E2E)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏗️
App-Level Tests

Unit, integration, and e2e — "does the application behave correctly?" Run via pytest or the Django test runner, against increasingly real dependencies as you climb the pyramid.

📦
Image-Level Tests

Structure tests and Hadolint — "is the artifact itself sound?" Cross-cutting checks on the built image and Dockerfile, independent of whether the app's own tests ever ran.

easypj Container Tests — the Pyramid in Practice
              ╱────────────╲       e2e: full compose stack
             ╱  e2e (few)   ╲      (slow, most realistic)
            ╱────────────────╲
           ╱ integration: app ╲    + real PostgreSQL
          ╱────────────────────╲
         ╱  unit: views/models  ╲  (many, fast)
        └────────────────────────┘
     image tests (structure + scan + lint) wrap every layer

easypj runs hundreds of unit tests on JobPost/Skills logic, a dozen integration tests hitting real PostgreSQL, and a couple of e2e flows (post a job → search → apply) — all green before an image ships. Counting your own tests by layer is the fastest way to catch a pyramid inversion: the shape should be a pyramid (unit ≫ integration ≫ e2e), never an "ice-cream cone" (mostly slow e2e) — the cone is a CI-time smell.

💡 The Food-Safety Analogy

A food-safety program tastes each ingredient (unit), tastes the mixed dish (integration), serves a test table the full meal (e2e), and inspects the kitchen itself (image tests) — more effort as you climb, so you run fewer tests at the top.

⚠️ Postgres In, Sqlite Out

easypj uses PostgreSQL, so tests must run against a real Postgres test database — never sqlite. Sqlite would pass tests that break on Postgres-specific SQL and migrations, letting a whole class of bugs reach production undetected.

24.2 Testing with docker compose run

docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test starts a one-off container on the Compose network — so it can reach the postgres service exactly the way the running app would — runs the Django test command inside it, and removes the container afterward. The command's exit code IS the test result: 0 means pass, non-zero means fail, and CI checks that exit code to gate the build.

TERMINAL
# Run Django unit tests (creates a fresh container)
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test
Ran 214 tests in 12.4s — OK

# Run tests for specific Django app
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost

# Run with pytest
$ docker compose run --rm django pytest --cov=jobpost

# In CI: exit code determines pass/fail
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test --noinput
$ echo $?   # 0 = all passed, non-zero = CI fails the job

The test container connects to the Compose postgres service — a real PostgreSQL, not a mock — so migrations and Postgres-specific queries are exercised exactly as they will be in production.

💡 The Rental-Car Analogy

docker compose run is like renting a car for a single test drive: you get the exact same model (image) wired to the real roads (the postgres service), then hand it back (--rm) — no residue, repeatable every time.

⚠️ Ports Aren't Published, Deps Aren't Waited For

docker compose run does NOT publish the service's ports by default, and it starts its OWN dependency containers on demand. Without a depends_on (ideally with condition: service_healthy, Chapter 11), the test container can start before postgres is ready to accept connections — and the first test fails on a refused connection, not a real bug.

24.3 Testcontainers — Real Database in Tests

Testcontainers is a library that spins up REAL database/service containers for integration tests — programmatically, from your test code — instead of mocking PostgreSQL or sharing one long-lived test database. It starts a container before the tests run, hands the test process a live connection, and destroys the container afterward. Available for Python, Java, Node.js, Go, and more.

Python (Django + Testcontainers)
# conftest.py — Spin up real PostgreSQL for tests
import pytest
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def postgres_container():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:15-alpine") as postgres:
        yield postgres

# tests.py — Test against REAL PostgreSQL, not SQLite!
def test_create_jobpost(postgres_container):
    DATABASES['default'] = {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'HOST': postgres_container.get_container_host_ip(),
        'PORT': postgres_container.get_exposed_port(5432),
        'NAME': 'test',
        'USER': 'test',
        'PASSWORD': 'test',
    }
    # Now test with real PostgreSQL — catches DB-specific bugs!

CI runs the JobPost/User integration tests against a fresh postgres:15-alpine container that exactly matches the version easypj runs in production — catching Postgres-specific migration and query bugs early, with no shared, stateful test database for one run to pollute for the next.

💡 The Rehearsal-Stage Analogy

Each test crew gets a brand-new rehearsal stage built on demand and demolished after — no fighting over one shared stage that the last crew left a mess on.

⚠️ Testcontainers Needs a Docker Daemon

Testcontainers needs a Docker daemon reachable from the test process — in CI that means dind or a socket mount, with the exact same isolation-vs-host-risk trade-off discussed for build strategies in 22.6. Budget for container startup time too — it adds a few seconds to every test run.

🔧 Under the Hood — how Testcontainers actually cleans up after itself

Testcontainers talks to the same Docker API easypj's own tooling uses (via docker.sock or DOCKER_HOST) to start a real container — e.g. postgres:15-alpine — publishing its port to a RANDOM free host port so parallel CI runs never collide. It then applies a wait strategy (poll a port, or watch for a log line like "database system is ready") before handing the test code a connection URL. To guarantee cleanup even if the test process crashes mid-run, Testcontainers starts a small companion container (the "Ryuk" resource reaper) that watches for the test process's session to end and force-removes every container and network it created — so a crashed test run does not leave orphaned PostgreSQL containers behind.

 test process ──▶ Docker API ──▶ start postgres:15-alpine (random port)
      │                                    │
      │                              wait strategy (port/log-ready)
      ▼                                    ▼
 run Django migrations + tests ──▶ tear down (+ Ryuk reaper cleanup)
🔑 The Ryuk reaper is why Testcontainers is safe in CI even after a hard crash: it doesn't rely on your test code reaching a finally block — it watches the session from outside and force-removes everything if that session simply disappears.

24.4 Container Structure Tests

Google's Container Structure Test framework runs a YAML spec against a built image: command tests (run X, assert output/exit), file existence tests (path present), and metadata tests (USER, EXPOSE, CMD/ENTRYPOINT). It validates the IMAGE — independent of whether the application's own tests ever ran.

tests.yaml
schemaVersion: 2.0.0
metadataTest:
  exposedPorts: ["8000"]
  cmd: ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
  user: "app"               # Must NOT be root!

commandTests:
  - name: "Python version"
    command: "python"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python 3.11"]

  - name: "Django check"
    command: "python"
    args: ["manage.py", "check"]
    expectedOutput: ["System check identified no issues"]

fileExistenceTests:
  - name: "requirements installed"
    path: "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/django"
    shouldExist: true

# Run: container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1 --config tests.yaml

The structure test above asserts /app/manage.py-adjacent packages exist, Python is 3.11, and USER is "app" — catching a broken Dockerfile (missing COPY, wrong base image, forgotten USER) before the image is ever deployed. Metadata tests like this are essentially unit tests for your Docker image, and belong in CI right after the build step, before any functional testing runs.

CategoryExample assertionWhat it catches
File/app/manage.py existsMissing COPY / build context
Commandpython --version ~3.11.*Drifted base image
MetadataUSER app, EXPOSE 8000Forgotten USER / missing port
💡 The Fourth, Rarer Category

The framework actually ships a fourth kind — fileContentTests (regex match against a file's contents, e.g. confirming DEBUG=False survived into the built settings.py) — rarer than the three above, but the only one that proves a config VALUE, not just a file's existence.

⚠️ Structure Tests Check the Image AT REST

A passing structure test proves USER is SET to "app" — it does not prove the app actually WORKS correctly running as that user. Structure tests validate the image at rest, not running behavior; pair them with integration tests, don't substitute one for the other.

24.5 Dockerfile Linting

Hadolint parses a Dockerfile and applies best-practice rules (DLxxxx) plus embedded ShellCheck on RUN lines: pin apt package versions, avoid :latest, use --no-install-recommends, don't run as root, combine RUN layers, prefer COPY over ADD. It exits non-zero on findings, so it drops straight into CI as a fast pre-build gate.

TERMINAL
# Install Hadolint
$ brew install hadolint     # macOS
$ sudo apt install hadolint # Linux

# Lint your Dockerfile
$ hadolint Dockerfile
Dockerfile:1 DL3007 warning: Using latest is prone to errors
Dockerfile:5 DL3008 warning: Pin versions in apt-get install
Dockerfile:8 DL3002 warning: Last USER should not be root

# In CI/CD (GitHub Actions):
- uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
  with:
    dockerfile: Dockerfile

# CI gate — fail the build on warnings and above:
$ hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile

# Fix all warnings and errors before merging!

Hadolint flags an unpinned apt-get install libpq-dev and a missing USER in the easypj Dockerfile — the exact issues that cause non-reproducible builds and root containers discussed back in Part 7. Fixing the top warnings and re-running until the warning count drops to zero, with --failure-threshold warning exiting 0, is what a passing CI lint gate looks like.

💡 The Spell-Checker Analogy

Hadolint is a spell-checker for your Dockerfile: it will not run the build, but it underlines the sloppy phrasing (unpinned apt, stray ADD, root user) that turns into bugs and bloat later.

⚠️ Linting Is Static, Not a Build Guarantee

A clean Hadolint run does NOT mean the image builds or runs — it means the Dockerfile follows best practices. Keep build, structure, and integration tests alongside it; linting is the cheapest fix in the pipeline, not the only check.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer real-Postgres integration tests, a handful of e2e, plus cross-cutting image tests wrapping every layer.
  • easypj tests must run against real PostgreSQL, never sqlite — Postgres-specific SQL and migrations won't be caught otherwise.
  • docker compose run --rm gives disposable, network-connected test runs whose exit code is the CI gate.
  • compose run does NOT publish ports by default and starts its OWN deps — pair with depends_on or the first test hits a refused connection.
  • Testcontainers gives version-matched, disposable Postgres per test run, with automatic cleanup via the Ryuk reaper even on a crash.
  • container-structure-test validates the IMAGE at rest (files, commands, metadata) — not runtime behavior; pair with integration tests, don't substitute.
  • Hadolint is static analysis on the Dockerfile — a clean run does not prove the image builds or runs correctly.
  • Always test the EXACT image that will be deployed, never a locally rebuilt version — the artifact under test and the artifact you ship must be the same digest.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • An "ice-cream cone" test shape (mostly slow e2e, few unit tests) → Is a CI-time smell — invert it toward the pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, fewest e2e.
  • Assuming Testcontainers works without exposing the Docker daemon to the test process → It needs dind or a socket mount reachable from the test process — the same trust trade-off as 22.6.
  • Forgetting depends_on with compose run → Can fail the first test on a refused DB connection even though the service exists in the file.
  • Treating a passing structure test as proof the app works → It only proves USER is SET to "app," not that the app actually WORKS correctly running as that user.
  • Testing only on dev machines → Always test the EXACT image that will be deployed — not a rebuilt version with different layers.
  • Skipping Dockerfile linting as "just style" → Hadolint catches security issues, deprecated instructions, and best-practice violations before they cost you in prod.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Run hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile as a fast pre-build CI gate before spending minutes on a full image build.
  • Periodically count tests by layer (unit vs integration vs e2e) to catch a pyramid inversion before it slows down every CI run.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 24)

the Chapter 24 cheat-card 
docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test          # full suite, real Postgres
docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost   # just the jobpost app
echo $?                                                          # 0 pass / non-zero fail
container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1 --config tests.yaml
hadolint Dockerfile                                              # lint, non-zero on findings
hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile                  # CI gate on warnings+
docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/Dockerfile:/Dockerfile hadolint/hadolint Dockerfile   # hadolint, no local install
docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock gcr.io/gcp-runtimes/container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1 --config tests.yaml   # structure test via container

🧠 Chapter 24 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the testing pyramid to Hadolint's static-analysis limits — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Describe the container testing pyramid for easypj from 24.1 — what sits at each layer, and why does the count shrink going up?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

e2e (few) — full compose stack, slowest, most real. Integration (fewer) — app container + real PostgreSQL. Unit (many, fast) — Django views/models logic. Image tests (structure + scan + lint) wrap every layer. Higher layers cost more time and realism per test, so you deliberately run fewer of them.

EXPLANATION

Matches 24.1's pyramid diagram directly — hundreds of unit tests, a dozen integration tests, a couple of e2e flows.

Q2
Why must easypj's tests run against real PostgreSQL rather than sqlite?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Sqlite would pass tests that break on Postgres-specific SQL and migrations, since it doesn't share Postgres's SQL dialect or migration behavior.

EXPLANATION

24.1's gotcha states this exactly — easypj is PostgreSQL-only, so any test database must be Postgres too.

Q3
What does docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test actually do, step by step?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Starts a one-off django container on the Compose network (so it can reach the postgres service), runs the Django test command inside it, exits with the test result's exit code, then removes the container (--rm).

EXPLANATION

This is 24.2's mechanism verbatim — the exit code becomes the CI gate.

Q4
Why can the FIRST test fail with a refused connection even though postgres is defined in the compose file?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose run does not publish ports by default and starts its own dependency containers — if there's no depends_on/wait step, the test container can start before PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

EXPLANATION

24.2's gotcha calls this out directly as the reason to pair --rm with depends_on.

Q5
What problem does Testcontainers solve that a shared, long-lived test database does not?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It gives each test run its OWN fresh, version-matched PostgreSQL container, so tests can't pollute each other's data or drift from production's Postgres version.

EXPLANATION

24.3 frames this as "no shared, stateful test DB to pollute between runs," backed by the code example that spins up postgres:15-alpine per run.

Q6
What Docker-level requirement does Testcontainers have, and what's the trade-off it inherits from 22.6?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It needs a Docker daemon reachable from the test process — in CI that means dind or a socket mount, with the exact same isolation-vs-host-risk trade-off discussed in 22.6.

EXPLANATION

24.3's gotcha explicitly cross-references this: "the same trust trade-off as 22.6."

Q7
List container-structure-test's assertion categories with an easypj example of each.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
CategoryExample assertionCatches
File/app/manage.py existsMissing COPY / context
Commandpython --version ~3.11.*Drifted base image
MetadataUSER app, EXPOSE 8000Forgotten USER / port

Plus fileContentTests — regex on file contents, e.g. confirming DEBUG=False landed in settings.py — the only one that proves a config VALUE, not just a file's existence.

EXPLANATION

Matches 24.4's table plus its callout about the fourth, rarer fileContentTests category.

Q8
Why doesn't a passing container-structure-test guarantee the easypj app works correctly at runtime?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Structure tests check the image AT REST — files present, a command's output, metadata values — not actual running behavior; USER being "app" doesn't prove the app functions correctly running as that user.

EXPLANATION

24.4's gotcha: "pair them with integration tests, do not substitute."

Q9
What kind of issues does Hadolint flag on a Dockerfile, and why does it matter for easypj specifically?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Best-practice rules like unpinned apt/pip versions, use of :latest, missing --no-install-recommends, running as root, and stray ADD instead of COPY. For easypj it caught an unpinned apt-get install libpq-dev and a missing USER — the exact non-reproducible-build and root-container risks from Part 7.

EXPLANATION

Straight from 24.5's example output and its easypj callout.

Q10
Why is an "ice-cream cone" test distribution (mostly e2e, few unit tests) considered a smell, and what does it cost in CI?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

e2e tests are the slowest and least isolated layer; a cone inverts the pyramid so MOST of your test time is spent on the most expensive, flakiest layer instead of the cheapest one — CI runs take longer and fail for less specific reasons.

EXPLANATION

24.1's practice step frames the pyramid shape check directly as "the cone is a CI-time smell."

🔬 Practice Drill 24.1 — Fail On Purpose, Then Lock Down USER (12 min)

Add one deliberately failing Django test, run it via docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test, and confirm $? is non-zero. Then write one container-structure-test metadata rule asserting USER is non-root, and confirm it PASSES against the current image — then remove USER from the Dockerfile, rebuild, and watch it FAIL. Done when you've seen both a red app test and a red structure test on demand.

🚧 Practice Drills 24.2–24.5 — Coming Soon

Four additional practice drills for this chapter are planned for a future revision.

✅ Chapter 24 — Verify Your Knowledge
  • Can you place unit, integration, e2e, and image tests on the container testing pyramid and explain why the count shrinks as you climb?
  • Can you run the easypj suite in a disposable container against real PostgreSQL with docker compose run --rm, gating CI on the exit code?
  • Can you spin up a throwaway, version-matched PostgreSQL with Testcontainers instead of a shared test database?
  • Can you write container-structure-test specs asserting facts about the built image (files, command output, non-root USER)?
  • Can you lint the easypj Dockerfile with Hadolint and fix its top warnings?
  • Can you recognize an "ice-cream cone" test shape as a CI-time smell and correct it?
📌 Chapter 24 Visual Summary — the shipped digest is the tested digest
                 ╱────────────╲       e2e (few, slow, most realistic)
                ╱  integration  ╲     + real PostgreSQL
               ╱──────────────────╲
              ╱   unit (many, fast) ╲
             └────────────────────────┘
        image tests (structure + Hadolint) wrap every layer above
        compose run --rm (exit code) │ Testcontainers (disposable DB)

In one line: Chapter 24 makes sure the thing you ship is the thing you tested — a pyramid of many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against real PostgreSQL (via compose run --rm or Testcontainers' disposable, version-matched containers), a handful of full-stack e2e runs, and image-level checks — container-structure-test for the built image's shape, Hadolint for the Dockerfile's hygiene — that catch what application tests never see.

The takeaway: app-level tests prove the code behaves; image-level tests prove the artifact is sound — Chapter 23's promoted digest only deserves production traffic once both have passed.

🔴 Part 8 · Recap · Complete

CI/CD with Docker — What You Now Know

You started with hand-run docker build/push commands and a pile of images called :latest; now you can wire easypj into GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins with a safe build strategy, promote a single tested digest through dev → staging → production by retagging instead of rebuilding, and prove the shipped artifact actually works with a layered test pyramid plus image-level checks.

🔑 Part 8 — Key Takeaways

  • Build once, promote by tag: bake the easypj image ONE time on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins, then run test/scan/push/deploy against that exact same artifact — rebuilding at any later stage silently reintroduces drift (Ch 22).
  • Every platform faces the same build-access choice: dind (isolated, but privileged), a docker.sock mount (fast, but root on the runner host), or a rootless builder like kaniko/buildah (neither) — picked by the code's trust level, not convenience (Ch 22).
  • A tag is a movable pointer; a digest is the real identity. Promotion means RETAGGING one already-tested digest across environments — never rebuilding to "promote" (Ch 23).
  • Split dev/prod registries, bound retention that exempts release tags, and sign on push with Docker Content Trust so the pipeline becomes the only route an image can take to production (Ch 23).
  • The container testing pyramid — many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against real PostgreSQL (compose run --rm or Testcontainers), a handful of e2e — with image tests (container-structure-test + Hadolint) wrapping every layer to validate the built artifact itself, not just app behavior (Ch 24).
  • 🎯 Exam: CI/CD platforms aren't graded by name, but tagging, promotion, and registry discipline (Ch 23) sit squarely inside the 20% Image Creation, Management & Registry domain — Ch 22 and Ch 24 are the production muscle that makes that domain's images trustworthy in the first place.
📌 Part 8 Visual Summary — one image, built once, tested, promoted, trusted
   📝 push ──▶ 🏗️ build (ONE image)             (Ch 22: build once, everywhere)
                   │  GitHub Actions │ GitLab CI │ Jenkins │ Build Cloud
                   │  underneath: dind │ socket mount │ kaniko/buildah
                   ▼
   🧪 unit ──▶ 🔗 integration (real Postgres) ──▶ 🌐 e2e   (Ch 24: the pyramid)
                   │        image tests wrap every layer:
                   └── 📐 structure-test  +  🧹 Hadolint
                   ▼
   🔖 tag:ci-sha ── tag:1.2.3-sha ── tag:production           (Ch 23: one digest)
        (all point at the SAME sha256 manifest — retagged, never rebuilt)
                   ▼
   dev registry ──promote (retag)──▶ prod registry     ✍️ signed (DCT) on push
                                                          🔒 enforced on pull
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the digest that shipped is the digest that was tested — nothing rebuilt, nothing untraced. 🚀

In words: Chapter 22 turns "works on my machine" into "works everywhere" by building easypj exactly once inside a container, on whichever platform you use, and picking a build strategy — dind, socket mount, or rootless kaniko/buildah — by weighing isolation against root-on-host risk. That same image then climbs Chapter 24's testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against a real PostgreSQL (via compose run --rm or Testcontainers), a handful of full-stack e2e runs, with image-level checks — container-structure-test and Hadolint — wrapping every layer to confirm the artifact itself, not just the code, is sound.

Once proven, Chapter 23 takes over: the image is tagged deterministically (SHA for traceability, semver for releases, combined for production), and moves dev → staging → production by retagging that one tested digest — never rebuilding. Registries stay split with sane, release-exempt retention, and Docker Content Trust signs the image on push and blocks unsigned pulls, so the pipeline itself becomes the only path an image can take to production.

The one idea to keep: everything in this Part exists to make one guarantee true — the digest that reaches production is the exact digest that was built once, tested at every layer, and never silently swapped out along the way.

Chapter 25 · Docker → Kubernetes Transition

Docker packages your app; Kubernetes runs it at scale. This chapter bridges the gap — from single-host containers to multi-node clusters. Understand why Kubernetes exists, how Docker concepts map to K8s, and how to take your Dockerized app from compose.yaml to production Kubernetes.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~45-60 min ☸️ K8s 🌉 CKA On-Ramp

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ State the one-sentence line that separates what Docker still owns from what Kubernetes takes over (25.1)
  • ✅ Translate any Docker noun (container, image, volume, network, compose file) to its Kubernetes equivalent without hesitating (25.2)
  • ✅ Walk the 6-step Dockerfile→build→push→Deployment→Service journey and label each step Docker-only or Kubernetes-only (25.3)
  • ✅ Explain why kubectl apply never builds or pushes an image (25.3)
  • ✅ Run kompose convert on a real compose.yaml and name what it gets right and what it can't guess — replicas, limits, probes (25.4)
  • ✅ Recognize why depends_on has no direct Kubernetes equivalent (25.4)
🎓 DCA Relevance
Beyond DCA Scope 0%
🎯 The On-Ramp to CKA, Not a Graded DCA Domain

Kubernetes concepts sit entirely outside the Docker Certified Associate exam blueprint — nothing here is required to pass the DCA exam itself. This chapter exists to make the DCA→CKA transition painless, the on-ramp to the companion CKA (Certified Kubernetes Administrator) guide.

  • Why this chapter exists: every image, container, network and volume so far lived on ONE machine — yours. The moment easypj must survive a server dying, or handle more traffic than one box can hold, Docker runs out of answers on its own. This chapter draws the exact line: what Docker still owns (the image, the Dockerfile, the single-host runtime) and what Kubernetes takes over (scheduling, healing, scaling across many machines).
  • The load-bearing question: "do I throw away Docker to learn K8s?" — no. Everything Part 3 taught you (Dockerfile, build, push) stays exactly as it was; Kubernetes only adds what comes AFTER the push.

🧭 Section Map

25.1 why leave Docker alone → 25.2 noun-for-noun mapping → 25.3 the 6-step deploy journey → 25.4 compose.yaml → manifests (kompose) — each section hands the next one a piece of the vocabulary you need before Chapter 26 writes a real manifest.
