25.1 Why Kubernetes After Docker?

Docker excels at running containers on ONE machine. Kubernetes excels at running containers across MANY machines. When your app outgrows a single server — you need auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, and multi-host networking — Kubernetes is the answer:

Docker (Single Host) vs Kubernetes (Cluster)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🐳 DOCKER (Single Host)  vs  ☸️ KUBERNETES (Cluster)           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DOCKER:                        KUBERNETES:                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │   ONE SERVER     │           │         CLUSTER (Many Servers)        │ │
  │  │                  │           │                                      │ │
  │  │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ │           │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│ │
  │  │  │C1│ │C2│ │C3│ │           │  │      🧠 CONTROL PLANE            ││ │
  │  │  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ │           │  │  API Server | etcd | Scheduler   ││ │
  │  │                  │           │  └──────────────────────────────────┘│ │
  │  │  IF SERVER DIES: │           │                                      │ │
  │  │  💀 Everything   │           │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐      │ │
  │  │     goes down!   │           │  │ 💪 Node 1  │  │ 💪 Node 2  │      │ │
  │  │                  │           │  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│      │ │
  │  │  SCALING: Manual │           │  │ │C1││C3││C5││  │ │C2││C4││C6││      │ │
  │  │  NO auto-healing │           │  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│      │ │
  │  │  NO rolling upd. │           │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘      │ │
  │  └──────────────────┘           │                                      │ │
  │                                 │  IF NODE DIES: Pods move to Node 2 ✅ │ │
  │                                 │  SCALING: kubectl scale --replicas=10│ │
  │                                 └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
DimensionDocker (Standalone)Kubernetes
Single Host✅ Yes✅ Yes (Minikube)
Multi-Host Cluster❌ No✅ Yes (core feature)
Auto-Scaling❌ Manual only✅ HPA + VPA built-in
Self-Healing⚠️ Restart policies✅ Auto-recreates pods
Service Discovery⚠️ Limited (Compose)✅ DNS + CoreDNS
Load Balancing⚠️ Compose/Manual✅ Built-in Services
Rolling Updates⚠️ Swarm only✅ Deployment native
Rollback❌ None✅ kubectl rollout undo
Secret Management⚠️ Swarm secrets✅ Secrets + etcd
Config Management⚠️ .env files✅ ConfigMaps
Storage Orchestration❌ Manual volumes✅ PV + PVC + CSI
Namespace Isolation❌ None✅ Namespaces
RBAC❌ None✅ Roles + Bindings
Cloud-Native❌ Not designed for✅ Built for cloud
Learning Curve🟢 Low🔴 High
💡 The Kitchen vs Restaurant-Chain Analogy

Docker is one kitchen with one chef — if the chef collapses, dinner stops. Kubernetes is a restaurant chain with a head office (the control plane) that reassigns any order to any open kitchen (node). Docker Engine schedules containers onto exactly the host you ran docker run on — there is no concept of "another machine" inside the engine itself. Kubernetes adds a control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) that turns MANY hosts (nodes) into one schedulable pool.

🔬 easypj today: docker run easypj:v1 dies with the laptop. On a 3-node cluster, the SAME image becomes 3 Pods — killing one node just moves its Pods to the survivors (see the table's Self-Healing row). Of the 15 dimensions above, Docker marks 13 ❌ or ⚠️ — but Auto-Scaling and Rollback are the two a growing easypj would hit FIRST, because they're the two Docker cannot do at all without Swarm or Kubernetes.

📊 Section 25.1 Summary

Docker = one host, one daemon; Kubernetes = a cluster with a control plane doing the picking for you. Gotcha: Kubernetes does NOT replace Docker's image format — it still runs the exact OCI images your Dockerfiles already build.

25.2 Concepts Mapping: Docker → Kubernetes

Every Docker noun has a Kubernetes translation. Learn this vocabulary once — it runs through every later Kubernetes/CKA page without you having to stop and re-derive it:

Docker ConceptKubernetes EquivalentKey Difference
ContainerPodPod can contain multiple containers sharing network/IPC
ImageContainer ImageSame concept — identical across both
docker-compose.ymlDeployment + ServiceCompose is single-file; K8s splits concerns
Docker NetworkCNI (Container Network Interface)K8s uses pluggable CNI drivers (Calico, Cilium)
Docker VolumePersistentVolume + PVCK8s separates storage provisioning from consumption
docker runkubectl apply -f (or run, imperative)K8s prefers declarative YAML over imperative commands
Restart PolicyPod restartPolicy + Deployment replicasK8s combines restart behavior with a desired replica count
compose.yaml Splits Into 4 Kubernetes Objects
  ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │services:           │───────▶│Deployment  (django Pods, 26.7)             │
  │django, postgres    │───────▶│  replicas: 3, image: easypj:v1             │
  │ports: 8000:8000    │───────▶│Service  (stable :8000 access)              │
  │environment:        │───────▶│ConfigMap+Secret (26.5): DEBUG,             │
  │DEBUG, SECRET_KEY.. │───────▶│  ALLOWED_HOSTS, SECRET_KEY                 │
  │volumes:            │───────▶│PVC: claims postgres_data (17.2)            │
  └────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🚚 The Moving-House Analogy

Relabeling a moving-house inventory: "box" becomes "crate", "van" becomes "fleet" — same cargo, new shipping company with its own paperwork and bigger trucks. The mapping is NOT 1:1 everywhere: one Docker container maps to a Pod's main container, but a Pod can hold several containers sharing localhost and a volume — a shape Docker alone cannot express (the sidecar pattern).

🔬 easypj: the postgres_data VOLUME becomes a PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume — same idea (durable disk outside the container), different YAML, same Postgres data files. 💡 kompose convert (25.4) automates roughly this exact split from a real compose.yaml — but it cannot invent replica counts, resource limits or health probes; those still need the Chapter 26/27 review a human does by hand before anything ships.

📊 Section 25.2 Summary

Same 5 nouns (image, container, network, volume, compose file), new names, bigger scope. Gotcha: "Docker Compose" itself has NO direct K8s object — its job splits across Deployment, Service, ConfigMap and PVC.

25.3 From Dockerfile to Kubernetes Deployment

Six steps carry your Dockerfile from a build command to a running, network-reachable Kubernetes Deployment. The first two are pure Docker — unchanged from Part 3. The last four are genuinely new Kubernetes concepts:

Dockerfile → K8s Deployment — Full 6-Step Journey

  │          🐳→☸️ DOCKERFILE TO KUBERNETES DEPLOYMENT — FULL JOURNEY           │

  │  STEP 1: Dockerfile           STEP 2: Build + Push                       │

  │  │ WORKDIR /app     │        │   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 .│               │
  │  │ COPY req.txt .   │        │ $ docker push            │               │
  │  │ RUN pip install  │        │   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1  │               │
  │  │ COPY . .         │        └───────────┬──────────────┘               │
  │  │ CMD ["gunicorn"] │                    │                               │

  │  │     - image: ghcr.io/    │     │ $ kubectl apply \        │          │
  │  │       you/easypj:v1      │     │   -f service.yaml        │          │

  │  │       - containerPort:8000│    │ NAME        READY STATUS │          │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘     │ easypj-xxx  1/1   Running│          │
  │                                   │ easypj-yyy  1/1   Running│          │
  │  STEP 5: K8s Service              │ easypj-zzz  1/1   Running│          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐     └──────────────────────────┘          │
  │  │ apiVersion: v1           │                                            │
  │  │ kind: Service            │     RESULT: easypj running on 3 pods,      │
  │  │ spec:                    │     accessible via Service on port 8000!   │
  │  │   selector:              │                                            │
  │  │     app: easypj          │                                            │

  │  │     targetPort: 8000     │                                            │
  │  │   type: LoadBalancer     │                                            │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘                                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏭 The Factory Line Analogy

The journey diagram above is a factory line: stations 1-2 (Dockerfile, build+push) are the loading dock you already run; stations 3-6 hand the crate to a NEW shipping department (K8s) deciding how many trucks (replicas) and which docks (Service) receive it.

🔬 easypj: docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 . does not change at all; only what happens AFTER docker push is new — a Deployment named easypj requests replicas: 3 of that tag. In the diagram's Deployment YAML, the image: line is just the Dockerfile's build output, traced straight back to the build+push chapters you already know cold; replicas: 3 is the new concept this chapter adds on top.

📊 Section 25.3 Summary

Build+push stays Docker; "how many, where, reachable how" becomes Kubernetes' job via Deployment + Service YAML. Gotcha: kubectl apply never builds or pushes images — if the tag in deployment.yaml was never pushed, every Pod sits in ImagePullBackOff forever.

🔧 Under the Hood — what actually changes when the SAME image moves from docker run to a Kubernetes Pod

Both Docker Engine and a Kubernetes node run containers through containerd underneath — dockerd talks to it via Docker's own API layer, kubelet talks to it directly via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). Neither one reinvents how a container starts: both ultimately call runc to create the Linux namespaces + cgroups the process runs inside. This is WHY an OCI image built once with docker build runs unmodified in both worlds — the image format never changed, only WHO is asking containerd to run it.

 docker run easypj:v1          kubectl apply (Pod easypj-xxx)
      │                              │ (via CRI)
      ▼                              ▼
 dockerd (Docker API)          kubelet (per-node agent)
      └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                     ▼
               containerd (shared)
                     ▼
           runc → namespaces + cgroups
                     ▼
          SAME OCI image, SAME running process

On the Kubernetes side, kubectl apply doesn't create the Pod directly either: it writes desired state to the API server, which persists it in etcd; the scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods and assigns a node; THAT node's kubelet then pulls the image and asks containerd to run it — the same watch-and-reconcile loop that makes a deleted Pod under a Deployment come back within seconds.

🔑 Two different daemons (dockerd, kubelet) both end up calling the exact same containerd + runc underneath — this is why an image built once with docker build never needs to be rebuilt for Kubernetes.

25.4 docker-compose.yml → Kubernetes Manifests

Convert a real easypj compose.yaml into K8s manifests two ways — automatic and manual — and know when to trust each:

Side-by-Side: Compose → K8s
# docker-compose.yml                    # Kubernetes (deployment.yaml)
services:                               apiVersion: apps/v1
  django:                               kind: Deployment
    build: .                            metadata:
    ports: ["8000:8000"]                  name: easypj
    environment:                        spec:
      - DB_HOST=postgres                  replicas: 3
    depends_on: [postgres]                selector:
  postgres:                                 app: easypj
    image: postgres:15                   template:
    volumes:                               spec:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  containers:
  redis:                                    - image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
    image: redis:7                             ports: [8000]
volumes:                                       env:
  postgres_data:                              - name: DB_HOST
                                                value: postgres

# Convert automatically:
# $ kompose convert -f docker-compose.yml
# Generates: deployment.yaml, service.yaml, pvc.yaml
🔧 The Rough Translator Analogy

kompose is a rough translator: it gets the nouns right (django, postgres, postgres_data) fast, but a human still edits the grammar (replicas, health checks, secrets) before it ships. This mirrors the exact django+postgres core Chapter 11 built — kompose reads that same compose.yaml and emits a Deployment + Service per service, plus a PVC per named volume.

🔬 easypj: kompose turns depends_on: [postgres] into nothing — K8s has no depends_on; Chapter 27's readiness probes replace it. Try it: run kompose convert -f compose.yaml on your easypj file. Verify: count the generated files (one Deployment + Service per service, one PVC for postgres_data) and confirm the postgres depends_on silently disappeared.

📊 Section 25.4 Summary

kompose bootstraps manifests from a file you already own; manual translation (Chapter 26) gives production control kompose's guesses don't. Gotcha: never ship kompose's raw output — no resource limits and no health checks means an unbounded, unmonitored Pod.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Docker = one host; Kubernetes = many hosts under one control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager).
  • Of the 15 comparison dimensions, Auto-Scaling and Rollback are the two Docker cannot do at all without Swarm or Kubernetes.
  • The Docker→K8s noun mapping is not always 1:1 — a Pod can hold several containers sharing one network namespace and volumes.
  • "Docker Compose" itself has no single K8s object — its job splits across Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, and PVC.
  • Steps 1-2 of the Dockerfile→Deployment journey (build, push) stay 100% Docker; steps 3-6 are new Kubernetes concepts.
  • kubectl apply never builds or pushes images — ImagePullBackOff always traces back to a tag problem, not a cluster bug.
  • kompose convert bootstraps manifests fast but guesses replicas: 1, no resource limits, no probes — a first draft only.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Kubernetes replaces Docker's image format → Kubernetes still runs the exact OCI images your Dockerfiles already build — the image format never changed.
  • kompose's output is production-ready → Never ship kompose's raw output — no resource limits and no health checks means an unbounded, unmonitored Pod.
  • kompose preserves depends_on as a readiness gate → depends_on silently disappears when kompose converts a compose.yaml — Chapter 27's readiness probes replace it.
  • ImagePullBackOff means Kubernetes itself is broken → It means the tag in your YAML was never pushed (or a private registry has no imagePullSecret) — check the registry, not the cluster.
  • Swarm == Kubernetes → Swarm and K8s solve similar problems differently. Concepts map but implementations differ.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Memorize the noun-mapping table cold before touching Chapter 26's YAML — the vocabulary swap is most of the learning curve.
  • Treat kompose convert as a fast first draft, never a final manifest — always add limits and probes by hand afterward.
  • When a Pod won't start, check the image tag before questioning the cluster.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 25)

the Chapter 25 cheat-card 
kubectl cluster-info                    # confirms a cluster is reachable
kubectl config current-context          # confirms kubectl points at the right cluster
docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 . # unchanged from Part 3
docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1       # image must exist in a registry before any Deployment references it
kompose convert -f compose.yaml         # auto-generates a first-draft Deployment/Service/PVC set
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml        # hands the Pod template + replica count to the API server
kubectl get pods -o wide                # confirms which node each Pod landed on
kubectl explain deployment.spec         # inline docs for any object's spec fields
kubectl create secret generic db-secret --from-literal=password=mypass  # bridge a Docker-era credential into a K8s Secret

🧠 Chapter 25 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From the one-sentence Docker/K8s line to the compose.yaml→4-objects flow — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What's the one-sentence line separating what Docker still owns from what Kubernetes adds?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker packages and runs a container on one host; Kubernetes schedules, heals, and scales containers across a cluster of many hosts via a control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager).

EXPLANATION

This is the exact GOAL statement 25.1 opens with — memorize it as the single sentence that separates the two tools' jobs.

Q2
Complete the mapping: Container → ?, docker-compose.yml → ?, Docker volume → ?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Container → Pod; docker-compose.yml → Deployment + Service (+ Helm chart); Docker volume → PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim.

EXPLANATION

Straight from 25.2's noun-for-noun mapping table — the vocabulary swap every later Kubernetes page assumes you already have.

Q3
From the 15-dimension comparison table in 25.1, which two rows show Docker flat-❌ that a growing easypj would hit FIRST?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Auto-Scaling and Rollback.

EXPLANATION

13 of the 15 rows mark Docker ❌ or ⚠️, but Auto-Scaling and Rollback are the two Docker cannot do AT ALL without Swarm or Kubernetes — the two a scaling easypj would feel first.

Q4
Why can one Kubernetes Pod outgrow "one Docker container"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Pod can hold multiple containers sharing one network namespace (localhost) and volumes — a shape a single Docker container cannot express alone (the sidecar pattern).

EXPLANATION

25.2's mapping is explicitly NOT 1:1 everywhere — this is the one place it breaks in Kubernetes' favor.

Q5
In the Dockerfile→Deployment 6-step journey, which steps are pure Docker and which are pure Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Steps 1-2 (Dockerfile, docker build + push) stay 100% Docker, unchanged from Part 3. Steps 3-6 (write + apply Deployment YAML, write + apply Service YAML) are pure Kubernetes — kubectl reads the YAML and drives the API server toward that state.

EXPLANATION

This is 25.3's 6-step diagram, split cleanly down the middle: build/push vs write/apply.

Q6
What error appears if deployment.yaml references a tag that was never pushed, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ImagePullBackOff — kubectl apply never builds or pushes images, it only schedules images already in a registry; if the tag doesn't exist there, every Pod trying to pull it fails permanently in that state.

EXPLANATION

25.3's closing gotcha — always check the image tag before questioning the cluster.

Q7
What does kompose convert -f compose.yaml produce from easypj's compose file, and what 3 things does it NOT set?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

One Deployment + Service per service (django, postgres) plus a PVC for postgres_data; it does NOT set real replica counts, resource limits, or health probes.

EXPLANATION

25.4's core takeaway — kompose is a fast first draft, never a final manifest.

Q8
Why does depends_on: [postgres] disappear when kompose converts easypj's compose.yaml, and what replaces it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Kubernetes has no depends_on concept; Chapter 27's readiness probes replace it by controlling when a Pod is added to a Service's endpoint list.

EXPLANATION

25.4's gotcha — a silent disappearance, not an error, so it's easy to miss until you go looking for it.

Q9
Compare a Docker volume to its Kubernetes equivalent for easypj's postgres_data.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

postgres_data as a Docker VOLUME becomes a PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume — same idea (durable disk outside the container lifecycle), different YAML, same underlying Postgres data files.

EXPLANATION

25.2's real-world example of the volume→PVC row in the mapping table.

Q10
Using the compose.yaml→K8s flow diagram from 25.2, match each key to what it becomes.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

services: django → Deployment (Pod template); ports: 8000:8000 → Service; environment: DEBUG, SECRET_KEY → ConfigMap + Secret; volumes: postgres_data → PersistentVolumeClaim.

EXPLANATION

The compose file's single block of YAML fans out into 4 separate K8s objects — exactly what 25.2's diagram shows.

26.1 Prerequisites for K8s Deployment

Confirm all 4 prerequisites before writing a single YAML line — most "kubectl apply hangs" reports trace back to skipping this step.

☸️
K8s Cluster

Minikube, kind, k3s, or cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS). Verify: kubectl cluster-info.

🔧
kubectl Configured

kubectl version --client. Context set: kubectl config current-context.

🗄️
Registry Access

Image pushed to a registry K8s can pull from. For private: create imagePullSecrets.

🐳
Docker Image Ready

Image built and pushed: docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 . && docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.

💡 The Right Key, Right House

Checking all 4 prerequisites is checking you have the right house key AND the right house before knocking — a valid kubectl config for the WRONG cluster fails exactly like no config at all, just more confusingly.

📋 Before You Write Any Manifest
  • ☐ a cluster exists — kubectl cluster-info returns a URL
  • ☐ kubectl context points at it — kubectl config current-context
  • ☐ you can push to a registry — docker login ghcr.io succeeds
  • ☐ the easypj image is already pushed — docker push completed

🔬 easypj: docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 must succeed BEFORE any Deployment references that tag — kubectl never builds images, it only schedules ones already in a registry.

⚠️ Local Clusters Can't See Your Laptop's Image Cache

A local Minikube cluster cannot pull an image that only exists in your local docker images — push it to a reachable registry, or minikube image load it directly.

26.2 Building & Pushing the easypj Image

Produce one correctly-tagged, pushed image that 26.3's Deployment can reference by exact name.

TERMINAL
$ docker build -t ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0 .
$ docker login ghcr.io -u username
$ docker push ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
$ docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0   # confirms it pushed cleanly
💡 The Mailing-Address Analogy

Mailing a package: the tag is the exact street address on the label. "v1.0" is a house number; "latest" is "somewhere on this street" — the carrier (kubelet) needs the number.

🛑 :latest Is Banned Here

The tag is the ONLY link between this chapter and the Deployment YAML — image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0 must match character-for-character, including the registry host. :latest is banned: K8s cannot tell "new latest" from "old latest".

🔬 easypj: reuse Chapter 9.7's multi-stage Dockerfile unchanged — only the registry host (ghcr.io/you/) is new; the build itself is identical to every prior chapter.

26.3 Creating the Kubernetes Deployment

Write a Deployment that names the exact image, exposes the right port, and never lets one runaway Pod starve the node.

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: easypj-secrets
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
💡 Selector/Labels Are a Name Tag, Not a Leash

The Deployment scans the room for Pods wearing "app: easypj" and claims them — mismatched labels means it creates orphan Pods forever, never recognizing the ones it already made.

📖 selector.matchLabels Must Equal template.metadata.labels

selector.matchLabels must equal template.metadata.labels — this is how the Deployment finds ITS OWN Pods among all Pods in the namespace. requests reserve capacity the scheduler counts against; limits are a hard ceiling the kubelet enforces.

🔬 easypj: gunicorn's own --workers setting (Chapter 6) now works ALONGSIDE replicas: 3 — each Pod runs N gunicorn workers, times 3 Pods, for the real concurrency ceiling.

⚠️ Skipping resources: Is Not Optional

Skip resources: and one memory-leaking Pod can starve every other Pod on its node — this is not optional in production.

26.4 Creating the Kubernetes Service

Give the 3 easypj Pods ONE stable address, and pick the right Service type for dev vs production.

service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
  type: LoadBalancer  # ClusterIP (internal) | NodePort | LoadBalancer
Service typeReachable by
ClusterIPInside the cluster only (default, most services)
NodePortCluster + any node IP:30000-32767 (dev/testing)
LoadBalancerThe public internet, via a cloud LB (production)
💡 The Hotel Front Desk Analogy

Pods are hotel guests reassigned rooms nightly; the Service is the FRONT DESK phone number — always the same, no matter which room today's guest is actually in.

🔬 easypj: nginx's old proxy_pass http://django:8000 (Chapter 11) becomes proxy_pass http://easypj:8000 — same pattern, the DNS name now resolves to a Service, not a container.

⚠️ A Selector Typo Fails Silently

A Service's selector uses the SAME label-matching rules as a Deployment — a typo silently creates a Service with zero endpoints (kubectl get endpoints easypj shows empty).

🔧 Under the Hood — how a Service's virtual IP actually routes traffic

A Service's ClusterIP has no process listening on it anywhere — it's a virtual address. kube-proxy runs on every node, watches the Endpoints object (built automatically from the Service's selector matching currently-Ready Pods), and programs iptables or IPVS rules that DNAT traffic bound for the ClusterIP straight to one of those real Pod IPs. CoreDNS is what resolves easypj.default.svc.cluster.local to that ClusterIP in the first place.

 client → DNS lookup "easypj.default.svc.cluster.local"
      │ (CoreDNS)
      ▼
 Service ClusterIP (virtual, nothing listens here)
      │ (kube-proxy iptables/IPVS DNAT rule)
      ▼
 one of: Pod-A IP | Pod-B IP | Pod-C IP  (Endpoints)
🔑 This is exactly why a failing readiness probe (27.3) removes a Pod from rotation with zero code changes anywhere: kube-proxy simply stops including that Pod's IP the next time it reprograms the DNAT rules.

26.5 ConfigMaps & Secrets for easypj

Split easypj's settings into non-secret (ConfigMap) and secret (Secret) — never mix SECRET_KEY into a plain YAML again.

configmap.yaml + secret.yaml
# configmap.yaml — Non-sensitive config
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-config
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: easypj.settings
  DEBUG: "False"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com,localhost"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
---
# secret.yaml — Sensitive data (base64 encoded)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: easypj-secrets
type: Opaque
data:
  SECRET_KEY: ZGphbmdvLWluc2VjdXJlL...  # echo -n "value" | base64
  DATABASE_URL: cG9zdGdyZXM6Ly9lYXN5cGpfdXNlcjpwYXNzQHBvc3RncmVzOjU0MzIvZWFzeXBq
AspectConfigMapSecret
Stored in etcdPlain textBase64 (NOT encrypted)
describe outputShows real valuesMasked: <set to key ...>
get -o yamldata: plain textdata: base64 (needs -d)
Mutable?Yes, in placeYes, in place
easypj exampleDEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTSSECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL
💡 Directly Maps to Chapter 11's .env Split

ConfigMap is the postcard (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS), Secret is the sealed envelope (SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL) — same two piles as Chapter 11's .env, now two cluster-native objects instead of one file.

🔬 easypj: settings.py's os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] call does not change at all — only WHERE the env var comes from changes, via envFrom in the Deployment (26.6).

⚠️ envFrom Uses Your Keys AS the Env Var Names — Verbatim

envFrom injects every key in a ConfigMap/Secret's data: directly as an environment variable name, unchanged. A key like database-url becomes a literal env var named database-url — which os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] will never find. That's why 26.5's ConfigMap/Secret keys are written DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE, DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, LOG_LEVEL, SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL — matching Django's expected names exactly, not a REST-style lowercase-hyphen convention.

⚠️ envFrom Needs a Rollout Restart

Both objects share one blind spot: a Pod already running with envFrom does NOT see an update until it restarts — only a volume-mounted ConfigMap/Secret refreshes live (~1 min sync). easypj's SECRET_KEY via envFrom needs a rollout restart to rotate.

26.6 Deploying & Verifying

Go from zero to "easypj answering HTTP requests through K8s" using only the 4 YAMLs this chapter built.

TERMINAL
# Create the namespace first — nothing else collides
$ kubectl create namespace easypj

# Config & secrets before anything that references them
$ kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml -f secret.yaml -n easypj

# Deployment & Service
$ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n easypj

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
easypj-5d8f7b9c-abcde     1/1     Running   0          30s
easypj-5d8f7b9c-fghij     1/1     Running   0          30s
easypj-5d8f7b9c-klmno     1/1     Running   0          30s

$ kubectl get svc easypj -n easypj
NAME     TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)          AGE
easypj   LoadBalancer   10.96.100.50   8000:30080/TCP   1m

$ kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:8000 -n easypj
# Open http://localhost:8000 — easypj is live on K8s! 🚀

$ curl -I http://localhost:8000/jobs/
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
📖 envFrom Is What Actually Wires It Together

envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: easypj-config}}, {secretRef: {name: easypj-secrets}}] in the container spec is what actually wires 26.5's objects into the Pod's environment — without it, ConfigMap/Secret exist but nothing reads them.

💡 port-forward Is a Temporary Phone Line

port-forward is a temporary phone line straight to one Service, bypassing the front desk's real routing — perfect for verification, never used for production traffic.

🔬 easypj: the same /jobs/ view Chapter 11's nginx served now answers through kubectl port-forward → Service → Pod → gunicorn — one more hop, same Django code, unmodified.

⚠️ Forgetting -n easypj Runs Against default

Forgetting -n easypj on any command runs it against the default namespace — objects "disappear" only because you're looking in the wrong namespace.

26.7 Pods vs Deployments — Scaling easypj

Explain why you scale the Deployment, never a Pod, and trace the object chain that makes --replicas=5 create Pods.

The Ownership Chain — Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods
  Deployment easypj (desired: replicas=5)
          │ creates & owns
          ▼
  ReplicaSet easypj-7d9f4 (current: 5)
          │ creates & owns
          ▼
  Pod  Pod  Pod  Pod  Pod   (each independently schedulable)
🚫
Single Pod

Ephemeral, not recommended. No controller watches it — kill it and it stays dead.

✅
Deployment

Manages a ReplicaSet, which ensures replicas. Killing a Pod under a Deployment gets it replaced within seconds.

TERMINAL
$ kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
deployment.apps/easypj scaled

$ kubectl get pods -w   # watch pods come up
💡 The HR Policy Analogy

A bare Pod is a single hire with no manager — vanish and the seat stays empty. A Deployment is HR policy: "this desk always has 5 people" — someone quits, HR (the ReplicaSet) posts the job again automatically.

🔬 easypj: kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5 takes easypj from 3 to 5 Pods — Django code untouched, gunicorn config untouched, only the REPLICA COUNT changed.

⚠️ Deleting a Pod Doesn't "Clean Up" Anything

Deleting a Pod created by a ReplicaSet doesn't clean anything up — it triggers an immediate replacement, the opposite of what a beginner usually expects.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • All 4 prerequisite gates (cluster reachable, correct context, registry access, image pushed) must pass before any YAML runs.
  • Image tags must be exact and never :latest — K8s can't tell "new latest" from "old latest".
  • selector.matchLabels must equal template.metadata.labels or the Deployment creates orphan Pods forever.
  • requests reserve scheduler capacity; limits are a kubelet-enforced ceiling — skipping them risks one Pod starving a node.
  • ClusterIP (default/internal), NodePort (dev/test), LoadBalancer (public/production) — pick the narrowest type that works.
  • ConfigMap = non-secret, Secret = base64-encoded (NOT encrypted) — envFrom wires both into the Pod's environment, but a running Pod needs a rollout restart to pick up changes.
  • Never scale a bare Pod — scale the Deployment; the ReplicaSet is the reconciliation layer that replaces killed Pods.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming a local cluster (e.g. Minikube) can pull an image sitting only in your laptop's docker images → Push it to a reachable registry, or load it directly into the cluster's runtime (minikube image load).
  • Assuming a successful docker push from your laptop means the cluster can pull → Private registries need an imagePullSecret in-cluster too — pushing and pulling are separate auth paths.
  • A label typo between a Service's selector and a Deployment's Pod labels → Creates a Service with zero endpoints silently — no error, just kubectl get endpoints showing empty.
  • Forgetting -n <namespace> on any kubectl command → Runs it against the default namespace — objects appear "missing" only because you're looking in the wrong namespace.
  • Deleting a Pod owned by a ReplicaSet, expecting cleanup → Triggers an immediate replacement — the ReplicaSet just made a new one.
  • Pods stuck Pending with no obvious cause → Usually insufficient CPU/memory for the requests — check kubectl describe pod for scheduling events.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • kubectl get pods,svc -A when anything "disappears" — it's usually a namespace mismatch, not a deleted object.
  • docker manifest inspect right after pushing — a 404 there predicts ImagePullBackOff before you even apply anything.
  • Check kubectl get endpoints <svc> first whenever a Service "isn't working" — empty endpoints means the selector is the bug, not the network.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 26)

the Chapter 26 cheat-card 
kubectl cluster-info                                      # confirms a reachable cluster
kubectl config current-context                            # confirms kubectl points at the right cluster
docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0                       # must succeed before any Deployment references the tag
kubectl apply -f k8s/                                      # apply every manifest in the directory at once
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n easypj # deploy both objects into the right namespace
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj                            # confirm replica count & Running status
kubectl get endpoints easypj                              # confirm the Service actually found Pods
kubectl logs -n easypj deployment/easypj                  # tail the app's logs by deployment name
kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:8000 -n easypj       # temporary local access, verification only
kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5              # scale the Deployment, never a bare Pod

🧠 Chapter 26 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From prerequisite gates to scaling a live Deployment — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What are the 4 prerequisite gates that must pass before writing any K8s YAML for easypj?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) a cluster exists (kubectl cluster-info), (2) kubectl context points at it (kubectl config current-context), (3) you can push to a registry (docker login succeeds), (4) the easypj image is already pushed.

EXPLANATION

This is 26.1's exact CHECKLIST — skipping any one of the four is the root cause behind most "kubectl apply hangs" reports.

Q2
Why is tagging an image :latest banned in Kubernetes manifests?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

K8s can't tell "new latest" from "old latest" — the tag is the only link between a pushed image and the Deployment's image: field, so it must be exact and stable (e.g. v1.0).

EXPLANATION

26.2's mailing-address analogy makes this concrete: v1.0 is a house number, latest is "somewhere on this street" — kubelet needs the number.

Q3
Fill in which Service type reaches which audience: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ClusterIP → inside the cluster only (default); NodePort → cluster + any node IP on 30000-32767 (dev/test); LoadBalancer → the public internet via a cloud LB (production).

EXPLANATION

This table is 26.4's own Service-type comparison — pick the narrowest type that still does the job.

Q4
Why must selector.matchLabels in a Deployment equal template.metadata.labels?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

That's how the Deployment recognizes its OWN Pods among all Pods in the namespace — a mismatch means it can never find the Pods it already created and keeps creating orphans.

EXPLANATION

26.3's name-tag analogy: the Deployment scans the room for Pods wearing the right label and claims them; mismatched labels means it never recognizes its own.

Q5
What's the difference between a Secret and a ConfigMap in etcd, and why doesn't that make Secrets "safe"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are base64-ENCODED (not encrypted) in etcd by default vs ConfigMaps' plain text — base64 is trivially reversible, so Secrets should be treated as obscured, not safe from a cluster admin without real encryption-at-rest.

EXPLANATION

26.5's comparison table spells this out row by row — describe output masks a Secret's value, but get -o yaml still round-trips with a single base64 -d.

Q6
Trace what happens when a client requests easypj.default.svc.cluster.local.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DNS name → CoreDNS → Service ClusterIP → kube-proxy DNAT → Pod IP. CoreDNS resolves the name to the Service's ClusterIP; kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules DNAT that virtual IP to one of the Ready Pod IPs in the Service's Endpoints list — no client ever addresses a Pod IP directly.

EXPLANATION

This is 26.4's Under the Hood box in full — the same mechanism is why a failing readiness probe (Chapter 27.3) removes a Pod from rotation with zero code changes.

Q7
Why does a Pod already running with envFrom NOT see a ConfigMap/Secret update immediately?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

envFrom copies values into the Pod's environment at container start; only a volume-mounted ConfigMap/Secret refreshes live (~1 min sync) — envFrom needs a rollout restart to pick up new values.

EXPLANATION

26.5 calls this out as "one blind spot" both objects share — rotating easypj's SECRET_KEY via envFrom always needs a rollout restart.

Q8
What does kubectl get endpoints easypj returning empty actually mean, and what's the usual cause?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The Service's selector matched zero Pods — usually a label typo between the Service's selector and the Deployment's Pod template labels.

EXPLANATION

26.4's closing gotcha and 26.6's SPEED TIP both point here first whenever a Service "isn't working."

Q9
What object actually keeps a deleted Pod "coming back" under a Deployment, and why does a bare Pod not do this?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The ReplicaSet, which the Deployment creates and owns — it continuously reconciles "Pods running" against "replicas: desired." A bare Pod has no controller watching it, so deleting it leaves the seat empty.

EXPLANATION

26.7's HR-policy analogy: a bare Pod is a single hire with no manager; a Deployment is HR policy that reposts the job automatically.

Q10
In order, what are the 4 deployment steps 26.6 runs, and why does that order matter?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) create namespace, (2) apply ConfigMap + Secret, (3) apply Deployment + Service, (4) verify with get pods,svc + port-forward — config/secret must exist before the Deployment's envFrom can reference them, and Pods must be Running before port-forward is meaningful.

EXPLANATION

This is 26.6's full TERMINAL sequence — the same order every real rollout follows.

🔬 Practice Drill 26.1 — Zero to Serving Traffic (10 min)

Apply easypj's 4 manifests (configmap, secret, deployment, service) into a fresh easypj namespace in order, port-forward, and curl /jobs/ for a 200. If any step fails, name which of the 4 prerequisite gates (26.1) it violates before troubleshooting further.

📌 Chapter 26 Visual Summary — 4 YAMLs, one running stack

  │ namespace → ConfigMap+Secret → Deployment+Service →            │
  │  (26.6)        (26.5)             (26.3+26.4)                  │

The takeaway: verification never trusts "applied without error" — it checks get pods for Running, get endpoints for a non-empty list, and a real curl response, because a Service or ConfigMap can silently exist while doing nothing.

Chapter 27 · Kubernetes Deployment Strategies

easypj is now running in Kubernetes — but "running" and "safely changeable" are different problems. This chapter covers what happens the SECOND time you deploy: shipping v2 without downtime, undoing a bad release in seconds, proving a Pod is actually healthy before it takes traffic, and keeping dev/staging/prod from sharing one fragile YAML.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~60-75 min ☸️ K8s 🌉 Beyond DCA

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Predict Pod counts of each version at every step of a rolling update from maxSurge/maxUnavailable alone (27.1)
  • ✅ Undo a bad release with kubectl rollout undo, to a specific past revision if needed (27.2)
  • ✅ Distinguish readinessProbe (Service membership) from livenessProbe (Pod restart) and their different consequences (27.3)
  • ✅ Run the SAME easypj manifests across dev/staging/prod using Namespaces + Kustomize overlays without copy-pasting YAML (27.4)
  • ✅ Predict a Pod's QoS class (Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort) from its requests/limits alone (27.5)
  • ✅ Set a namespace-wide ResourceQuota so one team can't starve another (27.5)
🎓 DCA Relevance
Not a Graded DCA Domain CKA-track
🎯 Where the DCA→CKA Bridge Gets Closest to Real On-Call Work

Rolling updates, probes, and QoS are Kubernetes operational concerns entirely outside the Docker Certified Associate blueprint — treat this chapter as CKA-track depth, not exam prep.

  • Why this chapter exists: the first deploy worked — now how do you change anything without breaking production? That's the problem solved here.
  • The load-bearing line: a rolling update alone does not protect against a bad image that passes startup but fails under real load — pairing it with 27.3's readiness probes is what closes that gap.

27.1 rolling updates → 27.2 rollback → 27.3 health probes → 27.4 dev/staging/prod (Namespaces + Kustomize) → 27.5 resource management/QoS.

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway

27.1 Rolling Updates — Zero Downtime

kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=ghcr.io/username/easypj:v2.0 changes the Pod template inside the Deployment. The ReplicaSet controller then creates a NEW ReplicaSet (v2) and shrinks the OLD one (v1) in lockstep, bounded by two numbers: maxSurge (extra Pods allowed above the replica count) and maxUnavailable (Pods allowed to be missing below the replica count). Run kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj right after the set image command — it blocks and prints progress until "successfully rolled out." Ctrl+C only stops your terminal's VIEW, not the rollout itself.

Rolling Update — Step by Step (5 Pods, Zero Downtime)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 🔄 ROLLING UPDATE — Step by Step                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BEFORE (v1):  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  5 pods running easypj:v1      │
  │                │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│                                  │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  New v2 pod created        │
  │  (maxSurge=1)  │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (6 pods total)            │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  One v1 terminated             │
  │  (maxUnavail=1)│v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (5 pods total)                │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  New v2 pod (#2)           │
  │                │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│ │v2│                             │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ...continues one-by-one until...                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  AFTER (v2):   ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  All 5 pods running v2!        │
  │                │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│  ZERO DOWNTIME ✅               │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY CONFIG:                                                              │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    strategy:                                                              │
  │      type: RollingUpdate                                                 │
  │      rollingUpdate:                                                       │
  │        maxSurge: 1       # Extra pods allowed during update               │
  │        maxUnavailable: 1 # Pods that can be unavailable during update     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Relay Handoff Analogy

Think of the diagram above as a relay handoff: with maxSurge=1 a 6th runner (v2) joins the track BEFORE the 1st runner (v1) steps off — the team is never running fewer than 5, per maxUnavailable=1. For easypj: kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0 starts this exact sequence — 5 Pods stay 5 Pods, never dropping below 4 Ready with the defaults shown.

⚠️ Rolling Update Alone Isn't a Safety Net

RollingUpdate is USELESS against a bad image that passes startup but fails at runtime under load — it only checks that the container process started, not that it's actually healthy. Pair it with 27.3's readiness probes, or it ships broken Pods as "healthy."

27.2 Rollback — Undoing a Bad Deploy

Every kubectl apply or set image that changes the Pod template creates a NEW ReplicaSet revision. Kubernetes keeps the last N (default 10, via revisionHistoryLimit) around so rollout undo can re-point the Deployment at an old ReplicaSet — the same rolling-update machinery from 27.1, run in reverse.

TERMINAL
# See rollout history
$ kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         initial v1.0
2         v2.0 (bad)

# Rollback to the previous revision
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj
# Rollback to a specific revision
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=1

# Watch the rollback
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj
ReplicaSet State — the Active Pointer Moves, ReplicaSets Never Die
  ┌───────────────────┐            apply v2.0            ┌───────────────────┐
  │RS rev.1 (v1.0)    │                                  │RS rev.2 (v2.0)    │
  │scale: 3           │─────────────────────────────────▶│scale: 3           │
  │● ACTIVE           │                                  │● ACTIVE (bad)     │
  └───────────────────┘                                  └───────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────┐           rollout undo           ┌───────────────────┐
  │RS rev.2 (v2.0)    │                                  │RS rev.1 (v1.0)    │
  │scale: 0           │─────────────────────────────────▶│scale: 3           │
  │  idle, kept       │                                  │● ACTIVE again     │
  └───────────────────┘                                  └───────────────────┘
💡 Neither Apply Nor Undo Ever Deletes a ReplicaSet

Both only edit each ReplicaSet's scale between 0 and the desired count. Undo is near-instant because rev.1's Pod spec was already sitting at scale 0 — no image pull needed, just a scale-up. For easypj: v2.0 shipped a migration that broke /jobs/ with a 500 — kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj restores v1.0 Pods with zero downtime, using the same mechanism as the original deploy.

⚠️ You Can't Undo Past What's Been Pruned

revisionHistoryLimit can prune old ReplicaSets — you cannot undo to a revision Kubernetes has already garbage-collected. Check kubectl rollout history before undoing twice; you might already be one revision away from the good one, and it still shows both revisions after an undo — undo adds a new revision, it does not delete history.

27.3 Health Checks — Liveness & Readiness Probes

A Kubernetes probe answers one of two very different questions. readinessProbe controls Service membership — a failing readiness check removes the Pod's IP from the Service's endpoint list (traffic stops) WITHOUT restarting it. livenessProbe controls the Pod's own lifecycle — a failing liveness check gets the container KILLED and restarted.

deployment.yaml (with probes)
containers:
- name: django
  image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0
  readinessProbe:             # Is the app ready for traffic?
    httpGet:                  # If fails → remove from Service
      path: /healthz/
      port: 8000
    initialDelaySeconds: 5
    periodSeconds: 10
  livenessProbe:               # Is the app still healthy?
    httpGet:                   # If fails → restart container
      path: /healthz/
      port: 8000
    initialDelaySeconds: 15
    periodSeconds: 20
💡 The Front-Desk Analogy

Readiness is a "back of house, not seated yet" sign — the front desk stops sending guests, staff keeps working. Liveness is a "this employee is unresponsive" alarm — pull them out and bring in a replacement. For easypj: GET /healthz/ is a tiny Django view checking DB connectivity — during a slow migration it fails readiness (correctly hides the Pod) without triggering any restart. Make it return 500 temporarily and check kubectl get endpoints easypj: the Pod's IP disappears from endpoints while kubectl get pods still shows it Running.

⚠️ Identical Thresholds Cause Restart Storms

A slow-but-recovering Pod that would have simply been hidden by a failing readiness check instead gets killed by liveness at the same threshold — restarting doesn't fix the underlying slowness, so it can repeat. Give liveness a longer initialDelaySeconds/periodSeconds than readiness, as in the YAML above.

27.4 Environment-Specific Deployments

A Namespace scopes NAMES — two easypj Deployments in different namespaces never collide. Kustomize scopes FILES — a base manifest plus small per-environment patches (replica count, resource limits, image tag) merged at apply time. Together they let dev/staging/prod share one manifest source instead of maintaining copy-pasted, drifting YAML.

TERMINAL
# Namespace isolation
$ kubectl create namespace dev
$ kubectl create namespace staging
$ kubectl create namespace prod

# Deploy to a specific namespace
$ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n staging

# Kustomize overlays for environment differences
# kustomize/base/                deployment.yaml, service.yaml, kustomization.yaml
# kustomize/overlays/staging/    kustomization.yaml, patch.yaml
# kustomize/overlays/prod/       kustomization.yaml, patch.yaml
$ kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/staging
💡 The Apartment Building Analogy

Namespaces are separate apartments in the same building — same address format, no shared furniture. Kustomize overlays are one blueprint with sticky notes per apartment ("prod: add 2 bedrooms") instead of redrawing the whole plan three times. For easypj: base/ ships replicas: 1 and DEBUG=True; overlays/prod patches replicas: 5 and DEBUG=False — one Deployment source, two real behaviors. Create staging and prod namespaces, apply each overlay with kubectl apply -k, then check kubectl get deploy -A: easypj shows up in BOTH namespaces with DIFFERENT replica counts.

⚠️ Namespaces Are Organizational, Not a Resource Wall

Namespaces do NOT isolate node resources or network traffic by default — that needs a ResourceQuota (27.5) and a NetworkPolicy on top.

27.5 Resource Management in K8s

The scheduler places Pods using requests (guaranteed capacity, never oversold); the kubelet enforces limits (a hard ceiling — CPU is throttled, memory over-limit gets the container OOMKilled). A namespace-wide ResourceQuota caps the SUM of requests/limits across every Pod in that namespace, so one team cannot starve another.

deployment.yaml (with resource limits)
resources:
  requests:             # Minimum guaranteed (scheduler uses this)
    memory: "256Mi"
    cpu: "250m"
  limits:                # Maximum allowed (container throttled/killed)
    memory: "512Mi"
    cpu: "500m"
requests vs limitsQoS classEviction order
requests == limits (both set)Guaranteedlast
requests < limits (both set)Burstable2nd
no requests, no limits set at allBestEffortfirst
resourcequota.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: easypj-quota
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 2Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
💡 The Hotel Room Analogy

requests are a reserved hotel room (always yours); limits are the room's maximum occupancy (fire code); a ResourceQuota is the whole floor's total occupancy cap shared across every room on it. For easypj: setting requests==limits on the django container (as in Chapter 26.3) makes it Guaranteed — the LAST Pod evicted if the node runs low, exactly what you want for the web tier.

⚠️ Silence Is the Worst QoS Class

A Pod with NO requests/limits (BestEffort) is the FIRST killed under node pressure — leaving resources unset is not safety, it's the worst-protected QoS class by default. Apply the ResourceQuota above, then try to scale easypj past what it allows: kubectl describe resourcequota easypj-quota shows used vs hard, and over-quota Pods sit Pending with a quota-exceeded event.

🔧 Under the Hood — how resources: is actually enforced (cgroups)

A Pod's resources: block isn't a Kubernetes-only concept — the kubelet translates it straight into Linux cgroups on the node. limits.cpu becomes a CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) quota: the container gets THROTTLED (paused, not killed) once it exceeds its slice in a period — this is why a CPU-limited Pod gets sluggish under load instead of dying. limits.memory becomes a cgroup memory hard cap enforced by the kernel itself: exceed it and the kernel's OOM killer ends the container's process immediately — the literal mechanism behind "OOMKilled" in kubectl describe pod.

 Deployment YAML: resources.limits {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
      │ kubelet translates on Pod start
      ▼
 Linux cgroup for this container
      ├─ cpu quota   → throttle at 500m (no kill)
      └─ memory cap  → hard limit at 256Mi (OOM kill)
🔑 This is also why QoS classes matter under real pressure: the kubelet's node-level eviction manager reads these SAME cgroup numbers to decide who gets killed first when a node runs low on memory — BestEffort Pods (no requests/limits at all) have the weakest cgroup protection and are evicted before Burstable or Guaranteed Pods.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually, bounded by maxSurge (extra Pods above replicas) and maxUnavailable (Pods allowed missing below replicas).
  • Rolling update alone doesn't catch runtime failures under load — pair it with readiness probes or it ships broken Pods as "healthy".
  • Every image/template change creates a new ReplicaSet revision; rollout undo re-points the Deployment at an old one (kept up to revisionHistoryLimit).
  • readinessProbe controls Service endpoint membership (no restart); livenessProbe controls the Pod's own lifecycle (kills + restarts).
  • Identical liveness/readiness thresholds risk restart storms — a slow-but-recovering Pod can get killed by liveness before readiness would've simply hidden it.
  • Namespace = isolation boundary for names; Kustomize overlays = one base manifest + per-environment patches, avoiding copy-paste drift.
  • requests reserve scheduler capacity, limits cap actual usage via cgroups, QoS class decides node-pressure eviction order, and ResourceQuota caps the whole namespace's totals.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Rolling update alone is a complete safety net → It's useless against a bad image that passes startup but fails under load — always pair with readiness probes.
  • Assuming any past revision is always undo-able → revisionHistoryLimit can prune old ReplicaSets — you cannot undo to a revision K8s already garbage-collected.
  • Namespaces alone isolate resources or network → They do NOT, by default — that needs ResourceQuota and NetworkPolicy.
  • Leaving requests/limits unset "to be safe" → A Pod with no requests/limits (BestEffort) is the FIRST killed under node pressure — silence is the worst QoS class, not safety.
  • Changing the image tag doesn't trigger an update → If imagePullPolicy is IfNotPresent and the tag is unchanged, pods won't redeploy — bump the tag or force a rollout restart.
  • Deleting a Pod manually to "fix" it → The ReplicaSet just recreates it from the same broken template — to change the Pod spec, update the Deployment instead.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Run kubectl rollout status right after a set image — it blocks until success/failure instead of guessing from get pods.
  • Set requests==limits (Guaranteed QoS) on anything you can't afford to lose, instead of leaving resources unset.
  • Check kubectl rollout history before undoing twice — you might already be one revision away from the good one.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 27)

the Chapter 27 cheat-card 
kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0    # triggers a rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj                               # blocks until the rollout finishes or fails
kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj                              # lists past revisions + change-cause
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj                                  # reverts to the immediately-previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=1                  # reverts to a specific older revision
kubectl scale deployment/easypj --replicas=5 -n easypj                  # scale replica count up/down
kubectl describe pod <pod>                                             # shows OOMKilled / probe failure events
kubectl create namespace staging                                        # isolates an environment by name
kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/prod                                 # applies a base + environment-specific patch

🧠 Chapter 27 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

Rolling updates, rollback, probes, environments, and QoS — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
With replicas=5, maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=1, what's the MIN and MAX Pod count mid-rollout?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Minimum 4, maximum 6 Pods.

EXPLANATION

5 replicas − 1 (maxUnavailable) = 4 min; 5 + 1 (maxSurge) = 6 max — the 27.1 diagram never drops below 4 or exceeds 6 Ready+terminating Pods during the rollout.

Q2
Why doesn't a rolling update alone protect against a v2 image that starts fine but crashes under real traffic?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Because RollingUpdate only checks that the container process started — not that it's actually healthy under load.

EXPLANATION

Pairing it with a readiness probe (27.3) is what keeps a broken Pod out of the Service's endpoints; rollout status only reports "successfully rolled out," never "actually working."

Q3
Fill in the consequence of each probe failing: readinessProbe and livenessProbe.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

readinessProbe failing → Pod's IP removed from the Service's endpoint list, no restart. livenessProbe failing → container killed and restarted.

EXPLANATION

This is the entire distinction 27.3 draws between "can it serve traffic right now?" and "is it stuck and needs a restart?" — different questions, different consequences.

Q4
Why can identical liveness and readiness thresholds cause a "restart storm"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A slow-but-recovering Pod that would have simply been hidden by a failing readiness check instead gets killed by liveness at the same threshold.

EXPLANATION

Restarting doesn't fix the underlying slowness, so the cycle can repeat — give liveness a longer delay/period than readiness so a slow-but-alive Pod gets hidden, not killed.

Q5
What does kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=1 actually do at the ReplicaSet level?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It scales the rev.1 ReplicaSet back up to the desired replica count and scales the currently-active ReplicaSet down to 0.

EXPLANATION

Neither ReplicaSet is deleted, only their scale changes — which is why undo is near-instant and needs no image pull.

Q6
Why can't you always rollout undo to any past revision you remember shipping?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) prunes old ReplicaSets.

EXPLANATION

Once a revision is garbage-collected, Kubernetes has nothing left to scale back up — check kubectl rollout history first to confirm the revision still exists.

Q7
What's the difference between how a Namespace and a Kustomize overlay solve "run easypj in dev/staging/prod"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Namespace scopes NAMES; Kustomize scopes FILES.

EXPLANATION

Two easypj Deployments in different namespaces never collide (names); one base manifest plus small per-environment patches for things like replica count or image tag (files) — they solve different problems and are normally used together.

Q8
Using the requests-vs-limits table from 27.5, what QoS class does a Pod with requests==limits get, and why does that matter operationally?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Guaranteed — evicted LAST under node memory pressure.

EXPLANATION

The kubelet's eviction manager reads the same cgroup limits that make Guaranteed Pods the safest to run; requests<limits (Burstable) is evicted 2nd, and nothing set (BestEffort) is evicted first.

Q9
What does a namespace-level ResourceQuota actually cap, and what happens to a Pod that would exceed it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It caps the SUM of requests/limits across every Pod in that namespace.

EXPLANATION

For example, a total requests.cpu: "2" across ALL Pods combined; a Pod that would push the namespace over quota sits Pending with a quota-exceeded event instead of being scheduled.

Q10
Chain together what happens on a node running low on memory to a BestEffort Pod vs a Guaranteed Pod.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The kubelet's eviction manager checks QoS class first — BestEffort Pods are evicted FIRST, Burstable next, Guaranteed Pods LAST.

EXPLANATION

BestEffort Pods have no requests/limits at all and therefore the weakest cgroup protection — the direct operational consequence of the QoS table in 27.5.

🔬 Practice Drill 27.1 — Ship, Fail, Undo (8 min)

Ship a deliberately broken image tag to easypj, watch kubectl rollout status report failure, then kubectl rollout undo it — time how long the undo takes and confirm kubectl rollout history still shows both revisions afterward.

📌 Chapter 27 Visual Summary — safely changeable, not just running
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ship v2 → RollingUpdate (maxSurge/maxUnavail) → probes          │
  │                  │                                 │           │
  │            bad? rollout undo              readiness/liveness   │
  │                  │                                 │           │
  │                  ▼                                 ▼           │

In one line: Chapter 27 is the "safely changeable" half of running easypj on Kubernetes: rolling updates and rollback handle WHEN code changes, readiness/liveness probes handle WHETHER a Pod is trusted with traffic or life at all, Namespaces/Kustomize handle WHERE (which environment) a manifest applies, and requests/limits/QoS/ResourceQuota handle HOW MUCH of the cluster any one Pod or namespace is allowed to consume.

The takeaway: none of these are Docker concepts — they only exist because a cluster, unlike one host, has to make these decisions on your behalf.

☸️ Part 9 · Recap · Complete

Docker → Kubernetes — The Bridge Is Crossed

You started Part 9 with easypj running happily on one Docker host; you finish it having deployed that exact same image to a real Kubernetes cluster, given it a stable address, and made it safely changeable — rolling updates, instant rollback, health probes, and per-environment overlays all wired in. None of this is Docker Certified Associate material — it's the on-ramp that makes the jump to the companion CKA guide painless instead of a cold start.

🔑 Part 9 — Key Takeaways

  • Kubernetes only takes over where Docker's single host runs out of answers — multi-host scheduling, auto-scaling, self-healing, rollback — while the same OCI image and Dockerfile carry over unchanged; every Docker noun has a K8s translation (container→Pod, volume→PVC, compose.yaml→Deployment+Service+ConfigMap+Secret+PVC), and kompose convert only ever bootstraps a first draft (Ch 25).
  • A real deploy is 4 YAMLs applied in order — namespace → ConfigMap/Secret → Deployment+Service — with an exact image tag (never :latest), matching selector/labels, real requests/limits, and the right Service type; you scale the Deployment, never a bare Pod (Ch 26).
  • Running isn't the same as safely changeable: RollingUpdate (bounded by maxSurge/maxUnavailable) ships v2 with zero downtime, rollout undo reverts it instantly, readinessProbe gates Service traffic while livenessProbe gates the Pod's life, and Namespaces + Kustomize + requests/limits/QoS/ResourceQuota keep dev/staging/prod from colliding or starving each other (Ch 27).
  • 🎓 Scope: none of Part 9 is graded DCA material (0% weight — "Beyond DCA Scope") — it's CKA-track depth, built entirely on the same easypj image Part 3 already produced.
  • 🔑 kompose convert · kubectl apply -f · kubectl rollout status / undo · kubectl scale deployment · kubectl get endpoints

In words: Chapter 25 draws the line without touching easypj's code at all — the image and Dockerfile stay exactly as Part 3 left them, and every Docker noun gets a Kubernetes name (Pod, PVC, CNI, Deployment+Service). Chapter 26 turns that vocabulary into 4 real YAMLs, applied in a fixed order so nothing references something that doesn't exist yet, ending in 3 Pods answering real HTTP traffic through a Service.

Chapter 27 is the second-deploy problem: a RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually within maxSurge/maxUnavailable bounds, rollout undo re-points the Deployment at an old ReplicaSet in seconds, and readiness/liveness probes decide whether a Pod earns traffic or gets killed. Namespaces plus Kustomize let dev/staging/prod share one manifest source, and requests/limits/QoS/ResourceQuota stop any one Pod — or team — from starving the rest of the cluster.

The one idea to keep: Docker got you a running container on one machine; Kubernetes gets you a cluster that keeps that same container running, reachable, and safely upgradeable — none of it required for the DCA exam, all of it the exact ground the companion CKA guide starts from.

Chapter 28 · Docker Swarm — Native Orchestration

Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in orchestrator — simpler than Kubernetes, using the same Docker CLI you already know. Kubernetes is powerful but heavy — sometimes a small team needs multi-host orchestration WITHOUT a new tool, a new CLI, or a new YAML dialect. Swarm is that answer: it is Docker itself, turned into a cluster with three extra commands. This chapter builds Swarm from init to production-grade quorum, update and rollback configuration — knowledge the DCA exam weights at 25%, its single largest domain.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3-4 hours 🐝 Swarm 🎯 DCA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain the manager/worker split and exactly what Raft-replicated state each role holds
  • ✅ Justify Swarm vs Kubernetes for a given team size using evidence, not preference
  • ✅ Bootstrap a real multi-node Swarm with swarm init/swarm join and verify it with docker node ls
  • ✅ Deploy, scale, update and stack-deploy services with the same verbs docker run/docker compose already taught
  • ✅ Explain why the routing mesh answers on every node regardless of where a task actually runs
  • ✅ Deliver secrets/configs as mounted files instead of visible env vars
  • ✅ Compute quorum for any manager count and know exactly when swarm unlock is required
  • ✅ Configure update pacing, failure-action and order so a bad deploy pauses or rolls back itself
  • ✅ Pin and spread tasks with hard constraints vs soft placement preferences, and separate ingress from docker_gwbridge
🎓 DCA Relevance
Orchestration 25%
🎯 This Chapter IS the Orchestration Domain

Chapter 28 carries more exam points per page than any other chapter in this guide — it IS the DCA's single largest domain (25%), and Swarm is most of what that domain tests.

  • Why this chapter exists: Kubernetes is powerful but heavy — sometimes a small team needs multi-host orchestration without a new tool, a new CLI, or a new YAML dialect. Swarm is Docker itself, turned into a cluster with three extra commands.
