28.1 What is Docker Swarm?

Swarm mode turns a group of Docker hosts into a single virtual host. You use docker service commands (similar to docker run) and Swarm distributes containers across nodes, handles failover, and provides built-in load balancing. A manager node runs the Raft-replicated cluster store, the orchestrator (reconciling desired vs actual tasks), and the scheduler (assigning tasks to nodes); workers only run tasks and report health back. docker service create is declarative — you state the desired replica count, and Swarm keeps making it true.

Docker Swarm Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🐝 DOCKER SWARM ARCHITECTURE                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                     SWARM CLUSTER                                 │    │
  │  │                                                                  │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────┐ │    │
  │  │  │  🧠 MANAGER NODE 1 (Leader)  │  │  🧠 MANAGER NODE 2        │ │    │
  │  │  │                              │  │  (Follower, standby)      │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Maintains cluster state   │  │                           │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Raft consensus DB         │  │  • Takes over if Leader   │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Scheduler (assigns tasks) │  │    fails!                 │ │    │
  │  │  │  • API endpoint              │  │                           │ │    │
  │  │  │  • docker service create     │  │  ⚠️ Managers also run     │ │    │
  │  │  │                              │  │     tasks (can opt out)   │ │    │
  │  │  └──────────────┬───────────────┘  └───────────────────────────┘ │    │
  │  │                 │                                                 │    │
  │  │                 │  Assign tasks                                   │    │
  │  │                 ▼                                                 │    │
  │  │  ┌───────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │  💪 WORKER NODE 1        │  │  💪 WORKER NODE 2         │    │    │
  │  │  │                           │  │                           │    │    │
  │  │  │  easypj:v1 (replica 1)   │  │  easypj:v1 (replica 2)   │    │    │
  │  │  │  postgres:15 (replica 1) │  │  postgres:15 (replica 2) │    │    │
  │  │  │  redis:7                 │  │  nginx:latest             │    │    │
  │  │  │                           │  │                           │    │    │
  │  │  │  Reports health to mgr   │  │  Reports health to mgr    │    │    │
  │  │  └───────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ROUTING MESH: curl ANY_NODE:8000 → routes to easypj container ✅        │
  │  OVERLAY NETWORK: Containers on different nodes communicate seamlessly  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Restaurant HQ Analogy

The architecture diagram above is a restaurant chain HQ (managers, Raft-synced so any one can answer) directing several kitchens (workers) — orders (services) go to HQ, and HQ decides which kitchen cooks which dish (task placement).

easypj: docker service create --name easypj --replicas 3 easypj:v1 looks exactly like docker run, but Swarm spreads the 3 tasks across however many worker nodes exist.

⚠️ Managers Also Run Tasks By Default

Under load, this steals CPU cycles from the control plane (Raft, scheduling, the API). In production, drain manager nodes so they only manage: docker node update --availability drain <manager>.

28.2 Swarm vs Kubernetes

Given a real team's constraints, you should be able to choose Swarm or Kubernetes in one sentence, using evidence rather than preference. The 20-dimension table below is not close on ecosystem, multi-tenancy, or auto-scaling — Swarm loses those outright. It is genuinely competitive on the first five rows: installation, CLI familiarity, learning curve, scaling, and rolling updates — because Swarm reuses the docker CLI you already know.

Dimension🐝 Docker Swarm☸️ Kubernetes
InstallationBuilt into Docker ✅kubeadm/minikube
CLIdocker service createkubectl apply -f
Learning Curve🟢 Low (hours)🔴 High (weeks/months)
Scalingdocker service scalekubectl scale + HPA
Rolling Updates✅ Built-in✅ Built-in
Rollback✅ docker service rollback✅ kubectl rollout undo
Service Discovery✅ DNS built-in✅ CoreDNS
Load Balancing✅ Routing Mesh✅ Service + Ingress
Secrets✅ docker secret✅ K8s Secrets
Configs✅ docker config✅ K8s ConfigMaps
Multi-Tenancy❌ None✅ Namespaces
RBAC❌ Limited✅ Full RBAC
Storage Orchestration⚠️ Volume plugins✅ PV+PVC+CSI
Auto-Scaling❌ Manual only✅ HPA built-in
Auto-Healing✅ Basic (restart)✅ Advanced (reschedule)
Ecosystem🔴 Small🟢 Massive (CNCF)
Cloud Support⚠️ Limited✅ EKS/GKE/AKS
GitOps Support❌ Minimal✅ ArgoCD/Flux
Community🟡 Medium🟢 Huge
Best For3-10 nodes, simple10-1000+ nodes, complex
💡 The Pickup Truck Analogy

Swarm is a reliable pickup truck: no towing rating for a highway of microservices, but it starts every morning with a key you already own. Kubernetes is the highway fleet — more capability, more paperwork, more training to drive it.

easypj: a 3-node team demo needs zero-downtime deploys and secrets — row-for-row, Swarm's ✅ column covers exactly that; the ❌ rows (RBAC, multi-tenancy, HPA) don't matter at 3 nodes.

📖 Building a Migration Checklist

From the table, every row where Swarm is ❌ or ⚠️ is a checklist item for "when to migrate to Kubernetes" — once 2+ of those rows start to matter for your team, it's time to move.

⚠️ The DCA Exam Tests Swarm, Not Kubernetes

Don't let K8s knowledge from Chapters 25-27 substitute for hands-on docker service/docker stack practice — this domain is graded on Swarm mechanics specifically.

28.3 Creating a Swarm Cluster

Standing up a real cluster and proving every node is visible from the manager takes under 5 commands:

TERMINAL
# On Manager node: initialize swarm
$ docker swarm init --advertise-addr 192.168.1.100
Swarm initialized: current node is now a manager.
To add a worker: docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-xxx... 192.168.1.100:2377

# On Worker nodes: join the swarm
$ docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-xxx... 192.168.1.100:2377
This node joined a swarm as a worker.

# View cluster nodes
$ docker node ls
ID        HOSTNAME    STATUS    AVAILABILITY   MANAGER STATUS
abc...    manager-1   Ready     Active         Leader
def...    worker-1    Ready     Active
ghi...    worker-2    Ready     Active
📖 Two Tokens, One CA Fingerprint

swarm init generates TWO join tokens — one for workers, one for managers (docker swarm join-token manager). Each token embeds the cluster's CA fingerprint, so a node cannot join by guessing an address alone. Ports 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp, and 4789/udp must be open between all nodes.

💡 The Wristband Analogy

The join token is a wristband with a hidden watermark — knowing the door address (IP:2377) alone doesn't get you in; you need the exact token from that specific cluster.

easypj: once 3 nodes show in docker node ls, deploying easypj as a Swarm service (28.4) can spread its replicas across all 3 — the same laptops that ran docker compose up in Chapter 11 now form a real cluster.

28.4 Deploying Services in Swarm

docker service create is docker run plus a desired replica COUNT — Swarm's orchestrator keeps re-creating tasks until docker service ps shows that many Running. Where docker run promises "start THIS container," docker service create promises "always have N of these running, somewhere" — a standing order, not a one-time request.

TERMINAL
# Create a service (like docker run, but multi-host)
$ docker service create --name easypj --replicas 3 -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1

# List services
$ docker service ls
ID        NAME    MODE        REPLICAS  IMAGE
abc...    easypj  replicated  3/3       ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1

# which node runs what
$ docker service ps easypj

# Scale up
$ docker service scale easypj=5

# Rolling update to new version
$ docker service update --image ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0 easypj

# Rollback
$ docker service rollback easypj

# Deploy a full stack (like docker compose, for Swarm)
$ docker stack deploy -c stack.yaml easypj

docker stack deploy reads a compose-format file and creates one service PER top-level service key — multi-service Compose, cluster-wide. easypj: docker stack deploy -c stack.yaml easypj turns Chapter 11's compose.yaml (with deploy: keys added) into django, postgres, redis and nginx services in ONE command.

FlagMeaning
-c / --compose-filepath, or - for stdin; repeatable to layer multiple compose files
-d / --detachdefault true; returns immediately instead of waiting for convergence
--pruneremove services no longer referenced by the file
-q / --quietsuppress progress output
--resolve-imagedefault always (always/changed/never) — query registry for image digest and platform info
--with-registry-authsend registry auth to Swarm agents
📖 Stack Deploy Requirements

Requires Compose file version 3.0+ and must run on a swarm MANAGER node; unsupported Compose keys (e.g. links) are reported as ignored, not treated as errors.

⚠️ Rolling Update by Default

docker service update --image triggers a rolling update by DEFAULT — it is not an in-place restart, it follows 28.8's update-config rules.

28.5 Swarm Networking & Storage

Swarm's routing mesh makes every node in the cluster able to serve any service — even if that node isn't running the container. The overlay network connects containers across hosts transparently, over VXLAN (UDP 4789). Storage uses volume drivers for multi-host persistence.

Routing Mesh — Any Node Answers
  client ─▶ curl node3:8000 (node3 runs NO easypj task)
          ▼
  node3's IPVS load balancer (every node runs one)
          ▼
  overlay network "ingress" ─▶ routes to a node WITH a task
          ▼
  easypj task (on node1 or node2) answers
💡 Routing Mesh Magic

With Swarm, curl worker-2:8000 works even if worker-2 isn't running an easypj container. The routing mesh intercepts the request and forwards it to a node that IS running the container. This means you can point your load balancer at ANY Swarm node — built-in high availability.

easypj: expose easypj with -p 8000:8000 in service create; curl http://<any-node-ip>:8000/jobs/ succeeds from all 3 nodes even though only 2 nodes hold an easypj task.

⚠️ The Mesh Needs Its Own Ports Open

The routing mesh needs ports 7946 (tcp/udp) and 4789 (udp) open between ALL nodes — one blocked node breaks the mesh in ways that look like random 502s, not a connectivity error.

28.6 Swarm Secrets & Configs

A Swarm secret is encrypted at rest in the Raft log and mounted as an in-memory tmpfs FILE at /run/secrets/<name> — ONLY inside services that declare it, never as a visible env var (docker inspect cannot leak it). Configs (docker config create) use the same delivery mechanism for non-secret files.

TERMINAL
# Create a secret (encrypted at rest, in transit)
$ echo "super-secret-key" | docker secret create django_secret -

# Create a config (non-sensitive)
$ docker config create nginx_conf nginx.conf

# Use in a service
$ docker service create --secret django_secret --config nginx_conf easypj

# Secrets mounted as files in /run/secrets/
# Configs mounted as files at / (config name becomes filename)
stack.yaml (django with a Swarm secret)
services:
  django:
    image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
    secrets: [django_secret_key]
    environment:
      SECRET_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/django_secret_key
secrets:
  django_secret_key:
    external: true
# created once, out-of-band:
# $ printf 'django-insecure-CHANGE-ME' | \
#     docker secret create django_secret_key -
💡 The Corkboard Analogy

A Swarm secret is a note passed hand-to-hand and never pinned to the office corkboard (env vars, visible in inspect); a Config is the same delivery method for a memo that isn't sensitive, just needs to reach exactly the right desk.

easypj: settings.py reads open(os.environ["SECRET_KEY_FILE"]).read().strip() instead of os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] — one line changed, and the value never appears in docker service inspect easypj.

🛑 Secrets Are Immutable

There is no docker secret update. Updating one means creating name_v2, updating the service to reference it, then removing the old one.

28.7 Raft Consensus & Swarm Lock/Unlock

Swarm uses the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain cluster state across manager nodes. The Raft log stores ALL cluster state — service definitions, node membership, secrets, and configs. Raft requires a strict MAJORITY ((N/2)+1, integer division) of managers reachable to commit any write to cluster state. Understanding Raft is critical for the DCA Orchestration domain.

Raft Consensus — Manager Quorum
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RAFT CONSENSUS IN DOCKER SWARM                 │
  │                                                             │
  │  N managers → tolerates floor((N-1)/2) failures             │
  │                                                             │
  │  1 manager:  quorum 1, 0 failures tolerated (not production)│
  │  2 managers: quorum 2, 0 failures tolerated (even = no      │
  │              quorum if split!)                              │
  │  3 managers: quorum 2, 1 failure tolerated  ★ minimum prod  │
  │  4 managers: quorum 3, 1 failure tolerated  ⚠️ same as 3,   │
  │              wastes a machine                               │
  │  5 managers: quorum 3, 2 failures tolerated ★ recommended   │
  │  7 managers: quorum 4, 3 failures tolerated ★ large clusters│
  │                                                             │
  │  Raft requires (N/2)+1 managers for quorum.                 │
  │  NEVER use an even number — wastes resources.               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔒
Autolock & Swarm Lock

Autolock encrypts the Raft log on disk. When a manager restarts, it requires an unlock key to decrypt and rejoin. Enable: docker swarm init --autolock. Unlock after restart: docker swarm unlock (paste key). View key: docker swarm unlock-key. Rotate key: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate. Without autolock, the Raft log AND all secrets/configs are stored in plaintext on disk.

🔄
Swarm Lock/Unlock Workflow

Enable: docker swarm update --autolock=true. Disable: docker swarm update --autolock=false. After daemon restart: docker swarm unlock ← REQUIRED before any swarm commands work. Store the unlock key safely — if lost, you cannot recover the cluster (must force new cluster).

⚠️ DCA Critical: Autolock

The DCA exam WILL test autolock. Know: (1) it encrypts the Raft log at rest, (2) without it, secrets/configs are plaintext on manager disks, (3) after manager restart, docker swarm unlock is required, (4) rotating the unlock key is docker swarm unlock-key --rotate. This is a top-5 most-tested Swarm topic.

TERMINAL
# Initialize swarm with autolock
$ docker swarm init --autolock
Swarm initialized: current node is now a manager.
To unlock: docker swarm unlock
Unlock key: SWMKEY-1-xxxx...  ← SAVE THIS!

# Enable autolock on existing swarm
$ docker swarm update --autolock=true

# Rotate the unlock key
$ docker swarm unlock-key --rotate

# View current unlock key (if you have it)
$ docker swarm unlock-key

# After manager daemon restart — MUST unlock:
$ docker swarm unlock
Please enter unlock key: [paste key]

# Check autolock status
$ docker info | grep -A2 "Swarm"
  Autolock Managers: true
  Unlock Key: SWMKEY-1-xxxx...
💡 The Company Board Analogy

Quorum is a company board vote: 5 members need 3 to agree — losing 2 still passes votes. Adding a 6th member (even count) needs 4 to agree, so you gained a salary without gaining tolerance. Autolock is a safe that relocks itself on every reboot — useful against a stolen disk, useless if you lose the combination.

easypj: a 3-manager Swarm running easypj survives ONE manager dying at 3 AM with zero manual action — the surviving 2 still form quorum; a 2-manager Swarm survives ZERO manager failures (quorum would need both).

easypj's 5-Manager Swarm — Quorum Intact vs Quorum Lost
 ┌──────────────────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ INTACT (3/5 up)          │                    │ LOST (2/5 up)            │
 ├──────────────────────────┤   lose 1 mgr  ─▶   ├──────────────────────────┤
 │ service ls      OK       │                    │ service ls      OK       │
 │ service scale   OK       │  ◀─ recover 1 mgr  │ service scale   HANGS    │
 │ service update  OK       │                    │ service update  HANGS    │
 │ tasks: RUNNING           │                    │ tasks: RUNNING           │
 └──────────────────────────┘                    └──────────────────────────┘
📖 Reads Survive, Writes Hang

Reads survive quorum loss because worker nodes execute tasks and route traffic independently of Raft — only WRITES to cluster state (scale, update, new service) need a manager majority to commit.

🔧 Under the Hood — Raft consensus, leader election & the manager log

Every manager runs the SAME replicated log via the Raft protocol: the cluster store (services, networks, secrets, task assignments) is a sequence of log entries, and a write only COMMITS once a majority of managers have persisted it to disk — the exact majority behind 28.7's quorum math. Managers elect a single LEADER by randomized election timeout: if a manager doesn't hear from a leader within its window, it becomes a candidate, increments the current TERM number, and requests votes; whichever candidate first collects a majority becomes leader for that term. Only the leader accepts writes and dispatches tasks — followers transparently redirect commands like docker service create to the leader, so any manager's socket works. docker node promote <id> / docker node demote <id> move a node between worker and Raft-participating manager without rebuilding the cluster — the safest way to resize manager count is always odd → odd (3→5, never 3→4).

  RAFT LOG REPLICATION — one write, three managers

  docker service scale easypj=5   (sent to any manager)
           │
           ▼
   LEADER appends entry to its Raft log (term N)
           │
     ┌─────┼─────┐
     ▼     ▼     ▼
  Mgr1    Mgr2    Mgr3    replicate + persist the SAME entry
 (leader)(follower)(follower)
     │     │     │
     └──▶ majority ACKs (2 of 3) ──▶ entry COMMITTED ──▶ applied
🔑 A write only becomes real cluster state once a MAJORITY of managers hold the same log entry on disk — that single mechanic is the reason quorum math, autolock, and odd manager counts all matter.

28.8 Advanced Service Update Configuration

docker service update has extensive flags controlling exactly how rolling updates behave. Swarm updates ONE batch (parallelism tasks) at a time, waits update-monitor to see if new tasks stay healthy, then either proceeds after update-delay or acts on update-failure-action once failures exceed update-max-failure-ratio. These flags appear frequently on the DCA exam:

FlagDefaultPurposeExample
--update-parallelism1How many replicas to update simultaneously--update-parallelism 2
--update-delay0sWait time between update batches--update-delay 30s
--update-failure-actionpauseWhat to do if an update fails (pause|continue|rollback)--update-failure-action rollback
--update-max-failure-ratio0Max fraction of tasks that can fail (0-1)--update-max-failure-ratio 0.2
--update-monitor5sHow long to monitor new tasks before declaring success--update-monitor 30s
--update-orderstop-firststop-first (stop old then start new) or start-first (start new then stop old)--update-order start-first
stop-first vs start-first Update Order
  stop-first (default):                     start-first:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Before: [v1][v1][v1]     │              │ Before: [v1][v1][v1]     │
  │ Step 1: [  ][v1][v1] STOP│              │ Step 1: [v2][v1][v1] NEW│
  │ Step 2: [v2][v1][v1] START│             │ Step 2: [v2][  ][v1] STOP│
  │ Capacity drops temporarily│              │ Step 3: [v2][v2][v1] NEW│
  │ ⚠️ 1 less replica during  │              │ Capacity NEVER drops!   │
  └──────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────┘
  Use stop-first when resources are         Use start-first when you can't
  tight and you can't run extras.           afford any capacity reduction.
TERMINAL
# Aggressive update: fast, parallel, auto-rollback on failure
$ docker service update \
    --update-parallelism 3 \
    --update-delay 5s \
    --update-failure-action rollback \
    --update-order start-first \
    --image ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0 easypj

# Conservative update: slow, safe, manual intervention on failure
$ docker service update \
    --update-parallelism 1 \
    --update-delay 60s \
    --update-failure-action pause \
    --update-monitor 30s \
    --image ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0 easypj
💡 The Cautious Surgeon Analogy

parallelism+delay+monitor is a cautious surgeon: operate on one patient, watch their vitals for the monitor window, only move to the next batch if they're stable — failure-action is the "abort the procedure" protocol if too many patients react badly.

easypj: --update-order start-first matters most for easypj's web tier — users never see a moment with fewer gunicorn workers than before, unlike the default stop-first.

⚠️ The Default Is pause, Not rollback

A bad update just STOPS mid-way unless you set --update-failure-action rollback explicitly (see 28.9).

28.9 Service Rollback Configuration

Rollback is triggered by docker service rollback OR automatically by --update-failure-action rollback. --rollback re-applies the service's PREVIOUS spec using the same batching machinery as a forward update — every --update-* flag has a --rollback-* twin. All configs, secrets, and mounts revert:

FlagDefaultPurpose
--rollback-parallelism1How many tasks to rollback at once
--rollback-delay0sWait time between rollback batches
--rollback-failure-actionpauseWhat to do if rollback itself fails (pause|continue)
--rollback-max-failure-ratio0Max fraction of rollback tasks that can fail
--rollback-monitor5sHow long to monitor rolled-back tasks
--rollback-orderstop-firststop-first or start-first during rollback
TERMINAL
# Manual rollback (instant — uses previous spec)
$ docker service rollback easypj

# View rollback history
$ docker service ps easypj
# Look for tasks with "Shutdown" state — shows which version was running

# Configure auto-rollback on failed update
$ docker service update \
    --update-failure-action rollback \
    --update-max-failure-ratio 0.3 \
    --update-monitor 15s \
    easypj

# Configure rollback behavior itself
$ docker service update \
    --rollback-parallelism 2 \
    --rollback-delay 10s \
    --rollback-failure-action pause \
    easypj
💡 Rollback Is Update, Run Backwards

Rollback isn't a separate "undo" engine — it's the exact same relay-handoff machinery as 28.8, just running backwards: same batching, same pause points, same order flag.

easypj: an automatic rollback restores easypj:v1 the moment enough v2 tasks fail their startup, often before an on-call engineer even opens their laptop.

Update flag (28.8)Rollback flag (28.9)
--update-parallelism 1--rollback-parallelism 1
--update-delay 20s--rollback-delay 10s
--update-monitor 30s--rollback-monitor 30s
--update-failure-action rollback--rollback-failure-action pause
--update-max-failure-ratio 0.2--rollback-max-failure-ratio 0.2
--update-order start-first--rollback-order start-first
📖 One Previous Spec Only

Unlike Kubernetes' revisionHistoryLimit (which keeps several past revisions), Swarm remembers only ONE previous spec. A rollback that itself fails has no --rollback-to-revision escape — ship a fixed image forward instead of undoing further back.

⚠️ Task History Ages Out Fast

docker service ps only keeps a short task history by default — diagnose a failed update FAST, before the Shutdown/Failed tasks needed for docker service logs age out.

28.10 Placement Constraints, Preferences & docker_gwbridge

Control WHERE services run with placement constraints and preferences. A constraint is a hard FILTER — Swarm leaves a task Pending forever rather than place it where the constraint fails. A placement preference is a soft SORT — Swarm spreads tasks as evenly as possible across the label's values but still places them if perfect spread is impossible.

📍
Placement Constraints

Restrict which nodes can run a service:
--constraint node.labels.ssd==true
--constraint node.role==worker
--constraint node.hostname!=db-server
Add labels: docker node update --label-add ssd=true node1
View labels: docker node inspect node1

📊
Placement Preferences

Spread tasks across labeled nodes:
--placement-pref spread=node.labels.rack
Ensures tasks distribute across racks/zones for HA. Unlike constraints (hard rule), preferences are soft — scheduler tries to satisfy but won't block scheduling.

Swarm Network Architecture — ingress + docker_gwbridge
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           SWARM NETWORKING INTERNALS                         │
  │                                                             │
  │  EVERY Swarm node has TWO special networks:                 │
  │                                                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  ingress (overlay)                                   │   │
  │  │  • Carries published port traffic (routing mesh)     │   │
  │  │  • IPVS load balances across ALL replicas            │   │
  │  │  • Every node joins this automatically               │   │
  │  │  • Subnet: 10.255.0.0/16 (default)                   │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  docker_gwbridge (bridge)                            │   │
  │  │  • Connects containers to host's external network    │   │
  │  │  • Provides outbound internet access for tasks       │   │
  │  │  • Every node has one docker_gwbridge                 │   │
  │  │  • Subnet: 172.18.0.0/16 (default)                   │   │
  │  │  • Check: docker network inspect docker_gwbridge     │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                             │
  │  PUBLISHED PORT FLOW:                                      │
  │  Request → ANY_NODE:8000 → ingress → IPVS → Task Container │
  │                                                             │
  │  OUTBOUND FLOW:                                            │
  │  Task Container → docker_gwbridge → Host Network → Internet│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TERMINAL
# Add node labels for placement
$ docker node update --label-add ssd=true --label-add rack=r1 node1
$ docker node update --label-add ssd=false --label-add rack=r2 node2

# Constrain service to SSD nodes only
$ docker service create --name db \
    --constraint node.labels.ssd==true \
    postgres:15

# Spread across racks for HA
$ docker service create --name web \
    --placement-pref "spread=node.labels.rack" \
    --replicas 6 nginx

# Inspect special Swarm networks
$ docker network inspect ingress
$ docker network inspect docker_gwbridge

# Customize docker_gwbridge subnet (in daemon.json):
# {"default-address-pools":[{"base":"10.10.0.0/16","size":24}]}
💡 The Locked Door Analogy

A constraint is a locked door (db data only enters the db room); a preference is a maître d' seating parties evenly across sections without ever turning a guest away. docker_gwbridge is the building's street-facing exit; ingress is the internal hallway connecting every room.

easypj: --constraint 'node.labels.type==db' keeps postgres's volume on the ONE node with the actual disk; easypj's --placement-pref keeps web tasks balanced across zone a/b so a single zone outage doesn't take all replicas at once.

⚠️ An Impossible Constraint Fails Silently

A typo'd label or zero matching nodes leaves the task Pending FOREVER with no error — confirm with docker node ls --filter before assuming a scheduler bug.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Swarm is the Docker Engine itself, clustered — no new CLI, no new control plane to install.
  • Managers hold Raft-replicated state and schedule tasks; workers only execute and report health.
  • Swarm trades ecosystem, RBAC, and auto-scaling for CLI familiarity and a near-zero learning curve versus Kubernetes.
  • swarm init + swarm join --token is the entire cluster bootstrap; docker node ls is the entire verification.
  • docker service create/scale/update and docker stack deploy reuse docker run/docker compose vocabulary at cluster scale.
  • The routing mesh (IPVS + the ingress overlay) makes every node a valid entry point regardless of where a task actually runs.
  • Secrets and configs mount as tmpfs files, never as visible env vars, and are immutable once created.
  • Quorum needs a strict majority ((N/2)+1) — always deploy odd manager counts; --autolock protects the Raft log at rest.
  • Update pacing (parallelism/delay/monitor), failure-action, and order decide whether a bad deploy pauses, rolls back, or ships zero-downtime; hard constraints vs soft preferences plus gwbridge vs ingress finish the placement picture.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming managers only manage, never run application tasks → Managers run tasks by default too — under load this steals CPU from the control plane; drain them (docker node update --availability drain) in production.
  • Adding a 4th manager "for extra safety" → An even manager count buys zero extra fault tolerance over one fewer odd count — 4 managers still tolerates only 1 failure, identical to 3. Always deploy odd counts (3, 5, 7).
  • Expecting --update-failure-action to default to rollback → The default is pause — a bad update just STOPS mid-way unless you explicitly set --update-failure-action rollback.
  • Trying to roll back more than one step with --rollback-to-revision → Swarm keeps only ONE previous spec — no such flag exists; ship a fixed image forward instead.
  • Expecting an error when a placement constraint matches zero nodes → The task just stays Pending FOREVER, silently — confirm with docker node ls --filter instead of waiting for an error.
  • Waiting to investigate a failed update → docker service ps keeps only a short task history — pull docker service logs FAST before Shutdown/Failed tasks age out.
  • Assuming docker stack deploy will build: images from a Dockerfile → Stack deploy ignores build: entirely — images must be pre-built and pushed to a registry before stack deploy.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker node ls --filter role=manager isolates managers instantly when checking quorum health.
  • docker service ps <svc> --no-trunc shows the full error message for a failing task instead of a truncated one.
  • docker service update --force <svc> re-schedules every task even with no spec change — a fast way to redistribute after adding nodes.
  • Alias dsls='docker service ls' and dnls='docker node ls' — both get typed dozens of times per Swarm session.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 28)

the Chapter 28 cheat-card 
docker swarm init --advertise-addr <ip>          # become the first manager
docker swarm join --token <token> <ip>:2377      # add a worker or manager
docker swarm join-token manager                    # print the manager token
docker node ls                                      # list cluster + roles
docker node update --availability drain <node>    # stop scheduling new tasks here
docker service create --replicas N --name X img   # deploy a new service
docker service scale X=N                            # change replica count
docker service update --image img:vN X             # rolling update
docker service update --rollback X                  # manual rollback
docker stack deploy -c stack.yaml X                 # compose file, cluster-wide

🧠 Chapter 28 — DCA Practice Questions (12)

From manager/worker state to quorum math to placement constraints — 12 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What state does a Swarm MANAGER hold that a WORKER does not, and what mechanism keeps that state consistent across managers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Managers hold the Raft-replicated cluster store — service definitions, network/secret/config objects, task-to-node assignments — kept consistent via Raft consensus, which commits a write only once a majority of managers persist it. Workers hold no cluster state; they run assigned tasks and report health.

EXPLANATION

This is why docker service create works against ANY manager socket but is meaningless against a worker's — workers never see the full desired-state picture (28.1, 28.7).

Q2
A team is choosing between 3, 4, 5 and 7 managers. Which counts are correct and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
ManagersQuorum ((N/2)+1)Tolerated failures
321
431 (same as 3!)
532
743

Correct choices: 3, 5 or 7 — never 4.

EXPLANATION

4 needs the same quorum as 3 but tolerates the SAME single failure — pure added cost with zero added resilience (28.7).

Q3
What does docker swarm init --autolock protect, and what must every manager do after a reboot while it's enabled?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It encrypts the on-disk Raft log with a passphrase-derived key. After ANY manager restart, that manager blocks at "Swarm is locked" until docker swarm unlock supplies the passphrase (or the key, rotatable with unlock-key --rotate).

EXPLANATION

Autolock defends a stolen/copied disk, not a lost passphrase — store it somewhere that survives losing every manager at once (28.7).

Q4
Compare docker service scale easypj=5 and docker service update --replicas 5 easypj. Which is correct?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both — they produce the identical result.

EXPLANATION

The exam may present either spelling of the same operation; recognizing they're equivalent prevents second-guessing a "select all that apply" question (28.4).

Q5
docker service ps easypj shows tasks on node1 and node2 only, yet curl node3:8000 still returns 200. Why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

client → curl node3:8000 (no easypj task here) → node3's IPVS load balancer (every node runs one) → ingress overlay → routes to node1/node2 (has a task) → easypj task answers.

EXPLANATION

The routing mesh runs on EVERY node and forwards over the built-in ingress overlay — task placement and valid entry points are two different questions (28.5).

Q6
Why does a Swarm secret protect SECRET_KEY better than an env var, mechanically?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A secret is delivered as a file on an in-memory tmpfs at /run/secrets/<name>, visible only inside services that declare it; docker service inspect cannot print its value. An env var is visible to anyone who can docker inspect the container.

EXPLANATION

docker config create uses the same file-delivery mechanism for non-secret data — the difference is encryption, not delivery (28.6).

Q7
An update runs with --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 20s --update-failure-action pause --update-max-failure-ratio 0.25. Batch 2 fails 30% of its tasks. What happens?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The update PAUSES — it does not roll back or continue — because 30% exceeds the 25% max-failure-ratio and the configured action is pause.

EXPLANATION

Parallelism/delay/monitor control pacing; failure-action decides the RESPONSE — pause is the default and must be overridden for automatic rollback (28.8).

Q8
Under what exact condition does Swarm roll back a service automatically, with zero manual command?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Only when the original update was started with --update-failure-action rollback, and the observed failure ratio then exceeds --update-max-failure-ratio.

EXPLANATION

Rollback reuses the same batching machinery as a forward update — automation is opt-in per update, not a Swarm-wide default (28.9).

Q9
Reading this docker service ps easypj output, what happened?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
NAMEIMAGEDESIRED STATECURRENT STATE
easypj.1easypj:v1RunningRunning 2m ago
easypj.1easypj:v2ShutdownFailed 3m ago

Task easypj.1 was updated to v2, that task FAILED, and Swarm shut it down and replaced it with a new task on the previous image, v1.

EXPLANATION

service ps keeps a short history of both the failed and replacing task — read DESIRED vs CURRENT STATE together (28.9).

Q10
postgres has --constraint 'node.labels.type==db' but no node carries that label. What happens, and how would you know?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The task stays Pending FOREVER — no error is raised. Confirm via docker service ps postgres (Pending, no node) and docker node ls --filter label=type=db (zero results).

EXPLANATION

A constraint is a hard filter with no fallback, unlike a placement preference which always schedules — silent Pending is the most common "invisible" Swarm bug (28.10).

Q11
What's the functional difference between ingress and docker_gwbridge, and which explains random 502s from the mesh?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ingress is the overlay the routing mesh uses to route published-port traffic task-to-task across nodes; docker_gwbridge is the per-node bridge to the outside world. Random 502s from the mesh point to ingress (or its ports: 7946 tcp/udp, 4789 udp), not gwbridge.

EXPLANATION

They serve different traffic directions — ingress is intra-cluster east-west, gwbridge is north-south egress (28.5, 28.10).

Q12
"Half my easypj replicas vanished and won't come back, but docker service ls still works." Walk the diagnostic order.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
CheckWhat it tells you
docker node lsare nodes still Ready?
count Reachable/Leader managersis quorum intact?
docker service ps easypj --no-truncPending, Failed, Running?
docker node inspect / labelsdid a constraint drift?
docker service inspect --pretty easypjdid an update change specs?
EXPLANATION

service ls working proves quorum is intact, so the cause is scheduling-side, not consensus-side — check node availability and constraints before assuming cluster failure (28.7, 28.10).

🔬 Practice Drill 28.1 — Full Lifecycle + Auto-Rollback (10 min)

On a 3-node Swarm, deploy easypj with 3 replicas, scale to 6, then intentionally update to a broken tag with --update-failure-action rollback --update-max-failure-ratio 0.2. Stop the clock once docker service ps easypj shows the automatic rollback complete, unprompted.

Chapter 29 · Docker Compose Bridge to Production

Chapters 25-28 gave you two full orchestration paths — Kubernetes and Swarm. This chapter answers the question every team eventually asks: do we run Compose everywhere, or is there a real bridge from a laptop's compose.yaml to whatever orchestrator production actually uses? Compose is for development; Kubernetes (or Swarm) is for production. This chapter bridges the gap — converting Compose files to K8s manifests, using Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and understanding when to reach for which tool.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5-2 hours 🌉 Bridge

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ State which tool owns each stage of easypj's path from laptop to production, and why the image never changes across stages
  • ✅ Translate any daily docker compose command to its kubectl equivalent without pausing to think
  • ✅ Generate a first-draft Kubernetes manifest set from a real compose.yaml with kompose convert, and name exactly what it omits
  • ✅ Package easypj as a versioned, parameterized Helm chart and use helm upgrade/rollback
  • ✅ Patch replica counts and resources per environment with Kustomize base/overlays, with no templating engine at all
🎓 DCA Relevance
Orchestration background Image Creation, Management & Registry background
🎯 Not Its Own Domain, But the Bridge Every Team Needs

This chapter isn't a standalone graded domain, but it reinforces Domain 1 (Orchestration, stack deploy) and Domain 2 (image portability) — expect scenario questions that assume you know WHICH tool a given deployment story is using.

  • Why this chapter exists: your team knows Compose — how much of that knowledge survives the move to real production infrastructure? This chapter is the honest answer.
  • The one constant object: the Dockerfile from Chapter 5 never changes across dev/staging/prod — only WHO reads it (compose locally, kubectl/Swarm after CI pushes it) changes per stage.

🧭 Section Map

29.1 dev-vs-prod tool ownership → 29.2 compose-to-kubectl command mapping → 29.3 kompose's automatic (and incomplete) conversion → 29.4 Helm's templated, versioned packaging → 29.5 Kustomize's template-free overlays — each section moves from zero tooling (29.2) to increasingly powerful conversion tools (29.3-29.5).

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway
29.1 Compose for Local, K8s for ProdWho owns each stage of the pipeline?Same image, three consumers, different jobs.

29.1 Docker Compose for Local, K8s for Prod

Goal: state which tool owns each stage of easypj's path from a laptop to production, and why the SAME image crosses all three.

Dev → Staging → Production Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🎼 DEV → ☸️ PRODUCTION PIPELINE                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐   │
  │  │ 💻 DEVELOPMENT    │    │ 🧪 STAGING        │    │ 🚀 PRODUCTION     │   │
  │  │ docker compose up │───▶│ docker compose up │───▶│ kubectl apply    │   │
  │  │ Compose + volumes │    │ Compose + test DB │    │ K8s + Helm       │   │
  │  │ Hot reload        │    │ CI/CD pipeline    │    │ 3+ replicas      │   │
  │  │ DEBUG=True        │    │ DEBUG=False       │    │ Rolling updates  │   │
  │  └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 Same Docker image flows through all three environments!              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Zoomed into the actual command chain, the same pipeline reads as a straight line from a laptop to production:

The Command Chain — laptop to prod
   laptop: docker compose up  ─▶  CI: docker build + push  ─▶
   staging: kubectl apply -k overlays/staging  ─▶
   prod: kubectl apply -k overlays/prod (or docker stack deploy)
⚡
Compose Optimizes for Feedback Speed

Bind mounts, hot reload, no registry round-trip — everything on ONE machine, tuned so you see a code change in seconds.

🛡️
K8s/Swarm Optimize for Resilience

The same image, no bind mounts, health-checked and self-healing — tuned for staying up across MANY machines, not for editing code in place.

💡 The Workshop Bench vs Assembly Line Analogy

Compose is a workshop bench — fast, one craftsperson, tools within arm's reach. K8s/Swarm is the assembly line — slower to set up, built for volume and to keep running when one station goes down. Same product design, different stage.

easypj in practice: the Dockerfile from Chapter 5 never changes across this diagram — only WHO reads it (compose locally, kubectl/Swarm after CI pushes it) changes per stage.

⚠️ Bind-Mounting Source Code in Production Defeats the Point

Bind-mounting source code (Chapter 11.6's dev-workflow trick) in a production Deployment defeats the point of an immutable image — production always COPIES code in at build time. One image, one Dockerfile, three consumers: compose for feedback speed, K8s/Swarm for resilience at scale.

29.2 docker compose up vs kubectl apply

Goal: translate any daily docker compose command to its kubectl equivalent without pausing to think.

OperationDocker ComposeKubernetes
Startdocker compose up -dkubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
Statusdocker compose pskubectl get pods
Logsdocker compose logs -f appkubectl logs -f deploy/easypj
Shelldocker compose exec app shkubectl exec -it deploy/easypj -- sh
Restartdocker compose restart appkubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj
Stop/Removedocker compose downkubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
Scaledocker compose up --scale app=3kubectl scale deploy/easypj --replicas=3
Builddocker compose buildno equivalent — docker build (K8s never builds)
💡 Same Muscle Memory, New Gym

The MOVEMENT (start, stop, watch logs, get a shell) is identical, only the equipment name changed — you're not learning new exercises, just labels.

easypj in practice: docker compose logs -f django becomes kubectl logs -f deploy/easypj — same tail-the-output habit from Chapter 11.5, same gunicorn "Listening at :8000" line at the end.

📖 compose down vs kubectl delete -f

compose down deletes containers, networks (and, with -v, volumes) it created; kubectl delete -f deletes exactly the objects the YAML defines — a PVC survives Deployment deletion unless its own manifest is deleted too, mirroring compose's volume-survives-down default.

🛑 Gotcha — docker compose build Has No kubectl Equivalent

Kubernetes never builds images, it only schedules ones that already exist in a registry (back to 25.3/25.4). The build step always happens in CI, before kubectl ever runs.

29.3 kompose — Automatic Conversion

Goal: generate a first-draft manifest set from easypj's real compose.yaml, then know precisely what still needs hand-editing.

TERMINAL
$ kompose convert -f compose.yaml -o k8s/
INFO Kubernetes file "django-deployment.yaml" created
INFO Kubernetes file "django-service.yaml" created
INFO Kubernetes file "postgres-deployment.yaml" created
INFO Kubernetes file "postgres-service.yaml" created
INFO Kubernetes file "postgres-claim0-persistentvolumeclaim.yaml" created

# Review and modify generated files, then deploy:
$ kubectl apply -f k8s/

kompose maps each compose service to a Deployment (+ Service if ports: exist) and each named volume to a PersistentVolumeClaim; it does NOT set resource requests/limits, probes, or replicas beyond 1 — those are manual additions from Chapters 26-27.

💡 A First-Draft Translator, Not a Production Generator

kompose is a first-draft translator, exactly like 25.4's image-format translation — fast and literal, never production-ready without a human editor adding the parts (health, resources, replicas) the source document never had to specify.

easypj in practice: kompose correctly builds postgres's PVC from volumes: [postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data], but the generated Deployment has NO readinessProbe — add 27.3's probe by hand before trusting it.

⚠️ What kompose Does NOT Handle

Kompose cannot convert: (1) depends_on (K8s has no direct equivalent — use init containers), (2) healthcheck in compose (manually add liveness/readiness probes), (3) Swarm-specific keys (the deploy section), (4) build: (the image must already be pre-built and pushed). Treat kompose's output as roughly 80% of the job — the remaining 20% is production-specific refinement: resource limits, probes, ConfigMaps/Secrets, Ingress.

🛑 Gotcha — Re-running kompose convert OVERWRITES Your Edits

Re-running kompose convert after hand-editing generated files OVERWRITES those edits — there's no merge step. Treat its output as a one-time starting point, not a regenerable source of truth.

29.4 Helm — The Package Manager for K8s

Goal: package easypj as one installable, versioned, configurable unit — the way apt install packages a binary. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — like apt/yum for K8s. It bundles K8s manifests into "charts" with parameterized values.

TERMINAL
# Create a Helm chart
$ helm create easypj-chart

# Chart structure:
# easypj-chart/
#   Chart.yaml            # name, version
#   values.yaml            # replicaCount: 3, image.tag: v1.0
#   templates/              # K8s manifests (with Go templates)
#     deployment.yaml       # {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
#     service.yaml
#     configmap.yaml

# Install with custom values
$ helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --set image.tag=v2.0

# Upgrade an existing release
$ helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --set replicaCount=5

# Roll back to a previous release
$ helm rollback easypj 1

Helm templates are Deployment/Service YAML with {{ .Values.x }} placeholders filled from values.yaml at install/upgrade time — one chart, N environments, via --set or per-env values files (values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml). helm upgrade tracks a release history, so helm rollback works like 27.2's rollout undo but chart-wide.

Helm's Render Pipeline — one directory to a live app
 ┌────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐
 │values.yaml         │──▶│templates/deploy.yaml   │──▶│rendered manifest   │
 │replicaCount: 3     │   │replicas: {{ .Values.   │   │replicas: 3         │
 │image.tag: v2.0     │   │  replicaCount }}       │   │image: easypj:v2.0  │
 └────────────────────┘   │image: easypj:{{ .Val-  │   └────────────────────┘
                           │  ues.image.tag }}      │
                           └────────────────────────┘
                                               ▼
                                helm install applies the manifest
💡 Fill-in-the-Blanks, Not Sticky Notes

Kustomize (29.5) is sticky notes on a fixed blueprint; Helm is a blueprint with FILL-IN-THE-BLANKS built in from the start — replicaCount, image tag and resource sizes are parameters, not patches bolted on after the fact.

easypj in practice: values-prod.yaml sets replicaCount: 5 and resources.limits.memory: 512Mi; values-dev.yaml sets replicaCount: 1 — one chart installs BOTH shapes of easypj.

📖 helm template vs helm install --dry-run --debug

helm template renders the SAME output with zero cluster contact — pure client-side substitution. helm install --dry-run --debug renders AND talks to the API server, catching what a template-only pass cannot.

🛑 Gotcha — helm --set Silently Accepts Typos

Helm's --set silently accepts typos in a values KEY (unlike a YAML schema error) — a misspelled key just gets ignored, and your override never applies. Always verify with --dry-run --debug or helm template, don't trust --set blindly.

🔧 Under the Hood — Helm 3's template rendering, with no server component

Helm 3 (unlike Helm 2) has no in-cluster "Tiller" service — the helm CLI itself renders every {{ .Values.x }} placeholder locally using Go's text/template engine (plus the Sprig function library for string/math/date helpers), producing plain Kubernetes YAML entirely client-side before anything touches the API server. helm install/upgrade then apply that rendered YAML AND write a release record (chart + values used) into a Kubernetes Secret in the target namespace — that Secret is what helm rollback reads to reconstruct a previous release's exact manifest. helm template stops after the render step and never contacts the cluster at all — the fastest way to sanity-check a chart offline.

 values.yaml + templates/*.yaml
      │ text/template (Sprig funcs)
      ▼
 rendered plain Deployment/Service YAML
      │ apply + record
      ▼
 live objects + release record, stored in a Secret
🔑 Nothing runs inside the cluster to make Helm work; the chart plus a stored Secret of "what we last applied" is the entire mechanism behind versioned installs, upgrades and rollbacks.

29.5 Kustomize — Template-Free Customization

Goal: patch easypj's replica count and resource limits per environment using ONLY kubectl and plain YAML — no templating engine, no values file, no server-side component to run.

TERMINAL
# Built into kubectl!
$ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod

# Kustomize structure:
# kustomize/
#   base/
#     kustomization.yaml     # Shared config
#     deployment.yaml        # replicas: 1
#     service.yaml
#   overlays/
#     staging/
#       kustomization.yaml   # Patches: replicas=2
#     prod/
#       kustomization.yaml   # Patches: replicas=5, resources

# Preview without applying:
$ kubectl diff -k overlays/prod

Kustomize is BUILT INTO kubectl (apply -k, since kubectl 1.14) — it merges a base manifest with strategic-merge or JSON patches declared in an overlay's kustomization.yaml; no templating language, no {{ }} syntax, purely YAML-on-YAML patches.

💡 Sticky Notes on a Photocopy

If Helm (29.4) is fill-in-the-blanks, Kustomize is sticky notes and highlighter marks directly on a photocopy of the base blueprint — same base, a visibly different overlay per environment, no separate templating tool required.

easypj in practice: base/deployment.yaml ships replicas: 1; overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml patches it to replicas: 5 and adds the resources block from Chapter 27.5 — the base file stays untouched.

📖 Zero Extra Tooling

kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod works on any machine with kubectl — no installation, no server-side component, no templating language to learn. The output is plain YAML (kubectl kustomize shows it) — compatible with any GitOps tool (ArgoCD/Flux).

🛑 Gotcha — No Release History, No Rollback Command

Kustomize has NO release history or rollback command like Helm — reverting a bad overlay means editing the patch and re-applying, or reaching for git revert on the overlay file, then kubectl apply -k again. Know this trade-off before picking it for a team that needs fast rollbacks.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Compose optimizes for feedback speed on one machine; Kubernetes/Swarm optimize for resilience across many — same image, different job (29.1).
  • compose and kubectl share the same VERBS (up/down, logs, exec, scale) — only object names and flags differ (29.2).
  • docker compose build has no kubectl equivalent — Kubernetes never builds images, only schedules ones already in a registry (29.2).
  • kompose convert bootstraps Deployments/Services/PVCs in seconds but adds NO resource limits, probes or replica planning — that's still on you (29.3).
  • Helm = templated manifests + a versioned release history + one command to install, upgrade or roll back an entire chart (29.4).
  • Kustomize = base + overlays, patch-based, needs no extra binary beyond kubectl itself, but has no rollback command (29.5).
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Bind-mounting source code in a production Deployment → Defeats the point of an immutable image — production always COPIES code in at build time.
  • Re-running kompose convert after hand-editing generated files → OVERWRITES those edits — treat its output as a one-time starting point, not a regenerable source.
  • Trusting a Helm --set flag without --dry-run --debug → A misspelled values key is silently ignored — no schema error, the override just never applies.
  • Expecting a Kustomize rollback command like Helm's → Kustomize has no release history — reverting means editing the patch and re-applying, or git revert.
  • Running Compose in production without any orchestration → Compose is for dev/CI on one host. Use Swarm or Kubernetes for resilient multi-host production deployments.
  • Deploying without running docker compose config first → config prints the merged, resolved YAML — always validate before deploying, it catches interpolation and syntax errors early.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • helm install ... --dry-run --debug renders AND validates against the live API server — stronger than helm template alone.
  • Keep a values-<env>.yaml per environment instead of long --set chains — it's diffable and reviewable in git.
  • kubectl diff -k overlays/prod (before apply) previews a Kustomize overlay's exact effect with zero risk.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 29)

the Chapter 29 cheat-card 
kompose convert -f compose.yaml -o k8s/         # first-draft manifests
helm create easypj                               # scaffold a new chart
helm install easypj ./chart --set image.tag=v2   # install w/ override
helm upgrade easypj ./chart                      # apply a new chart version
helm rollback easypj 1                           # revert to release 1
helm template ./chart                            # render only, no cluster contact
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod                   # apply a Kustomize overlay
kubectl diff -k overlays/prod                    # preview overlay effect

🧠 Chapter 29 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From tool ownership to Kustomize's missing rollback command — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Chapter 9 built easypj's image once. Name every consumer of that SAME image across dev, staging and prod, per 29.1.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

laptop (docker compose up), CI (build + push), staging (kubectl apply -k overlays/staging or docker stack deploy), prod (kubectl apply -k overlays/prod or docker stack deploy) — the Dockerfile and image never change, only who reads it.

EXPLANATION

This is the entire point of an immutable image — it removes "works on my machine" by construction (29.1).

Q2
Fill in the kubectl equivalents for: docker compose up -d, docker compose logs -f app, docker compose exec app sh, docker compose build.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose up -d → kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. docker compose logs -f app → kubectl logs -f deploy/easypj. docker compose exec app sh → kubectl exec -it deploy/easypj -- sh. docker compose build → no equivalent — K8s never builds.

EXPLANATION

The verbs map cleanly except build — the one operation kubectl fundamentally does not do (29.2).

Q3
kompose convert on easypj's compose.yaml produced django-deployment.yaml with no readinessProbe. Is this a bug?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — expected. kompose maps structure (services→Deployments, ports→Services, named volumes→PVCs) but can't infer health-check behavior; probes, resource limits and replicas beyond 1 are manual additions from Chapters 26-27.

EXPLANATION

Treat kompose as a first-draft translator, not a production generator (29.3).

Q4
Why can't you safely re-run kompose convert after hand-editing its output?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It regenerates files from compose.yaml every time and OVERWRITES whatever you added by hand — there's no merge step.

EXPLANATION

Use it once as a starting point, then manage the generated YAML yourself going forward (29.3).

Q5
What's the difference between helm install and helm upgrade, and what makes helm rollback possible afterward?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

install creates a NEW release; upgrade re-renders the chart against new values/chart version for an EXISTING release. Both write a release record into a Kubernetes Secret, which helm rollback <name> <revision> reads to reapply a prior state.

EXPLANATION

Rollback isn't magic — it's replaying a stored prior render (29.4, this chapter's Under the Hood).

Q6
Draw Helm's render pipeline from values.yaml to a live object, and mark the step needing no cluster contact.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

values.yaml (replicaCount: 3) ──▶ templates/deploy.yaml ({{ .Values.replicaCount }}) ──▶ rendered manifest (replicas: 3) [no cluster contact through here] ──▶ helm install applies it [cluster contact starts here].

EXPLANATION

helm template stops right after the rendered-manifest step — pure client-side substitution (29.4).

Q7
A helm install --set relicaCount=5 (typo) silently installs with the chart's DEFAULT replica count. Why no error?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--set writes into the values tree by key path; a misspelled key just creates/overrides a key nobody's template reads — there's no schema validation catching the typo.

EXPLANATION

Always verify with --dry-run --debug or helm template, don't trust --set blindly (29.4).

Q8
What does Kustomize need installed beyond kubectl itself to patch a base manifest per environment?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing — kubectl apply -k has Kustomize built in since kubectl 1.14.

EXPLANATION

This is Kustomize's core pitch versus Helm: zero extra binary, zero templating language (29.5).

Q9
overlays/prod patches replicas to 5; overlays/staging patches to 2. Does base/deployment.yaml change?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — base/deployment.yaml stays at replicas: 1; each overlay applies its patch independently at apply-time.

EXPLANATION

That's the base+overlay model — one source of truth, N environment-specific views (29.5).

Q10
A bad Kustomize overlay just shipped to prod. What's the rollback command, Helm-style?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

There isn't one — Kustomize has no release history or rollback verb. Fix means editing the patch and re-applying, or git revert on the overlay file, then kubectl apply -k again.

EXPLANATION

This is the one capability Kustomize trades away for its simplicity — know it before picking it for a team that needs fast rollbacks (29.5).

🔬 Practice Drill 29.1 — Two Roads to the Same Deployment (15 min)

Run kompose convert on easypj's real compose.yaml, list every field 27.3-27.5 would add that kompose did NOT generate (resource limits, probes, replica count beyond 1). Then apply the same replica/resource change twice — once by hand-editing the kompose output, once via a Kustomize overlay. Stop the clock once both produce identical kubectl get deploy output.

The takeaway: compose.yaml (29.1) feeds three different conversion tools (29.3-29.5) that trade off speed, parameterization and rollback support differently — but all three ship the exact same image Chapter 9 built once.

30.1 Docker Certifications Overview

The Docker Certified Associate (DCA) exam validates your Docker skills for employers. It is administered by Docker/Mirantis via a third-party proctor and tests PRACTICAL command recall and troubleshooting scenarios, not conceptual essays — exactly the hands-on drills this guide has run since Chapter 1.

FactDetail
CertificationDocker Certified Associate (DCA)
Format55 multiple-choice questions (mix of classic MC and discrete-option MC)
Duration90 minutes (~98 seconds per question)
Passing Score~65-70% (Docker does not publish an exact fixed percentage)
DeliveryOnline proctored, or a Pearson VUE testing center
PrerequisitesNone enforced; 6-12 months hands-on Docker experience recommended
Validity2 years from certification date, then re-certification required
Retake Policy14-day wait after a failed attempt
Cost$195 USD (may vary by region)
💡 A Driving Test, Not a Physics Exam

The DCA checks trained reflexes on realistic situations. You cannot cram reflexes — you can only have driven (done the labs). Examiners care that you can execute the maneuver (docker service update --rollback) under time pressure, not define orchestration in an essay.

✅
Readiness Heuristic

You can rebuild easypj's stack — image, compose, swarm service, secured daemon — from an empty shell without notes. If yes, schedule the exam.

🔬
easypj as Study Log

Your study log IS this guide's lab trail. The exam's scenarios (broken service, wrong network, missing volume) are the same failures you triaged in Chapters 6, 13-15 and 16-18 — every terminal block in Parts 1-9 that used a real easypj command is direct exam rehearsal, just with the names swapped.

🧪 Practice Lab — Cold Baseline

Take any 10 practice questions from Appendix H cold, timed at 98s each. Verify: ≥7/10 → begin 30.2's domain plan; below → note WHICH domains leaked and reread them.

⚠️ Gotcha

Discrete-option questions punish guessing patterns — every option is scored, so "pick the longest answer" folklore actively hurts here. There is also no experience CHECK at registration — Docker will take your money for an exam you aren't ready for; 30.2's domain weights are the real gatekeeper.

30.2 Docker Associate Exam Domains (Official)

These six core domains come directly from the official DCA exam website. Convert the weights below into a personal study budget — hours per domain proportional to weight × your own weakness:

30.3 Essential Docker Commands for the Exam

These are the commands you MUST know from memory. The exam provides a browser-based terminal — know the syntax cold. The CLI is a grammar: docker <noun> <verb> — container/image/volume/network/system/service/stack/secret/config/node/swarm. The exam exploits near-misses.

EXAM ESSENTIALS
# Container: docker run/create/start/stop/rm/ps/logs/exec/inspect/stats/top/cp
# Image: docker build/pull/push/tag/rmi/images/history/inspect/save/load/prune
# Network: docker network create/ls/inspect/connect/disconnect/rm/prune
# Volume: docker volume create/ls/inspect/rm/prune
# System: docker system df/prune/info/events
# Swarm: docker swarm init/join/leave, node ls/update, service create/ls/ps/scale/update/rollback
# Stack: docker stack deploy/ls/ps/services/rm
# Secret: docker secret create/ls/inspect/rm
# Config: docker config create/ls/inspect/rm
# Compose: docker compose up/down/ps/logs/exec/build/pull/push/config
# Trust: docker trust sign/inspect/revoke, DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
# Scout: docker scout quickview/cves/recommendations/compare
💡 Conjugation Tables for a Language You Already Speak

You know the words; the exam checks the irregular verbs — asymmetries like stop (SIGTERM + grace) vs kill (SIGKILL now).

Verb/flag AVerb/flag BThe ONE difference
psps -a-a also lists STOPPED containers
rmrmicontainer vs image (different noun)
saveexportlayers+history vs 1 flat layer
stopkillSIGTERM+grace vs SIGKILL now
image pruneimage prune -adangling only vs all unused
logs <ctr>service logs easypjone task vs every task
💡 The One Command Without a Matching Noun

docker inspect <id> breaks the noun-first grammar on purpose: given no noun, it auto-detects container vs image vs volume vs network by trying each type in turn.

🧪 Practice Lab — Command Recall

From Appendix A, cover the example column and write the command for 20 random rows. Verify: ≥18/20 exact, flags included — exam questions quote flags verbatim. Drill set: docker system df | docker system prune -a | docker events --since 1h | docker service ps --no-trunc | docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' <container>

⚠️ Gotcha

Prune scopes — docker image prune removes DANGLING only; add -a and it removes all UNUSED. The exam loves that one word.

30.4 Dockerfile Writing for the Exam

Know every instruction and be able to spot errors in a Dockerfile. The exam will show you broken Dockerfiles and ask what's wrong. The axis to answer from is build-time vs run-time: RUN executes at BUILD, CMD/ENTRYPOINT at START; COPY vs ADD (ADD = COPY + URL + auto-untar — prefer COPY); EXPOSE documents, -p publishes; ARG dies when the build ends, ENV persists; exec form vs shell form decides who receives SIGTERM.

💡 A Recipe's Prep Column vs Serve Column

RUN chops (baked into layers); CMD plates the dish when a guest (container start) arrives. Multi-stage = prep kitchen and serving counter in separate rooms — COPY --from=builder carries artifacts, dev toolchains never ship.

🏆 Exam Dockerfile Checklist

✅ FROM (always first, must be specific tag). ✅ WORKDIR (not RUN cd). ✅ COPY > ADD. ✅ Chain RUN with &&. ✅ CMD vs ENTRYPOINT. ✅ Multi-stage (COPY --from). ✅ EXPOSE is documentation. ✅ ARG vs ENV. ✅ USER for non-root. ✅ HEALTHCHECK for production. ✅ .dockerignore exists. ✅ No secrets in ENV.

💡 Memorize the Six ENTRYPOINT/CMD Combinations

Chapter 4's ENTRYPOINT × CMD table IS an exam question — rebuild it from memory the week before. The Ch9 production Dockerfile contains every examable instruction — recite it line by line and give the WHY of each (cache order, non-root USER, exec-form CMD).

🧪 Practice Lab — Two-Stage Dockerfile

Write a two-stage Python Dockerfile on paper in 5 minutes: builder installs into a venv, runtime copies it, non-root, exec-form gunicorn. Verify against Appendix D.1 — every deviation is a study item.

⚠️ Gotcha

"EXPOSE opens the port" is the most common WRONG answer on the exam — EXPOSE alone publishes nothing.

30.5 Docker Compose for the Exam

Know the compose.yaml structure and docker compose commands. compose.yaml is four top-level key groups: services, networks, volumes, configs/secrets. The exam picks: named volume vs bind mount syntax (short vs long form), depends_on ≠ "wait until ready", the default per-project user-defined bridge (DNS by service name), ports "8000:8000" vs expose, override/profiles precedence.

💡 An Org Chart, Not a Script

The file is an org chart, not a script: services are departments, networks the hallways, volumes the archive room — questions ask who CONNECTS to whom, not what runs first.

🏆 Compose Exam Checklist

✅ services → containers. ✅ networks → custom networks. ✅ volumes → named volumes. ✅ depends_on with condition: service_healthy. ✅ environment vs env_file. ✅ ports mapping. ✅ build vs image. ✅ docker compose config (validate). ✅ docker compose up/down/ps/logs/exec.

🧪 Practice Lab — Minimal Compose From Memory

From memory, write the minimal compose.yaml for django + postgres with a named volume and a healthcheck-gated depends_on. Verify: docker compose config accepts it — it validates without starting anything. The Chapter 11 full-stack compose file is your flashcard: django, postgres (PostgreSQL, as always), redis, nginx — every examable key appears in it at least once.

⚠️ Gotcha

The exam still shows version: "3.8" headers — legacy in modern Compose but valid on the test; don't let it rattle you.

30.6 Docker Swarm for the Exam

Swarm is 25% of the exam — the single largest domain. Know these commands and concepts. The examable loop: swarm init/join (+ tokens) → node ls/update (drain, labels) → service create (replicas, publish, secrets, constraints) → scale → update → rollback → stack deploy. Plus the theory spine: quorum math, routing mesh vs host-mode publishing, secrets' tmpfs delivery.

🏆 Swarm Exam Checklist — 25% of DCA (EXPANDED)

Cluster Management:
✅ swarm init (--advertise-addr, --autolock). ✅ swarm join (manager/worker tokens). ✅ swarm unlock/unlock-key. ✅ swarm leave (--force). ✅ node ls/ps/inspect/update/demote/promote. ✅ node --availability (active/pause/drain). ✅ Manager quorum (NEVER even number: 3,5,7). ✅ Raft consensus basics.

Services:
✅ service create (--name, --replicas, -p, --network, --secret, --config, --constraint, --placement-pref, --restart-condition, --restart-delay, --restart-max-attempts). ✅ service update (--image, --replicas, --update-parallelism, --update-delay, --update-failure-action, --update-order, --update-max-failure-ratio, --update-monitor). ✅ service rollback (--rollback-parallelism, --rollback-delay, --rollback-failure-action, --rollback-order). ✅ service scale. ✅ service ps (task status across nodes). ✅ service logs. ✅ service inspect.

Stacks:
✅ stack deploy (deploy: section: replicas, update_config, rollback_config, restart_policy, placement, resources). ✅ stack ls/ps/services/rm.

Networking:
✅ Routing mesh (ingress network). ✅ docker_gwbridge (outbound connectivity). ✅ Overlay networks (--opt encrypted). ✅ Port publishing (host mode vs ingress mode).

Security:
✅ secrets create/ls/inspect/rm. ✅ configs create/ls/inspect/rm. ✅ Autolock (encrypted Raft log). ✅ MTLS between nodes (automatic in Swarm).

💡 The Exam's Parallel-Park

A fixed maneuver sequence, practiced until it needs no thought — because a quarter of the marks sit on it. The five most-asked: quorum for N managers, drain a node, rotate a join token, publish mode ingress vs host, roll back a failed update.

🧪 Practice Lab — Full Lifecycle Loop

Run the ENTIRE loop once on your 3-node lab swarm with the jobpost stack — init to rollback in one sitting is the single highest-value hour of DCA preparation. Time it. Verify: under 15 minutes without notes, and each command's OUTPUT (not just the command) feels familiar when the exam screenshots it.

⚠️ Gotcha

docker service scale easypj=5 and docker service update --replicas 5 easypj are BOTH correct — the exam may list both; read for "select ALL that apply".

30.7 Exam Strategy & Tips

90 min / 55 Qs = 98s each. Three-pass method: pass 1 answers everything answerable in <60s and FLAGS the rest (~70 min); pass 2 revisits flags (~15 min); pass 3 is a sanity sweep (~5 min). Discrete-option MCs: judge each option as its own true/false — half-knowledge still harvests points. No penalty for wrong answers: never leave blanks.

⏱️
Time Management

55 questions / 90 minutes = ~1.6 min per question. Flag and skip hard ones — return later. Don't spend more than 3 minutes on any question. Answer everything (no penalty for wrong answers).

📖
During the Exam

Docker documentation IS available in the exam! You can access docs.docker.com. Know WHERE to find information quickly — don't memorize everything. Practice navigating the docs.

⚠️
Common Traps

EXPOSE vs -p publishing. CMD vs ENTRYPOINT behavior. depends_on without healthcheck. ENV vs ARG. save vs export. COPY vs ADD. Bridge default vs custom bridge DNS. Swarm manager quorum requirements.

💡
Pro Tips

Read ALL answer choices before selecting. Eliminate obviously wrong answers first. Watch for "NOT", "EXCEPT", "BEST" keywords. Trust your hands-on experience — the exam tests practical knowledge, not trivia.

💡 A Buffet With a Countdown

Sweep the room once taking everything easy, THEN queue for the carved roast (the hard, flagged questions) — starting with the roast starves you. Elimination heuristics that work: absolute words ("always", "only") are usually wrong; an option naming a nonexistent flag is instantly false — your Appendix A drills make fakes glow.

🧪 Practice Lab — Full Timed Mock

One full Appendix H mock, strict 90-minute timer, three-pass method. Verify: ≥75% AND fewer than 8 flags left after pass 1 — both numbers matter (accuracy AND pace).

⚠️ Gotcha

Burning 5 minutes on question 3 is how prepared candidates fail — the flag button is a skill; practice IT, not just content.

Online proctoring needs: a machine passing the vendor's system check (webcam, mic, screen share), ONE display, a clean desk, government ID matching your registration, stable bandwidth and a quiet room — verified in the ~15-minute onboarding before the clock starts.

No new browser, no untested webcam, no first-time VPN. Every variable you can rehearse, rehearse.

📋 The Night Before

Make your last technical act the 30.6 Swarm loop on the jobpost stack — end prep on your strongest, heaviest domain.

T-minus-1-day dress rehearsal: system check, desk cleared, one 90-minute mock at the same hour as the real slot. Verify: no step surprised you — that is the point.

A second monitor left plugged in — even merely switched off — can void the session at check-in. Unplug it, don't just switch it off.

💡 The Driving Test's Hand Signals

Nobody signals by arm in real traffic, but the examiner asks — and candidates fail on exactly the parts daily driving never exercises. Shipping jobpost taught you ~85% of the DCA by osmosis; this table is the other 15% that only deliberate study covers — every row cites the chapter that already did.

🧪 Practice Lab — Final Audit

Tick each row you can explain aloud in two sentences; reread the cited section for every non-tick, then do 3 Appendix H questions from that domain. Verify: a fully ticked table AND ≥80% on a fresh Appendix H mixed set.

⚠️ Gotcha

Don't study this table FIRST — without Parts 1-10 underneath it, memorized corners collapse under scenario-style questions.

🔧 Under the Hood — how Discrete-Option Multiple Choice (DOMC) is scored

A classic multiple-choice question has ONE correct option among several distractors — picking it earns full credit, picking any other earns zero. A DOMC question instead presents a stem with several OPTIONS, and each option is judged independently as true or false against the stem — functionally several true/false questions sharing one prompt. That independence is why "longest answer" or "eliminate two, guess between the rest" folklore fails here: an option's truth doesn't depend on how plausible the others look, and partial knowledge (getting 3 of 4 options right) still harvests partial credit rather than zero.

 CLASSIC MC                       DOMC
 Stem: pick the ONE               Stem: judge EACH option
 correct answer                   true/false, independently

 ○ Option A                       ☐ Option A   → True/False
 ○ Option B  (only 1 scored)      ☐ Option B   → True/False
 ● Option C  ← credit here        ☐ Option C   → True/False
 ○ Option D                       ☐ Option D   → True/False
                                   (each judged, each scored)
🔑 Treat every DOMC option as its own tiny true/false question: read it in isolation against the stem, decide, move on — don't compare options against each other the way classic multiple choice trains you to.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • 55 questions / 90 minutes / ~65-70% passing / 2-year validity — know the logistics cold so exam day has zero surprises (30.1).
  • Orchestration (25%) + Image Management (20%) ≈ 45% of the exam — study where the points are (30.2).
  • The exam's favorite trap is near-miss command PAIRS, not obscure commands — rm/rmi, save/export, stop/kill, prune scopes (30.3).
  • "EXPOSE opens the port" is the single most common wrong answer on the exam — EXPOSE documents, -p publishes (30.4).
  • docker compose build has no kubectl equivalent, and depends_on never promises "wait until ready" (30.5).
  • The full Swarm lifecycle (init→join→create→scale→update→rollback) is worth rehearsing until it needs zero thought — it IS a quarter of the exam (30.6).
  • Three-pass pacing (easy first, flag the rest, sweep last) beats answering in question order — practice the FLAG button, not just content (30.7).
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Registering for the exam because there's no experience check → Docker will take your money before you're ready; 30.2's domain weights are the real gatekeeper (30.1).
  • Practicing Kubernetes instead of Swarm → The DCA tests SWARM specifically — this is the single most common reason candidates fail Orchestration (30.2, 30.6).
  • Burning 5 minutes on a hard question 3 → Flag and move on. You have ~98 seconds per question on average (30.7).
  • Leaving a second monitor merely switched off → It can void an online-proctored session at check-in — unplug it, don't just switch it off (30.8).
  • Studying the 30.9 gap table FIRST → Without Parts 1-10 underneath it, memorized corners collapse under scenario questions (30.9).
  • Not using docs.docker.com during the exam → The docs ARE accessible. Know where to find the CLI reference and Dockerfile reference fast — that's a huge, underused advantage.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Time yourself at 98s/question during practice sets so the real clock never feels unfamiliar (30.1, 30.7).
  • Keep a running "wrong-answer list" from every Appendix H attempt — re-take ONLY those the night before (30.8).
  • Score yourself per-domain before studying anything — it tells you exactly which two domains earn your next two sessions (30.2).
