🧠 Chapter 30 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From readiness math to exam-day logistics — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
You're at month 4 of hands-on Docker with a DCA slot open next week. Per 30.1, should you book it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker recommends 6-12 months hands-on; at month 4 the honest move is to run 30.1's readiness heuristic (rebuild easypj's stack — image, compose, swarm service, secured daemon — from empty, without notes) before spending the exam fee.

EXPLANATION

There's no experience gate at registration, so the check has to be self-imposed (30.1).

Q2
You have 20 study hours and self-scored weakness 1-5 per domain: Orchestration=2, Images=4, Install=3, Networking=4, Security=2, Storage=5. Which two domains get the most hours?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Orchestration and Security get the most hours.

DomainWeightSelf-score (lower=weaker)Priority
Orchestration25%2Highest
Security15%2High
Installation15%3Medium
Images20%4Lower
Networking15%4Lower
Storage10%5Lowest
EXPLANATION

Budget = weight × weakness, not weight alone (30.2).

Q3
An exam question asks "which command removes an image?" with options docker rm, docker rmi, docker image rm, docker container prune. Which are correct?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker rmi and docker image rm (same operation, different noun spelling); docker rm removes a CONTAINER; docker container prune removes stopped containers, not images.

EXPLANATION

Exactly the near-miss noun trap 30.3 warns about (30.3).

Q4
True or false — "EXPOSE 8000" makes port 8000 reachable from the host.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

False.

EXPLANATION

EXPOSE is documentation/metadata only; only -p/--publish (or Compose ports:) actually maps a host port — the exam's most common wrong answer (30.4).

Q5
depends_on: [postgres] is set on django. Does Compose wait for postgres to be READY before starting django?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

No — by default depends_on only waits for the container to START, not for the app inside it to be ready; that needs a healthcheck-gated condition: service_healthy.

EXPLANATION

This exact gap is a favorite DCA trap on Compose questions (30.5).

Q6
Draw the full Swarm command loop you should run in under 15 minutes without notes.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

swarm init/join → node ls → service create (replicas, publish, secrets) → service scale → service update (28.8 flags) → service ps → service update --rollback (28.9) → stack deploy.

EXPLANATION

This loop alone represents Orchestration's 25% — rehearsed until each command's OUTPUT, not just syntax, feels familiar (30.6).

Q7
An exam question lists both docker service scale easypj=5 and docker service update --replicas 5 easypj and says "select all that apply." What do you pick?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both — functionally identical.

EXPLANATION

DOMC-style questions judge every option independently; both being true is valid, not a trick (30.6, this chapter's Under the Hood).

Q8
With 90 minutes and 55 questions, describe the three-pass method in one line each.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Pass 1 (~70 min): answer everything solvable under 60s, flag the rest. Pass 2 (~15 min): revisit flags. Pass 3 (~5 min): a sanity sweep confirming nothing was left blank.

EXPLANATION

Pacing to 98s/question only works if the flag button is used deliberately (30.7).

Q9
What THREE things should be true the night before an online-proctored exam?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) The vendor system check passed on the EXACT machine you'll use, (2) government ID matches registration exactly, (3) any second monitor is physically unplugged, not just off.

EXPLANATION

Logistics failures are free points lost before the exam even starts (30.8).

Q10
Per the 30.9 gap table, which chapter covers Raft quorum math, and which covers Docker Content Trust?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Raft quorum math → Chapter 28 (28.7); Docker Content Trust → Chapters 20 and 23.

EXPLANATION

The 30.9 table exists because these are commonly missed despite being taught earlier — use it as a final audit, not a first read (30.9).

🔑 Part 10 — Key Takeaways

Its favorite traps are near-miss command pairs (rm/rmi, save/export) and "EXPOSE opens the port" — every one of them defused by material you already practiced hands-on in Parts 1-9 (Ch 30).
  • 🎯 Exam: Part 10 alone covers a quarter of the DCA outright (Orchestration) plus a meaningful share of Image Management — rehearsing the full Swarm lifecycle, init to rollback, until it needs zero thought pays for itself twice on exam day.

Chapter 31 · Observability & Monitoring for easypj

31.1 Beyond docker stats — Building a Metrics Pipeline

docker stats is live, single-host, and single-snapshot — the moment you close the terminal, that data is gone forever. Past roughly 10 containers, or the moment you have more than one host, there is no history, no alerting, and no chart to look back at. cAdvisor (Container Advisor) is Google's per-container metrics exporter — it reads the SAME cgroup files Chapter 6.6's --memory/--cpus limits are enforced through, and re-exposes them as a scrapable /metrics endpoint.

docker stats vs the Metrics Pipeline That Actually Scales
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               📉 docker stats — THE ONE-HOST, ONE-SNAPSHOT VIEW          │
  │                                                                          │
  │ $ docker stats --no-stream        → live only, THIS host, THIS second    │
  │ past ~10 containers or >1 host    → no history, no alerts, no chart      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                   📊 THE PIPELINE THAT ACTUALLY SCALES                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │ 🐳 easypj-web  easypj-db  redis  nginx   (cgroup stats: CPU/mem/I/O)     │
  │       │ scraped via Docker API + /sys/fs/cgroup                          │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │ 📦 cAdvisor:8080/metrics → scraped/15s → 📊 Prometheus TSDB (history)    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 💡 cAdvisor is the ONLY new piece — Prometheus pulls FROM it; no         │
  │    change to easypj, postgres, redis or nginx themselves.                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯
GOAL

Explain why docker stats cannot be the production monitoring story, and name the one container that fixes it.

🔧
TECH

docker stats streams the cgroup counters (6.6) straight to your terminal with zero retention — it is a cat of live state, not a database. cAdvisor reads the same cgroup files PLUS the Docker API, converts them into stable time series labeled by container name, and serves them as a scrapable HTTP endpoint in Prometheus's OpenMetrics text format.

💡 The Security-Camera Analogy

docker stats is looking through a single window at a single instant; cAdvisor bolts a security camera on that window so someone else (Prometheus) can record everything it ever showed.

easypj: docker run -d --name cadvisor -p 8080:8080 -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro -v /:/rootfs:ro -v /sys:/sys:ro gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1 starts watching easypj-web, easypj-db, redis and nginx with zero app changes.

TERMINAL
# Start cAdvisor watching every container on this host
$ docker run -d --name cadvisor -p 8080:8080 \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
    -v /:/rootfs:ro -v /sys:/sys:ro \
    gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1

# Browse http://localhost:8080/metrics and confirm easypj-web appears
$ curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep easypj-web
container_memory_usage_bytes{name="easypj-web"} 8.912896e+07
🧪 PRACTICE — LAB

Run the cadvisor command above, then browse http://localhost:8080/metrics. Verify: you can find a line matching container_memory_usage_bytes{name="easypj-web"} — that line is what Prometheus will scrape in 31.2.

⚠️ Gotcha

cAdvisor needs read access to the Docker socket and the host's /sys and /rootfs — treat that mount with the same care as 20.3's socket-mount warning; it sees every container.

📊 Summary: docker stats is a live look; cAdvisor + Prometheus is the recorded history that alerting and dashboards need.

🔧 Under the Hood — how docker stats and cAdvisor read the SAME data

Both tools ultimately read the same kernel-maintained accounting files under the container's cgroup — docker stats calls the daemon's /containers/{id}/stats API endpoint, which is itself a JSON-formatted read of files like memory.current and cpu.stat (cgroup v2, or their v1 equivalents) — the exact files 6.6's --memory/--cpus limits are enforced through. cAdvisor does the identical read, on a timer, for every container on the host, then re-exposes the numbers as Prometheus's OpenMetrics text format instead of a one-shot JSON blob.

 /sys/fs/cgroup/<container>/memory.current, cpu.stat, io.stat
        │                              │
        ▼ (one-shot read)              ▼ (read every N sec)
  docker stats API call          cAdvisor → /metrics endpoint
  (dockerd, on demand)            (own process, on a timer)
🔑 Neither tool invents new data — they read the SAME kernel accounting; the only difference is retention and re-exposure format.

31.2 Prometheus + Grafana via Compose

Add prometheus, grafana and cadvisor as services alongside the django/postgres/redis/nginx stack from Chapter 10.4. A prometheus.yml file declares static scrape configs pointing at cadvisor and django's own /metrics (via django-prometheus); Grafana reads Prometheus as a data source and renders dashboards.

easypj compose.yaml + The Monitoring Side-Car
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            🎼 easypj compose.yaml + THE MONITORING SIDE-CAR              │
  │                                                                          │
  │ django:8000  postgres:5432  redis:6379  nginx:80   (Part 4 stack)        │
  │      │            │              │           │                          │
  │      └────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘                          │
  │                    │ scraped by                                         │
  │                    ▼                                                    │
  │ 📦 cadvisor:8080 → 📊 prometheus:9090 → 📈 grafana:3000                  │
  │ (per-container      (scrapes cadvisor +   (queries prometheus,           │
  │  cgroup metrics)      django /metrics)      renders dashboards)          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Browser → localhost:3000 → Grafana dashboard → PromQL → Prometheus       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
compose.yaml (monitoring side-car additions)
services:
  # ...django, postgres, redis, nginx unchanged from 10.4...

  # ─── cAdvisor — per-container cgroup metrics ───
  cadvisor:
    image: gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - /sys:/sys:ro
      - /var/lib/docker/:/var/lib/docker:ro

  # ─── Prometheus — scrapes cadvisor + django, stores history ───
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.53.0
    volumes: ["./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"]
    ports: ["9090:9090"]
    depends_on: [cadvisor]

  # ─── Grafana — queries prometheus, renders dashboards ───
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:11.1.0
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    environment: ["GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme"]
    depends_on: [prometheus]
prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'cadvisor'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['cadvisor:8080']
  - job_name: 'django'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['django:8000']
    metrics_path: /metrics
📦
cAdvisor — the security desk

Watches every camera (per-container cgroup metrics) and answers when asked.

📊
Prometheus — the archive room

Records everything the desk reports, on a 15s scrape interval, into queryable history.

📈
Grafana — the viewing room

Draws charts from the archive on demand — it never talks to cAdvisor directly, only to Prometheus.

Compose's service-name DNS (10.4) is what makes this work: prometheus.yml says targets: ['cadvisor:8080'], not an IP, exactly like nginx.conf says django:8000. Grafana never touches cadvisor directly — it always queries Prometheus's stored time series via PromQL.

PromQL — sample query
# CPU used by the easypj web container, averaged over the last 5 minutes
rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{name="easypj-web"}[5m])
# reads as: "average CPU-seconds/second consumed, last 5 minutes"

# Memory used, as a percentage of a 512 MiB limit
container_memory_usage_bytes{name="easypj-web"} / (512*1024*1024)
💡 Sample Dashboard Panel

Title: "easypj Web — CPU & Memory". Top graph = the CPU PromQL query above (unit: cores, alert threshold line at 0.8). Bottom graph = the memory query above, rendered as a percentage gauge, red above 90%.

🧪 PRACTICE — LAB

docker compose up -d, open localhost:3000, add Prometheus (http://prometheus:9090) as a data source, paste the CPU query into a new panel. Verify: the graph moves when you run ab -n 2000 -c 20 http://localhost/jobs/ against easypj.

⚠️ Gotcha

Grafana's default admin/changeme password is a demo convenience only — rotate it before this stack ever leaves your laptop, the same rule as 20.1's secrets discipline.

📊 Summary: three Compose services turn cgroup numbers into a live, queryable, visual dashboard for the exact stack from Chapter 4.

31.3 Centralized Logging — the Loki/ELK Pattern

Chapter 2.7 covered log-driver basics (json-file, rotation); this section covers SHIPPING logs off the host. json-file stays on local disk only, rotated, and never leaves the container. gelf pushes UDP/TCP to a Graylog-compatible endpoint (e.g. Loki via a gelf-to-Loki bridge, or Graylog directly). fluentd pushes to a Fluentd/Fluent Bit collector, which routes to Loki, Elasticsearch, S3, or all three at once. WHY stdout-only logging (Chapter 6's rule) is the precondition: a log driver captures a container's stdout/stderr stream — an app that writes to its OWN log file instead is invisible to ALL of this, driver swap or not.

Flow — gunicorn Access Logs → Loki
  ① gunicorn logs access lines to STDOUT (Ch6's rule, not a file)
  ② Docker's log driver captures that stream (per-container)
  ③ driver=fluentd → ships each line to a Fluent Bit collector
  ④ Fluent Bit forwards to Loki, labeled {app="easypj",tier="web"}
  ⑤ Grafana (already in 31.2) queries Loki with LogQL, next to
     the metrics dashboard — logs and metrics, one screen

  🐍 gunicorn ──①──▶ stdout ──②──▶ log driver ──③──▶ Fluent Bit
                                                          │④
                                                          ▼
                                    Loki {app="easypj",tier="web"}
                                                          │⑤
                                                          ▼
                                              📈 Grafana (LogQL)
DriverWhere logs goBest for
json-fileLocal disk, rotated (2.7)Dev, single host, default
gelfUDP/TCP to Graylog/LokiQuick push, low setup
fluentdFluentd/Fluent Bit collectorMulti-destination routing
awslogsAWS CloudWatch Logs directlyECS/EC2 on AWS
localBinary format, disk-cappedReplaces json-file, faster
🎯
GOAL

Ship easypj's gunicorn access logs to Loki without touching a single line of jobpost's code.

🔧
TECH

The log driver is a daemon-level or per-container setting (--log-driver, or daemon.json from 2.7) that intercepts a container's stdout/stderr file descriptor — it never reads application files. Swapping json-file for fluentd in the FLOW diagram above changes step ② only; step ①, gunicorn's own behavior, never moves.

💡 The Microphone Analogy

Stdout is a single, fixed-position microphone gunicorn always talks into (2.7); the log driver is whichever recording device is plugged into that microphone today — cassette (json-file) or a live radio broadcast (fluentd/gelf). The microphone's position never changes, only the recorder.

easypj: docker run --log-driver=fluentd --log-opt fluentd-address=localhost:24224 --log-opt tag="easypj.web" easypj:v1 — gunicorn's access_log output starts arriving in Fluent Bit within one request, no gunicorn.conf.py change.

TERMINAL
# Ship easypj-web's stdout to a local Fluent Bit collector instead of json-file
$ docker run --log-driver=fluentd \
    --log-opt fluentd-address=localhost:24224 \
    --log-opt tag="easypj.web" \
    easypj:v1

# docker logs now shows NOTHING for this container — expected, not broken
$ docker logs easypj-web
# (empty — the stream now goes to Fluent Bit instead)
🧪 PRACTICE — LAB

Run a local Fluent Bit container listening on 24224, then start easypj with the fluentd driver above and hit /jobs/. Verify: docker logs easypj-web now shows NOTHING (the driver took the stream) while Fluent Bit's own log shows the forwarded access line.

⚠️ Gotcha

docker logs reads from the LOCAL driver's storage; switch to fluentd/gelf and docker logs goes silent — that is expected, not broken; go read the shipped destination instead.

📊 Summary: json-file for local dev, gelf/fluentd to ship off-box — all three work ONLY because easypj logs to stdout (Ch6).

31.4 Alerting on What Actually Matters for easypj

The four golden signals (Google SRE) are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation — the smallest metric set that catches most outages. Applied per tier: django (latency/errors), postgres (saturation: connections), redis (saturation: memory), nginx (traffic).

SignalMetricSource
Latencyp95 request duration on /jobs/django (nginx log)
Trafficrequests/sec to nginxnginx access log
Errors5xx rate on /jobs/django/nginx logs
Saturationpostgres active_connections / maxpostgres_exporter
Saturationredis used_memory / maxmemoryredis_exporter
prometheus-alerts.yml — high error rate on /jobs/
groups:
  - name: easypj-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: JobsEndpointHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(django_http_responses_total_by_status_total
            {job="django",status=~"5..",view="jobs"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(django_http_responses_total_by_status_total
            {job="django",view="jobs"}[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 2m
        labels: {severity: page}
        annotations:
          summary: "easypj /jobs/ 5xx rate above 5% for 2m"
🎯
GOAL

Turn the four golden signals into ONE alert that fires before users file a support ticket about /jobs/.

🔧
TECH

The rule expression divides the 5-minute rate of 5xx responses on the jobs view by ALL responses on that view — a RATIO, not a raw count, so it stays meaningful whether traffic is 10 req/s or 10,000. for: 2m requires the breach to persist, filtering single blips.

💡 The Dashboard Analogy

The four signals are a car's dashboard: speed (traffic), how hard the engine strains (saturation), the check-engine light (errors), and how long the trip is taking (latency) — watch only these four gauges and you catch nearly every real problem before it strands you.

easypj: the SIGNALS table's saturation row is what predicts Chapter 32.1's incident BEFORE it happens — active_connections climbing toward postgres's max_connections is the warning 32.1's cascade ignored.

🧪 PRACTICE — LAB

Load the alert rule into Prometheus, then send deliberate 500s (curl -X POST localhost/jobs/999999/apply/ against a job ID that doesn't exist, repeated 20x). Verify: the Prometheus /alerts page shows JobsEndpointHighErrorRate move from Inactive → Pending → Firing over the 2-minute window.

⚠️ Gotcha

Alerting on RAW counts instead of ratios pages you every traffic spike (Black Friday) and stays silent during a LOW-traffic outage (2 requests, both failing) — always ratio.

📊 Summary: four signals, one metric each, cover latency, traffic, errors and saturation across the whole easypj stack.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • docker stats is a live, single-host, zero-retention view — use it for right-now debugging, never as a monitoring strategy.
  • cAdvisor is the ONLY new container required to start collecting history; it reads the same cgroup data docker stats reads, just continuously.
  • Prometheus PULLS metrics from targets on a scrape interval; Grafana never talks to cAdvisor directly, only to Prometheus's stored time series.
  • Compose's service-name DNS is what lets prometheus.yml say targets: ['cadvisor:8080'] instead of a hardcoded IP.
  • Log shipping (gelf/fluentd) only works because every easypj container logs to stdout/stderr — an app writing its own log file is invisible to every driver.
  • The four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — cover nearly every real outage with one metric per tier.
  • Alert on RATIOS, not raw counts, or you page on Black Friday traffic and stay silent during a low-traffic outage.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Treating docker stats as a monitoring strategy → It has zero retention — cAdvisor + Prometheus is the recorded history alerting and dashboards need.
  • Mounting the Docker socket and host /sys/ /rootfs for cAdvisor without a second thought → That access can see every container on the host — treat it like 20.3's socket-mount warning.
  • Leaving Grafana's admin/changeme password in place → It's a demo convenience, not a production credential — rotate it immediately (20.1).
  • Assuming a log driver switch broke docker logs → Switching to fluentd/gelf makes docker logs go silent for that container — expected, the stream now goes to the shipped destination instead.
  • Writing app logs to a file instead of stdout, then swapping log drivers to "fix" shipping → No driver swap fixes an app that never talks to stdout — Chapter 6's rule is a hard precondition, not a suggestion.
  • Alerting on raw 5xx counts → Raw-count thresholds miss low-traffic outages and mis-fire on legitimate traffic spikes — always alert on a ratio.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker stats --no-stream for a single non-scrolling snapshot instead of Ctrl+C-ing a live stream mid-debug.
  • Keep Prometheus's /alerts page and Grafana's dashboard one bookmark apart — most incidents start with one and end in the other.
  • Grep a metric name straight off cAdvisor's raw /metrics page before writing PromQL — confirms exact label spelling (e.g. name="easypj-web") instead of guessing.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 31)

the Chapter 31 cheat-card 
docker stats --no-stream                            # one-shot snapshot, no history
docker run -d --name cadvisor -p 8080:8080 \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
  -v /:/rootfs:ro -v /sys:/sys:ro \
  gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1                   # start metrics collection
curl localhost:8080/metrics | grep easypj-web        # confirm cAdvisor sees it
docker compose up -d                                  # bring up prometheus+grafana too
docker logs easypj-web                                # only shows LOCAL drivers' data
docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Type}}' easypj-web  # which driver?

🧠 Chapter 31 — Practice Questions (10)

From "why docker stats doesn't scale" to ratio-based alerting — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why can't docker stats be the production monitoring solution for easypj, even though the numbers it shows are correct?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It is live-only and single-host — close the terminal or restart the daemon and the data is gone forever; past ~10 containers or more than one host there is no history, no alerting, and no chart to look back at.

EXPLANATION

This is exactly the gap 31.1's DOCKER STATS vs THE METRICS PIPELINE diagram draws — a snapshot vs a recorded stream.

Q2
What is cAdvisor's actual job, and what does it NOT do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

cAdvisor reads the same cgroup files (plus the Docker API) docker stats reads, and re-exposes them as a scrapable /metrics HTTP endpoint. It does NOT store history — Prometheus does that by scraping cAdvisor on an interval.

EXPLANATION

Confusing cAdvisor with a database is the most common misunderstanding of this section — it is a re-exposer, not a store: cgroup files → cAdvisor:8080/metrics (no history kept) → scraped every 15s → Prometheus TSDB (history lives HERE).

Q3
In prometheus.yml, why does targets: ['cadvisor:8080'] work without an IP address?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose's service-name DNS (10.4) resolves 'cadvisor' to the right container automatically — the same mechanism that lets nginx.conf say django:8000.

EXPLANATION

No config in this chapter hardcodes an IP anywhere — every target is a Compose service name.

Q4
What does rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{name="easypj-web"}[5m]) actually compute?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The average CPU-seconds-per-second consumed by the easypj-web container over the trailing 5-minute window — a smoothed rate, not an instantaneous or cumulative value.

EXPLANATION

rate() over a counter always yields a per-second average across the chosen window, which is why 5m windows smooth out single-second spikes.

Q5
Match each log driver to its behavior: json-file, gelf, fluentd.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

json-file: local disk, rotated, the default. gelf: UDP/TCP push to a Graylog/Loki-compatible endpoint. fluentd: push to a Fluentd/Fluent Bit collector, multi-destination routing.

EXPLANATION

Straight from 31.3's driver-comparison table — each row trades "how much setup" for "how far the logs travel."

Q6
Why is Chapter 6's "log to stdout only" rule a hard PRECONDITION for every log driver in 31.3, not just a best practice?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A log driver only ever captures a container's stdout/stderr file descriptor; an app that writes to its own log file bypasses that capture entirely — no driver swap fixes an app that never talks to stdout.

EXPLANATION

This is why the FLOW diagram's step ① (gunicorn logging to stdout) never changes even when step ② (the driver) does.

Q7
A teammate switches easypj-web's log driver from json-file to fluentd, then reports "docker logs is broken, it shows nothing." What's actually happening?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing broken — expected behavior. docker logs only reads the LOCAL json-file driver's stored data; under fluentd the stream is shipped elsewhere. Check the shipped destination (Fluent Bit/Loki) instead.

EXPLANATION

This is 31.3's closing gotcha, verified directly by the section's own PRACTICE step.

Q8
List the four golden signals and their easypj-specific metric + source.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Latency: p95 request duration on /jobs/, from django (nginx log). Traffic: requests/sec to nginx, from nginx access log. Errors: 5xx rate on /jobs/, from django/nginx logs. Saturation: postgres active_connections/max, from postgres_exporter. Saturation: redis used_memory/maxmemory, from redis_exporter.

EXPLANATION

One metric per tier is deliberate — the smallest set that still catches most real outages (Google SRE's model).

Q9
Why does the JobsEndpointHighErrorRate rule divide 5xx responses by ALL responses instead of alerting on a raw 5xx count?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A ratio stays meaningful regardless of traffic volume; a raw count either pages constantly on high-traffic days or stays silent during a low-traffic outage where only 2 requests fail but both are 5xx.

EXPLANATION

31.4's closing gotcha states this directly: always ratio, never raw count.

Q10
What does for: 2m in the alert rule accomplish, and what would happen without it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It requires the error-rate breach to PERSIST for 2 minutes before firing, filtering single-request blips. Without it, one transient 500 could page someone for a problem that self-resolved before anyone even looked.

EXPLANATION

31.4's PRACTICE step verifies this exact transition: Inactive → Pending → Firing over the 2-minute window, not an instant fire.

Starting from a cold laptop, run the cadvisor command from 31.1, bring up the Compose monitoring stack from 31.2, and paste ONE working PromQL query into a new Grafana panel — no notes. Stop the clock the moment the graph moves.

32.1 The Anatomy of a Container Outage

Every sequence this chapter drills traces back to one realistic easypj incident: a bad deploy leaks memory, one OOMKilled Pod cascades into a full-stack outage. The first-responder steps below use nothing you haven't already learned — docker logs, docker inspect, kubectl describe, and kubectl rollout undo (27.2) — in a specific, deliberate order. Reading Exit Code 137 and Reason: OOMKilled correctly (6.6, Appendix F.8) is the one piece of kernel trivia that turns this from guesswork into a two-minute triage.

Anatomy of an OOMKilled Cascade — 00:00 to 00:14
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        🔥 ANATOMY OF AN OOMKilled CASCADE — 00:00 TO 00:14               │
  │                                                                          │
  │ 00:00  deploy easypj:v47 (/jobs/search) — no --memory cap set            │
  │ 00:03  search view holds the full queryset in memory per request         │
  │ 00:06  gunicorn worker RSS climbs past the 512Mi node limit              │
  │ 00:07  kubelet OOMKills the worker → Pod restarts                        │
  │ 00:08  readiness probe fails mid-restart → Pod pulled from Service       │
  │ 00:09  remaining 2 Pods absorb 3x traffic → THEY hit the same wall       │
  │ 00:11  3/3 Pods cycling OOMKilled → easypj returns 503 to users          │
  │ 00:14  on-call rolls back to v46 (27.2) → Pods stabilize, 503s stop      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 🔬 first response: docker logs → docker inspect (OOMKilled?) →           │
  │    kubectl describe pod (Events:) → kubectl rollout undo (27.2)          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The command order in the transcript below is deliberate, not habit. kubectl get pods names the failure MODE first — CrashLoopBackOff, and a RESTARTS count that's still climbing. logs --previous reads the DEAD container's own output, because the live one hasn't logged anything yet. describe confirms the KERNEL's verdict — Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, straight out of Appendix F.8. rollout undo is the fastest safe mitigation once root cause is a bad deploy, not infrastructure.

TERMINAL — the first 90 seconds of triage
# Step 1 — name the failure MODE
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj
NAME              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
easypj-7f9-a1b2   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6

# Step 2 — read the DEAD container's evidence
$ kubectl logs easypj-7f9-a1b2 -n easypj --previous
MemoryError: unable to allocate 340MB for queryset

# Step 3 — confirm the KERNEL's verdict
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-7f9-a1b2 -n easypj | grep -A3 "Last State"
Last State:  Terminated
  Reason:    OOMKilled
  Exit Code: 137

# Step 4 — fastest safe mitigation
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj -n easypj
🚗 A Car-Crash Reconstruction, Not a Redesign

The timeline diagram above is a car crash reconstruction: each timestamp is a skid mark. You do not redesign the road at 00:07 — you clear the wreck (rollback) first, and investigate second in 32.3. Reproduce this exact sequence, unassisted, in under two minutes on a Pod you have never seen before — Appendix F.8 should already live in your head by the time you finish this chapter.

🔬 easypj: the leak in this scenario is real, not contrived — an unpaginated JobPost.objects.filter(...) in the search view materializes every matching row before slicing. Chapter 26.3's requests/limits caught the SYMPTOM (a Pod got killed instead of eating the whole node), but they never fix the QUERY that caused it.

⚠️ The Single Most Wasted Minute in a Real Incident

kubectl logs WITHOUT --previous on a restarted Pod shows the NEW container's (empty) log, not the crash. Always reach for --previous first on any Pod with a nonzero RESTARTS count.

🔧 Under the Hood — what OOMKilled + Exit Code 137 actually means

When a cgroup's memory usage crosses its configured ceiling — 6.6's --memory flag on a standalone container, or a Pod's memory limit underneath — the KERNEL's OOM killer, not Docker and not Kubernetes, selects a process inside that cgroup and sends it SIGKILL (signal 9). Exit codes above 128 encode "killed by signal N-128"; 128+9 = 137 is that SIGKILL, which is why "Exit Code: 137" and "Reason: OOMKilled" always appear together in kubectl describe pod — one is the raw exit status, the other is Kubernetes' label for the same kernel event.

 cgroup memory.max exceeded → kernel OOM killer → SIGKILL
           │                                          │
           ▼                                          ▼
  kubelet observes container death        exit code 137
           │                                     recorded
           ▼
  Reason: OOMKilled  (Kubernetes' label for the SAME event)
🔑 Also worth knowing: repeated crashes trigger CrashLoopBackOff, an exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s… capped at 5 minutes) BEFORE Kubernetes retries the container again — that growing delay is why a crash-looping Pod takes progressively longer between restarts, not a fixed interval.

32.2 Chaos Engineering — Practicing Failure on Purpose

Chaos engineering means one simple, uncomfortable idea: kill things ON PURPOSE, in a controlled window, so the FIRST time a container dies isn't during a real incident. What SHOULD happen automatically differs by layer — a restart policy (6.2) heals a standalone container that dies on one host; a ReplicaSet or Deployment (26.7, 28.4) heals a missing orchestrated Pod anywhere in the cluster. Chaos testing exists to prove that distinction actually holds, instead of trusting it as a theory.

🔁
Restart Policy (6.2)

Standalone docker run --restart unless-stopped reacts to a killed CONTAINER on one host. It restarts the SAME container in place — no scheduling, no cluster awareness.

🧬
ReplicaSet (26.7)

A Kubernetes ReplicaSet reacts to a missing POD anywhere in the cluster, reconciling desired-vs-actual replica count. It schedules a BRAND-NEW Pod — possibly on a different node — not a restart of the old one.

The Chaos Loop — Kill One, Watch the System Answer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         🌀 THE CHAOS LOOP — KILL ONE, WATCH THE SYSTEM ANSWER            │
  │                                                                          │
  │ pick a random easypj-web replica or Pod                                  │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼   docker kill <id>   OR   kubectl delete pod <name>               │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼   restart policy (6.2) / ReplicaSet (26.7) notices ONE gone       │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼   new container/Pod scheduled, readiness passes, traffic returns  │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼   measure: how many seconds was capacity below 100%?              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 💡 if recovery takes >30s or users see errors, that gap — not the        │
  │    kill itself — is the incident chaos engineering just found for free.  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
chaos.sh — kill a random easypj Pod every 5 minutes
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NAMESPACE="easypj"
while true; do
  victim=$(kubectl get pods -n "$NAMESPACE" -l app=easypj \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '\n' | shuf -n1)
  echo "$(date -Iseconds)  killing pod: $victim"
  kubectl delete pod "$victim" -n "$NAMESPACE" --grace-period=0
  sleep 300
done
🔥 A Fire Drill, Not a Real Fire

The CHAOS LOOP diagram above is a fire drill: you do not wait for a real fire to learn the exit route works — you trigger the alarm on purpose, on a Tuesday, and time it. Run chaos.sh against a 3-replica easypj Deployment while watch kubectl get pods -n easypj runs in a second terminal; verify RESTARTS climbs, READY never drops to 0/3 across all Pods simultaneously, and curl against the Service never returns anything but 200 during the test.

🔬 easypj: with 3 replicas and the readinessProbe from 27.3, killing one Pod should show traffic dip to roughly 67% capacity for a few seconds, then return to 100% — never a 503 to a real user. If recovery takes longer than 30 seconds or users see errors, that gap — not the kill itself — is the incident chaos engineering just found for free.

⚠️ Redundancy Is a Prerequisite, Not Optional

Never point chaos.sh at a namespace with only 1 replica — you are not testing resilience, you are just causing an outage. Chaos testing needs spare capacity to demonstrate; without it, there's nothing left to absorb the kill.

32.3 Writing a Blameless Postmortem

A postmortem has one standard shape regardless of company or tool: Timeline, Impact, Root Cause (5 Whys), and Action Items. "Blameless" is a specific promise inside that shape — the document names FAILURES OF THE SYSTEM (a missing memory limit, no query review) and never a person. Below is that format applied end-to-end to the 32.1 OOMKilled scenario, written the way it would actually ship.

postmortem-2026-07-02-jobs-search-oom.md
# Postmortem: /jobs/search 503 outage

## Timeline (UTC)
00:00  easypj:v47 deployed (new /jobs/search endpoint)
00:07  first Pod OOMKilled (see 32.1 diagram for full timeline)
00:11  full outage — 3/3 Pods cycling, 503s served
00:14  on-call rolled back to v46 — service restored

## Impact
- 14 minutes of degraded/down /jobs/search for all users
- ~1,100 failed requests (503), 0 data loss

## Root Cause — 5 Whys
1. Why did users see 503s?      → all 3 Pods were OOMKilled.
2. Why were they OOMKilled?     → v47's search view held every
                                  matching JobPost row in memory.
3. Why unbounded rows?          → `.filter(...)` was never
                                  paginated or `.iterator()`'d.
4. Why did review miss it?      → no load test against a large
                                  Skills/JobPost fixture set.
5. Why no load test gate?       → CI (Ch22) checks tests pass,
                                  never checks memory under load.

## Action Items
- [ ] paginate /jobs/search (owner: web team, due: this sprint)
- [ ] set memory requests/limits on ALL Deployments (26.3)
- [ ] add a load-test stage to CI before prod deploy (Ch22)
- [ ] alert on postgres/redis saturation BEFORE next incident (31.4)

The 5 Whys technique only works if each "why" interrogates the ANSWER to the previous why, not the original symptom again. Notice how questions 4 and 5 above move from the CODE bug (an unpaginated queryset) to the PROCESS gap that let it ship (no load-test CI gate) — a postmortem that stops at "why 1" fixes nothing structural, it just restates that Pods were OOMKilled.

✈️ An Airline Investigation, Not a Trial

Blameless is an airline crash investigation, not a trial: the goal is a checklist change that prevents the NEXT crash, never a name in a report. Punishing the reporter only teaches the next person to hide the next near-miss — which is exactly how the SAME incident happens twice.

🔬 easypj: the postmortem above traces one 503 all the way to "no load-test CI gate" — that action item, not a scolding email, is what actually stops incident #2 from being the same incident. As practice, write a full postmortem for a different easypj incident — a bad docker compose down -v that deleted the postgres_data volume (see Chapter 17) — and verify your own 5 Whys ends on a PROCESS or TOOLING gap, never a person's name.

🛑 A Wish Is Not a Fix

An action item without an OWNER and a DUE DATE is a wish, not a fix — it will still be open at the next incident. Every row in the Action Items table needs both, or it doesn't count as closed.

32.4 On-Call Runbooks for easypj

A runbook trades "figure it out" for "follow the steps" at 2 AM. The format is always the same four stages — Symptom, Diagnostic commands, Mitigation, Escalation — and it ties directly back to Appendix F's seven troubleshooting categories (F.1 container errors, F.2 network, F.3 volume, F.5 daemon, F.7 Kubernetes). A runbook IS that appendix, pre-filtered for one specific alert.

runbook — JobsEndpointHighErrorRate (31.4's alert)
SYMPTOM
  Alertmanager: "JobsEndpointHighErrorRate — page"

DIAGNOSTIC COMMANDS (run in order, stop when one explains it)
  1. kubectl get pods -n easypj
     → any CrashLoopBackOff or 0/1 READY? go to F.7.
  2. kubectl logs -n easypj -l app=easypj --previous --tail=50
     → OOMKilled / MemoryError? go to 32.1's triage sequence.
  3. kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj -- \
       python manage.py dbshell -c "SELECT 1;"
     → fails? postgres is the problem, go to F.5/F.1 (db).
  4. curl -w "%{http_code}\n" -o /dev/null -s localhost/jobs/
     → 502/504? nginx→django path is broken, go to F.2.

MITIGATION
  - Bad deploy confirmed  → kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj
  - DB saturation (31.4)  → scale down non-critical workers,
                            raise postgres max_connections temp.
  - Unknown after step 4  → escalate now, do not keep guessing

ESCALATION
  - No resolution in 15 min → page secondary on-call
  - Data integrity in doubt → page team lead + freeze deploys
StepCheckIf true, route to…
1kubectl get pods -n easypjCrashLoopBackOff or 0/1 READY → Appendix F.7
2kubectl logs ... --previous --tail=50OOMKilled / MemoryError → 32.1's triage sequence
3kubectl exec ... dbshell -c "SELECT 1;"Fails → postgres is the problem, Appendix F.5/F.1
4curl -w "%{http_code}\n" ...502/504 → nginx→django path broken, Appendix F.2

Each diagnostic step is ordered cheapest-and-most-likely first (Pod status) to most-specific-last (the HTTP path), and each one names EXACTLY which Appendix F category to open next. The runbook is a routing table into knowledge you already wrote, not new knowledge invented under pressure.

✈️ A Pilot's Emergency Checklist

Nobody re-derives aerodynamics mid-flight — they run the printed steps in order, because a printed order beats a scared brain's improvisation every single time. That's the entire value proposition of a runbook.

🔬 easypj: step 2 of the runbook above is 32.1's ENTIRE first-response sequence, condensed into one command — writing the runbook IS turning last incident's manual triage into next incident's reflex. As practice, hand this runbook to a teammate who has never seen the 32.1 incident and have them "resolve" a simulated alert using ONLY the document; verify they reach the correct mitigation step without asking you a single clarifying question — any gap they hit is a gap in the runbook, not in them.

⚠️ A Stale Runbook Is Worse Than None

A runbook that references a removed service or an old command burns exactly the 15 minutes escalation was supposed to save — worse than having no runbook, because it costs time AND trust. Review runbooks every time the referenced service or alert changes.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The triage order is deliberate: get pods (failure MODE) → logs --previous (dead container's evidence) → describe (kernel's verdict) → rollout undo (fastest safe mitigation) — same four steps regardless of which service failed.
  • kubectl logs WITHOUT --previous on a restarted Pod shows the NEW, empty container's log, not the crash.
  • A restart policy (6.2) heals a single CONTAINER; a ReplicaSet (26.7) heals a missing POD by reconciling desired-vs-actual count — chaos testing exploits exactly this distinction.
  • Chaos engineering means killing something ON PURPOSE, in a controlled window, so the first real failure isn't a surprise.
  • Blameless means naming FAILURES OF THE SYSTEM (a missing memory limit, no load-test gate), never a person.
  • 5 Whys must keep asking "why" against the PREVIOUS ANSWER, not the original symptom, or it stops at a code bug instead of the process gap that let it ship.
  • A runbook (Symptom → Diagnostics → Mitigation → Escalation) turns last incident's manual triage into next incident's reflex — and a stale one is worse than none.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Running kubectl logs <pod> without --previous on a restarted Pod → You're reading the NEW, empty container's log — the crash evidence is in the DEAD container's log; always add --previous first.
  • Pointing a chaos script at a namespace with only 1 replica → That isn't testing resilience — it's just causing an outage; chaos testing needs redundancy to demonstrate.
  • Writing an action item with no owner and no due date → It's a wish, not a fix — it will still be open at the next incident.
  • Trusting a runbook that references a removed service or a stale command → It burns exactly the 15 minutes escalation was supposed to save — keep runbooks updated after every incident.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Alias klp for kubectl logs --previous — it's the step everyone forgets under pressure.
  • Keep chaos.sh's sleep interval generous (5 min) on first runs — you want time to WATCH the recovery, not just trigger the kill.
  • Draft the postmortem's Timeline section FIRST, straight from kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp — reconstructing it from memory afterward loses minutes that matter.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 32)

the Chapter 32 cheat-card 
kubectl get pods -n easypj                                    # failure MODE first
kubectl logs <pod> -n easypj --previous --tail=50              # dead container's evidence
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj | grep -A3 "Last State"   # kernel verdict
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj -n easypj               # fastest safe mitigation
kubectl delete pod <name> -n easypj --grace-period=0            # chaos: kill on purpose
watch kubectl get pods -n easypj                                # observe recovery live
kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by=.lastTimestamp           # postmortem timeline source

🧠 Chapter 32 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From "the alert fired" to a closed, blameless postmortem — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
A Pod shows CrashLoopBackOff with RESTARTS climbing. What is the correct FIRST command?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl get pods -n easypj — it names the failure MODE and the restart COUNT before you spend time on slower commands.

EXPLANATION

This is 32.1's first triage step for a reason — cheapest, fastest check first, and it tells you whether you're even looking at a crash loop before you go hunting for evidence.

Q2
You run kubectl logs <pod> on a just-restarted Pod and see nothing useful. What went wrong?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

You read the NEW container's (empty) log; the crash evidence is in the DEAD container's log. Re-run with --previous.

EXPLANATION

This is the single most common wasted minute in a real incident (this chapter's #1 Gotcha) — the fix is one flag, but only if you remember it exists.

Q3
(diagram) Walk through what Exit Code 137 + Reason: OOMKilled means.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

cgroup memory ceiling exceeded → kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL → exit code 137 recorded → kubelet labels it OOMKilled.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ over memory.max → OOM killer → SIGKILL(9) │
│   → exit 137 → Kubernetes: "OOMKilled"    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
EXPLANATION

Exit Code 137 and Reason: OOMKilled are not two separate facts — they're the SAME kernel event described twice, once as a raw exit status and once as Kubernetes' human-readable label (see the Under the Hood box in 32.1).

Q4
Why is kubectl rollout undo correct in 32.1's scenario, and when would it NOT be the right call?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Correct here because the root cause is a bad deploy (v47's unbounded query) — rollback removes the bad code immediately. It would be wrong if the cause were infrastructure (e.g. a full disk), since rollback doesn't fix an environment problem.

EXPLANATION

rollout undo treats the SYMPTOM (bad Pods) by reverting to a known-good ReplicaSet — it says nothing about disk space, node health, or external dependencies.

Q5
What's the difference between what a restart policy (6.2) heals and what a ReplicaSet (26.7) heals?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A restart policy reacts to a killed CONTAINER on one host; a ReplicaSet reacts to a missing POD anywhere in the cluster, reconciling desired-vs-actual replica count.

EXPLANATION

This is the exact distinction 32.2's chaos script exploits — deleting one Pod and timing how fast the controller notices.

Q6
(table) Per the CHAOS LOOP diagram, what should happen at each step?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
StepExpected outcome
kill one Podone replica goes missing
ReplicaSet noticesschedules a replacement
new Pod readytraffic returns to 100%
recovery >30s or errors seenTHAT gap — not the kill itself — is the real incident chaos engineering just found for free
EXPLANATION

This is 32.2's PRACTICE step made concrete — the last row is the whole point of chaos engineering: the GAP is the incident, not the kill.

Q7
Why must chaos testing never target a namespace with only 1 replica?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

With 1 replica, killing it just causes a real outage — there is no redundancy left to demonstrate resilience against.

EXPLANATION

Chaos testing requires spare capacity as a precondition; without it, you're not testing anything, you're just breaking production on purpose.

Q8
Why does stopping the postmortem's 5 Whys at "Why 1" fail to prevent a repeat incident?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It only restates the symptom (Pods were OOMKilled); the real fix comes from following the chain to Why 4 and 5 — no load-test fixture, no CI gate for memory under load — which are PROCESS fixes, not a one-line code patch.

EXPLANATION

32.3's worked example shows exactly this: stopping at Why 1 fixes nothing that prevents incident #2.

Q9
What are the four required sections of a blameless postmortem, and what does "blameless" protect against?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Timeline, Impact, Root Cause (5 Whys), Action Items. Blameless protects against naming a PERSON in the document.

EXPLANATION

Punishing a reporter only teaches the next person to hide the next near-miss — which guarantees the SAME incident happens again, just later and hidden.

Q10
Why does the JobsEndpointHighErrorRate runbook check kubectl get pods before checking postgres connectivity?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Pod status is the fastest, cheapest check and rules out the most common cause first (a bad deploy); only if that's clean do you spend time on slower, more specific checks like a dbshell query.

EXPLANATION

This is the same cheapest-first ordering principle from 32.1 applied to runbook design — each diagnostic step should be more expensive or more specific than the last.

Verify: you reach kubectl rollout undo or a clear "not OOMKilled, escalate" call inside two minutes, using nothing but the four commands from this chapter's cheat-card.

Chapter 33 · Cost & Performance Tuning

Chapters 26-27 taught you to SET requests and limits; Chapter 8 taught you to optimize a Dockerfile for correctness and security. Run easypj at real scale and both become money — an oversized request wastes a node's capacity every hour it runs, and a fat image wastes storage, egress, and CI minutes on every single build. This chapter turns yesterday's best-practice advice into today's budget line, with real measured numbers, so nobody has to ask "why is our Docker bill bigger than expected?" again.

🔴 Advanced/Production ⏱️ ~75-100 min 💰 Cost & Performance 🎯 Not DCA-Graded

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Replace a guessed requests/limits configuration (26.3) with numbers derived from sampled kubectl top data
  • ✅ Translate Chapter 8's image-size optimization into a monthly dollar figure across storage, egress, and CI-minutes cost lines
  • ✅ Reshape a multi-stage Dockerfile so BuildKit runs independent stages in parallel instead of serially
  • ✅ Decide when Build Cloud (22.5) is worth paying for versus running local BuildKit
  • ✅ Design and run a fair bare-metal-vs-containerized benchmark and interpret the result correctly
  • ✅ Separate "Docker overhead" from other root causes (a --cpus limit, a slow query) when performance looks off
🎓 DCA Relevance
Not DCA-Graded 0%
🎯 Beyond the Exam — the Discipline the DCA Assumes You'll Add

The DCA exam tests that you CAN set requests/limits (26.3, 27.5) and optimize a Dockerfile (Chapter 8); it never tests whether the numbers you chose were right. This chapter is that measurement discipline — production/day-2 depth, pure cost/performance engineering built on top of Chapters 8, 22, and 26-27.

  • Why this chapter exists: Chapters 26-27 taught requests/limits and Chapter 8 taught image optimization as CORRECTNESS and SECURITY concerns. Run easypj at real scale and both become MONEY — an oversized request wastes a node's capacity every hour it runs; a fat image wastes storage, egress and CI minutes on every single build.
  • The problem this solves: "our Docker bill is bigger than expected, and nobody can say exactly why."

33.1 Right-Sizing Requests & Limits from Real Usage Data

Chapters 26.3 and 27.5 taught you how to SET requests and limits; this section teaches you how to MEASURE what to set them TO, from real traffic. The goal is to replace 26.3's guessed configuration with numbers derived from a week of sampled kubectl top data — never a guess.

TERMINAL — measuring easypj-web over a real day
$ kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers
POD              NAME     CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
easypj-7f9-a1b2  django   210m         340Mi
easypj-7f9-c3d4  django   195m         355Mi
easypj-7f9-e5f6  django   640m         480Mi   ← traffic spike
$ kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers \
    --sort-by=memory | head -1     # repeat hourly, log the peak

kubectl top reads live metrics-server data — an instantaneous reading, exactly like docker stats (31.1's limitation) — so it must be SAMPLED repeatedly and logged, not read once. Requests should sit near the observed TYPICAL load so the scheduler doesn't over-reserve nodes, while limits should sit above the observed PEAK with margin so legitimate spikes don't get OOMKilled per 6.6/27.5:

ResourceGuessed (26.3)MeasuredRight-sized
CPU request250m210m typical200m
CPU limit1000m640m peak800m
Memory request256Mi355Mi typical384Mi
Memory limit512Mi480Mi peak640Mi
💡 The Suitcase Analogy

The measured table above is packing a suitcase from a week of actually worn outfits instead of guessing. 26.3's 250m/256Mi was a guess made before the trip; 33.1's 200m/384Mi is what the week actually proved you needed.

easypj in production: the 640m CPU spike row in the terminal example above is real traffic — a job-alert email blast hitting /jobs/. Set the limit UNDER that number and 32.1's OOMKilled cascade recurs on every future blast.

🧪 Practice — Lab

Sample kubectl top pod for easypj-web every hour for one full day, and record min/typical/peak. Verify: your recommended request sits near typical and your limit sits above peak — recompute if either measurement was a fluke.

📊 Summary: measure with kubectl top over TIME, set requests near typical and limits above observed peak — never a guess.

⚠️ Gotcha

Sampling for one hour catches nothing — right-sizing needs a full traffic cycle (usually a week) to see both quiet nights and peak-hour spikes.

🔧 Under the Hood — where kubectl top's numbers actually come from

kubectl top is not a new measurement — it queries the Kubernetes metrics-server, which polls each kubelet's /stats/summary endpoint, which is populated by cAdvisor embedded INSIDE the kubelet (the same cAdvisor Chapter 31 ran as a standalone container against plain Docker). 33.1's "measure, don't guess" numbers and 31.1's Prometheus dashboard ultimately trace back to the identical cgroup files — kubectl top just samples them on demand instead of continuously.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ cgroup memory.current / cpu.stat (same files as 31.1's cAdvisor)│
  │             │                                                   │
  │             ▼                                                   │
  │  kubelet's embedded cAdvisor → /stats/summary                  │
  │             │                                                   │
  │             ▼                                                   │
  │  metrics-server (cluster-wide aggregator) → kubectl top         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 This is also why kubectl top shares 31.1's core limitation: metrics-server keeps only a short in-memory window, so 33.1's instruction to sample REPEATEDLY and log the results yourself is not a suggestion — long-term history is Prometheus's job (31.2), not metrics-server's.

33.2 The Real Cost of Image Size at Scale

Chapter 8 optimized easypj from 850 MB down to 180 MB for SECURITY and speed reasons; this section prices that exact same win in dollars. The goal is to state Chapter 8's optimization win as a monthly dollar figure a manager, not just an engineer, will act on. There are three cost lines — registry storage, egress bandwidth, and CI minutes — worked here for a team doing 50 image builds/day:

Cost line850 MB image180 MB image (Ch8)
Registry storage
(200 tags kept)		850 MB × 200 tags = 170 GB180 MB × 200 tags = 36 GB
Egress / pull
(50 builds/day)		50 × 850 MB = 42.5 GB/day pulled50 × 180 MB = 9 GB/day pulled
CI minutes
(pull time, 8.1)		~11 min pull × 50 builds = 550 min~2.4 min pull × 50 builds = 120 min
Monthly CI minutes~16,500 min/month~3,600 min/month

The three cost lines compound: storage bills per GB-month kept across every retained tag; egress bills per GB actually transferred (every CI pull, every node pull, every developer pull); CI minutes bill per minute of RUNNER time, and pull time IS runner time even though no build step has run yet. Chapter 8.1's "~11 min vs ~2.4 min" pull numbers are the CI-minutes line above.

💡 The Airline-Baggage Invoice

The cost table above is the airline-baggage analogy from 8.1, converted into an invoice: every kilo (MB) you stopped checking is a fee you stop paying, 50 times a day, forever — not once, EVERY build.

📦
~33.5 GB/day Reclaimed

At 50 builds/day, the 670 MB Chapter 8 removed from easypj is not "670 MB smaller" — it is ~33.5 GB/day of pulls that never happen.

⏱️
~7.2 hours/day Reclaimed

That same 670 MB removal frees roughly 7.2 hours/day of CI runner time that was previously spent just pulling the fat image, not building anything.

🧪 Practice — Lab

Take YOUR team's real builds/day and registry retention policy, and plug them into the cost table's formula (size × builds/day, size × tags kept). Verify: you can name a monthly GB figure and a monthly CI-minutes figure, not just "smaller is better."

📊 Summary: image size is a recurring multiplier — storage × tags kept, egress × builds/day, CI minutes × pull time — never a one-time number.

⚠️ Gotcha

Teams that fix image size ONCE and never re-audit regress silently as dependencies grow — re-run docker history (7.6) every quarter, not just at the Chapter 8 rewrite.

33.3 Build Time Optimization Beyond Caching

Chapters 8 and 22 covered layer caching; this section covers making independent build STAGES run in parallel, not just cached. BuildKit runs stages with no shared dependency concurrently — multi-stage Dockerfiles should be shaped to exploit this. --platform matrix builds (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) also run each architecture as its own parallel build graph, not sequentially.

Serial vs Parallel Multi-Stage Builds
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                🏗️ SERIAL vs PARALLEL MULTI-STAGE BUILDS                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │ SERIAL (one lane):                                                       │
  │ deps ─▶ compile ─▶ test ─▶ collectstatic ─▶ final   (4 stages, 1 lane)   │
  │                                                                          │
  │ PARALLEL (BuildKit default — independent stages overlap):                │
  │ deps ─▶ compile ─┐                                                       │
  │ deps ─▶ lint ─────┼─▶ final      (wall-clock = longest lane, not sum)    │
  │ deps ─▶ test ─────┘                                                      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 💡 parallelism only helps stages that do NOT need each other's           │
  │    output — lint and test run BESIDE compile, never before it.           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

BuildKit builds a DEPENDENCY GRAPH from the Dockerfile, not a top-to-bottom script — any two stages that do not COPY --from= each other are scheduled concurrently, exactly the PARALLEL half of the diagram above. --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 doubles the graph into two parallel trees; 22.5's Build Cloud adds MORE concurrent workers plus a cache shared across the whole team, not just one machine.

Team profileVerdict
<10 builds/day, 1 local machinelocal BuildKit, Cloud unneeded
50 builds/day, multi-arch imagesCloud's shared cache wins big
Many devs rebuilding same depsCloud cache reused across TEAM
CI runners already fast + cachedCloud adds cost, not much speed
💡 The Three-Cooks Analogy

The diagram's SERIAL lane is one cook doing every step in order; the PARALLEL lanes are three cooks working side-by-side who all hand their trays to the same plating station (final) — the meal is ready as soon as the SLOWEST cook finishes, never the sum of all three.

easypj in production: splitting jobpost's Dockerfile into deps, lint (ruff), and test (pytest) stages that all COPY --from=deps but never from each other lets BuildKit run lint and test beside compile — CI wall-clock drops even though total CPU work is unchanged.

🧪 Practice — Lab

Split a single-lane Dockerfile's lint/test steps into separate stages that both depend only on deps, then run docker buildx build --progress=plain .. Verify: the build log shows lint's and test's stage numbers interleaved in the timestamps, not sequential.

📊 Summary: cache reuse (Chapters 8/22) makes REPEAT builds fast; parallel stage design makes even a COLD build fast.

⚠️ Gotcha

A stage that COPY --from= an unrelated stage "just in case" silently serializes two lanes that could have run side by side — audit COPY --from lines when builds feel slower than the graph should allow.

33.4 Benchmarking Container Overhead

Does containerizing a Django workload cost real CPU/memory versus running it bare-metal? Measure it, don't assume it. The goal is to produce a real, repeatable overhead number for easypj instead of citing "containers are basically free" from memory — a reproducible benchmark uses the same gunicorn command, the same hardware, container vs host process, and the same load generator:

TERMINAL — reproducible overhead benchmark
# 1) bare-metal baseline (no Docker at all)
$ gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3 &
$ wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/
Requests/sec:  1842.30   Latency p99: 68ms

# 2) same command, containerized, no limits
$ docker run -d -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
$ wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/
Requests/sec:  1798.11   Latency p99: 71ms

# 3) resource usage during the container run
$ docker stats --no-stream easypj-web
CPU %: 68.40%   MEM USAGE / LIMIT: 310MiB / 512MiB
MetricBare-metalContainerizedOverhead
Requests/sec1842.301798.11~2.4% lower
p99 latency68ms71ms~4.4% higher
Memory (RSS)~290 MiB~310 MiB~7% higher

The comparison MUST hold everything constant except the container boundary: same gunicorn --workers, same host, same wrk parameters, run back-to-back to cancel out ambient noise. The small overhead observed (namespaces + cgroup accounting + the bridge network's extra hop) is the real, measurable cost of 1.3's isolation — not zero, but small next to a full VM.

💡 The Receipt for "Near-Native"

The 1.3 VM-vs-container diagram showed containers' "near-native" CPU overhead as a claim; this section is that claim's receipt — the table above is what "near-native" measures out to on an actual easypj workload.

easypj in production: a ~2-4% overhead is the price for 1.3's entire benefit — portability, isolation, the whole rest of this guide — worth comparing against BEFORE assuming Docker caused a slowdown that a slow query or missing index (33.1's real culprit) actually caused.

🧪 Practice — Lab

Run the three terminal commands above on your own machine, bare-metal then containerized. Verify: your overhead lands in a similar small single-digit-percent range — a double-digit gap means something else is wrong (bridge network MTU, --cpus throttling from 6.6, not "Docker is slow").

📊 Summary: measured, containerization costs low single-digit percent overhead on a Django workload — not free, but rarely the real bottleneck.

⚠️ Gotcha

Benchmarking WITH a --cpus limit already set (6.6) measures your limit, not Docker's overhead — benchmark unlimited first, then re-test with production limits as a SEPARATE number.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Right-size requests near TYPICAL measured usage and limits above measured PEAK with margin — never a guess.
  • kubectl top (and docker stats) are instantaneous reads — sampling repeatedly over a full traffic cycle (usually a week) is what makes the numbers trustworthy.
  • Image size is a recurring multiplier, not a one-time number: storage × tags kept, egress × builds/day, CI minutes × pull time.
  • Re-audit image size quarterly (docker history, 7.6) — teams that fix it once regress silently as dependencies grow.
  • BuildKit schedules independent Dockerfile stages CONCURRENTLY by default; a stray COPY --from= on an unrelated stage silently re-serializes two lanes that could run side by side.
  • Build Cloud (22.5) pays for itself with high build volume, multi-arch matrices, or many developers sharing one dependency cache — not for a single low-volume local setup.
  • A fair overhead benchmark holds everything constant except the container boundary, separating Docker's real (small, single-digit-percent) overhead from unrelated causes.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Sampling kubectl top for only an hour and calling it "measured" → Right-sizing needs a full traffic cycle to see quiet nights and peak-hour spikes.
  • Fixing image size once and never re-auditing → Dependency creep regresses the win silently — re-check every quarter with docker history.
  • Adding COPY --from= an unrelated stage "just in case" → It silently serializes two lanes BuildKit could otherwise run in parallel.
  • Benchmarking WITH a --cpus limit already set → That measures your limit, not Docker's real overhead — benchmark unlimited first, then re-test with production limits separately.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers --sort-by=memory on a schedule instead of manually re-running it every hour.
  • docker buildx build --progress=plain to actually SEE stage timestamps interleave — the default output hides parallelism.
  • Keep a standing docker history <image> --no-trunc habit before every quarterly image-size review.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 33)

the Chapter 33 cheat-card 
kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers      # sample usage
kubectl top pod --containers --sort-by=memory | head -1   # find the peak
docker history <image> --no-trunc                          # audit layer sizes (7.6)
docker buildx build --progress=plain .                     # see stage parallelism
wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/            # load generator
docker stats --no-stream easypj-web                        # usage during a benchmark

🧠 Chapter 33 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From a guess to a measured, priced stack — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Why does 33.1 insist on sampling kubectl top repeatedly instead of reading it once?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Like docker stats, it's an instantaneous reading — one sample could catch a quiet moment or a fluke spike. Only repeated sampling over a full traffic cycle reveals TYPICAL vs PEAK usage.

EXPLANATION

This is exactly why 33.1's PRACTICE step asks you to sample hourly for a full day rather than run the command once and call it done.

Q2
Using 33.1's measured values, what CPU request/limit would you set, and why not the original 26.3 guess?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER
ResourceGuessed (26.3)MeasuredRight-sized
CPU request250m210m typical200m
CPU limit1000m640m peak800m
EXPLANATION

Requests sit near typical so the scheduler doesn't over-reserve; limits sit above observed peak with margin.

Q3
Why does setting a memory limit below the 640m CPU spike observed in 33.1 risk recreating 32.1's incident?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

That spike is real legitimate traffic — a job-alert email blast. A limit set under it OOMKills the container on every future occurrence of that same pattern.

EXPLANATION

This connects 33.1's right-sizing rule directly back to Chapter 32.1's OOMKilled cascade — the fix for one is the prevention for the other.

Q4
Using the SERIAL vs PARALLEL diagram, why does splitting lint/test into their own stages speed up CI wall-clock without reducing total CPU work?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

BuildKit builds a dependency graph, not a script; independent stages with no shared dependency run concurrently, so wall-clock equals the longest lane, not the sum — total CPU work is unchanged, just spent in parallel.

EXPLANATION 
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ deps ─▶ compile ─┐                     │
  │ deps ─▶ lint ─────┼─▶ final             │
  │ deps ─▶ test ─────┘  (longest lane wins)│
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
Q5
Give one condition where Build Cloud (22.5) is worth paying for, and one where it isn't.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Worth it: 50+ builds/day with multi-arch images, or many devs rebuilding the same deps. Not worth it: fewer than 10 builds/day on one local machine — local BuildKit is enough.

EXPLANATION

This is 33.3's Build Cloud verdict table condensed into the two extreme rows.

Q6
Why does an unrelated COPY --from= hurt build time even though it looks harmless?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It creates an artificial dependency edge in BuildKit's graph, forcing that stage to wait for the unrelated one — serializing two lanes that could otherwise run beside each other.

EXPLANATION

This is 33.3's closing gotcha — audit COPY --from lines whenever a build feels slower than the dependency graph should allow.

Q7
Why must the bare-metal and containerized benchmark runs use the SAME gunicorn --workers count, host, and load parameters?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

To isolate the container boundary as the ONLY variable — any other difference would contaminate the measured "overhead" number with something unrelated to Docker.

EXPLANATION

33.4's three-step terminal sequence is designed around this exact constraint: same command, same hardware, same load generator, back-to-back.

Q8
The 33.4 table shows ~2-4% lower throughput for the containerized run. What causes this overhead?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Namespace and cgroup accounting plus the bridge network's extra hop — the real, measurable cost of Chapter 1.3's isolation, small next to a full VM.

EXPLANATION

This is the "receipt" for the near-native claim Chapter 1.3 made without numbers.

Q9
A benchmark shows a DOUBLE-DIGIT percent slowdown under Docker. What should you suspect FIRST?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A --cpus throttling limit already applied (6.6), a bridge-network MTU issue, or another environmental difference — a double-digit gap signals something else is wrong, not "Docker is slow."

EXPLANATION

33.4's own gotcha names --cpus specifically: benchmark unlimited first, then re-test with production limits as a separate number.

Q10
Why re-run docker history every quarter instead of trusting Chapter 8's original optimization forever?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Dependencies grow over time and image size regresses silently — a one-time fix without ongoing audits eventually erodes back toward the original bloated size.

EXPLANATION

33.2's closing gotcha turns Chapter 7.6's docker history command into a recurring quarterly habit, not a one-off check.

In one line: Chapter 33 replaces four different guesses — a resource guess (26.3), an unpriced image-size win (Chapter 8), an unexamined serial build, and an assumed "containers are basically free" — with four measured numbers: a request/limit pair backed by real traffic, a monthly cost figure a manager will act on, a build that runs its independent stages side by side, and a small, honest overhead percentage that puts Docker's real cost in writing instead of folklore.

The takeaway: every number in this chapter came from measuring something real — kubectl top samples, a cost formula, a build log's timestamps, a back-to-back benchmark — never from memory or assumption.

Chapter 34 · Docker & AI Workloads

Every workload so far assumed a CPU-bound Django process. AI workloads break two assumptions at once: the "image" can BE a multi-gigabyte model instead of application code, and the container may need a PHYSICAL GPU passed through the isolation boundary Chapter 1.3 built on namespaces and cgroups alone. This chapter extends easypj with a hypothetical AI sidecar to show both changes without abandoning anything already built. Problem solved here: "our stack needs a model running next to it — does everything I've learned still apply?"
