34.1 Docker Model Runner — Running LLMs as Local Services

🎯 Goal: Run a local LLM as a service and call it exactly like the OpenAI API, with zero cloud dependency or API key.

Docker's built-in way to pull and run local LLMs is the same mental model as docker run, applied to models. docker model treats a quantized model file as an OCI artifact — pulled, cached, and versioned identically to easypj:v1, per 1.9's OCI standards, even though the payload is model weights, not a filesystem layer of app code. The runner serves an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions route, so any code written against the OpenAI SDK works by changing only the base URL.

TERMINAL — pulling and serving a local model
$ docker model pull ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M
Pulling ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M... done (1.9 GB)
$ docker model run ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M &
Model server listening on http://localhost:12434/engines/...
$ curl http://localhost:12434/engines/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"ai/llama3.2","messages":[{"role":"user",
         "content":"Summarize this job post in one line."}]}'
{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"Backend Django role..."}}]}
docker model pull/run — the Same Two Verbs, a Different Payload
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🤖 docker model pull/run — SAME VERBS, NEW PAYLOAD           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ docker model pull ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M                               │
  │        │                                                                 │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │  OCI REGISTRY  ── manifest → quantized weights blob (not code layers) ──▶│
  │        │                     cached locally, exactly like `easypj:v1`    │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │  $ docker model run ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M &                             │
  │        │                                                                 │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │  Model server :: http://localhost:12434/engines/v1/chat/completions      │
  │        │              (OpenAI-compatible — SDK code just changes         │
  │        ▼               its base_url, nothing else)                      │
  │  $ curl .../chat/completions  →  {"choices":[{"message": {...}}]}        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The docker pull / docker run Analogy

The TERMINAL example is docker pull / docker run wearing a model's clothes: same two verbs, same registry concept (1.4), the "image" just happens to be weights instead of a Python interpreter and Django.

📦
OCI Artifact, Not App Image

The payload is model weights, but the pull/cache/version machinery underneath is identical to any other image — same registry API, same content-addressable storage.

🔌
OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint

Existing OpenAI-SDK code points at localhost:12434 instead of the cloud by changing only the base URL — the request/response shape never changes.

🔬 easypj: a "summarize this job post" feature can call localhost:12434 in development and a real OpenAI endpoint in production — same request shape, per 34.3's sidecar pattern.

🧪 Practice — Summarize a Real Job Post

Run the TERMINAL commands above and swap the prompt for a real JobPost description from your fixtures. Verify: the response arrives from localhost, and docker model ls lists the cached model with no re-download on a second docker model run.

🛑 Gotcha — The Model Runner API Is Unauthenticated

Any client that can reach it, including other containers on the SAME Docker network, can pull, load, and run models. Never expose port 12434 (or the container-internal DMR endpoint) beyond a trusted network boundary.

⚠️ Gotcha — Quantized Still Means Real RAM

A 3B-Q4 model is still ~2 GB resident. Treat it like any other container in 33.1's right-sizing exercise — it is not free just because it's "local."

34.2 GPU Passthrough with --gpus

🎯 Goal: Get a container to see a host GPU and prove it with one command, understanding exactly what --gpus changed.

Two prerequisites gate everything in this section: an NVIDIA driver on the HOST, plus the nvidia-container-toolkit package, which registers the "nvidia" OCI runtime alongside runc (per 1.9's runtime landscape). Once both are in place, --gpus all exposes every GPU visible on the host, and --gpus "device=0" exposes exactly one specific GPU — the same isolation model as always, just one more device class.

--gpus Flag — From Host GPU to Container Process
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            🎮 --gpus FLAG — FROM HOST GPU TO CONTAINER PROCESS           │
  │                                                                          │
  │ 🖥️ host: NVIDIA driver + nvidia-container-toolkit installed             │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼                                                                   │
  │ $ docker run --gpus all easypj-inference:v1        (all GPUs)            │
  │ $ docker run --gpus "device=0" easypj-inference:v1  (GPU 0 only)         │
  │      │                                                                   │
  │      ▼                                                                   │
  │ runtime becomes nvidia (not runc directly) — CUDA libs and               │
  │ /dev/nvidia* devices are injected into the container automatically       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ $ docker exec easypj-inference nvidia-smi   → GPU listed = success       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
FlagWhat it exposesTypical use
--gpus allEvery GPU visible on the hostSingle-tenant host, one workload owns the box
--gpus "device=0"Exactly one specific GPU (by index)Multi-GPU host, isolating workloads per card

Under the hood, --gpus tells dockerd to hand the container to the nvidia OCI runtime (installed alongside runc per 1.9) instead of runc directly; that runtime injects the driver's character devices (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidiactl) and CUDA userspace libraries into the container's namespace — the same namespace isolation from 1.3, just with one more device class made visible on purpose.

💡 The Hotel Gym Analogy

The diagram above is a hotel giving a room a KEY to the gym (--gpus) instead of building the room its own gym — the room (container) still shares the building's one gym (GPU), same as it always shared the building's one kernel (1.3).

🔬 easypj: 34.3's resume-matching sidecar runs docker run --gpus "device=0" easypj-inference:v1 only if the embedding model benefits from GPU acceleration — the web/postgres/redis/nginx tier from Chapter 4 never touches this flag at all.

🧪 Practice — Prove the Passthrough Chain

Install nvidia-container-toolkit on a GPU-equipped host, then run docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.5.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi. Verify: the output lists your actual GPU model and driver version, proving the passthrough chain end-to-end before touching easypj at all.

⚠️ Gotcha — Silent Failure Without the Toolkit

--gpus silently does nothing (no error) on a host missing the toolkit. Always confirm with nvidia-smi INSIDE the container — never assume the flag was honored.

🔧 Under the Hood — how one registry stores both Django images and model weights

The OCI Distribution Spec supports ARBITRARY artifact types, not just container image layers — a manifest just needs a mediaType field. A normal image manifest points at gzipped filesystem layers; docker model pull's manifest points at a quantized weights file instead, but both are pushed/pulled/cached through the exact same registry API and content-addressable storage (1.9's OCI standards) — the registry doesn't know or care that one "image" is Python + Django and the other is a few billion numbers.

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  OCI Registry (same API for both)                              │
 │    ├─ easypj:v1        manifest → gzipped filesystem layers    │
 │    └─ ai/llama3.2:3B   manifest → quantized weights blob       │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

--gpus works on a similar "reuse the existing plumbing" principle: the OCI Runtime Spec supports prestart hooks, and nvidia-container-toolkit registers one that runs before the container starts, injecting /dev/nvidia* devices and CUDA userspace libraries into the container's mount namespace — no special-case code in dockerd itself, just a runtime swap (runc → nvidia) plus a hook, exactly like 1.9 described for pluggable runtimes.

🔑 Same plumbing, two payloads: pull/cache/version and prestart runtime hooks are generic OCI mechanisms — Docker didn't write special-case code for either AI models or GPUs, it reused what 1.9 already built.

34.3 Containerizing an ML Inference Sidecar for easypj

🎯 Goal: Add a matching service to the easypj stack that jobpost calls over the network, without merging it into django's image.

Consider a hypothetical resume-matching service: it scores a JobPost against an uploaded resume, and is called by jobpost — never called directly by a browser. It gets its own Dockerfile, separate from easypj's, with a different base image, a different dependency set, and a different resource profile: CPU-bound inference versus I/O-bound Django, with no need to scale 1:1 with web replicas.

The Resume-Matching Sidecar Next to easypj
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             🧩 THE RESUME-MATCHING SIDECAR NEXT TO easypj                │
  │                                                                          │
  │ 🌐 nginx:80 → django:8000 (easypj/jobpost) → postgres:5432               │
  │                   │                                                      │
  │                   │ POST /api/match  (internal network only)             │
  │                   ▼                                                      │
  │           🧠 inference:9000  (resume-matcher, own Dockerfile)            │
  │           CPU: 2 cores | RAM: 3Gi | no GPU (CPU-only model)              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 💡 the web tier stays thin; the heavy model lives in its OWN             │
  │    container so one slow inference call never blocks /jobs/.             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
inference/Dockerfile — the sidecar's own build
FROM python:3.12-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      libgomp1 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt   # sentence-transformers, fastapi
COPY app/ .
EXPOSE 9000
USER 1000:1000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "9000"]

The sidecar diagram above adds ONE new service to Chapter 10.4's compose.yaml — inference: — reachable only on the internal backend network (10.4's network isolation), never exposed via nginx. Its Dockerfile is intentionally separate from easypj's (8.2's base-image choice) because a sentence-transformers model needs different, heavier dependencies than Django ever will.

💡 The Kitchen Line Analogy

The diagram is a restaurant's kitchen line: the grill station (django, fast, high-volume) never stops to also run the slow sous-vide station (inference) — each has its own equipment and its own pace, connected only by an order ticket (the POST /api/match call).

📁
Its Own Dockerfile

Different base image, different dependency set, different resource profile from easypj's web tier — never bolted onto Chapter 8's optimized image.

🔒
Network-Only Access

Reachable only on the internal backend network, never published or proxied through nginx — jobpost calls it, nothing external can.

🔬 easypj: jobpost's Skills model gets a match_score(job, resume) helper that POSTs to http://inference:9000/match — if the inference container is slow or down, that ONE feature degrades gracefully (Skills scoring), /jobs/ itself never notices.

📖 Calling Docker Model Runner From a Real Sidecar

A REAL sidecar calling Docker Model Runner itself (rather than easypj's own custom inference service above) would call http://model-runner.docker.internal from inside a container on Docker Desktop — no port needed, unlike 34.1's host-side localhost:12434 (on Docker Engine, use http://172.17.0.1:12434 instead).

🧪 Practice — Confirm Internal-Only Reachability

Add the inference service to compose.yaml on the backend network only, build it, and call it from a shell inside the django container with curl http://inference:9000/health. Verify: the SAME curl fails from your HOST machine (no published port) — proof the sidecar is truly internal-only.

🛑 Gotcha — Don't Fatten the Web Image

A pip install sentence-transformers inside easypj's OWN Dockerfile is the anti-pattern this section exists to prevent — it fattens 8.1's 180 MB web image with weight only the sidecar ever needed.

34.4 Resource Planning for GPU-Bound Containers

🎯 Goal: Set a GPU-bound inference container's resource plan so it never crashes from VRAM oversubscription under load.

33.1's CPU/memory right-sizing math needs a THIRD dimension for GPU workloads: GPU memory (VRAM), not just host RAM. Unlike CPU, which the kernel time-slices fairly (6.6), a GPU has no throttling equivalent for VRAM — it is closer to 6.6's --memory: a hard wall. Two containers each assuming they own the full 24 GB card will both allocate, and the SECOND one's cudaMalloc fails outright, crashing that process.

DimensionCPU/RAM (33.1)GPU (this section)
Over-limit resultthrottled (CPU) or OOMKilled (memory, 6.6)CUDA out-of-memory — the process just crashes
Shareable?yes — CFS time-slices many containers on 1 CPUonly via careful VRAM budgeting per container
Oversubscriptionsafe for CPU (bursty), risky for memoryUNSAFE — no swap, no throttle, hard crash
Right-size usingkubectl top over timemodel's known VRAM footprint + batch size

Requests/limits (26.3/27.5) can request whole GPUs via nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in Kubernetes, but do not sub-divide VRAM the way CPU/memory limits sub-divide a core — plan by the MODEL's known footprint, not a guessed fraction.

💡 The Parking Spot Analogy

The comparison table above says it plainly: CPU is a shared meeting room (everyone gets a turn, 6.6's throttling); GPU memory is assigned PARKING SPOTS — once every spot is taken, the next car doesn't wait in line, it simply cannot park, full stop.

🔬 easypj: if 34.3's resume-matcher model needs a known 6 GB of VRAM per loaded instance, a single 24 GB GPU safely hosts THREE replicas with margin (18 of 24 GB) — a fourth replica is not "throttled," it fails to start.

🧪 Practice — Find Your Replica Cap

Check your model's documented VRAM footprint (or measure with nvidia-smi while one instance runs), divide your GPU's total VRAM by that number, and cap replicas at the floor of that division minus one for headroom. Verify: running one MORE replica than your calculated cap produces a clean CUDA out-of-memory error, not a graceful throttle — confirming why the margin matters.

⚠️ Gotcha — --gpus all Shares the Whole Card

--gpus all on MULTIPLE containers gives every one of them a view of the WHOLE card's memory — Docker does not enforce a per-container VRAM limit for you; that discipline is entirely on the deployer.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • docker model pull/run reuses Docker's exact pull/cache/version mental model — the payload is weights, not application code, but the OCI machinery underneath is identical.
  • The Model Runner serves an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so existing OpenAI-SDK code works locally by changing only the base URL.
  • --gpus all vs --gpus "device=0" controls WHICH GPUs are exposed; nvidia-container-toolkit is what makes the flag do anything at all.
  • Always verify GPU passthrough with nvidia-smi INSIDE the container — a missing toolkit makes --gpus fail silently.
  • An AI feature gets its OWN Dockerfile and its OWN resource profile, reachable only over the internal network — never merged into the web tier's image.
  • GPU memory (VRAM) has no throttling or swap equivalent — oversubscription causes a hard crash, not graceful degradation.
  • Right-size GPU-bound replicas by the MODEL's documented VRAM footprint divided into the card's total, with margin — never a guessed fraction.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming the Model Runner API needs a login like a real cloud endpoint → It's unauthenticated — never expose port 12434 (or the internal DMR endpoint) beyond a trusted network boundary.
  • Treating a quantized local model as "free" because it's not cloud-billed → A 3B-Q4 model still needs ~2 GB real RAM — it's a container like any other in 33.1's right-sizing exercise.
  • Assuming --gpus errors out on a host with no toolkit installed → It silently does nothing — always confirm with nvidia-smi inside the container.
  • pip install sentence-transformers directly inside easypj's own Dockerfile → This is the exact anti-pattern 34.3 exists to prevent — give the model its own sidecar Dockerfile instead.
  • Running --gpus all on multiple containers and assuming Docker isolates their VRAM → Every one of them sees the WHOLE card's memory — Docker enforces no per-container VRAM limit; that discipline is on the deployer.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • docker model ls before every docker model run — confirms the model is already cached and won't trigger a multi-GB re-download.
  • Test GPU passthrough with the small nvidia/cuda:...-base image and nvidia-smi BEFORE wiring it into a real inference container — isolates a toolkit problem from an app problem.
  • Keep the inference sidecar off nginx entirely (internal network only) from the very first Compose draft.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 34)

the Chapter 34 cheat-card 
docker model pull ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M       # cache a local model (OCI artifact)
docker model run ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M &      # serve OpenAI-compatible endpoint
docker model ls                                # confirm cache, avoid re-pull
docker run --gpus all <image>                  # expose every host GPU
docker run --gpus "device=0" <image>           # expose one specific GPU
docker exec <container> nvidia-smi              # verify GPU visibility INSIDE
curl http://inference:9000/health               # sidecar reachable only internally

🧠 Chapter 34 — DCA Practice Questions (10)

From local models to GPU right-sizing — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
How does docker model pull fit the same mental model as docker pull easypj:v1, despite pulling weights instead of code?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both are OCI artifacts pulled/cached/versioned through the identical registry mechanism — the manifest just points at a different payload type (weights vs filesystem layers).

EXPLANATION

This is 34.1's core TECH point, made concrete in the Under the Hood registry diagram after 34.2.

Q2
Why can existing OpenAI-SDK code call a local Model Runner instance with only a one-line change?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The Model Runner serves an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions route, so switching the base URL to localhost:12434 is the only required change.

EXPLANATION

34.1's TERMINAL example calls this exact route with a plain curl request, proving no special client is needed.

Q3
What does --gpus actually change under the hood?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It tells dockerd to hand the container to the nvidia OCI runtime instead of runc directly; that runtime injects the driver's character devices and CUDA userspace libraries into the container's namespace.

EXPLANATION

34.2's diagram and its Under the Hood block both trace this exact runtime swap, tying it back to 1.9's pluggable runtime model.

Q4
What is the prerequisite for --gpus to do anything, and what happens if it's missing?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

nvidia-container-toolkit must be installed on the host; if missing, --gpus fails silently with no error — always verify with nvidia-smi inside the container.

EXPLANATION

This is 34.2's closing gotcha, and exactly why its Practice Drill insists on proving the chain with a small base image first.

Q5
Why does the resume-matching sidecar get its own Dockerfile instead of joining easypj's image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It needs different, heavier dependencies (sentence-transformers, fastapi) than Django ever will; bundling them into easypj's image would fatten Chapter 8's optimized 180 MB image with weight only the sidecar needs.

EXPLANATION

34.3's closing gotcha names this exact anti-pattern, and its diagram shows the sidecar living entirely outside the web tier's build.

Q6
What happens differently when CPU/RAM vs GPU are oversubscribed?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CPU/RAM: throttled (CPU) or OOMKilled (memory), and shareable via CFS time-slicing. GPU: a clean CUDA out-of-memory crash, shareable only via manual VRAM budgeting — there is no throttle or swap equivalent.

EXPLANATION

This is 34.4's full comparison table, the load-bearing content of the whole section.

Q7
If the resume-matcher needs 6 GB VRAM per instance, how many replicas safely fit on a 24 GB GPU, and what happens to the next one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Three replicas fit with margin (18 of 24 GB); a fourth doesn't get throttled — it fails to start with a CUDA out-of-memory error.

EXPLANATION

34.4's easypj example, and the exact scenario its Practice Drill has you reproduce with one extra replica.

Q8
Why does curl http://inference:9000/health succeed from inside django but fail from the host machine?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The inference service is only on the internal backend network with no published port — proof the sidecar is truly internal-only.

EXPLANATION

34.3's Practice step verifies exactly this split — same curl, different result depending on which side of the network boundary it runs from.

Q9
What is the security gotcha with the Model Runner API?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It is unauthenticated — any client that can reach it, including other containers on the same Docker network, can pull, load, and run models; never expose port 12434 beyond a trusted network boundary.

EXPLANATION

34.1's first gotcha — the flip side of how convenient the Model Runner's zero-auth local endpoint is to develop against.

Q10
Why can't a GPU-bound container's memory be sub-divided the way CPU/memory limits are in Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

nvidia.com/gpu: 1 requests a WHOLE GPU; there's no built-in mechanism to sub-divide VRAM the way CPU shares or memory limits divide a core — right-sizing must be done by the model's known footprint, not a fractional resource request.

EXPLANATION

34.4's TECH paragraph ties this straight back to 26.3/27.5's requests/limits, showing where the analogy to CPU/memory breaks down.

🔬 Practice Drill 34.1 — Prove the GPU Chain First (10 min)

On a host with nvidia-container-toolkit installed, run docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.5.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi and confirm your real GPU model appears — do not touch easypj's inference sidecar until this passes cleanly.

📌 Chapter 34 Visual Summary — the same Docker mental model, pointed at AI
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │      🤖 CHAPTER 34 — THE SAME DOCKER MENTAL MODEL, POINTED AT AI          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  (34.1) docker model pull/run → OCI artifact → OpenAI-compatible API    │
  │  (34.2) --gpus all/device=N → nvidia runtime → CUDA libs in namespace   │

In one line: Chapter 34 proves that nothing about Docker's core model changes for AI workloads: pull/run still means pull/run even when the payload is model weights, --gpus still means "give this container a device" the same way volumes give it storage, a sidecar is still just a container with its own Dockerfile and network scope, and resource planning still means measuring a real footprint.

The takeaway: the only new fact to internalize is that GPU memory, unlike CPU, has no throttle and no swap, so oversubscription fails hard instead of failing gracefully.

Advanced Practices & Production Mastery — What You Now Know

You started this part already able to run easypj — deployed, scaled, secured. You finish it able to watch it in production (Ch 31), fix it under pressure without repeating the same outage twice (Ch 32), price it in real dollars instead of guesses (Ch 33), and extend it to GPU/AI workloads without breaking anything already built (Ch 34). That's the guide's last new skill — everything from here to the end is reference material, not new ground to learn.

🔑 Part 11 — Key Takeaways

  • Observability turns two silent kernel data sources — cgroup counters and stdout — into a queryable pipeline: cAdvisor + Prometheus + Grafana for metrics, log drivers for shipped logs, and ratio-based alerts (never raw counts) on the four golden signals (Ch 31).
  • Incident response is one rehearsed sequence built entirely from tools you already had — logs --previous → inspect → describe → rollout undo — proven safe in advance by chaos testing, then closed out with a blameless postmortem and a runbook the next on-call can follow cold (Ch 32).
  • Cost & performance tuning replaces every guess with a measurement: requests/limits sized from sampled kubectl top data, image size priced as a recurring multiplier, BuildKit stages parallelized, and Docker's real overhead isolated in a fair benchmark (Ch 33).
  • AI workloads don't break Docker's model, they extend it — docker model pull/run reuses the same OCI pull/cache/version machinery for weights instead of code, --gpus passes through a physical device, and an inference sidecar gets its own Dockerfile and a VRAM budget with no throttle or swap to soften an overshoot (Ch 34).
  • 🎯 Exam: none of Part 11 is separately DCA-graded — it's the day-2 discipline the exam assumes you'll add once the badge is earned: watch, respond, price, extend.
  • 🔑 docker stats · kubectl top · kubectl logs --previous · kubectl rollout undo · docker model run · --gpus
📌 Part 11 Visual Summary — watch it, fix it, price it, extend it
   📊 cAdvisor+Prometheus+Grafana ──▶ 🚨 ratio-based alert fires          (Ch 31: SEE it)
                                            │
                                            ▼
   🚑 logs --previous→inspect→describe→rollout undo ──▶ postmortem → runbook   (Ch 32: FIX it, don't repeat it)
                                            │
                                            ▼
   💰 kubectl top (measured, not guessed) ──▶ right-sized requests/limits + priced image + parallel builds   (Ch 33: PRICE it)
                                            │
                                            ▼
   🤖 docker model run / --gpus ──▶ inference sidecar, own Dockerfile, VRAM-capped   (Ch 34: EXTEND it)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the same easypj app from Part 1 — now watched, defended, priced, and ready for whatever runs on it next. 🏁

In words: Chapter 31 gives you eyes on easypj in production — cAdvisor feeds Prometheus, Grafana renders it, log drivers ship the text half of the same story off-box, and a ratio-based alert on the four golden signals is what actually pages a human before a user files a ticket. Chapter 32 gives you hands for the moment that alert fires: the same triage sequence every time, rehearsed on purpose via chaos engineering before it's ever real, and closed out with a blameless postmortem and a runbook so the next on-call needs none of this from memory.

Chapter 33 turns earlier best-practice advice — right-sized requests/limits, a small image — into an actual dollar figure, replacing every guess with a kubectl top sample, a cost formula, or a back-to-back benchmark. Chapter 34 proves none of that foundation breaks when the workload changes shape entirely: a model pull is still a pull, --gpus is still just handing a container a device, and a sidecar is still just a container with its own Dockerfile — the only new fact is that GPU memory has no throttle, so oversubscription fails hard instead of gracefully.

The one idea to keep: production doesn't ask for new skills, it asks you to run the ones you already have — watch, respond, price, extend — continuously, on the same easypj app you first containerized back in Part 1. From here, the Appendices are reference material for a guide whose chapter content is now complete.

A.1 Container Commands

Commands for managing the complete container lifecycle — create, run, inspect, debug, and destroy.

CommandDescriptionExample
docker runCreate and start a containerdocker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name app easypj:v1
docker psList running containersdocker ps -a --filter "name=easypj"
docker stopStop a running container (SIGTERM)docker stop easypj-app
docker startStart a stopped containerdocker start easypj-app
docker restartRestart a containerdocker restart easypj-app
docker rmRemove a containerdocker rm -f easypj-app
docker execRun a command in a running containerdocker exec -it easypj-app bash
docker logsView container logsdocker logs -f --tail 100 easypj-app
docker cpCopy files between host and containerdocker cp easypj-app:/app/data ./backup
docker inspectView detailed container metadatadocker inspect easypj-app
docker statsLive resource usagedocker stats easypj-app
docker topShow processes inside containerdocker top easypj-app
docker pausePause all processes in containerdocker pause easypj-app
docker unpauseResume paused containerdocker unpause easypj-app
docker killForce kill container (SIGKILL)docker kill easypj-app
docker createCreate container without startingdocker create --name temp easypj:v1
💡 DCA Tip: docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful, 10s timeout then SIGKILL). docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately. docker rm -f does stop + rm in one command. Always prefer docker exec -it CONTAINER sh over docker attach for debugging — attach connects to the main process, exec starts a new one.

A.9 Docker Trust Commands

Commands for Docker Content Trust — cryptographic signing and verification of images using Notary/TUF.

CommandDescriptionExample
docker trust signSign an imagedocker trust sign ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1
docker trust inspectView trust metadatadocker trust inspect easypj:v1
docker trust verifyVerify image signaturesdocker trust verify easypj:v1
docker trust key generateGenerate signing keydocker trust key generate alice
DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1Enable DCT globallyexport DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
⚠️ Important: With DCT enabled, Docker refuses to pull unsigned images. This prevents supply-chain attacks. Sign images before pushing to production registries. Store root keys offline; repository keys can be delegated.

A.10 Docker Context Commands

Commands for managing multiple Docker engines/environments — a context stores an endpoint (+ TLS config) under a name, so you can target a remote daemon by name instead of juggling DOCKER_HOST exports.

CommandDescriptionExample
docker context createCreate a context for remote Dockerdocker context create remote --docker host=ssh://user@server
docker context lsList all contextsdocker context ls
docker context useSwitch to a contextdocker context use remote
docker context inspectView context detailsdocker context inspect remote
docker context rmRemove a contextdocker context rm remote
💡 Tip: A named, persistent context beats ad-hoc SSH + DOCKER_HOST exports — it's switchable per command (docker --context prod ps) with no env-var leakage between terminals or scripts. docker context use switches the default target for every following command; docker context ls marks the active one with *. See A.20 for the full docker context create flag reference.

A.17 docker checkpoint (Experimental)

⚠️ Experimental: Requires CRIU 2.0+ installed separately — Docker does not bundle it, so most default installs cannot run this today. Needs a recent kernel with seccomp support; -t/--tty containers cannot be checkpointed. Treat as a lab curiosity, not a production backup strategy.
CommandPurpose
docker checkpoint create CONTAINER CHECKPOINT [--leave-running] [--checkpoint-dir]freeze state to disk (--leave-running keeps it running afterward)
docker checkpoint ls CONTAINERlist saved checkpoints
docker checkpoint rm CONTAINER CKPTdelete a checkpoint
docker start --checkpoint CKPT_ID CONTAINERrestore a container from a checkpoint

A.18 docker system prune — Removal Scope

The exact blast radius per flag combination, since guessing here has cost real teams real volumes.

CommandRemoves
docker system prunestopped containers + unused networks + DANGLING images only + unused build cache
docker system prune -asame, but ALL unused images (not just dangling) — next run re-pulls
docker system prune --volumesabove, PLUS anonymous volumes not used by any container
docker system prune -a --volumesmaximum blast radius: all unused images + anonymous volumes
-f/--forceskip the "Are you sure?" prompt
--filter until=<time>only touch things older than <time>
--filter label=<k>=<v>same key = OR; different keys = AND
--filter label!=<k>=<v>exclude matching items by label
⚠️ Gotcha: --volumes only removes ANONYMOUS volumes (no --name, no compose service reference keeping it alive). easypj's named pgdata volume survives every combination above — but confirm with docker volume ls before running -a --volumes on a shared host.

A.19 docker stack deploy — Flags

Deploys a Compose-format stack of services onto a swarm; must run on a swarm MANAGER node; supports Compose file version 3.0+. Unsupported Compose keys (e.g. links) are reported as ignored, not treated as errors.

FlagMeaning
-c/--compose-filepath, or "-" for stdin; repeatable to layer multiple compose files
-d/--detachdefault true; returns immediately instead of waiting for convergence
--pruneremove services no longer referenced
-q/--quietsuppress progress output
--resolve-imagedefault always (always|changed|never) — query registry for image digest and platform info
--with-registry-authsend registry auth to Swarm agents

A.20 docker context create

A context stores an endpoint (+ TLS config) under a NAME — see A.10 for the day-to-day context use/ls workflow. Syntax: docker context create [OPTIONS] CONTEXT

FlagMeaning
--descriptionhuman-readable description for the context
--dockerset the docker endpoint: host=<endpoint>
--fromcreate from an existing named context
bash
$ docker context create \
    --docker host=unix:///var/run/docker.sock my-context
$ docker context create --from existing-context my-context
$ docker context create \

In one line: Appendix A is the exam-day and daily-work lookup table — nine command categories (A.1–A.9) covering the everyday CLI surface, then nine deep-dive flag references (A.10–A.21) for the commands whose full official flag set is too large to memorize but too important to guess at.

The takeaway: when in doubt about a flag's exact name or default value — for run, build, exec, ps, network/volume create, system prune, stack deploy, context create, or model — come back here before guessing on the exam or in production.

🎯 DCA Exam Tip: Know the difference between docker stop (SIGTERM, graceful) and docker kill (SIGKILL, immediate). Know docker service commands for Swarm orchestration (25% of exam). Remember docker system df for disk troubleshooting and docker system prune for cleanup — and remember that --volumes only ever touches anonymous volumes, never named ones.

📝 Appendix B: Dockerfile Quick Reference

Dockerfile — All Instructions & Templates

Complete reference of every Dockerfile instruction with syntax, plus production-ready templates for Python/Django, Node.js, Java, Go, and static sites. Includes multi-stage patterns, .dockerignore templates, and the modern BuildKit-era features (mount types, network/security modes, parser directives, env-var expansion, and ADD's Git/URL/checksum powers) that the DCA exam and real production Dockerfiles both expect.

📝 Reference🎯 DCA Essential
🏗️ FROM

Base image (mandatory)

FROM python:3.11-slim

📁 WORKDIR

Set working directory

WORKDIR /app

📋 COPY

Copy files from context

COPY . /app

⚙️ RUN

Execute build commands

RUN pip install -r req.txt

🚀 CMD

Default runtime command

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

🎯 ENTRYPOINT

Fixed executable

ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]

🌍 ENV

Runtime env variable

ENV DEBUG=False

🔨 ARG

Build-time variable

ARG VERSION=1.0

📊 Quick visual overview — full syntax in B.1 below

B.1 Complete Instruction List

InstructionSyntaxDescription
FROMFROM python:3.11-slim AS builderBase image (MANDATORY, first). Multi-stage: use AS for stage name.
WORKDIRWORKDIR /appSet working directory. Creates if missing. Better than RUN cd.
COPYCOPY requirements.txt .Copy files from build context. Preferred over ADD for local files.
ADDADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /app/Like COPY + URL download + tar auto-extract. Use COPY when possible.
RUNRUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r req.txtExecute commands during build. Chain with && to reduce layers.
CMDCMD ["gunicorn", "app:application"]Default command (overridable). Exec form preferred.
ENTRYPOINTENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]Fixed executable (not easily overridden). CMD becomes arguments.
ENVENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=app.settingsSet environment variable (persists at runtime). Visible in history.
ARGARG VERSION=1.0Build-time variable. NOT in final image (unless persisted to ENV).
EXPOSEEXPOSE 8000Document port (metadata only). Use -p to actually publish.
USERUSER appuserSwitch to non-root user. Create first: RUN groupadd && useradd.
VOLUMEVOLUME ["/app/data"]Create mount point. Prefer named volumes in compose/docker run.
HEALTHCHECKHEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost/Container health monitoring. Interval, timeout, retries configurable.
LABELLABEL version="1.0" maintainer="team"Add metadata to image. Visible in docker inspect.
SHELLSHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]Change default shell for RUN commands.
STOPSIGNALSTOPSIGNAL SIGTERMSignal to stop container. Default: SIGTERM.
ONBUILDONBUILD COPY . /app/srcAdd trigger for downstream builds. Executes when image is used as base.
Advanced Dockerfile Features from Official Docs

ONBUILD: registers instructions that execute when your image is used as a base (FROM). Triggers run ONCE in the child build and are cleared afterwards. RUN --mount=type=secret: injects build secrets without baking them into layers (see B.7). COPY --chown: sets file ownership. COPY --chmod: sets file permissions (see B.6). Parser directives (# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1): pin Dockerfile syntax version for reproducible builds (see B.9). Here-Documents: multi-line RUN/COPY without messy backslash escaping (see B.6).

B.2 Dockerfile Templates

Production-ready single-stage starting points by language/framework. Non-root user, minimal base image, and requirements/dependency-first layer ordering are baked into every one.

Python/Django (easypj)
FROM python:3.11-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
Node.js
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Java (Spring Boot)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/*.jar app.jar
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
Go (Multi-Stage)
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o server .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/server"]
Static HTML (Nginx)
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY ./html /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

B.3 Multi-Stage Dockerfile Templates

Two multi-stage shapes cover most real projects: a compiled-artifact stage that discards its build tools (Python/Go/Java) and a static-asset stage that discards its entire Node.js toolchain, keeping only the built output.

Multi-Stage Pattern — Python/Django (Generic)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Runtime (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
COPY . .
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
Multi-Stage Pattern — Node.js Build → Nginx Serve
# Stage 1: Build static assets (full Node toolchain)
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: Serve with Nginx (no Node, no node_modules)
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
💡 Same Shape, Different Payload

Both templates follow the identical rule: the FINAL stage's FROM never sees a compiler, a package manager cache, or source files that aren't needed at runtime — only COPY --from=builder artifacts. See 8.5/13.x for the size/CVE numbers this buys (a 4-5× smaller, 3-4× fewer-CVE image is typical).

B.4 Dockerfile for Django (easypj)

Complete production-ready Dockerfile for the easypj/jobpost Django application — reproduced verbatim from 9.7 / Appendix D.1, the guide's one authoritative copy: multi-stage build, non-root user, an entrypoint script that runs migrate + collectstatic before serving, and a HEALTHCHECK.

easypj/Dockerfile (Production)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Run (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
COPY . .
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
Best PracticeImplementationWhy
Pin base imagepython:3.11-slimReproducible builds; slim reduces attack surface
Multi-stageBuilder → RuntimeFinal image has no pip, no build tools
Non-root userUSER appContainer breakout doesn't give host root
Entrypoint scriptdocker-entrypoint.shWaits for Postgres, runs migrate + collectstatic, THEN execs gunicorn (D.5)
Health checkHEALTHCHECK instructionOrchestrators can detect and replace unhealthy containers/pods
Python hardeningPYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Prevents .pyc files; reduces image size
Workers=3Gunicorn workersRule of thumb: (2 × CPU cores) + 1
🏆 Chapter Cross-Reference

This is the same Dockerfile 9.7 finalizes and Appendix D.1 reproduces — 11.2/22.x build/push it unchanged; only the registry host changes. If your local copy diverges from this listing, 9.7 is the narrative walkthrough of how it got here.

B.5 .dockerignore Templates

Excluding unnecessary files from the build context makes builds faster and images smaller. Place .dockerignore in the same directory as your Dockerfile.

Python/Django .dockerignore
# Python

Dockerfile

B.6 Modern Dockerfile Features (BuildKit)

BuildKit is Docker's default build engine and unlocks Dockerfile syntax that the legacy builder can't parse. Every feature below requires a parser directive (B.9) pinning a modern frontend — without it, Docker silently falls back to legacy parsing and these lines error out.

FeatureWhat It ReplacesWhy It's Better
Here-doc RUN <<EOFLong &&-chained RUN linesMulti-line scripts without backslash escaping; one layer, readable
COPY --chmod --chownA separate RUN chown/chmodOwnership/permissions set at copy time — no extra layer
RUN --mount=type=cacheRe-downloading deps every buildPersistent build cache across builds (see B.7)
RUN --mount=type=secretARG/ENV holding a credentialSecret never lands in any image layer (see B.7)
Here-Doc RUN Block
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.11-slim
RUN <<EOF
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
EOF
COPY --chmod --chown at Copy Time
COPY --chmod=755 --chown=app:app docker-entrypoint.sh /app/docker-entrypoint.sh
Parser Directives Gate Everything Here

All of B.6's features depend on # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 being the literal first line of the Dockerfile (B.9). Heredoc syntax isn't RUN-only either — CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, and ADD all accept the same <<EOF ... EOF block form (B.11).

B.7 RUN --mount — All 5 Types

RUN --mount attaches a filesystem to that one RUN step only; unlike COPY/ADD, nothing lands in the final image unless explicitly copied out again — purpose-built for build-only inputs, caches, and secrets.

TypePurposeKey Options
bindMount build context or another stage, read-only by defaulttarget, source, from, rw
cachePersistent directory for compiler/package-manager cachesid, target, ro, sharing, from, source, mode, uid, gid
tmpfsTemporary in-memory filesystem, scoped to this RUNtarget, size
secretSecure file/env var, exposed only during this RUNid, target, env, required, mode, uid, gid
sshForwards SSH agent/keys into this RUNid, target, required, mode, uid, gid
bind Mount — Replaces a Throwaway COPY
RUN --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=/tmp/req.txt \
    pip install -r /tmp/req.txt
💡 easypj Already Uses Two of the Five

easypj's Dockerfile already uses cache and secret (5.7's pip cache and pip.conf credentials). A bind mount is the natural next step for any build-only file that shouldn't cost a layer of its own.

B.8 RUN --network & --security Modes

Two more independent RUN flags — not --mount types — that control network reachability and privilege scope for a single RUN step.

RUN --networkEffect
defaultStandard network access (the default)
noneNo network; loopback only, fully isolated
hostShares the host's network stack; requires a BuildKit allow-entitlement flag
RUN --securityEffect
sandboxDefault secure, unprivileged mode
insecureElevated/privilege-breaking mode; requires a BuildKit allow-entitlement flag
Proving a Layer Never Touches the Network
RUN --network=none pip install --no-index \
    --find-links=/wheels -r requirements.txt
The easypj Proof

Because every wheel comes from a local /wheels cache, --network=none proves this install step never reaches PyPI at build time — a supply-chain assertion the build itself enforces, not just a policy on paper.

B.9 Parser Directives

Three parser directives exist, and all three must sit before any other line — even a comment — or Docker silently ignores them.

DirectivePurpose
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1Pins the Dockerfile frontend version; unlocks newer syntax (e.g. B.6's heredoc RUN blocks)
# escape=\ (or # escape=`)Sets the escape character; backtick avoids clashing with Windows-style paths
# check=skip=<name>;error=true(v1.8.0+) Skips one check, or skip=all; error=true fails the build on any check warning
⚠️ Order Is Not Optional

Parser directives are only recognized while they're the very first lines of the file. A stray blank line or comment above them, and Docker treats the directive as a regular comment instead — no error, no warning, the pinned syntax version simply never activates.

💡 easypj's Line 1

easypj's Dockerfile should open with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 as line 1 — B.6's heredoc RUN blocks and B.7/B.8's mount/network/security flags all depend on it.

B.10 Environment Variable Expansion

$var or ${var} expand inside ADD, COPY, ENV, EXPOSE, FROM, LABEL, STOPSIGNAL, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR, and ONBUILD. Four bash-style modifiers refine the default behavior:

ModifierMeaning
${var:-word}word if var is UNSET or EMPTY, else var
${var-word}word if var is UNSET only (an empty string is kept as-is)
${var:+word}word if var is SET and non-empty, else empty
${var+word}word if var is set at all (even empty), else empty
easypj Examples
ENV PORT=${PORT:-8000}       # default when PORT unset
ENV DEBUG=${DJANGO_ENV:+1}   # "1" only if ARG was passed

B.11 ADD's Git/URL/Checksum Capabilities

ADD does two things COPY cannot: auto-extract local tar archives, and accept a remote URL or Git repo URL directly as <src> (COPY only accepts paths inside the build context).

ADD-Only/Extra FlagPurpose
--keep-git-dirKeeps .git when <src> is a Git repo URL
--checksumVerifies a remote file's digest before adding it; fails the build on mismatch
--unpackControls tar auto-extraction; true by default for LOCAL tars, false for URLs
--chmodSets permissions at add-time (shared with COPY)
--chownSets owner:group at add-time (shared with COPY)
--linkReuses already-built layers (shared with COPY)
--excludePattern-based exclusion (shared with COPY)
A Genuine One-Off Fetch
ADD --checksum=sha256:<digest> \
    https://example.com/geoip.mmdb /app/geoip.mmdb
⚠️ COPY Stays the Default

easypj still uses COPY for its own source: local files need no extraction or remote fetch, so COPY's narrower behavior is the safer default (4.2's audit-red-flag warning stands — an ADD pulling from a bare URL with no --checksum is exactly the kind of line a Dockerfile audit should flag). ADD earns its place only for a genuine one-off remote/Git fetch.

📋 Appendix B Summary — Dockerfile Best Practices

  • 1️⃣ Pin base images — use python:3.11-slim, not python:latest
  • 2️⃣ Order for caching — dependencies first, source code last
  • 3️⃣ Multi-stage builds — separate build tools from the runtime image (B.3)
  • 4️⃣ Non-root USER — create an app user; never run as root
  • 5️⃣ Use .dockerignore — exclude node_modules, .git, venv (B.5)
  • 6️⃣ HEALTHCHECK — enable orchestrator health awareness
  • 7️⃣ BuildKit features — cache/secret mounts, heredocs, COPY --chmod/--chown save layers and keep secrets out of the image (B.6-B.7)
  • 8️⃣ Parser directive first — # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 must be line 1 or every modern feature above silently falls back to legacy parsing (B.9)

🎼 Appendix C: compose.yaml Quick Reference

Docker Compose — Complete File Reference

Every essential compose.yaml key, grouped and cross-referenced to where it's taught in the guide, plus copy-ready templates for the easypj stack (django + postgres + redis + nginx). This appendix is reference material — look up a key, copy a template, move on.

C.1 Complete compose.yaml Reference

The full set of service-level and top-level keys you'll actually reach for, organized by what they control.

KeyExampleDescription
imageimage: postgres:15-alpineUse a pre-built image instead of building one
buildbuild: . or build: {context: ., dockerfile: Dockerfile}Build from a Dockerfile — see C.8 for the full sub-key list
container_namecontainer_name: easypj_appFixed container name instead of the auto-generated one
portsports: ["8000:8000"]Publish ports, HOST:CONTAINER
exposeexpose: ["8000"]Make a port reachable to other services only, no host publish
environmentenvironment: {DEBUG: "False"}Set environment variables (map or list form)
env_fileenv_file: .envLoad environment variables from a file
volumesvolumes: [postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data]Mount named volumes or bind mounts — see C.9 for all six types
networksnetworks: [backend, frontend]Attach a service to one or more networks
depends_ondepends_on: {postgres: {condition: service_healthy}}Startup order, optionally gated on health
commandcommand: gunicorn easypj.wsgi:applicationOverride the image's CMD
entrypointentrypoint: ["/docker-entrypoint.sh"]Override the image's ENTRYPOINT
healthcheckhealthcheck: {test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user"]}Health monitoring — see C.4 for per-service templates
restartrestart: unless-stoppedRestart policy: no / always / on-failure / unless-stopped
develop.watchdevelop: {watch: [{action: sync, path: .}]}Hot-reload rules for docker compose watch — see C.5
