profilesprofiles: ["debug"]Service only starts when its profile is activated
labelslabels: {com.easypj.tier: "backend"}Arbitrary metadata attached to the container
secrets / configssecrets: [db_password]Mount Swarm/Compose-managed secret or config files
pull_policypull_policy: buildControls when the image is pulled vs built — see C.10
name (top-level)name: easypjSets the project name inside the file itself — see C.6
volumes (top-level)volumes: {postgres_data:}Declares named volumes referenced by services
networks (top-level)networks: {backend: {driver: bridge}}Declares custom networks referenced by services
🧭 Where each key is taught

Core service keys are introduced in Chapter 10, wired into the full easypj stack in Chapter 11, and health/watch/scaling are covered in Chapter 12. This appendix doesn't re-teach the concepts — it's the lookup table for syntax you've already learned.

C.2 compose.yaml Templates

Two ready-to-copy stack sizes: the minimal two-service pair, and the full four-service easypj production shape.

compose.yaml — django + postgres
services:
  django:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://easypj_user:${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/easypj
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: easypj
      POSTGRES_USER: easypj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  postgres_data:
compose.yaml — full easypj stack (django + postgres + redis + nginx)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    container_name: easypj_app
    command: gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3
    environment:
      DEBUG: "False"
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://easypj_user:${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/easypj
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/static
      - media_volume:/app/media
    depends_on:
      postgres: {condition: service_healthy}
      redis: {condition: service_healthy}
    networks: [backend, frontend]

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: easypj
      POSTGRES_USER: easypj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
    networks: [backend]

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
    networks: [backend]

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/static:ro
      - media_volume:/media:ro
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on: [django]
    networks: [frontend]

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  static_volume:
  media_volume:

networks:
  backend: {driver: bridge}
  frontend: {driver: bridge}

C.3 Compose Override Templates

The same base compose.yaml in every environment, layered with an environment-specific file — never three separate stack definitions.

compose.override.yaml — dev (auto-loaded)
services:
  django:
    volumes:
      - .:/app                        # live host code, read-write
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
    environment:
      DEBUG: "True"
compose.staging.yaml
services:
  django:
    command: gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --workers 2
    environment:
      DEBUG: "False"
      LOG_LEVEL: info
compose.prod.yaml
services:
  django:
    command: gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --workers 4
    environment:
      DEBUG: "False"
      SECRET_KEY: ${SECRET_KEY:?set it in .env}
    restart: always
    ports: []                          # nginx is the only public door in prod
CommandFiles loadedUse case
docker compose up -dcompose.yaml + compose.override.yaml (auto)Local dev — no flags needed
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.staging.yaml up -dExplicit list, left → rightStaging deploy
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -dExplicit list, left → rightProduction deploy
⚠️ Merge Rules Aren't Uniform

Scalars (strings, numbers, booleans) in a later file replace the earlier value. Maps (environment, labels) merge key-by-key. Sequences written as a plain YAML list (a service's ports: or volumes:) are replaced wholesale by a later file's list, never appended. When in doubt, run docker compose config — it prints the merged, interpolated file the engine will actually run.

🚨 Gotcha

compose.override.yaml loads automatically on any bare docker compose up — including on a server, if the file is present. Forgetting to exclude it from a production checkout can silently deploy runserver and DEBUG=True.

C.4 Health Check Templates

One healthcheck: block per easypj tier — the exact commands that turn "started" into "ready."

ServiceTest commandWhat "healthy" means
postgrespg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypjServer accepts connections for that role/DB
redisredis-cli ping (expects PONG)Server responds on its client port
djangocurl -fs localhost:8000 || exit 1Gunicorn is bound and serving HTTP
nginxcurl -fs localhost/healthz || exit 1Reverse proxy is serving requests
healthcheck: blocks for all four easypj services
services:
  postgres:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U easypj_user -d easypj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  django:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fs localhost:8000 || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 30s      # grace window while migrate runs
      start_interval: 2s     # faster probes during that window

  nginx:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fs localhost/healthz || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
Sub-keyMeaning
testCommand to run inside the container; CMD-SHELL wraps it in a shell, CMD runs it directly
intervalTime between checks (default 30s)
timeoutTime before a single check is considered failed
retriesConsecutive failures before the container is marked unhealthy
start_periodGrace window where failures don't count toward retries — for slow-booting services
start_intervalFaster probe cadence used only during start_period
disabletrue turns off a HEALTHCHECK baked into a base image without forking the Dockerfile
💡 Gate on service_healthy, Not Just depends_on

depends_on alone only waits for the container to START. Pair every healthcheck with depends_on: {postgres: {condition: service_healthy}} on the dependent service, or the healthcheck block does nothing for startup ordering.

C.5 Watch Configuration Templates

docker compose watch routes file changes to one of three actions — sync for code, rebuild for dependencies, sync+restart for config.

develop.watch — django service
services:
  django:
    build: .
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync              # .py, templates → copy in, no restart
          path: .
          target: /app
          ignore: [".git/", "*.pyc", "__pycache__/"]
        - action: rebuild            # dependency change → new image
          path: requirements.txt
        - action: sync+restart       # config change → copy + bounce process
          path: easypj/settings.py
          target: /app/easypj/settings.py
ActionTriggers onEffect
syncSource/template editsCopies changed files into the running container, no restart
rebuildrequirements.txt / Dockerfile changesRebuilds the image and replaces the container
sync+restartConfig file edits (e.g. settings.py)Copies the file in, then restarts the service process
🚨 Gotcha

Synced files land in the container's writable layer. A rebuild discards that layer — your disk copy (the source of the sync) is the only durable one, by design. Never treat a running container's writable layer as a place to leave unsaved work.

C.6 Compose File Power Features

Three features that keep a large compose.yaml DRY without changing what any service actually runs.

FeatureSyntaxPurpose
Extension fieldsTop-level x-* keysReusable chunks the Compose parser ignores at the top level, referenced elsewhere via anchors
YAML anchors & aliases&defaults / <<: *defaultsDefine a block once, merge it into many services — pairs naturally with x-* fields
Top-level name:name: easypjSets the project name inside the file itself, replacing reliance on the directory name or -p flag
x-* extension fields + YAML anchors — easypj logging & env defaults
name: easypj

x-common-env: &defaults
  TZ: UTC
  PYTHONUNBUFFERED: "1"

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  django:
    build: .
    environment:
      <<: *defaults
      DEBUG: "False"
    logging: *default-logging

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      <<: *defaults
      POSTGRES_DB: easypj
    logging: *default-logging
💡 x-* Fields Are Parser-Invisible Until Aliased

Compose skips any top-level key starting with x- when validating the file — it's a scratch area. The value only takes effect once a service references it with <<: *anchor-name, which YAML-merges the anchored map into that service's own map at that key.

C.7 The deploy: Key — Full Reference

deploy: is read by docker stack deploy (Swarm mode). Plain docker compose up does not act on most of it — the CLI-flag versions students run day-to-day (docker service scale, --constraint, --placement-pref) are their Swarm-command equivalents. This is the YAML-file form of those same flags.

KeyValues / meaning
modereplicated (default, N copies) | global (one task per node) | replicated-job | global-job (run-to-completion)
replicasInteger — YAML form of docker service scale
endpoint_modevip (one virtual IP, load-balanced) | dnsrr (DNS round-robin to each task's own IP)
placement.constraints / placement.preferencesYAML form of --constraint (hard) and --placement-pref (soft)
labelsService metadata under deploy: — distinct from a service's own top-level labels:
resources sub-keyMeaningeasypj django-tier example
cpusCPU share, decimal stringlimits.cpus: "1.00"
memoryRAM, string with unitlimits.memory: 512M
pidsMax PIDs in the tasklimits.pids: 100
devicesGPU/device reservationscapabilities / driver / count
restart_policy sub-keyValues / meaning
conditionnone | on-failure | any (default)
delayWait between restart attempts, e.g. 5s
max_attemptsGive up after N tries (default: unlimited)
windowTime window used to judge attempt success
update_config / rollback_config sub-keyValues
parallelismTasks touched per batch
delayPause between batches
failure_actionupdate: continue | rollback | pause  ·  rollback: continue | pause
monitorHow long to judge a new task
max_failure_ratioTolerated failure share before acting
orderstop-first | start-first
compose.yaml — deploy: key for the easypj django service
services:
  django:
    image: registry.example.com/easypj:v1
    deploy:
      mode: replicated
      replicas: 3
      endpoint_mode: vip
      placement:
        constraints: ["node.role == worker"]
      resources:
        limits: {cpus: "1.00", memory: 512M, pids: 100}
        reservations: {cpus: "0.25", memory: 256M}
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
        delay: 5s
        max_attempts: 3
        window: 120s
      update_config:
        parallelism: 1
        delay: 10s
        failure_action: rollback
        order: start-first
🧭 easypj cross-reference

The CLI form --update-failure-action rollback --update-order start-first becomes, in a stack file, deploy.update_config: {failure_action: rollback, order: start-first} — same knobs, YAML instead of flags.

C.8 The build: Key — Full Reference

Sub-keyMeaning
context: / dockerfile:Same two inputs as docker build's PATH and -f
dockerfile_inline:Writes the Dockerfile inline in compose.yaml instead of a separate file
args:Build-time ARG values
labels:OCI labels baked into the built IMAGE, not the running container
target:Build only one stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile, same as docker build --target
platforms:List form of --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64; needs a buildx builder
cache_from: / cache_to:YAML form of --cache-from; e.g. type=registry,ref=... or type=gha for CI caches
secrets: / ssh:YAML form of --secret / --ssh — build-time credentials that never land in an image layer
no_cache / pull / privileged / network / shm_size / ulimitsOne-to-one with their docker build flag namesakes
provenance / sbomAttestation toggles (bool, or a string like mode=max / generator=...), off by default
additional_contexts:Extra named build contexts (NAME=VALUE), usable as COPY --from=NAME beyond the base context
entitlements:Opts BuildKit into extra privileges (e.g. network, security.insecure) a build step explicitly requests
compose.yaml — easypj's build: key using more than context/dockerfile
services:
  django:
    build:
      context: .
      target: production
      args:
        DJANGO_ENV: production
      cache_from:
        - type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/you/easypj:buildcache
      platforms: ["linux/amd64", "linux/arm64"]

C.9 Volume Mount Types — Full List

The six type: values available under a long-syntax volumes: entry.

typePurpose
volumeDocker-managed named volume (postgres_data)
bindHost path mounted straight through (dev source code)
tmpfsRAM-only, gone when the container stops
imageMount another built IMAGE's filesystem (newer)
npipeWindows named pipe (Windows container hosts)
clusterSwarm CSI cluster volume, multi-host (newer)

Long syntax is always type: + source: + target: (+ read_only:) plus a type-specific sub-block (bind.*, volume.*, tmpfs.*, image.*). easypj's postgres_data, written long-form:

long-syntax volume mount — postgres_data
services:
  postgres:
    volumes:
      - type: volume
        source: postgres_data
        target: /var/lib/postgresql/data

and the nginx.conf bind mount, long-form:

long-syntax bind mount — nginx.conf
services:
  nginx:
    volumes:
      - type: bind
        source: ./nginx.conf
        target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
        read_only: true
🧭 The two newest types

image shares a built image's filesystem read-only — no extra COPY needed to hand static assets to another service. cluster names a CSI volume for Swarm's multi-host storage drivers.

C.10 pull_policy & Other Attributes

pull_policy valueBehavior
alwaysAlways pull, even if cached locally
neverNever pull, fail if the image is missing
missingPull only if not already cached (default)
buildAlways build, even if image: is set
dailyPull if the cached image is more than a day old
weeklyPull if the cached image is more than a week old
every_<duration>Pull if the cached image is older than that duration
AttributePurpose
gpus:Short form takes a driver, a count, or the literal all — the Compose-file shortcut for a GPU request; the long form's full capabilities/device_ids table lives in Chapter 34
models:Compose's hook into Docker Model Runner; short form names a model, long form sets endpoint_var: / model_var: so a service's environment gets the model's endpoint URL and name injected instead of hardcoding localhost:12434
credential_spec:file: or registry: — Windows gMSA credentials for a container joining an Active Directory domain; unrelated to secrets: despite the similar name
compose.yaml — pull_policy: build on the django service
services:
  django:
    build: .
    image: easypj:v1
    pull_policy: build
💡 easypj cross-reference

pull_policy: build on the django service guarantees docker compose up never runs a stale cached easypj:v1 image after a Dockerfile change with no new tag.

Appendix D · Dockerfile for easypj (Production)

The five files that, together, reproduce the easypj image from a clean checkout: the multi-stage production Dockerfile built in 9.7, a single-stage development variant with hot reload, the .dockerignore that keeps secrets and cruft out of the build context, a pinned requirements.txt, and the entrypoint script that wires migrations and static collection into container startup. Nothing here is new — this appendix collects the canonical, final version of each file so you can copy them straight into a project without hunting back through the chapters that derived them.

D.1 Full Multi-Stage Production Dockerfile

This is the exact Dockerfile derived in 9.7 — The Complete easypj Dockerfile (Final Version), reproduced verbatim so the guide has one authoritative copy. Stage 1 (builder) installs dependencies into --user site-packages; Stage 2 copies only that installed tree plus the source into a fresh python:3.11-slim base, drops to a non-root app user, and hands off to docker-entrypoint.sh (D.5), which runs migrate and collectstatic before exec-ing gunicorn.

Dockerfile (Production)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Run (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
COPY . .
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
📖 Why No collectstatic in the Build Stage

Earlier drafts of this Dockerfile ran collectstatic during the build and COPY --from=builder'd the result. The final version moves it into docker-entrypoint.sh (D.5) instead — one fewer build-time dependency on STATIC_ROOT being correctly configured, and static files stay in sync with whatever code actually starts the container, not whatever code happened to be present at build time.

D.2 Development Dockerfile (Hot Reload)

The dev image trades every production concern for iteration speed: one stage instead of two (rebuild the whole thing in seconds), DEBUG=True, runserver instead of gunicorn (its autoreloader IS the hot-reload mechanism), and no non-root lockdown since it never leaves your machine. Pair it with a bind mount — docker run -v $(pwd):/app ... or a compose override's volumes: [.:/app] — so edits on the host appear inside the container instantly; the COPY . . below only seeds the image so a bare docker build still produces something runnable without the mount.

Dockerfile.dev
# Development Dockerfile — single stage, hot reload, DEBUG on
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Same baseline env as production, DEBUG flipped on
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
ENV DEBUG=True

# libpq-dev/gcc still needed to compile psycopg2 (same as 9.2)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# requirements/dev.txt extends base.txt with debug-toolbar, pytest, black
COPY requirements/base.txt requirements/dev.txt ./requirements/
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements/dev.txt

# Seeds the image; the real source arrives via a bind mount at runtime
COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
AspectD.1 ProductionD.2 Development
Stages2 (builder + runtime)1
Servergunicorn, 3 workersmanage.py runserver (autoreload)
DEBUGFalse (via env)True
Usernon-root approot (local machine only)
Source codeBaked in via COPY . .Bind-mounted over the seeded copy
Entrypointdocker-entrypoint.sh (D.5)None — bare CMD
⚠️ Never Ship Dockerfile.dev

DEBUG=True leaks stack traces, settings, and installed apps to anyone who can trigger a 500. Keep D.1 and D.2 as two separate files (-f Dockerfile.dev at build time) — never merge them behind a build arg that could default the wrong way in CI.

D.3 .dockerignore File

Identical to the file written in 9.3 — Writing .dockerignore. It does three jobs at once: shrinks and stabilizes the build context, keeps the layer cache from invalidating on irrelevant file changes, and — most importantly — keeps .env and its secrets out of every layer COPY . . would otherwise bake in.

.dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/

# Django
media/
staticfiles/

# Virtual Environment
env/
venv/
.env

# Git
.git/
.gitignore

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# OS
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Docker
Dockerfile
Dockerfile.dev
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml
🛑 The .dockerignore Security Rule

If .env holds SECRET_KEY or DB_PASSWORD, it MUST be in this list. A single unprotected COPY . . bakes secrets into the image — visible forever via docker history or a registry pull. Secrets belong in runtime injection (docker run -e, Compose's env_file:, or Kubernetes Secrets), never in a shippable layer.

D.4 requirements.txt Example

The pinned dependency set actually shipped in the easypj image — these are the same four packages the SBOM in 21.4 reports back out of the built image, confirming the file below is what really ends up on disk. psycopg2 (not the -binary wheel) is why D.1/D.2 both install gcc and libpq-dev before pip install: it compiles against libpq at install time and only needs the runtime libpq5 afterward.

requirements.txt
Django==5.2.0
gunicorn==21.2.0
psycopg2==2.9.9
Pillow==10.3.0
💡 Splitting for Dev vs. Prod

The file above is what D.1's COPY requirements.txt . expects. For the dev/prod split referenced in 8.4's speed tip, break it into requirements/base.txt (the four lines above), requirements/prod.txt (-r base.txt, nothing else — production stays lean), and requirements/dev.txt (-r base.txt plus django-debug-toolbar, pytest-django, and black — exactly what D.2 installs). A prod-only build is then one -r requirements/prod.txt away with no editing required.

D.5 Entrypoint Script

Identical to the pattern built in 4.7 — The Entrypoint Script Pattern. This is what D.1's ENTRYPOINT ["/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"] actually runs before handing off to CMD: wait for PostgreSQL, run migrations, collect static files, then exec into gunicorn so it — not the shell — becomes PID 1 and receives docker stop's SIGTERM directly.

docker-entrypoint.sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
until pg_isready -h "$DB_HOST" -p 5432 -q; do
  echo "waiting for PostgreSQL..."; sleep 1
done
python manage.py migrate --noinput
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
exec "$@"        # replace shell with CMD → gunicorn = PID 1
⚠️ It Needs the Executable Bit

A script copied by COPY . . keeps whatever permissions it had on the host. If docker-entrypoint.sh isn't executable there, the container fails at startup with permission denied, not a Python traceback. Run chmod +x docker-entrypoint.sh once in the repo (and commit the mode bit) before the first build — Git tracks executable permissions, so this only has to happen once.

Appendix E: easypj Kubernetes Manifests

Complete Production-Ready Kubernetes Manifests for the easypj/jobpost Django Application

Chapter 26 built four minimal, teaching-sized YAMLs to get easypj running on a cluster for the first time. This appendix is the reference-grade expansion of that same easypj stack: every manifest needed to take the image built in §26.2 (ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0) from a fresh cluster to a production-shaped, TLS-terminated, auto-scaling deployment — Namespace, ConfigMap, Secret, Deployment, Service, Ingress, a Kustomize base+overlay pair, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. Every resource name below (easypj namespace/Deployment/Service, easypj-config ConfigMap, easypj-secrets Secret) is the exact same object Chapter 26 already introduced — this appendix only adds the fields a real production rollout needs.

Apply order: (1) namespace.yaml → (2) configmap.yaml & secret.yaml → (3) deployment.yaml → (4) service.yaml → (5) ingress.yaml → (6) kustomization.yaml overlays, once base resources exist → (7) hpa.yaml, last, since it targets the Deployment created in step 3.

📦 Reference Appendix ☸️ 8 Manifests 🎯 easypj Production Deployment

E.1 namespace.yaml

Creates the isolated easypj namespace for all application resources — the declarative equivalent of §26.6's kubectl create namespace easypj. Namespaces scope names, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies.

namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: easypj
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jobpost
    environment: production
💡 Tip: Always label namespaces with app.kubernetes.io/* recommended labels for discoverability and tooling support.

E.2 configmap.yaml

Stores non-sensitive configuration for the same easypj-config object §26.5 introduced — this version carries the full production key set (database/cache hosts, CSRF origins, log level) on top of §26.5's original four, consumed the same way: envFrom in the Deployment (E.4), exactly as §26.3/26.6 already do.

configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-config
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
    component: config
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"
  DEBUG: "False"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com,localhost"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  POSTGRES_HOST: "postgres.easypj.svc.cluster.local"
  POSTGRES_PORT: "5432"
  REDIS_HOST: "redis.easypj.svc.cluster.local"
  REDIS_PORT: "6379"
  CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS: "https://easypj.example.com"
KeyValuePurpose
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULEeasypj.settingsTells Django which settings file to load
ALLOWED_HOSTSeasypj.example.com,localhostDjango security: blocks host-header attacks
POSTGRES_HOSTpostgres.easypj.svc.cluster.localK8s internal DNS for the Postgres Service
REDIS_HOSTredis.easypj.svc.cluster.localK8s internal DNS for Redis cache

E.3 secret.yaml

Stores sensitive data for the same easypj-secrets object §26.5 introduced: Django SECRET_KEY, the DATABASE_URL connection string, and email credentials. stringData is plain text on write — kubectl base64-encodes it into data automatically at apply-time, so it's equivalent at rest to §26.5's manually pre-encoded data: block, just easier to author.

secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: easypj-secrets
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
    component: secrets
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SECRET_KEY: "django-insecure-REPLACE-WITH-REAL-SECRET-KEY"
  DATABASE_URL: "postgres://easypj_user:STRONGpassword123!@postgres.easypj.svc.cluster.local:5432/easypj"
  EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD: "smtp-password-here"
⚠️ Warning: Never commit stringData to Git! Use kubectl create secret or a sealed-secrets controller in production. This file is for reference only.
🔐 Production Secret Strategy: (1) use Sealed Secrets or the External Secrets Operator; (2) enable etcd encryption at rest; (3) restrict access via RBAC; (4) rotate secrets every 90 days.

E.4 deployment.yaml

The core workload resource — the same easypj Deployment §26.3 created, extended to production shape: a ReplicaSet of 3 django-container Pods with the identical 256Mi/250m requests and 512Mi/500m limits from §26.3, plus a rolling-update strategy, three health probes, and PVC-backed static/media volumes. Config and secrets arrive via envFrom, pulling in every key from E.2's easypj-config and E.3's easypj-secrets at once.

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
        tier: backend
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
          protocol: TCP
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: easypj-secrets
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 2
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 0
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 12
        volumeMounts:
        - name: static-files
          mountPath: /app/static
        - name: media-files
          mountPath: /app/media
      volumes:
      - name: static-files
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: easypj-static-pvc
      - name: media-files
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: easypj-media-pvc
FieldValueWhy
replicas3High availability; survives node failure
strategyRollingUpdateZero-downtime deploys
maxUnavailable0Never drop below desired replica count during update
resources.requests256Mi/250mGuaranteed minimum; informs scheduler — same values as §26.3
resources.limits512Mi/500mHard cap; prevents noisy-neighbor issues — same values as §26.3
startupProbe60s windowGives Django time to start before liveness kicks in
terminationGracePeriodSeconds30sAllows graceful connection draining

E.5 service.yaml

Exposes the Deployment via the same easypj Service name §26.4 created, load-balancing across all 3 Pods. §26.4's minimal version exposed a single 8000→8000 port for local kubectl port-forward testing; this production variant fronts the same Pods on ports 80/443 instead, so E.6's Ingress has a stable port to terminate TLS against and route through.

service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: easypj
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
  - name: https
    port: 443
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800
Service typeReachable by
ClusterIPInside the cluster only (default, most services)
NodePortCluster + any node IP:30000-32767 (dev/testing)
LoadBalancerThe public internet, via a cloud LB (production — used here)

E.6 ingress.yaml

Routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the E.5 Service with TLS termination and path-based routing. Requires an Ingress Controller (nginx, traefik, AWS ALB) and, for automatic certificates, cert-manager.

ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: easypj-ingress
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - easypj.example.com
    secretName: easypj-tls
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /static
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj
            port:
              number: 80
📖 Routing: all three paths (/, /static, /api) currently point at the same easypj:80 backend — Django itself dispatches by URL. Split them onto a separate static-file backend once static assets move to object storage or a CDN.

E.7 kustomization.yaml

Kustomize overlays enable environment-specific customization without copying YAML. A base/ layer holds E.1–E.5 unmodified; overlays/prod (shown below) patches replicas and memory limits and bumps the image tag, all without touching the base files.

base/kustomization.yaml
# base/kustomization.yaml — Common configuration
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: easypj
resources:
- namespace.yaml
- configmap.yaml
- secret.yaml
- deployment.yaml
- service.yaml
commonLabels:
  app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: kustomize
images:
- name: ghcr.io/username/easypj
  newTag: v1.0
overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml — Production-specific overrides
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: easypj
resources:
- ../../base
patches:
- patch: |-
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/replicas
      value: 5
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: easypj
- patch: |-
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory
      value: "1Gi"
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: easypj
images:
- name: ghcr.io/username/easypj
  newTag: v1.2.3
nameSuffix: -prod
commonLabels:
  environment: production
OverlayReplicasMemory LimitImage Tag
dev1256Milatest
staging2512Miv1.2.3-rc1
prod51Giv1.2.3
🚀 Deploy with Kustomize: kubectl apply -k overlays/prod or kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | kubectl apply -f -

E.8 hpa.yaml — HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Automatically scales the E.4 Deployment between 2 and 10 pods based on CPU and memory utilization — extending the fixed replicas: 3 from §26.3/§26.7 with a live, metrics-driven floor and ceiling. Requires the Metrics Server installed in the cluster.

hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: easypj-hpa
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: easypj
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 60
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15
      - type: Pods
        value: 4
        periodSeconds: 15
      selectPolicy: Max
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
ParameterValueMeaning
minReplicas2Never drop below 2 pods (HA minimum)
maxReplicas10Never exceed 10 pods (cost control)
cpu target70%Scale up when average CPU exceeds 70% of the 250m request
memory target80%Scale up when average memory exceeds 80% of the 256Mi request
scaleDown stabilization300sWait 5 min before scaling down (prevents flapping)
scaleUp policyMax(100%, 4 pods)Aggressive scale-up; uses whichever adds more pods
⚠️ Warning: the HPA and §26.7's manual kubectl scale --replicas=5 both write to the same spec.replicas field — once the HPA is applied, a manual scale is overwritten on its next reconcile. Delete the HPA before scaling manually, or edit minReplicas/maxReplicas instead.

Appendix F: Docker Troubleshooting Guide

Systematic Diagnosis & Repair — From Container Crashes to K8s Deployment Failures

Every common Docker error, categorized by subsystem, with root cause analysis, diagnostic commands, and step-by-step solutions. Work the decision tree first — it routes you to the right F.N section in one hop: a crashed container starts with docker logs / inspect / events (F.1); a build/image failure starts with docker build --no-cache --progress=plain (F.4); a runtime/network symptom starts with docker inspect network / exec ... ping (F.2). Once the root cause is identified: apply the fix, then verify with the same diagnostic command that surfaced the problem.

F.1 Common Container Errors

The most frequent container-level failures — exit codes, OOM kills, permission denials, and port conflicts.

SymptomExit CodeLikely CauseDiagnosticSolution
Container exits immediately0 or 1Wrong CMD, missing file, app crashdocker logs <id>Check CMD/ENTRYPOINT; run docker run -it --entrypoint sh <img>
OOM Killed137Memory limit exceededdocker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <id>Increase --memory limit; check for memory leaks
Permission denied126Non-root user without accessdocker exec <id> whoamiRUN chown -R app:app /app or adjust USER
Port already in useN/A (fails to start)Host port conflictnetstat -tlnp | grep :8000Use a different host port: -p 8001:8000
Segfault / core dump139Native library incompatibilitydmesg | grep segfaultRebuild for correct arch (amd64 vs arm64)
Connection refusedN/ABinding to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0docker exec <id> netstat -tlnpUse --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 in Django/Gunicorn
Image pull failsN/AAuth or tag issuedocker pull <img>docker login; verify the tag exists on the registry
Healthcheck failsunhealthyWrong endpoint or timingdocker inspect --format='{{.State.Health}}' <id>Adjust interval/timeout; verify the endpoint
Quick Diagnostic Checklist
# 1. Check container state
docker ps -a --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
# 2. Inspect exit reason
docker inspect --format='{{json .State}}' CONTAINER | jq
# 3. View last 50 log lines
docker logs --tail 50 CONTAINER
# 4. Check resource usage
docker stats --no-stream CONTAINER
# 5. Shell into the running container
docker exec -it CONTAINER sh

F.2 Network Troubleshooting

DNS resolution failures, inter-container communication, port mapping, and overlay issues.

SymptomDiagnostic CommandLikely CauseSolution
DNS resolution failsdocker exec <id> nslookup postgresContainers on different networksJoin the same network: docker network connect net <id>
Cannot reach host portcurl localhost:8000Port not published, or wrong interfaceCheck the -p HOST:CONTAINER mapping
Intermittent connectivitydocker network inspect bridgeIP address pool exhaustedPrune unused networks: docker network prune
Swarm overlay brokendocker node lsPort 4789/7946 blockedOpen UDP 4789 (VXLAN), TCP/UDP 7946 (gossip)
Container cannot reach the internetdocker exec <id> ping 8.8.8.8iptables rules or IP forwarding disabledsysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
Slow DNS resolutiondocker exec <id> cat /etc/resolv.confDNS server misconfiguredSet --dns 8.8.8.8
🌐 Why Two Containers Can't Talk: Network Isolation

Docker's default bridge (docker0, e.g. 172.17.0.0/16) lets any two containers attached to it reach each other directly — but a container on a separate custom network (e.g. mynet, 172.18.0.0/16) is invisible to them by design, even though both are running on the same host. This isolation is deliberate (Compose gives every project its own network for exactly this reason); the fix is never "there's a network bug," it's docker network connect <network> <container> to put both containers on a shared network.

Network Debug Toolkit
# List all networks and the containers on them
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge --format='{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
# Test connectivity from inside a container
docker exec CONTAINER ping -c 3 TARGET_IP
docker exec CONTAINER nslookup TARGET_HOSTNAME
# Check iptables rules
iptables -L DOCKER -n -v
# Inspect DNS config
docker exec CONTAINER cat /etc/resolv.conf

F.3 Volume/Mount Troubleshooting

Data loss, permission errors, slow I/O, and mount point confusion.

SymptomDiagnosticCauseSolution
Volume appears emptydocker run -v vol:/data ... ls /dataBind mount path does not exist on the hostCreate the host directory first, or use a named volume
Permission denied on mountdocker exec <id> ls -la /mntUID/GID mismatch, host↔containerdocker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g)
Data lost after container rmdocker volume lsUsed an anonymous volume (--rm flag)Always use named volumes in production
Volume not reattacheddocker inspect VOLNAMEVolume still attached to a stopped containerRemove the old container: docker rm <old_id>
Slow volume I/Odocker run --volume-driverWrong storage driver on macOS/WindowsUse :cached or :delegated on bind mounts
Bind mount not reflecting changesdocker exec <id> stat /mnt/fileFilesystem notification issue (macOS)Use :consistent, or switch to a named volume

Named volumes and bind mounts fail differently because Docker manages one and merely references the other:

AspectNamed Volume (/var/lib/docker/volumes/…)Bind Mount (direct host path)
Survives docker rm✅ Yes — Docker-managed storage⚠️ Only if the host path itself persists
Backup-friendly✅ Yes — docker volume tooling❌ Manual host-path backup required
Cross-platform safe✅ Yes❌ Path-dependent (differs Windows/Mac/Linux)
Live code editing❌ Requires a copy-in step✅ Yes — host edits appear instantly
Permission handling✅ Docker manages ownership❌ UID/GID mismatches are common

F.4 Build Errors

Dockerfile syntax issues, cache corruption, COPY failures, and multi-stage pitfalls.

Error MessageCauseSolution
COPY failed: file not foundPath is relative to the build context, not the DockerfilePaths are relative to the docker build <CONTEXT> directory
returned a non-zero code: 1RUN command failedAdd set -ex at the top of the script; split a long RUN into steps
no such file or directoryMissing dependency, or wrong base imageVerify the package is available in the chosen base image variant
manifest for ... not foundWrong platform/architectureUse --platform linux/amd64 on ARM Macs
Cannot connect to Docker daemonDocker daemon not runningsudo systemctl start docker
Build context huge/slowMissing .dockerignoreCreate .dockerignore; exclude node_modules, .git, venv
exec format errorBinary compiled for the wrong architectureUse FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM with BuildKit
Layer cache not usedCOPY/ADD invalidates the cacheOrder the Dockerfile: install deps FIRST, then COPY source
Build Debug Techniques
# Build with full output (no cache)
docker build --no-cache --progress=plain -t app .
# Inspect a specific layer
docker history IMAGE
docker run -it IMAGE sh  # explore interactively
# Build with BuildKit for better error messages
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t app .
# Check what's in the build context
du -sh . && ls -la  # ensure .dockerignore is working

F.5 Docker Daemon Issues

Daemon won't start, disk space exhaustion, API unresponsiveness, and performance degradation.

SymptomDiagnosticSolution
Daemon won't startsudo journalctl -u docker --no-pager -n 50Check daemon.json syntax; verify the storage driver
Disk fulldocker system dfdocker system prune -a --volumes (caution — destructive!)
API unresponsivedocker info hangssudo systemctl restart docker; check for deadlocks
Too many open filesdocker info | grep -i "file"Increase LimitNOFILE in docker.service
Images won't deletedocker rmi -f IMAGEStop containers using the image first; remove child images
Docker Desktop won't startWSL2 / Hyper-V issuesRestart WSL: wsl --shutdown; check virtualization in BIOS
⚠️ docker system prune -a --volumes Is Irreversible

It deletes every stopped container, unused network, dangling AND unused image, and — with --volumes — every volume not currently attached to a running container. Confirm nothing important is only "temporarily" stopped before running it.

Daemon Health Check
# Check daemon status & logs
sudo systemctl status docker
sudo journalctl -u docker --since "10 min ago" --no-pager
# Check disk usage
docker system df -v
# Verify daemon config
cat /etc/docker/daemon.json | python -m json.tool  # validates JSON
# Test the API
docker version && docker info

F.6 Compose Troubleshooting

Startup ordering, environment variable leaks, healthcheck deadlocks, and network creation failures.

SymptomDiagnosticSolution
Service stuck waitingdocker compose psCheck depends_on: condition: service_healthy
Env vars not injecteddocker compose run web envVerify the .env file location; check env_file vs environment
Port conflict between servicesdocker compose configCheck for duplicate published ports
Volume data disappearsdocker compose down -v was usedDon't use the -v flag; use external named volumes
Network not founddocker network lsdocker compose down, then docker compose up
Build cache staleCode changes not reflecteddocker compose build --no-cache
Compose Debug Flow
# Validate the compose file
docker compose config  # shows merged config; catches YAML errors
# View logs for all services
docker compose logs --tail=20
# Recreate a single service
docker compose up -d --force-recreate django
# Check health status
docker compose ps --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.Status}}"
# Test individual service connectivity
docker compose exec django python manage.py check --database default

F.7 Kubernetes Deployment Troubleshooting

ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, pending pods, probe failures, and service routing issues — the same container-level root causes from F.1–F.6, one layer up.

SymptomPod StatusDiagnosticSolution
Pod stuck in PendingPendingkubectl describe pod <name>Check resource requests, node capacity, PVC binding
Cannot pull imageImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePullkubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 EventsVerify the image tag and registry auth (imagePullSecrets)
Container keeps restartingCrashLoopBackOffkubectl logs <pod> --previousFix the application error; check CMD in the Dockerfile
Probe failingRunning but not Readykubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A10 "Liveness\|Readiness"Adjust probe path, port, initialDelaySeconds
Service not routingPods running but unreachablekubectl get endpoints <svc>Check that the selector matches the pod labels
ConfigMap/Secret not updatingOld config in running podskubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>K8s does not auto-restart pods on ConfigMap change
HPA not scalingLoad high but no new podskubectl top pods -n <ns>Verify the Metrics Server is installed and running
Ingress 404/503Request returns an errorkubectl describe ingress <name>Check the backend service name and port match
K8s Debug Quick Reference
# Pod debugging
kubectl describe pod POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE
kubectl logs POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE --previous  # crash logs
kubectl exec -it POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE -- sh   # shell in
# Deployment debugging
kubectl rollout status deployment/DEPLOY_NAME -n NAMESPACE
kubectl rollout history deployment/DEPLOY_NAME -n NAMESPACE
# Service debugging
kubectl get endpoints SVC_NAME -n NAMESPACE   # are pods registered?
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -O- http://SVC_NAME:PORT
# Events, newest last
kubectl get events -n NAMESPACE --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

F.8 Exit-Code Decoder

Docker and Kubernetes surface the same POSIX exit codes; codes above 128 follow the 128 + signal-number convention. Read this table left to right: the code tells you WHAT happened before you spend a single second guessing.

Exit CodeMeaningCommon CauseDiagnosticFix
0Clean exitProcess completed successfullydocker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' <id>None needed — this is success; a Job's restartPolicy: Always would still restart the container, which is a common source of confusion
1Application errorUncaught exception, bad config, generic app-level failuredocker logs <id> / kubectl logs <pod> --previousRead the app's OWN logs first — the fix lives in application code or config, not in Docker
125docker run itself failedBad CLI flag, malformed image reference, or a daemon-level error — the container process never startedRead the docker run stderr output directlyFix the invocation (flag syntax, image tag); there are no container logs to check because the container never ran
126Command found but not executableBinary lacks execute permission, or CMD points at a non-binary filedocker exec <id> ls -la <path> / whoamichmod +x the entrypoint script, or fix a broken shebang line
127Command not foundTypo in CMD/ENTRYPOINT, missing binary, or wrong PATH inside the imagedocker run -it --entrypoint sh <img>, then which <cmd>Install the missing binary in the base image, or fix the PATH
137SIGKILL (128 + 9)OOM-killed, OR a manual docker kill / stop-timeout expirydocker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <id> / kubectl describe pod → look for reason OOMKilledRaise the --memory / K8s memory limit, or fix a leak — .State.OOMKilled (or the pod's Terminated reason) is the ONLY reliable way to tell an OOM kill from a manual kill
139SIGSEGV (128 + 11)Segfault — native library incompatibility or a runtime bugdmesg | grep segfaultRebuild for the correct architecture (amd64 vs arm64), or patch the native dependency
143SIGTERM (128 + 15) honoredA graceful docker stop or kubectl delete pod completed within its grace perioddocker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' <id>Expected behavior, no fix needed — unless shutdown legitimately needs longer, in which case extend --stop-timeout / terminationGracePeriodSeconds
🛑 Exit 137 Has Two Unrelated Causes

128 + 9 = SIGKILL fires both when the kernel OOM-killer terminates a container AND when something runs docker kill / the stop-timeout expires after a plain docker stop. Never assume "137 = out of memory" — always confirm with docker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' (Docker) or the pod's status.containerStatuses[].lastState.terminated.reason (Kubernetes) before resizing memory limits.

Exit-Code Quick Decode
# Docker: exit code + whether OOM caused it
docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}}' CONTAINER
# Kubernetes: last termination reason + exit code
kubectl get pod POD_NAME -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason} {.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.exitCode}{"\n"}'
# crictl (node-level, works even if the apiserver is unreachable)
crictl inspect CONTAINER_ID | grep -i exitCode
🛠️ Golden Rules of Docker Troubleshooting

1. Always check docker logs first — most answers are already in the logs.
2. Use docker inspect for structured state (exit codes, mounts, networks) instead of guessing.
3. Isolate: run with -it --entrypoint sh to enter a container that won't start normally.
4. For Kubernetes: work describe → logs → exec → events, in that order.
5. Prune regularly — docker system prune -a — to prevent disk-full failures before they happen.

Appendix G: Docker Glossary A-Z

Every Docker Term You'll Ever Need — Defined Clearly with Context

50+ essential terms organized alphabetically, a comprehensive acronym reference, and a curated set of modern, exam-critical terms drawn from this guide's CI/CD, testing, orchestration-tooling, observability, incident-response, and AI-workload chapters. Each definition includes practical context for the DCA exam and for real-world easypj/jobpost work.

G.1 50+ Docker Terms — A to Z

#TermDefinition
1Bridge NetworkDefault Docker network type. Containers on the same bridge can communicate by IP or container name. Uses NAT (iptables) for external access.
2Build ContextThe directory (and all its contents) sent to the Docker daemon when running docker build. Controlled by .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files.
3BuildKitNext-generation Docker builder supporting parallel builds, secrets injection, remote cache, and advanced Dockerfile syntax. Enabled via DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1.
4CMDDockerfile instruction that sets the default command (and arguments) for a container. Overridable at docker run. If ENTRYPOINT is set, CMD becomes its arguments.
5ContainerA running instance of a Docker image. Has its own writable layer, network namespace, process space (PID), and resource constraints (cgroups).
6Container RuntimeThe low-level software that actually runs containers. Docker uses containerd (which uses runc). Alternatives: CRI-O, gVisor, Firecracker.
7containerdAn industry-standard container runtime managing the complete container lifecycle. Docker donates containerd to CNCF; used by Kubernetes as well.
8Control Groups (cgroups)Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for, and isolates resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network) of a collection of processes (containers).
9Copy-on-Write (CoW)Storage optimization: files in read-only image layers are copied to the writable container layer only when modified. Maximizes layer sharing between containers.
10Docker ComposeTool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file (compose.yaml). Single command: docker compose up.
11Docker Content Trust (DCT)Integrity system that signs Docker images using Notary. Ensures images haven't been tampered with. Enabled via DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1.
12Docker DesktopGUI application for macOS/Windows that packages Docker Engine, CLI, Compose, Kubernetes, and credential helpers into a single install.
13Docker EngineThe core Docker runtime: a client-server application consisting of the Docker daemon (dockerd) and the Docker CLI (docker).
14Docker HubDocker's official public registry. Hosts millions of container images. Free for public repos; paid plans for private repos and vulnerability scanning.
15Docker ScoutBuilt-in image vulnerability scanner that analyzes SBOM, checks against CVE databases, and provides remediation advice. Replaces the older docker scan.
16Docker SwarmDocker's native orchestrator for multi-host container management. Provides service discovery, load balancing, secrets, rolling updates, and self-healing.
17DockerfileText file containing a set of instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, etc.) that Docker uses to automatically build an image layer by layer.
18ENTRYPOINTDockerfile instruction that defines the fixed executable. Unlike CMD, ENTRYPOINT is not overridden by docker run arguments (unless --entrypoint is used).
19ExposeDockerfile instruction that documents which ports the container listens on. Does NOT publish ports — only -p or ports: in Compose does that.
20HealthcheckDockerfile instruction that defines how Docker tests if a container is still working. Supports CMD, CMD-SHELL, and NONE. Status: starting/healthy/unhealthy.
21Host NetworkNetwork mode (--network host) where the container shares the host's network stack directly — no isolation. Faster but less secure.
22ImageA read-only template composed of stacked layers, built from a Dockerfile. Used as the blueprint to create containers. Identified by name:tag or digest.
23Image DigestContent-addressable SHA256 hash uniquely identifying a specific image version. Immutable — unlike tags which can be moved. Format: sha256:abc123...
24Image LayerEach instruction in a Dockerfile produces a read-only layer. Layers are cached, shared between images, and combined via a union filesystem (Overlay2).
25Init ProcessA lightweight init (tini/dumb-init) that runs as PID 1 to handle zombie processes and signal forwarding. Enabled via docker run --init.
26MACVLANNetwork driver that assigns a MAC address to each container, making it appear as a physical device on the network. Used for legacy applications.
27ManifestA JSON document describing an image's layers, architecture, OS, and digests. Multi-arch images have a manifest list pointing to platform-specific manifests.
28Multi-Stage BuildDockerfile technique using multiple FROM statements. Build dependencies in one stage, copy only the final artifacts to a minimal runtime stage.
29Namespace (Linux)Kernel feature isolating process visibility: PID, NET (network), MNT (mount), IPC, UTS (hostname), USER, CGROUP. Docker uses all 7 namespaces per container.
30OrchestrationAutomated deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters. Docker Swarm and Kubernetes are the two main orchestrators.
31Overlay NetworkMulti-host Docker network using VXLAN encapsulation (UDP port 4789). Enables containers on different Swarm nodes to communicate securely.
32Overlay2Default Docker storage driver on most Linux distributions. Uses a union mount filesystem with copy-on-write semantics for efficient layer stacking.
33Port MappingPublishing a container port to the host using -p HOST:CONTAINER. Traffic to HOST:PORT is forwarded to CONTAINER:PORT via Docker's proxy.
34Private RegistrySelf-hosted Docker image storage. Can be a simple registry:2 container, or a managed service (AWS ECR, GCR, GHCR, Azure ACR).
35RegistryA stateless, highly scalable server-side application that stores and distributes Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.
36RepositoryA collection of related Docker images with the same name but different tags. Example: python repository contains python:3.11, python:3.12, etc.
37Restart PolicyControls when Docker automatically restarts a container: no, on-failure[:N], always, unless-stopped. Set via --restart flag.
38SBOMSoftware Bill of Materials — a detailed inventory of all packages, libraries, and dependencies inside a container image. Generated by Docker Scout.
39SeccompLinux kernel security feature that filters which system calls a process can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile blocking ~44 of ~300+ syscalls.
40Service (Swarm)The definition of a desired state for an application in Docker Swarm. A service specifies the image, replicas, ports, networks, and update strategy.
41StackA group of interrelated Swarm services defined in a Compose file and deployed together via docker stack deploy. Stacks span the entire swarm.
42Storage DriverThe plugin that manages how image layers and the container writable layer are stored. Common drivers: overlay2 (default), aufs, devicemapper, btrfs, zfs.
43TagA human-readable label applied to an image (e.g., python:3.11-slim). Tags are mutable — a tag can be moved to a newer image. Use digests for immutability.
44Tmpfs MountA temporary filesystem stored in the host's RAM (not disk). Used for sensitive data that should never hit disk. --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid.
45Union FilesystemFilesystem that allows files from separate filesystems (branches/layers) to be overlaid into a single coherent view. Overlay2 is the Linux union FS Docker uses.
46User NamespaceMaps a container's root user (UID 0) to a non-privileged user on the host. Reduces blast radius of container breakout. --userns-remap.
47VolumeDocker-managed persistent storage that exists outside the container's UnionFS. Survives container deletion. Managed via docker volume commands.
48Volume DriverPlugin enabling Docker volumes to use external storage systems: NFS, AWS EBS, Azure Disk, Ceph, GlusterFS. Specified via --volume-driver.
49Worker NodeA Docker Swarm node that runs containers as scheduled by manager nodes. Workers don't participate in Raft consensus or cluster management.
50Manager NodeA Docker Swarm node that handles cluster management: scheduling, maintaining cluster state, API serving, and Raft consensus. First node is always a manager.
51Docker ContextA configuration that bundles Docker endpoint (daemon) connection details, letting you switch between multiple Docker environments with docker context use.
52Build ArgsBuild-time variables passed via --build-arg or ARG instruction. Unlike ENV, ARGs are NOT persisted in the final image. Use for conditional builds.
53Secrets (Docker)Encrypted blobs (max 500KB) managed by Swarm for sensitive data. Stored in Raft log, mounted as tmpfs into /run/secrets/. Never written to disk.
54Configs (Docker)Non-sensitive configuration data (max 500KB) managed by Swarm. Similar to secrets but not encrypted. Mounted into /<name> in the container.

G.2 Docker Acronyms Explained

Every acronym you'll encounter in Docker documentation, exams, and interviews — expanded and explained.

AcronymExpansionWhat It Means
CI/CDContinuous Integration / Continuous DeliveryAutomated pipeline: build image → test → push → deploy. Docker is the backbone of most CI/CD pipelines.
CNCFCloud Native Computing FoundationLinux Foundation sub-foundation that hosts containerd, Kubernetes, Prometheus, and other cloud-native projects.
CoWCopy-on-WriteStorage strategy: data is copied only when modified. Core to Docker's layer efficiency.
CRIContainer Runtime InterfaceKubernetes API for pluggable container runtimes. containerd implements CRI via the CRI plugin.
CVECommon Vulnerabilities and ExposuresPublicly disclosed security flaws. Docker Scout checks images against CVE databases.
DABDistributed Application Bundle(Deprecated) Early Docker format for multi-service apps. Replaced by Compose files + docker stack deploy.
DCADocker Certified AssociateDocker's official certification exam covering orchestration, image management, networking, security, and storage.
DCTDocker Content TrustImage signing and verification using Notary/TUF. DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1.
OCIOpen Container InitiativeLinux Foundation project creating open standards for containers (image-spec, runtime-spec, distribution-spec).
SBOMSoftware Bill of MaterialsInventory of all software components in an image. Generated via docker scout sbom.
TUFThe Update FrameworkSecure software update specification. Docker Content Trust uses Notary, which implements TUF.
VXLANVirtual Extensible LANEncapsulation protocol (UDP 4789) used by Docker overlay networks for multi-host container communication.

G.3 Modern & Exam-Critical Terms

Terms this guide introduces in its CI/CD (Ch22), testing (Ch24), manifest-generation and Kubernetes-packaging (Ch25, Ch27, Ch29), observability and incident-response (Ch31-32), and AI-workload (Ch34) chapters — the vocabulary a basic Docker glossary won't cover, but that a working easypj/jobpost engineer (and a well-prepared exam candidate) needs.

#TermDefinition
1Blameless PostmortemA standardized incident report — Timeline → Impact → Root Cause (5 Whys) → Action Items — written after every production incident. "Blameless" means it names failures of the system (a missing memory limit, no query review), never a person (Ch32).
2Chaos EngineeringDeliberately killing a container or Pod on purpose, in a controlled window, to prove restart policies (Ch6) or a ReplicaSet/Deployment's self-healing (Ch26, Ch28) actually work — so the first time something dies isn't during a real incident (Ch32).
3CIS BenchmarkThe Center for Internet Security's Docker security-configuration standard. Docker Bench Security (docker/docker-bench-security) automates PASS/WARN/INFO checks against it, covering host config, daemon.json, and runtime settings (Ch21).
4dind (Docker-in-Docker)Running a full Docker daemon inside a container (e.g., the docker:27-dind service image), typically to build images in a CI job. Requires --privileged, which disables the seccomp/capability protections from Part 7 for that job — high isolation, high risk (Ch22).
5Docker Build CloudDocker's hosted remote-builder service. Offloads buildx builds to remote, beefy builders with a shared, persistent cache across an entire team. Pays for itself with high build volume or slow local hardware (Ch22).
6Docker Model RunnerDocker's built-in way to pull and run local LLMs as a service — docker model pull / docker model run — treating quantized model weights as OCI-distributed artifacts, cached and versioned exactly like an application image. Exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint on localhost (Ch34).
7DOCKER-USER ChainThe iptables chain Docker reserves specifically for an administrator's own firewall rules. It is evaluated before Docker's own rules, so custom container-traffic restrictions survive daemon restarts instead of being silently overwritten.
8Error BudgetThe SRE counterpart to an SLO: the maximum amount of unreliability a service is allowed (e.g., 0.1% of requests may fail) before a team must pause feature work and prioritize reliability. Consumed by every incident and every failed request (Ch31-32).
9Golden SignalsGoogle SRE's four-metric framework for the smallest signal set that catches most outages: Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. Applied per tier — e.g., Django (latency/errors), Postgres (saturation: connections), Redis (saturation: memory), nginx (traffic) — to drive alerting (Ch31).
10HelmThe de facto package manager for Kubernetes. Packages Deployment/Service/etc. YAML as a templated, versioned "chart" with fill-in-the-blank values.yaml, released via helm install/upgrade with rollback history. Helm 3 has no in-cluster Tiller component — all rendering happens client-side (Ch29).
11KomposeA CLI tool (kompose convert) that auto-translates a compose.yaml into first-draft Kubernetes manifests (Deployment/Service/PVC). A fast starting point, never a final artifact — it silently drops fields like depends_on and adds no resource limits (Ch25, Ch29).
12KustomizeA template-free Kubernetes customization tool built directly into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Layers environment-specific "overlay" patches on top of one shared "base" manifest set — no extra binary needed, but also no release history or rollback command like Helm (Ch27, Ch29).
13Live-RestoreA daemon.json flag ("live-restore": true) that lets already-running containers keep running through a dockerd restart or upgrade, instead of being stopped along with the daemon.
14Manifest ListA single image tag that points to multiple architecture-specific manifests (e.g., amd64 and arm64) — what docker pull resolves automatically depending on whether the host is Apple Silicon or x86.
15Routing MeshDocker Swarm's ingress feature: any node in the swarm can accept traffic on a published service port and route it — via the ingress overlay network and IPVS — to a healthy task, even one running on a completely different node.
16RyukThe lightweight "resource reaper" companion container that Testcontainers starts alongside every test run. It guarantees cleanup of test containers and networks even if the test process itself crashes mid-run (Ch24).
17SLO (Service Level Objective)A target reliability threshold for a service (e.g., "99.9% of requests succeed"), measured against a Service Level Indicator (SLI) such as error rate or latency. Sets the error budget available before reliability work must take priority over new features.
18TestcontainersA library that starts real, disposable, version-matched database/service containers programmatically for automated tests — e.g., a real Postgres container per test run instead of a shared test database or mocks. Needs a Docker daemon reachable from the test process — dind or a socket mount in CI, the same trust trade-off as Ch22 (Ch24).

This appendix is a three-layer glossary: G.1 covers the 50+ foundational Docker terms every DCA candidate must know cold, from Bridge Network through Configs. G.2 expands the 12 acronyms — CI/CD, CNCF, CoW, CRI, CVE, DAB, DCA, DCT, OCI, SBOM, TUF, VXLAN — that show up throughout Docker documentation and exam questions. G.3 is this guide's own addition: 18 terms that a basic Docker glossary would miss entirely because they come from newer, exam-adjacent territory — CI build strategies (dind, Docker Build Cloud), testing (Testcontainers, Ryuk), Kubernetes packaging tools (Helm, Kustomize, Kompose), production operations (golden signals, SLO, error budget, chaos engineering, blameless postmortem, CIS Benchmark), Swarm networking internals (routing mesh, DOCKER-USER chain, live-restore, manifest list), and AI workloads (Docker Model Runner). Together the three tables give a single alphabetized and topically grouped reference for every term used across this guide's 34 chapters.
