H.1 Domain 1: Orchestration — 25 Questions

Swarm mode, services, stacks, nodes, rolling updates, scheduling, and the Compose-to-Kubernetes bridge covered in Chapters 10-12 and 25-30. 25% of the DCA exam — the single largest domain.

📝 DCA Domain 1 — Orchestration Practice Questions (25)

Swarm init/join, services, stacks, scheduling, rolling updates, and the Compose/Kubernetes bridge — 25 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command initializes a Docker Swarm on the current node?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker swarm init. This makes the current node a Swarm manager, generates join tokens, and starts the Raft consensus database.

EXPLANATION

The node becomes the first manager. Swarm uses Raft consensus (an odd number of managers is recommended — 3, 5, or 7). The command outputs docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-... for workers and a separate token for additional managers.

Q2
How do you add a worker node to an existing swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

On the manager: docker swarm join-token worker to get the token. On the worker: docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-... MANAGER_IP:2377.

EXPLANATION

Port 2377 is the Swarm management port (TCP). Workers need connectivity to all managers on this port. Join tokens differ for workers vs managers — manager tokens should be guarded carefully since they grant full cluster control.

Q3
What is the difference between a Swarm service and a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A service is a declarative definition of desired state (image, replicas, ports, networks). A container is a single running instance. Services manage containers across the swarm.

EXPLANATION

In Swarm, you don't run containers directly — you create services. The swarm manager ensures the desired number of replicas are running, rescheduling them if nodes fail. This is the core of orchestration: declaring WHAT you want, letting the system handle HOW.

Q4
What command creates a Swarm service running nginx with 5 replicas on port 80?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service create --name web --replicas 5 -p 80:80 nginx

EXPLANATION

The service is automatically load-balanced across all 5 replicas via Swarm's routing mesh. Any node receiving traffic on port 80 forwards it to a healthy replica, even if that node isn't running the container.

Q5
How do you perform a rolling update on a Swarm service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service update --image nginx:1.25 --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 10s web

EXPLANATION

Swarm performs rolling updates by default. --update-parallelism controls how many replicas update at once; --update-delay adds a pause between batches. Failed updates auto-rollback if --update-failure-action rollback is set.

Q6
What is the Swarm Routing Mesh?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The routing mesh makes every Swarm node listen on published service ports and forward traffic to healthy replicas — even if the receiving node doesn't run that replica. Uses IPVS for load balancing.

EXPLANATION

You can hit ANY node on port 80 and reach the nginx service, even if that node has zero nginx containers. This is key for external load balancers — they can point to any swarm node.

Q7
How many manager nodes should a production Swarm have, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

3 or 5 manager nodes (odd number). Raft consensus requires (N/2)+1 managers to be available (quorum). With 3 managers, you can lose 1; with 5, you can lose 2.

EXPLANATION

Never use an even number — it wastes capacity with no fault tolerance gain. 4 managers has the same fault tolerance as 3 (can lose 1) but needs 3 for quorum instead of 2. More managers means slower consensus, so 7+ is rarely needed.

Q8
What command deploys a Compose file as a Swarm stack?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml mystack. This creates services, networks, and secrets defined in the Compose file across the entire swarm.

EXPLANATION

Key difference from docker compose up: stack deploy is Swarm-aware — it respects the deploy: section (replicas, update_config, restart_policy, placement constraints). Compose up ignores deploy: unless using docker compose --compatibility up.

Q9
How do you scale a Swarm service to 10 replicas?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service scale web=10 or docker service update --replicas 10 web

EXPLANATION

Swarm schedules the additional replicas across available nodes, respecting placement constraints and resource availability. If there aren't enough resources, replicas may stay in a "pending" state.

Q10
What is a Swarm placement constraint? Give an example.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A rule restricting which nodes can run a service. Example: docker service create --constraint node.labels.ssd==true --name db postgres ensures the database only runs on nodes with SSD storage.

EXPLANATION

Placement constraints use node labels (docker node update --label-add ssd=true node1). You can also use --placement-pref for spreading across racks/zones. Constraints help with compliance, performance, and licensing requirements.

Q11
How do you drain a Swarm node for maintenance?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker node update --availability drain NODE_NAME. All containers on that node are gracefully stopped and rescheduled to other nodes.

EXPLANATION

Drain prevents new tasks from being scheduled and migrates existing ones. After maintenance: docker node update --availability active NODE_NAME. The node's state persists — only containers move.

Q12
What are the three Swarm node availability states?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Active — normal operation, can receive tasks. Pause — existing containers stay, no new tasks. Drain — all containers moved away, no new tasks.

EXPLANATION

Pause is useful for temporarily suspending a node (troubleshooting without evacuation). Drain is for decommissioning or maintenance. Managers in drain state still participate in Raft but don't run workloads.

Q13
What happens to a Swarm service if a worker node fails?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Swarm detects the failure, marks the node as Down, and reschedules the failed containers onto healthy nodes to maintain the desired replica count.

EXPLANATION

This is self-healing. The manager monitors heartbeats — if none arrive for ~20s the node is marked Down (~60s for leader election if a manager itself fails). Containers from failed nodes are recreated on healthy nodes automatically.

Q14
How do Swarm secrets differ from environment variables for sensitive data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are encrypted in transit and at rest in the Raft log, mounted as tmpfs files in /run/secrets/, and never exposed in docker inspect or env vars. Env vars are visible in docker inspect and process lists.

EXPLANATION

Secrets exist only in memory on worker nodes (tmpfs), are encrypted in the Raft database, and are only sent to nodes that need them. Env vars can leak via ps aux, /proc, or logging. Always use secrets for passwords, API keys, and certificates.

Q15
What command lists all services in a swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service ls — shows service name, mode (replicated/global), replicas, image, and ports.

EXPLANATION

Add --format for custom output. For detailed inspection: docker service inspect SERVICE_NAME. For task-level view: docker service ps SERVICE_NAME shows each replica's node, state, and error messages.

Q16
How do you scale a specific Compose service to N instances without editing the compose file?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose up -d --scale web=5. Overrides the replica count for that service at deploy time.

EXPLANATION

This only works cleanly for services without a fixed container_name and without a static published host port (each replica needs its own port, or none published at all — let a reverse proxy or the Swarm routing mesh handle distribution instead).

Q17
How do you make Compose wait for a dependency to actually be ready, not just started?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Define a healthcheck: block on the dependency (e.g. postgres), then depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy on the dependent service.

EXPLANATION

Plain depends_on only waits for the container to start, not for the application inside it to be ready — a classic race-condition source (app connects before Postgres finishes initializing). service_healthy ties startup order to the actual HEALTHCHECK status.

Q18
What is a Docker config object and how does it differ from a secret?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker config create nginx-conf ./nginx.conf, then docker service create --config nginx-conf .... Mounted as a regular, unencrypted file — for non-sensitive configuration, not passwords.

EXPLANATION

Contrast with a secret, which IS encrypted at rest/in transit and mounted only at /run/secrets/. Configs are meant for config files (nginx.conf, application.yaml) that are fine to version-control alongside the service definition.

Q19
What is the difference between global mode and replicated mode for a Swarm service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service create --mode global ... runs exactly one task per eligible node (e.g. a monitoring agent or log shipper). The default, replicated, runs a fixed --replicas count spread across nodes by the scheduler.

EXPLANATION

Global mode scales automatically with cluster size — every new node automatically gets an instance. You cannot docker service scale a global service since its replica count is derived from the node count, not set manually.

Q20
How do you view the aggregated logs of every replica of a Swarm service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service logs -f SERVICE_NAME — shows stdout/stderr from ALL replicas across every node, prefixed with the node/task ID.

EXPLANATION

Requires the json-file or journald log driver (not all drivers support service logs). This is far faster for debugging than SSHing to individual nodes to run docker logs on each replica.

Q21
How do you add a custom label to a node, and how do you promote a worker to manager?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker node update --label-add zone=us-east node1 adds a label. docker node promote node2 turns a worker into a manager; docker node demote node2 reverts it.

EXPLANATION

Labels combine with placement constraints (node.labels.zone==us-east). Promote/demote lets you rebalance manager quorum without having the node leave and rejoin the swarm.

Q22
What are Compose profiles and how do you activate one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add profiles: ["debug"] to a service, then run docker compose --profile debug up. Services with no profiles: key always start; profiled services only start when explicitly requested.

EXPLANATION

Useful for optional tooling (an adminer UI, a debug sidecar) that shouldn't start in every environment from the same compose.yaml — no need to maintain separate override files just to toggle a service on or off.

Q23
What is the difference between --update-order start-first and the default rolling update order?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service update --update-order start-first --image app:v2 web starts the new task BEFORE stopping the old one (brief overlap, zero downtime). The default stop-first stops the old task first (brief service gap).

EXPLANATION

start-first needs enough spare capacity for the overlap. True blue-green or canary deployment still needs an external load balancer and versioned service names, since Swarm's rolling update always converges to one image per service.

Q24
What does kompose convert do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kompose convert -f compose.yaml translates a Docker Compose file into Kubernetes Deployment/Service YAML manifests — a bridge for teams moving from Compose to Kubernetes.

EXPLANATION

kompose is a separate CLI tool, not part of Docker itself. It handles ports/volumes/env automatically, but anything Kubernetes-native with no Compose equivalent (probes, HPA, Ingress rules) needs manual review and editing afterward.

Q25
What is the difference between docker stack rm and docker stack ps?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stack rm mystack removes all services, networks, and configs/secrets belonging to that stack in one shot. docker stack ps mystack lists every task with its node placement and current state.

EXPLANATION

stack ps is the go-to first command when a stack deploy looks "stuck" — it shows failed or rejected tasks and their error messages, mirroring docker service ps but for every service in the stack at once.

H.2 Domain 2: Image Creation & Management — 20 Questions

Dockerfile best practices, multi-stage builds, layer caching, registry operations, and image security covered in Chapters 4-9. 20% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 2 — Image Management Practice Questions (20)

Dockerfile instructions, build optimization, multi-stage builds, and registry operations — 20 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q26
What is the purpose of the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

FROM specifies the base image to build upon. Every Dockerfile must start with a FROM instruction (or an ARG before FROM). It initializes a new build stage.

EXPLANATION

Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements. Always use specific tags (python:3.11-slim) rather than latest for reproducibility. FROM scratch creates an empty base, used for statically-compiled binaries.

Q27
What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENTRYPOINT defines the fixed executable — arguments after docker run IMAGE become arguments to it. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT (or the default command if no ENTRYPOINT is set). CMD is overridden by docker run IMAGE command.

EXPLANATION

When both are used: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"] runs python app.py. docker run img test.py overrides CMD, running python test.py. Use ENTRYPOINT for the executable, CMD for default args.

Q28
Why should you use COPY instead of ADD in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

COPY is simpler and predictable — it copies local files/directories. ADD has extra magic (auto-extracting tar archives, fetching remote URLs) that makes builds less deterministic. Docker recommends COPY unless you specifically need tar extraction.

EXPLANATION

ADD's URL fetch doesn't cache well and can be a security risk. For remote files, use RUN curl/wget in a single RUN with cleanup. ADD is only appropriate when you need auto-extraction of local tar files.

Q29
What is layer caching and how do you optimize it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. If a layer hasn't changed and all previous layers are cached, Docker reuses it. Optimize by ordering instructions from least to most frequently changed: install dependencies first, COPY source code last.

EXPLANATION

Example: COPY requirements.txt → RUN pip install → COPY . . This way, code changes don't invalidate the pip install cache. Copying everything first would force a full reinstall on every code change.

Q30
What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Dockerfile with multiple FROM statements. The first stage(s) build/compile the application with full toolchains. The final stage copies only the compiled artifacts, producing a much smaller production image without build tools.

EXPLANATION

Example: Stage 1 uses golang:1.21 to compile a Go binary. Stage 2 uses alpine:3.19 and copies just the binary. Result: a 10MB image instead of 800MB — and better security since compilers and dev tools are gone from the final image.

Q31
How do you tag an image for a private registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker tag myapp:latest registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0 — then docker push registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0. The registry hostname must be part of the tag.

EXPLANATION

The image name format is [HOST[:PORT]/]NAME[:TAG]. Without a host, Docker Hub is assumed. For AWS ECR: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1. Always docker login to the private registry first.

Q32
What does the dot (.) mean in docker build -t app .?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The dot is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon. All COPY/ADD instructions reference paths relative to this directory.

EXPLANATION

The Dockerfile doesn't have to be in the context root — use docker build -f path/to/Dockerfile .. The context is sent as a tar to the daemon, so keep it small with .dockerignore (exclude node_modules, .git, venv).

Q33
How do you reduce Docker image size? List 5 techniques.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Use slim/alpine base images.
2. Multi-stage builds.
3. Combine RUN commands to reduce layers.
4. Remove package caches in the same RUN (apt clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*).
5. Use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files.

EXPLANATION

Each layer adds permanent size — deleting a file in a later layer doesn't shrink the image, since the file still exists in the earlier layer. Combine operations into ONE RUN line so caches never get committed to a layer in the first place.

Q34
What is the difference between ENV and ARG in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENV persists into the final image and is available at runtime. ARG is build-time only — it exists only during docker build, not in the final image. ARGs can be passed via --build-arg.

EXPLANATION

Use ARG for build-time configuration (version numbers, build dates). Use ENV for runtime configuration the container needs. ARG can even set the base image dynamically: ARG PYTHON_VER=3.11 then FROM python:${PYTHON_VER}.

Q35
What command pushes an image to Docker Hub?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker push username/imagename:tag. Requires docker login first. The image must be tagged with the Docker Hub username as a prefix.

EXPLANATION

If not logged in: denied: requested access to the resource is denied. For organizations: docker push orgname/imagename:tag. Use docker logout to remove stored credentials.

Q36
What does docker build --no-cache do, and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build --no-cache -t app . forces Docker to rebuild every layer from scratch, ignoring the local build cache entirely.

EXPLANATION

Use it when a RUN step depends on external state that changed but the Dockerfile itself didn't (e.g. an upstream apt package list update) — the cached layer would otherwise silently stay stale.

Q37
What does the HEALTHCHECK instruction do, and why isn't a running process enough?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1 tells Docker how to probe the container's actual application health, not just whether the process exists.

EXPLANATION

docker ps shows (healthy)/(unhealthy)/(starting). Swarm uses this health status to decide whether to route traffic to a task or replace it — a hung process that never responds is still "running" but not actually healthy.

Q38
What is a .dockerignore file used for?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A .dockerignore file (same syntax as .gitignore) excludes files/directories from the build context sent to the daemon — e.g. node_modules, .git, *.log.

EXPLANATION

It shrinks build context upload time, prevents accidentally COPYing secrets or huge dev-only directories into the image, and avoids invalidating the cache from files that don't belong in the image at all.

Q39
What is the difference between docker image prune and docker image prune -a?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker image prune removes dangling images (untagged, unreferenced layers). docker image prune -a removes ALL unused images not referenced by any container.

EXPLANATION

Dangling images accumulate from repeated docker build -t app . overwriting the same tag — the old layer set becomes <none>:<none>. Regular pruning reclaims significant disk space on build servers.

Q40
What does docker history show, and when is it useful?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker history IMAGE shows every layer of an image with its size and the Dockerfile instruction that created it.

EXPLANATION

It's the fastest way to find WHY an image is bloated — spot a RUN apt-get install layer that's unexpectedly large, or confirm a multi-stage build actually dropped the build tools from the final stage.

Q41
What does the LABEL instruction do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

LABEL maintainer="team@example.com" version="1.0" attaches arbitrary key-value metadata to an image, viewable via docker inspect.

EXPLANATION

Used for org-standard metadata (OCI annotations like org.opencontainers.image.source), automated cleanup scripts, and linking an image back to its build or commit without needing an external tracking system.

Q42
Why should you use WORKDIR instead of RUN cd /app && ...?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

WORKDIR /app sets the working directory for all subsequent RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, and ADD instructions, and creates the directory if it doesn't exist.

EXPLANATION

RUN cd /app && ... only affects that single RUN layer, not later instructions, because each RUN starts a brand-new shell — the "cd" doesn't carry over. WORKDIR persists across the whole rest of the Dockerfile.

Q43
How do you pass a build-time value into a Dockerfile, and is it safe for secrets?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In the Dockerfile: ARG APP_VERSION=latest. At build time: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=2.3.1 -t app .. Not safe for secrets.

EXPLANATION

ARG values are NOT secret — they end up visible in docker history unless you use BuildKit secret mounts (--mount=type=secret). Never pass passwords or API keys via --build-arg.

Q44
How do you build a multi-platform image (e.g. amd64 and arm64) in one command?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t app:latest --push . builds and pushes a single manifest list covering multiple CPU architectures.

EXPLANATION

buildx uses BuildKit and, for cross-architecture builds, QEMU emulation. Without it, building an arm64 image on an amd64 host requires a separate emulated builder or native arm64 CI hardware.

Q45
What is the difference between an image tag and an image digest?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A tag (app:1.0) is a mutable pointer that can be overwritten. A digest (app@sha256:abc123...) is an immutable content hash that always refers to the exact same bytes.

EXPLANATION

Pin production deployments to a digest (or an enforced immutable-tag policy) to guarantee you're never silently running different content than what was tested — docker pull app:1.0 today can return different bytes than yesterday if someone re-pushed that tag.

H.3 Domain 3: Installation & Configuration — 15 Questions

Docker Engine setup, daemon configuration, logging drivers, storage drivers, and Docker Desktop management covered in Chapters 1-3. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 3 — Installation & Configuration Practice Questions (15)

Daemon configuration, install methods, and the Engine/containerd/runc stack — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q46
Where is the Docker daemon configuration file located?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux. Docker Desktop manages this through its Settings UI. The file is JSON and requires a daemon restart (sudo systemctl restart docker) to apply changes.

EXPLANATION

Common settings: {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m"}, "storage-driver": "overlay2", "insecure-registries": ["myreg:5000"], "dns": ["8.8.8.8"]}. Validate JSON syntax before restarting — bad JSON prevents the daemon from starting.

Q47
How do you configure Docker to use a specific logging driver?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In /etc/docker/daemon.json: {"log-driver": "json-file"} for a daemon-wide default. Per-container: docker run --log-driver=syslog --log-opt syslog-address=tcp://....

EXPLANATION

Available drivers include json-file (default), syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, splunk, gcplogs. Set log rotation with {"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}} to prevent disk exhaustion.

Q48
What is the default storage driver and how do you change it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Default: overlay2 on most modern Linux. Change in daemon.json: {"storage-driver": "overlay2"}. Requires a daemon restart; existing images/containers are NOT migrated.

EXPLANATION

Supported drivers: overlay2 (recommended), aufs (legacy), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfs (slow, for testing). Check the current driver with docker info | grep "Storage Driver". Changing drivers loses all existing data — back up first.

Q49
How do you start/stop/restart the Docker daemon on Linux?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

sudo systemctl start docker, sudo systemctl stop docker, sudo systemctl restart docker. Enable at boot with sudo systemctl enable docker.

EXPLANATION

Check status: sudo systemctl status docker. View logs: sudo journalctl -u docker -f. Docker socket: /var/run/docker.sock (group: docker). Add a user to the docker group: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER.

Q50
What is the difference between Docker CE and Docker EE?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker CE (Community Edition) — free, open-source, community-supported. Docker EE (Enterprise Edition, now Mirantis Container Runtime) — paid, with certified plugins, RBAC, image scanning, and support SLAs.

EXPLANATION

For the DCA exam: know that EE includes Docker Trusted Registry (DTR) and Universal Control Plane (UCP). CE is sufficient for learning and most production use cases. Mirantis now manages the enterprise Docker products.

Q51
What is the difference between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Engine is the core daemon (dockerd) + CLI + API, running natively on Linux. Docker Desktop is a full application for macOS/Windows that runs a Linux VM behind the scenes to host the Engine, plus a GUI, a Kubernetes toggle, and file-sharing integration.

EXPLANATION

On Linux, docker run talks directly to a local dockerd. On macOS/Windows, there's no native Linux kernel — Desktop's VM (or WSL2 integration on Windows) is what makes running Linux containers possible at all.

Q52
What is the difference between docker version and docker info?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker version shows Client and Server (Engine) version/API/Go version pairs. docker info shows daemon-wide configuration: storage driver, cgroup driver, container/image counts, registry mirrors, and the daemon.json settings in effect.

EXPLANATION

docker version failing while docker ps works (or vice versa) is a quick signal of a client-server connectivity issue. docker info is usually the first command run when troubleshooting an unfamiliar host.

Q53
What is the recommended way to install Docker on Ubuntu?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add Docker's official apt repository and GPG key, then sudo apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin — NOT the outdated docker.io package from Ubuntu's default repos.

EXPLANATION

The official repo tracks upstream Docker releases. Ubuntu's own docker.io package lags significantly behind and may be missing the buildx/Compose v2 plugins that the exam and modern workflows assume are present.

Q54
How do dockerd, containerd, and runc relate to each other?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

dockerd delegates actual container lifecycle work to containerd (a separate daemon), which shells out to runc to create the low-level OCI-compliant container process (namespaces, cgroups).

EXPLANATION

This layering is why Kubernetes can use containerd directly as a CRI runtime without going through the Docker daemon at all — dockerd is essentially a client-facing API layer sitting on top of containerd + runc.

Q55
Why is membership in the "docker" group a security-sensitive setting?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/var/run/docker.sock is owned by root:docker. Having access to it is EQUIVALENT to root on the host, because you can launch a privileged container that bind-mounts the host's /.

EXPLANATION

This is a classic install/config question that's secretly a security question — adding a user to the docker group deserves the same scrutiny as granting sudo access.

Q56
How do you configure the Docker daemon to use an HTTP proxy for pulling images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create a systemd drop-in at /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf with Environment="HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy:3128", then sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart docker.

EXPLANATION

This configures the DAEMON's outbound proxy. It's separate from configuring a proxy INSIDE containers, which is set via ~/.docker/config.json proxies settings or per-container -e HTTP_PROXY flags.

Q57
What is docker context used for?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker context create remote-host --docker "host=ssh://user@remote", then docker context use remote-host points the local CLI at a remote daemon over SSH or TCP without needing to SSH in manually for every command.

EXPLANATION

docker context ls shows all configured endpoints; switch back with docker context use default. Useful for managing multiple environments (dev VM, staging, CI) from one workstation.

Q58
What is rootless Docker mode?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon itself as a non-root user (via user namespaces plus slirp4netns/rootlesskit networking), so a daemon compromise doesn't automatically grant host root.

EXPLANATION

Installed via dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install. Trade-offs include some networking/cgroup features needing extra configuration and generally lower network throughput than standard rootful Docker.

Q59
How do you check the Docker Engine API version, and why does it matter?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker version shows the API version for both client and server. The CLI negotiates down to the lowest common API version automatically, but very old clients/servers outside the supported skew can fail with a version mismatch error.

EXPLANATION

This matters most when scripting against the Engine API directly (curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock) or using an SDK — always check the API version rather than assuming "latest" behavior.

Q60
How do you secure the Docker daemon's remote API with TLS?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

dockerd --tlsverify --tlscacert=ca.pem --tlscert=server-cert.pem --tlskey=server-key.pem -H=0.0.0.0:2376, with clients connecting using matching --tlsverify flags.

EXPLANATION

NEVER expose the Docker API on TCP without TLS — an unauthenticated -H tcp://0.0.0.0:2375 is equivalent to handing out root on the host to anyone on the network. This remains one of the most common real-world Docker misconfigurations.

H.4 Domain 4: Networking — 15 Questions

Bridge, overlay, host, and MACVLAN networks; port mapping; DNS resolution; network troubleshooting covered in Chapters 13-15. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 4 — Networking Practice Questions (15)

Network drivers, port publishing, service discovery, and troubleshooting — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q61
What is the default Docker network type and how does it work?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The bridge network (docker0). Containers on the same bridge can communicate by IP. The default bridge does NOT support DNS-based service discovery — use custom user-defined bridges for that.

EXPLANATION

Default bridge: containers can only reach each other by IP, not by name. User-defined bridge: automatic DNS resolution between containers. Always create custom networks (docker network create mynet) for production apps.

Q62
How do containers on different networks communicate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

They cannot communicate directly — Docker networks are isolated. To connect containers across networks, attach a container to both: docker network connect net2 container1.

EXPLANATION

Or publish a port to the host so other containers reach it via the host IP. In Swarm, overlay networks span nodes and enable cross-host communication via VXLAN tunnels (UDP 4789).

Q63
What is an overlay network and when is it required?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An overlay network uses VXLAN encapsulation to connect containers across multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes). Required for multi-host Swarm services to communicate with each other.

EXPLANATION

Overlay networks can encrypt data-plane traffic with IPSec (--opt encrypted). Control plane uses TCP 2377 (Swarm management); data plane uses UDP 4789 (VXLAN) and UDP 7946 (gossip for service discovery).

Q64
What does -p 8080:80 mean in docker run?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Maps host port 8080 to container port 80. Traffic to localhost:8080 is forwarded to port 80 inside the container via Docker's iptables NAT rules.

EXPLANATION

The format is -p HOST:CONTAINER. To bind a specific interface: -p 192.168.1.100:8080:80. For a random host port: -p 80. Check mappings with docker port CONTAINER.

Q65
What is host network mode and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--network host removes network isolation — the container shares the host's network stack directly. Use for maximum network performance or when a container needs to bind many ports.

EXPLANATION

Trade-offs: faster (no NAT), but no isolation — port conflicts with the host, no network namespace. Linux-only. Common uses: network monitoring tools, high-throughput proxies. Not recommended for multi-tenant environments.

Q66
How do you create a custom bridge network with a specific subnet?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network create --driver bridge --subnet 172.20.0.0/16 --gateway 172.20.0.1 mynet creates a user-defined bridge with an explicit IP range.

EXPLANATION

Without an explicit subnet, Docker auto-assigns from its default address pools, which can silently collide with corporate VPN ranges — a common real-world networking bug and a good exam trap to know about.

Q67
How does Docker's embedded DNS server let containers resolve each other by name?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Every container on a user-defined network gets an entry in Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11, letting containers resolve each other by container/service name automatically.

EXPLANATION

This is what makes db:5432 work as a hostname in application config without hardcoding IPs. It does NOT work on the default bridge network — only user-defined ones — a frequent source of "why can't my containers see each other by name" issues.

Q68
What is the MACVLAN network driver and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network create -d macvlan --subnet=192.168.1.0/24 --gateway=192.168.1.1 -o parent=eth0 macnet assigns containers their own MAC address and IP directly on the physical LAN.

EXPLANATION

Bypasses the Linux bridge/NAT entirely — useful for legacy apps expecting a real LAN IP, but requires the interface to support promiscuous mode and typically doesn't work over Wi-Fi.

Q69
How do you encrypt traffic on a Swarm overlay network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network create -d overlay --opt encrypted secure-net encrypts the VXLAN data-plane traffic between nodes with IPSec, on top of a control plane already secured by mutual TLS by default.

EXPLANATION

Encryption adds CPU overhead (IPSec encrypt/decrypt on every packet), so it's opt-in per network rather than a default — enable it for overlay networks crossing untrusted network segments, like cross-datacenter links.

Q70
What tools and commands do you use to troubleshoot container networking?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec -it CONTAINER sh, then use ping, curl, nslookup/dig, or wget inside the container. docker network inspect NETWORK shows connected containers and their IPs.

EXPLANATION

Minimal images (alpine, distroless) often lack these tools — install temporarily (apk add curl bind-tools) or attach a debug sidecar container on the same network as a workaround.

Q71
What does --network none do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --network none isolates a container completely — it gets only a loopback interface, with no external connectivity at all.

EXPLANATION

Used for maximum isolation of untrusted workloads (e.g. processing an unknown file) that should have zero network access by design, not just restricted access.

Q72
What is the difference between EXPOSE in a Dockerfile and -p on docker run?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

EXPOSE 80 in a Dockerfile is DOCUMENTATION ONLY — it doesn't actually publish anything. Only -p HOST:CONTAINER (or -P to auto-publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports) actually opens a port from the host.

EXPLANATION

A common exam trap: EXPOSE alone does not make a service reachable from outside the container's network. Containers on the SAME Docker network can already reach each other on any port regardless of EXPOSE/-p.

Q73
What is the Swarm ingress network and how does it relate to the routing mesh?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Swarm automatically creates a special overlay network called ingress. Every published Swarm service port is load-balanced through it via IPVS, which is what lets ANY node answer traffic for a service even without running a replica locally.

EXPLANATION

Bypass the routing mesh with --publish mode=host to bind the port only on nodes actually running the task — useful when you need the real client source IP, since the mesh otherwise SNATs traffic.

Q74
How do you disconnect a running container from one network and connect it to another, without restarting it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network disconnect mynet CONTAINER removes a running container from a network; docker network connect othernet CONTAINER adds it to another. Neither requires a restart.

EXPLANATION

Useful for live-migrating a container between networks, or forcibly cutting off network access for a suspicious running container during an incident with zero downtime.

Q75
How do you set a custom DNS server for a single container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --dns 8.8.8.8 --dns-search example.com myapp sets a container-specific resolver, overriding the daemon-wide default from /etc/docker/daemon.json.

EXPLANATION

Useful in split-horizon DNS environments, or when a container needs to resolve internal corporate hostnames that the host's default resolver doesn't know about.

H.5 Domain 5: Security — 15 Questions

Docker Content Trust, secrets management, seccomp profiles, AppArmor, image signing, RBAC, and TLS covered in Chapters 19-21. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 5 — Security Practice Questions (15)

Content trust, isolation mechanisms, least-privilege patterns, and secrets — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q76
What is Docker Content Trust (DCT) and how do you enable it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DCT uses digital signatures (via Notary/TUF) to verify image integrity and publisher identity. Enable it with export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. When enabled, Docker only pulls/pushes signed images.

EXPLANATION

With DCT=1, unsigned images are rejected. Signing keys: repository key (per-repo), root key (offline), timestamp key. DCT prevents supply-chain attacks by ensuring images haven't been tampered with since signing.

Q77
What is seccomp and how does Docker use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) filters which Linux syscalls a container can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls out of 300+, significantly reducing kernel attack surface.

EXPLANATION

Apply custom profiles: --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json. Disable (NOT recommended): --security-opt seccomp=unconfined. The default profile is well-tested and suitable for most applications.

Q78
How do you run a container as a non-root user?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In the Dockerfile: RUN useradd -m app && USER app. At runtime: docker run --user 1000:1000 nginx. Always create the user in the Dockerfile so file permissions are set correctly during the build.

EXPLANATION

Root in a container is root on the host unless user namespaces are enabled. A container breakout as root gives full host access. The USER instruction should come after permission-critical operations (package installs) and before COPY/CMD.

Q79
What are user namespaces and how do they improve security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

User namespaces remap a container's root user (UID 0) to a non-privileged user on the host (e.g. UID 100000). Enable via {"userns-remap": "default"} in daemon.json. A "root" breakout then only gives a low-privilege host user.

EXPLANATION

A powerful defense-in-depth measure. Trade-offs: some filesystem operations may need adjustment, and it's incompatible with some volume drivers. Enabled per-daemon, not per-container.

Q80
How do Swarm secrets protect sensitive data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are encrypted in transit (mutual TLS), encrypted at rest (Raft log encryption), mounted as tmpfs (in-memory only), and only sent to nodes that need them — never exposed via env vars or docker inspect.

EXPLANATION

Create: echo "mypassword" | docker secret create db_pass -. Use in a service: docker service create --secret db_pass. Mounted at /run/secrets/db_pass. Max size: 500KB per secret.

Q81
What is AppArmor and how does it differ from seccomp?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker applies a default AppArmor profile (docker-default) on Ubuntu/Debian hosts that restricts file access, mount operations, and capabilities beyond what seccomp covers. Apply a custom profile with --security-opt apparmor=my-profile.

EXPLANATION

AppArmor is Mandatory Access Control (path-based rules), while seccomp filters syscalls — complementary layers, both enabled by default on supported distros (AppArmor on Ubuntu/Debian; SELinux is the RHEL/CentOS equivalent).

Q82
What is Docker Bench for Security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -it --net host --pid host --cap-add audit_control -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker/docker-bench-security runs an automated CIS Docker Benchmark audit against host and daemon configuration.

EXPLANATION

Checks host config, daemon config, image/container config, and runtime — outputs PASS/WARN/INFO per CIS control. A commonly referenced tool for the DCA security domain and for real-world audits alike.

Q83
How do you scan an image for known vulnerabilities?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker scout cves myimage:latest (or a third-party tool like trivy image myimage:latest) scans image layers against known CVE databases and reports vulnerable packages by severity.

EXPLANATION

Scanning should run in CI before push, not just after — catching a critical CVE post-deployment is far more costly than blocking the build. Docker Hub and most registries also offer automated scan-on-push.

Q84
How do you make a container's filesystem immutable at runtime?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp makes the container's root filesystem immutable; only explicitly mounted volumes/tmpfs remain writable.

EXPLANATION

Prevents malware from writing to the filesystem or an attacker from modifying application binaries post-compromise. Requires identifying and tmpfs/volume-mounting any paths the app legitimately needs to write to (logs, cache, /tmp).

Q85
How do you drop unnecessary Linux capabilities from a container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp removes all default capabilities and adds back only the one actually needed (binding to a low port as non-root).

EXPLANATION

Docker grants ~14 capabilities by default (a subset of the kernel's ~40), already more than most apps need — capability minimization follows the same least-privilege principle as seccomp filtering or running non-root.

Q86
Why should you avoid the --privileged flag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--privileged disables ALL isolation mechanisms (seccomp, AppArmor, capability restrictions, device cgroups) — the container gets essentially the same access as a process running directly on the host.

EXPLANATION

Only needed for niche cases (nested Docker-in-Docker, certain hardware/device access). If you're reaching for --privileged, first check whether a specific --cap-add or --device flag solves the actual need instead.

Q87
How do resource limits function as a security control, not just a performance one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--memory=512m --pids-limit=100 --cpus=1 prevents a single compromised or buggy container from exhausting host RAM, forking a fork-bomb's worth of processes, or starving CPU from other containers.

EXPLANATION

This is a denial-of-service defense, distinct from access-control defenses (seccomp/AppArmor/capabilities). Without limits, one noisy or malicious container can take down every other workload on the same host.

Q88
Why is mounting the Docker socket into a container a major security risk?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock gives that container FULL control over the host's Docker daemon — equivalent to root on the host, since it can launch new privileged containers that mount the host filesystem.

EXPLANATION

Common in CI runners and monitoring tools (to let a container manage sibling containers), but should be treated as a major trust boundary — never do this for untrusted or user-supplied container images.

Q89
What key hierarchy does Docker Content Trust use, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DCT is built on Notary/TUF (The Update Framework), using a hierarchy of keys — root key (offline, rarely used), repository/targets key (signs each release), snapshot and timestamp keys — to prevent both tampering and stale/replay attacks.

EXPLANATION

Delegation lets a team share signing responsibility (multiple people can hold targets keys) without ever exposing the offline root key, which should be stored securely and used only to rotate other keys.

Q90
How does Swarm enforce role separation between managers and workers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Only manager nodes can issue Swarm API commands (docker service, docker node, etc.) and participate in Raft consensus. Worker nodes only run assigned tasks and cannot query or modify cluster state.

EXPLANATION

This is Swarm's built-in RBAC boundary — compromising a worker does not grant control of the cluster, whereas compromising a manager (especially its TLS certs) does. Keep the manager count minimal and tightly access-controlled.

H.6 Domain 6: Storage & Volumes — 10 Questions

Volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs, storage drivers, volume plugins, and data persistence strategies covered in Chapters 16-18. 10% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 6 — Storage & Volumes Practice Questions (10)

Mount types, volume lifecycle, and backup/restore patterns — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q91
What are the three types of Docker mounts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Volumes — Docker-managed, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/, portable, best for persistence.
2. Bind mounts — mount any host path, great for development (live code editing).
3. tmpfs — in-memory only (RAM), never written to disk, for sensitive temporary data.

EXPLANATION

Volumes are the recommended production choice: managed by Docker, work across OSes, can use volume drivers for cloud storage, and are easy to back up. Bind mounts are path-dependent and can have permission issues across different OSes.

Q92
How do you create and use a named volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create: docker volume create pgdata. Use: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres. List: docker volume ls. Inspect: docker volume inspect pgdata.

EXPLANATION

Named volumes survive container deletion. Remove: docker volume rm pgdata (must be unused). Prune all unused: docker volume prune. Backup pattern: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .

Q93
What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Volume: Docker-managed location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), created via docker volume create, portable, recommended for production. Bind mount: any host path (/home/user/data), depends on host directory structure, great for development.

EXPLANATION

Volumes work consistently across all platforms and don't depend on host filesystem structure. Bind mounts can break when moving between macOS, Windows, and Linux due to different path conventions.

Q94
What is a tmpfs mount and when should you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

tmpfs stores data in the host's RAM only — never written to disk. Use: docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid. Best for sensitive data that should never persist (tokens, temp credentials).

EXPLANATION

Unlike volumes/bind mounts, tmpfs data is lost on container stop AND host reboot, and it cannot be shared between containers. Swarm secrets use tmpfs internally. Mount options (noexec, nosuid, nodev) add security hardening.

Q95
How do you back up a Docker volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use a temporary container mounting both the volume and a backup directory: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/source -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /source .

EXPLANATION

This pattern works for any volume. Restore: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/target -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /target. For databases, prefer native tools (pg_dump, mongodump) over raw filesystem backup for consistency.

Q96
What is a volume driver, and when do you need one other than the default?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker volume create --driver rexray/ebs --name pgdata (or nfs, azurefile, etc.) creates a volume backed by external/cloud storage instead of the local disk, via a volume plugin.

EXPLANATION

The default local driver only works on a single host. A cloud/network-backed driver is required for Swarm services, where a task might be rescheduled to a different node and still needs access to the same data.

Q97
Can multiple containers use the same named volume at the same time?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Yes — docker run -v shareddata:/data container1 and docker run -v shareddata:/data container2 both mount the SAME named volume simultaneously; writes from either are immediately visible to the other.

EXPLANATION

Useful for a sidecar pattern (e.g. a log-shipping container reading files an app container writes), but the application must handle concurrent access safely — Docker provides no file locking or write coordination on its own.

Q98
How do you restore a volume from a backup tarball?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --rm -v pgdata:/target -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /target extracts a tarball into a named volume.

EXPLANATION

The target volume should be empty, or you should understand tar -x's overwrite semantics — it merges into existing content rather than clearing it first. For a true restore, remove and recreate the volume before extracting.

Q99
What does docker volume prune do, and what's the risk?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker volume prune removes all volumes not currently referenced by at least one container, running or stopped. docker system prune -a --volumes includes volumes in a broader cleanup.

EXPLANATION

DESTRUCTIVE and irreversible — always confirm which volumes are truly unused first (docker volume ls plus checking dependent stacks), since Compose/Swarm-managed volumes for stopped-but-not-removed stacks can get caught up in a prune.

Q100
How do you mount a volume as read-only inside a container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -v config-vol:/etc/app/config:ro myapp mounts the volume read-only inside the container — the app can read its config but any write attempt fails, even though the volume itself is writable from other mounts.

EXPLANATION

A simple but effective defense-in-depth measure for configuration or reference data that a compromised/buggy app should never be able to modify. The same :ro suffix works for bind mounts too.

📋 Appendix H Summary — DCA Exam Strategy

📝
100 Questions
Across all 6 DCA exam domains with weighted distribution (25/20/15/15/15/10)
🎯
Exam Format
55 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes — roughly 1.6 minutes per question
📖
Open Book
You CAN access docs.docker.com during the exam — know where to look, not just what to memorize
✅
Passing Score
Typically ~65-70%. Focus on Orchestration & Image Management (45% combined)

This appendix mirrors the real DCA exam's domain weighting: Orchestration and Image Management together make up nearly half the exam, so mastering docker service/docker stack commands and multi-stage Dockerfiles pays off more than any other single study effort. The remaining four domains — Installation, Networking, Security, and Storage — are each worth 10-15%, but collectively still outweigh either of the top two domains, so don't skip them in favor of over-studying Swarm. Because the exam is open-book against the official docs, the goal of these 100 questions isn't rote memorization of every flag — it's building enough command-level fluency that you recognize the right command family instantly and only need the docs to confirm exact flag syntax under time pressure.

🎯 DCA Exam Tips:
1. Practice all docker service and docker stack commands — Orchestration is 25% of the exam.
2. Know multi-stage Dockerfiles cold — Image Management is 20%.
3. Memorize daemon.json structure and the Engine/containerd/runc stack — Installation is 15%.
4. Understand overlay vs bridge networks and the routing mesh — Networking is 15%.
5. Know secrets, DCT, seccomp, and user namespaces — Security is 15%.
6. Master volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs — Storage is 10%.

Appendix J: 4-Week DCA Study Plan

A week-by-week study cadence mapping directly onto this guide's own Parts and Chapters — the same plan Section 6.7 in the front matter points to. Budget ~10-15 hours/week; adjust down if you're already comfortable with a given week's domain per your 30.2 self-score.

📅 4 Weeks + Exam Week ⏱️ ~10-15 hrs/week 🎯 Maps to Ch1-30 📋 Reference Appendix
🧱
J.1 · Week 1

Foundations & hands-on. Vocabulary and CLI grammar, cold.

🖼️
J.2 · Week 2

Images, Compose & Networking (20% + 15% of the exam).

🔒
J.3 · Week 3

Storage, Security & Shipping (10% + 15%, plus CI/CD fluency).

⚓

J.1 Week 1 — Foundations & Hands-On (Parts 1-2, Ch1-6)

Goal: own the vocabulary and the CLI grammar cold. This week is entirely Part 1 (Docker Concepts) and Part 2 (Docker Hands-On) — everything later in the guide assumes this mental model is already automatic.

DayTopicChaptersDeliverable
Day 1-2The mental model, images/containers/registries, install + first containerCh1–Ch3Drill: Ch1 & Ch3 Lab Q&A, both chapters
Day 3-5Dockerfile, docker build, docker run & container lifecycleCh4–Ch6Build easypj's own Dockerfile from memory once
Day 6-7Part 1-2 Key Takeaways review + docker run/build flag references skimCh1–Ch6 Key Takeaways + App. A.11-A.15Comfortable reciting Part 1-2 vocabulary cold
🎯 Week 1 Checkpoint

Rebuild, tag, and run easypj:v1 from an empty checkout, without notes, in under 10 minutes.

J.2 Week 2 — Images, Compose & Networking (Parts 3-5, Ch7-15)

Goal: own Image Creation/Mgmt/Registry (20%) and Networking (15%) — 35% of the exam in a single week. Parts 3-5 (Docker Images, Docker Compose, Docker Networking) build on each other, so keep the order.

DayTopicChaptersDeliverable
Day 1-2Image management, optimization, the full easypj build-and-run walkthroughCh7–Ch9easypj image built, tagged & optimized
Day 3-4Compose fundamentals → easypj's real stack → profiles/overrides/scalingCh10–Ch12easypj's Compose stack running locally
Day 5-7CNM model, easypj's two-network design, host/macvlan/overlay + the debugging ladderCh13–Ch15Comfortable diagnosing container network issues
🎯 Week 2 Checkpoint

Stand up easypj's full 4-service Compose stack cold, then intentionally break DNS resolution and fix it using only the 15.4 debugging ladder.

J.3 Week 3 — Storage, Security & Shipping (Parts 6-8, Ch16-24)

Goal: own Storage & Volumes (10%) and Security (15%); build CI/CD fluency along the way. CI/CD isn't its own graded domain, but Part 8's tagging & promotion material is load-bearing for Domain 2 (Image Creation, Management & Registry) in practice.

DayTopicChaptersDeliverable
Day 1-2Volumes/bind mounts/tmpfs, easypj's real assignments, overlay2 internalsCh16–Ch18easypj's persistent data fully mapped out
Day 3-4The security onion, hardening checklist, Docker Scout/Bench/Trivy/SBOMCh19–Ch21Security scan run against easypj's image
Day 5-7CI/CD pipelines, tagging & promotion (graded), testing pyramidCh22–Ch24easypj pipeline builds, tags & tests automatically
🎯 Week 3 Checkpoint

Harden easypj to non-root + cap-drop ALL + read-only, then run docker scout quickview and explain every finding.

J.4 Week 4 — Orchestration, Bridge & Exam Prep (Parts 9-10, Ch25-30)

Goal: own Orchestration (25%, the single biggest domain) and Installation & Configuration (15%); close every remaining gap before exam week.

DayTopicChaptersDeliverable
Day 1-2The Docker→Kubernetes bridge — context, not exam content, but reinforces the noun modelCh25–Ch27Concepts-mapping table memorized
Day 3-5Docker Swarm, ALL 10 sections (25% of the exam by itself) + Compose portabilityCh28 (28.1-28.10) + Ch29Full Swarm lifecycle rehearsed
Day 6Exam strategy, domain weights, pacingCh30Personal pacing plan set
Day 7Full mock exam (100+ questions), timed, three-pass methodAppendix HEvery miss logged against the 30.9 gap table
🎯 Week 4 Checkpoint

Run the full Swarm lifecycle (init → service create → scale → update → rollback) in under 15 minutes, no notes.

🎯 Pacing Week 4 — Don't Shortchange Swarm

Orchestration is worth 25% of the DCA — more than any other single domain — and nearly all of it lives in Chapter 28's 10 sections. Give Swarm the full 3-day block (Day 3-5) it's budgeted here rather than compressing it to make room for review; review is what Exam Week (J.5) is for. On Day 7, use the three-pass method from 30.7 Exam Strategy & Tips: pass 1 answers everything you're sure of, pass 2 tackles flagged questions, pass 3 is a final sanity sweep with whatever time remains.

J.5 Exam Week — Final Review

No new material this week — only consolidation. The four actions below are ordered by how close to exam day they belong; treat the last one as non-negotiable.

ActionReferenceTiming
Re-run every Appendix H question you missed the first timeAppendix HEarly exam week
Re-read domain weights + coverage audit onceSection 6.2-6.4 (front matter)Early exam week
Confirm exam-day logistics — system check, ID, second monitor unplugged30.8 Exam Day ChecklistAt least 24 hours before your slot
Rest — no cramming—Final 24 hours
🎯 The Final 24 Hours — Rest Beats Cramming

Cramming new material in the final 24 hours has a worse ROI than showing up as a calm, rehearsed test-taker. By exam week you've already spent 4 weeks building the muscle memory this test actually checks — a rested brain that executes the three-pass method cleanly will consistently outscore a tired one that "knows one more edge case."

Appendix K: DCA Exam Simulator — 15 Practical Tasks

A scenario-based practice set modeled on the DCA's performance expectations, weighted by domain the same way the real exam is (Section 6.2). Time yourself: 90 minutes total, all 15 tasks, no notes — then check your results against the K.16 Scoring Guide to see which domain needs another pass.

⏱️ 90 Minutes, No Notes 📝 15 Tasks + Scoring Guide 🎯 Weighted by Domain (§6.2) 🐍 easypj / jobpost
📖 How to Run This Simulator

Set a 90-minute timer and work all 15 tasks back to back, exactly as the real DCA exam presents them — no reference docs, no notes. Each task states a scenario/goal and a Verify check; don't move on until your own environment actually satisfies that check (don't just read the solution and assume). When the clock stops, total your score against the K.16 Scoring Guide and cross-reference any domain scoring below 80% against Section 6.3's domain-to-chapter map before re-attempting.

K.1 Swarm Init & Deploy

🐳 Task K.1 — Swarm Init & Deploy

🎯 Domain: Orchestration · Weight 25%
Scenario

Initialize a single-node Swarm, then deploy easypj as a service named easypj-web with 3 replicas, image easypj:v1, publishing port 8000.

swarm init & service deploy
# 1. Initialize a single-node Swarm
docker swarm init

# 2. Deploy easypj-web with 3 replicas, publishing port 8000
docker service create \
  --name easypj-web \
  --replicas 3 \
  --publish 8000:8000 \
  easypj:v1
✅ Verify: docker service ls shows easypj-web at 3/3 replicas running.

K.2 Scale & Rollback Replicas

🐳 Task K.2 — Scale & Rollback Replicas

🎯 Domain: Orchestration
Scenario

Scale easypj-web to 5 replicas without editing its original service definition, then roll it back to 3.

scale up, then back down
# 1. Scale up to 5 — no need to touch the original `service create` definition
docker service scale easypj-web=5
docker service ps easypj-web

# 2. Scale back down to 3
docker service scale easypj-web=3
docker service ps easypj-web
✅ Verify: docker service ps easypj-web shows the running task count changing both times — 3 → 5, then 5 → 3.

K.3 Rolling Update & Auto-Rollback

🐳 Task K.3 — Rolling Update & Auto-Rollback

🎯 Domain: Orchestration
Scenario

Update easypj-web to image easypj:v2 with --update-parallelism 1 --update-delay 10s --update-failure-action rollback. Simulate a bad tag and confirm the automatic rollback fires.

controlled update with rollback policy
# 1. Update to v2 under a controlled, auto-rollback policy
docker service update \
  --image easypj:v2 \
  --update-parallelism 1 \
  --update-delay 10s \
  --update-failure-action rollback \
  easypj-web

# 2. Simulate a bad tag — this update should fail health checks and trigger rollback
docker service update --image easypj:broken-tag easypj-web

# 3. Watch the tasks converge back to the last-known-good image
docker service ps easypj-web
✅ Verify: docker service ps easypj-web shows Shutdown tasks on the broken tag and Running tasks back on easypj:v1 (the rollback target).

K.4 Docker Secrets in Swarm

🐳 Task K.4 — Docker Secrets in Swarm

🎯 Domain: Orchestration
Scenario

Create a Docker secret named db_password from a local file and mount it into a new postgres service.

secret create & mount
# 1. Create the secret from a local file
echo "S3cr3t-Pg-Pass" > db_password.txt
docker secret create db_password db_password.txt
rm db_password.txt

# 2. Mount it into a new postgres service
docker service create \
  --name postgres \
  --secret db_password \
  --env POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password \
  postgres:15
✅ Verify:
  • docker exec into the postgres task and confirm /run/secrets/db_password exists.
  • docker service inspect postgres --pretty never prints the secret's value — only its name and ID.

K.5 Multi-Stage Build & Tagging

🏷️ Task K.5 — Multi-Stage Build & Tagging

🎯 Domain: Image Mgmt & Registry · Weight 20%
Scenario

Build easypj with a multi-stage Dockerfile, tag it three ways (git-SHA, semver, and semver+SHA combined), and confirm all three share one Image ID.

one build, three tags
# 1. Build once from the multi-stage Dockerfile
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
docker build -f Dockerfile.multistage -t easypj:$SHA .

# 2. Re-tag the SAME image two more ways — no rebuild, just new labels for one Image ID
docker tag easypj:$SHA easypj:1.2.0
docker tag easypj:$SHA easypj:1.2.0-$SHA

# 3. Confirm all three tags resolve to one Image ID
docker images | grep easypj
✅ Verify: docker images | grep easypj shows one Image ID against three tags (<sha>, 1.2.0, 1.2.0-<sha>).

K.6 Promote by Digest

🏷️ Task K.6 — Promote by Digest

🎯 Domain: Image Mgmt & Registry
Scenario

Promote an image from a staging tag to a production tag by digest, without rebuilding.

re-tag by digest, no rebuild
# 1. Capture staging's Image ID / digest before promoting
docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:staging

# 2. Promote — re-tag the identical image content as production (no rebuild)
docker tag easypj:staging easypj:production

# 3. Confirm production resolves to the SAME Image ID
docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:production
✅ Verify: docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' on both easypj:staging and easypj:production returns the identical local Image ID.

K.7 Image History Audit

🏷️ Task K.7 — Image History Audit

🎯 Domain: Image Mgmt & Registry
Scenario

Run docker history on any image you've built this session and identify its two heaviest layers.

layer-by-layer audit
# Full, untruncated layer history with real sizes
docker history --no-trunc easypj:v1
✅ Verify: name both heaviest layers' originating Dockerfile instruction (for example, a base-image FROM layer and a RUN pip install -r requirements.txt layer are the usual culprits).

K.8 daemon.json Configuration

⚙️ Task K.8 — daemon.json Configuration

🎯 Domain: Installation & Config · Weight 15%
Scenario

Configure a daemon.json with "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}, and "icc": false, then restart the daemon.

/etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  },
  "icc": false
}
apply & restart
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}}'
docker run -d --name k8-check alpine sleep 300
docker inspect k8-check --format '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig}}'
✅ Verify: docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}}' confirms the daemon picked up json-file, and docker inspect <container> --format '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig}}' on a freshly-started container shows max-size:10m and max-file:3 actually applied. icc: false doesn't show up in either command — confirm it separately with docker network inspect bridge --format '{{index .Options "com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc"}}' (should print false).

K.9 3-Manager Swarm Quorum

⚙️ Task K.9 — 3-Manager Swarm Quorum

🎯 Domain: Installation & Config
Scenario

Create a Swarm with 3 managers, verify quorum with docker node ls, then stop one manager and confirm the cluster still accepts writes.

3-manager quorum test
# 1. Init the first manager, then join two more as managers
docker swarm init --advertise-addr <MANAGER-1-IP>
docker swarm join-token manager     # run the printed command on managers 2 & 3

# 2. Confirm all three are Ready + Reachable
docker node ls

# 3. Stop the Docker daemon on ONE manager (2/3 still reachable = quorum holds)
ssh manager-3 'sudo systemctl stop docker'

# 4. Prove the cluster still accepts writes with 2/3 managers up
docker service create --name quorum-test --replicas 1 nginx
✅ Verify: docker service create still succeeds while only 2 of 3 managers are reachable — Raft quorum (majority) is intact.

K.10 Custom Bridge Networks

🌐 Task K.10 — Custom Bridge Networks

🎯 Domain: Networking · Weight 15%
Scenario

Create two user-defined bridge networks (frontend, backend), attach a django container to both and a postgres container to backend only, and prove django can reach postgres by name while an nginx container on frontend alone cannot.

two networks, three containers
# 1. Create the two user-defined bridge networks
docker network create frontend
docker network create backend

# 2. postgres — backend ONLY
docker run -d --name postgres --network backend postgres:15

# 3. django — BOTH networks (attach the second after the first at run-time)
docker run -d --name django --network frontend easypj:v1
docker network connect backend django

# 4. nginx — frontend ONLY
docker run -d --name nginx --network frontend nginx

# 5. Prove reachability by name (Docker's embedded DNS resolves container names per-network)
docker exec django ping -c 1 postgres      # succeeds — shares `backend`
docker exec nginx ping -c 1 postgres       # fails — no shared network
✅ Verify: three docker exec ... ping results matching this exactly —
  • django → postgres succeeds (shares backend)
  • nginx → postgres fails (no shared network)
  • django → nginx succeeds (shares frontend)

K.11 Bind Port to Localhost

🌐 Task K.11 — Bind Port to Localhost

🎯 Domain: Networking
Scenario

Publish a container's port bound only to 127.0.0.1, then confirm it is unreachable from another machine on the LAN but reachable from the host itself.

loopback-only publish
# 1. Bind the published port to 127.0.0.1 explicitly (not 0.0.0.0)
docker run -d --name loopback-app -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8000 easypj:v1

# 2. From the HOST itself — should succeed
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080

# 3. From ANOTHER machine on the LAN, using the host's real IP — should fail
curl http://<HOST-LAN-IP>:8080
✅ Verify: the remote curl from another LAN machine fails (connection refused/timeout), while the local curl against 127.0.0.1:8080 succeeds.

K.12 Re-Run Hardened Container

🔒 Task K.12 — Re-Run Hardened Container

🎯 Domain: Security · Weight 15%
Scenario

Take any running container and re-run it with --user 1000:1000 --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp, and confirm it still serves traffic.

hardened re-run
# Re-run under a hardened, least-privilege profile
docker run -d \
  --name hardened-app \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  easypj:v1

# Confirm the non-root UID inside the container
docker exec hardened-app id

# Confirm the app still responds
curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/
✅ Verify: docker exec ... id shows a non-root UID (uid=1000), and the app still responds to a request despite --cap-drop ALL and a read-only root filesystem.

K.13 Vulnerability Scan

🔒 Task K.13 — Vulnerability Scan

🎯 Domain: Security
Scenario

Run docker scout quickview (or Trivy) against an image and identify whether its Critical/High findings originate from the base image or your own added layer.

scan & attribute findings
# Option A — Docker Scout (built in)
docker scout quickview easypj:v1
docker scout cves easypj:v1

# Option B — Trivy
trivy image easypj:v1
✅ Verify: state, for each Critical/High finding, which layer it traces to — the base image (fix: bump/patch the base tag) or a layer you added (fix: pin the package version or drop the dependency).

K.14 Named Volume Mount

💾 Task K.14 — Named Volume Mount

🎯 Domain: Storage & Volumes · Weight 10%
Scenario

Create a named volume, mount it into a postgres container, insert data, remove the container, and mount the SAME volume into a brand-new postgres container.

volume survives the container
# 1. Create the named volume and mount it into postgres
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name pg1 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pass \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15

# 2. Insert a row so there is something to lose (or keep)
docker exec -it pg1 psql -U postgres -c \
  "CREATE TABLE t(id int); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);"

# 3. Remove the container — the NAMED VOLUME is untouched
docker rm -f pg1

# 4. Mount the SAME volume into a brand-new container
docker run -d --name pg2 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pass \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
docker exec -it pg2 psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM t;"
✅ Verify: the row from step 2 is present in pg2 without any restore step — the data lived in the volume, not the container.

K.15 pg_dump Backup

💾 Task K.15 — pg_dump Backup

🎯 Domain: Storage & Volumes
Scenario

Take a pg_dump backup of a running database, drop and recreate the database, then restore from the dump.

dump → drop → restore
# 1. Baseline row count, then dump the running database
docker exec pg2 psql -U postgres -d easypj -c "SELECT count(*) FROM t;"
docker exec pg2 pg_dump -U postgres easypj > easypj_backup.sql

# 2. Drop and recreate the database
docker exec pg2 psql -U postgres -c "DROP DATABASE easypj;"
docker exec pg2 psql -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE easypj;"

# 3. Restore from the dump
cat easypj_backup.sql | docker exec -i pg2 psql -U postgres -d easypj

# 4. Re-check the row count
docker exec pg2 psql -U postgres -d easypj -c "SELECT count(*) FROM t;"
✅ Verify: a row-count query returns the same number before the drop and after the restore.

K.16 Scoring Guide

Total 15 tasks across 6 domains, weighted to match the real DCA's blueprint (Section 6.2). Score each task 1 point if its Verify check genuinely passed in your own environment — no partial credit.

Domain Tasks Weight Your Score
Orchestration K.1 – K.4 25% ___ / 4
Image Mgmt & Registry K.5 – K.7 20% ___ / 3
Installation & Config K.8 – K.9 15% ___ / 2
Networking K.10 – K.11 15% ___ / 2
Security K.12 – K.13 15% ___ / 2
Storage & Volumes K.14 – K.15 10% ___ / 2
💡 Reading Your Score

Any domain below 80% here is your next study session — cross-reference the missed task's chapter citation against Section 6.3's domain-to-chapter map and re-read that section before re-attempting. Because these weights mirror the real exam's (Section 6.2), a low Orchestration or Image Mgmt & Registry score costs you the most — prioritize re-drilling those two domains first.
